title: The Dutch Design Awards 2015 gave the Future Award to a refugee camp documentary and the public vote to a defibrillator drone
subtitle: The 2015 awards read through the organizer's entry pages and jury texts, the festival's own releases, the makers' pages and the official photo archive
description: Who won the Dutch Design Awards in 2015, what the jury wrote, how the public prize went to a drone, and what the record does not show.

sections.x: The Dutch Design Awards of 2015 gave their Future Award to a documentary about a refugee camp, and the Frame Public Award to a drone built to carry a defibrillator. [S1][S3][S13]

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2015 awards from public sources only: the festival's closing release, the organizer's entry pages with their committee and jury statements, the makers' own pages and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where the sources disagree I say which one settled the question. [S1][S2]
A Saturday night in the Effenaar, and a new hall for the exhibition

The festival's closing release says the annual Dutch Design Awards were presented on Saturday evening, October 24, 2015, at a festive award show in the Effenaar. [S1] It calls Submarine Channel the big winner of the night. [S1] The same release counts the fourteenth Dutch Design Week at an estimated record of more than 275,000 visitors, 2,500 designers and 99 locations, and it names the new Veemgebouw as a valuable addition, where the exhibition Dutch Design Awards showed an overview of the best Dutch design of the past year. [S1]

No page I opened for 2015 states which edition of the awards this was. The festival's own announcements for later years give the count: the 2016 awards were the 14th, the 2017 awards the 15th and the 2018 awards the 16th. [S19][S18][S20] Counting back, 2015 was the 13th, which I treat as an inference from three consistent pages and not as a quoted fact. The awards themselves date from 2003, and the organizer's later release says the Dutch Design Awards office has been in Eindhoven since 2008. [S18] The organizer's current organization page tells it slightly differently: the awards were established in 2003 thanks to BNO and DesignLink, and have been based in Eindhoven since 2005. [S43] The two pages give different years for the move to Eindhoven (2008 and 2005), and I could not settle which is right, so I give both.

The festival around the awards had its own frame. The closing release says DDW 2015 ran under the banner What if, and that its ambassadors were Koert van Mensvoort, who launched Next Nature Network that week, and the designers Rianne Makkink and Jurgen Bey of Studio Makkink & Bey. [S1] It also records a new festival prize that year, the Best of Dutch Design Week Award, which the ambassadors gave to Modebelofte: Performing Advancers. [S1] That prize belongs to the festival and not to the Dutch Design Awards, and the two are easy to confuse. [S1] Makkink & Bey turn up on the awards side as well: PROOFFLab Magazine, made with the furniture maker PROOFF, was a 2015 Product nominee, and the studio won Design Research in 2022. [S41][S42]
How a prize was chosen: committees, a jury and five criteria

The organizer's pages for 2015 show a two-step process. Every winner's entry carries a Committee text, written by the category's selection committee, and most carry a Jury text, written by the international jury that chose the winner from the finalists. [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7][S8] The announcements of the next two years describe the same design: committees draw up the shortlist and an international jury picks the winners in October. [S19][S18]

The criteria are named on the Young Designer entry: impact, aesthetics, production method, innovation and collaboration. [S10] The 2017 announcement lists the same five (aesthetics, impact, innovation, method of manufacture and collaboration) for all categories. [S18]

The archive lists 30 entries for 2015 across eight groups: Communication, Design Research, Fashion, Habitat, Product, Service & Systems, Best Commissioning (called the Best Client Award in the 2015 entry text) and Young Designer. Nine carry the tag Winner. [S2][S9] Add the Future Award, which went to a project that had already won its category, a public prize and the biennial Piet Zwart prize, and the evening handed out ten awards by my count. [S1][S12][S13]

The exhibition's printed colophon, which I read in a photograph on October 9, 2026, names the jury chairs: Joost Alferink for Product and Fashion, Richard van der Laken for Communication and Service & Systems, Jan Konings for Habitat and Design Research, Saskia van Stein for Young Designer, Timo de Rijk for the BNO Piet Zwart prize and Frank Houben for the international jury. [S21] I could not check that panel against a second source in this pass.
Refugee Republic won twice, and the jury explained why

Refugee Republic, by Submarine Channel, won Communication and also took the Future Award, which the closing release describes as the prize for the most promising design for the future. [S1][S3] The entry describes an interactive online documentary about daily life in the Syrian refugee camp Domiz in northern Iraq, where drawings, photographs, film, sound and text let a visitor roam the camp. [S3]

The makers' own pages add the names and the money. The visual artist Jan Rothuizen, the journalist Martijn van Tol and the photographer Dirk Jan Visser made it; the producers were Bruno Felix and Femke Wolting; de Volkskrant was a co-producer; and the Non-fiction Transmedia Programme, a collaboration of the Creative Industries Fund, the Dutch Media Fund and the Netherlands Film Fund, made it possible. [S14] The credits date the production to 2014. [S14]

The committee praised a visibly good cooperation among the three makers and said research, communication, visualization, technology and interaction with users all hold up. [S3] The jury went further. It said it was unanimous that the project was relevant with a clear social purpose, and that current events may have fueled the message but were not why it was chosen. [S3] It gave weight to the fact that the team lived in the camp while working, which it said adds an intensity that embedded journalism does not. [S3] It rewarded the project with the Future Award as one rooted in empathy, and it described refugees shown as human beings and not as victims. [S3]

One number does not agree between pages. The organizer's entry gives around 58,000 refugees in Domiz, while the makers' two pages say around 64 thousand. [S3][S14][S15] The makers know their own project best and their pages describe the camp as it grew, so I would read 58,000 as an earlier count. That reading is my inference, since neither page dates its figure.
The other winners

Design Research went to Arna Mackic for Mortal Cities & Forgotten Monuments, a book on the role architecture played at turning points in the history of the Balkans, with a proposal for Mostar. [S4] The committee said she does not take a side and builds on collective habits and memories and not on ethnicity or religion. The jury called it well conceived, visually appealing and subtle, and noted that invitations to apply the approach elsewhere showed it travels. [S4]

Fashion went to Lucas Ossendrijver for Lanvin's men's collection for autumn and winter 2015, shown at Paris Fashion Week on January 7, 2015. [S5] The jury said he had translated the quality of haute couture into ready-to-wear, an innovator with many imitators. [S5] The committee wrote that, thanks to Ossendrijver, Lanvin's menswear had been put on the map. [S5]

Habitat went to the Pani community center by SchilderScholte architecten, in Rajarhat in north Bengal. The entry calls it a technical school and neighborhood center whose workshop makes bamboo bicycles that are sold in its shop. [S6] Domus describes the same building as an educational building and community center, with materials taken from within a 15 mile radius: bamboo, hand-shaped brick, mango wood, reused steel and recycled corrugated panels. [S16] The committee noted that the colors had a function, yellow against mosquitoes and blue against flies, and the jury said every part of the integrated concept was exceptionally well executed. [S6] The two descriptions, school and community center, are not in conflict. The building is both. [S6][S16]

Product went to the Sorting Machine for PostNL by Flex/the Innovationlab, which processes post and packages to reduce the physical burden on PostNL employees. [S7] The committee said there had been no computerized system within PostNL for large and small packages while web shops grew. [S7] The jury's argument was about attention: design is often used to streamline logistics but gets little notice when the result is not media-friendly, and this was a blueprint of meaningful design. [S7]

Service & Systems went to Fabrique for the Van Gogh Museum's multimedia tour, a touchscreen player with three tours in ten languages that replaced a rental device, introduced when the museum presented a new arrangement of its permanent collection in November 2014. [S8] The committee spoke of two worlds, the digital and the historic, interconnecting. [S8]

The prize for the best commissioner, the Best Client Award, went to Eindhoven365, the city marketing organization, for building a Virtual Design Agency, a collective of local studios that gave Eindhoven one visual identity as a technology, design and knowledge city. [S9] The jury called it a bold, radical step, and listed studios including Edhv, HeyHeydehaas, George & Harrison, Raw Color and Scherpontwerp. [S9]

Teresa van Dongen won the Young Designer Award. She graduated with distinction from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2014, and the entry describes her work as a bridge between nature, science and design, with a living lamp and a lamp that uses bioluminescence in development. [S10] The jury said her portfolio was still modest but held great potential and that every one of the five criteria showed in it. [S10]

A separate page honors Paul Mijksenaar, the specialist in information design and wayfinding, with the Piet Zwart prize. [S12] The text calls him an ambassador of the end user and ties contemporary data visualization to his analytical approach. [S12]
The public prize and the drone

Frame's headline says Alec Momont's Ambulance Drone seized voters' hearts to win the Frame Public Award. [S13] I could read only the headline. The article body did not load for me, so I have no vote count, no date and no description of how the vote ran. [S13]

The organizer's archive complicates the picture. It tags the Ambulance Drone Winner under Service & Systems, next to the Van Gogh Multimediatour. [S2][S11] But the drone's page holds a Committee text and no Jury text, while the Van Gogh page holds both. [S8][S11] Every other category winner's page has a jury paragraph. [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7][S9][S10] I read the tag on the drone as the archive's way of marking the public prize, with the Van Gogh tour as the Service & Systems jury winner. That is the only reading that fits the Frame headline and the missing jury text together, and it is my reading, not the organizer's stated rule.

The drone was Alec Momont's graduation prototype at the faculty of Industrial Design at TU Delft, developed with the innovation platform Living Tomorrow. [S11] It flies autonomously to deliver a defibrillator, with a video and voice connection so people at the scene get instructions, locating the caller by phone signal and navigating by GPS. [S11] The entry gives about 100 kilometers an hour, a weight of four kilograms and a payload of up to four kilograms. [S11] The committee said it was a complete system, not just a product, and remarked that it was still a prototype with, given legislation, a long way to go. [S11]

The most quoted number around the drone is Momont's own projection that a defibrillator could reach a patient within a 12 square kilometer zone in one minute, raising survival after cardiac arrest from 8 percent to 80 percent. [S17] The same 2014 report notes that Dutch law then forbade autonomous drones and that obstacle avoidance still had to improve. [S17] As a medical educator, I treat a survival figure like that as a projection until a trial says otherwise. Nothing I found shows a clinical result for this prototype, and I make no claim that it has saved anyone. [S17]
Nominees that show the range

The nominee lists are where the year's range is easiest to see. In Product, Studio Drift's Shylight, a robotic light installation, had been bought by the Rijksmuseum, and Dirk Vander Kooij's RvR chair was described as the first 3D-printed chair in the world, printed in half an hour from recycled plastic. [S22][S23] Floris Schoonderbeek's Groundfridge revived the cool cellar as a product. [S33]

In Habitat the committee stressed that it was Arno & Iris's artwork on the Rotterdam market hall, made with MVRDV, that was shortlisted, and not the whole building. [S30] MoodBuilders' Heijmans ONE offered a movable single-person home for people who earn too much for social housing and too little to buy. [S34]

In Communication, CLEVER°FRANKE mapped how people read migration data, with the University of Sheffield and the Migration Observatory, and Rob van Hoesel's New Horizons is a book of three hundred pictures chosen from the 8,785 that a machine took of the North Sea horizon, hour by hour, through 2012. [S28][S29] In Fashion, MAISON the FAUX turned a backstage dressing room into the catwalk. [S27]

Two nominees turn up again. Manon van Hoeckel's In Limbo Embassy, a mobile embassy for asylum seekers, was a 2015 Communication nominee, and she won the Young Designer Award in 2018, where her list of projects includes Limbo Embassy. [S25][S26] MAISON the FAUX was a 2015 Fashion nominee and a 2018 Fashion winner. [S27][S2] In the Design Research list, Circus Engelbregt's Medicijnfabriek, a workshop in which participants choose a plant in a park and process it into a medicine, sat beside Reframing Studio's Project Network, an app for young people recovering from mental health problems. [S31][S32]

Some nominees were projects about places. Inside Outside's Agora 2014 Espace Public was an exhibition design in a former transport depot in Bordeaux, separating a formal city downstairs from an informal one upstairs with a white curtain 247 meters long. [S37] Anne Holtrop and Anouk Vogel's pavilion for Bahrain at Expo Milan 2015 was designed to be rebuilt in Bahrain afterward as a botanical garden. [S38] Overtreders W's Almeerse Wolunie was a wool association in Almere with 200 members who paid 50 euros a year for four workshops; the same studio later built the People's Pavilion that won Habitat in 2018. [S35][S36]

The Best Client list included the Rijksmuseum, whose entry names Irma Boom, Christian Borstlap, Droog Design and Fabrique among the designers it worked with, and the Industriepark Kleefse Waard, whose committee praised it for linking industry and young designers through a furniture series made only from waste materials. [S24][S40] In Communication, the committee admired Marie-Jose Jongerius and Hans Gremmen's two-volume Edges of the Experiment as a self-initiated, long-term study despite the financial risk. [S39]
What the exhibition photographs add

The Veemgebouw exhibition album holds 19 photographs, which I read in full on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version. [S21] In one, a white panel headed Colofon lists the jury chairs named above, says the exhibition was designed by La Bolleur in collaboration with Exposize, and names the municipality of Eindhoven as initiator. [S21]

In another, a wooden shelf under a red sign that reads FRAME public award and VOTE NOW carries labeled jars, with labels for Mortal Cities & Forgotten Monuments, Ambulance Drone and Lanvin. [S21] That is how I know the public vote ran in the room. It also explains why the drone is in the archive as a winner: its jar was on the shelf, and the shelf's sign names the prize Frame awarded. [S21][S13] The photographs show no count.
Where 2015 sits in the archive

The organizer's archive lists 30 winner and nominee entries for 2015, close to the 31 for 2014 and well below the 39 for 2013 and the 127 listed for the first edition in 2003. [S2] Those numbers are my count of the listing and not an organizer statistic. [S2]

Several 2015 names have long runs in the archive. Flex/the Innovationlab, the Product winner, is listed in 2003, 2005 (as a winner for 1-2 Paint), 2007, 2010 and 2015. [S2] Fabrique, which won Service & Systems, is first listed in 2003 and appears as a winner in 2005, 2006 and 2013 before 2015. [S2] Lernert & Sander, nominated in Fashion for The Sound of Cos, had been on the lists in 2010, 2011 (a winner for a video clip), 2012 and 2014. [S2] Studio Drift, a Product nominee for Shylight, had been a Young Designer nominee in 2010. [S2] MVRDV, a collaborator on the market hall artwork nominee, had appeared in 2010 with The Why Factory. [S2]

Reading the archive this way shows what the Product and Service & Systems prizes of 2015 were rewarding. They went to studios that had been in the awards' orbit for more than a decade, and the committees said what they valued was applied work: a sorting machine redesigned around the people who use it, and a museum tour built around the people who borrow it. [S2][S7][S8]
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

**Who won Service & Systems.** The archive tags two winners. The jury text exists only for the Van Gogh tour, and Frame's headline gives the drone the public prize, so I treat the Van Gogh tour as the category winner and the drone as the public prize winner. [S2][S8][S11][S13]

**Who won the other categories.** The closing release names only Communication, the Future Award and Young Designer. The organizer's entry pages, each with a jury statement, settled Design Research, Fashion, Habitat, Product, Service & Systems and Best Client. [S1][S4][S5][S6][S7][S8][S9] Earlier secondary summaries that named other winners are contradicted by those pages and are not used.
**The size of the camp.** Around 58,000 on the organizer's page and around 64 thousand on the makers' pages. I follow the makers and say so. [S3][S14]
**The edition number.** Not stated for 2015. Inferred as the 13th from three later announcements. [S19][S18][S20]
**Since when in Eindhoven.** 2008 in the 2017 release, 2005 on the current organization page. Unresolved. [S18][S43]
What the record does not show

I do not know how many entries the 2015 awards received, how many people sat on each committee, or who sat on the international jury beyond the chairs on the colophon. None of the 2015 pages I opened gives these numbers. [S1][S2]
I do not know the public vote's count, its dates, or whether people could vote online as well as in the room, because the only readable record is a headline and a photograph. [S13][S21]

I could not locate the organizer's own 2015 announcement of finalists or its winners release, and I could not read Frame's article. What I could use for 2015 is the entry pages, the closing release and the photographs. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show. [S1][S2]

If you open the archive for a year you care about, read the jury paragraph of one winner and one nominee side by side. Which of the two reasons would you have been willing to defend in public, and would you have defended it the same way a year later? [S2]

title: The Dutch Design Awards 2016 gave the Future Award to a flax chair and the public vote to a glass brick facade
subtitle: The 2016 awards read through the festival's releases, the organizer's entry pages and jury texts, a museum record and the official photo archive
description: Who won the Dutch Design Awards in 2016, why the jury picked the FLAX Chair, how the Crystal Houses won the public vote, and what the record leaves open.

sections.x: The Dutch Design Awards of 2016 gave their Future Award to a chair made of flax and polylactic acid, and the public vote to a facade of glass bricks. [S1][S4][S5]

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2016 awards from public sources only: the festival's releases, the organizer's entry pages with their committee and jury texts, press reports, a museum record and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question. [S1][S3]
A Saturday in October, 26 finalists and a hall in the Veemgebouw

The festival's closing release says the annual Dutch Design Awards were presented on Saturday, October 29, 2016, and that prizes went to six categories, with the Young Designer Award, the Best Client Award and the Public Award on top. [S1] The same release counts the 15th Dutch Design Week at an estimated record of 295,000 visitors, with 2,500 designers across more than 430 curated exhibitions and presentations at 100 locations, under the theme The making of. [S1]

The June announcement counted the field. A selection committee shortlisted 26 finalists in six categories for what the festival calls the 14th Dutch Design Awards: four in Fashion, five in Product, five in Habitat, four in Design Research, four in Communication and four in Service & Systems. [S2] An international jury would choose the winners in October. [S2] The organizer's archive lists 32 entries for 2016, the 26 finalists plus three Best Client finalists and three Young Designer finalists. [S3]

The committees wrote a short state of the field for each category. They noted a striking number of young designers in Fashion, a stronger showing for consumer products and less traditional industrial design in Product, and in Habitat a plea that clients keep involving designers so that impact can happen at scale. [S2] In Design Research they saw designers engaged with current political themes, and in Service & Systems the committee called design a team sport. [S2]

Press reports place the exhibition of finalists and winners at the Veemgebouw during the festival, October 22 to 30, where the public could vote for a favorite design. [S14] No photo caption I read names the venue, so the press report fills that gap. [S21][S14]
The Future Award: a chair with a long paper trail

The closing release says Christien Meindertsma convinced the international jury on all fronts, and that her FLAX Chair won the Product category and the Future Award, the prize for the most promising design of the future. [S1] The press reports repeat this, and IO+ headlined that the FLAX Chair was the big winner. [S13][S15]

The jury's long paragraph is the best statement of why. It said the project is more than another chair: it is the result of years of research into flax, a search for a way to reinstate the value of the short flax fibre, and a drive to connect with Dutch companies to bring a product to market, done with Label/Breed and Enkev. [S4] It called the chair an excellent example of what contemporary design can achieve. [S4] A second jury paragraph praised an almost waste-free production process that marries sustainability and relevance with an elegant look. [S4] The committee had noted that the two materials, flax fiber and polylactic acid, are both environmentally responsible and insufficiently valued, and it singled out the role of Label/Breed, which links designers to Dutch manufacturers. [S4]

The makers and a museum fill in the construction. Meindertsma's own page says the chair began as a collaboration with the natural fiber specialist Enkev, initiated by Label/Breed, and that a new composite was made from four layers of woven flax textile and five layers of newly developed dry-needle felted flax, heat pressed into a rigid shape from a 60 by 100 centimeter sheet with very little waste. [S19] The Victoria and Albert Museum's record adds that the chair is the first research project of hers to result in a product that can be made at scale, that the seat is cut from one panel and the rest is folded into the legs so that nothing is left over, and that only two screws are used. [S18]

One detail differs between sources. The press reports say Meindertsma bought a flax farm. [S13][S15] The jury's English text says she bought a flax plot. [S4] The museum record is the most specific and says she began the Flax Project in 2010 by buying the entire harvest, 10,000 kilos, from a Dutch flax farm to understand the dwindling European flax industry. [S18] I follow the museum record: she bought a harvest, not a farm.

The chair kept its standing after the evening. The museum record notes that the chair won the Product category and the Future Award in 2016, and Meindertsma's page lists it in the collections of the Vitra Design Museum, the National Gallery of Victoria and Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen. [S18][S19] She is back in the archive in 2023 as one half of The Soft City, a Best Commissioning winner made with Rotterdam Circulair. [S44]
The public vote: Crystal Houses

Crystal Houses by MVRDV, with ABT, TU Delft and Poesia, won the Public Award, the closing release says. [S1] IO+ reports it received the most votes both online and in the exhibition, and TLmag says the votes were aggregated from on-site and online voting. [S13][S14]

MVRDV's own news item describes the prize as the Public Award for best product. [S16] That wording is looser than the festival's. The festival's release and the press reports describe a public vote across all finalists and not a product prize. [S1][S13][S14] The facade was one of the five Product finalists, which may be where MVRDV's wording comes from; that is my inference. [S2]

The organizer's archive complicates it in the same way it did in 2015. It tags Crystal Houses Winner under Product beside the FLAX Chair. [S3][S5] But the Crystal Houses page holds a Committee text and no Jury text, while the FLAX Chair page holds both. [S4][S5] I read the tag as the archive's way of marking the public prize. The committee text itself calls the solid glass brick a revolutionary new material that enables completely new cityscapes. [S5]

The project page describes what was built: a flagship store facade on Amsterdam's PC Hooftstraat in glass bricks, glass window frames and glass architraves, copying the layering of the original brick building, with 620 square meters of retail and 220 square meters of housing. [S17] Poesia in Resana near Venice cast the bricks, and research by Delft University of Technology with the engineering firm ABT and the contractor Wessels Zeist led to a high-strength transparent adhesive from Delo that replaced mortar. [S17] The entry gives the brick size as 24.7 by 11.6 by 5.3 centimeters. [S5]
The other category winners

Communication went to Studio Joost Grootens for the Dikke Van Dale, the 15th edition since 1864, with 241,558 headwords on 4,880 pages and, for the first time, four-color printing, illustrations and a new typeface. [S6] The committee said that in a digital era the studio had turned the paper dictionary into a must-have. [S6] The jury added that Grootens had also developed a technique to streamline the layout process for the publisher. [S6]

Design Research went to Jan Willem Petersen of Specialist Operations for Uruzgan's Legacy, a study of the results of reconstruction projects in Afghanistan, which looks at the impact of the interventions and not at statistics such as the number of schools built. [S7] The committee called it a must-read for future missions and praised the research in a difficult place. [S7] The jury said Petersen went to great lengths to embed himself in his environment and that the maps, photography and plain texts make complex information accessible. [S7]

Fashion went to Jan Hoek and Duran Lantink for Sistaaz of the Castle: photographs and a collection about transgender sex workers in Cape Town, shown at the photo museum Foam and during Amsterdam Fashion Week. [S8] The jury wrote that making and customizing garments is part of the cultures of the African continent, that the project explores the idea that everyone is a designer, and that its respect for the Sistaaz comes across in the couture and the photography and in the sense of pride the project gave them. [S8]

Habitat went to Studio Marco Vermeulen for the Biesbosch Museumeiland. The museum reopened in summer 2015 after eight months of building, with a glass-fronted new wing and a grass and herb roof on old and new parts. [S9] The jury said that with limited resources and by reusing the original structure, the architects had made a museum in synergy with the landscape, and that it answers the national need for affordable ways to transform obsolete 1970s buildings. [S9]

Service & Systems went to Frank Kolkman for Designs For Flies, a toolkit that would let patients with rare illnesses take part in research by testing compounds on fruit flies. [S10] The commissioner is credited as the Kyoto Institute of Technology, and the Kyoto Design Lab's own page describes a collaboration with Professor Masamitsu Yamaguchi, the Center for Advanced Insect Research and Charcot-Marie-Tooth Japan around a home screening kit for a neurodegenerative disorder. [S10][S20] The committee called it promising and pioneering but still preliminary, and the jury said it spotlights the need for new approaches to drug research. [S10] Nothing I found shows the kit in use by patients, so I read it as a design proposal and not a validated service. [S10][S20]

The Best Client Award went to Brabantia, the family firm founded in 1919 and led since 2012 by Tijn van Elderen, the fourth generation, for repositioning its brand with three agencies: Proud Design for logo and packaging, Studio Aandacht for styling and photography and Bovil for copy. [S11] The jury called the rebranding a commercial success and credited the careful choice of designers. [S11]

Tom van Soest won the Young Designer Award. He graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2012 with research into using building waste for bricks, which became the company StoneCycling with Ward Massa and the WasteBasedBrick. [S12] The jury, led by Giovanni Colauto, CEO of De Bijenkorf, according to IO+, praised him for designing the production process as well as the product and for getting a grip on the legal approval of new construction materials in a short time. [S12][S47]
The finalists that did not win

In Communication, Moniker's Place a Stone let 15,509 visitors place virtual stones that formed the names of victims of the shooting of May 7, 1945 on the Dam, and the result was set in the pavement on March 1, 2016. [S22] Moniker returns in 2018 as a winner for Paperstorm.it. [S40]

In Habitat, [ZUS]'s Luchtsingel, a 400 meter pedestrian bridge in Rotterdam partly paid for by crowdfunding, sat beside Jonas Staal's People's Parliament of Rojava and NEXT architects' Bat Bridge over the Vlotwatering. [S23][S24][S45] World of Food turned a former parking garage in the Bijlmer into an indoor market. [S46]

In Product, the finalists included 2016/Arita, in which Scholten&Baijings linked sixteen designers to craftspeople in the Japanese porcelain village Arita, with Meindertsma among the Dutch four. [S25] Space Encounters' Boring Collection was a deliberately plain, soft gray office furniture line that the committee called funny and daring. [S26] Simone Post's Post-Vlisco Carpet turned textile waste from Vlisco into rugs, and Post won the Young Designer Award in 2019. [S27][S42]

In Service & Systems, Yellow Backie put free yellow luggage carriers on Amsterdam bikes so strangers could ride along, and ACHTUNG!'s Mijn Volkswagen App was praised for showing relevant information only when the car is not moving. [S28][S29] Social Label's >VEEG with Dick van Hoff made brooms from old bicycle frames, and Social Label won Best Commissioning in 2018. [S30][S43]

In Design Research, the finalists included Thought Collider's Kindred Spirits on smell and memory in a rehab clinic, Studio Marco Vermeulen's Dutch Smart Thermal Grid on geothermal heat, and MacGuffin Magazine, which the 2018 committee said won after an earlier nomination. [S31][S32][S33][S41] In Fashion, Futura's Racing Ankersmit used archive cotton prints from the textile maker Ankersmit. [S38]

The Best Client finalists besides Brabantia were Transavia and MultiTankcard, and the Young Designer finalists besides Van Soest were Marius Jopen and Sophie Hardeman. [S34][S35][S36][S37] A third Young Designer thread: Frank Kolkman, who won Service & Systems here, won the Young Designer Award the next year. [S39]
What happened next to a few finalists

The organizer tracked its alumni in later items. In a January item about Paris Men's Fashion Week, it notes that the duo Schepers Bosman, Sanne Schepers and Anne Bosman, showed an autumn-winter 2020 collection of work clothes with stage esthetics, each garment linked to a musician or band, made with Hacked By_, and that Bosman had been nominated in 2016 as part of Futura. [S51][S38] That fits the Futura entry, which names Anne Bosman among the label's founders. [S38]
What the exhibition photographs add

The 2016 albums, which I read on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version, hold an exhibition set and an award show set. [S21] In one photograph a tilted white panel headed INTRODUCTION carries the exhibition's own text. It says the award show was on October 29, that designs are judged on five criteria (aesthetics, impact, innovation, manufacturing process and cooperation), that Glamcult Studio designed the exhibition, that Exposize and Baars & Bloemhoff made it possible and that the winners' awards were 3D metal printed by Addfab. [S21]

A banner in the same album reads Design Research above a text saying there are four finalists, which matches the June announcement. [S21][S2] A wall of mirrored glass bricks in another photograph looks like the Crystal Houses material. I could not read a caption for it, so I treat it as a match to check, not a finding. [S21]
Where 2016 sits in the archive, and where people went next
The organizer's archive lists 32 entries for 2016, close to the 30 of 2015 and the 34 of 2017, and the number drops to 24 a year from 2018. [S3] The count is mine, from the listing. [S3]

Several 2016 names are long-running. Christien Meindertsma is listed as a 2008 winner twice, for the book PIG 05049 in Communication and as a Young Designer, and again in 2013 for a knitting book in Product, before 2016 and 2023. [S3] Studio Joost Grootens, the Communication winner, was listed in 2003, won in 2006 for the Metropolitan World Atlas and was a 2010 nominee. [S3] NEXT architects, a Habitat nominee for the Bat Bridge, had been listed in 2008 and twice in 2010 and won in 2018 with the Zaligebrug. [S3] Moniker, a nominee for Place a Stone, had won in 2013 for Do Not Touch and would win again in 2018. [S3]

The organizer later asked past Young Designer winners and nominees to reflect. In a 2024 paired conversation the 2016 winner Tom van Soest said that to have a big impact his recipes for recycled bricks had to fit the existing industry, that ten years later he knows how hard that is, and that he had recently returned to working at a smaller scale. [S48] Frank Kolkman, who won Service & Systems in 2016 and Young Designer in 2017, said in his own paired conversation that he is more married to the concept of collective imagination and how to express it in design. [S49] Marius Jopen, a 2016 Young Designer finalist, talked in a third conversation about working as a VJ and with AI tools, and about hand-tracing more than a thousand frames of an AI-made video to get an analog look. [S50]
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

**Two Product winners.** The archive tags the FLAX Chair and Crystal Houses Winner. Only the FLAX Chair page has jury text, and the festival's release assigns the Public Award to the Crystal Houses. [S3][S4][S5][S1]
**Flax farm, plot or harvest.** Press: farm. Jury English text: plot. Museum record: the whole harvest, 10,000 kilos. I follow the museum record. [S13][S4][S18]
**What MVRDV's prize was.** MVRDV calls it a Public Award for best product; the festival calls it the Public Award. I follow the festival. [S16][S1]
**Where the exhibition stood.** No caption in the photo archive names it, and TLmag gives the Veemgebouw. I follow TLmag and say it is a press report. [S14][S21]
What the record does not show
I do not know who sat on the 2016 international jury or how many projects were entered, and I found no jury list in the releases or on the entry pages. [S1][S2][S3]
I do not know the Public Award's vote count or dates. The reports say only that online and exhibition votes were combined. [S13][S14]

I could not verify the exhibition's hall within the Veemgebouw, or the details of the photo-based statements above, in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show. [S21]
If you read one year of an award archive this way, what would you look for first: the winner's reasons, or the labels that tell you which winners were chosen by a room and which by a crowd? [S3]

title: The Dutch Design Awards 2017 gave the Future Award to a renovated Bijlmer flat and the public vote to a coat for people without a home
subtitle: The 2017 awards read through the festival's releases, the organizer's entry pages and jury texts, press reports, the publisher's catalog and the official photo archive
description: Who won the Dutch Design Awards in 2017, who judged them, how DeFlat Kleiburg and Sheltersuit 4.0 won the top and public prizes, and what the record leaves open.

sections.x: The Dutch Design Awards of 2017 gave the Future Award to the renovation of a 500-apartment block in Amsterdam's Bijlmermeer, and the public vote to a jacket that turns into a sleeping bag for people who live outside. [S5][S8][S17][S18]

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2017 awards from public sources only: the festival's releases, the organizer's entry pages with committee and jury texts, press reports, a publisher's catalog and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question. [S1][S4]
October 28, 2017: the 15th edition and a jury of nine

The June announcement counted 27 nominated projects for the 15th Dutch Design Awards in six categories: Product, Communication, Habitat, Fashion, Design Research and Service & Systems. [S2] It said the work of all nominees would be shown in a retrospective exhibition during Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29, and that winners would be announced on October 28. [S2] Three Young Designer finalists, chosen from 73 submissions, came with a separate announcement. [S3]

The announcement describes how the shortlist was made: three committees with twenty design experts together selected from the submissions and from scouted projects, judging on aesthetics, impact, innovation, method of manufacture and collaboration. [S2] The committee also asked itself a question in public, whether the emphasis on designers' responsibility for social issues is desirable, since good designs that find their way into daily use also matter. [S2]

The winners were chosen by an international jury of nine: Bart Ahsmann of BEDA, Saskia van Stein of bureau Europa, Carolien Ligtenberg of Bureau Zwirt, Rosa Bertoli of Wallpaper, Deyan Sudjic of the Design Museum London, Beatrice Leanza of Beijing Design Week, the product designer Joost Alferink, the graphic designer Roosje Klap and Marco Coello of Design Week Mexico. [S5][S6] They announced the results on Saturday, October 28, during Dutch Design Week. [S5]

The awards marked 15 years. The announcement says that since 2003 the awards have rewarded Dutch designers, that the anniversary year celebrates the future with a new batch of designers, the publication of archives and the stories behind 15 years of Dutch design, and that the biennial BNO Piet Zwart Award was presented again. [S2] The festival's closing release counts 335,000 visitors, 2,600 designers and 610 exhibitions, presentations, tours and activities at 110 locations, and it lists Smurfit Kappa with Dutch Design Awards among the new collaborations between designers, brands and labels. [S1]
The ambassadors that year included Marcus Fairs of Dezeen, Winy Maas of MVRDV and Lonny van Ryswyck and Nadine Sterk of Atelier NL. [S21] Atelier NL won Design Research the same week. [S10][S21]
DeFlat Kleiburg: the Future Award and the Habitat prize

DeFlat Kleiburg by NL Architects and XVW architectuur won both the Habitat category and the Future Award, which made it the big winner of the evening. [S5][S8] The jury's line quoted in the press was that the project sends a clear, positive message: community building is the future. [S5]

The entry describes the approach. Kleiburg is the only block of the Bijlmermeer development that kept its original look after refurbishment. The team modernized only the main structure, meaning lifts, balconies, walkways and building systems, and left the vacant apartments for the future occupants to finish. The lift shafts moved inside, which restored the long horizontal lines, and the concrete, painted white, was sandblasted. [S8] The committee wrote that the building had finally become what its designers intended in the 1960s, an open building where people from different cultures and backgrounds live together, and that the project was carried out at the height of the financial crisis. [S8]

The jury pointed to what happened afterward: positive reactions of residents and the community and rising land prices as the best testimony to success. [S8] It also said that after several attempts at revitalizing the Bijlmer, DeFlat Kleiburg was the first to succeed, and that it offers a tangible answer to the international problem of scalable re-use of 1960s and 1970s buildings. [S5]

The building later won a larger prize. The European Commission and the Fundacio Mies van der Rohe announced DeFlat Kleiburg as the 2017 winner of the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture, the Mies van der Rohe Award, naming the client as Kondor WesselsVastgoed, the block as a bend slab of 500 apartments, and the way it was rescued as a Klusflat, where residents renovate their own apartments. [S18] The announcement adds that it was the first time the main award went to the renovation of an existing building. [S18] That is a fact about a different award, and I mention it only because it shows how the Dutch jury's choice was read abroad.
The credits differ by outlet. Some reports name only NL Architects, while the organizer's entry and IO+ add XVW architectuur. [S5][S8][S18] I follow the entry and the two firms together.
The other winners

Communication went to Michiel Schuurman for Vlisco un a un, an exhibition on 170 years of Vlisco at the Museum Helmond, with a giant Vlisco pattern that he designed for the floor. [S9] The jury called it a majestic oeuvre exhibition staged at a time when the industry faces challenges, and noted the justified number of visitors for a modest regional museum. [S9] Schuurman was a former fabric designer at Vlisco, and the committee praised the client for giving him a free hand. [S9]

Design Research went to Atelier NL for Zandglas, tableware made of glass melted from natural sand taken from dunes, beaches and other places in Europe, each object stamped with its origin. [S10] The committee said the work puts local prospecting for materials on the map as a design and production method. [S10] The jury applauded the thorough, time-intensive research and encouraged the pair to involve scientific institutions. [S10] The sand sources named in the entry include the Sand Motor and the Savelsbos at Maastricht. [S10]

Fashion went to the collective Das Leben am Haverkamp, four designers, Anouk van Klaveren, Christa van der Meer, Dewi Bekker and Gino Anthonisse, for their Bravado collection and show. [S11] The jury said the group puts artistic expression first, shows how unflinching research can look, and called the mix of individual and collective output radical and engaging, while asking the collective to develop a signature style. [S11] The same group was a Young Designer finalist. [S44]

Product went to Quooker Flex, a tap that supplies boiling water at 100 degrees and has a pull-out hose. [S12] The jury credited years of collaboration between many parties and the safe separation of boiling water from cold, and ended by asking when Quooker will start dispensing sparkling water. [S12]

Service & Systems went to Richard Vijgen's White Spots, an app, made with the filmmaker Bregtje van der Haak and the photographer Jacqueline Hassink, that lets people seek out the limits of the Internet, as an interactive map and a virtual reality experience. [S13] The entry notes that one third of the world's population does not enjoy continuous access to the Internet. [S13] The jury called it evocative and lyrical and said it shows the necessity of going offline. [S13]

The Best Client Award went to Royal FloraHolland, which had asked the Vandejong Creative Agency at the end of 2015 to design a strategy for new consumers as the company shifted from the auction in Aalsmeer to digital trading, a program that became the brand Let it Grow. [S14] IO+ gives the award's criteria as professionalism, strategy, sustainability and innovation. [S7] The jury called Royal FloraHolland the undisputed winner of the 2017 Best Client Award. [S14]

Frank Kolkman won the Young Designer Award, a year after Designs For Flies won Service & Systems. [S15] The jury said his critical, provocative way of thinking merges science and design, and that in innovation and research he was in a class of his own among talented submissions. [S15] The IO+ report quotes the jury listing his projects, among them Open Surgery, a do-it-yourself robot surgery installation, and Designs for Flies, a kit for patients to develop medicine for rare diseases. [S6]

The biennial BNO Piet Zwart Award went to the design collective LUST. The organizer's page, in Dutch, says the jury chose it from thirty nominations as a forerunner for a new generation, that it was the first time a collective received the prize, and that the founders had decided to stop LUST in September 2017. [S16]
The public vote: Sheltersuit 4.0

The Public Award went to Sheltersuit 4.0 by designer Bas Timmer, which IO+ says received the most public votes online and in the exhibition. [S5][S6][S7] The Sheltersuit was one of five Product finalists. [S17][S4]

The entry describes a water- and windproof jacket that can be transformed into a sleeping bag for people without a home. Every suit is unique because it is made from donated high-quality materials, more than 1,200 had been handed out by then, and they are made by people distanced from the labor market, mostly asylum seekers with a residence permit. [S17] The committee called it a kind of family in which everyone contributes to the process, with a strong product and tremendous goodwill. [S17]

The press reports give no vote count, and I found none. [S5] The Sheltersuit foundation's own news page about the prize, which a search returned, no longer loads, so the organizer's wording and IO+ carry this.
Finalists across the categories

In Communication, Mevis & Van Deursen's poster for the Ed van der Elsken retrospective used a bright pink frame with chalk-like lettering, and Radio Garden, from Studio Puckey and Moniker, let people turn a globe through about 12,000 stations; the entry says it had been visited more than eighty million times. [S23][S24] Richard Niessen's The Palace of Typographic Masonry was a self-initiated structure of graphic elements, and it returns in 2019 as a nominee. [S25]

In Design Research, XML's Parliament compared the plenary halls of the parliaments of 193 United Nations member states. [S26] Envisions worked with the board manufacturer Finsa, and Babette Porcelijn's De Verborgen Impact aimed at behavior change toward an eco-neutral life, with the committee voicing reservations about its graphic design but not its research. [S27][S28]

In Fashion, the finalists were Sies Marjan's autumn-winter collection under creative director Sander Lak. [S29] In Habitat, MVRDV's De Trap put 140 steps up to the roof of the Groot Handelsgebouw in Rotterdam to mark 75 years since the start of reconstruction, and Sander Breure and Witte van Hulzen's work put four actors on a platform entrance at Utrecht Centraal every day for six months. [S30][S31] Stadslab Buiksloterham circular treated a hundred-hectare area in Amsterdam as a living lab for the circular city, and Vluchtmaat gave undocumented refugees, artists and start-ups a redeveloped vacant office building. [S32][S33]

Civic Architects' Willem II shopping arcade in Tilburg connected the inner city with the Spoorzone, and the same firm is among the winners of the 2019 Habitat category for the LocHal, in the same city. [S34][S46] The People's Pavilion, built by Bureau SLA and Overtreders W for the World Design Event in the middle of Strijp-S during DDW 2017, won Habitat in 2018. [S48]

In Product, the finalists beside Quooker and Sheltersuit were the Bugaboo Boxer luggage system, Fatboy's Lamzac 2.0 air-filled lounger and Miniot's Wheel turntable. [S35][S36][S37] In Service & Systems, the finalists were Me You and the Robot's guidelines for working with AI, Ermi van Oers's Living Light, which generates its electricity from plants, and Chloe Rutzerveld's Strooop!, a stroopwafel made from vegetables. [S38][S39][S40] The Best Client finalists beside Royal FloraHolland were Koninklijke Mosa and the Nationale Opera & Ballet. [S41][S42]

The committee texts say why each was shortlisted. For the Ed van der Elsken poster it was the boldness of a bright pink frame with chalked letters, and for Ornithology, Jeremy Jansen's design of a bird photography book by Anne Geene and Arjan de Nooy, it was that the book changes how you look at birds. [S23][S49] For the Bugaboo Boxer it was that a push system makes luggage feel lighter and the parts stack, for Lamzac 2.0 an air-filled lounger that fills with a wave of the arm and carries up to 200 kilos, and for Miniot's Wheel a turntable that holds the tone arm, motor and amplifiers inside the object and plays the record from the underside. [S35][S36][S37] United Nude's Rock Shoe was designed for an Issey Miyake show and the committee liked its chunky, sculpted heel. [S50] Sies Marjan's collection won praise for asymmetrical lines and dancing fabrics. [S29]

Among the Service & Systems finalists, the committee said Living Light addresses an overlap of design and science through plant microbial fuel cells, where a caress, not a switch, turns the light on, and it said Strooop! uses unusually sized vegetables and by-product streams to make a traditional stroopwafel from vegetable juice and fibres. [S39][S40] The Nationale Opera & Ballet entry credits Lesley Moore with a new house style, and Koninklijke Mosa, the Maastricht tile maker, kept an in-house design team and a long relationship with the agency Zuiderlicht. [S42][S41]

Super Local was a Young Designer finalist in 2017, and in 2023 it won Product with From the Himalayas. [S43][S45] Moniker, a co-author of Radio Garden, won Communication in 2018 with Paperstorm.it. [S24][S47]
After the award night

The organizer kept reporting on its winners. Michiel Schuurman, the Communication winner, was invited by PostNL to design a stamp sheet called Gewoontjes, six stamps for international destinations inspired by marbles, launched on October 18; PostNL, the item says, had begun that year to give winners of design competitions a free commission. [S53] The organizer does not state the year in the text I captured.

Sheltersuit, the Public Award winner, announced a partnership with the fashion house Chloé under its new art director Gabriela Hearst, in which two Sheltersuits go to people without a home for every bag sold, made from leftover fabrics of earlier collections. [S51] The foundation also staged its first Dutch Sleep Out in Enschede on the night of March 14 to 15, where participants slept outdoors to raise money. [S52] Both items reached me from the organizer's own pages, and I have not checked them against the foundation or the fashion house. [S51][S52]

Two 2017 finalists also turn up in later items. Chloé Rutzerveld, whose Strooop! was a Service & Systems finalist, was named to the Food100 list of food innovators under 30, an organizer item says. [S54][S40] Sander Lak of Sies Marjan was among the Dutch designers the organizer listed for Paris Men's Fashion Week in January. [S55][S29]
What the exhibition photographs add, and one correction

The Dutch Design Awards Exhibition album, which I read on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version, shows a white panel that opens with the words Be the Future and welcomes visitors to the retrospective exhibition, saying that visitors could vote for a Public Award and that winners would be revealed at the Awards Show on October 28. [S22] Two curtains read BE THE FUTURE and BACK TO THE FUTURE. [S22]

The publisher's catalog suggests what the two curtains refer to: Dutch Design Today, the awards' yearbook, was published in 2017 as a double publication with two covers and two titles, Be the future and Back to the future, to mark 15 years of the awards, and the curtains carry the same two titles. [S19][S20][S22] That is a match of titles, not a statement by the organizer about the curtains.
The same album's trophies are diamond shapes on colored bases stamped 2017, with bases for Product, Communication and Public Award. [S22]
Where 2017 sits in the archive

The organizer's archive lists 34 rows for 2017, which is 33 distinct entries because DeFlat Kleiburg appears under two labels, Future Award and Habitat. [S4] That is the high-water mark of the years in this series, and the count drops to 24 a year from 2018. [S4] The count is mine, from the listing. [S4]

Several 2017 winners had long histories on the lists. Michiel Schuurman, who won Communication, had been a nominee in 2008 and 2011. [S4] Richard Vijgen, behind White Spots, was a double winner in 2009 for two Communication projects and a nominee in 2009 and 2012 before winning Service & Systems. [S4] LUST, which received the Piet Zwart prize in the year its founders chose to stop, had won Communication in 2006, 2008, 2010 and 2011 and been a nominee in 2003, 2012 and 2014. [S4][S16] Atelier NL, which won Design Research with Zandglas, had been a Young Designer nominee in 2009. [S4] Moniker, a co-author of the Radio Garden nominee, had won in 2013, was a 2016 and 2017 nominee and won in 2018. [S4]

That pattern fits what the committee said in its June announcement, that the nominated designers have the intention and potential to shape the future and that the awards had in 15 years rewarded projects people use or live with today. [S2] Most of the winners in this archive had been on the lists for years. [S4]
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

**The 2017 winners.** The festival's closing release names none of the category winners. The organizer's entry pages, each with a jury statement, and two IO+ reports that list all winners settled Product, Service & Systems, Best Client, Young Designer, the Piet Zwart prize and the Public Award. [S5][S6][S7][S12][S13][S14][S15][S16]

**The Best Client row in the archive.** The archive page capture shows the 2017 Best Client rows with the winner year in the wrong field, and a Young Designer row with the project title missing. The entry pages and IO+ reports make the winners clear. [S4][S14][S7]
**What Be the Future was.** The curtains' two slogans match the yearbook's two titles, so I read them as a nod to the publication and not as a standalone joke about time. [S19]
**Credits for DeFlat Kleiburg.** Some outlets name NL Architects alone. The entry and the Mies announcement name NL Architects and XVW architectuur. [S8][S18]
What the record does not show

I do not know where the 2017 retrospective exhibition stood. The announcement names dates and no building, a search for the venue found nothing, and the festival's program release lists many locations without placing the awards. [S2]
I do not know the Public Award vote count, or how many entries the committees reviewed beyond the 73 Young Designer submissions. [S3][S5]
I did not verify the photo-based statements in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show. [S22]
If an award yearbook and an exhibition share the same two slogans, which of them do you read first, and does the answer change what you think the slogans mean? [S19]

title: The Dutch Design Awards 2018 stopped naming nominees, named 24 winners in June, and let visitors choose a 3D-printed bridge with paper ballots
subtitle: The 2018 awards read through the festival's releases, the organizer's updates and entry pages, press reports, the bridge's own records and the official photo archive
description: How the 2018 Dutch Design Awards replaced nominees with 24 winners, what the juries wrote, why the Future Award became three International Jury Awards, and how a bridge won the public vote.

sections.x: The Dutch Design Awards of 2018 stopped separating nominees from winners: the organizer named 24 winners in June, three in every category, then showed them for nine days in October and let visitors choose one with a paper ballot. [S1][S6][S8]

I like an award that can be checked against its own paperwork. This essay reads the 2018 awards from public sources only: the festival's releases, the organizer's updates and entry pages, press reports, the records of the winning bridge and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and where sources disagree it says which one settled the question. [S1][S11]
Why there were no nominees

The call for entries for what the organizer called the 16th edition asked its own question: why make a distinction between nominations and winners? Projects in a field as wide as design are often near impossible to compare, it said, so selecting multiple winners lets each designer be judged on their own merits. [S8] Committees of independent experts would select three winners per category from the submissions and from scouted work. [S8] The call set submissions from Thursday, March 8 to Tuesday, April 24, and named the criteria as aesthetics, impact, innovation, manufacture and cooperation. [S8]

The arithmetic shows in the archive. Every one of the 24 entries for 2018 carries the winner tag, three in each of Communication, Design Research, Fashion, Habitat, Product, Service & Systems, Best Commissioning and Young Designer. [S11] The festival's June item says the same, adding that this 16th edition presents several prizes per category. [S1]

The June item also describes what the winners had in common. It names circularity, the way technology increasingly affects our lives and a search for trust in a time of fake news and Instagram. [S1] Bright, whose editor-in-chief Erwin van der Zande sat on the jury according to the outlet, reported the same three themes under the heading that the winners show the future of the design industry. [S10]
The festival around the awards

The festival those winners were shown in ran October 20 to 28, 2018, under the theme If not us, then who?, which the closing release calls a tribute to designers. [S4] It counts 355,000 visitors, 2,600 designers and 499 exhibitions, lectures, tours and labs across 120 locations, and numbers it the 17th Dutch Design Week. [S4] The ambassadors were Ravi Naidoo of Design Indaba, Laurens van den Acker of Renault and Wendy Plomp of Dutch Invertuals. [S4][S15] The awards are a separate count: the festival's own items call the 2018 awards the 16th edition. [S1]
Thursday, June 28: an Awards Night and a cash prize for young talent

The organizer's update on the Young Designer prize says the winners were presented on Thursday, June 28, 2018, at the festive Dutch Design Awards Night. [S5] The evening also announced a new multi-year collaboration with the Keep an Eye Foundation: for the first time each Young Designer winner received 10,000 euros for professional development, and three prizes went to Lisa Konno, Olivier van Herpt and Manon van Hoeckel. [S5]

The same update names the Young Designer committee: Saskia van Stein as chair, with Jeroen Junte, Jeroen van Mastrigt and Georgette Koning, selecting the winners under jury chair Job Meihuizen of the Dutch Design Awards. [S5] It describes the prize as a stimulus for people who graduated no more than five years ago, judged on the whole portfolio. [S5] I did not find where the Awards Night took place. [S5]
The 24 winners

Communication went to What now, Koetsier? by Chives Archives with Rene Put, a series of 45 small advertisements by more than forty designers in the newspaper Het Parool that paid tribute to the conceptual artist Hans Koetsier; to Moniker's Paperstorm.it, a campaign site that simulates scattering paper flyers over Washington and, the entry says, saw visitors distribute over 22 million flyers in three weeks in defense of net neutrality; and to Hansje van Halem's identity for Lowlands 2018, a toolkit built on a grid of lines. [S17][S18][S19]

Design Research went to Urgentcity, a research project and program by Amateur Cities and New Generations that built a shared vocabulary for city-making around four themes; to the MX3D Bridge by Joris Laarman Lab and MX3D; and to MacGuffin Magazine's Magazine N 5, The Cabinet, whose committee said it won after an earlier nomination. [S20][S21][S22] That earlier nomination was in 2016. [S42]

Fashion went to MAISON the FAUX for Fauxmosapien (The Evolution), shown on the last evening of the 27th FashionWeek Amsterdam; to Schueller de Waal for Compulsory shenanigans' show, a staged large show whose committee called the label one of its favorite Dutch labels; and to Johannes Offerhaus for An Experiment with Parabolas, five outfits and five art installations set in motion by the models. [S23][S24][S25] MAISON the FAUX was a 2015 finalist. [S44]

Habitat went to the micro-home Slim Fit by Ana Rocha Architecture, about 50 square meters over three floors on a footprint smaller than two parking bays; to the People's Pavilion by Bureau SLA and Overtreders W, built from loaned and repurposed materials that were returned undamaged; and to the Zaligebrug by NEXT architects, a 200 meter bridge at Lent near Nijmegen that shows fluctuating water levels. [S26][S27][S28] The architects' own page dates the bridge's completion to March 2016 and calls it part of the national Room for the River program. [S14]

Product went to Aleksandra Gaca's BLOKO sound-absorbing 3D woven textile for Renault's SYMBIOZ concept car, made at the TextielLAB in Tilburg; to Circa, a smart alarm clock by Robert Bronwasser Design and Circa that offers an alternative to keeping the phone at the bedside; and to The Incredible Machine's Transparent Charging Station for ElaadNL and Alliander, which shows how a smart charging algorithm allocates power. [S29][S30][S31] The committee for the charging station asked whether a doctor should always have priority over an unemployed person. [S31]

Service & Systems went to Cow&Co by Anastasia Eggers and Ottonie von Roeder, a speculative project in which cows run their own circular milk production; to Swapfiets, a bicycle subscription from a fixed monthly fee, with a repair or swap offered within twelve hours and a blue front tire; and to VIIA with Freshheads, a digital tool for assessing earthquake reinforcement of buildings in Groningen, which twenty organizations were using. [S32][S33][S34] The Swapfiets committee called the idea an updated version of the White Bicycle Plan of the 1960s. [S33] The company said in October 2024 that it had been founded by three student friends from Delft and had grown to more than 270,000 members in 45 European cities. [S53]

Best Commissioning, which the festival's 2018 items call the Best Client Award, went to Museum Catharijneconvent with Fabrique for Het Grootste Museum van Nederland, which turned thirteen churches and synagogues into one museum; to Social Label, a laboratory that designs work for people on the margins of the labor market with designers including Piet Hein Eek and Kiki van Eijk; and to Royal Delft with Flex/design and Twnkls for Augmented Blueware, each dinner service paired with a hand-painted vase and augmented reality. [S1][S35][S36][S37] The committee noted that Social Label lacks the usual client and designer relationship. [S36] The museum's 2017 press release dates the opening of Het Grootste Museum van Nederland to July 6, 2017, with eleven churches and two synagogues, an audio tour developed with Fabrique and the 2016 book Kerkinterieurs in Nederland as its starting point. [S51] A June 2018 release says three more sites joined, making sixteen, after about one hundred thousand visits in the first year. [S52]

The Young Designer winners were Lisa Konno, whose Nobu collection puts her Japanese father at the center of an ironic comment on the integration debate; Manon van Hoeckel, who designs encounters, including a working launderette at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen and a traveling embassy for refugees; and Olivier van Herpt, who built his own 3D printer for ceramics. [S38][S39][S40] The Limbo Embassy had been a Communication finalist in 2015. [S41]
What the committees valued

The committee texts, the only reasoning the 2018 entries carry, are candid about limits. The committee said of Cow&Co that it does not offer a realistic solution to overconsumption but is a poetic contemplation of an alternative reality. [S32] It said of VIIA that the designers do not offer a simple answer but a functional tool for a complex problem. [S34] It was critical of the inconsistency in Lisa Konno's earlier work before praising her latest collection. [S38] And it put an ethical question to The Incredible Machine, asking whether a doctor should always get priority at a charging point and an unemployed person should not. [S31]

A second thread is the commissioning party. For Lowlands the committee admired the festival's courage in choosing one designer, not a large agency. [S19] For Het Grootste Museum it spoke of a traditional institution acquiring new meaning through the right partner. [S35] For Royal Delft it described a deep-rooted brand meeting innovative technology, with the outcome about unicity versus the multiple. [S37] For the People's Pavilion it said the designers give new meaning to circular building by keeping every material intact. [S27]

A third thread is patience with research. The MX3D committee spoke of years of impatient waiting for digital manufacturing to deliver, the MacGuffin committee of impact that builds with each issue, and the Offerhaus committee of fashion, technology and mathematics meeting in an installation, adding that he deserves to be picked up by smart-textile parties. [S21][S22][S25]
October: an International Jury Award, and a missing Future Award

The June item said the overall winner of the Future Award would be announced during Dutch Design Week, and Bright said an international jury would choose an overall winner from all the winners. [S1][S10] What happened instead, according to the festival's item of October 21, is that for the first time in the awards' history an International Jury Award went to three projects: Het Grootste Museum van Nederland, Cow&Co and the Zaligebrug. [S2] FashionUnited adds that the awards usually announce one. [S9]

The jury's reasoning is specific. It said the three projects share a habit of nudging designers around the world toward a new perspective, that it is time for designers to dare to question themselves and their role, and that this useful doubt is characteristic of what it calls the Dutch school. [S2] On Het Grootste Museum it remarked that a category for the best client is itself typical of the Dutch design climate. [S2] On Cow&Co it called the project a wonderful thought experiment. [S2] On the Zaligebrug it said that building a bridge that fails to do its job can only happen in the Netherlands, and that the meeting where it was proposed deserved a prize. [S2]

The jury, chaired by Job Meihuizen of the awards, consisted of Cameron Sinclair (United States), Lilli Hollein (Austria), Ikko Yokoyama (Hong Kong), Yuval Saar (Israel), Pieter Aarts, Joost Alferink, Saskia van Stein, Roosje Klap and Jaapjan Berg (Netherlands). [S2] The organizer's Dutch update describes the prize as placing the winners in an international context, with the international jury exchanging views with the Dutch jury before choosing. [S7]

I found no 2018 page that names a Future Award winner, and no page that says the International Jury Award replaced it. The June item and Bright anticipated one overall winner, and the October items describe three. [S1][S10][S2] I treat the International Jury Award as the practical successor for that year, but that is my reading and not the organizer's statement.
The public vote: a bridge and a paper ballot

The MX3D Bridge won the Public Award by a narrow majority, the festival says. [S3] The organizer's Dutch update adds a rule change: visitors voted for the first time only on a paper ballot form in the exhibition, to encourage people to see the projects themselves and to prevent the prize from going to the best online promotion. [S6] The exhibition was very busy, it says. [S6] No vote count is given. [S3][S6]

The entry describes the bridge as the world's first steel bridge 3D printed by robots, to span a canal in the center of Amsterdam, with partners including Arup, Autodesk, Heijmans, ArcelorMittal and Imperial College London. [S21] The jury text called it a utopian construction that opens the door to other large or public applications. [S21]

The bridge took longer than the 2018 wording suggested. Imperial College London reports that the 12 meter footbridge was unveiled by Queen Maxima in July 2021 and is designed to act as a living laboratory with a network of sensors and a digital twin. [S12] MX3D says the bridge has been in place over the Oudezijds Achterburgwal since 2021. [S13] The 2018 entry said it would soon span the canal. [S21] That gap is worth knowing when reading any award text: a jury judges what is shown, and the world finishes the story later.
Threads that run through the archive

Because 2018 gave winners where other years gave finalists, it is a good year to follow people. Manon van Hoeckel, MacGuffin and MAISON the FAUX were all earlier finalists. [S41][S42][S44] Social Label appears as a 2016 finalist through its >VEEG project, as a 2018 winner and again as a 2019 finalist through the Werkwarenhuis. [S43][S36][S45] Schueller de Waal returns as a 2020 finalist with Litter, Lisa Konno as a 2023 finalist with Henk, and Moniker had been a 2017 finalist with Radio Garden. [S46][S47][S48]
After the award night

The organizer's later items follow two of the winners. Overtreders W, whose People's Pavilion won Habitat, received the jury prize for Sustainability at the Frame Awards in Amsterdam on Thursday, February 20 for Brasserie 2050, a restaurant it designed as a food barn of the future that first opened at Lowlands in 2018. [S27][S54] Lisa Konno presented her newest short film BABA on Saturday, February 8 at the Compagnietheater in Amsterdam, after the earlier film NOBU, as part of a project that combines fashion, film and photography. [S38][S55] MAISON the FAUX made a chalk-stripe dress worn by the online host Nikkie de Jager at Eurovision: Europe Shine a Light, the alternative show staged from a studio in Hilversum after the Rotterdam contest was canceled because of the coronavirus, the organizer reports. [S23][S56] The items do not give the year in the text I captured; the weekdays and the Eurovision reference match 2020. [S54][S55][S56]
What the exhibition photographs add

The Dutch Design Awards album for 2018, which I read on October 9, 2026 and did not reopen for this version, shows an exhibition built from cardboard cubbies, wooden beams and black cardboard columns. [S16] Easel signs read Partners and Voting Point. [S16] One photograph shows boxes taped with a blue quote, signed Lilet Breddels, saying that collaboration between disciplines is crucial to understand the urgencies that face cities. [S16] The Young Designer boards are numbered, board 12 for Manon van Hoeckel and board 19 for Olivier van Herpt. [S16] The photographs show a Voting Point, which fits the paper ballot rule. [S16][S6]
Where 2018 sits in the archive, and what the young winners said later

The organizer's archive lists 24 entries for 2018, against 34 for 2017, and every one is tagged winner. [S11] From this year on the archive lists 24 entries each year through 2023. [S11] The counts are mine, from the listing. [S11]

Returning names stand out. Ernst van der Hoeven of MacGuffin Magazine had been a nominee in 2014 for a Habitat project, Indigo Cascade, and in 2016 for the magazine. [S11][S42] Hansje van Halem had been a nominee in 2011 for posters. [S11] Schueller de Waal's 2018 win was followed by the 2020 nomination for Litter. [S11][S46] NEXT architects had been listed in 2008 and twice in 2010. [S11] Overtreders W had been nominated in 2011 and 2012 before the Almeerse Wolunie in 2015 and the People's Pavilion win. [S11] Freshheads, behind the VIIA tool, was a 2019 Best Commissioning nominee with Interpolis. [S11]

Two of the young winners spoke later. Olivier van Herpt told the organizer in May 2019 that, besides recognition, the financial support mattered for taking the next step, that his team was industrializing ceramic 3D printing and that they were about to move to a new space in Eindhoven with room for research, development and demonstration. [S49] In a 2024 paired conversation, Manon van Hoeckel described a method she compares to a Trojan horse: she sets a goal, for example bringing people to a museum who normally do not come, and first joins the new target group to see what already fits their lives. [S50]
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it
**The top prize.** June sources anticipate a Future Award winner; October sources give three International Jury Awards. No source names a 2018 Future Award winner. [S1][S10][S2]
**Best Client or Best Commissioning.** The festival's 2018 items use Best Client; the archive entries use Best Commissioning. They are the same category. [S1][S11]

**Committee or jury.** The 2018 entry pages carry committee statements and no separate jury paragraph, because there was no single winner to defend. Any copy that says the jury wrote an entry text should say the committee. [S17][S36]
**How the public voted.** The festival says visitors could vote only in the exhibition. The organizer adds that it was paper only. The two agree. [S3][S6]
What the record does not show
I do not know where the Awards Night of June 28 was held, where the October exhibition stood, how many people voted, or how many entries the committees reviewed. [S5][S3][S1]
I did not verify the photo-based statements in this pass. Nothing here describes what the Dutch Design Awards 2026 will show. [S16]
If an award stops separating nominees from winners, what do you lose when you can no longer see who was almost chosen, and what do you gain? [S8]
