title: Love is not the same thing as payment
subtitle: Manshee Zheng's I Do It Because I Love It borrows a sentence used to justify unpaid creative work. Dutch copyright law, a sector code of conduct and national labor statistics show what the sentence leaves out.
description: Manshee Zheng's I Do It Because I Love It at Dutch Design Week 2026, read against Dutch copyright law, the Fair Practice Code and CBS data on artists' work.

sections.x: A person can love making something and still want the work counted. Dutch law says so in one clause: a maker has the right to fair remuneration for granting permission to exploit a work, and the amount is to be set in the contract. [S2]

Manshee Zheng's I Do It Because I Love It is in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program at VEEM floor 8 on Strijp-S, the home of Manifestations. The program describes an installation in which images print onto the objects that made them: a mirrored portrait onto a human-sized mirror, a liked Instagram story of a Scottish landscape onto a glass tabletop, a couch selfie printed onto a blanket draped over a sofa. [S1] It says the title borrows the phrase used to justify unpaid, feminized, creative labor performed under the guise of passion, with the influencer's caption, the intern's shrug and the artist's excuse for working through the night as examples. [S1] That is the artist's stated position. Zheng is listed as born in Beijing in 2002, and image captions on the page name I Have Nothing To Hide (2025) at Frascati in Amsterdam and at an ArtEZ graduation. [S1]

This essay uses public documents only: the program page, the Copyright Act, the Fair Practice Code, two Statistics Netherlands publications and the International Labour Organization's care-economy page. It reports no visit and no interview, and it does not speak for any worker. I want to take the question seriously without using an artwork as a shortcut to somebody else's life. [S1]
What the artwork claims, and what it does not

The program says that each object was already doing quiet, unpaid work, reflecting, displaying and holding, before the image arrived to make that labor visible and then disappear it again. [S1] It says the labor of framing, editing and mirroring folds back into the object until it looks effortless. [S1] The installation, in its own words, stages a domestic scene where care, self-exposure and content production collapse into one gesture performed for its own sake, "or so it claims." [S1]

That is an argument made in objects. It says nothing about what any named person was paid, and it offers no data. An artwork can make a relationship visible. It cannot tell me what a particular creator agreed to or how much choice she had. [S1]
What the law says about a maker's share

In Dutch law the question has an answer for people who make works protected by copyright. Under the Copyright Act in the version valid from January 1, 2026, a maker is entitled to a fair remuneration, to be set in the contract, for granting an exploitation right. A remuneration negotiated between an association of makers who are solo self-employed and an exploiter, or an association of exploiters, is presumed fair. [S2]

The Act adds three further protections. A maker who has granted exploitation rights must be informed by the other party at least once a year about how the work is exploited, the income generated and the remuneration owed, and the information must be current, relevant and complete. [S2] A maker can ask a court for an additional fair remuneration if the agreed payment is disproportionate to the revenue from exploiting the work. [S2] And a maker can terminate an agreement, in whole or in part, if the other party does not exploit the work sufficiently within a reasonable time. [S2]

I am not giving legal advice, and these provisions apply to makers of copyright works who grant rights by contract. They do not decide whether a given unpaid request is lawful, and they do not reach every kind of creative labor. They matter here for what they assume. The provisions read to me as starting from the idea that a creative person's affection is not the price, and they give the maker tools for later, when a short text becomes a longer one or an image becomes a promotional asset. [S2]
What the sector's own code says

The Fair Practice Code, published by Kunsten'92 for the cultural and creative sector, is a code of conduct and not a law. Its principles page names three principles, fair pay, fair share and fair chain. It says fair pay is the most obvious: relationships between people who work together last only with fair payment, equal pay for equal work is a condition of solidarity, and salaries and rates should be set in a way that is clear and transparent. [S3]

The page also makes an argument about who can afford to love their work for free. It says that without fair pay the sector becomes inaccessible to people who have no financial safety net, which leaves no room for diverse new talent. [S3] That is a statement about the sector from the code's authors, and I did not find a study that tests it. It does put the passion phrase in a different light. If only people with a cushion can say "because I love it," the sentence sorts the field.
What the national statistics show, and do not

Statistics Netherlands (CBS) counted, for 2021 to 2023, an average of 194 thousand artists and 337 thousand other workers in creative occupations, about 1 in 50 working people being an artist. More than half of the artists work as solo self-employed, well above the average for workers. [S4] Artists have, in the middle of the distribution, a relatively low income, though higher than other creatives at lower occupational levels, and they work at the highest occupational level, which requires higher or university education. [S4]

The CBS data also complicate the passion story. Most self-employed artists and creatives are satisfied with their work and working conditions, though less often than self-employed people in general, especially about working conditions. [S4] On income the gap is clearer. Among self-employed artists, 63 percent were satisfied or very satisfied with their income, compared with 78 percent of all self-employed people. Among employees, 71 percent of artists were satisfied with their salary, against 76 percent overall. [S5] People can like the work and be dissatisfied with what it pays, and the statistics show both at once.
These numbers do not measure unpaid labor, and they do not split the results by gender in the pages I read. The program's word "feminized" is a claim I cannot test with them. [S1][S4][S5]
Care work is a different category

The ILO's care-economy account helps with one distinction. The ILO defines care work as paid and unpaid, direct and indirect, delivered in the public and private sectors and in households. [S6] Its topic page reports 748 million people outside the labor force because of care responsibilities and a 24 percent gender pay gap in the health and care sector. [S6] Those figures concern care. Zheng's installation connects care, self-exposure and content production, and the program does not say the creative work in it is care work. Unpaid status alone does not make an activity care. Borrowing the moral weight of one category for an unsupported claim about another keeps the argument from being checked.
A clearer invitation

For a request to make something, a plain invitation says what the deliverable is, what uses are intended, how review works and what the payment is, before asking for commitment. If there is no payment it says so. If the scope changes, the conversation reopens. The Copyright Act's annual information duty and disproportion claim describe the same idea from the maker's side, and the Fair Practice Code's call for clear and transparent rates describes it from the sector's side. [S2][S3]

The same holds for a person who is asked to be visible. Making invisible labor visible can create another task, and the program does not say how participants in the installation, or the people whose images appear in it, were asked or credited. [S1] A self-image offered inside an artwork is not a reusable portrait for an article about unpaid work, and I would not treat it as one.
What the record does not show
What any person involved was paid, and under what terms the images and objects were used. [S1]
Whether the CBS figures differ by gender for self-employed creatives; they are not split in the pages I read. [S4][S5]
How common unpaid creative work is in the Dutch design sector, and how much of it is requested in exchange for exposure. [S4]
How the Fair Practice Code is applied in practice or by whom, beyond its published principles. [S3]
Whether copyright remuneration rules would cover a given request; that depends on the facts and the contract. [S2]

I want the affection to stay in the story. It may be what makes someone return to a hard piece or find a better sentence. I also want the arrangement beside it. Love can explain why making matters. The law, the sector's code and the statistics all point to the same follow-up question: who asked for the result, and what do they owe the person who made it? [S2][S3][S4]

title: What does a new material story forget?
subtitle: An exhibition at the Gasfabriek in Eindhoven tells fifty years of Dutch biological and biobased building. VIBA's own chronology shows ministers, pavilions and a permanent expo in the 1990s, and national monitors show how small the share still is.
description: Fifty years of biological and biobased building in the Netherlands: VIBA's own chronology, ministers and a 1 percent share of new homes in 2025.

sections.x: When a ministry says that in 2030 at least 30 percent of new homes should be built from at least 30 percent biobased materials, "new" is a strange word to hear. The Dutch association that argued for building with natural materials was founded on December 15, 1976, and by 1994 a minister was opening its permanent exhibition hall. [S2][S3][S5]

The exhibition 50 jaar biologisch en biobased bouwen in Nederland (fifty years of biological and biobased building in the Netherlands) is in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program at the Gasfabriek in Eindhoven. It describes a group of architects, building biologists and construction companies presenting drawings, publications and projects to make this Dutch heritage visible again. [S1] This essay uses public documents only: the program page, VIBA's own chronology, two Dutch government publications and the national building-environment database. It reports no inspection of any drawing, building or material sample. Where a claim is the exhibition's own, I say so. [S1]
What the exhibition claims

The program says that long before biobased building became a current topic, a group of architects, designers and researchers in Eindhoven explored how buildings could be healthier for people and the environment, linking natural materials, a healthy indoor climate, ecological responsibility and human scale. It names Professor Peter Schmid as central, with his teaching and research as fertile ground for VIBA, founded in 1976, and it names De Kleine Aarde, De 12 Ambachten, later Stichting Mens & Architectuur, programs at TU Delft and Wageningen University and Sustainable Building Demonstration Projects. [S1] The organizers named are Barbara Wojtkowska and Mieke Weterings, with building biology consultants and biobased-material companies. [S1]

It says the architects around Schmid experimented with materials mainstream construction had lost sight of, such as clay and straw, agricultural residues and fast-growing plants such as miscanthus, even in India. In its words, what seemed experimental is now returning as biobased building, it took almost fifty years for these ideas to begin flourishing on a wider scale, and today they are no longer marginal. [S1] Those are the exhibition's statements. The rest of this essay checks them against records.
What the dated record shows

VIBA is the Vereniging Integrale Bio-Logische Architectuur. Its own chronology, written by Frank van Empel for the years 1966 to 2003, gives dates. In 1966 a study association with a similar name, IBA, was founded in Vienna, and the chronology names Schmid as its initiator. In 1972 Schmid became a full professor of finishing technology at the Eindhoven university, then still called the Technische Hogeschool, and he gave his inaugural lecture on October 10, 1975. VIBA's official founding date is December 15, 1976. [S3]

The early years were activist and educational. In 1977 the cooperatives BABC (a building cooperative, now a recognized contractor) and IBAC (an architects' office) were founded, an international congress ran in Eindhoven and the first traveling exhibition on corrugated cardboard panels toured the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and France. In 1982 Schmid's book Bio-logische Architektur appeared from a German publisher, and in 1983 a workshop began building an experimental loam house. [S3] The chronology also records a "very quiet period" before VIBA was re-founded on October 24, 1987. [S3]

Then the record shows official attention. A 1990 book by Michiel Haas and Schmid carried a preface by Ed Nijpels, a former minister of housing and the environment. In 1991 the VIBA Center opened in 's-Hertogenbosch as a national information center, with a committee to assess materials and products before admitting them to its permanent exhibition. A 1992 design competition drew 93 participants, and Minister Alders presented the prizes on February 3, 1993. A VIBA pavilion at a building fair in 1993, opened by Prince Constantijn, drew more than 100,000 visitors, and a model for an office building of the future was commissioned by the Rijksgebouwendienst, the state buildings agency. On April 6, 1994 Minister Andriessen of Economic Affairs, as the chronology has it, opened VIBA Expo, which showed building materials across 1,500 square meters, and the chronology quotes him giving VIBA a ten out of ten. [S3]

After that the chronology records strain and change. Schmid stepped down from the board in 1996. In 1997 both the association and the foundation ended the year in the red. A second international straw-building symposium took place at VIBA Expo on June 28, 1999, to investigate whether straw could be widely applied in construction, and the auditorium was named for Schmid in 2000, the year of his retirement. [S3]
What this means for the word "new"

Read against that, the exhibition's claim of near-forgotten pioneers needs a refinement. The ideas were not unknown. They had a university chair, a national exposition center, ministerial openings and 100,000 visitors to a pavilion. What the sources show disappearing is continuity: a very quiet period in the 1980s, financial difficulty in the 1990s and no mainstream adoption. I did not find an explanation of why. The chronology ends in 2003, and the exhibition says only that the ideas took almost fifty years to flourish more widely. [S1][S3]

The record also shows that the vocabulary changed. VIBA's chronology explains "bio-logical" as a combination of the Greek words for nature or life and for human reason, meaning everything in accordance with human life, and its 1976 statutes aim for architecture that brings people into harmony with themselves, others, nature and the cosmos. [S3] The 2020s language is about carbon and materials accounting. The national building-environment database explained in 2021 that under the European standard behind the Dutch method, carbon taken up by biomass such as wood is counted in a separate biogenic category, and that the effect of temporary carbon storage is not credited, because the uptake is offset by emissions later in the life cycle, so the balance over the product's life is zero. [S8] The metric by which a straw or wood wall is judged today is not the one in VIBA's statutes. That is a real change in what "better" means, and a new material story that forgets it will compare things measured in different units.
What the numbers say about "no longer marginal"

The Dutch government's National Approach to Biobased Building was announced on November 8, 2023, with 200 million euros: 25 million to set up a market until 2025 and 175 million reserved for 2025 to 2030. Its ambition is that by 2030 at least 30 percent of new homes contain at least 30 percent biobased materials, with the same percentage for insulation measures and for utility building. It aims to grow fiber-crop cultivation for building from about 2,000 to 50,000 hectares and processing capacity to at least 400,000 tons of fiber a year. [S5] Minister Hugo de Jonge said in the announcement that experience shows a market does not arise by itself. [S5]

The July 15, 2026 monitor of that approach gives the current position. In 2024, 0 percent of new homes were built with at least 30 percent biobased mass including the foundation, and in 2025 it was 1 percent. Apartments did better: more than 5 percent in 2025 excluding the foundation, up from 2 percent, which the monitor attributes to industrial builders moving from timber terraced houses to timber apartments. In renovation, the share of private owners choosing biobased insulation rose from almost 8 percent in 2024 to more than 11 percent in 2025. Many biobased materials are still produced abroad, and the national approach is being evaluated and updated in 2026. [S6]

So the exhibition's phrase "no longer marginal" has a measurable counterpart, and the measure is mixed. Renovation insulation and timber apartments are moving. New homes with a substantial biobased share are at about 1 percent. [S6]
The rules changed too

The rules around the material shifted in the same weeks as the exhibition. The state enterprise agency RVO says that from July 1, 2026 the environmental-performance requirements for new buildings change. The calculation uses 19 impact categories instead of 11. The requirement for homes is 1.6 under the new method, offices are tightened by 15 percent to 1.55 and requirements apply for the first time to schools, shops, health-care buildings and industrial halls. [S7] The same page also still states, in an earlier paragraph, a limit of 0.8 for homes and 1.0 for offices, which looks like text from before the change, and I could not reconcile the two from the page alone. [S7] The 2023 national approach says the demand for biobased insulation is to be stimulated by tightening this requirement with heavier steering on carbon. [S5]

A fair comparison between a 1980s straw or loam wall and a 2026 biobased panel therefore needs more than a date. It needs the question each was built to answer, the metric used to judge it and the rule it had to meet. [S3][S7][S8]
What the record does not show
Which drawings, projects and material samples the exhibition shows, and which of its claims about specific buildings can be checked. [S1]
Why the movement lost momentum after the 1990s, which the sources do not explain. [S1][S3]
How many buildings VIBA's members built, and how they have performed. [S3]
The current legal state of the environmental-performance limits for homes: the RVO page gives both 0.8 and 1.6. [S7]
Whether the 2026 evaluation of the national approach changes the targets. [S6]

The question in the title is practical. When a material is called new, ask which of five things changed: its composition, its production, its use, its measurement or its rules. A story that names the one that changed has already remembered the rest. [S1][S3]

title: Who represents a river in a proposal?
subtitle: Het Parlement der Dingen at Dutch Design Week 2026 asks participants to speak for museum objects. Rivers in New Zealand and India, Dutch water boards and a mock court for the North Sea show what happens when someone has to speak for something that cannot.
description: A Parliament of Things workshop at Dutch Design Week 2026, read against the Whanganui and Ganges rulings, Dutch water boards and a North Sea mock court.

sections.x: When a river gets a legal voice, someone has to be named to use it. In New Zealand the guardian of the Whanganui River is two people, one appointed by the Crown and one by the Whanganui tribe, who must act as one. [S3]

Het Parlement der Dingen (The Parliament of Things) is a workshop in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, on October 23, 2026 from 16:00 to 19:00. It is hosted by Gerard Rooijakkers and Kees Streng, spoken in Dutch, and needs a DDW ticket. [S1] The program describes a masterclass set in an artistic installation of a parliament in the museum's basement. Visitors select an item from a display of museum objects and take part as its spokesperson, with spectators welcome in the public gallery. Rooijakkers acts as arbitrator, and after an exploratory round of proposals the objects engage in dialogue with one another. [S1] The river in this essay is my comparison. The workshop description does not mention one. [S1]

This essay uses public documents only: the program page, an abstract by Bruno Latour, a 2018 comparative study of river rights, the Dutch Water Boards Act and a Dutch Design Awards entry. It reports no attendance and no interview, and it takes no position on the workshop's quality. [S1]
What the workshop says it is built on

The program says the idea is developed from Bruno Latour's Parliament of Things, in which non-human actors are given a voice articulated by human spokespersons who explore the "perplexity" of a specific thing. [S1] Its starting point is the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of the Valkenswaard region, which it names as falconry and the "corso" tradition, and it says the colonial world of tobacco will be explored, from the perspective of the things themselves. It adds that controversial heritage such as slavery and the erosion of biodiversity are addressed. [S1] A meet-and-greet with a delegation from the Dutch UNESCO Commission follows from 18:00 to 19:00 at the Van Abbe Café. [S1]

Latour's own abstract describes a shift in attention from opinions and positions to things, or "issues," and the assemblies in which they are shaped and decided. [S2] It offers a way to compare those assemblies with the traditional vocabulary of politics. It does not provide a legal procedure. [S2]
What happens when a real river gets a representative

Law has tried this, and the experience is documented. A 2018 article in Ecology and Society compared three cases: Victoria in Australia, the Whanganui River in New Zealand and the Ganges and Yamuna in India. [S3] Its summary is that legal rights have been granted to a river system with specific guardians appointed to act on its behalf. [S3]

In New Zealand, the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act of March 2017 followed eight years of negotiation between the Whanganui tribe and the Crown, after a dispute over the river that the article dates to 1873. It treats the river and its catchment as a legal entity with the rights, powers, duties and liabilities of a person, able to sue and be sued. [S3] The guardian, Te Pou Tupua, is two people, one appointed by each party, who must act as one and speak for the river's health and well-being. [S3] Around that guardian the Act builds an advisory group and a strategy group of up to 17 representatives, including tribes, central and local government, tourism, conservation, recreation and the operator of a power scheme that diverts 82 percent of the river's headwaters, and the Crown pays a 30 million New Zealand dollar contestable fund toward making the rights effective. [S3] The river's voice, in other words, is a negotiated structure with a budget.

In India, on March 20, 2017, the High Court of Uttarakhand declared the Ganges and Yamuna rivers legal persons and treated them as minors, naming three state officials to act on their behalf: the director of the national Ganga mission, the state's chief secretary and its advocate general. [S3] On July 7, 2017 the Supreme Court of India agreed to hear the state's appeal, which argued that its guardianship duties were unclear because the rivers extend beyond the state, and in doing so halted the effect of the ruling. [S3] The authors note the guardians were government officials, which could create conflicts of interest, and were given no extra funding. [S3] The article dates from 2018, and I did not find a later account of the rivers' status, so the stay is the last point I can document. [S3]
The comparison supports a plain point. Naming a representative is the beginning. Who appoints her, whom she answers to, what she can ask for and who pays decide whether the voice carries. [S3]
The Dutch version is older and less poetic

Dutch water governance already answers the representation question with human interests. Under the Water Boards Act, valid from January 1, 2026, the general board of a water board is composed of representatives of categories of interested parties: residents, those with the use of unbuilt property that is not nature terrain, and those with the use of nature terrain. The board has between 18 and 30 members, and the two non-resident categories have two representatives each, appointed by organizations designated in the board's regulations. [S4] The law does not give the water a seat. It gives seats to people and organizations with stakes in how the water is managed. That is an important Dutch fact for the exercise, because it shows that even a mature system of water representation speaks for interests and not for the river itself.

A Dutch design project has tested a different idea. The Embassy of the North Sea, a 2023 nominee for the Dutch Design Awards in Design Research, staged a mock court in the Peace Palace in The Hague as the final step of its 2018 to 2022 establishment. According to the awards entry, human and non-human witnesses were called and spoke on behalf of facets of the North Sea, and the experiment investigated how non-human voices could be heard in a courtroom. [S5] The Embassy's stated mission is to give nature a position in culture, politics and the legal system, and the awards panel called the sea an entity whose ownership and control are unclear. [S5] A mock court is a rehearsal. The entry does not describe any legal effect. [S5]
What a spokesperson needs to show

Put those cases beside the workshop's format and a set of questions follows. Which observation is the spokesperson speaking from? Who can challenge her interpretation? Who is the proposal addressed to, and can that person say yes? In the real cases the answers are written down: a statute names the guardian and funds the work, or a court names officials and the appeal shows where the arrangement was weak. [S3] The workshop is an experiment in attention, and the program describes it as such, with exploration, dialogue and an arbitrator. [S1] I think it deserves to be judged as that. An account of it that claimed a legal consequence would need a different kind of evidence.

For a reader who wants to carry the exercise away, the useful move is to separate three records: what the spokesperson observed, how she interpreted the interest and what she asked someone to do. A river, an object and a species all need that traceable step if the voice is to survive the room. [S3]
What the record does not show
What the participants decide in the workshop, and what is recorded. The program describes a format, not an outcome. [S1]
Whether any output of the workshop goes to a real decision-maker. [S1]
The present legal status of the Ganges and Yamuna rulings, beyond the 2017 stay and a 2018 article. [S3]
Any legal effect of the North Sea mock court. [S5]
How the Dutch UNESCO Commission meet-and-greet connects to the workshop beyond the program's mention. [S1]
The question the title asks is useful because it has no tidy answer. In each case above, someone wrote down who could speak, and the rest of the arrangement followed from that line. [S3][S4]

title: Who has to stand while the bus is late?
subtitle: Luca Ortmann's Waiting for the Bus puts steel-tube furniture at a temporary stop in Eindhoven. Research on perceived waiting, English seating guidance and Dutch accessibility agreements show what a stop has to offer before a seat counts.
description: Waiting for the Bus at Dutch Design Week 2026, read against Minnesota research on perceived waits, English seating guidance and Dutch accessibility agreements.

sections.x: In a study of 36 stops and stations in the Minneapolis and St. Paul area, the biggest difference in how long a wait felt was between any shelter and none at all. [S4] A bench was only one of the variables the researchers modeled. That finding is where I start when I look at a project about waiting.

Luca Ortmann's Waiting for the Bus is in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program at Demer in Eindhoven's center, free to visit. It presents steel-tube objects at a temporary replacement bus stop. According to the program, each object interprets an element of the city where people naturally pause: a bicycle rack becomes a seat, railings invite leaning and shopfront ledges become places to sit. The objects are bolted to aluminum base plates, can be rearranged to suit the surroundings and carry light elements. [S1] The program says the goal is to make waiting visible and valued, and to turn waiting into a positive and desirable action. [S1] Those are the designer's claims. This essay uses public documents only: the 2026 and 2025 program pages, a Minnesota study, English seating guidance, a Dutch accessibility agreement and a report from the Dutch human rights institute. It reports no visit, no measurement and no interview. [S1][S2]
What the program says, and what it leaves out

The program describes waiting as a fundamental experience of urban life, often associated with boredom and frustration, and says that places where waiting happens rarely offer more than basic functionality. [S1] It says the steel tubes create a playful and familiar space in an otherwise stressful urban setting, and that adding light elements places familiar forms in a new context. [S1]

The 2025 Dutch Design Week listing for the same project was at Area 51 on Strijp-S and was hosted by the German Design Council. It described three objects that extend the bus stop sign and create space for sitting, resting and social interaction. [S2] The 2026 listing names different elements, bicycle racks, railings and ledges, and does not mention the sign. [S1][S2] I cannot tell whether the objects changed between years or only the description did.

Neither listing says anything about weather protection, schedule or arrival information, seat height, back or arm support, or whether the objects stay clear of the route to the bus. A design shown in an exhibition need not answer each of these, and the research below says they matter to people who wait. [S1][S2][S4]
What research says people notice while waiting

The Minnesota study, reported by the University of Minnesota's Center for Transportation Studies in January 2015, surveyed more than 880 riders at 36 stops. A recruiter asked just-boarded passengers to estimate the time they had spent waiting, and a videographer recorded the actual time. [S4] Perceived and actual waits were related but the relationship varied. Even waits under a minute tended to feel like a minute or two. The presence of a shelter, even a simple one, made waits seem shorter, especially under 10 minutes. A real-time information sign also shortened perceived waits. Posted schedules had a mixed pattern: for short waits they led people to overestimate the wait, and after about 10 minutes they led people to underestimate it. The study found no significant effect of gender alone, but women at stops rated less safe perceived longer waits. [S4]

This is American research on perceived time, and the page I read does not report what benches did. It cannot tell us how a lean rail feels after 20 minutes in Eindhoven. It does suggest that the first things to check about a waiting place are shelter, information and safety. [S4]
What seating guidance says

Active Travel England's guidance on benches and resting points, written for walking, wheeling and cycling routes in England, lists informal arrangements as typically useful for short periods, alongside seating with back and arm rests and styles with a range of heights. It says resting points should ideally be less than 50 meters apart, should not obstruct walking, wheeling and cycling routes and must not form a hazard to disabled people. It adds that seats should contrast in color and tone with their surroundings, be vandal-resistant and easy to clean, and should not collect rainwater, and that seating should be provided at bus stops and shelters where possible. [S3] It describes benches as particularly important for older people and people with mobility issues. [S3]

That is British guidance used as a comparison. It certifies nothing about Ortmann's work and sets no Dutch rule. It does give a useful reading of the program's description. A rail or ledge to lean on is an informal arrangement, suited to short waits, and the guidance treats it as one option among several. [S3]
What Dutch agreements say about a stop

A stop in the Netherlands carries accessibility commitments. The Netherlands is bound by the UN convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, and the Bestuursakkoord Toegankelijkheid Openbaar Vervoer 2022 to 2032, signed by the state, the provinces, transport authorities and operators, aims for fully accessible public transport in 2040 in line with the convention. [S5] Its article 9 says the state will try to put clear minimum requirements for new or renewed stops into regulation, and that bus-stop standards for road managers are to be based on characteristics set by the regional transport authorities in 2020. It says the standards would not in principle apply retroactively to stops that are not accessible. The agreement adds that after the state's 2006 to 2015 stimulus period all new bus stops have been delivered accessible. [S5]

The Dutch human rights institute's 2023 report on the convention gives the state of play. It says that at the end of 2022 more than 90 percent of railway stations were accessible, while for bus stops the figures were lower: 21 percent were accessible for people with a visual impairment and 38 percent for people with a motor impairment, citing a national government overview. It also says that requirements for new, renewed and improved stops, vehicles and stations apply immediately. [S6]

Whether a temporary replacement stop counts as new or renewed is something I could not find answered in these documents. A temporary stop exists for weeks or months, and a person with a wheelchair or a cane uses it on the same days as everyone else. The question is who inspects it and against what standard, and the program says nothing about that. [S5][S6]
A posture has a duration

The question in the title stands, and the evidence sharpens it. A lean is one posture and the wait is an interval. A short wait under a shelter is a different experience from a long wait on a rail without one, and the research above says the difference is large. [S4] The English guidance would treat the lean as a short-stay option. [S3] The Dutch agreements put the bar for the stop itself at who can reach it and use it. [S5][S6]

So a fair way to read Waiting for the Bus is as a proposal about atmosphere and identity for a stop, set beside questions about shelter, information, safety and access that other documents answer in other ways. Its stated aim of making waiting valued does not conflict with them. Its listing just does not say how it meets them. [S1][S3][S4][S5]
What the record does not show
Which stop the objects stand at, why the stop is temporary and how long it will be in use. The listing gives only the street. [S1]
Seat heights, supports, spacing from the route and lighting levels. [S1]
Whether the objects were used by waiting passengers and for how long. [S1][S2]
Whether the project's stop counts as a new or renewed stop under Dutch accessibility rules. [S5][S6]
How Eindhoven or the bus operator informs passengers at the stop. [S1]
Any Dutch study of how waiting feels at stops like this one. The Minnesota study is American. [S4]
The question I would carry to the stop is plain. If the bus is late by twenty minutes, who can stay comfortably, who cannot, and how would anyone know? [S4][S6]

title: Biodegradable where, exactly?
subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week exhibits use plastics made by bacteria. The standards, a sea study, Eindhoven's bin rules and a new consumer law all say the word needs a setting, a period and a test.
description: Two DDW 2026 exhibits use bacteria-made plastic. What standards, a sea study, Eindhoven bin rules and a new law say about the word.

sections.x: “Biodegradable” makes me ask for a place. Soil? A home composter? An industrial plant? The sea? The word sounds finished until I try to imagine holding one object and deciding what to do with it. [S7]

Two Dutch Design Week exhibits give the question a face. Mozi Studio’s Zero Waste Lab shows stools, side tables and lamps made from PHA and PHB, polymers that bacteria make, and its program page calls them fully biodegradable and compostable. Shijia Huang’s Written in Decay is a book made from a bacteria-derived bioplastic, with pages that are placed in soil and left to decay. Both are free, both run October 17 to 25, 2026, and I have not seen either. This essay reports no visit, no interview and no test. It reads the makers’ own pages, the standards and studies that give the word its meaning, the rules in force in Eindhoven and a consumer law that started applying in the Netherlands on September 27, 2026. [S1][S2][S16]
Two exhibits made from the same family of material

The Zero Waste Lab is at Strijp T+R, building A3, inside Piet Hein Eek on Halvemaanstraat 30, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00. The program page credits the design to Ziemowit Liszek and Monika Gradzik, lists a scientific consultant, and describes a collection of stools and side tables made from sheets produced on Precious Plastics-type machines adapted for biopolymers, a series of 3D-printed lamps, and aluminum elements sourced from local scrapyards and cast in-house. It says every object is made on site in Gdynia, Poland. [S1]

Written in Decay is at Strijp T+R, building A1, in the BioArt Laboratories space at Oirschotsedijk 14-10, also daily from 11:00 to 18:00. Its page says the book is made from Vivomer, a bioplastic developed by Shellworks, and that its pages are placed in soils collected from different environments across London and exposed to microorganisms, moisture and time. Huang is described as an artist and biodesigner based in London. [S2]

The materials share a source. PHAs, the family that includes PHB, are polymers some bacteria make and store inside their cells as an energy reserve. Mozi’s page says so, and Shellworks says Vivomer is made of proprietary formulations of PHA. [S1][S3][S5] The two exhibits ask different things of the material. The furniture is offered as a viable, scalable alternative to conventional plastics in furniture production. The book is an artwork about life, matter and decay. [S1][S2] I will keep those purposes apart, because a claim that suits a product page does not automatically suit a gallery label, and the reverse is also true.
What the furniture claim rests on

The program page says PHA and PHB are fully biodegradable and compostable, and that they return to soil, water and compost once a product’s life cycle is complete. [S1] Mozi’s own page about the collection, dated Gdynia 2025, is more cautious about the stage of the work. It calls the collection a prototype series, describes the material as the studio’s blend of PHA and PHB, says research and development continue with designers, technologists and biochemists, and notes that the project was co-funded by Poland’s Ministry of Culture and National Heritage. The same page says the materials break down in water, soil and compost, and even in seawater, without leaving microplastics. [S3]

A Polish design magazine, whiteMAD, covered the premiere on November 18, 2025 and credits Mozi as its source. It adds that the studio used PHB granules to make solid semi-finished boards with Precious Plastics technology, that the premiere took place at the tuBaza space in Gdynia, and that work on the material is ongoing. Ziemowit Liszek is quoted saying the team chose the polymers because they are “free of marketing myths.” [S4]

I read all three pages looking for a test report, a certificate or a named laboratory for the finished furniture, and none of them names one. [S1][S3][S4] That does not mean none exists. It means the public record I could reach states the conclusion and not the evidence. The pages also differ in small ways. The program page says PHA and PHB, Mozi’s page says a blend of the two, and the magazine says PHB granules. Because PHB is a member of the PHA family, those descriptions can all be true together. What none of them says is which grade of polymer, which additives and which pigments went into the boards. [S1][S3][S4]
One word covers several different tests

The European Environment Agency’s 2020 briefing on biodegradable and compostable plastics is the plainest statement I found of why the setting matters. It says whether and how fast a plastic item biodegrades depends on whether it was designed for biodegradation or composting and on the conditions it meets afterward and for how long. It says conditions in home composters and in the open environment differ greatly from those in industrial composting plants, which changes the rate and extent of breakdown. And it says any claim of compostability or biodegradability should be precise and tied to the conditions under which it holds. The briefing also reports a German survey in which 58 percent of respondents thought all “bioplastics” were compostable, and it notes that evidence for or against the fear that such labels encourage littering is scarce. [S7]

Each setting has its own measuring stick. The international standard for compostable plastics, ISO 17088:2021, assesses four things: disintegration during composting, ultimate aerobic biodegradation, absence of adverse effects of the compost on terrestrial organisms, and control of constituents. Its published scope says these suit the conditions of industrial composting, that it gives no requirements for plastics that end up in the environment as litter, and that it does not apply to biological treatment in small installations run by householders. [S9] A Dutch waste-sector factsheet from March 2018 describes the related European packaging standard, EN 13432, as requiring that at least 90 percent of the material has fallen apart within 12 weeks in an industrial composting installation. [S14]

Home composting has a separate scheme. TÜV Austria’s OK compost HOME specification covers raw materials, intermediate products and finished products. It states that it considers only home compostability and passes no judgment on biodegradation in soil or water, and that a certified product may not use the mark to claim degradation in soil or water. A different certification would be needed for that. [S10] Shellworks says Vivomer carries the TÜV Austria home-compostable certification. [S5] I could not find a certificate for Mozi’s boards.

The Commission’s own summary shows how thin the legal ground is. Its page says there is no EU law applying comprehensively to bio-based, biodegradable and compostable plastics, that the policy framework adopted on November 30, 2022 (COM(2022) 682) is not legally binding, that a harmonized European standard exists for industrially compostable packaging and another for soil-biodegradable mulch films, and that there is no general standard for marine biodegradation. [S8] So “fully biodegradable” could be tested against several different standards, or against none that was written for a stool.
The same polymer, a very different sea

A field study makes the point with numbers. In 2021, Christian Lott and colleagues published half-lives for polyhydroxybutyrate film in the sea, from laboratory tests, climate-chamber tanks and field sites in the Mediterranean and Southeast Asia. For an 85-micrometer film of PHB, the modeled half-life ranged from 54 days on the seafloor in Southeast Asia to 1,247 days in the open-water tank test. In the laboratory tests the same film took a modeled 116 days to reach half-life on the seafloor and 222 days buried in beach sand; in the tanks the figures were 357 days on the seafloor, 737 on the beach and 1,247 in open water. Polyethylene showed no biodegradation at all. The authors concluded that results differed by orders of magnitude with climate, habitat and material, which made it imprecise to call any material “marine biodegradable” without qualification. [S11]

This does not describe Mozi’s boards. The study used a commercial PHB compound that the authors identified by infrared spectroscopy, in thin films. The Zero Waste Lab pieces are solid sheets and printed lamps of a material whose grade is not published. [S1][S11] What the study offers is a measure of how much a sentence like “breaks down in seawater” leaves out. Thickness, form and habitat each change the answer, and Shellworks says the same of its own material, noting that timing depends on factors including thickness, temperature, moisture and microbial activity. [S5][S11]

The European Commission’s scientific advisers reached a related conclusion in December 2020. The expert review behind their advice found that biodegradable plastic has a role in reducing the accumulation of plastics in the environment, but a limited one, and that calling something biodegradable does not mean it will biodegrade in every condition. The advisers recommended limiting open-environment uses to applications where reduction, reuse and recycling are not feasible, and supporting coherent testing and certification standards. [S12]
A stool has more than one part, and Eindhoven has bins

The Zero Waste Lab collection pairs polymer with aluminum cast from scrapyard material. [S1] That sets up a question the listing does not answer: whether the two can be separated, and who would do it. TÜV Austria’s home-compostability specification treats a finished product made of different components through a separate document that I could not open, and it asks applicants for the full composition including additives and colorants and the maximum thickness. [S10] The questions a certifier asks are the questions a buyer would ask.

Then comes the bin. The EEA notes that correct disposal of compostable plastics depends on the local waste system and treatment infrastructure. [S7] In Eindhoven, the collector Cure publishes what goes in the green GFT/E container. Compostable bags carrying the seedling logo are allowed. Compostable packaging without that logo is not, and its list of items that do not belong in the container includes bioplastic pots. [S13] The seedling logo is the mark for EN 13432. [S14] The Dutch waste association explained in 2018 why the sector advised against putting biodegradable packaging in the organics stream at all: much of what is collected is sieved out of the compost and ends up with residual waste that is burned for energy. It names PHAs among the materials in that group. [S14]

Those rules concern household organics, bags and packaging. They do not tell anyone what to do with a PHA stool, and I found no rule that does. The lesson I take from them is narrower. “Compostable” is a statement about a test, and a bin instruction is a different statement about a local system. Between the two sits a person with a broken lamp. [S7][S13]
What a damaged page can show

Written in Decay asks for a different kind of attention. The exhibition page frames the marks left by decay as inscription, and the work as a way to follow relationships between life, matter and microorganisms. [S2] I take that on its own terms. A page that has been in soil changes, and the change is worth seeing.

Shellworks’ description of its material helps explain how a book can be held at a chosen stage. Its FAQ says Vivomer is stable on a shelf and in the shower, and breaks down only where microorganisms are active, such as soil or home compost. It also says that if the material is removed from those conditions mid-breakdown, it stops breaking down and stays stable until it is returned, and that this is how the company photographs the middle of the process. [S5] That is the company’s account of its material. The exhibition page does not say how Huang’s pages were handled, for how long they were exposed, which soils were used or whether anything was measured. [S2]

Appearance and measurement are two different kinds of evidence. The EEA describes biodegradation as breakdown by microorganisms into water, carbon dioxide, mineral salts and new biomass. [S7] A stain, a hole or a change of texture on a page shows that something happened. It does not show how much of the polymer has been converted, or how fast. Shellworks itself separates the two. It says Vivomer is certified home compostable, breaks down at a rate similar to cellulose, and takes months and not decades in active home compost, and it declines to give blanket timelines for the ocean. [S5] An artwork does not owe anyone a laboratory curve. A product claim does.

As an anatomist, I am used to thinking of decay as something people work hard to slow down, so a project that makes it the subject has my attention. That is a reaction to the idea and a judgment on nothing about the material. [S2][S7]
The word now carries weight in Dutch law

Directive (EU) 2024/825, adopted on February 28, 2024, amends the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive to prohibit generic environmental claims when a trader cannot show recognized excellent environmental performance. Its recitals list “biodegradable” and “biobased” among the examples, next to “eco-friendly” and “green.” A claim does not count as generic when its specification appears in clear and prominent terms on the same medium, such as the packaging or the online selling page. The recitals add that “biodegradable” could not rest on an EU Ecolabel unless the label’s criteria for that product include biodegradability. Member states were to apply the measures from September 27, 2026. [S15]

The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets announced on September 24, 2026 that the Dutch implementing act would take effect on September 27, and called on businesses to check their sustainability claims. It said terms such as “green” can be used only with a clear explanation or when they meet strict European or national standards, and that sustainability labels need independent checks. [S16] The government’s business portal says stricter rules have applied since that date and that supervisors can enforce them, and that sustainability claims must be backed by verifiable evidence. [S17]

I am describing texts here and offering no view on how they apply to either exhibit. The two program pages I read describe free exhibitions and quote no prices, and none of the sources says how a festival listing is treated. [S1][S2][S15] What the directive does say, for anyone selling an object described as biodegradable, is that the rest of the sentence belongs on the same page as the word.
What the record does not show
I have not seen either exhibit and do not know what the labels beside the objects will say. [S1][S2]

No source I found gives test results for the Zero Waste Lab furniture. I do not know the polymer grade, the additives, the pigments or the thickness of the boards, whether the aluminum can be separated, or what the studio recommends an owner do at the end of use. Mozi’s page calls the collection a prototype series while the program page speaks of a scalable alternative. [S1][S3][S4] The program page credits a scientific consultant, and no page I read says what testing, if any, that role involved.

For Written in Decay, I do not know the exposure period, the soils, the number of pages or whether decay was measured. I do not know whether the home-compostable certificate Shellworks cites covers a bound book, its binding or any inks. [S2][S5]

I could not open the ISO website, which refused automated requests, so the scope of ISO 17088:2021 comes from the Swedish standards institute’s listing of the identical text. [S9] I read the TÜV Austria specification dated 2012, edition D, and not any newer edition. [S10] Cure’s page is undated, and the Dutch waste factsheet is from 2018, so both may have changed. [S13][S14] For the new consumer rules, I read the directive, the consumer authority’s announcement and the business portal, and not the Dutch Official Gazette text of the implementing act. [S15][S16][S17]

If you meet a biodegradable object at Dutch Design Week, try asking four questions in this order. Where is it meant to go, how long should it take there, what exactly was tested, and which bin in your own street will take it? Which of the four can the label answer? [S7]

title: The screw is visible. Is the replacement part available?
subtitle: Fairphone's Gen. 6+ is in the Dutch Design Week program as a phone you can open. The published record shows what an owner can order, what it costs, what the law requires and where the promises end.
description: Fairphone Gen. 6+ at Dutch Design Week: the part, price, tools and support dates behind one imaginary repair, and the EU rules around them.

sections.x: The screw is visible. The rest of the repair takes a little more looking. [S1][S3]

I like seeing a product that can be opened. It gives my curiosity somewhere to go. What it cannot tell me is what comes after the cover comes off: which part I would order, what it costs, how fast it arrives, and for how many years someone has promised to keep making it. Those answers sit in public documents, and this essay follows one imaginary fault through them. It reports no repair test and no interview, and I have not seen the exhibit. [S1]
What the program page promises

Fairphone appears in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program as “ID Hub - The smartphone. Reimagined.” It is part of Design meets Industry, at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S (building B4), open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 between October 17 and 25, 2026, and it asks for a DDW ticket. The page says the Fairphone (Gen. 6+) is designed to stay, with screws over glue, replaceable modules and recycled materials, under the line “Yours to open. Yours to keep.” [S1]

The Gen. 6+ is new. Fairphone launched it on August 18, 2026, a little over a year after the Gen. 6 launched on June 25, 2025. [S5][S7] The company’s product page says the two models differ in processor, memory, colors and price (Gen. 6+ with a Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and 12 GB of RAM at 649 euros, Gen. 6 with a Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 and 8 GB at 599 euros) and that everything else on the page is identical on both. [S2] That sentence matters for this essay, because it lets the repair and support terms on the Gen. 6 pages stand for the Gen. 6+ as well, on Fairphone’s own word.
One fault, followed through

Imagine a phone whose charging connection has stopped working. The situation is hypothetical. Fairphone’s repair page tells an owner to diagnose the problem first and says some repairs are covered by warranty. It then offers two routes. One is to send the phone to a repair center. The other is to do it yourself with the relevant spare part, a Phillips 00 or Torx T5 screwdriver and the right guide. [S3]

The page lists guides for the Gen. 6, including one for the loudspeaker and USB-C port with an estimated time of 10 to 15 minutes. It lists no separate entry for the Gen. 6+. [S3] The part itself is sold on Fairphone’s webshop for 19.95 euros. Its page says it is compatible with the Gen. 6 and Gen. 6+ and incompatible with any other device, describes the job as five minutes with a Torx T5 screwdriver, and gives the part a two-year warranty. [S4] On the company’s comparison table, 19.95 euros sits beside an “industry average” of about 120 euros for the same part. Fairphone says that average is an estimate drawn from official repair quotes from three flagship brands in July 2025, so it is the company’s figure and not an independent price survey. [S2]

iFixit, the repair-guide company, took the Gen. 6 apart in 2025 and found the USB-C port under the speaker assembly, a module that can be swapped alone. It said two T5 screws release the back cover, that the battery is held by four screws and one flex cable, and that the display is secured by eight screws. It gave the phone 10 out of 10 for repairability. [S8] Fairphone’s own page says the USB-C port, battery, display and back cover can each be swapped in under five minutes. [S2]

The page also prices the other parts in the table. The battery is 39.95 euros, the display 89.95, the main camera 69.95, the ultra-wide camera 44.95, the selfie camera 34.95, the top unit 39.95, the earpiece 19.95, the top back cover 9.95, the bottom back cover 14.95 and the SIM tray 7.95. [S2] That is eleven priced items against a text that speaks of twelve replaceable parts, and Fairphone’s story about the Gen. 6 names a loudspeaker as well, so I cannot say which twelve the company counts or what the twelfth costs. [S2][S14]

Time is the other number worth reading carefully. The repairs page gives 5 to 10 minutes for a battery, 10 to 15 for a display and 10 to 15 for the loudspeaker and USB-C port. [S3] iFixit reports that Fairphone’s real-time video of a battery change runs almost exactly two minutes from shut-down to reboot, and that its own team reassembled the phone four more times after the first. [S8] Those are favorable conditions: a clean table, the right screwdriver, and people who open phones for a living. The estimates describe the work and leave out the diagnosis, the wait for the part and the afternoon without a phone.

One count does not match. Fairphone’s launch release for the Gen. 6 says the battery can be replaced with just seven screws, while iFixit describes two T5 screws on the back cover and four on the battery. [S7][S8] They may be counting different things, and I have not opened one to check.
Where the owner stops

The Fairphone page counts 12 user-replaceable parts and names three parts, the microphones, the side buttons and the fingerprint sensor, that a repair center services. [S2] iFixit adds that Fairphone does not treat the mainboard as user-serviceable, and that warning labels mark it as a trickier repair. [S8] Two details in that teardown help show where the limits sit. The battery is glued to a thin metal strip, and the contact pads under the power button are glued down, which iFixit called a fiddly but small compromise. [S8]

The trade-off for a glue-free body is water protection. The Gen. 6 carries an IP55 rating, which iFixit contrasted with the IP68 of two flagship phones, adding that glue-free designs with higher ratings exist. [S8] I raise it because a repair story that mentions only the strengths is a catalog. An owner deciding between a sealed phone and an openable one is choosing between two sets of risks, and both belong in the account.

iFixit also reports a figure Fairphone commissioned from the Fraunhofer Institute: how many extra days of use it takes for a spare part to pay back the emissions of making it. Cameras and speakers pay back in 18 days, a display in 33 and a battery in 55, while a mainboard from the Gen. 4 took 719. [S8] That is a company-commissioned estimate relayed by a repair company, and I treat it as a reason Fairphone prioritizes some parts over others.
What European rules now require of every phone

Fairphone’s repair story sits on top of a legal floor that did not exist five years ago. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1670 sets ecodesign requirements for smartphones and has applied since June 20, 2025. For smartphones, it requires manufacturers to supply the battery, back cover, display assembly, charger and SIM tray to professional repairers and end users for at least seven years after the end of placing the model on the market. It requires the external charging port, cameras, buttons, microphones and speakers to be available to professional repairers over the same period. [S9]

The Regulation also sets delivery times (five working days during the first five years of that period and ten working days during the last two), requires indicative pre-tax prices for these parts to be published, requires repair information, and requires at least five years of operating system updates after the end of placement on the market. It sets a battery endurance minimum of 800 cycles at 80 percent remaining capacity. [S9] Its definition of “basic tools” includes a screwdriver for hexalobular recess heads, which is the Torx type. [S9]

The companion energy label rules, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1669, add a repairability class from A to E derived from a score that weighs disassembly depth, fasteners, tools, spare parts, software updates and repair information. Class A requires a score of at least 4.00. [S10] Fairphone’s page states a repairability class A and an energy label A for the Gen. 6 models. [S2]

Compare the floor with Fairphone’s promises. The company says spare parts and software support run to 2033 for both models. [S2][S5] The regulation counts its seven years and five years from the end of placement on the market, a date I found on no Fairphone page. So I cannot tell whether 2033 is above or below the legal minimum for either phone. That depends on when sales stop. The Gen. 6+ owner also gets a shorter run than the Gen. 6 owner did on launch day: both end in 2033, and the newer phone started more than a year later. That is arithmetic on published dates and not a criticism. [S5][S7]
Note too that the Regulation obliges a manufacturer to offer the external charging port to professional repairers only. Fairphone sells it to anyone who orders it. [S4][S9]
The right to repair, and the date it started

The European Right to Repair Directive, (EU) 2024/1799, gives a consumer the right to ask the manufacturer to repair goods covered by listed repairability rules, which include the smartphone Regulation. The repair is to be free or at a reasonable price, within a reasonable time, and the manufacturer may not refuse because another repairer worked on the phone earlier or use hardware or software techniques that block repair without a legitimate reason. Spare parts and tools must be offered at a price that does not deter repair. [S11] Member states had to apply the national measures from July 31, 2026. [S11]

In the Netherlands, a bill to implement it, the Implementatiewet richtlijn bevordering van reparatie, was listed on July 9, 2026 as parliamentary paper 36996. A legal-news listing I read on October 10, 2026 shows documents up to number 5 of the 2026-27 session. I found no sign that it has been published as law. [S12] So I cannot say whether the Dutch consumer right is in force yet.

A separate rule has just begun. The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets said on September 24, 2026 that the Dutch implementation of the Empowering Consumers directive takes effect on September 27, and described its information duties toward consumers on lifespan, repairability, availability of spare parts and use of non-original components. [S13] I have not read the Dutch act itself.

The Right to Repair Directive also touches the older, quieter rule that sits behind a purchase. It amends the sale-of-goods directive so that a consumer who chooses repair within the seller’s liability period gets that period extended by 12 months. [S11] Fairphone’s five-year warranty runs well past both, and Fairphone marks it with an asterisk on its product page, so the conditions behind it are worth reading before it is relied on. [S2]
Support has a date

Fairphone describes the Gen. 6 launch as an event in Amsterdam with software support through 2033 and a five-year warranty. [S7] For the Gen. 6+, the August 2026 press release repeats the five-year warranty and updates through 2033, and says the Gen. 6+ runs Android 16 out of the box with a promise of six operating system upgrades. [S5][S6] The product page uses the words “support till 2033” and “spare parts available till 2033.” [S2] Those are the company’s published commitments, and a commitment is not a stock listing or a completed repair.

A date like that changes the question a buyer can ask. Instead of whether a phone can be repaired, you can ask whether the part will still be sold in year six, at what price, with which guide. The comparison sheet I would keep is plain: the model, the part, the route, the instructions, the support period and the date I checked. [S2][S3][S4]
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibit and do not know what it will display. [S1]

I could not open Fairphone’s support site, which refused automated requests. Three things I have seen repeated about Fairphone repairs rest on that site and are therefore not stated here as fact: that the Core Module is not sold to individuals, that parts from other models are not interchangeable (the webshop page supports the narrower point for the USB-C port), and that an owner should update the phone before replacing parts. [S4]

I found no Fairphone page that gives the date when sales of either model will end, no independent measurement of how long a delivery takes, and no teardown by iFixit of the Gen. 6+ itself. The 10 out of 10 comes from the Gen. 6 teardown, and Fairphone’s own release carries it over to the Gen. 6+. [S5][S8] I found no price history for the part or evidence on whether the part is in stock today. Fairphone’s price comparison is the company’s estimate. [S2]
I cannot confirm the status of the Dutch implementation bill beyond the listing described above. [S12]

Pick one phone you own and look for three things: the part you would most likely need, the price of that part, and the last year its maker promises to sell it. Can you find all three before the screen cracks? [S9]

title: What happens after the exhibition closes?
subtitle: Three projects in the Dutch Design Week orbit already have a public afterlife: a marble run that toured a museum, a dataset with a one-year plan, and a library with no closing date. The record also shows what the handoff takes.
description: Packet Run, Are we autonomous yet? and the Biomaterials Library: what the public record shows about what happens after a design show ends.

sections.x: An exhibition ends on a calendar, but the work it showed may not. The room closes while someone still has to answer a question, find an earlier version or decide whether a record is still accurate. [S2][S3]

Three projects in or near the Dutch Design Week 2026 program let me ask what that takes, because each has left a public trail. One is Packet Run, a marble run about how the internet routes data, which was at Dutch Design Week in 2023 and has since been in a museum. One is Are we autonomous yet?, a map of which vendors Dutch organizations depend on, which opens at Dutch Design Week 2026 with a stated plan for the following year. One is the Biomaterials Library, a physical collection of material experiments in Vilnius that brings a selection to Eindhoven. I have not seen any of the 2026 exhibits, and I interviewed nobody. What follows reads funders’ pages, the makers’ public repositories and the DDW listings, and it separates what those records say from what they leave open. [S13][S17]
Packet Run has the longest record

Packet Run is an interactive installation in which a visitor places a marble in a star-shaped track and watches it travel through stations that stand for the real hops a data packet takes to reach a website. [S3] Its public repository says it was exhibited at the 2023 Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29, 2023, and afterwards became available to festivals, conferences and cultural institutions. [S5] The Dutch Design Week archive lists it as presented by Bureau Moeilijke Dingen, created with SIDN Labs and supported by a grant from SIDN fonds. [S1] SIDN fonds said on October 30, 2023, the day after the festival closed, that the work was a collaboration between the funder, the studio and SIDN Labs, built on PathVis, a tool SIDN Labs made so that non-specialists can see the routes data packets take. [S4]

SIDN fonds, the funder, closed its first grant in February 2024 with numbers: about 50,000 visitors at Dutch Design Week 2023, and 1,419 packets for which visitors traced the route from Eindhoven to a website of their choice. The same note says the project was not finished and that its makers were seeking museums, public institutions and organizations to show it temporarily or permanently. [S2] The repository itself names no later venue, but the funder does. A second SIDN fonds grant, dated 2025, paid for adapting the installation for long-term use in museums and art institutions, in cooperation with Studio Falkland and Oyfo Techniekmuseum in Hengelo. [S3]

The museum run is documented too. SIDN fonds says Packet Run was shown at Oyfo from July 2025 to January 2026, that visitors made 2,350 runs in that period, and that the museum had 16,472 visitors, most of them parents with children. [S3] A family-events listing gives the dates as July 4, 2025 to January 4, 2026, while SIDN fonds gives July 3 as the start, a one-day difference I cannot settle from either page. [S3][S11] On November 13, 2025, the museum hosted a symposium, Hoe Het Netwerkt, where four designers first presented visualizations of internet infrastructure made at the invitation of SIDN fonds and SIDN Labs. The four were Packet Panic, a game about repairing routes during famous routing hijacks, Digital Cathedrals, a travel guide to the routing protocol, How the Net Works, which compares the internet to a postal system, and the dependency database discussed below. The note adds that the visualizations would next be shown at a festival in The Hague on November 20. [S12]
What a handoff looks like in writing

The Packet Run repository is more than a code archive. It holds the software for the terminals and the server, the design files, and a documentation folder with a build-up guide, a start-up and shutdown guide, a tear-down guide, a troubleshooting guide, a parts inventory, a list of tools and materials and a track list. [S5][S10] The folder’s own note says some documentation lives outside the repository, mostly in a company wiki, and that exports of the build-up and tear-down guides are kept in a PDF directory. [S10] The repository is licensed under the MIT license. It was created on December 7, 2023, after the festival, and its latest commit is dated July 14, 2025, during the museum preparation. [S6]

The tear-down guide shows what a handoff has to carry. It says the superstructure is heavy and dangerous and must be assembled or disassembled by at least four people, that a track must always be removed by at least two, and that track segments should never be disconnected but moved as one piece. It tells the reader to attach numbered pairs of clips to each rope and its steel cable before any rope is released, so the web of tracks can be rebuilt, and warns that the receiving prongs for the marbles are brittle. It says ethernet cable lengths have been closely calibrated, so a cable must not be coiled on top of another. [S7] The start-up guide has a daily test: place a ball on each terminal’s scanner and expect the message “Invalid packet detected,” then make two full runs through the installation. [S8] The troubleshooting guide lists black terminal screens, a terminal window in place of the regular screen, a scanner that is not working, terminals throwing errors and a press that is not working. [S9]

None of that explains the organization behind it. SIDN fonds says the repository’s authors, Bureau Moeilijke Dingen, are adapting the installation with Studio Falkland, and directs inquiries to a Studio Falkland designer. [S3] The repository credits seven people from Bureau Moeilijke Dingen and four from SIDN Labs. [S5] I found no page that explains how those two studio names relate, and I will not guess.

One sentence in the SIDN fonds note is easy to pass over. It says an exhibition that starts a discussion about the internet benefits from technically minded attendants. [S3] That is a staffing requirement, written in a funder’s page and not in the repository. A document can tell a new venue how to start the machine. Someone who can answer a visitor’s question about routers is a different sort of handoff.
A dataset with a plan, and a gap

Are we autonomous yet? is listed in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program as a free exhibition by Studio Falkland at Gebouw SFF, building B18, Torenallee 49 on Strijp-S, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 between October 17 and 25, 2026. The listing says the project tracks which vendors about 10,000 organizations in the Netherlands use for e-mail and web hosting, and that during the week visitors will help build a map of their own digital dependencies. [S13]

The listing also says what comes next. The exhibition is the kick-off for a year-long collaboration with the journalists’ collective Vers Beton and data journalist Sytze Simonse, who will examine organizations in Rotterdam, and with SIDN Labs. It says the team will update its online platform during the coming year with new data, visualizations, investigations and stories. [S13] That is a stated plan for the afterlife, written down by the organizers before the exhibition opens.

A March 31, 2026 article from SIDN explains where the project came from. The designer, Lei Nelissen, had made Packet Run with SIDN Labs and asked what other internet stories the same data and design skills could visualize. The project was funded through SIDN Fund’s Visualising the Internet Infrastructure call, announced in 2024, with a grant confirmed in September of that year. The article says the project is live and describes next steps: widening the scope to other sectors such as energy and education, tracking where dependency is greatest and how it is changing, and working out what knowledge, processes and alternatives can help organizations reduce it. [S14]

The code repository shows the mechanics. It was created on September 5, 2024, holds 122 commits, and its latest push is dated May 27, 2026. [S15][S16] It is licensed under the EUPL 1.2 as of an April 27, 2026 commit. Its README says the site is a static application and the data is refreshed by running an extraction command, and that the date of the last data update is shown in the application. [S15][S16] It also records two limits. Some extraction relies on non-public datasets kept in a data/sources folder, and the README advises anyone who hits errors to comment out those tasks. The collected data is not released yet, pending certainty about reuse, and people who want it are told to get in touch. [S15]

That is what continuation looks like when it is honest. A command exists, and it does not run for a stranger without access to files the repository does not contain. Another credit detail needs attention. SIDN’s November 2025 symposium note credits this project to a company called Codified, while SIDN’s March 2026 article and the DDW listing credit Studio Falkland. [S12][S13][S14] I could not find a page that connects the names.
A library with no closing date

The Biomaterials Library: Lithuanian & Baltic Creators is a free exhibition at BioArt Laboratories, Strijp T+R, building A1, Oirschotsedijk 14-10, running October 17 to 25, 2026. [S17] The Dutch Design Week listing describes the library as a growing archive of material experiments that keeps different stages of development, from early tests and samples to refined applications and design objects, and says each material carries knowledge about its ingredients, processes, failures and possibilities. [S17] It describes the host as an independent platform in Vilnius with a growing physical collection, working through exhibitions, workshops, educational activities and international collaborations. [S17]

The Eindhoven show is a selection: a curated group of samples, prototypes and design objects by Lithuanian and Baltic creators, working with agricultural, food and industrial side streams, mycelium, algae and natural fibres. The page names five works, among them Amber Waste is Bliss, Vegetative Textiles, Coffee Waste Tiles, Giria and Pine Skins. [S17] The library’s own site offers a submission form for new material and invites visitors to book an appointment at its Vilnius address. [S18] Those two invitations are the nearest thing to an afterlife policy that I found: contributions go in, and people can come to see the collection in person.

The listing says nothing about how a sample is identified, how its test information travels with it, who may borrow it, or what happens to a sample that degrades. The page I read does not say when the library began or how many items it holds. [S17][S18] A collection that preserves failures needs a way to show that a failed sample is a failure on purpose, and I would want to see how a label does that.
What a later user needs

Putting the three together suggests a short list of what a later user needs, and it is my list and not a standard. For an installation, the operating and teardown steps and the name of someone who can answer questions. For a dataset, the date of the data, the method, and an honest account of what cannot be rerun. For a sample, an identifier, a maker, a version and a statement of what was tested. These are proposed criteria and I am not saying any of the three projects lacks them. [S5][S15][S17]

A revision is a different problem. Packet Run’s funder page says the project was finished in February 2024 and, in the same paragraph, that it was not done yet. [S2] That is not a contradiction. A project page records one phase, and the work moved on. Readers are better served when a page says which phase it describes and who is continuing, and a dated line on a record does that cheaply.

Stopping deserves an honest label too. A project may have met its purpose, lost its funding or moved into another form. The Packet Run repository carries the same present-tense sentence about availability that it carried in 2023, and the latest commit is from July 2025. [S5][S6] Whether Packet Run is available today for a new venue is something I could not confirm from public records.
What the record does not show
I have not seen any of the 2026 exhibits. The listings are the organizers’ descriptions. [S13][S17]

I found no public account of what it cost to adapt Packet Run for museum use, who maintained it between the Oyfo run and now, or whether it has booked another venue after January 2026. [S3] The visitor and run counts come from SIDN fonds and are not audited. [S2][S3]

For Are we autonomous yet?, I found no schedule for updates, no statement of how many people maintain the data, and no explanation of the Codified credit. The extraction code depends on data that is not public. [S12][S15]
For the Biomaterials Library, I found no information on sample numbering, storage, loan rules or conservation, and I found no founding date. [S17][S18]
If you had to hand one of these three projects to a stranger next month, what is the first document you would want them to read? [S5][S15][S17]
