title: Can residents say no to city AI?
subtitle: A new Amsterdam handbook records a citizens' panel, a camera bicycle and a resident preference that was not the one chosen. The record, the parking scan car figures and the EU rules show where a no can go.
description: A new Amsterdam handbook records a resident panel, a scan bicycle and a preference that was not chosen. What that shows about saying no.

sections.x: If a resident says no to a city’s AI system, what happens next? [S4]

A published handbook from the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences gives a documented answer, and it is more specific than most claims about participation. A resident of a citizens’ panel for a camera bicycle says the panel’s first meeting showed the decision to put the bicycle on the street had already been made. She and one other member wanted to discuss whether the bicycle should exist. The panel’s job was to discuss the conditions it must meet. [S4]

That is one account, and I treat it as one account. It is also the clearest description I have found of the gap between being invited and being able to refuse. This essay follows that gap through the handbook, through the Amsterdam parking scan car that the same researchers studied, and through the European and Dutch rules that decide where a resident’s objection can go. I have not seen the Dutch Design Week exhibit, I attended no workshop and I interviewed nobody. [S1][S4]
What the program says

Bewoners-in-the-loop (Residents-in-the-Loop: Deciding Together on AI in the City) is a free exhibition at Stadslab Eindhoven, Gasfabriek 6, hosted by the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and Studio Bits of Space. Its page asks who decides how camera cars and sensors in public space are used, and presents a Co-Creation Cycle for the Smart City in which defining, making and evaluating follow one another in a continuous loop. [S1] A workshop is scheduled for Wednesday, October 21, 2026, from 14:00 to 15:00 at The Square, the central DDW plaza, aimed at civil servants, designers and participation professionals, and each participant is to leave with a copy of the handbook. [S1]

The handbook is a 2026 publication under a Creative Commons license by Mike de Kreek, Tessa Steenkamp and Martijn de Waal, closing a four-year project called Human Values for Smarter Cities. Amsterdam’s chief technology officer wrote the foreword dated May 27, 2026, and received the first copy at a closing event at Pakhuis de Zwijger on June 23. [S4][S2][S3]
How many methods are there

The university’s news item says the handbook offers fifty practical methods. [S2] The handbook counts differently. The introduction to its second part says it contains fifteen ideas, eighteen experiments and twelve methods, which is 45 entries. A page of principles elsewhere in the book refers to thirty ideas, experiments and methods, and the project’s toolkit site speaks of a handbook with fifteen. [S4][S5] Four counts for one book is a small matter, but the correct unit is not obvious. The ideas are prompts, the experiments were run in the project, and the methods are instructions for repeating an experiment, so I use the book’s own breakdown and avoid a single number.
The scan bicycle, as documented

In 2022 the municipality of Amsterdam began developing a multipurpose scanning vehicle, and in 2023 its Computer Vision Team issued a tender. The first use was to find construction containers without a permit on vulnerable quays for the enforcement department. The tender went to a company that could build an electric scan bicycle. The municipality chose to develop its own blurring and recognition model and to build the first application with a citizens’ panel. [S4]

The participation plan was based on Amsterdam’s version of the participation ladder and aimed at the highest goal, which it calls zeggenschap (having a say), and the highest level of influence, meebepalen (co-deciding). Certain subjects, including whether scanning public space is desirable at all, were placed explicitly outside the scope. The project ran 20 meetings around three focus areas: making the service responsible, exploring new uses and evaluating the cooperation. [S4] Since early 2025 the bicycle has ridden with a web address on its frame. The rider has no task of talking to onlookers but carries a business card. The bicycle detects objects such as construction containers and toilet cabins, checks for permits, and when it finds a possible violation an enforcement officer follows up. It stores a supporting photo in which people are blurred immediately. [S4]

The handbook describes what happened with scope. Participants did not stay within the boundary set in advance. While the Computer Vision Team wanted to work on concrete design questions, residents raised basic questions about whether more automation in the city was desirable. The researchers then used collages and value cards to choose themes: data minimization, transparency, control over technology and human scale. [S4]
Where a resident’s preference met a department’s decision

One workshop produced four data-minimization scenarios, from blurring personal data in images (scenario A) to sharing only GPS data (scenario D). The residents preferred D. After consultation with the department that would use the bicycle, A was chosen as the most workable. The handbook says formal influence moved toward an advisory role, and adds that the joint development narrowed the municipality’s room for decision, because residents’ views shaped the options that reached the table. [S4]

Both statements can be true together. A resident who preferred D can fairly say the answer was no. The authors describe the same fact as influence that shaped the choices even though it did not decide among them. I read that as an honest disagreement inside the research team’s own account, and I would not choose between the two readings on the evidence I have. [S4]

The handbook records what the team promised next. The Computer Vision Team said that when new functions are added to the bicycle it would start from the scenario that collects the least data, and that residents’ perspectives would be included in future advisory letters to the city council about extending this kind of technology. [S4] Then it records the weak point. After staff changed, these long-term promises turned out not to be well anchored in the organization. [S4] Its reflection chapter says the project group had been dissolved by then and the ladder approach did not travel with time, so influence that depends on follow-up needs written commitments that someone tracks and reports on. [S4]

The same chapter reports that participants gained trust in individual project staff but not in the municipality as an institution, and that some wondered whether long cooperation had left them without critical distance. The project’s lead researcher is quoted as asking how to make sure people in a citizens’ panel remain residents, after saying the project may have accidentally turned them into consultants. [S4][S3]
The panel member’s account

The handbook prints an interview with a member of the panel. She says the first meeting surprised her because the bicycle already existed and the decision to deploy it had been taken, and that she would have liked to talk about the step before. The panel had about fifteen members and met for a year, each meeting about another detail: the color of the rider’s vest, whether the camera should be covered, which images are blurred and how long data is kept. She has no negative word about the friendliness of the facilitators, she says, but their assignment was the conditions and not whether the bicycle should exist. Attendance fell to five by the end, and she would have liked a final evaluation. [S4]

I quote only the parts she made public in the handbook, and I do not name her. Her account differs from the researchers’ in one factual respect: the book’s experiment title speaks of twenty selected residents, while she remembers fifteen people at the start. [S4] The handbook does not reconcile them. A panel can recruit twenty and see fifteen turn up, and I only note the difference.
Talking back to a car that cannot listen

One of the handbook’s experiments takes the problem literally. A parking scan car passes at speed, its driver is not allowed to stop or open a window, and the car takes photographs and does not film, so even a warning light is usually not visible. A resident who is loading a van has no way to say so before the process starts, and the next chance to speak is the objection. [S4] The researchers held two workshops with 35 participants who made small wooden signs to hang over a license plate. Many signs carried angry slogans and drawn rude gestures instead of explanations, which the authors link to having opened the workshop with an introduction to the system. Two constructive ideas came out: a loading-and-unloading sign with a timer, and a disabled-permit sign that could replace the separate website where permit holders now register a plate when visiting Amsterdam. [S4]

Whether the city would read such a sign is a separate question. The handbook notes that the photographs are reviewed by an enforcement officer at a central computer, which could in principle read a note, and it does not report that the city adopted the idea. [S4]
Where objections go when the room is not the place

Most residents will never sit on a panel. For them, the nearest thing to saying no is a formal objection to a single decision. The handbook gives Amsterdam’s figures for the parking scan car. About 500,000 parking charges are imposed each year, about 75,000 objections are filed, and about 45,000 are granted. Of those, roughly two-thirds are granted out of leniency, for example after mistakes, and one-third because of errors in the system or its execution. [S4] The authors read the 60 percent grant rate as evidence that the objection process is a core part of how the system functions and not a small correction afterward. [S4]

They add a point about context. Loading and unloading is allowed for five minutes without payment in Amsterdam. A person who walks inside alone to drop something off is not beside the car when the scan car passes, and the photos can then look like a violation. [S4]

The national picture comes from the Dutch Data Protection Authority, whose study the handbook cites. According to a legal-news summary of its April 2026 findings, municipal scan cars make 250 to 375 million scans a year, leading to 3 to 5 million parking charges. The authority estimates that more than one in ten is wrong, and people who object are right in 40 to 62 percent of cases. It says the cars capture a moment and cannot judge context such as loading or a disability permit, that paying is not suspended while an objection is pending, and that the burden falls most on people with disabilities and people who are less digitally skilled. [S6] In June 2026 the Minister of the Interior answered parliamentary questions by saying municipalities are responsible for the parking tax and for how it is enforced, including for reducing errors. [S7] I could not open the Authority’s own report, whose website disallows automated access, so I rely on the handbook and the summary. [S4][S6]
What European and Dutch rules add

A resident’s route also depends on law, and the law is in motion. The EU AI Act sets out rights for people affected by high-risk systems. Article 85 lets anyone with grounds to think the Act has been infringed complain to the market surveillance authority. Article 86 gives a person subject to a decision based on the output of an Annex III high-risk system the right to a clear explanation of the system’s role and the main elements of the decision. Article 27 requires public bodies deploying certain high-risk systems to assess the impact on fundamental rights first. [S8] The Act as adopted applied from August 2, 2026. The Council adopted a regulation amending it on June 29, 2026, and reports of its terms, which I could not read in the text, move the stand-alone high-risk rules to December 2, 2027. [S8][S9]

I found no source that places the scan bicycle or the parking scan car in a risk category under the Act, so I cannot say whether these rights apply to them. A member of the Amsterdam city council says in the handbook that Amsterdam started the first municipal algorithm register, that a national register now exists, that the council adopted a motion to use the Act’s classifications, and that high-risk algorithms are now shared with the council. She also says that when she asks why no high-risk algorithms appear in the national register, the answer is that there are none, and she asks how anyone knows. [S4]
The shape of an honest invitation

Put together, the record gives a reader a few things to ask of any invitation to take part in decisions about city AI. Which question is on the table, and which is outside it? Who will read the answer, and what happens to commitments made after the project team is disbanded? If a resident prefers one option and the department chooses another, is that written down with a reason? And where can a person take an objection that no workshop can address, whether a council, an ombudsman or a court? The handbook’s principle of leaving room to adjust and to stop is relevant here. It reports that Amsterdam’s scan bicycle experiment, introduced to reduce enforcement costs, created more work for the smaller number of remaining enforcers, and it warns against searching for a new business case to justify a solution that has lost its original purpose. [S4]

I add one observation of my own. A route for disagreement is only as good as the record of where it leads. The sources I read are unusually willing to publish their own limits, and that makes them useful. A project page that said every participant could shape the outcome would tell me less than a handbook that records a resident’s preferred scenario and the one the department picked. [S4]
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibit or the workshop, and the program page is the organizers’ description. [S1]

I could not open the Amsterdam municipality’s own page on the scan bicycle, because the site refused automated requests. The facts about the bicycle here come from the handbook, which describes it in detail. [S4] I found no public account of what happened after the promised advisory letters, no later evaluation of the scan bicycle, and no statement of how many objections the scan bicycle has produced. The bicycle does not issue charges, and the handbook gives no objection route for it. [S4]

The Data Protection Authority’s figures reach me through a legal-news summary and the handbook, and the Authority’s own pages were not available to my method. [S4][S6] The status of the European amending regulation rests on the Council’s voting-result note, and the revised dates rest on reports I could not check against the text. [S9]

If a city told you its camera bicycle was designed with residents, which of these would you ask first: what could they refuse, what did they ask for that was not given, or where do I go if I object? [S4]

title: Who gets to decide what gets seen?
subtitle: Table of Power at Dutch Design Week 2026 seats the international press at a long table. Hassink's boardroom photographs, the festival's press rules and a journalism guideline show where the choices sit.
description: Table of Power at DDW 2026 puts a dinner for international press on a long table. Hassink's boardroom photographs, DDW press rules and a journalism guideline frame the question.

sections.x: The table is easy to photograph. The invitation is what I want to understand. Who wrote it, who received it, who could say yes, and whose account of the evening becomes the one other people read? [S1]

Table of Power, an exhibition by the collective SHOW NOT SHOW at De Kruisruimte in Eindhoven, puts that question on a long table. Its Dutch Design Week page says the table is the setting for the official DDW opening dinner for the international press, which it describes as bringing together the people who influence what is seen, discussed and remembered in the design world. The title, it says, refers to Jacqueline Hassink’s project The Table of Power, and the collective turns the table from a symbol of institutional power into a platform for participation and interpretation. [S1] I have not seen the show or the dinner. This essay reads the program page, the record of Hassink’s earlier project, Dutch Design Week’s own press rules and the Dutch journalism guideline, and it reports no interview and no guest list. [S1][S8][S10]
What the program page says, and what it leaves out

Table of Power is on Generaal Bothastraat 7-E, in the space called De Kruisruimte, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 between October 17 and 25, 2026, and it requires a DDW ticket. SHOW NOT SHOW hosts it with outside partners: Studio Four for tableware and ceramics, Maarten Baptist for glassware and cutlery, Yasmine Chihoub as chef, and Hapax for a food experience. [S1] The page calls this the collective’s third Dutch Design Week presentation at De Kruisruimte. [S1]

The collective is a group of makers who show their own work. The 2025 listing names the members as Clovis Atelier, Frank Penders, Lucas Zito, Marc Meeuwissen (Dear Objects), MOKKO (Aad Bos) and Studio Luuk van Laarhoven, with a guest, and says the group launched at De Kruisruimte during DDW 2024. [S2] A preview of that first show described six designers under the name The Best Kept Spoilers, showing mainly functional and autonomous objects and inviting visitors into the making process. [S3] So the 2026 table comes from a group whose earlier shows concerned how things get made, now turning to who gets to talk about them.

The page does not give the date or time of the dinner, the number of seats, how guests are chosen, whether the public can watch, or what the guests are asked to do. [S1] Those omissions matter to the question, and I will not fill them in.
The table it borrows from

Jacqueline Hassink’s The Table of Power ran from 1993 to 1995. [S7] According to her biography at the Rencontres d’Arles, she photographed the boardroom tables of Europe’s forty largest multinational corporations, without people in the frame, asked each company to fill in a questionnaire about its table, and had an artist draw the table setting during board meetings. [S5] A book followed in 1996. The photobook history by Martin Parr and Gerry Badger, as quoted by a bookseller, says she approached Europe’s top forty companies from the Fortune list, that only 21 allowed a photograph, and that those who denied access appear in the book as black photographs. [S6]

That detail changes how I read the title, and so does the blurb’s emphasis on emptiness. [S12] Hassink’s project was partly a record of who would open the door, and the refusals were part of the work. The exhibition page uses her tables as a symbol, and the dinner puts people around its own table, in contrast with the empty boardrooms. [S1][S5][S6] I read that contrast as a deliberate move and not as a failing, though the page does not say what happens to the idea of refusal when the invitation is the organizers’ own.

Hassink returned to the subject in 2009 after the financial crisis. Her Hatje Cantz book The Table of Power 2, published in 2012 with design by Irma Boom, revisits the headquarters of about fifty companies from Fortune’s list, including banks, insurers and corporations such as Shell, BP, Volkswagen and ING. [S4] The publisher’s blurb, repeated by the International Center of Photography for a 2012 book signing, describes boardroom tables in deserted, soulless rooms, as if emptiness were one of the inherent features of power. [S12] The two blurbs disagree about the count: the publisher says about fifty companies, while the signing notice says the top 40. [S4][S12] She was born in Enschede in 1966 and died in November 2018, according to a gallery biography reproduced in a photobook library. [S7]
Visibility at a festival is already selected

Dutch Design Week presents work by about 2,500 designers to a stated 350,000 visitors at around one hundred locations over nine days. Its 2026 theme is R.A.W., short for Rebel Authentic Worth. [S9] A festival at that scale cannot be seen in full by anyone, and journalists, like visitors, see a selection.

The festival has its own gate for journalists. Its press accreditation page says accreditation gives access to all locations, talks, conferences, press tours on request and select networking events. The form asks for a professional role, the main media title and its country, and for recent coverage of DDW or proof of publication of a similar event under the applicant’s name. Press tours are offered only during the first weekend. [S8] I do not know whether the opening dinner is one of the select networking events, or how the international press for that table is chosen. The accreditation page does not say. [S8]

Media scholars call this selection gatekeeping. Pamela Shoemaker and Timothy Vos describe it as the process by which people turn information about billions of events into a manageable number of messages, which decides what is selected and also what the messages look like, and they argue that minor decisions add up to shape how an audience sees the world. [S11] A dinner that gathers editors, correspondents and curators in one room is a compact case of that: many small choices of who sits, who speaks and what gets repeated afterward.
The guest who is also a reporter

A journalist at a dinner holds two roles. The Dutch Council for Journalism publishes a guideline that is the standard by which it judges complaints, and the September 2026 edition says journalists carry out their work independently and avoid the appearance of conflicts of interest, that they identify themselves as journalists to potential interlocutors and are clear about their journalistic intentions, also when entering non-public spaces, and that quotations from interviews may not be used in a context other than the interviewee could expect from what the journalist told them. [S10] It also says journalists who accept an embargo must keep to it until the agreed date. [S10]

Those lines do not settle every case at a dinner. I found nothing in the guideline text about hospitality, and nothing about the status of table talk, so I cannot say how the Council would treat a remark made over food. What the lines do give is a vocabulary: who knows a person is a journalist, what the guest understood about how a remark would be used, and what was agreed beforehand. An honest account of a dinner like this would state those terms on the page. [S10]
What would show who shaped what

Describing the table is the easy part. The harder part is the sequence after it. An invitation might produce an interview, an introduction, a photograph, a commission or nothing, and a conversation can matter without becoming content. The fact that people met does not show what changed. Following one invitation to a published story, and saying which choices along the way belonged to the host, the guest and the editor, would show more than a photograph of a place setting. [S1][S11]

A published picture of the table also needs a caption that says when it was made and whether it shows the public exhibition or the separate dinner. The program page describes both and does not say they are the same room at the same time. [S1] A reader should not have to guess which one they are looking at.

There is an argument here that I find worth making. Visibility comes from a series of ordinary choices: who is on the list, what the form asks, which story leads, which photograph runs. The table makes those choices easy to point at. The record I could read says who built it and what it is for, and says almost nothing about how its guests were chosen. [S1][S8]
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibition or the dinner. The page is the organizers’ description. [S1]

The four partners are named on the program page only; searches did not turn up independent pages that confirm who they are or what they supply, so I describe them as the page does. [S1] I found no guest list, no invitation criteria, no date for the dinner, and no account of how the international press for it was chosen. I do not know whether other press events at the festival work on invitation, and I found no earlier DDW opening dinner for the press to compare. [S1][S8]

My account of Hassink’s first project rests on the Arles biography and on a bookseller’s quotation of Parr and Badger, not on the 1996 book. I did not open the book, and I could not reach her own website. [S5][S6] The date of her death comes from a gallery biography reproduced by a library listing. [S7]
I could not open the Chatham House Rule page, whose site refused automated requests, so this essay does not rely on that convention. The Dutch guideline I did read is silent on the matter. [S10]
If you were handed the guest list for that dinner tomorrow, which question would you ask first: who is missing, who chose, or who will write it up? [S1]

title: What makes a hemp textile right for interiors?
subtitle: A Czech design school, a family weaving mill and a coarse 70/30 wool and hemp yarn. The record shows how an awkward local fiber ended up pointed at carpets, and how far the proof goes.
description: A Czech design school, a family mill and a coarse 70/30 wool and hemp yarn. What the record says about hemp for interiors and what it leaves open.

sections.x: Say “hemp textile” and the mind goes straight to clothes. A shirt, a jacket, something to wear. That jump from material to garment is an assumption, and the people behind SOW HEMP! have written down why they stepped around it. [S1][S2]

The record I could read is better than a guess. It says a Czech design school was handed a local hemp fiber that textile machinery does not like, found a mill willing to try it with sheep’s wool, and ended up with a coarse yarn that students are testing in carpets, tapestries and objects. It also says, in two places, slightly different things about how far that yarn has been proven. This essay reads the program page, the school’s own account, the mill’s website, Czech customs data, a 2026 fiber study and the EU labelling rule, and it separates what each can carry. I have not seen the exhibition and interviewed nobody. [S1][S2]
What the program says

SOW HEMP! is presented by the Studio of Textile at the Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague, known as UMPRUM, at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S (building B4), open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 between October 17 and 25, 2026, with a DDW ticket required. Ten students of the Studio of Textile and eight of the Studio of Photography II are credited as exhibitors. [S1]

The page frames the project as an exploration of both the cultural context and the material qualities of hemp fiber. It says hemp is mainly grown in the Czech Republic for seeds, blooms and hempcrete, and that fiber is not processed for the textile industry there, except that one farm built a scutching mill from scratch to get short hemp fibers. The Studio of Textile took the chance to work with this non-textile material and to explore possibilities beyond clothing. [S1]

Two sentences on the page carry the interiors argument. One says research with the weaving mill Kubák set out to find whether a local hemp and wool blend could become an industrial yarn combining the qualities of both. The next says the resulting yarn, made by a local weaving mill, met qualities for architecture and interior design. [S1] Those are the organizers’ words. The page does not say which qualities, or how they were checked.
What the school’s own account adds

UMPRUM published a longer account on May 28, 2026, ahead of its ARTSEMESTR show in Prague from June 4 to 9. It describes SOW HEMP! (in Czech, Sej konopí!) as a year-long project that began in the winter semester as research and material experiment. The studio’s head, Linda Kaplanová, is quoted saying the studio had first examined sheep’s wool, which is processed very little in the Czech Republic and mostly burned, and then turned to a plant fiber, asking why the textile industry turned its back on hemp. [S2]

The account is specific about the raw material. Students visited a farm called Lapka and took home stems and already processed fiber. Because that fiber contained a higher share of shives, the woody part of the plant, it was not suitable for ordinary industrial textile processing. The account calls that limit important to the studio: instead of working with an ideal raw material, students asked what the local fiber could become in its present form. [S2]

In the summer semester, with support from a grant it names as AGS, the project added a collaboration with the weaving mill Tkalcovna Kubák in Strmilov. Together they tested whether a usable yarn could be made despite the contamination. The blend that worked best was 70 percent wool and 30 percent hemp, which the account describes as a visually distinct, coarser yarn that students are testing in objects, tapestries, carpets and other work. [S2]

Set side by side, the two descriptions differ in strength. The program page says the yarn met qualities for architecture and interior design. The school’s account says the blend worked best among those tried and that students are testing it. Neither names a standard or a test report. [S1][S2] I treat “is being tested in carpets and tapestries” as established and “met interior-design qualities” as the organizers’ claim.
What the students made with it

The interiors claim rests on a narrow part of the project. The school’s account says the students moved the local hemp into bioplastic, tapestries, acoustic panels, objects, animation and installations, and that themes of care, craftivism, feminism, posthumanism and craft as a political act surfaced on their own while they worked. Martin Pondělíček, the studio’s assistant, is quoted saying the breadth is what makes the project matter to them. [S2] The DDW page lists five works by name: The Hemp Bag, Hyakinthos, Modulus/Threadline, You Are My Star and Joy. [S1] It also describes experiments in dissolving hemp fiber into bioplastic, felting, spinning and carding hemp with wool, traditional tapestry weaving, and fusing raw fibers with a digital embroidery machine. [S1]

So the yarn is one thread among several. The program describes some projects as oscillating between fine art and functional products for a harmonious interior, and others as critical design about values, health and care. [S1] A visitor who sees a hemp rug should not assume the whole show is about floor coverings, and the maker’s account of which works use the 70/30 yarn is the missing piece. [S1][S2]
Why a rough fiber points toward a rug

The interiors direction makes sense of the raw material, which is my reading and not something the sources state. Hemp for textiles depends on how cleanly the bast fiber is separated from the shives. A study presented at an engineering conference in Jelgava on May 27 to 29, 2026 tested scutched fiber from two Ukrainian industrial hemp varieties. It found tensile strength sufficient for spinning but linear densities of about 65 and 77 tex, which it describes as high, and it concluded that the fiber suited medium to coarse yarn counts (Nm 2.8 to 3.5) and should be blended with finer fibers such as cotton. Fiber yield from intact stem segments averaged 34.7 percent, and cellulose content was about 70 to 72 percent. [S5]

That study is about other varieties grown elsewhere, and it says nothing about Lapka. What it shows is the general shape of the problem the Prague studio met: scutched hemp tends to be strong and coarse, and the finer, cleaner fiber used in clothing is harder to get. A coarse yarn that students can use in a tapestry or a carpet is a reasonable match for that. Whether this particular fiber behaves the same way is an open question that the school’s account does not measure. [S2][S5]
The mill

Tkalcovna Kubák’s own site describes a small family firm whose tradition reaches back to 1870, when the founder was the great-great-grandfather of the current owner, and which makes designer home textiles. It says it prefers local wool bought from local breeders, that it won the Czech Grand Design award as manufacturer of the year 2020 for collections made with the studios DurchDuo and IHOR, and that its suppliers meet OEKO-TEX standards. [S3] A mill that already works with local wool is a natural partner for a project that began with the problem of Czech wool, and the school’s account says the collaboration was about whether contaminated hemp could become a yarn. [S2][S3]

I did not find Kubák’s own description of this collaboration. What the mill contributed to the yarn’s development, such as spinning settings, blend ratios tried, or failures, is not on the pages I could read. [S2][S3]
The local crop behind the fiber

The DDW page says hemp cultivation is on the rise with new legislation. [S1] Czech customs data show a different pattern in recent years. The Customs Administration’s hemp figures give the harvested area as 280 hectares in 2022, about 168 in 2023 and about 125 in 2024, and the number of growers as 102, 67 and 49, with 128.67 hectares sown in 2024. They also show 545 hectares and 81 growers in 2015. [S4] The table repeats the years 2017 and 2018 with different values in two series, so I would not lean on the early years. [S4] The decline since 2022 does not contradict a rise that began later, and I have no data for 2025 or 2026. It does mean the supply behind a mill-scale yarn is small. Forty-nine growers is a thin base for an industrial textile.
What a label would have to say

If a yarn like this were sold in a carpet’s use-surface or a chair covering, EU rules on fiber names would apply. Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 treats furniture coverings containing at least 80 percent textile components, and the textile components of the upper layer of multi-layer floor coverings, in the same way as textile products. [S6] It allows only the fiber names in its Annex I on labels, and for hemp the legal name is “true hemp,” defined as fiber obtained from the bast of Cannabis sativa. [S6] It permits a manufacturing tolerance of 3 percent between the stated composition and the analyzed one. [S6] A 70/30 yarn would therefore be labeled as wool and true hemp with percentages, and the 30 percent figure would be judged against an analysis, not against a design intention. That is a description of the text and not a statement about any exhibited object.
What “right for interiors” would require

Nothing in the sources defines what the right qualities are, so I lay out only what a reader can ask. Abrasion resistance is commonly judged by the Martindale method, whose second part sets how the end-point of the test, specimen breakdown, is determined for most woven and knitted fabrics and nonwovens. [S7] I searched for published Martindale results for a wool and hemp yarn in upholstery or carpet and did not find any. [S7] That does not show the yarn fails, and it does not show it passes. It shows that a claim of interior suitability would need its own test on this yarn, and neither the program page nor the school’s account cites one. [S1][S2]

The question the exhibition raises is what makes this fiber, from this farm, in this blend, right for that job, and what the students learned along the way: the farm’s fiber arrived with limits, a mill agreed to try, a ratio emerged, and a set of objects came out of it. That sequence is documented in two sources and is more interesting than the idea that hemp is versatile. [S1][S2]
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibition. The program page and the school’s account are the organizers’ descriptions. [S1][S2]

I do not know which qualities the program means by “met qualities for architecture/interior design,” what tests were done, what the shives content of the Lapka fiber was, how many blends were tried, or what the AGS grant is. I found no independent page for the farm Lapka and none for its scutching mill, and no account from Kubák. [S1][S2][S3]

The Ukrainian fiber study concerns other varieties and a different processing chain. [S5] Neither the DDW page nor the school’s account says that any garment was tried and abandoned, so I do not suggest one was. [S1][S2]
If a wall hanging, a carpet and a shirt were all made from the same yarn, which of the three would you ask the maker to prove first? [S2]

title: Would you wear someone else’s hair?
subtitle: Human Material Loop's ādara® at Dutch Design Week 2026 is billed as a fiber for interiors. The record on the fiber, the hair supply and the labeling rules shows how far the question about wearing it goes.
description: Human Material Loop's ādara® at DDW 2026 is for interiors. What the record says about the fiber, the hair supply, the law and the question.

sections.x: Would you wear someone else’s hair? The question takes six words, and it can turn the whole conversation into a reaction: yes, no, never. [S5]

The question is older than this essay. When the jury of the Dutch Design Awards nominated Studio Zsofia Kollar’s Human Material Loop in the Design Research category in 2022, it asked whether we are ready to wear human material. [S5] A Limburg development agency opened its profile of the company by imagining the reaction to a warm coat made from human hair: “On second thought, no thank you.” [S4] So the company and its supporters have been asking the question for years. My interest here is narrower. The exhibit at Dutch Design Week 2026 is, on its own program page, about interiors, so the first thing I want to check is whether the question still fits. I have not seen the exhibit, handled a sample or spoken to the team. [S1]
What the program page says

ādara® is an exhibition at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S (building B4), with a DDW ticket required, hosted by Human Material Loop together with the designer Roger Haan and the studio WANDSCHAPPEN. The page describes ādara® as a keratin protein fiber made from hair waste for the interior industry. It says the company spent years developing laboratory technology to transform human hair waste into a new generation of materials, that the process has been engineered for industrial production using existing textile machinery and infrastructure, and that ādara® is a regenerative keratin protein fiber combining low environmental impact with strong functional and material performance. [S1]

The page frames the exhibit as what the fiber can become in the hands of designers, makers, builders and architects: surfaces, objects and spaces. [S1] It does not mention clothing. The company’s own site says ādara® is its first commercial application and that textiles are where it starts, because fibers must perform through processing, coloration, manufacturing and use. [S2] That is a company statement.
From a sweater to a wall

The company’s earlier public face was a garment. The Dutch Design Awards entry from 2022 shows the process of material development in the form of a sweater, and the jury wrote that the work concerns a much broader issue: what we do with our own waste flows. [S5] The jury text says the studio was developing a closed recycling system with specialist companies, and that around 72 million kilograms of human hair end up in waste in Europe every year. [S5]

The company then moved toward industry. The Limburg agency LIOF reports that it granted a prototype grant in 2023 and later a loan from its Early Phase Fund, which it says would help the company test production at industrial scale and build a patent portfolio. It reports that the company had so far made clothes from up to 7 kilograms of hair, that it planned to process 220 kilograms, and that the first yarn would be spun at a factory in Germany. [S4] The same article says the company focuses primarily on the interior segment, offering yarn, fabric or fibers for acoustic panels, wall coverings, curtains and similar uses, with apparel to follow later. [S4]

A separate project page describes TRESS, a pilot to produce a hair-derived textile at pilot scale and validate it in the high-end clothing market. The textile is made from hair waste collected at hair salons, resembles wool and can be produced on the same equipment, and is treated with a bio-based coating from the Dutch company Sustanix, while the designer Tess van Zalinge makes a collection to show it to the fashion industry and consumers. The project is supported by OPZuid and co-funded by the European Union and the Province of Limburg. [S3]

So the record shows two routes: interiors first, in the LIOF account and on the 2026 program page, and a clothing pilot, in the TRESS description. I cannot tell from public pages whether the exhibited fiber is the same as the TRESS textile, and I will not assume it. [S1][S3][S4]
What kind of fiber it is

The company’s site says keratin gives hair, wool and feathers their strength, that the challenge is engineering and not availability, and that hair is the starting resource because it is generated continuously by salons, donations and wig manufacturing and has little industrial value once separated from the body. [S2] As an anatomist, I know hair as keratin, the protein family it shares with nails and the outer layer of skin, so that part of the premise is ordinary biology. What is new is the industrial route, and the pages I could read describe it in broad terms only. [S2]

The word regenerative on the DDW page matters. In textile terms, a regenerated fiber is usually made by dissolving a raw material and re-forming it into fiber, and the DDW page does not say that this is what happens here. [S1] It is possible to dissolve human hair: a 2022 doctoral thesis at the University of Nottingham found that certain ionic liquids dissolve hair and that keratin can be recovered from the solution, noting that the anion, such as acetate or dimethylphosphate, does the work of breaking hydrogen and disulfide bonds. [S7] That thesis is not about Human Material Loop and says nothing about ādara®. It does show that dissolving hair is a research problem with several routes, and the company has not published which one it uses. [S2][S7]

The vocabulary matters for the law. Under the EU Textile Regulation, the name “wool” is reserved for fiber from the fleeces of sheep or lambs, and only the fiber names in its Annex I may be used on a label. [S8] Annex I does list a name “protein,” for fiber obtained from natural protein substances regenerated and stabilized through the action of chemical agents. [S8] Whether ādara® falls under that name is for the maker and the authorities to say. What I can say is that the phrase “human wool,” which LIOF’s article uses as a figure of speech, could not appear on a label. [S4][S8] A manufacturer who wants a new name has to apply to the Commission with a technical file that, under the Regulation’s recitals, includes scientific information on possible allergic reactions or other adverse effects. [S8]
The raw material, by the numbers

The three quantities I found do not line up. The Dutch Design Awards entry says about 72 million kilograms of human hair waste a year in Europe. [S5] LIOF’s article says more than 150,000 tons a year in Europe, which is about 150 million kilograms, twice as much. [S4] The same article quotes the founder saying a hairdresser throws away about 15 kilograms of waste hair a week and that there are 28,000 registered hair salons in the Netherlands. [S4] Multiplied out, 28,000 salons at 15 kilograms for 52 weeks is about 21.8 million kilograms a year, which would be roughly 30 percent of the lower European figure from a single country. That is my arithmetic on the company’s own numbers, and it suggests at least one of them is a rough estimate. [S4][S5]

The problem is not that the resource is small. It is that the sources give no common basis. The question for a designer is how much consistent, traceable hair a mill could count on, which none of these figures answers. [S2][S4]
What is in the input

The founder’s account describes hair as clean, non-toxic, light, insulating and strong, and says no human is allergic to it. [S4] Those are company claims, and I found no independent test of the hair that salons collect.

A January 2025 interview in Lampoon magazine fills in how the hair is gathered. The founder says a pilot with fifteen Amsterdam salons came first, and that the company now works with a logistics partner that serves more than a thousand salons in the Netherlands, collecting aluminum, plastic and paper for other manufacturers and sending the hair to Human Material Loop. She says the company does not sort the salon waste, so dyed and bleached hair goes in too, that hair needs only steaming before processing, that very short fibers cannot be spun and are put to another use, and that about 85 percent of the collected hair can be spun into yarn. [S9] She also says barber-cut hair usually lacks the follicle, so no nuclear DNA is present. [S9]

Every one of those statements comes from the company. The unsorted input is the one I would want tested. A salon cut can carry dyes, bleach and styling products, and I found no published analysis of what remains in the yarn or what the process removes. [S2][S4][S9] A reader should hold that as an open question and not as a finding that anything is wrong.

The accounts also differ on where the yarn is spun. LIOF says the first yarn from hair would be spun at a factory in Germany, and the Lampoon interview says the yarn is currently produced at a spinning mill in Italy. [S4][S9] The two statements may describe different batches or years, and I could not tell which.

An independent research demo gives a sense of how hair is handled when someone other than the company works with it. Sofía Guridi and Matteo Iannacchero of Aalto University published a demo in Biotechnology Design on July 21, 2026, in which hair as warp and wool as weft were woven by hand and tapped against a Teflon film, producing a root-mean-square voltage of 16.45 millivolts, and in which a pillow was built from the same layering. They state that the hair came from discarded material with no personal identification retained. [S6] It is a hand-woven research sample, and it does not describe Human Material Loop’s fiber, yarn or tests. [S6]
Does “wear” still fit

If the 2026 exhibit is about wall surfaces, objects and spaces, then wearing is the wrong test, and a wall does not touch skin the way a sweater does. [S1] Interior use raises its own questions: what the fiber does under light, abrasion, cleaning and fire, and what a specifier needs on a data sheet. I found no published test results for ādara® on any of those. [S1][S2] The person who hesitates at hair on the body might not hesitate at a wall covering, or might hesitate more at a stranger’s hair in the living room. I cannot tell, and no survey I found measures it.

The honest version of the question has more parts. Which material is it, how was it processed, what is it meant to do, and what do we actually know? The pages I read answer the first and the third in outline and the second and fourth only in company terms. [S1][S2][S4]
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibit, handled a sample or interviewed the team. The program page and the company pages are the organizers’ and the company’s descriptions. [S1][S2]

I do not know the composition of the exhibited fiber, the processing route, the share of hair in any yarn or fabric, the terms of the collection arrangement with salons beyond the founder’s outline, or the results of any durability, safety or environmental test. I found no patent text, no life-cycle assessment and no independent review of ādara®. I could not find independent pages for the designer or the studio credited alongside the company. [S1][S2][S3]

The dates of the LIOF article are not printed in the text I read, though it refers to a 2023 grant. [S4] The funding and pilot facts come from the funder and the project page, which are the best available but still the parties’ own accounts. [S3][S4]
If a wall covering were woven from salon hair, what is the first thing you would want to know about it? [S9]

title: Would you wear something you had to care for?
subtitle: KojiGotchi grows koji on body heat. The team's own experiments and user studies show what care asks of a wearer, and where the record stops.
description: KojiGotchi grows koji on body heat. The team's own experiments and user studies show what care asks of a wearer, and what they leave open.

sections.x: Would you wear something you had to care for? Charging a battery is the easy case. A harder case is a wearable organized around a living organism, where putting it on starts a relationship. [S1]

KojiGotchi is a concrete place to ask. It is a device worn on the body to grow the mold used for miso and sake, using body heat, and its makers have published more of their working than most projects do: their experiments, their sensor choices, two user studies and a resource page. This essay reads those pages, the Dutch Design Week listing, the Biodesign Challenge page and one review of the mold’s safety. I have not seen the exhibit, worn the device or spoken to the team, and I give no cultivation instructions. [S1][S2][S3][S4][S6]
What the program says

KojiGotchi is a free exhibition at BioArt Laboratories, Strijp T+R, building A1, Oirschotsedijk 14-10. The listing describes an open-source wearable that uses human body heat to grow Aspergillus oryzae, the fungus behind miso and sake, in a playful, Tamagotchi-inspired format. It says the project began with experiments at DTU Biosustain in Copenhagen, where the team tried to grow the mold on body heat alone, first in plastic bags in back pockets, and that the device is a transparent growth chamber with a digital avatar, KojiMoji, that reads live sensor data and turns conditions into emotional states. [S1]

The listing makes a claim about audience that deserves attention: it says the device is fully open-source, built from standard components, and designed for primary schools, maker spaces and home kitchens. [S1] It credits Maxim Velli with concept and biological experiments, Rasmus Tofthøj with electronics and engineering, Tania Safa with visual identity and Taylor Rayne with narrative, names Mark Torochkin as redesigning the casing for DDW, and lists Adrien Rigobello and Joshua Evans as supervisors. [S1] The Biodesign Challenge lists KojiGotchi among the 2025 projects of the team from the Technical University of Denmark and the Royal Danish Academy. [S7] I found no record of an award, and the listing does not claim one.
How the body-heat idea was tested

The team’s experiments page is candid. Its first try put steamed rice with spores in a zip bag in a back pocket for 48 hours and, it says, produced minimal to no visible growth, which it could not explain. [S4] The product-design page describes the same try as showing a small amount of growth with limited success, a small difference between two pages by the same team. [S4][S5] The second experiment suspended a 3D-printed egg containing only a temperature and humidity sensor under an armpit for 48 hours and found hourly readings staying within 25 to 35 degrees Celsius, which the team gives as the mold’s ideal range. [S4]

The team then added sensors for temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide and volatile compounds, a probe inside the rice, and a color sensor. It reports that overheating inside the rice clump made koji prone to contamination, that the color sensor gave a confusing reading, and that this led to a transparent chamber for direct viewing. [S4] The final proof of concept carried the chamber under the arm for 60 hours at an ambient temperature of about 16 degrees Celsius, and the team reports the result was as fragrant and tasty as koji from a traditional incubator, though growth took slightly longer. [S4][S5] Those are the team’s findings, from a handful of runs, and sample sizes are small: the sensor graph for the third experiment shows an average for three replicates. [S4]

The resources page describes two versions. The Essentials version is portable, with an air temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide and volatile-compound module, an OLED screen, three buttons and an ESP32-C3 microcontroller, and the team says it has been built and works. The Advanced version has more sensors, was made for the Biodesign Challenge finals, and is not yet portable. [S6] The DDW listing does not say which version will be shown, and it notes that the casing is being redesigned. [S1][S6] The project site also invites visitors to signal interest to help decide whether to produce the device, so it is a prototype and not a product. [S2]
What happened when people set it up

The user-studies page records an interaction session in which participants smelled, touched and optionally tasted koji, and were then invited to set up the device themselves with grains of their choice and a prop for spores, which was rice flour, and to choose where on the body to wear it. [S3] Most preferred the upper or lower abdomen. Most were excited by futuristic biodesign but wary of contamination and allergy. Many were reluctant to touch koji rice again after learning it was moldy rice, and they preferred white koji over black and green varieties, which looked too dangerous. [S3]

The finding that matters most for care sits in one line: not a single participant considered or attempted to work in a sterile manner while setting up the device. [S3] As a medical educator, I do not find that surprising. Sterile technique is a skill that is taught by demonstration and checked, and an organism that needs it will not be looked after properly because someone has been given a friendly avatar. That is my reading, and the team does not draw that conclusion. [S3]

The online survey gives numbers that do not agree between pages. The user-studies page reports that 84.78 percent of respondents were curious or fully comfortable with contributing body heat, breath or sweat to power microbial growth, that over 95 percent were comfortable using products containing living microorganisms, and that 39.13 percent would trust food fermented by such a device. [S3] The product-design page says 90 percent of 41 online respondents expressed curiosity or comfort. [S5] The percentages on the first page are what 39 of 46 and 18 of 46 respondents would give, which is my arithmetic and not a figure the team states, so the number of respondents is probably 46 rather than 41. The pages do not resolve it. [S3][S5]
Is the mold safe to live with

The question people raised, contamination and allergy, is a fair one, and the literature gives a limited answer. A review by Frisvad and colleagues in Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology in 2018 says Aspergillus oryzae, like the other industrial workhorses it covers, has a long history of safe use for enzyme production, that it has been wrongly reported as an aflatoxin producer because strains of the related Aspergillus flavus were misclassified, and that production strains should be checked so they cannot make mycotoxins. [S8] That is a statement about industrial strains. It is not a safety assessment of a body-worn chamber, of spores bought online and used by novices, or of what grows if the culture goes wrong. [S5][S8] The team’s own notes mention that overheating makes contamination likelier and that mold color is a cue to contamination. [S4][S5]

The resources page says the guidebook teaches principles of cleanliness and optimal conditions through do’s and don’ts, and that it encourages users to rely on smell and observation. [S6] I did not see the guidebook text. I also found no Dutch or other school guidance on culturing this mold in a primary-school classroom, either permitting or advising against it, so I cannot say how a teacher would be expected to handle it. [S1]
Where the device sits between exhibit and clothing

The device is carried in a harness, and the team gave the casing three hoops so users can choose how to carry it. [S5] It is a body-worn object, but the pages I read describe a wearable, never a garment, and the team’s tests had it under the arm for two days or more, which no ordinary garment is asked to do. [S4][S5] The team describes participants choosing the abdomen. [S3] The question I raised in the title is therefore about a device and a routine and not about a garment. What does a person do when the temperature in the chamber leaves the range, when they need to change activity, or when they want to stop? The pages describe the avatar’s prompts and the sensors that trigger them. They do not describe an exit. [S2][S5]

Care has an end as well as a beginning. The product-design page says the aim is to ease users into nurturing a living entity, and that the Tamagotchi format avoids extreme direct exposure to microbes. [S5] It also describes the end of the story as fermented food, since koji is the base of miso, soy sauce and sake. [S2] Whether a visitor, a pupil or a home user is meant to eat what grows is not stated, and the survey suggests that many would want more assurance of cleanliness before they did. [S3]
What the studies can and cannot show

The team plans education in primary schools, asking why children should learn to care only for plants and not for microbes. [S5] The user studies I read involved adults who set up a prop and survey respondents; the pages do not describe children, a classroom, or any measure of what anyone learned. [S3] Reaction, curiosity and stated comfort are real findings. They are not evidence that wearing the device teaches care, or that a beginner can keep a live culture healthy. [S3][S5]

This is a design proposition. KojiGotchi offers a reason to ask what a technology asks from a body, a schedule and a person’s attention, and the team deserves credit for publishing the awkward results. [S3][S4] The ordinary routine is where a proposed future has to introduce itself, and a reader deserves enough information there to decide whether they want the relationship.
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibit or worn the device, and the listing and project pages are the team’s descriptions. [S1][S2]

I do not know which version will be shown, how the redesigned casing differs, what the guidebook says, whether the DDW exhibit will contain live koji or a prop, or how it will be supervised. I found no independent review of the device, no safety assessment of body-worn cultivation, and no study of children using it. [S1][S3][S6]
The two pages disagree on the survey size and on the first experiment, and I could not tell which is right. [S3][S4][S5]
If you were handed a living thing to carry for two days, what would you want to be told about the moment you need to put it down? [S5]

title: Your material has a biography. Where is it?
subtitle: Biomaterials Library brings a Baltic selection to Eindhoven. The public record of one coffee-ground tile shows what a material biography keeps, and what it still leaves out.
description: Biomaterials Library at DDW 2026 and the coffee tiles in it: what the public record keeps about a material's origin, and what it leaves out.

sections.x: I can see the surface. I want to know how it got here. [S2]

That question comes up whenever a material arrives in an exhibition looking wonderfully self-contained: a tile, a sheet, a small object that makes you stop scrolling. The description names an ingredient, coffee waste or a plant or something that would otherwise have been discarded, and a complicated history becomes a beautifully short sentence. I understand the appeal. I also want the longer sentence: who had the ingredient before the designer did, what condition it was in, what happened between collecting it and making this object, and which parts of that history somebody else can check. [S2][S5]

Biomaterials Library: Lithuanian & Baltic Creators is a good place to ask, because the library says its job is to keep that longer sentence. I have not seen the exhibition, and I interviewed nobody. This essay reads the library’s own pages, the Dutch Design Week listing, one published record of a single material from the show, the EU waste rules that decide what coffee grounds are, and an open recipe database for comparison. [S1][S2][S5][S6][S8]
What the library says it keeps

The library’s about page calls it the first publicly accessible physical collection of its kind in the Baltic States, based at SODAS 2123 in Vilnius and continuously expanding online. It says materials are presented not only as finished surfaces or objects but through their biological, renewable or waste-derived sources, transformation processes, properties, possible applications and end-of-life pathways, and that its work includes open recipes. It names its founder and curator, Austėja Platūkytė, the organizing NGO Medžiagotyra, and the support of the Lithuanian Council for Culture. [S1] That is a stated ambition and it matches a biography: a sample with a source, a process and an end. The page does not describe how a sample is recorded, what a record contains, or who checks it. [S1]

The Dutch Design Week listing for 2026 repeats the idea in curatorial language. It calls the library a growing archive of material experiments that preserves stages of development, from early tests and samples to refined applications and design objects, and says each material carries knowledge about its ingredients, processes, failures and possibilities. [S2] The exhibition is free, at BioArt Laboratories, Strijp T+R, building A1, open October 17 to 25, 2026, and it presents a curated selection by Lithuanian and Baltic creators working with agricultural, food and industrial side streams, mycelium, algae and natural fibers. The page names five works: Amber Waste is Bliss by Agnė Kučerenkaitė, Vegetative Textiles by Indrė Spitrytė-Mikuckė, Coffee Waste Tiles by Waste Matters Studio, Giria by Evelina Kudabaitė and Pine Skins by Sarmite Polakova. [S2]

A note on dates. Another copy of the exhibition’s page, on DDW’s older site address and with no date, carries nearly the same text and the same four credited images. [S3] I found no 2025 archive version of the listing on the festival’s archive path, so I treat that copy as a mirror of the 2026 program page and not as proof of an earlier showing. [S2][S3]
One record: the coffee tiles

The most useful public record of a single work from the show is a materials-directory entry for the Coffee Waste Tiles by Waste Matters Studio, published on MaterialDistrict on November 11, 2025 under the code ONA1148. It says the tiles are made from locally collected coffee grounds bound with natural bio-resins, handcrafted, with variation in tone from piece to piece. It says they are thermoplastic biocomposites that can be cast, layered or hand-formed and are re-meltable for reprocessing, and lists suitable uses as wall panels, decorative surfaces and tableware. It calls the tiles low-emission and biodegradable. [S5]

The studio’s description gives part of the biography. It says the studio works directly with local cafés, restaurants and food producers; that the residues, such as coffee grounds and fruit peels, are cleaned, dried, ground and turned into bio-resin-based thermoplastic composites; and that each material is developed and produced in-house, for transparency from waste collection to final application. [S5] The same page rates the material’s fire resistance as poor, its UV and weather resistance as good, and its scratch and chemical resistance as moderate. [S5]

What the entry leaves out is the ingredient that is not coffee. “Natural bio-resins” does not say which resin, in what proportion, or from what source. The grounds come from “local cafés,” and the page names none, gives no batch, and states no test behind “low-emission” or “biodegradable.” [S5] A re-meltable thermoplastic and a biodegradable one are different claims, and the essay on biodegradation I wrote for this series asks the same question about another material: where, over what period, and on what evidence. I flag the gap and do not suggest the tiles fail either test, since I found nothing that tests them. [S5]

One more fact belongs in any honest provenance note. MaterialDistrict says Waste Matters Studio was founded by Austėja Platūkytė, who is also the founder and curator of the Biomaterials Library and the curator of this exhibition. [S2][S5] That does not weaken the work. It does mean that the library, the studio and the exhibition share a person, and a reader weighing the library’s description of its collection should know that.
What makes coffee grounds waste

“Coffee waste” sounds like a category, and in law it is one. The EU Waste Framework Directive, in its consolidated text of July 5, 2018, says a substance resulting from a production process whose primary aim is not to produce that substance is a by-product and not waste only if four conditions are met: further use is certain, it can be used directly without processing beyond normal industrial practice, it is produced as an integral part of a production process, and the further use is lawful. [S6] A separate article sets conditions for waste to stop being waste after recovery: use for specific purposes, a market or demand, compliance with technical requirements and product standards, and no overall adverse environmental or human health impact. [S6]

I found nothing that says how the grounds in this studio’s tiles are classified, and the directive does not decide it for café grounds in general. What it shows is that “collected from cafés” and “cleaned, dried, ground” are not neutral phrases. Whether a café’s grounds are waste handed over, or a by-product with a certain further use, affects who may collect them, how they travel and what a biography would have to record. [S5][S6] I am describing the text and not advising on any case.
Two other works, as far as the record goes

Two more works on the list have public accounts that show the same pattern. Sarmite Polakova’s Pine Skins is described in a 2022 profile in Lampoon magazine as a leather-like material from pine bark. The profile says her studio received a Worth Partnership grant in 2019 and worked with a network of Latvian tree cutters and with the Spanish wood manufacturer Seistag, that the bark goes through cleaning, softening and waxing with natural ingredients, and that its width and structure are limits she works within. [S9] The same profile quotes her saying she extracts the bark herself and that it is not regularly harvested, which sits beside the line about a network of tree cutters without settling how the two fit. [S9]

Evelina Kudabaitė’s Giria is described by the Lithuanian Culture Institute as a tree-bark homeware project first presented in 2015 as her bachelor’s thesis at the Vilnius Academy of Arts, made from bark dust from different sawmills with an organic binder she found with traditional craftsmen. [S10] Both accounts name a type of supplier, tree cutters or sawmills, and neither names one supplier. Giria’s binder, like the coffee tiles’ resin, is described and not identified. [S10] I found no public record under the title Vegetative Textiles. [S2]
Two ways to choose a supply

Another exhibitor’s public record shows a different logic. Agnė Kučerenkaitė’s Ignorance is Bliss project, entered for a New European Bauhaus prize, glazes ceramic tiles with pigments derived from industrial metal waste, with up to 40 percent waste in the glaze. The entry says it focuses on industrial waste and by-products because they are usually consistent, giving a reliable and qualitative supply, whereas secondary materials from other sources are often contaminated and therefore dumped or downcycled. [S7] A designer who collects from cafés and one who works with industrial residues are making different bets about consistency, and each bet leaves a different trace in a record. That is my comparison and not the authors’. [S5][S7] It also shows why “made from waste” cannot stand alone: the kind of waste, and how it was secured, is part of the material.
Open recipes and what they do not replace

The library says its work includes open recipes. [S1] Open databases of biomaterial recipes do exist: Materiom describes an open-access database of recipes covering what they are made of, how they are made and their performance properties. [S8] A recipe tells another maker what to try. A biography tells a reader what happened to one sample. The two overlap but they are not the same document, because a recipe describes a repeatable process while a sample carries the accidents of one batch. I could not find whether the library publishes recipes for the works in this exhibition. [S1][S8]
What the photograph should carry

A close-up shows texture and a wider shot shows scale, and neither proves the object’s history. A photograph can pair the appealing surface with something less glamorous: a sample identifier, a labeled input, a dated process stage. The MaterialDistrict entry shows the minimum a public record can have, which is a code, a date, a maker and a list of properties. [S5] A caption could add what the entry lacks: which resin, which batch of grounds, and who vouches for the claim.
What the record does not show
I have not seen the exhibition, and the program page and the library’s own pages are the organizers’ descriptions. [S1][S2]

I do not know how the library records a sample, whether the exhibited works have identifiers, which resin binds the coffee tiles, which cafés supply the grounds, or how the tiles’ low-emission and biodegradable claims were tested. I could not open the studio’s own website or the library’s sample records. [S1][S4][S5]
I found no source on the history of any other exhibited work, and the five names on the DDW page are the only works I can identify. [S2]
The test I would apply is simple. After reading an account, could someone say where this particular sample came from, what changed it, and what we still do not know? [S2]
