title: Who does your website depend on?
subtitle: Studio Falkland's Dutch Design Week project counts the providers behind thousands of Dutch organizations. Its method, its open code, two real cases and a 2026 court ruling show what a dependency map can and cannot say.
description: What Studio Falkland's Dutch Design Week project measures, how its method works, and what the ICC and Solvinity cases show about dependence.

sections.x: On the project's own site, 65 percent of Dutch government organizations point their email at Microsoft's outlook.com, and the same page gives 70 percent for companies, 63 percent for education and 48 percent for healthcare. [S6]

Those figures come from Zijn we al autonoom? (Are we autonomous yet?), a project by the Eindhoven design studio Studio Falkland that is in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program. This essay reads how the number is made, what the red button in the project does, what two real cases of dependence look like in the record, and what a reader should ask before repeating a conclusion. It uses published sources only: the studio's pages, its open repository, standards documents, a ruling and press reports. It reports no visit and no interview, and it does not rerun the project's measurements. Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026. [S1][S3][S5][S8]
What the exhibition is

The program lists Are we autonomous yet? as a free exhibition at Gebouw SFF (Bosch) on Strijp-S, hosted by Studio Falkland, and describes it as visualizing how dependent the Netherlands is on non-European digital services. [S1] It asks what would happen if, with one press of a button, the US President disabled all US-based digital services for Dutch organizations, and says visitors will help co-create a map of their personal dependence. It also says the exhibition kicks off a year-long collaboration with the journalistic collective Vers Beton and data journalist Sytze Simonse, with SIDN Labs contributing research on internet protocols and infrastructure. [S1]

Studio Falkland describes itself as a design studio for internet technology and personal data in Eindhoven. Its page lists earlier work shown at Dutch Design Week, among them Aeon in 2020 and 2021, Packet Run in 2023, made by BMD Studio with SIDN Labs and developed further by Falkland, and ApathOS in 2025 at the Next Nature Museum. [S2] The project's own About page says it was developed as part of the call Internet Infrastructuur in Beeld from SIDN Fonds, in which design teams work with SIDN Labs on visualizations of the internet, and that it is a research project working from public data. [S4]
How a dependency gets counted

The Sources page is specific. The team keeps a database of organizations and their URLs, categorized by sector and location. It aims to recheck all URLs monthly: it performs DNS lookups of MX records, which name the mail servers, and A records, which give web server addresses, then does reverse lookups on the IP addresses to find the provider and the autonomous system number, and aggregates the results. [S5] It says the data is collected with the greatest care, that errors are unavoidable at this size, and that the aim is a large-scale picture of dependence. [S5]

Two details in that method matter. An MX record names a mail relay. The standard for mail transfer says a relay server is usually the target of an MX record rather than the final delivery system, and may pass the mail on. [S14] So a measurement of the MX host tells you the first hop, and a filtering service or forwarder in front of another provider would be counted as the provider. I have no evidence that this distorts any particular figure. It is the kind of thing a method note should state. And the country assigned to a provider comes from registry data: the CAIDA dataset the project uses infers a mapping from autonomous systems to organizations by processing WHOIS records from the regional internet registries. [S13][S5]

The input lists differ by sector. Government organizations come from the national register of government organizations and the register of government internet domains. Schools come from the education agency DUO's open data. The 500 largest companies come from an Elsevier ranking. Healthcare organizations come from OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API. The whole .nl domain comes from a SIDN Labs export. [S5] The page also lists when each dataset was last updated. The .nl datasets show February 17, 2025, the Elsevier list December 12, 2024, the OpenStreetMap pull March 4, 2026, the government and education lists June 9, 2026, and the CAIDA and IPInfo files September 23, 2026. [S5] A reader comparing sectors is comparing different vintages built from different kinds of list.
What the numbers add up to

The home page gives each sector a count and a concentration label. Email: government 533 organizations, healthcare 2,304, education 5,277, companies 488. Web hosting: government 557, healthcare 2,435, education 5,869, companies 496. [S3] Those four rows add up to 8,602 organizations for email and 9,357 for web hosting. The listing's "about 10.000" is therefore a round figure. [S1][S3] The page separately reports the whole .nl domain as 3,519,094 entries for email and 5,756,751 for web hosting, a different unit from an organization. [S3]

The concentration label uses the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, which the US merger guidelines define as the sum of the squares of market shares, reaching 10,000 for a single firm. [S16] The project's code labels 5,000 and above monopoly, 4,000 and above oligopoly, 2,500 and above high concentration, 1,500 and above moderate concentration, and anything lower competitive. [S10] The 1,500 and 2,500 cutoffs match the bands in the 2010 US Horizontal Merger Guidelines. The 2023 guidelines moved the line for a highly concentrated market to 1,800. [S15][S16] The words monopoly and oligopoly are the project's own, since by the guidelines' definition an index of 10,000 is a single firm. Those guidelines apply the index to shares of a market in merger review, and the project applies it to counts of measured URLs per provider. [S16][S11]

I checked whether the pages agree with each other. A provider with a 65 percent share contributes 4,225 points on its own, and the government email index is 4,350. Education at 63 percent gives 3,969 against 4,347. Companies at 70 percent give 4,900 against 5,054, and healthcare at 48 percent gives 2,304 against 2,410. [S6][S3] The remainders are small shares from other providers. The numbers cohere. The sector breakdown of government email shows how small groups behave: 292 municipalities score 5,798, 17 water boards 6,886, 11 ministries 2,727 and 5 provinces 6,800. [S7] An index computed on five organizations moves a great deal with a single change.

The code also shows what is counted. The frequency query starts from organizations and their URLs, takes the latest measurement for each URL, counts how often each provider's autonomous system occurs and drops unmeasured organizations unless asked to include them. [S11] An organization with several URLs therefore counts several times, and one with no usable measurement counts not at all. That is a choice, and a reasonable one for a large-scale picture, but it means the index describes the spread of measured addresses and not the share of mailboxes, traffic or services.
What the red button does

In the interface code, the red button is a toggle. Pressing it flips a state value, and the helper that colors a measurement returns red when the measurement's autonomous-system country code is US and blue otherwise. [S9] The Dutch label on the button is Grote rode knop, the big red button. [S3] On the live site I read, the effect I can verify from the code is a change of presentation based on that country code. I did not find in the files I read a model of which services fail, for how long, or what an affected organization could do instead. The listing frames the button as a simulation of denied access, and it should be read as a way to see the US-coded share, not as a forecast of an outage. [S1][S9]

The word "US" in that code is a country code attached to an autonomous system. It is not a statement about who controls a contract, where data sits or which law reaches it. The next two cases show why that difference matters. [S9][S13]
Two cases from the record

The first is the one the listing itself cites. It says that "in June of last year" a US executive order disabled email and document access to the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court. [S1] The record I could read is different in dates and in mechanism. Executive Order 14203, "Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court," was signed on February 6, 2025, and on February 13, 2025 the US Treasury's sanctions office added Prosecutor Karim Khan to its sanctions list under it. [S17] In May 2025 the news agency AP reported, as relayed by the German outlet heise, that Microsoft had blocked Khan's email account, forcing him to switch to the Swiss provider Proton, according to ICC employees. [S19] Microsoft's president Brad Smith then said the company had neither terminated nor suspended its services to the court, and a spokesperson said Microsoft had been in contact with the court since February throughout the process that led to excluding the sanctioned official from Microsoft services. [S18] So the order imposed sanctions, the disconnection of one official followed in the way Microsoft describes it, and the company disputes any wider cutoff. The listing's sentence compresses that sequence, and its date does not match the sources I found. I could not see the studio's own source for it.

The second case is Dutch and recent. On May 25, 2026, the State Secretary for Economic Affairs, acting on advice from the investment screening office BTI, banned the takeover of the cloud company Solvinity, which stores the data DigiD uses, by the US company Kyndryl. The ban rests on Article 14a.4 of the Telecommunications Act. [S20][S21] The ruling of the Rotterdam court on July 14, 2026 recounts the State Secretary's reasoning: that US law has extraterritorial reach over data held by US companies, naming the CLOUD Act, FISA and other statutes, that a US-based owner could be compelled to hand over data even from European servers, often under a gag order, and that this made a threat to the public interest. [S21] The court did not decide the merits. It refused to suspend the ban while the objection is pending, because the parties could wait for the decision without irreversible consequences, and it rejected the argument that the State Secretary lacked authority. [S22][S21] The State Secretary promised a decision on the objection at the end of September, and I found no report that it has been issued. [S22]

Set beside the dependency map, the Solvinity case shows the gap between network registration and control. NOS describes Solvinity as originally Dutch and by then in British hands, and the legal concern was about a US parent, not about where the servers were. [S20][S21] A map keyed to the country of an autonomous system could not see that change until the ownership showed up in registry data.
Asking the question of one site

The same questions can be asked at small scale of a site the reader is allowed to inspect. Which records point where, and when was that checked? Is the first hop a relay for something else? What would a visitor be unable to do if one service failed, and what evidence exists of a fallback? The project's own method gives a template: say what was looked up, on what date, from which data, and which consequence the lookup supports. [S5][S14] A named example from a real site would need the owner's permission to publish, so I give none.
What the record does not show

I did not rerun any measurement, and the project says its dataset is not currently available for reuse, though the code is open under the EUPL-1.2 license and its extraction step depends partly on non-public inputs. [S8][S12] The site is labeled beta. [S3] I do not know how many of the government, healthcare or education organizations use a filtering relay in front of another provider. The healthcare list rests on OpenStreetMap coverage. [S5] The red-button behavior is from the interface code, not from the exhibition build. [S9] The studio's source for the ICC sentence in its listing is unknown to me. [S1] The court's summary of the State Secretary's reasoning is the State Secretary's reasoning, and the court did not rule on it. [S21] I did not check the objection decision beyond the sources named.

The question I would take to the exhibit is the practical one. For the one dependency that matters most to you, what is the evidence of who controls it, and what is the date of that evidence? [S5][S21]

title: A workshop is a form of publishing
subtitle: Atelier Fig brings its Fringe technique to Dutch Design Week 2026. What a visitor can learn there, what the studio has already published, and what showing a practice gives away.
description: Atelier Fig brings Fringe to Dutch Design Week 2026. What a visitor can learn there and what showing a practice gives away.

sections.x: Entry to Atelier Fig's Dutch Design Week exhibition is free, and the personal presentation by one of its founders sits inside a breakfast ticket priced at 38.29 euros. [S1][S7]

That pairing is the practical version of this essay's argument. A workshop that opens to the public is a publication, in the sense that it arranges knowledge for an audience, and every publisher decides what is free, what is framed and what stays unsaid. This essay reads the studio's own pages, the festival listing, a note on how skill is classed as knowledge, and two European legal texts on what exposure does to a design and to a trade secret. It uses published sources only. It reports no tour, no visit and no interview, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026. [S1][S3][S9][S10][S11]
What is on offer

The program lists Atelier Fig. Presents Fringe as a free solo exhibition at Hallenweg 11 in Eindhoven, with the studio bringing its workshop to the festival to show how the Fringe technique evolves from experiment into objects, tableware and furniture. [S1] The text says Fringe emerged from experiments in cutting material with self-developed tools, that it is shown for the first time as the studio's whole practice in one presentation, and that experiments, tools, material studies and finished pieces are presented together so the development behind the collection is visible. [S1] It names two new works: Fringe Tableware 2.0, produced in collaboration with Studio Zand in Amersfoort, and the studio's largest work to date, a cabinet that carries the technique to a larger scale. [S1] The listing records the venue as tactile, with dogs allowed and full wheelchair access. [S1]

On the first weekend, October 17 and 18, the studio hosts Breakfast at Atelier Fig: an extensive breakfast by Atelier Nori, coffee and latte art by Ruben, and a personal tour with Gijs, with tickets sold on the studio's website. [S1] The ticketing page gives the times as 09:30 to 11:00 on both mornings and the price as 38.29 euros, marked with an asterisk I could not explain. It describes an aperitif, a buffet, freshly prepared coffee and an intimate presentation by Gijs on the materials, experiments and craftsmanship behind the new collections. [S7] So the tour is not a free add-on to the exhibition. It is part of a ticketed event on two mornings. Nothing I read lists a hands-on making session, and the listing never calls the exhibition a class. [S1][S7]

The studio's home page describes Atelier Fig as a design studio where material research, experimentation and craftsmanship come together to create objects, collections and spatial applications. [S2] Its own About page names the founders, Ruben Hoogvliet and Gijs Wouters, who met at the ArtEZ art academy in Arnhem. [S3] The first names match those in the listing, which I take to be the same people without a source that says so. The page lists an earlier Dutch Design Week show in 2022, Messmerizing, and a Rising Talent Award from Maison & Objet that year. [S3] It states an aim that bears on this essay: the studio's aesthetic experience raises awareness of the tactility and transformation within the creative process and shows what often remains unexposed. [S3]
What the studio has already published

Publication already exists in small form on the studio's product pages. The Fringe coffee mug page says the mug is handmade in the studio in the Netherlands from high-quality stoneware with a matt glaze, part of a tableware collection with a tactile appearance that is rough yet refined. [S4] The Square Vase page describes porcelain Ikebana vases made with the studio's dip technique and a method it says it is currently exploring, kurinuki, a traditional Japanese carving approach, in an edition of five. [S5] The frame cabinets page describes beechwood beams of 2.5 by 2.5 centimeters, milled to slide over handmade metal dowels, inspired by a linen cupboard of Gijs's grandmother. [S6] I do not claim that the frame cabinet is the cabinet in the exhibition, because the listing does not say so.

What I did not find on any of these pages is a description of the Fringe cutting tools or of the cutting action. [S1][S4][S6] The listing says the tools exist and that they will be shown. The record in public text names a result, a material and in some cases a method, and leaves the tool itself to the room.
One earlier technique, three published accounts

The studio's earlier Gravity collection shows how a technique gets published once it leaves the studio. The studio's own page says it makes work by immersing moisture-absorbing structures in liquid clay and leaving the clay-soaked forms to drip-dry, and that gravity always has the final say, so that each piece differs. [S12] A product page for one of its porcelain figures lists the material as porcelain with a glaze and engobe finish. [S13] In a Maison&Objet Rising Talent report carried by a design magazine, the studio is described as building each object's drippy coating of liquid clay over a foam armature that is consumed during firing, with Wouters saying the porcelain is extremely thin and the technique is at the limit of what is possible. [S14] A 2024 article in the Italian magazine IFDM says the clay-soaked forms are left to dry without kilns, under gravity. [S15]

Those accounts do not quite agree about firing, and the public text cannot settle it. Glazed porcelain objects are normally fired, which I take as general ceramic knowledge and not as something these sources say, so the IFDM sentence most likely describes the drying stage. [S13][S15] The point for this essay is that the studio's own page publishes a principle and leaves out the armature and the firing, and the press fills the gap differently. A technique published in outline gets completed by others.
Show, tell and teach

Philosophers separate knowing that from knowing how. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on knowledge-how says it is customary to add, beside knowledge of facts, a kind of knowledge possessed when one can be truly described as knowing how to do something, such as play the piano or make a pie, and that Ryle's 1949 argument that this differs from knowing facts has been contested and revived in the last twenty years. [S9] I draw only a modest point from that: whether a skill can be fully put into sentences is an open question among specialists. A workshop can publish what a methods page cannot. It can let a visitor see an adjustment that a maker makes without announcing it, and it can leave the visitor with a feeling for the material that no caption holds. A visitor who watches a repeated operation learns what the operation looks like. Whether the visitor learns to do it depends on a form of invitation the listing does not offer.

The editorial decisions follow from that. A maker who shows a tool beside the mark it leaves has chosen to publish a relationship. A maker who shows only finished pieces has chosen to publish results. Starting from the objects makes the earlier experiments look like inevitable steps, and starting from the uncertain experiment makes the objects look like one answer among several. The listing's phrase, a technique evolving through research, chance and repetition, signals an intention to show the second order, and the exhibition itself will show whether it does. [S1]
What showing gives away

Showing a practice in public has legal consequences, and the texts are older than the debate about workshops. The Community designs Regulation of 2002 treats a design as made available to the public if it has been exhibited, used in trade or otherwise disclosed in a way that could reasonably have become known to the specialist circles in the sector within the Union. [S10] It gives the designer a 12-month period before filing a registered design during which the designer's own disclosure is not held against it, and it protects an unregistered design for three years from first making it available, though only against copying. [S10] It excludes features of appearance dictated solely by technical function. [S10] The Regulation protects how a product looks. It does not protect a cutting technique as such, and the 2002 text has since been amended by a design reform, so the current wording needs checking. [S10]

The Trade Secrets Directive of 2016 covers the other kind of knowledge. It defines a trade secret as information that is secret, has commercial value because it is secret, and has been subject to reasonable steps by the person in lawful control to keep it secret. [S11] Its preamble says reverse engineering of a lawfully acquired product is a lawful way to acquire information unless contractually agreed otherwise. [S11] I do not say what Atelier Fig has filed, or what it considers secret, because I do not know. The two texts make a general point. What a studio shows in a room, and what it sells as an object, begins to leave its control, and each studio decides in advance how much that matters.
Credit and collaboration

The listing credits Studio Zand in Amersfoort as the collaborator for Fringe Tableware 2.0. [S1] The gallery that announced the 2026 Van Achterbergh Prize describes studioZAND as the joint studio of Frans Ottink and Erna Huppelschoten in Amersfoort, says Ottink has designed functional ceramics and porcelain tableware in editions in his own workshop since 1989, and says Huppelschoten makes jewelry from porcelain, silver and other materials. [S8] I take the two names to be the same studio, spelled differently, and note the assumption. Neither page says which stage of making each studio carried out. The listing's word, produced in collaboration, covers a wide range. [S1][S8] A credit that said who developed the glaze, who made the molds and who fired the pieces would tell a visitor more than a studio name alone.

The breakfast has its own credits. Atelier Nori provides the food, Ruben the coffee and Gijs the presentation. [S1][S7] A reader asking who is publishing what should note that the part of the event that explains the work is also the part the studio sells.
What the record does not show

I did not see the exhibition. The listing does not say whether any activity beyond watching and the ticketed presentation is offered. [S1] It does not describe the Fringe tools, the materials the technique cuts or the cabinet's construction. [S1] The ticket price comes from a ticketing page I read on October 10, 2026, and the asterisk beside it is unexplained. [S7] The legal paragraphs describe the 2002 Regulation and the 2016 Directive as published, and say nothing about the studio's own filings or agreements. [S10][S11] The studioZAND details come from a gallery's announcement, not from the studio. [S8]

The question I would take to the room is the one the studio's own description invites. For one operation shown or explained, what would a stranger need in order to describe it accurately tomorrow, and what has the maker chosen not to say? [S3][S12]

title: The field is only the beginning of the hemp story
subtitle: A Prague textile studio's hemp show at Dutch Design Week 2026, the processing steps between a plant and a yarn, and what Czech and European records say about who can do that work.
description: What a Prague hemp show at Dutch Design Week, a processing review and Czech and EU records say about the work between field and yarn.

sections.x: In the Czech Republic the harvested area of hemp was 124.56 hectares in 2024, down from 550.78 in 2019, according to the customs administration that collects the grower data. [S7]

That is the background to a hemp exhibition from Prague. The page for SOW HEMP!, hosted by the Prague academy UMPRUM and in the Dutch Design Week 2026 program, says hemp cultivation is on the rise, and also says that in the Czech Republic hemp fiber is not processed for the textile industry. [S1] The distance between a field and a yarn is made of equipment, people and decisions, and this essay follows what the public record says about it. It uses published sources only. It reports no visit and no interview, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026. [S1][S5][S7]
What the exhibition says

The program lists SOW HEMP! at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 25, 2026, with a Dutch Design Week ticket required. [S1] The same text, with the same contributors, also sits at an older site.ddw.nl address, which could be mistaken for an archive page, but the current ddw.nl page carries the 2026 dates and venue, so this is a live 2026 listing and not an account from an earlier festival. [S1][S2]

The text is plain about its raw material. Hemp is mainly grown for seeds, blooms and hempcrete; with new legislation in favor of hemp and more demand for local and sustainable materials, cultivation is on the rise. It adds that in the country hemp fiber is not processed for the textile industry, and that one farm managed to build scutching machinery from scratch to get short hemp fibers. [S1] The Studio of Textile took this chance to work with a non-textile material and explored possibilities beyond clothing. [S1] Students worked with yarn and other hemp materials, fibers and shives, which the text also calls hurds, in processes it lists: dissolving fiber into bioplastic, felting, spinning and carding hemp with wool, traditional tapestry weaving and fusing raw fibers with a digital embroidery machine. [S1] Separately, a research project with the weaving mill Kubák asked whether a local hemp and wool blend could become an industrial yarn, and the page says the resulting yarn, made by a local weaving mill, met the qualities needed for architecture and interior design. [S1]
The steps between plant and yarn

A 2022 review in the journal Materials by Małgorzata Zimniewska lays out the chain that such a project depends on. Fiber has to be separated from the woody part of the stem. Retting, a biological process in which microorganisms degrade the pectin and other compounds that bind the fibers to the stem, is the usual first step, and the method chosen determines fiber quality. [S5] Dew retting on the field is the most common method and the cheapest, needing no special equipment, but its parameters cannot be controlled, so duration and yield depend on weather. [S5] Water retting was historically common and was largely replaced because of its environmental cost, and enzymatic, chemical and physical methods are newer. [S5] The alternative is to decorticate the stalks mechanically without retting, which the review says gives bundles of lower quality and high impurity, unsuitable for textiles unless degummed afterward. [S5]

After retting come breaking and scutching to separate fiber from the woody parts. Long scutched fibers go on to hackling for high-quality textiles. The short fibers created during scutching have to be carded to prepare thicker yarns for thick fabrics such as upholstery and other woven applications. [S5] The review then describes the spinning options: cottonized hemp can be spun alone or blended with other cotton-like fibers on a cotton system, and wool-like hemp fibers can be mixed with wool and processed on the woolen system. [S5] It adds a trade-off: yarn from cottonized fibers is of lower uniformity and strength than yarn from long fibers, and the cottonization process costs hemp some of its inherent properties, such as high tensile strength and cool touch. [S5]

Read against that, the exhibition's account is coherent. Short fibers from a scutching step, carded and blended with wool, are the kind of input that reaches a woolen spinning system, and a thicker yarn for interiors is the kind of use the review names. [S1][S5] That is my reading of two documents. It is not a description of what the farm, the mill or the students actually did. The page does not say which fibers went into the yarn, in what proportion, by which spinning system, or what tests it met. [S1]

The scale of the whole chain is small. The review puts world production of hemp fiber and tow at 60,000 tons in 2019, 1.7 percent of natural fibers and 0.05 percent of all textile fiber production. [S5] The European Commission's hemp page reports that EU hemp area for fiber rose from 20,540 hectares in 2015 to 33,020 in 2022 and production from 97,130 tonnes to 179,020 tonnes, with France accounting for more than 60 percent of EU production, Germany 17 percent and the Netherlands 5 percent. [S6]
What the Czech record shows about capacity

The Czech customs administration publishes the grower statistics. Its March 2025 sheet gives harvested hemp area of 550.78 hectares in 2019, 280.01 in 2022, 167.95 in 2023 and 124.56 in 2024, with 57, 102, 67 and 49 growers in those years, and gives the 2024 area sown as 128.67 hectares. The table is untidy: 2017 and 2018 each appear twice, with 2018 at 670.04 hectares in one place and 437.03 in another, and 2020 and 2021 are missing. I rely only on the entries that appear once. [S7] The series falls from 2022 to 2024. The page's sentence that cultivation is on the rise matches the EU series to 2022 and does not match the Czech customs series after 2022. [S1][S6][S7] The text may mean something else, and a sentence about a trend needs a year attached.

A grower interviewed by Forbes Czech Republic in October 2018 describes the bottleneck in the terms of this chain. Václav Říha of Hemp Production, vice chairman of the Czech flax and hemp association, said the alpha and omega of growing hemp in Czechia is a line that splits the stem into fiber and shives, and a harvester converted for hemp, of which they had one, used abroad. He said one of the last stem-processing lines in the country, near Příbram, was idle for want of a part, and that the area had gone from 1,500 hectares ten years earlier to 100 and then back to about 600. [S8] That is one grower in 2018, and the roughly 600 hectares he gave lies between the two 2018 values in the customs sheet. [S7][S8] It is the nearest independent description I found of the missing middle that the exhibition page names, and it does not identify the farm in the exhibition.

The legal frame differs by level. The European Commission says hemp complying with the common agricultural policy must have a THC content not exceeding 0.3 percent, and that growers of such varieties are eligible for area-based direct payments. [S6] A law firm's overview says the Czech definition of industrial hemp is a THC content not exceeding 1 percent of dry matter, applied since 2022, and that cultivating over 100 square meters requires notification to the customs office. [S9] I draw no inference about the exhibition, which says only that new legislation favors hemp. [S1]
Who made the next step possible

The page names a farm without a name, a weaving mill in one sentence and a studio. UMPRUM's 2024 page for its wool show, shown at Dutch Design Week from October 19 to 27, 2024, thanks the Weaving factory Kubák Strmilov, k.s., which fits the mill the 2026 page calls Kubák, though the 2026 page does not say so. [S1][S3] Forbes Czech Republic described the Kubák workshop in 2016 as a family business in Strmilov, founded in 1870, that makes wool blankets and throws and handles the process from fleece through carding and spinning to weaving. [S4] So a wool-processing mill taking on a hemp and wool blend is a plausible fit with its existing skills. I flag that as inference and not as something either source states.

Credit for this part of the story is thin. The colophon lists teachers, designers, writers and students, 30 people in all, and not the farm or the mill. [S1] The question for any article is where the change happened that made the next step possible: who built the scutching line, who ran the blend trials, who spun the yarn. The record I could read does not answer it.
What the claims about hemp and the environment can carry

The Commission's hemp page says one hectare of hemp sequesters 9 to 15 tonnes of CO2 in about five months, that hemp fiber is very similar to linen, and that hempcrete, hemp wool and fiberboard insulation are used in construction. [S6] Those are the Commission's statements about the plant and its uses. The review gives the process-level counterweights: dew retting depends on the weather, water retting polluted water, and cottonization costs fiber properties. [S5] A comparison between a hemp textile and another textile would need to name both products, the job each does and which stages count, and no document I read does that for the exhibited yarn. [S5][S6]
Following one object

A narrow route works best: follow one named object from its starting material through the transformations that can be documented, to the people involved and its intended use, and say what remained difficult. Three plain questions frame the handoff at each step: what arrived, what changed, what left. That is more informative than twenty close-ups whose identities cannot be recovered. The SOW HEMP! page itself offers five named works with makers and photographers, which is where such a route could begin. [S1]
What the record does not show

I did not visit the exhibition or speak to anyone involved. The page does not name the farm, the yarn's fiber ratio, the spinning system or any test result, and it does not say how much of the exhibited work uses the yarn. [S1] The Czech customs series has gaps for 2020 and 2021, and the grower interview is from 2018. [S7][S8] The THC limit for Czech industrial hemp comes from a law firm's summary and not from the statute. [S9] The review is a 2022 overview of hemp fiber processing in general, not of the Czech chain. [S5] I could not open the Radio Prague article on the decline of the Czech hemp industry, because the site returned HTTP 403, so I do not rely on it.
If the field gets the opening shot, the question for the middle is plain: who owned the machine, and what did they need to be given for the next step to work? [S1][S8]

title: Show me what changed between the samples
subtitle: The Biomaterials Library says it keeps early experiments beside refined work. Its public pages, a data-stewardship standard and a study of how research reports its results show what a reader needs in order to ask what changed.
description: What the Biomaterials Library records about its samples, and what a comparison between an earlier and a later sample needs.

sections.x: None of the eleven sample pages I read on the Biomaterials Library's website carries a date or a version label, although the Library's Dutch Design Week listing says its collection preserves stages of development from early tests to refined applications. [S1][S6][S7][S8][S9][S10][S11][S12][S13][S14][S15][S16]

I do not read that as a fault. The listing describes a physical collection in Vilnius, and a web page is a different object. It is a reason to be specific when a reader says, show me the earlier one, because the earlier one has to be identified before anyone can compare it with the later one. This essay uses the Library's own pages, the Dutch Design Week listing, the FAIR data principles and a study of how often published research reports positive results, and it asks what a comparison between two samples needs. It uses published sources only. It reports no handling of any sample, no visit and no interview, and Dutch Design Week itself runs October 17 to 25, 2026. [S1][S3][S17][S18]
What the Library is

The Library describes itself as the first publicly accessible physical collection of its kind in the Baltic States, based at SODAS 2123 in Vilnius and expanding online, founded and curated by Austėja Platūkytė, organized by the NGO Medžiagotyra and supported by the Lithuanian Council for Culture. [S3] It says material libraries often sit inside universities and laboratories, where the knowledge stays inside academic or professional circles, and that it was created to open that knowledge to a much wider public. It presents materials through their biological, renewable or waste-derived sources, transformation processes, properties, possible applications and end-of-life pathways. [S3] It also says that biomaterials are not universal solutions but evolving practices shaped by local resources, skills, technologies and contexts. [S3]

The program lists Biomaterials Library: Lithuanian & Baltic Creators as a free exhibition at BioArt Laboratories on Strijp T+R, with hours of 11:00 to 18:00 during the festival. [S1] The listing is on the live 2026 program of ddw.nl, and the older site.ddw.nl address carries the same text. [S1][S2] It describes a growing archive of material experiments that preserves different stages of material development, from early tests and samples to refined applications and design objects, and says each material carries knowledge about its ingredients, processes, failures and possibilities. [S1] It names makers in image captions: Indrė Spitrytė-Mikuckė for Vegetative Textiles, Waste Matters Studio for Coffee Waste Tiles, Evelina Kudabaitė for Giria and Sarmite Polakova for Pine Skins. [S1] The Library's news page lists the same exhibition title at Shoreditch Town Hall in London on September 15 to 17, 2026, during London Design Festival. [S4]
What a sample page records

I read the Library's pages for eleven samples. Each ends with a Created by line. [S6][S7][S8][S9][S10][S11][S12][S13][S14][S15][S16] What they record falls into several kinds of statement, and the kinds are worth separating, because they support different claims.

Some state composition and process. The Amber Waste Is Bliss page says the composites are made with a heat press in an environment without oxygen, with cellulose from sewage waste and the solid remains of hemp after oil extraction added, and with more than 50 percent amber dust. [S8] The Giria page lists collecting bark waste from sawmills, drying, grinding, sieving, boiling a binder, mixing, molding and a few weeks of drying. [S6] The Pine Skins page says freshly harvested inner bark is treated with a bio-softening solution and enhanced with pigments and natural wax. [S7]

Some state an observation. Giria says objects deform as they dry, depending on thickness, so no two items are the same. [S6] Some state an intention or a promise. The Compost Board page says the sheet is designed to be returned for recycling and to feed worms and bacterial life. [S12] Coffee Waste Bio-Resin is described as lightweight, durable and fully recyclable, able to be reheated and reformed. [S10] Hemp Fur, a substitute for animal and synthetic fur, is described by its producer as anti-allergenic and as biodegrading after use. [S13] Hempforma says its study demonstrates how integrating hemp into design can contribute to more responsible construction and healthier indoor environments, and mentions material testing without giving any result. [S14] The Amber page gives numbers: a melting temperature of about 150 degrees Celsius and a start of melting at 250 to 300 degrees, without a stated method. [S8]

That is a working vocabulary for the question the old essay asked: which sentence is an intention, which an observation, which a measurement? Nearly all of the sentences on these pages are the first two kinds. The Amber page comes closest to numbers, and they are the maker's, without a method or a date. [S8]
A change that the pages do record

Within the Amber Waste Is Bliss page there is a before and after. It says amber is initially soft and brittle, and that to address this, cellulose from sewage waste and the solid remains of hemp after edible oil extraction are added to the formulation, which changes the properties of the resulting biocomposite. [S8] That sentence is the sort of change the headline of this essay asks for: a starting material, a problem and an addition. It does not say when the change was made, how many versions came between, how the properties were compared or what the earlier sample looked like. [S8]

The (Un)woven page gives another kind of record, in the form of collaboration. It says Studio Sarmīte developed a dyeing method for mixed-blend fibers together with Roua Atelier, that the dyeing is integrated into the making of the biotextile, and that the project was funded by the European Commission. [S11] A reader learns who contributed a method and who paid, though not which version of the dyeing method is shown. [S11]
Which sample are we discussing

The FAIR principles for scientific data management, published in 2016, are written for data. They say data and metadata should be assigned a globally unique and persistent identifier, that data should be described with rich metadata, and that metadata should be released with detailed provenance. [S17] The logic carries over to a physical sample in ordinary terms. A name for the project identifies the family. A name, date or version for the sample identifies the member. A statement about the earlier sample that is attached to a photograph of the later one is a quiet error that nobody intends to make. [S17]

The Library has one device for this at the level of recipes. Its Recipes page says the recipes collected there were developed and tested during Library workshops in 2025, are shared as open resources for learning and adaptation rather than as fixed formulas, and ask users to credit the Library and the named contributors. [S5] That gives a year and a credit rule. I did not open the linked PDF, so I do not know what versioning it carries. [S5]
On the word failure

The listing says each material carries knowledge about its failures. [S1] The word needs care in two directions. A maker, not an observer, decides whether an iteration failed or opened another direction. And science as a whole under-reports the unsuccessful: a 2010 study of 2,434 papers that declared they had tested a hypothesis found that the share reporting positive support ranged from 70.2 percent in space science to 91.5 percent in psychology and psychiatry. [S18] That study concerns research papers and says nothing about design samples or about this Library. It shows why a collection that keeps earlier and unsuccessful work is making an editorial choice against a common pattern, and why a reader asking for the earlier sample is asking for something that is often not recorded. [S18]

The Library's own text frames it as part of its purpose: it presents materials through processes and end-of-life pathways and not only as finished surfaces. [S3] How much of that appears on the public site, and how much in the physical collection, is a question for the Library. The Library's home page invites visitors to book an appointment at the Vilnius space and offers a form for submitting a material, and its news page notes that its curators are still calling for new display submissions. [S19][S4]
One comparison, set out

A usable comparison needs two columns. For the earlier sample: its name or identifier, the date or version, what it was made from, how, and what the maker observed. For the revised sample: the same fields. A third line records what changed and who explained it. This is a proposed worksheet and not a Library workflow, and where the maker has not approved a comparison, the fields stay empty. [S3][S17] Hypothetically, a sheet could be made with one recipe and later finished differently; the three photographs would then show related objects with different descriptions, and the photograph that goes with a sentence has to be the sample the sentence describes. This is a made-up example about documentation in general.

Credit and context travel with the sample. The Library asks, for its recipes, that the Library and contributors be credited. [S5] Its news page shows the collection traveling to Vilnius, Milan, Dubai, London and Eindhoven. [S4] Each trip moves an object into a new frame, and the information that qualified it either goes along or does not. [S4]
What the record does not show

I did not see the physical collection or the exhibition. I read eleven sample pages and found no dates, versions or test methods on them, and I cannot say what the physical labels at the exhibition carry. [S6][S8][S11] The Amber numbers are the maker's and come without a method. [S8] The Recipes PDF was not opened. [S5] The FAIR principles are written for research data, and the positive-results study concerns journals. [S17][S18] The listing names five makers in captions and one person in the colophon; it does not say who approves descriptions of individual samples. [S1] The question the title asks has one clean form for a visitor: could you show me the earlier version, and what would you want me to know about it? [S1][S3]

title: Dutch Design Week 2015 asked What if, and the record shows how a week of questions was organized
subtitle: The What if... edition read through DDW's own press releases and program, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards archive, a university exhibition brochure and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2015 (What if...) from DDW releases, Dutch press, the awards archive and a university brochure, with what the record does not show.

sections.x: A design week that picks What if... as its theme has chosen a question and not an answer, and the 2015 edition spent nine days testing how many kinds of answers a city can hold. [S1][S6]

I like a theme that can be checked against a room. This essay reads the fourteenth edition of Dutch Design Week from published sources only: twelve press releases from DDW's own archive, the organizer's description of its history, Dutch press, the Dutch Design Awards gallery, an exhibition brochure from the Eindhoven University of Technology and its partners, and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. [S6][S19] A short earlier version of this essay leaned on the photographs; this one starts from the documents and brings the photographs back in the second half, where they can be checked against something. [S19]
The numbers, and which ones to trust

The edition ran from Saturday, October 17 to Sunday, October 25, 2015, under the theme What if... [S1] DDW called it the fourteenth edition in several releases, and the releases for 2014 and 2016 call those years the thirteenth and the fifteenth. [S1][S11][S20] That is a consistent count inside the archive of this period, so I use it.

The release of July 23 expected 2,400 participants across 80 locations. [S1] The ticket release of late August repeated those figures. [S2] The opening-day release raised them to 2,500 designers in almost 100 locations. [S3] The closing release of October 25 gave the final tally under the heading "DDW in numbers": 275,000 visitors, 2,500 designers, 99 locations and 400 events, and it described the visitor number as an estimated record. [S6] Those four numbers are the organizer's own and the release does not say how the visitor estimate was made, so I treat them as DDW's account and not as an audited count.

The comparison with the year before is in DDW's own archive. The closing release for 2014, the UP edition, reported more than 250,000 visitors, 2,400 designers, 387 events and 86 locations. [S11] Set side by side, the 2015 figures show about 10 percent more visitors, 13 more locations and 13 more events than 2014. That arithmetic is mine, from two organizer releases, and both rest on the same kind of estimate. Omroep Brabant, writing at the start of the week, expected about 250,000 visitors, which is the 2014 figure. [S14] The record was a surprise only in the sense that it exceeded last year's number.
A theme chosen to praise imagination

DDW's announcement said the theme celebrated the imagination of designers and called What if... the ultimate question from which creativity and innovation start. [S1] The campaign was made with the Rotterdam design agency Fabrique, and the site was built with the Tilburg agency Freshheads; a September release says the new site grouped the program by theme and added search and design routes. [S1][S10] The managing director at the time, Martijn Paulen, was quoted in both the July and October releases saying that posing the right questions is the motor for the imagination, and that designers dare to question everything and shape a different answer. [S1][S6]

It is worth reading what the theme did to the program. The releases do not use the word "answer" as a promise. They list exhibitions in which a design question is posed and left open: the Playing Life exhibitions about working with living materials, the exhibition It's Your World with its four strands (trash, health, industry, neighbor), and Thing Nothing at the Van Abbemuseum, which the July release says examines the role of design in a dematerializing world. [S1][S3][S6]
Who stood behind the week

Since 2009, DDW says, it has appointed two ambassadors each year to represent the week and to take part in its content. [S20] For 2015 they were Studio Makkink & Bey, the partnership of architect Rianne Makkink and designer Jurgen Bey, and Koert van Mensvoort, the founder and director of the Next Nature Network. [S8][S12] The announcement says the choice of Makkink & Bey responded to growing interest in interdisciplinary working, teaching and thinking, and that Van Mensvoort's appointment fit a wish for new schools of thought on social issues. [S8]

The closing release lets the ambassadors describe the week in their own words. Makkink said that during DDW the designer becomes a curator, puts issues on the agenda and also generates new work, and she named the OXI exhibition at Sectie-C, Dutch Invertuals' work on movement, Modebelofte at the Philips Stadium and a program of football-themed content called FC DDW as examples. [S6] Van Mensvoort said what struck him was the openness of DDW and added that the question had shifted from the world of design to the design of the world. [S6] These are their statements as the organizer quotes them, and I report them as such.
One city, three areas

Omroep Brabant's guide to the week described the program as spread over three areas: Strijp-S, the city center between the Witte Dame and the city hall, and a group of old factories in the east of the city near the Broekakkerseweg. [S14] DDW's own opening-week releases split the program the same way: one release for Strijp-S and one for the center. [S3][S4]

At Strijp-S, the former Philips complex, the releases place four anchors. The Klokgebouw was open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 and held It's Your World, which DDW says was developed with support from the Stichting DOEN. [S3] The Ketelhuisplein held the VPRO Peepshow, the CoLab Toon Design Challenge by the energy company Eneco and a collaboration between the studio HeyHeydeHaas and the designer Morag Myerscough, with music from 16:00. [S3][S6] The Veemgebouw, on its eighth floor, was a new DDW location that the release called a hub: the retrospective exhibition for the Dutch Design Awards finalists, In No Particular Order supported by the Creative Industries Fund NL, Hands Off: New Dutch Design at the Confluence of Technology & Craft, and three Playing Life exhibitions. [S3] MU, the art space in the same complex, had attracted more than 35,000 visitors during DDW 2014 according to the release, and in 2015 hosted the design studio KNOL, which planned to study individual and collective behavior through spatial interventions. [S3]

In the center, the release names the Philips Stadium for Modebelofte, the Paterskerk for The Allegory of the South, the Steentjeskerk for an exhibition by Floris Hovers, the Stroomhuisje for London Calling Part 2, and the Kazerne for Open Ended by Lidewij Edelkoort. [S4] The details are the kind that make an archive worth reading. The stadium was closed on Saturday, October 17 because of a football match, and opened at 14:00 on Sunday; the church served as a farmers' market by day, and in the evening a restaurant with a Michelin star served a set menu at a dining table more than twenty meters long. [S4] VPRO's guide gives the price of those dinners as 150 euros including drinks, and says they were almost entirely booked. [S13]
What the week was arguing about

DDW's debates release says the program held more than 100 lectures, meetings and seminars. [S5] It names Agatha Haines, Rachel Armstrong, Anab Jain of Superflux, Koert van Mensvoort, Stephan Petermann of OMA/AMO, Victor Knaap and Jurgen Bey among the speakers. [S5] Three threads in that release read well next to the theme.

The first is technology and what it does to people. The third Now Future talk show, on Thursday, October 22 in the ABN AMRO House at the Klokgebouw, was hosted by Van Mensvoort, and the release says he would launch a new nature movement that evening. [S5] The Next Nature Network release says the first ECO coin, a coin meant to express the ecological value of nature, was presented symbolically that night to Yoyo Yogasmana, who conserves more than 130 rice varieties in Indonesia without insecticides. [S7] Yogasmana was one of the six creatives of Age of Wonderland, a four-year program curated by Arne Hendriks for Hivos and Baltan Laboratories with DDW. [S5][S7] The release counts what the Natlab program did in nine days: one exhibition, 21 activities, 14 guided tours and one seminar. [S5]

The second is the city. The Smart City and the Participation Society conference at the Van Abbemuseum on Friday, October 23 was set up by Het Nieuwe Instituut and the municipality of Eindhoven, who the release says had been working on that question in a multiyear program since June 1, 2015. [S5] A Smart Board of six scientists, thinkers and designers was to be appointed there to examine the city's ambitions and formulate an action plan. [S5]

The third is the refugee crisis, which reached the Dutch news in the weeks before the week began. The release notes that VPRO would broadcast the Tegenlicht episode "Gimme shelter" on Sunday, October 18, with a meet-up on what designers could do for refugees. [S5] The closing release says Van Mensvoort directed special attention to design in relation to the refugee issue. [S6] Omroep Brabant's guide points to a Design Academy Eindhoven graduation project, the Limbo Embassy by Manon van Hoeckel, as a neutral meeting place meant to hold a debate without the polarization of a talk show. [S13]
Mind the Step and the technical universities

Mind the Step is the part of the edition that I can read in the most detail, because its organizers published a brochure. The Design United page says the 2015 exhibition at the Klokgebouw continued an experiment that began in 2014 as a collaboration between faculties of the Eindhoven University of Technology and Design United, the design research institute of the three technical universities of Delft, Eindhoven and Twente. [S17] The brochure is bilingual and signed by the vice president of the TU/e executive board, Jo van Ham, by the science director of Design United, Daan van Eijk, and by Lucas Asselbergs as project leader. [S18] It says the emphasis lay on the step the visitor can make, and the products, systems and services on show concern how people learn, move, live, stay healthy and reproduce. [S17][S18]

Omroep Brabant names three of the exhibits: a touring motorcycle powered by electricity alone that goes around the world in 80 days, an emergency hospital that takes different shapes depending on the disaster, and a soft robotic hand that can make subtle movements. [S14] The brochure confirms an electric motorcycle project and a soft robotics project by Rob Scharff of Delft, among its entries. [S18] I count the brochure's entries as a program and not as a ranking of what was best.
Awards, and a new prize

The Dutch Design Awards were presented on Saturday, October 24, in the Effenaar, the first time the show was held there. [S5][S6] Submarine Channel won the Communication category and the Future Award for Refugee Republic, an interactive online documentary about the Domiz camp in northern Iraq, where the Dutch Design Awards entry says about 58,000 refugees lived. [S6][S15] The jury wrote that the team lived in the camp while working, which gives an intensity that embedded journalism does not, and that refugees were portrayed as human beings and not as victims. [S15] Teresa van Dongen received the Young Designer Award. [S6] The release notes that the Van Gogh Museum's multimedia tour, made by Fabrique, won the Service & Systems category, and the agency itself said so in a statement that Emerce ran as a submitted item. [S16]

For the first time the ambassadors also gave a prize for the most surprising or impressive presentation, the Best of Dutch Design Week Award. It went to Modebelofte: Performing Advancers, curated by Niek Pulles and Harm Rensink of the concept store You Are Here, praised for its presentation in an unusual place, the Philips Stadium, and for the organizers' generosity toward the fashion talent taking part. [S6] VPRO described that show as 42 designers in six tunnels of the stadium, on a sportswear theme. [S13]
Tickets, music and the festival feel

The week also added things for visitors who came for more than the exhibitions. DDW Music, a collaboration among DDW, the Effenaar and the booking agency Friendly Fire, put daily live performances in cafes, the Van Abbemuseum, the Stroomhuis and the Ketelhuisplein, free for ticket holders. [S1][S9] The line-up was long, with Rufus Wainwright at the Muziekgebouw on Sunday, October 25 and Two Gallants at the Effenaar on Thursday, October 22, and The Closing Party followed the awards on Saturday, October 24. [S9]

A DDW ticket cost 16 euros online and 18.50 euros at the door, and no day tickets were sold. It gave nine days of access to the Klokgebouw, the Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show, Thing Nothing at the Van Abbemuseum and the Veemgebouw, and a 50 percent discount at the Philips Museum. [S2] Everything else was free unless the program said otherwise. [S2] That structure matters when reading the visitor estimate. The closing release does not say how a free-entry week with a ticketed core was counted, which is why the 275,000 figure should stay labeled as an estimate.
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a collection of press photographs for 2015 with 45 albums, and the account's pages say the images may be published for non-commercial purposes with the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week stated. [S19][S12] I opened six of the 45 albums on October 9, 2026, covering 191 photographs by the counts on the pages, and I did not return to them for this version. [S19]

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 33 photographs by Cleo Goossens, Tommy Köhlbrugge and Almicheal Fraay. A high view by Goossens looks across the square in autumn, with yellow trees in the foreground, white tents and a stage, and two red and white chimneys behind. A photograph by Köhlbrugge shows a tower of scaffolding hung with colored panels and letters, one of them a large question mark. The releases do not name a tower, so I use the picture for its question mark and nothing more. A third photograph shows a bulb-lit stand for the VPRO Peepshow, which the October 17 release places on the Ketelhuisplein. [S19][S3]

The Klokgebouw album holds 50 photographs by Sjoerd Eickmans, titled Klokgebouw_div with a number. One shows black and white patterned fabric on a mannequin and a sign reading Zeeuws Museum Handwerk; I can say whose stand it is and not who designed the print. A separate album, 3TU & TU/e: Mind the Step, holds 31 photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann, including a mannequin torso in a dark purple shirt with a strip of small circuit boards stitched down the middle. The brochure and the album fit the same exhibition, and no caption says what those circuits do. [S19][S17]

The Kazerne Expo album holds 30 photographs by Ralph Roelse. An earlier draft said no release named the Kazerne. That was wrong: the October 15 release names the Kazerne for Open Ended by Lidewij Edelkoort, and the July release lists it among the hot spots. [S4][S1] The album shows a dark gallery with a brick wall, a red glazed bowl on a white plinth, and a red wool coat on a mannequin arm. I still cannot say which of the Kazerne's exhibitions the coat belongs to, because the photo title carries only the venue. [S19]

The MU album, titled Collective [Ir]Rationality, holds 18 photographs by Köhlbrugge and Daan Paans, one of them of visitors walking beside a pale factory wall toward an entrance marked by white posts and an orange barrier. [S19] An earlier draft said the October 17 release lists Playing Life exhibitions at MU. That was also wrong. The release puts the three Playing Life exhibitions in the Veemgebouw and describes MU's program separately, as the work of the studio KNOL, which fits the album's title about collective behavior. [S3]

The Sectie-C album holds 49 photographs, among them Iris Rijskamp's pictures titled 91_OXI. One shows a glass case on a dark table, and another a case holding a gray bird hung on wires next to a printed card reading OXI and SALUTES. [S19] The earlier draft said it did not know what OXI is. The record now answers that. The closing release names OXI on Sectie-C as an exhibition by Justine Kontou, Tessa Koot and Club-C, and Makkink described it as a challenge to the revenue model for designers. [S6] VPRO adds that OXI's curator was Kontou, that one work, Dadabase by Govert Flint, scanned a visitor's face to recognize age, gender and emotion as a way to produce data that has value, and that Sectie-C was home to 180 creative entrepreneurs, craftspeople and artists opening their studios. [S13] The card and the case in the photograph are consistent with that description. They do not tell me which object is Flint's.
A visit from parliament

On Monday, October 19, a delegation of members of parliament from the standing committees for Economic Affairs and for Education, Culture and Science made a working visit to the creative industry at DDW. [S21] The Dutch release says the mayor of Eindhoven, Rob van Gijzel, the chair of the Dutch Creative Council, Jeroen van Erp, and Martijn Paulen presented their view on the importance of the creative industry for the Netherlands and for Brainport Eindhoven, and that the members saw research and design projects by the three technical universities and the Graduation Show of the Design Academy Eindhoven. [S21] The release gives the festival's standing scale as more than 2,400 designers presenting to some 260,000 visitors a year, more than 400 events and 100 locations. [S21] That 260,000 sits between the 250,000-plus of 2014 and the 275,000 of 2015, and it is a description of a typical year, not a count. [S21][S11][S6]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Expected versus final scale.** The July release expected 2,400 participants in 80 locations, and the closing release reports 2,500 designers in 99 locations. The closing release is later and says it is a tally, so I use it. [S1][S6]

**Opening day.** Omroep Brabant wrote that the week began on a Friday evening, while DDW's releases give Saturday, October 17 as the first day and say, on that date, that the week gets underway "today". [S14][S3] DDW's own dates settle the program days. The Friday evening report may describe an opening event, which the sources I opened do not describe.
**Playing Life.** The earlier draft placed it at MU. DDW's October 17 release places it in the Veemgebouw. [S3]
**The Kazerne and OXI.** Both were unexplained in the earlier draft and both are named in DDW releases. [S4][S6]
**Edition number.** The archive's own releases agree on the fourteenth, the thirteenth and the fifteenth for 2015, 2014 and 2016. [S1][S11][S20]
What the record does not show
I do not know how DDW produced the visitor estimate, and neither the July nor the October releases explain it. [S6]
I do not know which of the roughly 100 locations received the most visitors. The only per-venue figure in the sources is MU's 35,000 visitors in 2014, from the opening release. [S3]
I cannot say what the 39 Flickr albums I did not open show, or whether other photographers recorded exhibits I did not read about. [S19]

I do not have a complete list of Dutch Design Awards winners for 2015 from a primary page. The gallery entry I opened covers Refugee Republic, and the other winners I name come from DDW's closing release and one submitted press item. [S6][S15][S16]

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If you look at the 2015 archive this month, pick one room and ask the question the theme asked: what if the thing in that photograph had been designed for a different person, and who would that person be? [S1]
