title: Dutch Design Week 2020 had to learn what intimacy means at a distance, and the record shows how fast it moved
subtitle: The New Intimacy edition read through DDW's releases and magazine, the Dutch Design Awards, Dutch trade press and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2020 (The New Intimacy) from DDW releases and the awards: the June plan, the September 30 cancellation and the virtual week.

sections.x: A festival about the new intimacy had to learn, seventeen days before it opened, that nobody would be allowed to stand close to anything, and the record shows how a design week rebuilt itself on a screen in under three weeks. [S1][S3][S4]

I like a theme that gets tested by events. This essay reads the nineteenth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten items from DDW's press archive, news and magazine, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement, a trade-press report on the online program and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview, and for this edition nobody could have visited in the usual way. An earlier short draft used four releases, an ambassadors page and the photographs. This one adds the timeline, the numbers and the people. [S11]
A timeline in four releases

On June 8, 2020 the Dutch Design Foundation announced that DDW would go ahead as a combination of a live and an online festival. [S2] The release said that consultation with the municipality of Eindhoven and the Brabant Southeast Safety Region had confirmed that a DDW with more than 350,000 visitors, large central locations and organized transport was unrealistic. [S2] The live part would be a "studio exhibition model": designers would open studios by appointment to a limited number of professional visitors, with a maximum number of visitors per time slot based on floor space, in categories of 10, 30 and 100, and a daily cap for the city. [S2] The rest would be an improved online platform. [S2]

On July 7 DDW announced the theme The New Intimacy for what it called the 19th Dutch Design Week. [S1] The text describes a search for a new equilibrium in a time when Covid-19 is one of the major factors accelerating the exploration of ways of relating to each other and the world, and it says the theme illustrates the uniqueness of the edition, which would manifest itself in intimate physical and extensive online forms. [S1] It also noted that recent easing of national guidelines allowed a larger live component. [S1]

On September 30 the mayor of Eindhoven, John Jorritsma, decided that the live version could not take place, on advice of the Safety Region and on the basis of an emergency ordinance issued earlier that week after new national measures. [S3] The release quotes the mayor saying that the images of the overflowing healthcare system in spring were still fresh in his mind, and the director Martijn Paulen saying that canceling with two and a half weeks to go was deeply saddening. [S3] DDW said it had been developing a virtual experience for months, which would now become the main stage. [S3]

The closing release of October 25 looked back on a virtual edition. [S4] That sequence is DDW's own account, and it is consistent across the four documents: a hybrid plan in June, a theme in July, a cancellation of the live part in late September, and a virtual week in October. [S1][S2][S3][S4]
A recognition arriving in the middle of it

Between the June plan and the July theme, on June 4, 2020, the Council for Culture advised the Minister of Education, Culture and Science to include the Dutch Design Foundation in the national cultural basic infrastructure from 2021. DDW's news item called it the first time a national design festival would be included. [S5] The item says the council praised a year-round program embedded in the region, the combination of a curated and a free-form part of the festival, and quality delivered consistently, and that the minister would decide on Prinsjesdag in September. [S5] This is DDW's summary of the advice, and I did not read the council's text. The timing matters for the story: the organization lost its physical festival in the same season in which it gained a place in the national funding structure. [S3][S5]
What DDW counted

The closing release counts over 1,500 designers, 750 3D Viewing Rooms, 600 events and 400 livestreams by designers, 125 DDW TV programs with 3,500 minutes of content, and 50,000 DDW TV viewers. [S4] It says the festival reached "several hundreds of thousands" through several outlets, mainly professionals, and gives no visitor count. [S4] Paulen said the combination of virtual and live would be the future of DDW and that meeting in real life remains indispensable. [S4] The release also records a virtual visit by the minister of education, culture and science, Ingrid van Engelshoven, and the decision to keep the 750 Viewing Rooms online for ninety days instead of nine. [S4]

Two other figures circulated. The trade site IO+ reported on the program before it started and counted more than 450 online events. [S8] DDW's own final count is 600. [S4] The two do not conflict: the earlier number was a preview of the program and the later number is DDW's tally of the week, and neither says how an event was defined. IO+ also gave 355,000 as the 2018 attendance, which is the last full-size comparison the sources offer. [S8]

These numbers describe reach and not presence, and the difference matters for a theme about closeness. A livestream can reach a person without putting them in a room, and a 3D Viewing Room can show a stand without anyone walking through it. [S4] The figures say what DDW counted. They do not say what a viewer felt, and the release does not claim to know.
Three ambassadors, announced the year before

The 2020 ambassadors were announced at the closing event on October 27, 2019: Lidewij Edelkoort, the designer Sabine Marcelis and Sean Carney, who leads healthcare transformation services at Philips. [S7] The magazine's profile written in the week itself shows how each had to change course. [S6]

Edelkoort, with Charlotte Grün, made a traveling library from the private book collection of the graphic designer Anthon Beeke, to open at the Van Abbehuis opposite the Van Abbemuseum and then travel to Dutch libraries. [S6] With the museum's director Charles Esche she curated New Melancholy, an exhibition at the Van Abbemuseum and Kazerne Home of Design that puts museum artworks in dialogue with design objects she has collected, which she described as an offer of new ways of thinking about design and art in times of pandemic. [S6] Marcelis made a three-dimensional digital interaction called Tactility with the technology partners 5GHUB and Dimenco, and worked with a gallery on letting remote visitors control cameras placed in a physical gallery space. [S6] Carney gave a keynote calling on designers to design with purpose in healthcare, and announced the winners of a student design challenge. [S6]
A week made of programs

DDW's daily guides to the week show what a virtual festival looked like on a timetable. Each day began at 11:00 with a program called For starters, in which the design journalist Jeroen Junte talked with young and familiar names from the design field, and gave a daily wake-up call to the previous day's Dutch Design Awards winner. [S12] The guides list, for a single day, a news program from the Embassy of Health on intimacy, a daily talk show from Design United with design researchers from the Delft, Eindhoven, Twente and Wageningen universities, an Antenna series of ten international graduates from five continents, and the Class of 2020 presentations. [S12] DDW had invited all Dutch design schools to make an exhibition on the theme, and when the physical DDW stopped, five of the participating schools decided to show their physical installations in the schools, filmed. [S12] A talent program of 22 designers, Driving Dutch Design, researched the theme of value in podcasts, articles, a virtual group exhibition and six episodes on DDW TV. [S12]
Awards on a screen

The Dutch Design Awards presented their 2020 winners from October 17 to 24 in a live show on DDW TV, one category a day at 16:00, according to the awards' own announcement. [S9] The eight winners were The Interceptor by The Ocean Cleanup with Fabrique (Product), Forum Groningen by NL Architects with deMunnik-deJong-Steinhauser (Habitat), DEMO by Studio Dumbar (Communication), Collection 005 by Ninamounah (Fashion), Insectology: Food for Buzz by Matilde Boelhouwer (Design Research), MONNIE by Afdeling Buitengewone Zaken with Garage2020 (Service & Systems), Water as Leverage by the national government (commissioning) and Simon Dogger (Young Designer). [S9] The jury, chaired by Ine Frings, wrote of "doing is the motto" and of designers who take responsibility. [S9] I did not find a Future Award for 2020 in the announcement, and I do not state one.
Where the program touched the ground

IO+ highlighted a handful of online projects: Aiki, a soft toy that breathes with a child during medical treatment; the IKEA Virtual Greenhouse; Ilse Kremer's Fabulous Fungi, which uses fungal pigments for textile dye; the Bank of Care, which registers unpaid care work; the app Agora for mental wellness of cancer patients; Manifestations, whose 2020 theme was Monsters; and WatAlsStad, in which five designers made workshops for children to shape a city of the future. [S8] That list is a trade site's selection of an online program, and I did not open the projects' own pages. [S8]
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a 2020 collection of 25 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated. [S11][S10] I opened seven on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. [S11]

The Viewing Rooms album holds nine renders at 2560 by 1440 pixels, images of virtual rooms and not photographs of rooms, so I did not use them. [S11] What the archive does hold is photographs made in real halls, so the physical objects existed even when the audience was online. [S11]

The New Melancholy album holds 24 photographs by Ralph Roelse, titled for the Van Abbemuseum, Lidewij Edelkoort and Kazerne. They show dark halls hung with pale, weathered curtains, a ring of stacked blocks lit from above, a vase on the floor, hanging pods and a wall of small frames, and no visitor appears in the ones I looked at. The magazine names the exhibition and its curators, so the earlier draft's matching by names is now confirmed. [S11][S6] For an exhibition titled New Melancholy an empty room is a fitting record, and for a theme about intimacy it is an uncomfortable one.

The album for the Dutch Design Awards show, titled Live_Habitat, holds 20 photographs by Jeroen van der Wielen and Oscar Vinck of a television studio with a red set, yellow-fronted desks, a DDA logo screen, presenters and guests at mid distance and a camera operator. The awards' announcement confirms that the show was made for DDW TV. [S11][S9] The Self Design Academy at MU has 27 photographs by van der Wielen, among them round wooden benches facing a projection in a concrete hall. The Piet Hein Eek album has 33 photographs by Max Kneefel. A World Design Embassy on circular and biobased building has 26 photographs, and TAC, the Temporary Art Centre, has 22, among them a wall text that reads VIROPHILIA. [S11]
Before June, and the call to designers

Before the June plan, DDW's corona update told designers that the foundation was working on physical and virtual scenarios. [S13] It said that, taking national guidelines and 1.5-meter distancing into account, it would be naive to think 350,000 visitors could run free around exhibitions for nine days, and that the aim was a meaningful physical DDW different from earlier editions alongside a digital route. [S13] The update is undated, and it reads as written in spring 2020. [S13] After the July theme, a call for designers said DDW20 would combine a virtual and a live festival, that every approved participant would get a digital space for a virtual 3D exhibition, that a limited number of venues would be coordinated for the live part, and that applications closed on September 1. [S14] That is the program the mayor's decision then cut back to the virtual half. [S14][S3]
The universities' research talks

Design United held its 2020 edition, Up Close & Personal, from October 19 to 23, one theme a day, as a debate around design research: hybrids, eco-logica, living matter(s), silent power and crisis. [S15] The page lists projects such as Roboat, on autonomous mobility on water for Amsterdam, and a robotic play object for education. [S15] DDW's daily guide gives the show a host, Isolde Hallensleben, and a time of 13:00 to 14:00 each afternoon. [S12]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**The number of events.** IO+ counted more than 450 online events in its preview, and DDW counted 600 events at the close. DDW's is the later and the organizer's own tally, and I use it, labeled as DDW's. [S4][S8]
**Live or virtual.** The June plan promised a live studio component and the September decision removed it. The 2020 edition was virtual, not hybrid. [S2][S3][S4]

**What stopped on September 30.** The mayor's decision removed the live events around DDW, and the schools' filmed installations show that physical objects still existed in rooms. DDW's own guide is the source for the schools. [S3][S12]
**Visitor count.** There is none. The closing release gives reach and viewers of DDW TV, not visitors. [S4]

**The anniversary count.** The theme release calls 2020 the 19th Dutch Design Week, which agrees with the series from 2015 (14th) and 2019 (18th), while the June release speaks of "the last 19 years". [S1][S2]
What the record does not show
I do not know how many people watched or how many were professionals, because DDW gave no breakdown. [S4]
I do not know what the New Melancholy exhibition looked like to a visitor, or whether any visitor saw it in person. [S6][S11]
I did not open any of the Viewing Rooms, which may no longer be online after the ninety days DDW promised. [S4]
I did not read the 18 Flickr albums I skipped and I did not re-read the seven I used. [S11]

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival has to rebuild itself in seventeen days, which part of it would you save first, the objects, the meetings or the audience? [S3]

title: Dutch Design Week 2021 borrowed its theme from a lost exhibition, and the record shows what it built instead
subtitle: The Greater Number edition read through DDW's releases, a 1968 Milan exhibition, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2021 (The Greater Number) from DDW releases, the 1968 Milan exhibition behind the theme, the awards and the photo archive.

sections.x: A theme called The Greater Number asks for a count, and the record of the 2021 edition gives plenty of numbers and none of the one a reader would ask for first, the number of visitors. [S1][S3][S4]

I like a theme that sets a trap for the person writing about it. This essay reads the twentieth Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten items from DDW's press archive, a design magazine's guide, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement, a review of a book on a 1968 Milan exhibition and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases and the photographs. This one adds the origin of the theme, the timeline from the April plan to the October close, and the people. [S10]
The trap: the one number that is missing

The edition ran from Saturday, October 16 to Sunday, October 24, 2021. [S1][S3] DDW's announcement of the live plan on April 13 said the organizers hoped to welcome visitors in line with the Covid measures in force and that alternative plans were in place. [S2] The September 21 release said the work was spread over eight areas of Eindhoven. [S3] The closing release of October 24 gives no visitor count, no count of designers and no count of locations. [S1] Its figures are the DDW TV episode a day and the thanks to participants and volunteers. [S1]

What numbers exist are expectations. The standard description DDW supplies to event listings said more than 350,000 visitors and more than 2,000 designers in more than 100 locations. [S9] Omroep Brabant quoted Paulen in a 2021 profile saying he did not know how many would come and that growth was not the goal, since DDW wanted to connect good designers with good visitors. [S7] Both are statements made before or during the week, and neither is a count. The reason the closing release stays silent is stated on DDW's press page for facts and figures: the organizers write that more is not better, that constant growth in visitors and participants is not what DDW is about, and that they therefore no longer share exact numbers for each edition, only that a few hundred thousand visitors come each year apart from 2020. [S14] The page is undated, so I cannot say from which edition the policy applies. I also looked for DDW's public annual report for 2021 and could not open it. [S7][S9]
A theme with a history

The Greater Number is the English form of De Carlo's phrase for the 14th Milan Triennale of 1968. The design magazine Wallpaper explains that the architect Giancarlo De Carlo coined it for that exhibition, which dealt with population growth, advances in science and the gap between Western abundance and poverty. [S8] Wallpaper says student protesters destroyed the exhibition a few days after it opened. [S8] A review of Paola Nicolin's book on the Triennale puts it differently: the opening-day protest ended with eviction on June 8, followed by De Carlo's resignation with the whole executive committee, and the exhibition was seen by almost no one. [S11] I use the book review's account of events, because it rests on archival research. The magazine's one-line version is a fair summary of the outcome and not of the timing.

DDW's own statement uses the phrase for a different purpose. Its April release asks whether, after the corona crisis, we will continue on the road built by economic growth, and answers that change should focus on social values and care for the planet, with "a constant search for a better number", sometimes less, sometimes more but of higher quality, and sometimes simply different. [S2] Four sub-themes grew out of it, on the pandemic, the wellbeing economy, climate and inclusivity and the design field. [S2][S3] The closing release repeated the framing, aiming at designers looking for the right balance, towards better and away from simply less or more. [S1] That is the organizer's wording, and I report it as such.
The twentieth edition and its new look

DDW called 2021 its twentieth edition and its twentieth anniversary, which agrees with the count of 14th in 2015, 18th in 2019 and 19th in 2020. [S2][S4] The agency thonik, founded by Nikki Gonnissen and Thomas Widdershoven, was chosen without a pitch to design a new visual identity based on continuity and innovation, while Vruchtvlees kept the digital platform. [S5] The release says an independent brand strategist, Roel Stavorinus, would write about the design process as it went along. [S5] After the fully virtual 2020 edition, Paulen said the virtual week could not replace the feeling of a live festival, and that DDW stands for serendipity. [S2]
Three ambassadors, three exhibitions

The ambassadors, announced on July 16, were the architect Floris Alkemade, Natsai Audrey Chieza of Faber Futures and Christien Meindertsma. [S4] Alkemade, the former Chief Government Architect, presented a labyrinth in the Klokgebouw with the Board of Government Advisors and World Design Embassies, a translation of his essay The Future of the Netherlands: The Art of Changing Direction. [S4][S3] Chieza led Bio Stories at MU, a three-day forum on synthetic biology and what relationships people want with nature. [S4][S4] Meindertsma, with the interactive designers Joel Gethin Lewis and Reza Ali, made the interactive installation Sharing Elements in Microlab, about the matter that connects bodies to the rest of the world. [S4][S3] Meindertsma's earlier book on a pig, the release recalls, showed how many products an average pig ends up in. [S4]
Areas, halls and a village

The September 21 program release named the pieces. In the Klokgebouw, the technical universities showed work as Design United, and the exhibition It's in our nature explored human relationships with nature, with Emma van der Leest's fungal bio-coating, Living Color's bacteria-dyed textiles and work from Baltan Laboratories and Mediamatic. [S3] On the Ketelhuisplein, Arne Hendriks presented Hara Hachi Bu, a small village where people practice designing, producing and consuming less, and Nieuwe Helden showed The Exploded View, a house built entirely from biobased materials. [S3] The Embassy of Inclusive Society, also on the square, showed Angel-Rose Oedit Doebés, Lydienne Albertoe on the portrayal of people of color in Dutch children's books, Janine Zielman on facial recognition and Karim Aducchi's Social Distancing Fabric, an embroidery project by 200 refugees during the pandemic. [S3] In Microlab Hall, Things that matter included Ineke Hans's injection-molded chair for the label Circuform, which is returned to the store after use. [S3]

In Fuutlaan Hall, Cabinet of collaborations, designed and co-curated by Envisions and Studio Rick Tegelaar, set an extra-large conversation table among works by designers and industry, including pairings such as Vincent Schwenk with Microsoft. [S3] The October 14 release adds the Van Abbemuseum program on inclusiveness and geopolitics, Kiki & Joost, a Natlab costume lab by Baltan Laboratories and Mediamatic, and the Design United talk show Up Close & Personal, streamed daily from the Effenaar. [S6] It places the Graduation Show of the Design Academy Eindhoven in the Beursgebouw, with Manifestations, Isola Talents Factory and Class of 21 as young-talent programs. [S6] DDW TV ran an hour every day at 19:00, including the awards. [S6] I leave out the MU project on substance use that the same release describes, because the release gives me nothing I can check beyond its title and framing.
Awards in the week

The Dutch Design Awards presented their winners on October 23, 2021. [S12] They were BYBORRE Create for Product, Marker Wadden for Habitat, Stay Sane Stay Safe by Studio Lennarts & De Bruijn with overdeschreef for Communication, Leela by The Fabricant for Fashion, Affect Lab's community-building project for Design Research, Globalance World by Clever Franke for Data & Interaction, the Circulair Warenhuis for commissioning and Audrey Large as Young Designer, with Hella Jongerius receiving the BNO Piet Zwart Award. [S12] MINI gave The Fabricant an extra prize, a year with an electric car and an ambassador role. [S12] Two of those winners appear in the DDW program: the release lists Het Circulair Warenhuis among the projects in Microlab Hall as DDA-nominated. [S3][S12] The rest of the announcement is the awards' own summary, and I did not read the jury reports.
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a 2021 collection of 36 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated. [S10][S13] I opened six on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. [S10]

The Graduation Show album holds 135 photographs by Cleo Goossens. The one I chose shows a dark hall with a lit table of tall vases and glazed pots and a large film screen behind it, with visitors as silhouettes. The release places the show in the Beursgebouw, and the album titles name no building. [S10][S6]

The Bio.Stories album holds 141 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 18. The photograph I chose shows a concrete hall with a long dark ribbon on the floor and a ring of pale wooden stools, with a few people small and far away. [S10] The release attributes the project to Chieza's team. [S6]

The Klokgebouw album holds 278 photographs, and two sets inside it are titled Cabinet of Collaborations and Class of 21. A wall in the first set lists 16 pairings of designers and companies, among them ByBorre with Natuzzi and VVAND with Microsoft, and a sign in the same set reads Location Fuutlaan. [S10] The program release places Cabinet of collaborations in Fuutlaan Hall, which resolves the earlier draft's puzzle about the sign. [S3] A tall close view in the Class of 21 set shows small glass and mesh vessels on a transparent shelf, with no maker named. [S10]

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 38 photographs, mostly by Kneefel, dated October 16 and 17. Two aerial photographs show small timber houses with moss roofs among crowds. The release says Hara Hachi Bu is a small village on the square, and The Exploded View is a house, so the timber houses fit one of the two, but no title names either, and the magazine's description of Hara Hachi Bu as a circle of eleven sheds favors that reading. [S10][S3] The Manifestations album holds 83 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge dated October 16 and 17, and the Kiki & Joost album 68 under the title Meanwhile. [S10]
Voices from the magazine

DDW's own magazine ran columns and interviews around the week, and they fill in what the releases leave out. [S15][S16][S17][S18] The design writer Jeroen Junte wrote that The Greater Number translates simply as less is more but is not only about reducing, since more solutions are needed for the climate crisis, privacy violations and inequality. [S15] He described the Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences' project Slowductivity, on slowness, boredom and manual labor, and ArtEZ's Greater Less, Greater More, on mixed reality as a way to reduce consumption, citing an average of 173 items of clothing in Dutch wardrobes. [S15] He described Alkemade's Labyrinth in the Klokgebouw as a corridor system of white canvases with artworks hidden as signposts, ending with Atelier Van Lieshout's Apocalypse and an alternative exit through a work by Constant on the playing human, and Arne Hendriks's Hara Hachi Bu on the Ketelhuisplein as a circle of eleven sheds. [S15] That description supports the earlier draft's reading of the small timber houses in the aerial photographs as Hara Hachi Bu, though no photo title says so. [S15][S10]

The 1m2 Collective, formed by Jeffrey Heiligers, Studio Jeroen van Veluw and ST-DUO, who knew each other from the talent program Driving Dutch Design, showed in the Van Abbemuseum a totem of 18 works chosen by five independent jurors and curators, free of participation costs. [S16] Heiligers said the starting question was how inclusive design events are, and that this applied to DDW itself. [S16] That is a critique of the festival published by the festival, and the magazine item says so plainly. [S16]

Natsai Audrey Chieza, in a magazine interview, said her Bio.Stories forum related to the sub-theme It's in our nature, and that she had been invited in 2020 to the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Synthetic Biology, which partnered with her studio Faber Futures on the project. [S17] Christien Meindertsma, with the interaction designers Joel Gethin Lewis and Reza Ali, said her project Sharing Elements was about how people are matter themselves and connected to food, earth and products. [S18] The eight World Design Embassies, a program the foundation started five years earlier, included the Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building, whose curator Lucas de Man of Company New Heroes explained The Exploded View on the Ketelhuisplein, and the Embassy of Food, curated by Chloe Rutzerveld. [S19] Company New Heroes is the same collective that made the Growing Pavilion in 2019. [S19]
The universities' talk show

Design United returned to a five-day format. Its 2021 edition, Up Close & Personal, put a live talk show hosted by Isolde Hallensleben in the Effenaar for five days, one theme a day: entangled ecologies, connected interactions, changing things, embedded designers and evolving methodologies. [S20] The Design United page dates the edition to October 18 to 22 and gives the year as 2022 in its heading, which is a typo for 2021, since the days and the Effenaar broadcast match DDW's October 14, 2021 release. [S20][S6]
What changed after the virtual year

DDW's "what's new" guide lists the practical differences from earlier editions. [S21] A ticket or wristband gave nine days of access to the paid locations: the Klokgebouw, Things that Matter in Microlab Hall, the Graduation Show in the Beursgebouw, the Van Abbemuseum, Sectie-C, Dutch Invertuals and Cabinet of Collaborations on the Fuutlaan, Kazerne, the New Order of Fashion Lab and the Philips Museum. [S21] Corona testing was in principle not needed at the official exhibition locations, but an entry pass was mandatory for longer stays such as workshops and lectures. [S21] The bus company Hermes sold a day ticket for 5 euros, and the VEEM was no longer a DDW location, replaced by Microlab Hall, while the former Campina factory had become De Caai, home of Manifestations, Foundation We Are and the Embassy of Food. [S21] The TU/e campus was a new location, celebrating the university's 65th anniversary under the name Heroes of Change. [S21]

The guide to Strijp-S points out the Klokgebouw's Labyrinth, an art installation called Autonomous Tree in which visitors converse with a tree, and the Class of 2021 projects of all academies except the Design Academy Eindhoven. [S22] On the Ketelhuisplein it names Studio Speciaal's Portal, and Hendriks's village, where it says visitors learn that 80 percent is enough, and it places Antigoon and Ralph Roelse, two artists with roots in graffiti, in the basement of the skate park at Area 51. [S22] The guide counts eight areas in the city. [S22]

The design sector that DDW served was in a mixed mood. The BNO Sector Monitor 2021, republished by DDW, surveyed designers in the second half of 2020: half expected lower turnover in 2020 than in 2019, about two-fifths expected an improvement in 2021, and about 30 percent of self-employed designers without staff had used the temporary bridging scheme for the self-employed. [S23] The monitor's 2019 figures predate the pandemic. [S23]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**The theme's name.** DDW writes The Greater Number, and Wallpaper writes The Great Number. De Carlo's 1968 exhibition was the Great Number in Italian, and DDW's form is the one for this edition. [S4][S8]
**The Milan exhibition's end.** Wallpaper says days after opening, the book review says opening day. I use the review. [S8][S11]
**Visitor count.** None exists in the sources I opened, and DDW's press page says it no longer shares exact numbers per edition. The 350,000 figure is a standing description. [S7][S9][S14]
**Edition count.** DDW says the twentieth. Omroep Brabant's profile also says twentieth. [S2][S7]
What the record does not show
I do not know how many people visited, how many designers took part or how many locations there were, because the closing release says none of it. [S1]
I do not know which of the Ketelhuisplein buildings the aerial photographs show. [S10]
I did not read the jury reports of the Dutch Design Awards or DDW's annual report for 2021. [S12]
I did not read the 30 Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the six I used. [S10]
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival asks for a better number and publishes none, what would you ask it to count? [S1]

title: Dutch Design Week 2022 told designers to get set, and the record shows who was ready
subtitle: The Get Set edition read through DDW's releases and magazine, the Dutch Design Awards, a design critic's tips and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2022 (Get Set) from DDW releases, the awards and the photo archive: the theme, the area map, the Solar Pavilion and the missing count.

sections.x: A theme that says Get Set is a request to start, and the 2022 record shows a festival that started with a question to its own community before it asked anything of the public. [S1][S3]

I like a festival that tells its audience what to do next. This essay reads the twenty-first Dutch Design Week from published sources only: nine items from DDW's press archive and magazine, a trade-press report, a broadcaster's guide, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases, one release about the year before and the photographs. This one adds the context around the theme, the program map, the awards and the question of numbers. [S12]
A theme that came out of meetings

On June 7, 2022 Miriam van der Lubbe, Creative Head of DDW22, announced the theme in a live Q&A on Instagram with the designer Pete Fung. [S1] The release says the theme signals a shift from preparation to action and crystallized out of several meetings with members of the design community, held earlier in the year to test the temperature and ask how DDW could best relate to the design field. [S1] Van der Lubbe's own explanation was that people must be ready for the challenges, must also get their settings right, forge smart coalitions and, above all, get activated, because doing nothing is no longer an option and not everything will work out as planned. [S1] The closing release gave the theme as Get Set, with the line "We're on a mission". [S2]
The edition ran from Saturday, October 22 to Sunday, October 30, 2022, and DDW called it the 21st. [S3][S4] That agrees with the count of 14th in 2015 and 20th in 2021. [S4]
The ambassadors' mission

The ambassadors, announced on September 5, were the solar designer Marjan van Aubel and the Milan and Rotterdam studio Formafantasma, Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin. [S4] The release says the ambassadors were also asked to bring young talent into their mission, which was new that year. [S4] Van Aubel is co-initiator of the first Solar Biennale, held in September 2022, and its closing piece was the Solar Pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein. [S4][S5] Formafantasma's symposium at Kazerne on Sunday, October 23 investigated, in DDW's words, the possibilities and problems of design in answering crucial questions of ecological and social development. [S6]

The Solar Pavilion was designed by V8 Architects and Marjan van Aubel Studio. DDW's magazine describes four steel masts between which a sheet of glass solar panels is stretched, colored panels developed with Kameleon Solar, and a design that is fully circular and uses borrowed standard components to be returned. [S5] The same item describes Sunne Experience in the Klokgebouw, an immersive installation of lights that go through a day cycle with a soundscape based on recordings by NASA. [S5] The earlier draft matched a curved, tiled structure in the drone photographs to this pavilion by form alone. The magazine's description of colored panels supports that match, and I still have no title that names it. [S5][S12]
The program map

The program release of September 13 listed seven thematic exhibitions, all called Get Set for something, that could be seen only during DDW in the Klokgebouw and on the Ketelhuisplein: Durable Living, The Next Generation, Digital Evolvement, Smart Livability (with the exhibition The New Nature of Living), Creations of Trust, Global Wellbeing and Things that Matter. [S3] It also put the Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show in the Microtuin near the station and Manifestations in the VEEM, Next Nature's RetroFuture in the Evoluon, and the program of World Design Embassies, which it said uses eight embassies to explore complex social challenges. [S3] The release spoke of nine areas of Eindhoven. [S3]

The October 19 guide named the areas one by one: Station, Center, Canal, West, Hallenweg, Sectie-C, Strijp T+R and Strijp-S, followed by a group of separate locations under the heading Other. [S6] Eight named areas and one group of locations reconcile the two statements. The guide placed the Dutch Design Awards nominees in Microlab Hall, with the exhibition Things that Matter, and gave Eindhoven Central Station a first appearance as a DDW location. [S6] It also named the official opening party at MYLC on October 22, an Envisions retrospective, Expedition Aequalis by Dutch Invertuals and Fillip Studios' Arabidopsis Symphony on the Wilhelminaplein. [S6]

At the Van Abbemuseum, the exhibition The collection is... showed design objects from Lidewij Edelkoort's private collection in ten rooms of the old building alongside contemporary art, with an emphasis on alumni and teachers of the Design Academy Eindhoven. [S7] The museum's program page lists it as on show from October 8 to November 6, 2022 and says a second showing would run at Kazerne until spring 2023. [S7] The program release of September 13 called the roughly 50 works recently acquired. [S3] The page names the curators, Edelkoort and Steven ten Thije. [S7]
Numbers: what the closing release says and does not say

The closing release of November 3 says DDW22 was "on the level of peak year 2019" for visitor numbers and gives no figure. [S2] Peak year 2019 is a loose phrase: DDW's own closing release for 2019 gave 350,000 visitors, and the trade press reported that this was 5,000 fewer than the 355,000 of 2018. [S15] A broadcaster's headline, which I could read but not the text beneath it, says DDW drew 350,000 visitors and that a new generation of designers had risen. [S9] The standard description DDW supplies to the press, quoted by Innovation Origins that week, was more than 2,600 designers and more than 350,000 visitors across about 120 locations. [S10] Innovation Origins counted 598 exhibitions, from which it selected six. [S10] And DDW's own press page says the organization no longer shares exact numbers for each edition. [S11]

So the numbers available are these: a loose comparison from DDW, a headline, a boilerplate description and a count of exhibitions by a reporter. None is an audited count. I use 350,000 only as a media figure, and 598 as one reporter's count of exhibitions. [S2][S9][S10][S11]
Awards at night

The Dutch Design Awards announced and celebrated their winners at the DDA Award Night on October 27, 2022 during DDW. [S8] The winners were REX by Studio Ineke Hans and Circuform for Product, the Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen by MVRDV for Habitat, CAPS LOCK by Ruben Pater for Communication, The Utopia Ball by Yamuna Forzani for Fashion, Waterschool M4H+ by Studio Makkink & Bey for Design Research, Buycloud by Studio Noa Jansma for Data & Interaction, a campaign by Fonds Slachtofferhulp and Morrow for commissioning, and Cream on Chrome (Martina Huynh and Jonas Althaus) as Young Designer. [S8] The Public Award went to the Kleinkijkacademie by Sjaak Langenberg and Rosé de Beer. [S8] The jury text for the year calls it a time when designers take responsibility and collaborate more. [S8] The guide of October 19 put the nominees in Microlab Hall, so a visitor could see the work that the night would judge. [S6][S8]
A broadcaster's view

The VPRO's guide, ten tips for the week, opens with Manifestations in the VEEM, curated by Viola van Alphen, and gives the example of the Love Letter Generator, in which a language model writes a love letter, and gURL, a teenage bedroom of 2032. [S13] Its second tip is the Solar Pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein, where Van Aubel argues for what the guide calls solar democracy, a world in which people surround themselves with aesthetic solar technology. [S13] That is a critic's selection and the VPRO's reading of Van Aubel's position, and I report them as such.
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a 2022 collection of albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated. [S12][S14] I opened five on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. [S12]

The Klokgebouw album holds 134 photographs, and the titles split the building into Hal 1 to Hal 4, with dates from September 22 to October 26, 2022. The one I chose, titled Hal 3 and dated October 26, shows a teal bicycle on a black table beside a card reading DO NOT TOUCH. No title names the bicycle, and I cannot say which of the seven thematic exhibitions it belongs to. [S12] A hall name and a date are reliable, and the work on the table is not named. [S12][S3]

The Ketelhuisplein album holds 190 photographs, and several drone photographs by about.today show a tall, curved structure covered in blue, pink and brown tiles rising over the square, with the Philips clock tower in the background. In a closer aerial photograph three people wave from an opening in it. [S12] The Van Abbemuseum album holds 35 photographs, 13 of them titled for Lidewij Edelkoort and dated October 23, 2022, by Boudewijn Bollmann; in the one I chose, two visitors stand before a wall of framed objects, drawings and small sculptures, with a blue globe hanging in the corner. The museum's page shows the exhibition ran in ten rooms, which makes a wall of framed objects plausible. [S12][S7]

The Graduation Show album holds 132 photographs, and a set by about.today is titled Graduation Show Microtuin, which matches the release's location. The one I chose shows a long red banner reading WHO CAN AFFORD TO BE CRITICAL?, a table with papers on the floor and visitors far in the background. [S12][S3] The Embassy of Rethinking Plastic album holds 48 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 22 and 23, with file titles that read YKSI, which is a place and not a project. [S12]
What the magazine added

The magazine's interview with Creative Head Miriam van der Lubbe and the designer Pete Fung, published June 2, gives her account of the theme: DDW is a platform for the community of designers, companies and organizations, the theme asks designers and citizens to get in the right mindset for enormous challenges such as the climate crisis, the war in Ukraine and inequality, and DDW had held meetings with the design community to learn what its members were working on. [S16] Fung called the phrase poetic, the moment before action, in a field often about grand gestures. [S16]

Formafantasma's ambassador project was a symposium called Learning With, which the duo said would not be about them: their way of showing who they are is to present young talents such as their students. [S17] The magazine describes GEO-DESIGN, a two-year master's course at the Design Academy Eindhoven led by Formafantasma, which in 2022 delivered its first graduates, some of whom took part, among them Gudrun Havsteen-Mikkelsen's film on Arctic mining and Ayla Kekhia's amended legal text on border enforcement. [S17] The symposium included the researcher Angela Rui and the Design Museum London senior curator Rebecca Lewin. [S17]

The What if Lab, a program of the Dutch Design Foundation that pairs designers with organizations, showed results in the Klokgebouw's second hall, among them Muzus's installation with ReumaNederland on making life with rheumatism experienceable and Totaal Lokaal, a project with the engineering firm Sweco on self-sufficient cities. [S18] The eight World Design Embassies, a program the foundation began five years earlier, included the Embassy of Food, whose curator Chloe Rutzerveld laid out three scenarios for the supermarket of 2050, and an Embassy of Water. [S19] The Dutch Design Awards commissioned a column by the curator Nick Axel, who wrote that the nominees show the future has already arrived and that designers bridge the gap between theory and practice. [S20]
The universities in two places

Design United split its 2022 edition, Transitions, between a Klokgebouw exhibition on October 22 to 30 and an afternoon program of workshops, debate and project presentations in Microlab on October 24 to 28, 15:00 to 18:00, on five themes: more than human design, futuring, politics of design, entanglements with AI and neo craftsmanships. [S21] The 2022 page counts the Klokgebouw expo as part of the same edition. [S21]
The opening night, the leadership change and the Floriade link

The grand opening took place at MYLC in De Caai, hosted by Jess Oberlin of PLASMA and the chair Jennifer Muntslag, with Van der Lubbe explaining the theme and the State Secretary for Education, Culture and Science, Gunay Uslu, speaking about giving space to creativity, designers and makers. [S22] Van der Lubbe thanked Martijn Paulen for his dedication, and DDW's earlier announcement explains why: after nine years Paulen stepped down as frontman of Dutch Design Week to concentrate on the foundation's strategic development, including World Design Embassies and What if Labs, and DDW looked for a new creative leader. [S22][S23] Paulen said the government had acknowledged DDW as indispensable for the Dutch creative basic infrastructure. [S23] That sentence is his, and it refers to the Council for Culture's advice of June 2020 that DDW's own news item reported.

The Solar Pavilion has a backstory in DDW's own telling. V8 Architects' co-founder Michiel Raaphorst said Marjan van Aubel called them in May asking for help, that they met three days later with Van der Lubbe and sketched a surface that harvests solar energy and forms part of the environment, that the structure holds about five thousand kilos of solar panels and that more than ten parties worked on it. [S24] Visible connections and wires were left in place on purpose, and an app let visitors have their photo taken from a distance via a QR code. [S24]

Earlier in 2022 DDW pointed to its presence at the horticultural exposition Floriade Expo 2022 in Almere, open until October 9: the house The Exploded View: Beyond Building from the 2021 Ketelhuisplein, a biobased pavilion by Next Nature hosting 24 designers, and an art pavilion by Studio Ossidiana. [S25] The page places Floriade Expo 2022 in Almere, where the exposition took place. [S25]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**Nine areas or eight.** The September 13 release says nine, and the October 19 guide lists eight named areas plus Other. Both fit one list. [S3][S6]

**The Edelkoort exhibition's title.** The program release speaks of approximately 50 works, and the museum's page calls the exhibition The collection is... and gives ten rooms and the dates. The museum's page is the more specific. [S3][S7]
**Visitor numbers.** DDW's phrase "level of peak year 2019" is loose, and its press page says exact numbers are no longer shared. A broadcaster's headline says 350,000. [S2][S9][S11]
What the record does not show
I do not know how many people came, because DDW says it no longer shares exact numbers. [S11]
I do not know which Get Set exhibition the teal bicycle or the red banner belongs to. [S12]
I did not read the jury texts of the Dutch Design Awards beyond the announcement. [S8]
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the five I used. [S12]

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival tells its audience to get set and then stops publishing how many came, what would you look for instead as proof that anyone did? [S11]

title: Dutch Design Week 2023 asked visitors to picture this, and the record shows a festival that sorted itself into missions
subtitle: The Picture This edition read through DDW's releases, a royal visit notice, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2023 (Picture This) from DDW releases, a royal visit notice and the awards: the missions, PONT, the new management and the missing count.

sections.x: A theme that says Picture This invites the obvious test: what can a photograph of the future actually show, and what does a festival do to help a visitor read one. [S1][S5]

I like a festival that gives its visitors an instruction they can check. This essay reads the twenty-second Dutch Design Week from published sources only: ten items from DDW's press archive, a notice from the royal house, the Dutch Design Awards' announcements and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used four releases and the photographs. This one adds the program structure, the funding news, the management change and the question of numbers. [S13]
An urgent call, and a new way to sort a program

The edition ran from Saturday, October 21 to Sunday, October 29, 2023, and DDW called it the 22nd. [S2][S3] The theme was announced on May 17 in two live Q&A sessions on Instagram, in which Miriam van der Lubbe, Creative Head of DDW, spoke with the media partners DesignWanted and ArchDaily. [S1] The release calls Picture This an urgent call to face the future scenario that follows if we continue living as we do now, and asks what world we would see in 20, 50 and 100 years. [S1] It adds that designers are experts in formulating and visualizing perspectives and can lead people through a process of change and break through paralysis. [S1]

What changed was the structure of the program. DDW's April announcement said it would commit for the coming years to ten program lines, five missions and five design perspectives, and encouraged applicants to link their work to them so the program team could curate matches. [S2] The missions begin with verbs: achieving an equal society, boosting health and well-being, challenging the digital future, creating the living environment and enabling a thriving planet. [S2][S4] The design perspectives are signature and collectible design, speculative and social design, product and craft design, service and innovative design, and independent and critical design. [S2] The September 5 release described them as ten brand-new narratives that guide visitors and designers to find each other. [S3]
What the October guide put under each mission

The October 4 guide gave examples. Under the equal society it listed, among others, Portray Me by International Creative Women in the center and Dialogues of the Unheard by Fresh Grads at Sectie-C. [S4] Under health it listed Design your MRI Experience (for kids) by Aniek Bartels and the Philips Museum and Objects for Wellbeing by Alissa+Nienke. [S4] Under the digital future it listed Mainframe: Living Technology by Synthetic State and a project on game design by Enversed. [S4] Under the living environment it listed the What if Lab project Rethinking shared space with Sweco and Everyday Paradise, co-curated by Lili Tedde and Lidewij Edelkoort. [S4] Under the planet it listed Icon Re/Outfitted by The Visionary Lab with Vitra and Levi's, and Future > Factory > Furniture, a joint project by furniture makers. [S4]

It also described seven World Design Embassies. Among them: the Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building, with Possible Landscapes on a regenerative economy; the Embassy of Food, with The farm of the future; the Embassy of Health, with Health as currency; and the Embassy of Inclusive Society. [S4] The September 5 release added places: the Van Abbemuseum's The space between us, A Bite of Void at Albert van Abbehuis, Manifestations on Strijp-S, Perpetuum Mobile by Kiki & Joost at Canal and Next Nature's Spacefarming at the Evoluon on the future of food for 10 billion people in 2050. [S3]
Money and management, off the exhibition floor

Two announcements in September show the organization behind the week changing shape. On September 19, DDW said the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science would invest 9 million euros over three years in a program called PONT, The Public Design Practice, which the Dutch Design Foundation would coordinate. [S6] The aim, in the State Secretary's words as quoted, was to involve the creative industry more in societal challenges such as the energy transition and housing. [S6] PONT would officially launch during DDW on October 23. [S6] On September 28 the foundation announced that Katja Pahnke would join Martijn Paulen from November 1 as a second member of the management board, with Paulen responsible for strategy and innovation and Pahnke for general and organizational development. [S7] These are the organizer's announcements, and I did not look for the ministry's own text.
A queen, a forest and the hundred best products

Queen Máxima made a working visit on the afternoon of Thursday, October 26. [S8] The royal house's notice says she walked around with Van der Lubbe, exploring the role of AI, reuse of industrial residue, sustainable furniture design and unconventional materials in architecture, and that young international designers presented graduation projects and there was an overview of the hundred best designed products of the past two years. [S8] The notice also says DDW has existed since 2001 and draws about 350,000 visitors a year, and that the queen had visited in 2011 and 2016. [S8] The first statement differs from DDW's own edition count, which makes 2023 the 22nd. If the first edition was in 2001, the count would be 23. I come back to this below.

The Dutch Design Awards announced eight winners on September 22, and the retrospective in the week showed their work. [S9] The jury noted that crossovers made up the majority of entries and wrote about the art of weaving, in the sense of craft and technology flowing together. [S9] The Habitat winner, Bosk, by Arcadia, the municipality of Leeuwarden and Bruno Doedens, was a walking forest of more than a thousand trees that moved through Leeuwarden's center for a hundred days in the summer of 2022, helped by about 4,000 volunteers, according to the awards' gallery. [S10] On Thursday of the week it won the Public Award, announced as the opinion of DDW visitors aligning with the jury. [S5][S11] The closing release and the awards' announcement agree on that. [S5][S11]
The closing release and its absences

The closing release of October 29 describes designers' "shared mission of bettering ourselves" and thanks the beacons Muzus, Yinka Ilori and Stefan Diez. [S5] It names the new programs of the year: the narratives, the interCHANGES series of co-creation sessions, the Avenue of Fresh Perspectives and PONT. [S5] It gives no visitor count. [S5] DDW's press page says the organization no longer shares exact numbers per edition. [S12] The royal house's 350,000 is a yearly description. [S8] I do not state an attendance figure for 2023.
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a 2023 collection of albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated. [S13][S14] I opened seven on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. [S13]

The Evoluon album holds 13 photographs by about.today, dated October 20, 2023. In one, a sign reading SPACE FARMING hangs above a long, thin model of a bridge-like truss, with two visitors leaning over it. That sign matches the September 5 program entry for Spacefarming at the Evoluon. Two photographs show a yellow dome whose side panel reads The Embassy of Food, and inside it a plaque headed Future perspectives says the embassy chose five designers as guides. The October 4 guide names the Embassy of Food and its theme, the farm of the future. [S13][S4][S3]

Albert van Abbehuis is a villa, and its photographs show it: floral wallpaper, wooden parquet and stained glass, with mirror-steel and stone objects standing in the rooms. The album holds nine photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann dated October 21, and the file titles name Collective Doh. The program names A Bite of Void at the same address, and I found no source linking Collective Doh to that exhibition. [S13][S3]

At Canal, the Kiki & Joost album holds 20 photographs by Nick Bookelaar, dated October 22, one of them of a tall timber hall with pink-lit beams and a lone visitor. The program names Perpetuum Mobile by Kiki & Joost for the location. [S13][S3] The Ketelhuisplein album holds 58 photographs by Cleo Goossens, dated October 21, and many titles name the Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building; a second album for that embassy adds photographs by Max Kneefel of greenhouse pavilions with landscape models on round tables, a flax board and a terracotta tower with plants. That fits Possible Landscapes on a regenerative economy. [S13][S4] The Graduation Show album holds 35 photographs by Goossens, dated October 22 and 29. The Dutch Design Awards album holds 44 photographs by Bookelaar, dated October 21 and taken at MicroLab on Strijp-S. [S13]
How the week ran, from the daily guides

DDW published a daily guide for each of the nine days, and together they give a calendar that the releases do not. [S15][S17][S18][S19][S20][S21] The guide for Saturday, October 21 listed Archiprix 2023 at the Eindhoven University of Technology, a talk on mobility in 2050 with the Embassy of Mobility, the Baltan Laboratories and Onomatopee event The Body is a Movement at Sectie-C and a Kiki & Joost evening at Canal, with dinners at the Kazerne by the caterer Vaderland as the "DDW at Night" item. [S15] As its "hidden gem" it named Bubble Trouble at Koelhuis, a playground in the former Campina freezer warehouse about the illusion of comfort and safety. [S15]

The Grand Opening took place in the skate park at Area 51, hosted by Lynn Zebeda and Cesar Majorana, with a takeover by the collective The New Originals, and the captions name the mayor of Eindhoven, Jeroen Dijsselbloem, among the guests. [S16] Van der Lubbe explained the theme on stage and the three beacons, Stefan Diez, Sanne and Neele Kistemaker of Muzus and Yinka Ilori, stood together. [S16] DDW and the auction house Catawiki ran an online auction of design by exhibiting designers from October 21 to 29. [S15][S21]

On Monday, October 23 the guide listed DRIVE 2023 at the Effenaar, a day by CLICKNL and Design United, and the first of the area recap videos, for Strijp-S. [S17] On Tuesday the interCHANGES session on the living environment and the thriving planet ran at the Fifth NRE, and Design United's Dialogues ran at Microlab. [S18] The 1m2 Collective, which had shown in the Van Abbemuseum in 2021, returned with a hall at Sectie-C, again to give starting, self-taught and student designers exposure and to make a statement about the inclusivity of design festivals. [S18] On Thursday, October 26 the Embassy of Inclusive Society held a conference at the Van Abbemuseum, the same afternoon as the queen's visit. [S19][S8] The guide for Saturday, October 28 mentions the former Renault design chief Laurens van den Acker, a DDW ambassador in 2018, giving a talk at the Klokgebouw on the Scenic E-Tech electric car, and Next Nature's Evoluon program on the food dilemma. [S20] It describes the week's work as visions from over 2,000 designers. [S20] The last guide, for Sunday, October 29, promised rain, a last day of everything and the Catawiki auction's closing. [S21]

Design United's own account of 2023, Ever-changing Relationships, runs from October 21 to 29, with five days of themed dialogues from Monday, October 23: politics of design, climate futures now, more than human, disentangling AI, design and society, and making matters. [S22]
Beacons, a talent podium and a club for missions

DDW called the first generation of beacons, Yinka Ilori, Stefan Diez and Muzus, guiding lights, and it published profiles in their own words. [S23][S24] Ilori, a British-Nigerian artist and designer, described his public commission Happy Street in Battersea as his first permanent public commission and said its value lay in its effect on the neighbors. [S23] Diez, who has run his studio DIEZ OFFICE in Munich since 2002, said his work follows the principles of a circular economy, giving the BOA chair as made with at least 75 percent recycled material and AYNO and COSTUME as products made to be taken apart, and said there is no contradiction between good and sustainable design. [S24] Those are the designers' statements about their own work, published by the organizer.

The Secrid Talent Podium placed seven designers a year in the Klokgebouw with coaching and a monetary prize, funded by the card-wallet company Secrid, which says it invests 1 percent of its revenue in projects that serve its mission to shift industry from producing more to producing better and has been a certified B Corp since 2022. [S25] VPRO and DDW broadcast a live program on Sunday, October 22, on the relationship between Dutch design and the throwaway society, with the photographer Kadir van Lohuizen, Christien Meindertsma and a Repair Cafe, free to visitors with a ticket. [S26] On Wednesday, October 25 the foundation launched the Mission Club, a place where companies, governments and other organizations can meet the design community; Paulen opened it saying change is a contact sport between governments, the market and designers. [S27] Earlier in the year, on March 9, DDW was among eleven Eindhoven event organizers that signed the Green Events Deal with the city. [S28]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**The anniversary count.** DDW's April release calls 2023 the 22nd edition, and the royal house says DDW has existed since 2001. A count starting in 2002 gives 22, and a start in 2001 gives 23. DDW's own series is internally consistent from 2015 to 2023, so I use it, and I treat the royal house's year as the founding of the event and not as an edition count. [S2][S8]
**Visitor numbers.** DDW publishes none. The royal house says about 350,000 a year. [S8][S12]
**The Public Award.** The closing release and the awards' announcement agree that Bosk won. [S5][S11]
What the record does not show
I do not know how many people visited in 2023, because DDW says it does not share exact figures. [S12]
I do not know what Collective Doh was or whether it belongs to A Bite of Void. [S13]
I did not read the jury reports or the full winners list for the Dutch Design Awards 2023. [S9]
I did not open the ministry's own text on PONT. [S6]
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the seven I used. [S13]

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. When a festival sorts its program into missions, how would you check that a project belongs to the one it claims? [S2]

title: Dutch Design Week 2024 asked what was real, and the record shows eleven things built outdoors to answer
subtitle: The Real Unreal edition read through DDW's releases, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2024 (Real Unreal) from DDW releases and the photo archive: Grand Projects, Mission Days, beacons, a bamboo pavilion and the missing count.

sections.x: A theme called Real Unreal sets a trap for a photo archive, because a photograph of an unreal thing is still a photograph of a real one. [S1][S10]

I like a theme that forces a reader to check what a picture can prove. This essay reads the twenty-third Dutch Design Week from published sources only: seven items from DDW's press archive, the program page of one pavilion, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview. An earlier short draft used three releases and five photo albums. This one adds the call for entries, the beacons, the Mission Days, the pavilion's history and the awards' year of reflection. [S10]
A theme about several realities

The edition ran from Saturday, October 19 to Sunday, October 27, 2024. [S4][S6] DDW's June 28 release announced the theme Real Unreal and said it addresses how people find their way among the different realities the world now consists of, and where very diverse perspectives meet. [S1] It says designers explore and question what we accept as truths, and it invites visitors to discover things "so good, it's unreal" and to "see real amazing innovations". [S1] The slogan "don't believe everything you think" closes the release. [S1] The call for entries, opened on April 3, called the edition the 23rd and set the deadline for submissions at June 14. [S2]
Open doors for ideas that were too big for a booth

The call for entries made a point of inviting all kinds of ideas, with a special Call for Grand Projects that might land at one of Eindhoven's prominent squares. [S2] It also announced a more accessible application process, with tutorial videos and walk-in clinics. [S2] The closing release says the open call for Grand Projects got an amazing response and resulted in eleven outdoor projects that DDW could support, some together with the municipality of Eindhoven, which became the eyecatchers on prominent locations. [S6] I note that the count of eleven comes from the organizer and that I did not find a list of all eleven.
The program, by mission

The September 10 program release sorted highlights under five missions, with places. Living environment: Teunland 2.0 by Teun Zwets at Piet Hein Eek on Strijp-R, made from reused waste materials, and the Secrid Talent Podium in the Klokgebouw. Thriving planet: Cooling down the city at the NRE Terrain, a collaboration between designers and nature to tackle urban heat stress with a green spa around a revived oak tree, and Designing Society on the Ketelhuisplein. Digital future: Poetics of Prompting at MU and Pokka at Koelhuis. Health and wellbeing: Processing the Unprocessed at Sectie-C and Sharing Bloemfontein, a walking exhibition in Doornakkers. Equal society: the Trilix Bamboo Pavilion and Temple of Peace on the Ketelhuisplein, the latter described as 80 flags designed by teams of design graduates, artists and refugees. [S4]

The release also introduced Mission Days, five themed days from Monday, October 21 to Friday, October 25, with morning sessions, afternoon tours and an evening program called DDW at Night, meant to facilitate encounters between designers and professional visitors. [S4] The closing release says DDW co-created and hosted them with ClickNL and Design United. [S6] One of the days, the Digital Future day, included a Design and AI symposium on Wednesday, October 23 at Natlab. [S5]
The beacons

DDW calls its guest figures beacons, and the October 3 release introduced three new ones. [S5] Julia Watson of the Lo-TEK Institute, author of a book on indigenous technology, was to lecture at the Van Abbemuseum on Saturday, October 19. [S5] Bas van de Poel, innovation director of Modem, presented projects at the Klokgebouw and gave a keynote at the symposium. [S5] André Doxey, who had joined the LEGO Group that year as head of design, completed the three. [S5] The returning beacons were Muzus, with the interactive installation Meaningful Encounters on the Ketelhuisplein, and Stefan Diez, whose students from the University of Applied Arts in Vienna showed in the group exhibition Class of '24. [S5] The release describes the idea of a beacon as a guiding light that spends the first year in a deep dive into DDW and then develops a project. [S5]
A bamboo pavilion with a travel history

The program page for the Trilix Bamboo Pavilion, by studio akēka with the Dutch Bamboo Foundation, says it was first built in Uganda, then built again in Brussels for the New European Bauhaus Festival in spring 2024, and was in Eindhoven in its third iteration and its first showing in the Netherlands. [S7] It says most of the bamboo was harvested in Georgia and in the Netherlands and that the structure acts as a shading structure with workshops and discussions. [S7] This is a program text by its makers, and I did not find independent coverage. A bamboo structure had stood on the same square in 2016 as Bambooh Lala, a different project by the agency HeyHeydeHaas, according to a 2016 preview listing and DDW's 2016 closing release. [S11][S12]
Awards in a year of reflection

The Dutch Design Awards announced in July that 2024 would be a year of reflection: the strategy and processes would be redesigned and a new approach presented early the next year. [S3] In the meantime the exhibition at DDW paired ten earlier Young Designer winners or nominees each with a promising current name, ten plus ten designers, organized under DDW's five missions. [S3] The pairs include Yuta Ikeya spotlighted by Christien Meindertsma and Auke Bleij spotlighted by Bob Hendrikx. [S3] Bleij won the Public Award with Respyre, a concrete that turns urban surfaces into green infrastructure, and received a trophy designed by Meindertsma and printed by her FLOCKS Wobot. [S6] The closing release describes Meindertsma as the first Young Designer to win a Dutch Design Award. [S6]
What the closing release says about numbers

The closing release of October 29 calls the edition exceptionally high in quality, quotes Creative Head Miriam van der Lubbe saying it may have been the best so far, and announces the next edition as Saturday, October 18 to Sunday, October 26, 2025, with a first Super Early Bird ticket. [S6] It gives no visitor count. [S6] DDW's press page says it no longer shares exact numbers per edition. [S8]
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a 2024 collection of albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated. [S10][S9] I opened five on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. They hold 126 photographs: nine at Piet Hein Eek, 41 at the Klokgebouw, 11 at the NRE terrain, 30 at the Ketelhuisplein and 35 for Designing Society. [S10]

Only the NRE photographs name their projects in the file titles. At Piet Hein Eek, the photograph I chose shows a gray chair with an easel for a back, set against a blue block. The file title says Dirk Duif, and the program names Teunland 2.0 at the same site, so the picture and the program entry do not name the same work. [S10][S4] At the NRE terrain, the Cooling-Down-the-City photographs are dated October 23 and credited to Anwyn Howarth. The one I chose shows grasses, flowers and a young tree along the edge of a roof, which fits the program's description of designers working with nature. [S10][S4]

At the Ketelhuisplein, a bamboo pavilion with three tall, lit canopies stands on a paved square beside a container marked Drivers of Change. No file title names it, and I match it to the Trilix Bamboo Pavilion by form and place only. [S10][S4][S7] Designing Society has 35 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 19, 20 and 22, which show a glass greenhouse where visitors read boards, listen on headphones and look at a wooden model of a city. The release says the World Design Embassies, Labs and PONT presented together in this exhibition, exploring design as a tool for change. [S10][S6]
The ten named Grand Projects

The news page on the Grand Projects says an open call was issued in March and that "the final selection of eleven projects" ran from October 19 to 27 on the most prominent squares and locations. [S13] The page names ten: Rayonne by Marion Aeby, a textile installation on the Ketelhuisplein; POND by Nova Innova, a light installation at the Van Abbemuseum lake that translates the water's health into color; Temple of Peace by Peace Seekers, eighty flags made by eighty teams of recent graduates and refugees; We (don't) Want Wind by Noud Sleumer and Nikolai Gillissen; Outpost for Unreal Institutions by Pete Ho Ching Fung and Samein Shamsher at the station square; Inkijkjes in de Energietransitie by Bits of Space and Waag Futurelab; the Eigengrau Pavilion by Zalan Szakacs at Koelhuis; Krijt-je-Rijk by De Reuringdienst on 18 Septemberplein; the Wind Knitting Factory by Studio Merel Karhof on the Nieuwe Emmasingel; and Sex in the City by Noha and Lena Tunkers on the City Hall Square. [S13] That makes ten names against the stated eleven, and I did not find the eleventh. [S13][S6]

Designing Society, the Ketelhuisplein greenhouse, had around 40 projects and was free to visit. [S14] It came out of four of the foundation's programs: PONT, World Design Embassies, What if Lab and Maakruimte voor Mooi NL. [S14] Access was planned in: a tactile model at the entrance for visitors with visual impairments, project signs at wheelchair height and a free public tour every hour. [S14] DDW's look back at the exhibition called it the 7th edition of World Design Embassies, with all embassies, PONT and the labs under one roof. [S24]
A city's design school, a fire and a newspaper list

Not everything that mattered in 2024 happened inside the week. A DDW news item signed by Van der Lubbe, Paulen and Pahnke expressed serious concern about a possible departure of the Design Academy Eindhoven from the city, to Roermond, and argued that creative industries add about one billion euros a year to the region according to municipal research, and that DDW featured in more than 4,000 national and international publications the previous year. [S15] A later DDW news item says it was now certain that the academy would stay in Eindhoven, with the search for a location continuing, quoting the academy's chairman Joseph Grima. [S16] The items carry no date on the page, and the claims about value and publications are the signatories' own. [S15][S16]

Shortly before the week DDW reported that the Stroomhuis, an old squatted building and punk venue that had been a DDW location for years, was lost in a fire. [S17] The 2015 releases name the Stroomhuis as the venue of London Calling Part 2 and as a stage for DDW Music. [S25][S26]

On October 10 the Dutch newspaper Trouw placed DDW in its Sustainable 100 list at 22nd position as a newcomer, and Van der Lubbe accepted the prize for first place in the Art & Design category at Pakhuis de Zwijger. [S18] The jury chair was quoted saying the list shows the power of working together. [S18]
Who paid, who was invited

From the 2024 edition DDW selects an annual charity that visitors can support when buying a ticket, and the first was the Dutch Refugee Council, VluchtelingenWerk Nederland; the item gives no amount. [S19] DDW also said it supports Cultuur Inclusief Eindhoven each year, which provided 500 tickets to low-income residents, and partners with Refugee Team Eindhoven and Wasbeer & Pauw so refugees can gain work experience as volunteers. [S19] A ticket was valid for all nine days at the price of a day ticket. [S20] The three Creative Voices, the thing Magazine, Otis Dirk and Benito Walker, were invited to reflect on the program, including through a new DDW TikTok channel. [S21][S6] The Secrid Talent Podium, supported by the Secrid Impact Fund since 2022, again showed product designers, among them Pauline van Dongen's SUNTEX solar fabric, which links to her Umbra Pavilion a year later. [S22][S6]
Design United's 2024 edition, Changing Gears, put an expo in the Klokgebouw from October 19 to 27 and dialogues in the Natlab from October 21 to 25 on the five missions. [S23]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**The edition count.** The call for entries says the 23rd, which agrees with the series (22nd in 2023). [S2]
**Eleven outdoor projects.** The closing release gives the number, and I did not find a list. [S6]
**Visitor numbers.** DDW publishes none. [S6][S8]
What the record does not show
I do not know how many people visited, or how many of them came for the Mission Days. [S6][S8]
I do not know which photograph shows Teunland 2.0, the Secrid Talent Podium or Temple of Peace. [S10]
I do not know the list of the eleven Grand Projects. [S6]
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the five I used. [S10]
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a theme asks what is real, which of the eleven outdoor projects would you ask to show its working? [S2]
