title: Dutch Design Week 2025 called design unfinished, and the record shows a festival counting its own birthdays
subtitle: The Past. Present. Possible. edition read through DDW's releases and program pages, an interview with its co-founder, the Dutch Design Awards and the official photo archive
description: Dutch Design Week 2025 from DDW releases, program pages and the awards: the anniversary count, two sets of forecasts, Bridging Minds and the Grand Projects.

sections.x: A festival that calls design unfinished has to show unfinished things, and Dutch Design Week 2025 put several of them in the open air while it argued with itself about how old it was. [S1][S3][S4]

I like a theme that can be checked against an object. This essay reads the 2025 edition from published sources only: eight items from DDW's press archive, two program pages, an interview with the festival's co-founder, the Dutch Design Awards' announcement and the photo albums DDW publishes. It reports no visit and no interview of my own. An earlier short draft used five releases, two program pages and the photographs. This one adds the anniversary arithmetic, the awards, the leadership change and the forecasts that do not agree with each other. [S12]
A theme that refuses to wrap up

The edition ran from Saturday, October 18 to Sunday, October 26, 2025, under the theme Past. Present. Possible. [S1][S2] DDW's release on the theme says the 25th edition is grounded in the belief that design is never finished, and quotes Creative Head Miriam van der Lubbe: "Experiment is the engine of progress." [S1] It says the week presents raw ideas, bold questions and sensory experiments in studios, public squares, repurposed factories and central venues. [S1] The press archive's index dates the release July 8, 2025, and the dateline in the text reads July 10, 2025. I do not know which is the publication date, and I use July. [S1]
Counting the birthdays

The release calls 2025 the 25th edition and says what began in 2001 as Designers Present grew into an international platform. [S1] The royal house said in 2023 that DDW had existed since 2001. [S9] That does not match the ordinals DDW used in earlier years: the 14th edition in 2015, the 19th in 2020, the 20th and anniversary in 2021, the 22nd in 2023 and the 23rd in 2024. [S19][S20][S21][S22][S23] Those ordinals make 2025 the 24th and put the first edition in 2002, and a 2021 Omroep Brabant profile likewise says the event grew into an international one from 2002. [S18]

I can lay out the possibilities and not settle them. If DDW counts a 2001 event as its first edition, then 2025 is the 25th and the earlier ordinals were one short. If it counts from 2002, 2025 is the 24th, and the 2025 release counts a year-zero event. The co-founder, interviewed in a design trade piece, speaks of 25 years and of the 25th edition. [S6] None of the sources I opened explains the shift, and the release with the 2001 detail is the one source for the name Designers Present. [S1] I give the 25th as DDW's own label for the 2025 edition.
Forecasts, and two that disagree
No closing figure for 2025 appeared in the sources I opened, and DDW's press page says it no longer shares exact numbers per edition. [S10]

What exists are forecasts. The September 18 release said more than 2,500 designers, design schools, ministries and leading brands across 120 venues, with around 350,000 visitors expected. [S2] The September 24 release said work and concepts from 2,000 designers to 350,000 visitors at around 100 locations. [S4] Both are DDW's, six days apart, and they differ by 500 designers and 20 venues. The About DDW page gives more than 2,500 designers and more than 120 locations as the standing description. [S11] I take the larger standing description for the scale and the September 24 numbers as a looser phrasing, and I note that I cannot tell which DDW stands behind.
Eleven installations in public space

On August 7 DDW announced eleven large-scale installations by international designers at prominent places in the city, freely accessible, from an open call. [S3] It described five: Econario by Thijs Biersteker, about how political choices ripple through the living environment; the Umbra Pavilion by Pauline van Dongen, a pavilion of solar textile; Factory 5.0 by Aditya Mandlik, in which 10,000 mealworms eat through polystyrene; City At Sea Level by Bahar Orcun, a submerged city; and The Waiting Room by Nanne Brouwer, on privacy in asylum shelters. [S3] Van der Lubbe said the installations bring design to where people already are and invite passers-by to wander, discover and pause. [S3] The September 18 release added that some reach ten meters high. [S2] The 2024 closing release had counted eleven outdoor projects as well, so the number repeats from year to year. [S8]
Bridging Minds, and a queen

At the Van Abbemuseum the exhibition Bridging Minds, curated by Van der Lubbe as guest curator, showed 100 works across ten rooms of the Old Building. [S5] The program page names the rooms by theme: feeling safe, humans and technology, care and well-being, connection, inclusion, empowerment, innovation, nature, raw materials and freedom. [S5] Named makers include Hella Jongerius, Formafantasma, Jalila Essaidi and Bas Timmer. [S5] An assistant curator, Kirstin Romer, and scouts from the Nieuwe Instituut are credited. [S5] The page says the exhibition was on view from October 4. [S5]

Queen Maxima opened the festival on the evening of Thursday, October 16 at Domus Dela, after visiting Bridging Minds, according to the September 24 announcement and the opening release. [S4][S7] The opening release quotes her saying designers have remarkable power to tackle the challenges of our time and are a driving force in the Dutch economy. [S7] It calls the exhibition a selection of 100 designers and artists, while the program page counts 100 works, and I use works. [S5][S7]
Class of 25: sixteen or thirty-five

The September 18 release says a new generation of talent from 35 leading European design schools was featured in Class of 25. [S2] The program page for the Klokgebouw show lists 16 academies, from the Vilnius Academy of Arts and HKU Utrecht to the Academy of Fine Arts in Gdansk, and says each shows one project at the front of its presentation, together the Avenue of Fresh Perspectives, which capture "the current zeitgeist". [S13] The two numbers do not match, and the Design Academy Eindhoven, which the release names in Class of 25, is not among the 16. [S2][S13] I use 16 for the page and 35 for the release's claim, and I do not know the reason for the gap. The page's own date headers show the 2026 dates, so the listing may have been updated after the week.
Awards, in a new format

The Dutch Design Awards presented an Emerging Talent Award on Saturday evening, October 18. [S14] Fifteen nominees were shortlisted, and the jury, chaired by Borre Akkersdijk of BYBORRE, chose three winners: Vera van der Burg, Willem de Haan and Plasticiet (Marten van Middelkoop and Joost Dingemans). [S14] Each received 10,000 euros and a talent development program, funded by the Keep an Eye Foundation. [S14] This continues the 2024 year of reflection, after which the awards have a new approach. [S14][S15] The release describes the awards as founded in 2003. [S14]
The people behind the week

On August 26, 2025 the foundation announced that Martijn Paulen would step down as managing director on January 1, 2026 after 12.5 years, and that the supervisory board would recruit a successor. [S16] He had joined in 2013. [S16] The same year, Van der Lubbe described, in the trade interview, an initiative called Design Development Eindhoven to keep designers able to live and work in a city that expects 70,000 new homes in a decade, and a pavilion on the Ketelhuisplein dedicated to everyone who helped build DDW. [S6] These are her statements, and I did not find a document describing the initiative.

A related announcement of April 3 shows the festival's industrial side. Future > Factory > Furniture, driven by DDW with eight Dutch furniture and textile companies, took its circular-supply-chain project to Milan Design Week. [S17]
What the photographs add

DDW's Flickr account carries a 2025 collection of 58 albums, and its pages say the photographer's name and Dutch Design Week must be stated. [S12][S11] I opened seven on October 9, 2026 and did not return to them for this version. [S12]

The Umbra Pavilion album holds 16 photographs by Max Kneefel, dated October 18 to 24 in the file titles. In the one I chose, a canopy of pale blue louvered panels rises on a blue mast above curved light-blue benches, with a tower block planted with trees behind it. The photograph shows a public place that people can use. It cannot show a textile generating power, and the release makes that claim. [S12][S3]

Factory 5.0 has five photographs by Cleo Goossens, titled with the date October 26. My photograph shows a yellow-orange timber frame shaped like a four-legged animal, in front of a glass facade, carrying rows of white packets, with a visitor reading them. I cannot tell from the picture whether those packets are polystyrene or whether any worms are visible. [S12][S3]

The Waiting Room has eight photographs by Kneefel. The one I chose shows a timber room with a patterned cut-out roof, metal bunk beds with blue mattresses and a hanging sheet that begins with the words Once we had dreams, with six visitors at mid distance. That fits a piece about privacy in asylum shelters, and it is a match of subject and not proof of intent. [S12][S3]

The album for the Queen's visit holds 45 photographs by Kneefel, all dated October 16, and the Class of 25 album holds 56 photographs by Boudewijn Bollmann titled with the date October 26. [S12] The photograph I chose of the Class of 25 looks down on a long gray platform of small projects with visitors reading them from the edges. [S12][S13]
The installations, named

A DDW news page of July 7, built with Bureau Binnenstad Eindhoven, lists the Grand Projects for 2025 and again says eleven. [S24] It names ten: City at Sea Level; Econario; The Waiting Room; Factory 5.0; the Institute for Sand Grain Elevation Policy, where visitors scatter a bag of sand as "Sand Grain Distributors"; Rain Café, a rainwater tank that fills with every rainfall and doubles as a meeting place, by Floris Schoonderbeek; SONIC MAZE, an inflatable installation by mesure studio and ultimo intimo; the Umbra Pavilion; the Water Basin Totem by Salu Iwadi Studio, made from recycled construction materials and inspired by West African water basins; and Touching Cellulose, an EduCrafting Pavilion built with visitors from wood, hempcrete and cellulose, guided by TU Delft and TH Koln. [S24] As in 2024, the page states eleven and I count ten. [S24]

The page says The Waiting Room is an emergency tent lined with reclaimed wood from bed frames used at a Dutch asylum center in Bleskensgraaf, with bunk beds identical to those in more than 300 reception centers, and made with Planemos, the Netherlands Red Cross and the Eindhoven reception centers Wasbeer and Pauw. [S24] That detail adds to what my photograph shows of blue bunk beds in a timber room. [S24][S12] The page also spells the solar textile of the Umbra Pavilion HELIOTEX where the August release wrote Heliotex. [S24][S3]
New this year: hubs, former beacons and a furniture show

The foundation introduced HUBS, exhibitions that cluster designers around urgent developments, among them a Young Graduates hub at Fuutlaan 12 and a Textile and Material hub in the Klokgebouw. [S25] Forward Furniture, conceived and curated by Liv Vaisberg at De Caai, showed more than 100 designer studios, each asked to present at least three realized works. [S26] Former beacons returned: Bas van de Poel of Modem presented Dream Recorder, a bedside device that records dreams and plays them back, and a seminar on the design of a design practice; Stefan Diez presented an Exposé on a Circular Design Contract that ties a product's value to its use, durability and return; and the company Hydro showed R100, new work by designers including Keiji Takeuchi, Cecilie Manz, Daniel Rybakken, Sabine Marcelis and Stefan Diez, each limited to a 100-kilometer radius, at the Kazerne. [S27]

After the week DDW posted a short thank-you that called the 25th edition a milestone, repeated the dates of DDW 2026, October 17 to 25, and offered no figures. [S28] Design United's 2025 edition, Less Hope, More Action, ran five days of dialogues in the Natlab from October 20 to 24 and an expo in the Klokgebouw. [S29]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**25th or 24th.** DDW says 25th and dates the start to 2001, while its earlier ordinals imply 2002. Unresolved. [S1][S19][S23]
**2,500 designers and 120 venues, or 2,000 and 100.** Two DDW releases in one week disagree. Unresolved. [S2][S4]
**Sixteen academies or 35 schools.** The page and the release disagree. [S2][S13]
**Release date.** July 8 in the index, July 10 in the text. [S1]
What the record does not show
I do not know how many people visited, since DDW says it does not share exact numbers. [S10]
I do not know why the edition count and the founding year do not match. [S1][S10]
I do not know the reason for the gap between 16 and 35 schools. [S2][S13]
I did not read the Flickr albums I skipped and did not re-read the seven I used. [S12]

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and nothing here describes what it will show. If a festival adds a year to its age, what would you want it to show you to prove that the extra year happened? [S1]

title: Age of Wonderland had a known ending, and its record is better than its photographs
subtitle: Four years of a Hivos and Baltan Laboratories program at Dutch Design Week, read against the organizers' own reports and the three albums in the official photo archive
description: Four Dutch Design Week editions of Age of Wonderland, a Hivos and Baltan Laboratories program, 2014 to 2017, set beside the organizers' reports.

sections.x: Age of Wonderland is an unusual subject for the Dutch Design Week archive, because its organizers wrote down when it began, how many editions it had and when it ended. [S2][S15]

I like a record that ends, because it lets me ask whether the photographs cover the whole story. They do not, and the gap is the subject of this essay. It draws on public sources only: pages and annual reports from Baltan Laboratories, pages from Hivos, a Dutch Design Week press release, a 2014 review, a heritage article about the Natlab building, a capture of the program's own website and the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits. [S1][S5][S6][S7][S13]
It began with a festival in March, not with Dutch Design Week

The usual shorthand is that Hivos and Baltan Laboratories started the program in 2014. Hivos says exactly that, calling it a global learning program initiated by the two organizations that year. [S2] Baltan's annual report for 2014 gives the earlier step. In March 2014 Baltan held a festival called Age of Wonder, and six non-Western artists and scientists from the network of Hivos presented their projects there. The report says that visit led to a long collaboration with Hivos, and that the festival produced the pilot called Age of Wonderland as one of its main spin-offs. [S5]

The same report says Dutch Design Week took the project in as a program partner in 2014, and as one of the main themes on the way to the World Design Expo planned for 2017. It also reports about 2,500 visitors for the March festival and names three funders for the program: SNS REAAL, the Strijp-S Cultuurfonds and the Creative Industries Fund. [S5] Hivos, in the report's wording, is the Humanist Institute for Development Cooperation. [S5]

The program's own site, as the Internet Archive captured it after the end, lists the founders as Christine Wagner of Hivos and Olga Mink of Baltan Laboratories, with Arne Hendriks as curator. It calls Hivos and Baltan the initiators, developed for Dutch Design Week with the Dutch Design Foundation. [S15] That is the line I would use for credit: a program of two initiators with the festival organization as a third partner, and a named curator.
The numbering is simpler than it looks

It would be easy to read the sources as counting the editions differently. I read them as consistent. Hivos called the 2016 edition the third year in a row of the partnership, Baltan calls 2015 the second edition and 2017 the fourth, and the review of the first edition said it would be the first in a series running until 2017. [S3][S4][S8][S14] That is 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2017, four editions, and Hivos in 2017 calls the program four years long. [S2]

The 2015 annual report adds the phrase "2015-2017." It says that in 2015 Baltan started a three-year plan with Hivos, and its program heading carries those years. [S6] I read that as the span of the funded plan that followed the 2014 pilot, not as the start date of the program. The report itself describes the 2015 edition as the second. [S6]
2014: the pilot, six weeks and a lab

Baltan's report says six young, non-Western creatives from the Hivos network came to Eindhoven for six weeks, from mid-September to the end of October 2014, to work with the local creative community on existing projects. Their results were shared during Dutch Design Week, October 18 to 26, through public interventions, pop-up labs, workshops, lectures and exhibitions. [S5] The report's diary gives the exact residency dates as September 13 to October 26 and says the results were shown at Baltan Laboratories. [S5] A Baltan page for an open lab held that October says the two organizations had become the new program partner of Dutch Design Week 2014 with this project, with the six artists in residence since mid-September. [S12]

Studio International reviewed the edition on November 6, 2014. Its writer describes colored notes on the walls, tools on the tables and the noise of spinning bicycle wheels, and says six young talents from Indonesia, Uganda, Kenya, Guatemala and Nicaragua presented at Baltan in the Natlab. Six people from five countries means one country appears twice, and the review does not say which. [S14] The report resolves this: two of the six, Andreas Siagian and Seterhen Akbar Suriadinata, are from Indonesia. [S5]

Both documents give the projects some detail. Sandra Suubi, an eco-artist from Kampala, built a Dream Lab from plastic waste in which children's dreams could be heard, and after the week the organization Flipside took the Dream Lab over, according to the report. [S5] Roy Ombatti of Nairobi studied custom footwear for people affected by sand flea infections and, in the review's account, found that 3D-printed plastic shoes were hard and uncomfortable and moved toward a do-it-yourself toolkit. [S5][S14] Siagian, co-founder of Lifepatch in Yogyakarta, taught electronics workshops. [S5] David Marín of Guatemala worked on a project to remove clichés from Maya symbols, and José Montealegre of Nicaragua worked with Eindhoven's Griet Menschaert on a project about prisons, touring the city in a caravan. [S5]

The program's site gave the 2014 edition the title "The friendly invasion of a new world order." [S15] This edition falls outside the archive years, because the official photo archive holds no 2014 album for it, and I did not look for 2014 photographs elsewhere.
2015: a food program with a day-by-day record

The 2015 report is the best document in the set. It dates Age of Wonderland: Balancing Green & Fair Food to October 17 through 25, 2015, describes a week of presentations, workshops and conversations in an exhibition, and says Baltan and Hivos organized it. [S6] It names the Dutch Design Foundation, then still called DDW, as the third partner. [S6] The report's diary records that on July 15 Baltan learned the Creative Industries Fund would support the 2015 edition with 40,000 euros. [S6]

The six fellows were selected through an open call, according to the report. They were Yoyo Yogasmana of Kasepuhan Ciptagelar in Indonesia, Symbat Satybaldieva of Bishkek, Ahadi Katera of Dar es Salaam, Achmad Fadillah of Bandung, Sari Dennise of Mexico City and Arie Syarifuddin of Jatiwangi. [S6] Three of them arrived in Eindhoven on October 1, and on October 6 all six took part in a workshop with agribusiness managers at Tomato World in the Westland. [S6] The fellows returned home on October 30, except Katera, who spoke at a conference in The Hague. [S6]

The diary gives every day a focus. October 17 was compost, with Katera's workshop on fertilizer made from food waste. October 18 was rice, with Yogasmana cooking and eating rice with the public. October 19 was the Future Food Seminar, with a dinner and a tour; the report lists speakers from the Dutch foreign ministry, Next Nature and others. October 20 was water, October 21 agriculture, October 22 clay, October 23 plastic, October 24 abundance and October 25 resilience, closing with a finale and a nomadic food tasting. [S6]

Several details in the report line up with objects the photo archive may show. Fadillah's project LEBO, short for LEGO bottle, was a prototype of linkable, reusable plastic water bottles, and on October 23 he ran a bottle brick design workshop. [S6] Syarifuddin's Claynialism work investigated edible clay with Atelier NL and produced a manifesto signed by Eindhoven's culture alderman and by a representative of the Jatiwangi district. [S6] Yogasmana received the first Eco Coin from Koert van Mensvoort of Next Nature. [S6][S8] Baltan's follow-up post of November 24, 2015 adds that Katera's start-up Guavay drew interest from DSM and BAM, and the report says it won a contract with BAM International for supplying organic fertilizer to an airport tender in Dar es Salaam. [S6][S8]

Baltan's follow-up post credits its own photo archive to two photographers, Sas Schilten and Hanneke Wetzer. [S8] The Dutch Design Week album credits different people, in the photo titles, which is a reminder that Baltan's archive and the DDW archive are separate bodies of photographs.
2016: big data, and a longer cast

The Hivos page of October 17, 2016 describes the theme Big Data. Big DADA? and says six artists, designers and other creatives from Africa, Asia and Latin America would examine big and open data, with Natlab as their temporary atelier from September 26 and Dutch Design Week running October 22 to 30. [S3] The Dutch Design Week press release of October 6, 2016 calls it the third edition and names the fellows' home countries as Chile, Guatemala, Indonesia, Iran and Tanzania. [S13] The Hivos page names Branly López, Budi Prakosa and Ng'winula Kingamkono among them. [S3]

The two pages disagree in small ways. Hivos gives López's country as Guatemala in one sentence and Mexico in another. [S3] I leave that alone and note only that an organizer's own page can hold two answers to a simple question.

The press release adds the structure. The program was multi-year, with six fellows a year and two intensive residencies. [S13] The fellows worked with the Design Academy Eindhoven, among others, and master's students in information design were involved. [S13] There was also a live online radio station, produced with Ja Ja Ja Nee Nee Nee. [S13] Baltan's post of January 10, 2017 says the 2016 exhibition ran October 22 to 30, showed six non-Western applications of big data and had ten Dutch counterparts working with the six fellows. [S9]

The seminar The Big Data/Dada Dialogues took place on Monday, October 24, from 7:30 to 9:30 p.m. at Natlab, with Arne Hendriks, a Hivos program manager and the dean of research at ArtEZ among the guests. [S3] The 2017 annual report adds that two former fellows, Branly López and David Marín, shared their knowledge at a hackathon in the Natlab basement from March 28 to 30, 2017, with artists and students from the Design Academy and the university of technology. [S7]
2017: from a place to a calendar

The final edition changed shape. Baltan announced on February 13, 2017 that 100 Days of Learning would take place across the whole year, in the fellows' own cities and not only in Eindhoven, with sessions through four Hivos regional offices and a set of days during the World Design Event. [S10] The program's idea was a hundred people sharing knowledge that had changed their lives, turned into acts or tools others could repeat. [S10]

The October week was part of the first World Design Event, which Baltan describes as a new quadrennial event inside Dutch Design Week, with a focus on global social questions. [S4] The 2017 annual report says the event ran October 21 to 29 and drew a record 335,000 visitors. It also says Days of Learning took place in 20 countries across five continents that year. [S7]

Several details differ between the organizers' pages, and they matter if you caption photographs. Hivos promised ten daily talk shows. [S2] The program's own site lists nine daily talks, numbered one to nine, which matches the nine days of October 21 to 29. [S15] Baltan's event page and annual report say the daily talk, hosted by Arne Hendriks, was at 11:00 in the People's Pavilion, not in Natlab. [S4][S7] At Natlab, in the Dick Raaijmakers hall, there was a living archive exhibition and an editorial office, open daily. [S7] Baltan describes that archive as two walls where visitors could add their own story. [S4][S11]

That description matters for the 2017 photographs. The album holds six photos, four of which show numbered cards headed Moment of Learning on a wall. [S1] Baltan's page now lets me say the exhibition invited visitors to write on walls. It still does not say that these particular cards are those contributions, so I describe the cards and cite the invitation without joining them.
The program ended there. The program's site, after the last edition, says it was a wrap after four years, and Hivos calls 2017 the final edition. [S2][S15]
The building: a physics laboratory that became a program venue

The venue is part of the story. Architectuurcentrum Eindhoven says Natlab, short for Natuurkundig Laboratorium, was founded by Philips in 1914, moved into its own building on Strijp-S in 1923 and left for Waalre in 1963. [S16] The article also says the renovated building has been in new use since 2013, with a cinema, Baltan, the architecture center and an education institute among its tenants, to a design by the architect Peter Claassen that kept original floors, window frames and a wall painting. [S16]

Baltan's own history says its pilot years ran from 2008 to 2010 and that in 2014 to 2015 the renovated Natlab was officially opened with Baltan as a key inhabitant. [S17] On October 5, 2017, a few weeks before the final edition, Baltan posted that the European Physical Society had designated the Natlab a historic site and unveiled a pillar. [S18] The final edition's living archive therefore sat in a building that had just received a formal heritage recognition for its research history. That is a coincidence of dates, and no source links the two.
What the unevenness means

Four editions give four different amounts of evidence. 2014 has a review, an annual report and a program site, and no album. 2015 has a day-by-day report with named workshops, and a 23-photo album. 2016 has a theme, a seminar and a press release, and a 62-photo album that I could see only partly. 2017 has a format, two venues and a count of walls, and a six-photo album. [S1][S5][S6][S13]

That unevenness shapes how I would write each year. 2015 can carry specific captions, because the report and some photographs share words: a table headed This is LEBO matches a listed workshop. 2016 can carry a theme, a venue and a seminar. 2017 can carry a format, a place and the invitation to visitors. I give each year the claim its evidence supports and nothing more. [S1][S6][S13]
What the record does not show

I did not see any 2014 photographs, because the official archive holds no album for that year, and I did not open Baltan's own photo archive, which is a separate body of images. I do not know which fellow or session any 2016 photograph belongs to: the titles name the venue, the show and the photographer only. [S1]

I cannot say whether the cards in the 2017 photographs are the living archive, or whether Hivos's ten talk shows were planned and cut to nine. The sources do not say how many people attended the Age of Wonderland program itself in any year, apart from the 2,500 at the March 2014 festival. [S5] The Internet Archive capture of the program's site is from after the end, and I read only some of its pages, so details I did not open there stay out of the essay. [S15]

I also do not know what followed 2017 for the fellows. Baltan's 2017 report notes both the March hackathon and a six-day trip to Kyrgyzstan organized in August by a 2015 fellow, which are signs that some links outlived their residencies. [S7] A fuller history would follow those people, and I have not.
If you open one of these three albums, which photograph would you try to caption first, and which of these reports would you check it against? [S6]

title: Atelier NL at Dutch Design Week: a church studio, a soil archive and a sand project that left Eindhoven
subtitle: The official photo archive files seven albums over six editions. Studio pages, DDW's program, a museum press release and the press show what stood in the room, and when.
description: Atelier NL's church studio on Bergmannstraat and what the DDW archive, program and press show about its soil, sand, wood and river-clay projects.

sections.x: A photo archive can show that a studio was in the room without saying what the studio was doing there. [S27]

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds seven Atelier NL albums across six editions, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2019, 2023 and 2024, 83 photographs in all, credited in their titles to four photographers. [S27] The written record is much richer than those albums, and in two of the six years it changes what the pictures mean. This essay draws on public sources only: the studio's own pages, DDW's program and news archive, a museum press release, a Dutch broadcaster's festival guide, regional news, design press and a design-awards gallery. It reports no visit to the studio and no conversation with its designers, and it says nothing about the 2026 program beyond what DDW lists. [S1][S8]
I come from anatomy, where an unlabeled specimen is a problem, so I start with the label: the year first, the credit second, and only then the object. [S27]
Two designers who went looking for the ground under their feet

Atelier NL is an Eindhoven studio of Nadine Sterk and Lonny van Ryswyck. Its own about page says its work analyzes clay, sand and wood, aims to tie the earth's materials more closely to living communities, and is carried out with local producers and communities. It also says the two lead the Ceramic Minor Program and teach in the Department of Living Matter at the Design Academy Eindhoven. [S1]

The best account of how it began comes from a Sight Unseen profile of January 8, 2010. It says Sterk and van Ryswyck graduated from the Design Academy in 2006 and that the best-known work was Drawn From Clay, an extension of van Ryswyck's graduation project, for which she gathered soil from plots around the Netherlands to make ceramic cups in different hues. The profile traces the idea to an internship in poorer regions of Brazil, where the two saw ceramic workers make clay from favela soil. When they proposed going back to South America for their thesis, their tutor, the designer Dick van Hoff, reminded them they could do the same in their own country. [S19]

After graduation the duo were invited by the Rotterdam design couple Rianne Makkink and Jurgen Bey to live at their farm in the Noordoostpolder, where they spent a year studying the farmland and gathering soil from each plot with the farmers' help. The clays became a soil map and a rough tableware series, Polderceramics, and then a dinner service made with the manufacturer Royal Tichelaar Makkum. [S19] A gallery biography adds that Tichelaar launched works based on the Drawn From Clay prototypes at the Milan furniture fair in April 2009, after Gallery Libby Sellers in London had shown the prototypes earlier that year. [S20] The studio also announces on its home page, without a date, that Stedelijk Museum 's-Hertogenbosch and the Princessehof National Museum of Ceramics acquired what it calls its most pivotal work, the Noordoostpolder pieces. I did not check that with either museum. [S2] The studio's page for the later Clay Service says formal production began with Tichelaar and moved in-house at the studio after Makkum closed its homeware line in 2016. [S4]

Everything in this essay that happens at Dutch Design Week grows out of that first move: dig where you live, label what you find, and let the label travel with the object. The Clay Service page puts it in one detail, that each piece carries a stamp linking it to the place its clay came from. [S4]
A church in a residential street

For DDW the studio's address matters as much as its work. The DDW location page says Atelier NL is in the former Bergmann Church on Bergmannstraat, focuses on craftsmanship with locally sourced materials, and hosts social projects and exhibitions during the week. [S8] The studio's Earth Alchemy Factory page describes the same building as a place where design, education and production run together, with workshops, lectures, archives and material libraries open to the public and an active community of Design Academy students. [S7]

Sight Unseen already placed the studio in a church in 2010, describing a live-and-work loft in what it called the 4Apostelen church. [S19] I found no source that links that name to the Bergmann Church name used in 2015 and later, and I found no source that says when the building went up or who designed it, so I do not claim they are the same building and I give no construction date.

The building almost went away. Core77, reporting from Dutch Design Week 2015, says the studio had been there about eight years, that its lease was due to expire on November 1, and that it had launched a campaign to buy the building. [S18] The Core77 article says visitors could buy a €35 clay tile from a large tile wall of the clays the studio had collected over eight years, as an on-site complement to an online crowdfunding campaign. In the report van Ryswyck explains the wall plainly: the whiter it gets, the more people have funded the studio. [S18] I could not open the crowdfunding page itself, because the host answered with an access refusal, so I do not repeat any total raised, and I found no source that says whether the purchase went through. The studio still lists the Bergmannstraat address on its own pages, and DDW still lists it in 2026. [S1][S8]
2015 to 2017: tiles, a dinner and a request for sand

The first three albums are Iris Rijskamp's photographs of the church hall in 2015, 2016 and 2017, 14, 16 and 8 photos. [S27] The 2015 album shows what Core77 describes: a wall of clay tiles. [S18][S27]

For 2016 the studio's own page for Earth to Table explains the week. Atelier NL and the culinary group Dutch Cuisine invited visitors to curated meal events built around Dutch soil, with dishes by the chefs Luc Kusters, Jef Schuur and Peter Gast. The page says the events coincided with the release of the new SandGlass collection, glassware made from local sands, and the first Clay Service edition produced in-house at the Earth Alchemy Factory. There were two formats: a private Soil Soirée in the factory and a public Tasting Dinner in the hall of the nearby (H)eerlijk Anders cooking school. [S3] The 2016 album's long table of clay plates beside clear glass fits that description, but the archive does not say which pieces are which. [S27]

In 2017 Atelier NL became one of the DDW ambassadors. The IO+ news archive published the appointment on June 30, 2017, naming Sterk and van Ryswyck with the architect Winy Maas and the Dezeen founder Marcus Fairs, and said the studio would introduce a new interactive project, To See a World in a Grain of Sand. The announcement also says the two teach at the Design Academy and ArtEZ and run the Earth Alchemy Factory. [S15] TL Magazine, writing on October 25, 2017, called the project one of the most celebrated presentations of that year's week. It says the two had asked the public for months to send sand samples from around the world, with their stories, and that the first glassware of the project, the ZandGlas set, was handblown from sand dug at the Zandmotor near The Hague. It places a presentation by Sterk at the VEEM building. [S16]

The same ZandGlas research won the 2017 Dutch Design Awards in the Design Research category, according to the awards gallery. The jury text there praises the thorough and time-intensive research and calls the glassware design distinctive. The gallery says each glass object is stamped with the origin of its sand, and that the sands then in use came from the Sand Motor and the Savelsbos in Maastricht, among other localities. [S17] I did not find a page that gives the date of the 2017 award ceremony, so I do not give one.

The album for 2017 has eight photos of bottle shelving and a lit sign over a counter of glassware. [S27] The sources above place the sand project at the VEEM building and other sites, and they do not tell me whether the church hall held a part of it. Whether those shelves belong to this project or to something else in the church that week is unknown to me.
2019: a model forest, a cargo bike and a soil call
In 2019 the archive has two Atelier NL albums, and unlike in earlier years the written record explains both. [S27]

The second album, 13 photos by Iris Rijskamp of saplings in pots and stacked planks, matches the exhibition the VPRO festival guide recommended that year under the title Stormhout/WildHout. VPRO says the strong storm of January 18, 2018 had pushed van Ryswyck to dive into the world of wood, that Atelier NL planted a complete model forest in the large church hall together with the forest group Bosgroep Zuid-Brabant, and that next to the hall the studio showed a modular relay block designed so that even small trees can be used for timber. It also says the designer Tom van Duuren parked a mobile wooden house in front of the church where visitors could stay for 60 euros a night. [S23] The saplings in the album therefore belong to this exhibition, since a model forest in the church hall is what the guide describes. [S23][S27]

The studio's own page for WildHout WildWood adds the community side. It says the exhibition was first presented at Dutch Design Week 2019 as a response to a violent storm earlier that year that uprooted nearly a thousand trees in Eindhoven, that visitors were invited to adopt a tree and the municipality planted two more in return, and that adopters chose among six themes, timber, recreation, food, biodiversity, water storage and cultural history, each tagged with a color. [S6] The two dates do not conflict. The VPRO guide dates the spark of interest to a storm in January 2018, and the studio dates the adopt-a-tree campaign to a storm in 2019. Omroep Brabant confirms the second one: it reported that around a thousand trees fell in Eindhoven in a storm in early June 2019, and that the city also still had 400 trees to replace after a storm in 2018. [S25] A later Omroep Brabant survey counted almost two thousand fallen trees in Eindhoven and the surrounding municipalities and noted that part of the storm wood would go to an atelier making work for Dutch Design Week. The article does not name the atelier, so I do not claim it is this one. [S26]

The first 2019 album, titled Straatmakers, has 19 photos by Ralph Roelse. [S27] The studio's page for De StraatMakers describes a project in which it collected 150 soil samples from 30 sites across Eindhoven, drilling one meter deep at each, and sorted the soils into earth, sand, clay, humus and peat. It says the stone manufacturer Metten Stein+Design developed a family of paving tiles from that research, with a warm gray ground that matches Brabant loam and fragments in the colors of the city's soils. The page adds that Eindhoven residents could send in a jar of soil with a story. [S5]

DDW's own news item for DDW19 explains the mechanics. It introduces De StraatMakers, "a.k.a. former DDW ambassador Atelier NL," and says that starting that day the group would ride a cargo bike through Eindhoven collecting soil samples for a presentation at DDW. People registered a jar and its story on the A World of Sand website, received a location ID number, and either gave the jar to the riders or took it to Bergmannstraat 76 before October 8. [S9] That explains the green cargo tricycle with a Straat Makers op DDW sign that appears among the album's photos. The album's photo titles mention Wall Street. Neither the studio's project page nor DDW's news item uses that name, and I found no source that explains it, so I leave it unexplained. [S5][S9][S27]

A third program used the same address that week. Creative Residency Arita announced on October 12, 2019 an exhibition of seven recent residents' ceramic projects and two brands at Atelier NL, Bergmannstraat 76, October 19 to 27, 2019, 11:00 to 18:00. [S24] In 2019 the church hosted a forest, a soil collection and a Japanese residency show at once, which is why I think captions need three fields, venue, project and year, and not one. [S24][S23][S9]
2021: the week the studio was in Venlo

No album exists for 2021, but the DDW program does list the studio. Earth Alchemy: 15 Years of Digging, presented by Atelier NL, ran at the Museum van Bommel van Dam in Venlo until January 9, and DDW offered guided tours called Think Global, Dig Local on October 19, 21 and 24, with train times from Eindhoven. [S12] The program page does not state the year. October 19 fell on a Tuesday in 2021, and the listing carries the weekday, so I read it as 2021. A German trade-press report on the museum's reopening in the former post office says the Atelier NL retrospective was one of two shows it opened with. [S22] The studio's home page calls it its first retrospective and says the tenth ZandGlas edition, made from sand from Joamerdal (Valley of Sorrow) with the heritage foundation Het Limburgs Landschap, commemorates it. [S2] Here the archive's silence is only an archive gap: the studio was on the DDW program that year, in another city.
From Eindhoven sand to Norfolk, Virginia

The sand project did not stay in Eindhoven. The studio's home page says To See a World in a Grain of Sand was launched at the Oerol festival in 2017, that a 500-meter trail called ZandScheppers followed at Oerol 2023, and that the Chrysler Museum of Art in Norfolk, Virginia showed it from August 2022 to January 2023, the studio's first major exhibition in North America. [S2] The Chrysler's press release of August 8, 2022 gives the exact run, August 12, 2022 to January 22, 2023, and describes the method: people send in a small amount of sand from a place that matters to them, with its story and a photo of the spot, and the designers melt it into glass. [S21] It names the agencies that authorized local sand collection, among them Fort Monroe National Monument, Jamestown Rediscovery, Naval Station Norfolk, the Portsmouth Department of Museums and Tourism and the Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia. It also says Sterk visited the museum's glass studio from August 18 to 21, 2022. [S21] The studio's page adds that the museum show produced a limited ZandGlas #11 from Fort Monroe, the first in the series made from American soil. [S2]

I include this thread because it shows what an archive of one week cannot: the 2017 request for sand at DDW is a seed, and the Norfolk press release counts it as more than a decade of collecting. [S21][S15]
2023: a church hall shared with other designers

The 2023 album has 8 photos by Almicheal Fraay of a banner, a pink looping sculpture, tables of printed sheets and a row of cups. [S27] DDW's program page says The Product Chronicles, an exhibition presented by Zakka Stories, was held at Atelier NL's venue, the Bergmannkerk. It names Aniela Fidler Wieruszewska, Antoine Peters, Christien Meindertsma, Nienke Hoogvliet with Tim Jongerius, Noud Sleumer and the collective Re-gained among the contributors. [S11] That corrects how the pictures should be read: the banner and most of the work in the hall belong to a guest show. The same page says Atelier NL showed its current work, sold tableware and samples, and presented two social projects with Residency for the People, KoffieKopSalon 55+, in which older local residents work live in clay at the studio, and Amsterdam Table Ware, made with local clay and Amsterdam residents on the initiative of the Amsterdam committee for the May 4 and 5 commemorations. [S11]
2024: clay from a river widening

The 2024 album has five photos by Anwyn Howarth and is filed under Hallenweg. [S27] DDW's recap video of October 24, 2024 places Atelier NL in the Hallenweg area and names an exhibition, Meanderende Maas, and a dinner in the studio's church, Smaak van de Bodem. [S28]

The program page for Meanderende Maas, presented by Atelier NL under the theme thriving planet, says the exhibition was made with the Meanderende Maas project along the river between Ravenstein and Lith, using the clay excavated for river widening and dike reinforcement. It describes a Maas KleiServies made from that clay and packages of purified clay called Broodjes Maasklei, each carrying a message from a visitor to the person who will buy the clay. [S10] MaterialDistrict, writing on December 20, 2024, dates the show within Dutch Design Week, October 19 to 27, 2024, and credits its photos to Maikel Samuels. [S14]

The project behind the clay has its own record. Its website says the Meanderende Maas project strengthens the dike from Ravenstein to Lith, gives the river more room, and covers about 2,650 hectares including a Brabant dike of more than 26 kilometers. Ten organizations work on it, the contractor Boskalis began in January 2025, and completion is expected at the end of 2030. [S13] I found no source that says how much Maas clay Atelier NL actually received or used. The photos in the archive could be of either the exhibition or the dinner, and the album does not say. [S27][S28]
What the awards add

The studio's home page reports that Dezeen Awards named Atelier NL Designer of the Year in 2018 and also gave a Homeware Design of the Year award that year, and quotes the jury's reasons. [S2] The jury text on the Dutch Design Awards page and the one on the Dezeen page the studio quotes both point to the same things: local materials, responsible production and an unusually rigorous method. [S17][S2] I could not open Dezeen's own pages, because its server refused access, so the Dezeen award is known to me from the studio's page and not from the award organizer. There was no album and no program page that I could find for 2018, so the archive tells us nothing about what the studio showed at DDW that year.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**When the studio began.** Core77 in 2015 says van Ryswyck founded Atelier NL with Sterk in 2006. The gallery biography says it was formed in 2006 after graduation, and Sight Unseen in 2010 gives 2006 as the graduation year. The Chrysler's 2022 press release gives the founding year as 2007, and DDW's 2017 ambassador item says the pair started "ten years ago." [S18][S20][S19][S21][S15] I use 2006 and say who says it. The 2006 sources date from 2010 and 2015 (the gallery page is undated), and the 2007 figure is a single parenthetical in a press release. A company register extract would settle it, and I did not find one.
**Which storm.** VPRO points to January 18, 2018, the studio's page to a 2019 storm. Both happened, and both feed the project at different stages. [S23][S6][S25]
**Whether the saplings belong to WildWood.** Settled by the VPRO guide: a model forest in the church hall. [S23]
**Who made the 2023 show.** The program page names Zakka Stories as the presenter, and Atelier NL as host with its own side program. [S11]
**The Venlo retrospective.** The DDW program page carries no year; the weekday of the listed tour dates settles it as 2021. [S12]
What the record does not show

I do not know who designed the Bergmann Church or when it was built, whether the 4Apostelen church of 2010 is the same building, or whether the 2015 purchase campaign succeeded. I do not know what the 2017 album's shelves belong to, what "Wall Street" refers to in the 2019 photo titles, or which of the 2024 photographs show the exhibition and which the dinner. I could not read the studio's press kit, which its site says is available, because the site's robots file excludes the folder where such files sit. I found no DDW program page for Atelier NL for 2018, 2020, 2022 or 2025, and the archive's album list was the only way I had to look at those years, from a reading on October 7, 2026 that I did not repeat for this version. [S27][S1]
The 2026 listing shows the studio open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 during October 17 to 25, 2026, with wheelchair access. It says nothing I can use about what will be shown. [S8]

The archive gives us the church hall, year after year. The written record says what stood in it. When you look at a photograph of a studio's space, which sentence would you check first: the one that names the maker, or the one that names the year? [S8]

title: Baars & Bloemhoff at Dutch Design Week: a sheet-material wholesaler that commissioned a design show every October
subtitle: Five albums in the official photo archive, from the first Transitions in 2015 to Below the Surface in 2019. Company pages, trade press and design studios show who made what, and where.
description: A sheet-material wholesaler, a materials library on Strijp-S and five years of commissioned design shows at Dutch Design Week, 2015 to 2019.

sections.x: The name Baars & Bloemhoff reads like a design studio, and the company's own history page says it belongs to two men, Goodwin Baars and Gerard Bloemhoff, who started a wholesale business in decorative sheet material in 1972. [S1][S2]

As a content strategist I read an album title for what it promises, and a title made of two surnames promises authors. This essay asks who the authors were in the five albums the official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive files under this name, and what the archive can and cannot show about them. It uses public sources only: the company's pages, trade and design press, the studios that built the settings, a design academy's event listing and the archive's album pages. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 program beyond the fact that I found no listing for the company in it. [S27][S1]
A wholesaler with a founding story and a new owner

The company says Goodwin Baars and Gerard Bloemhoff started a wholesale business in decorative sheet material in 1972, and that they were the first to bring Pfleiderer products to the Netherlands on a large scale. It says the firm stayed an independent family company for 27 years, until the Stiho Groep, another family company, bought it in 1999. [S1] A second page, written for the 50th anniversary, repeats the 1972 start and the Pfleiderer link and calls the company the largest online player for the Dutch interior-building trade. [S2] Core77 reported the same founding year in 2015, which is the earliest independent date I found. [S3] These are the company's own statements about itself. I did not find a Chamber of Commerce extract, so the year rests on the company and on one magazine that may have taken it from the company. [S1][S2][S3]

What it sells is plain on the home page: constructive and decorative sheet material, advice and inspiration for interior builders in the Netherlands and, as the page puts it, recently Belgium. [S26] In 2015 its marketing manager, Johan van der Meer, told Core77 that the firm sold 25 brands and more than 3,000 different materials and traveled to look for new ones. [S3] Core77 called it Utrecht-based and said it counted the Eindhoven Broeinest as one of five permanent sales centers. [S3] That is a supplier's profile. It tells you why the DDW story is unusual: a wholesaler has no signature object to show, so it commissioned some. [S26][S3]
Broeinest: the idea behind the venue

In an interview in the company's anniversary magazine, Bart Dekkers, who led the company from 2012 to 2019, says the picture he had of it from his earlier job at Stiho was a plate wholesaler that lacked color and character, and that the company's motto became "from plate wholesaler to design hotspot" (translated from the Dutch). He says that in the same period the Dutch Design Foundation invited him to Strijp-S in Eindhoven, which was looking for DDW sponsors, that he concluded the company's inspiration center in Amsterdam was in the wrong place, and that if the company could inspire anywhere it was Strijp-S. [S20] The name was his: he says it came to him at night, that it was odd and rubbed a little, and that he likes a name that makes people ask a question. [S20] This is a recollection from the person who made the decision, published by his former company, and I treat it as the company's account. [S20]

Janou Bonnie, the first coordinator, says the official opening of Broeinest Eindhoven was in January 2015. [S20] MaterialDistrict independently says that since January 2015 Broeinest has been located on Strijp-S in Eindhoven. [S21] The interview itself was recorded in the Glasfabriek on Strijp-S, in what the interviewer calls the very first Broeinest location. [S20] A 2016 report from Architectuur.nl gives the address: Broeinest in the Glasgebouw on Strijp-S, Torenallee 45. [S7] A 2018 Wallpaper* listing uses the same street number. [S16] Taken together, these say Broeinest stood on Strijp-S from January 2015, in a building the sources call the Glasgebouw or Glasfabriek. [S20][S21][S7][S16]

Bonnie says the original ambition was to be the flexible workplace for interior architects, with free coffee, desks and WiFi, and that it turned out differently: what the place was, and still is, she says, is a materials library. She adds that the team brought in Materia, the international network for innovative materials, early on. [S20] MaterialDistrict dates that collaboration to February 2016 and says Materia mounted exhibitions in Broeinest that were swapped every quarter. [S22] The 2016 article on the second Transitions show said Broeinest was set up as a "material library / flex workplace" where Materia had an ongoing exhibition. [S6] The venue was an exhibition room before DDW arrived, and DDW week was one busy week in its calendar. [S20][S22][S6]
2015: Transitions, six studios and one theme

The company's own page says it created Transitions in 2015 inspired by the DDW theme, "What if...," and chose to show its materials in a different way during DDW. It names six invitees: Studio Mieke Meijer, De Intuïtiefabriek, Lex Pott, Visser & Meijwaard, OS ∆ OOS and Michiel Martens. [S4] Core77's October 28, 2015 report called it the company's first designer collaboration and described the exhibition as staged in a corner of the ground floor of the Broeinest community studio, marked off by freestanding cupboards in opposite corners. [S3] [S4][S3]

Core77 listed the six projects with the materials each used. Studio Mieke Meijer's Airframe 01 used Decospan oak veneer on a plywood structure and weighed 18.5 kilograms. De Intuïtiefabriek's Spatial used colored MDF that resembles stone and concrete. OS ∆ OOS's Otto was an extendable two-tier table with a different veneer on each side of its top, using Alpi veneers. Lex Pott's Chroma built on the edge-banding of the materials, with Abet Laminati décors and Homapal metal laminate. Michiel Martens's Flat Cabinets folded Homapal metal laminate, which is 1 millimeter thick. Visser & Meijwaard's Grey on Gray used HI-MACS, a solid surface that can be heat-formed and glued with almost no seams, in a cupboard inspired by industrial crates. [S3] Core77 spells the first project Aeroframe 01 in its heading and Airframe 01 in the caption; the company's page says Airframe 01 and lists the same six designers and project names. [S3][S4] [S3][S4]

Core77 also records the commercial logic. The marketing manager told the magazine that the projects served as prototypes for production, and that OS ∆ OOS's Otto table would soon be available through the brand Please Wait to Be Seated. [S3] The company says the series continued in Milan: its Transitions I page carries a Dutch heading saying Transitions made its debut in Milan at the Salone del Mobile 2016. [S4] I read the pattern as a supplier using a design festival to test whether materials look good when handled by designers, and then using a second, larger stage to reach buyers. That is my interpretation, and the sources give the pieces but not that sentence. [S3][S4]
2016: Transitions II and eight trend worlds in the same building

MaterialDistrict announced on October 7, 2016 that Transitions II would run during DDW, October 22 to 30, under the festival theme "The making of," and said the focus would be on the making process. [S6] Architectuur.nl placed the show in Broeinest in the Glasgebouw on Strijp-S, Torenallee 45. [S7] Six designers took part: Daphna Laurens (the duo Daphna Isaacs Burggraaf and Laurens Manders), Paul Heijnen, Sabine Marcelis, Studio rENs, David Derksen and Klaas Kuiken. [S6][S5] [S6][S7][S5]

The projects, as MaterialDistrict describes them: Daphna Laurens glued two sheets of Forbo Desktop together into a two-color double-sided slab for Everything But the Desktop, from which they made a chair and a lamp. Paul Heijnen's Unity Globe Light is a lampshade of 1,080 identical sides based on a dodecahedron, made from Finsa Color MDF Negro 3 millimeters thick, so that almost no waste remains after laser cutting. Sabine Marcelis's Filter combined HI-MACS with light in a chandelier and a wall lamp. Studio rENs's BLACK studied every black material in the company's range, from HI-MACS, Forbo, Abet Laminati, Sibu and Duropal, and turned them into play blocks. David Derksen's Grid used wood veneer as a base material rather than a finish, in hanging structures with LED lights and acoustic foam. Klaas Kuiken's Inside-Out used Finsa Greenpanel, two 4 millimeter MDF skins around a honeycomb core, sawn through so the core shows. [S6] [S6]

Johan van der Meer explained the premise to Architectuur.nl: the firm's materials surround people every day in hospitals, shops and offices, and because they are everywhere they are barely noticed, so bringing them down to small proportions puts the focus back on the material. He added that designers phone him with questions about cutting, milling and deliberately scratching the material. [S7] The company's own review page says the Transitions II exhibition was later shown at Ventura Centrale in Milan in 2017, in a setting designed by Daphna Laurens, with a shining abstract architectural setting. [S5] [S7][S5]

A company news page tells a second story from the same week. During DDW 2016, Broeinest also showed Broeinest 8:1, a joint presentation with its partners, curated and art-directed by the Eindhoven studio Raw Color, which was founded in 2007 by Christoph Brach and Daniera ter Haar. The eight worlds were New Natural, Vibrant Night, Modular Geometry, Concrete Poetry, Spectral Tech, Classic Symmetry, Rusty Earth and Industrial Standard, and the partners named were Forbo, DRT, Interface, Spectrum Design, Modular Lighting, Barrisol and Busch-Jaeger. [S8][S9] So the 2016 Broeinest album can hold two kinds of pictures, a designer's cabinet from Transitions II and a trend world from the 8:1 show, and a reader of the album alone could not tell which is which unless a label says so. [S8][S9]
2017: Transitions III and Matter Revealed in 700 square meters

The company's press release for the third edition names six studios again: Mae Engelgeer, Studio Truly Truly, Bart Joachim van Uden, Floris Wubben, Christian Heikoop and Job van den Berg. It gives DDW's dates as October 21 to 29, 2017 and says Studio Mieke Meijer was asked to create a spectacular environment at Broeinest Eindhoven in which the six designers' works would show to best effect. It says the results would travel to Milan during the Salone the following year. [S11] The project page lists the pieces: Engelgeer's The Showroom, Van den Berg's Hollow, Van Uden's Romancing the Stone, Wubben's Crystal Shift & Twist, Heikoop's Linear Wood and Truly Truly's Column. [S10] [S11][S10]

IO+ describes what visitors saw during DDW 2017: a dual exposition, Matter Revealed and Transitions III, that aimed to show what design materials are made of. It explains high-pressure laminate as a sandwich of kraft paper, pigments and a covering layer, and names the partner brands: Baars & Bloemhoff, Spectrum, Modular Lighting Instruments, Forbo Flooring Systems, Interface, Barrisol and Busch-Jaeger. It describes Hollow as a bulky-looking object that is light because it is made of oak veneer rolled into hollow tubes, and Linear Wood as light-looking but relatively heavy because of metal inside, covered seamlessly in veneer. [S12] [S12]

Studio Mieke Meijer's project page adds the numbers and the credits. The exhibition space was 700 square meters, built from plywood and mesh fabric, with art direction and signage by Raw Color and photography by Ronald Smits. Raw Color divided the room between final products and raw materials so that visitors could see the processes behind the products. The third Transitions was shown in the same space. [S13] The company's own DDW page says the same, in its own words: the Matter Revealed exposition was shown in Broeinest, all in a museum-like, serene setting designed by Studio Mieke Meijer. [S9] [S13][S9]

Raw Color's credit needs its year attached. The company's pages credit the studio with curating the 2016 trend worlds. For 2017 the credit comes from the architect's page, which names Raw Color as art director of the Meijer setting, while the company's own page credits the setting itself to Studio Mieke Meijer. [S8][S9][S13] [S8][S9][S13]
2018: #TIMEISNOW, a flat-pack concept and a conflict that the company's own page settles

The Transitions IV page describes a change of purpose. Where earlier Transitions projects were experimental and exclusive, the company says, this one targets accessible design and a new furniture concept called The not so Flat Collection, to narrow the gap between industrial standard furniture and unique high-end design. It names five designers: Daphna Laurens, Lex Pott, Johan Moorman, Tijs Gilde and Jasmijn Muskens. It says a pilot collection would be shown within the exhibition #TIMEISNOW at Broeinest EHV during the coming Dutch Design Week, and that the designs would later be sold on a Transitions online platform. [S14] [S14]

The page gives no year in its text, so the edition has to come from elsewhere, and two independent pages supply it. Wallpaper* places #TIMEISNOW and Transitions IV in its guide to Dutch Design Week 2018, which ran from October 20 to 28. KABK, the Hague art academy, lists the Transitions IV project in its guide to alumni at DDW 2018, with the same five designers and the location Broeinest, Strijp-S. [S16][S15] The company's wording, that the pilot collection would be shown at the coming DDW within #TIMEISNOW, fits that edition. [S14] [S16][S15][S14]

KABK says the Transitions IV results would be presented within the four thematic trend worlds of #TIMEISNOW, curated by Floor Knaapen and Grietje Schepers. [S15] Wallpaper* described the show as exploring sustainability, circularity and digitization in styled rooms, with designers working with materials taken directly from the warehouse in their natural, unprocessed state, and added that Transitions IV focused on digital production techniques and a flat-pack furniture collection to be sold online later that year. The listing gives the venue as Broeinest EHV, Torenallee 45. [S16] MVSA Architects, an architecture firm that wrote up its four favorite stops, named two of the four worlds, Tech & Texture and Trash & Treasure, and said the company ran a competition during DDW called the Maatwerk Award, with a Retail category won by a firm MVSA worked with. [S17] That is a visitor's blog and a firm's own news item, so I treat it as a lead and not as a record of the award. [S15][S16][S17]

The labels in the 2018 album fit this account. Signs in the photos read Tech & Texture and More Is More, and a board reads Maatwerk Awards. [S27] More Is More also appears in Wallpaper*'s picture caption, which spells the company "Baars & Bloemhof," the same one-f spelling that turns up in the 2019 file titles. [S16][S27] I take that as a plain misspelling that traveled, since the company's own pages use two f's. [S1] [S27][S16][S1]
2019: Below the Surface, eight worlds and a kitchen in each

The company's review says Broeinest Eindhoven was transformed into an organic landscape through which thousands of visitors wandered, with eight conceptual worlds that flowed into one another, held apart by organic room dividers and light frames, with crumpled paper, perforated strips, semi-transparent cloths and bundled reed around them. Studio IOIA assembled the worlds with the Broeinest team. In every world a kitchen returned, which the review calls a personal showpiece, built with Quooker; the base was the company's materials, Barrisol acoustic ceilings and continuous IVC flooring. Unique pieces by established designers and young talent completed each world. [S18] [S18]

The review names the worlds with the materials used in each, so a reader can check them against the photographs: Forgotten Colours, Beyond Natural, Matter in Motion, Crafting Rituals, Gradually Evolving, Majestic Mimicry, Reflecting Realities and Connecting Comfort. [S18] Studio IOIA's own page confirms the eight stylistic worlds, says each room contained a 3D mood board of the company's material range, and credits Quooker for the kitchens, Floor Knaapen for still-life photography and Willeke Machiels and Ronald Smits for exhibition photography. [S19] [S18][S19]

The DDW archive credits its 2019 album to a different photographer, Britt Roelse, whose name appears in the file names and the album note. [S27] The two credits do not conflict: the archive's photographers shoot for the festival, and the studio's credits cover the images commissioned for the company. It does mean that two sets of photographs of the same rooms exist, from different photographers, and a caption has to name the right one. [S19][S27] [S19][S27]
Broeinest after 2019

The record after 2019 is about the venue, not the festival. Broeinest Rotterdam opened on February 16, 2017, and Broeinest Amsterdam on May 24, 2018, according to MaterialDistrict's reports dated the day of or after each event. [S21][S22] The anniversary interview dates Amsterdam to June 2018 and describes Rotterdam as a year earlier than that, which does not match the dated reports, so I use the reports. [S20][S21][S22] The company's own news post on the Utrecht opening says more than 350 makers, designers and partners came on a Thursday, January 9, to see the machine park and the company's new head office in the Werkspoorfabriek, and the interview places it in 2020. [S23][S20] [S21][S22][S20][S23]

Today the company's Broeinest page and Broeinest's own pages list two places, a library in Amsterdam and an atelier in Eindhoven. [S25] The atelier page says that in June 2025, ten years and five months after the opening of the first Strijp-S location, Broeinest opened a smaller atelier, an intimate materials hub open on Tuesdays and Thursdays by appointment. [S24] I found no source that says why the archive has no Baars & Bloemhoff album after 2019, and I found no 2020 to 2025 DDW program entry for the company. The sources I opened show Broeinest changing; they do not link that change to DDW. [S24][S25] [S25][S24]
What the five albums can and cannot show

The archive holds one album for each year from 2015 to 2019, with 13, 23, 11, 17 and 9 photos, 73 in all, by Tommy Köhlbrugge in 2015 to 2017, Ruud Balk in 2018 and Britt Roelse in 2019. [S27] Reading them against the sources, three things stand out. The 2016 album sits across two shows, as the trend worlds and Transitions II shared a building. The 2017 album carries the title Transitions III while the venue held a second exposition, Matter Revealed. And the 2018 album shows styled rooms whose names appear on signs, but whose designers do not. [S27]

A label in a picture is the most reliable caption an archive photograph can have, because the exhibitor wrote it for visitors. In the 2016 album, a sign reads Baars & Bloemhoff Transitions II, and plinths read Klaas Kuiken and rENs. In the 2015 album a plinth reads De Intuïtiefabriek. [S27] Each label names one piece, and the cabinet next to a labeled plinth may belong to someone else. This is why I would not caption a photograph of a Baars & Bloemhoff show with the company's name as maker. The company supplied the material, a named designer shaped it, and in 2017 and 2019 a third party designed the room. [S27]
Questions the sources settle

Four questions came up, and each has an answer in the sources. Which edition Transitions IV belonged to: Wallpaper* and KABK both put it in 2018, and the company's wording fits. [S14][S15][S16] Whether Broeinest sat on Strijp-S: Architectuur.nl, MaterialDistrict and the company's interview say yes. [S7][S21][S20] When Rotterdam and Amsterdam opened: the dated trade reports settle it over a recollection in a later interview. [S20][S21][S22] Who handled the 2016 and 2017 Broeinest shows: Raw Color curated the 2016 trend worlds and art-directed the 2017 setting that Studio Mieke Meijer built. [S9][S13] [S14][S15][S16][S7][S21][S20][S22][S9][S13]
What the record does not show

I do not know who the fourth world of #TIMEISNOW was, since I could name only Tech & Texture, Trash & Treasure and More Is More across the sources I opened. [S15][S17][S27] I do not know which photographs in the 2016 and 2017 albums belong to which show. [S27] I did not verify the Maatwerk Award beyond one visitor blog. [S17] I did not find the company's DDW 2018 attendance figures in an opened source, and I found no Chamber of Commerce record that fixes the founding year. [S1][S3] [S15][S17][S27][S1][S3]

I also cannot say whether the company takes part in DDW 2026, because I found no program listing for it. [S25] If you are looking at one of these albums, which line in the picture tells you who made the object, and which tells you who supplied the material it is made of? [S25]
