title: Baltan Laboratories at Dutch Design Week: a lab that keeps its own books, and a wedding counted four ways
subtitle: The lab's annual reports, its funder's advice and the artists' pages agree on a great deal and on one number they do not. A reading of 2018 to 2025 against the official photo archive.
description: Baltan Laboratories at Dutch Design Week 2018 to 2025: Frankenstein, Homo Sensorium, a brainwave wedding, and what the lab, its funder and the artists say.

sections.x: Baltan Laboratories reports that 26 couples married during Dutch Design Week 2019, with the verb in quotation marks, and two other counts for the same days sit in the report and on the artists' own page. [S12][S13]

I like a number like that, because it shows what a lab's own record can and cannot settle. Baltan documents itself unusually well: it publishes an annual report for each year from 2017 to 2025, an event page for most of what it does and a clear account of who paid. This essay reads those documents against each other and against the official Dutch Design Week photo archive. It draws on public sources only, and it reports no visit and no interview. It says nothing about the 2026 program beyond what the sources I opened show. [S1][S31]
A name that is a building spelled backwards

The first fact about Baltan Laboratories is in its name. Baltan's 2018 annual report calls the name an anagram of NatLab, the former Philips physics laboratory known for combining applied and fundamental research, and says the name also honors Kid Baltan, the pseudonym of the composer Dick Raaijmakers. [S3] The letters of Natlab, reversed, spell Baltan. This is Eindhoven, the city's tourism site, says Philips opened the Natuurkundig Laboratorium at Strijp-S in 1923, a date I have not checked against a Philips source. [S29]

The lab's own history of itself gives two dates for the move. The 2018 report says Baltan opened its doors in 2008 in the Glass Building on Strijp-S, the former Philips terrain, and in 2013 took a first step toward a broader art-science lab in the former Natlab. [S3] The timeline on Baltan's About page says it was founded as a two-year research pilot (2008 to 2010), published a book called A Blueprint for a Lab of the Future after that phase, adopted what it calls a plug-in methodology around 2012 to 2014, and that in 2014 to 2015 the renovated Natlab building was officially opened with Baltan as a key inhabitant. [S1] These do not contradict each other if 2013 is when the lab moved in and 2014 to 2015 is when the building was officially opened, and I read them that way, though neither page gives a day.

Two address facts help a reader who is trying to place the photographs. Baltan's event pages for 2018, 2019 and 2024 all give Kastanjelaan 500, the Natlab address, and its legal notice says the foundation, Stichting Baltan, has existed since 2008 and is based in the Natlab on Strijp-S. [S1][S4][S5][S8][S25] Mediamatic's organization page for Baltan still says the lab is in the SWA building on Strijp-S. [S18] No source I opened says whether that building is the Glass Building of 2008, so I treat Mediamatic's line as out of date and use Baltan's own address.

The people have changed too. In October 2018 the director who spoke to Innovation Origins was Olga Mink. [S6] The About page now lists two co-directors, Marlou van der Cruijsen and Lorenzo Gerbi, a producer, a community builder and two board members. [S1]
Who pays, and what the funder said

Baltan's record includes unusually frank documents about its money. The 2019 report prints a financing mix of 77 percent public funds, 7 percent income from EU projects and 16 percent income from private partnerships, and it prints a second split, 79 percent public income and 21 percent own income, without saying how the two relate. [S12] The same page lists a team of six permanent staff, nine freelancers, two interns and eight volunteers. [S12] The report counts 72 activities for the year, among them four exhibitions, six presentations, three lectures, 18 workshops or events, six residencies and one publication. [S12]

The Homo Sensorium page that Baltan wrote for Dutch Design Week 2019 says the program is part of a multi-year trajectory supported by the Creative Industries Fund NL, Stichting Cultuur Eindhoven and the Province of Noord-Brabant. [S9][S10] The fund itself publishes its advice on applications, and three of them concern Baltan. The first is an application for a four-year institutional grant for 2020 to 2024, titled "van Homo naar Inter-esse," for 900,000 euros. The fund's advice was positive, but the application dropped out after prioritization. The same document records that Baltan was supported for a one-year program in 2018 and through the fund's multi-year program in 2019 and 2020. [S26] The second is a request for 350,000 euros for a two-year program in 2021 and 2022, and the third is a request for 100,000 euros for 2021. Both advice documents are negative. [S27][S28]

What the committee wrote is more useful than the verdicts. In the first document it praises how well Baltan is embedded in Eindhoven's cultural sector and notes that the lab's survival and international position depend on large European projects, in which Baltan often cannot set the agenda. It also asks for more attention to reaching existing and new audiences. [S26] The fund's summary of the application says that Baltan does not aim at a large public and places its impact in artistic research and in communities of professionals. [S26] In the two negative advices the committee finds the programs unclear in structure, says the themes seem arbitrarily chosen and criticizes the choice of makers as the usual suspects. It names Koert van Mensvoort and Arne Hendriks in both and Paolo Cirio in the two-year request. [S27][S28] The text of the three documents carries no date. The file metadata of the first dates it to September 1, 2020, and the programs they describe fit that year. [S26][S27][S28]

I note this here because it frames how to read the albums. A lab that tells its funder it does not aim at a large public is a different kind of Dutch Design Week participant from a studio selling to visitors, and its record is better judged on the quality of its documentation than on crowds. I found no visitor counts for the week in the reports I searched. [S12][S26]
2018: a symposium and an exhibition on Frankenstein

In 2018 Baltan marked its tenth year. Innovation Origins, in an article dated October 16, 2018, describes the Frankenstein Symposium as a fitting celebration of the lab's decade of connecting the high-tech and creative communities, and quotes Mink on Eindhoven as a maker city that is becoming aware that the impact of technology is long-lasting and severe. [S6] That is an interview with the director and carries the director's framing.

Baltan's pages give the program in detail. The Frankenstein Exhibition, titled It's Alive, ran from October 20 to 28, 2018 at Kastanjelaan 500 from 11:00 to 18:00, with free entrance and late opening until 23:00 on Monday, October 22. [S4] The page lists five works. We Are Data's Mirror Room is a space that measures the person who enters it. Cluster by Quintus Glerum is described as a robotic lifeform that clusters data into a neural network and turns physical data such as a heartbeat into movement. Perfect Paul by Arthur Elsenaar presents his research on the computer-controlled human face. The Artificial Intelligence Training Centre by Bureau Moeilijke Dingen asks visitors to teach everyday products the right behavior. Fictional Journal's issue 03, Uncanny, was made with Baltan. [S4]

The symposium took place on October 22, 2018, from 11:00 to 20:30, and Baltan's page gives the tickets as 50 euros, or 35 euros for students. [S5] It was organized with Robot Love, an Eindhoven exhibition run by Stichting Niet Normaal, and a symposium ticket gave a 20 percent discount on entry to that exhibition. [S5] The program named a lecture by the technology philosopher Martijntje Smits, a lecture by the bioethicist Jason Robert on loving our monsters, a performance by Elsenaar, an artist talk by Nicolas Maigret of the collective Disnovation.org, the launch of Fictional Journal's issue by Sophie Rzepecky, and the performance Eingeweide by Marco Donnarumma with Margherita Pevere, with Ruben Baart of Next Nature Network moderating. [S5]

Baltan's 2018 report adds three things the event pages leave out. It says Eingeweide had its Dutch premiere at the symposium after debuting at the opening of the Ars Electronica festival, that the Frankenstein Expo was on view in the Natlab for the whole of Dutch Design Week, and that it was a showing of five projects. [S3] It also says Baltan and Robot Love's organization, Stichting Niet Normaal, worked together in 2018, and Baltan's earlier post on its Sentient Machines residencies describes an artist-in-residence series set up together with Robot Love. [S3][S7]

The report also places the symposium inside a longer line of work. It says Baltan ran a residency program called Sentient Machines with Robot Love and the artists Marco Donnarumma and Marije Baalman, that Donnarumma's AI robot arm Amygdala was exhibited in the Raaijmakers Hall of the Natlab, that the same arm was part of the Eingeweide performance, and that the Frankenstein reflection was a prelude to the next topic, Homo Sensorium. [S3] That sentence is the link between the two years in this record. The 2019 program was announced in 2018 as the next chapter, and the report describes its starting point as sensory reality showing itself according to the senses, technological ones included, that a person has. [S3] The hall's name matches the composer the report credits as Kid Baltan, and no source I opened says the hall is named for him. [S3]

One small credit belongs to another item in this series. The symposium page's header image is credited to HeyHeydeHaas, and Baltan's December 2017 post says its new website was developed by the team of Heyheydehaas. [S2][S5] I mention it because the two names will meet again in this archive.

As for the photographs, the old dossier for this item records that the official archive holds 12 photos for 2018, credited in the titles to Ruud Balk, and that none of the titles names a work. I did not reopen Flickr for this version. [S31] That is why any pairing of a robot photograph with Cluster, or of a screen with a face with Perfect Paul, is a match by appearance. The text pages in this section are the only place where the work names are fixed.
2019: Homo Sensorium, a program with a report

In 2019 Baltan's own report says it started the Homo Sensorium program with its housemates Natlab and Broet, in and around Natlab, with workshops, presentations, debates, food experiences, performances, tours, Brainwave weddings, a piano concert and films. [S12] The theme is derived from the idea of Homo Universalis, a person whose expertise spans many fields. [S12][S8] Baltan's program page runs October 19 to 27, 2019 at Natlab and lists a long set of events with prices. The Cosmic Travel Kit, a 20-minute walk across Strijp-S by Klara Ravat, Pieter Verhees and Angela de Weijer based on an idea of the Eindhoven artist Peter Nagelkerke, was free with registration. The Facing Nature workshop with Madeline Schwartzman cost 17.50 euros, or 12.50 for students. The design dinner by the studio Joes + Manon cost 36.43 euros. Inevitably Blue by Sophia Bulgakova, a participatory performance on a swing, and the Homo Sensorium Space by Raphael Coutin, a barefoot tactile room, were free to enter. [S8][S9][S14] The Dutch Design Week program archive lists Homo Sensorium as presented by Baltan Laboratories, Natlab and Broet. [S15]

The report adds a claim that matters for any attendance figure: all the events were sold out before Dutch Design Week began, and the press took more notice of the program, with attention in Damn Magazine, on AD.nl and on Bright.nl. [S12] I did not find those press items, so I cannot say what they reported or whether they give a wedding count. The report also credits its own photographers for the week, Sas Schilten and Hanneke Wetzer, which means the official archive's photographs of the same week, credited to Britt Roelse, are a second visual record of the same events. [S12][S31]
The wedding, and four ways to count it

The Brainwave Wedding Lab is the best-documented project in this record, and it is also where the documents disagree most. Baltan's page of September 13, 2019 describes it as a high-tech wedding experience developed by Baltan with the artists Lancel/Maat. During the kiss the couple's brain activity is measured with EEG sensors, the two patterns are 3D printed as two rings, and the rings are said to encapsulate a code that stands for the marriage contract, stored in a blockchain system. [S10] The page says the marriage was inclusive, for two people or several, that it has no legal status, and that participants agree to be filmed and photographed and are invited to discuss the experience afterward. [S10] The artists' own page adds that the contract was drawn up with support from KissPatent, whose founder D'vorah Graeser also spoke at a Baltan talk on love, that the ring printing was developed with Vincent Hoenderop, and that the 3D print is often later made into a gold ring. [S13][S8]
The documents disagree on what the week looked like. [S10][S11][S13]
Question · Baltan's program and report · Baltan's call for testers · The artists' page
Days · October 19, 20, 23, 25, 26 and 27 [S10][S8] · October 24 to 27, from 12:30 to 18:30 [S11] · "during a week" [S13]
Length of one ritual · about 45 minutes [S10]; one hour [S8] · 30 minutes [S11] · 60 minutes [S13]
Price · 20 euros per couple [S10] · 20 euros per ritual, rings not included, first ten free [S11] · not stated
How many · "26 couples married" [S12] · not applicable · 40 contracts and 40 rituals [S13]; 25 couples and sometimes more than two people, in the artists' note inside Baltan's report [S12]

I cannot settle the days, the length or the price from these pages, because none of the Baltan pages carries a posting date that would show which was the later and corrected one. The program page and the September 13 page agree on six days and on the 13:00 to 19:00 hours, and I use those as Baltan's schedule. The call for testers describes a shorter window, and I leave it as an earlier or looser description. [S8][S10][S11]

The counts are the point of this essay's opening. Baltan's report says 26 couples "married" and puts the verb in quotation marks, while the artists' note inside the same report says 25 pairs, and sometimes more than two people, married through a self-made, non-religious contract. [S12] The artists' own page says they concluded 40 marriage contracts over a week, held 40 rituals of 60 minutes, and that participants often brought large groups of witnesses. [S13] These figures use different units: couples, pairs, contracts and rituals. A ceremony with three people is one contract and no couple at all. Nothing I opened reconciles them, and a booking record would be the primary document that could. For that reason I would use Baltan's own 26 only with Baltan's name next to it, as Baltan's report states it, and would not combine any two of the figures. [S12][S13]

I read the technical claim with an anatomist's question. Scalp electrodes record electrical signals from the muscles of the head and face as well as from the brain, and a kiss uses facial muscles. A research review of muscle artifacts in EEG reports that even resting recordings made near the center of the scalp showed significant muscle contamination in studies where participants were fully paralyzed for comparison. [S30] The artists' page says they developed a special brain-computer interface that translates the kiss into a code. [S13] No source I opened says how the device separated brain signals from muscle signals, and I make no claim either way. It is a question the documentation does not answer, and a rich one for a ritual that is also a measurement. [S13][S30]
After the albums: what Baltan did at Dutch Design Week from 2020 to 2025

The photo archive holds Baltan albums for 2018, 2019 and 2021, and the old dossier counts 12, 24 and 9 photos, from Ruud Balk, Britt Roelse and Max Kneefel. [S31] The annual reports show that a missing album does not mean a missing edition.

In 2020 the exhibition Economia was filmed in a purpose-built studio, shown in online events, and presented as part of the virtual Dutch Design Week in a 3D viewing room, according to the 2020 report. [S20] The same report's preface says the lockdown began a week after the opening of another exhibition, Infrastructures for Participation. [S20]

In 2021 Baltan and Mediamatic hosted Inhuman Carnaval. Mediamatic's event page dates it October 17 to 22, 2021 at Natlab, while Baltan's 2021 report lists the program as October 16 to 24, the dates of the whole week. [S17][S19] The Dutch Design Week program archive describes an open costume lab, workshops, exhibitions, a party and a parade, with the stated goal of turning the costumes into instructions for carnival 2022. [S16] Baltan's report says the program included the Open Costume Lab, embroidery workshops, Open Air Gentle Discos, the exhibition Extinction Claims, talks, performances and a party, and that dozens of people worked on it. [S19]

Extinction Claims by Paolo Cirio ran from October 17 to November 30, 2021, from 11:00 to 18:00 at Natlab, according to Mediamatic. [S32] The report describes visitors receiving postcards that show species or ecosystems and assigning a percentage of reparation payments from a fossil fuel producer of their choice, with the signed cards collected by the artist and presented to organizations in the European Union. It ties the work to the legal idea of environmental personhood and to data on more than 40,000 endangered species. [S19] A talk on October 23, 2021, Let's Talk About Climate Justice, brought Cirio together with Raphael Weyland, whom the report calls an environmental lawyer and former work partner of Cirio, Teresa Borasino of Fossil Free Culture NL and Selçuk Balamir. [S19][S18] The funder's committee, in advice whose file is dated September 2020, had named Cirio among the safe, established names in a two-year request. [S27] In 2021 Baltan showed his exhibition. The two facts sit side by side in the record, and I draw no conclusion from them. [S27][S19]

In 2022 Baltan's report lists a symposium during Dutch Design Week as part of Raise Your Voice, a project for nine designers and artists, and a workshop and conference contribution for the Embassy of Health. [S21] In 2023 it presented The Body is a Movement with Onomatopee, an exhibition of ten artists with a workshop program, part of which was shown afterward in Baltan's space in Natlab. [S22] In 2024 it showed Decentralized Futures, with eight international artists from the ARTeCHÓ Fellowship, in the Koelhuis, and the report says the opening of Dutch Design Week took place at the location of that exhibition. [S23] A guided tour on October 25, 2024, led by the exhibiting artist Michele Bazzoli, had slots at 10:30 and 17:30. [S25] The page's header gives Kastanjelaan 500, but its body and the report put the show at the Koelhuis, and I follow the body and the report. [S25][S23]

The 2025 report lists two items for Dutch Design Week 2025: a takeover at Onomatopee from October 20 to 23, and Silicon Souls at NulZES from October 23 to 26, a series of open dialogues organized by DES.ENG.AGE with Baltan about the materials behind silicon technologies. [S24] That second venue has its own entry in this series.
What a photograph of a ritual should keep back

A wedding is a private event held in public. The 2019 archive album, by the old dossier's description, contains close views of participants and a kiss. [S31] Baltan's page told couples they agreed to be filmed and photographed, so the photographs exist with their consent as the lab states it. [S10] I would still keep a public timeline to wide views, hands and the backs of heads, because a timeline of a lab does not need a face, and the project asked people to take part in a ritual, not to become an image. That is my judgment, and RN may weigh it differently. [S10][S31]
The same discipline applies to the words. A lab can publish that 26 couples took part without naming one of them. A caption can do the same, and should name the lab when it repeats the count. [S12]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**When Baltan moved into Natlab.** The 2018 report says a first step in 2013 and the About page says the renovated building was officially opened in 2014 to 2015. I read the first as the move and the second as the opening, and both are Baltan's own. [S3][S1]

**Where Baltan was based.** Mediamatic says the SWA building, Baltan's pages say Kastanjelaan 500 in Natlab, and the 2018 report says the first home was the Glass Building. Baltan's own address settles the present, and the question of the SWA building stays open. [S18][S3][S1]

**What the funder thought.** Positive on the four-year request, negative on the two shorter ones. The documents are the funder's own, and the verdicts do not conflict because they answer different applications. [S26][S27][S28]

**The wedding week.** Days, length, price and count differ across Baltan's pages and the artists' page, as the table shows. I use Baltan's 26 with attribution and do not reconcile the rest. [S10][S11][S12][S13]

**Dates of Inhuman Carnaval.** October 17 to 22 on Mediamatic's page and October 16 to 24 in Baltan's report. The second is the span of the whole week, and I use the first for the program and attribute it. [S17][S19]
What the record does not show

I do not know how many people visited Baltan's program in any year, because the reports I searched give no visitor counts. I do not know which of the wedding counts matches a booking record, or whether the dome ran one ritual at a time. I do not know which Baltan page about the wedding was written last. I did not find the AD.nl, Bright.nl or Damn Magazine items that the 2019 report says covered the program. [S12]

I did not reopen the Flickr archive for this version, so the album counts, titles and photographers come from the dossier's October 8, 2026 reading and should be checked again before posting. I do not know whether Baltan has albums under other titles, and the archive's own pages do not say why there are none for 2020 and for 2022 to 2025. The sources do not say what Baltan will show in 2026. [S31][S1]
If you opened one of these documents tomorrow, which would you want to see set beside it: the booking record, the funder's advice or the photograph? [S12]

title: Bart Hess at Dutch Design Week: a studio, a latex cave and a location named after him
subtitle: The photo archive holds four albums. Museum pages, press and Dutch Design Week's own listings show a wider record, and the 2026 listing at his address is another label's show.
description: Bart Hess at Dutch Design Week, 2012 to 2026: a studio at NRE, a latex cave, a VR film and a location page that lists another label's show.

sections.x: The 2026 Dutch Design Week page named Bart Hess | NRE lists one exhibition, and it belongs to a furniture label called OFFSITE. [S7][S8]

This essay began with four albums of photographs and turned into a reading of a place. As a content strategist I watch what a name on a map promises, and a location that carries a designer's name promises that the designer is behind what is shown there. This essay checks how often the sources keep that promise. It draws on public sources only: Dutch Design Week's own program and location pages, the designer's pages, museum records, local and international press, a heritage-minded city page and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what the published listings say. [S6][S7][S9][S15]
The archive has four albums, and the record is wider than that

The official Flickr archive holds Bart Hess albums for 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2021, with 7, 7, 6 and 10 photos, which makes 30. The 2016 titles read 82_BART_HESS and credit Iris Rijskamp. The later titles begin NRE_BartHess and credit Nick Bookelaar. I read those albums in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand. [S1]

The written record shows a longer and odder pattern. It has a 2012 production line for visitors whose festival link I could not confirm, a 2016 open studio, a 2018 installation in a former dairy factory that no Hess-titled album covers, a 2019 virtual reality film at a different address, a 2024 dance project that DDW lists and its photo archive does not, and a 2026 location page that carries his name and someone else's show. [S4][S5][S6][S7][S25][S26]
A designer who made his name early

Brabant Cultureel, a regional culture site, says Hess grew up in Geldrop, studied at the Design Academy in Eindhoven and graduated in 2007 from the Man and Identity department. After graduating he started a blog with Lucy McRae, who then worked for Philips Design, and each week one of them appeared in front of the camera dressed in everyday materials such as dish soap foam. In 2010 American Vogue approached the pair about doing something similar with the photographer Nick Knight, and in 2011 Lady Gaga approached them for a photo session for a new album. [S4]

The slime dress that came out of it was developed in his studio, then on the Kanaaldijk. The same article says he thickened the slime with flour so it would hold on the body during the shoot and took fifteen kilos of the mixture to New York on the plane. Omroep Brabant repeats the fifteen-kilo figure. [S4][S19] Hess's own account, in an interview on the design site WOTH, is that Lady Gaga's stylist picked his Slime Outfit for the cover of the album Born This Way while he was still at school. That is his recollection, and the two accounts differ on the order of events. [S21]

The Dutch Design Awards gallery lists him as the 2011 winner in the Young Designer category, and WOTH has him describing the prize as the Mini Young Designer Award. [S20][S21] Design Museum Den Bosch says the Slime Dress brought international fame barely four years after graduation. [S15] The same WOTH interview has him saying he no longer calls himself a designer because he does not think in products. [S21] That sentence matters for an archive that files him under "Bart Hess" and a place: the work he describes is a body of materials, films and installations, and a festival listing is a poor fit for it.
2012: a production line that asked visitors to work

The earliest record I could open of Work With Me People is a research record at the University of the Arts London. It dates the installation and performance to 2012 through 2017 and describes visitors instructed through headphones to perform simple, repetitive acts, in that version dripping liquid latex onto a stretched latex surface. It says the piece is meant to highlight the beauty of the differences between each participant's workmanship, and that once the latex dries the sheet is released and shrinks so the drops draw together into a skin of rubber bubbles. It adds that the automated version came out of his appointment as a Creative Fellow at the London College of Fashion. [S26]

A trend service, LS:N Global, ran an item dated October 24, 2012 under the headline "Alien concept: Show visitors make future fabrics." [S27] I could read only the headline and date, and I did not try to get around the wall in front of the text. Neither source I could open says the 2012 version ran during Dutch Design Week, so I treat that placement as a lead and not a fact. Hess's own site credits the Work With Me pop-up studio as a way he involved audiences in making. [S9]
2016: back in Eindhoven with the studio door open

Hess left Eindhoven in 2012 for London, spent a year in different places abroad and came back in 2016, according to Brabant Cultureel. His first studio on return was on the Stratumsedijk, and since the spring he had been at the former NRE terrein. [S4] A January 2016 interview on the Innovation Origins site has him saying the city had grown while he was away, calling it a drab-looking town with a lot going on beneath the surface. [S22]

Neon Moire's guide to the fifteenth Dutch Design Week lists "Bart Hess" at the NRE terrein from October 22 to 30, 2016, 10:00 to 18:00, as an exclusive look inside his new studio where he develops materials and installations. The same guide counts nine days, 100 locations and 2,500 designers for the festival. [S2] This is the earliest program text I found that places him at NRE.

Two reports describe what visitors found. Visi's report says he opened his studio to show "a treasure trove of artificial hides," with the flesh-colored Royal Latex Bed getting under the viewer's skin. [S3] Brabant Cultureel confirms he opened the studio to the public during Dutch Design Week and adds a detail from that visit: an intern was sewing sequins that looked like mussel shells onto a base for costumes for Khôra, another dance by the choreographer Nanine Linning, due in the Netherlands in 2017. It also says the pink latex he used for the strange creatures in Linning's Silver was the material he had used for the curtains of a canopy bed in his studio. [S4]

Those two reports disagree on color, flesh in one and pink in the other, and the 2016 album includes a photograph of a bed under pale pleated drapes whose title names no work. That is a lead and not a match, because a title is a source and a resemblance is not. [S1][S3][S4]

The place has its own history. The NRE terrein is a former gasworks site established in 1899, and it takes its name from the Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, the regional utilities that were there from 1989 to 2010. The municipality bought it afterward and turned it into a creative neighborhood. [S13] In 2016 Hess said the mix of studios there worked for him, with a ceramics workshop on one side and a graphic atelier due on the other. [S4]
2017: a museum survey, and photographs with no program page

In 2017 the written record sits in museums. Future Bodies: Bart Hess 2007 to 2017 ran from June 24 to October 1, 2017 and was billed as the first survey of ten years of his projects. Design Museum Den Bosch lists it under the Mondrian to Dutch Design year. [S15] The accompanying book names the museum then as the Stedelijk Museum 's-Hertogenbosch, names Fredric Baas as curator, and describes Hess as a new type of designer who experiments with materials to develop concepts that can take many media. [S16] Silver, the Linning production with his costumes, was scheduled for January 14, 2017 at the Parktheater in Eindhoven and January 17 in Den Bosch, and the TextielMuseum in Tilburg showed his new work in an exhibition running to May 28, 2017. [S4]

That Tilburg work came from a collection commission on the museum's braiding machine, which produced three new works that react to approaching visitors with small, irregular movements. [S19] Brabant Cultureel describes the electronics hidden in braided cord or in a wrinkled pink silicone skin and responding to warmth and movement. [S4]

The studio that designed the Den Bosch survey, Studio Harm Rensink, says it turned the museum's 500 square meters into a landscape in which visitors moved from one world to the next through Hess's video works, soundscapes and material experiments, working closely with him. [S29]

For Dutch Design Week 2017 itself I found no program page. The Flickr album holds seven photographs by Nick Bookelaar titled NRE_BartHess that show performers in crumpled silver foil costumes under projected light. [S1] A 2016 report says the robot-like dancers in Silver wore costumes of strips of reflective material, and that the Khôra costumes were in preparation, so a link is imaginable. No source I opened ties either production to these photographs, and I do not make the link. [S4]
2018: a latex cave in a former dairy factory

Hess's 2018 Dutch Design Week appearance sits outside any album with his name. Robot Love, an exhibition running from September 15 to December 2, 2018 at the Campina Melkfabriek on the Kanaaldijk-Zuid, reported thousands of visitors during the festival and published a photo captioned as visitors in Hess's Grotto. [S24] Core77 describes Grotto as a cave formed by enormous latex pillars in the center of the factory hall, made in 2015, and as one of his largest pieces. [S23]

Designboom adds the method. Pink latex sheets are stretched on six-meter wooden frames to double their size, a thick layer of liquid latex goes on, and Hess shapes vein-like lines with his fingers. When the sheet is released from the frame it springs back, and the surface distorts while the carved lines keep their size. The same article says Grotto grew out of a three-year process that began with his show at the 2015 design biennale in Saint-Etienne and presented it during Dutch Design Week as part of Robot Love. [S25]

As an anatomist I notice what that description borrows from tissue: a stretched sheet that recoils, with veins that hold their size while the skin around them puckers. That is the article's account of the method, and I cannot test it from a page. My narrower point is this. I did not find a 2018 album under his name in the archive, so anyone who searches the archive by name would miss a well-documented appearance. [S1][S23][S25]
2019: Reveries, and an address that is not the studio

VPRO's tip number seven for Dutch Design Week 2019 is Bart Hess, Reveries. The tip describes a 360-degree film of about six minutes, watched through a VR headset on a swivel chair at Gasfabriek 18. It says he made the film from a long trend report for Première Vision, a textile fair in Paris, that the music is by Wouter de Belder, and that only five headsets were available. In the reviewer's account the viewer sits in a forest surrounded by objects that dancers climb out of, and the landscape keeps changing as the dancers appear in new outfits. [S5]

The address matters. Dutch Design Week's 2026 location page for The GASFAB gives Gasfabriek 18 and calls it a former industrial gasworks in the NRE district, in the Canal area. [S14] The 2026 page for Bart Hess | NRE gives Gashouder 43A. [S7] So the 2019 film was shown in a different building on the same site from the one DDW now names after him. The sources do not say where his studio stood in 2019, and the photo titles NRE_Bart_Hess record an area, not a building. [S1][S5][S7][S14]
2020 and 2021: a prize, a book and a gap

In 2020 Hess and Harm Rensink did the exhibition design for BodyDrift, Anatomies of the Future, at Design Museum Den Bosch, and the studio's page credits the photography to Hess. [S17][S30] Rensink also co-curated Modebelofte in 2016, according to Neon Moire, which is the kind of thread that makes the Eindhoven design world look small. [S2][S17]

On June 19, 2021 the Cultural Fund of North Brabant gave Hess its Design Prize, which comes with 10,000 euros and alternates between an established designer and a breakthrough talent. Piet Hein Eek won it in 2017 and Simone Post in 2019. [S17][S18] Omroep Brabant quotes the jury on the alienation his work causes and mentions his body sculptures for the national opera and ballet. [S18] He used the occasion to select three emerging talents for a presentation at the museum from June 19 to September 19, 2021. [S17]

None of this places him at the festival that October. The 2021 album holds ten photographs by Bookelaar that show projected lettering, drawings and printed fabric. [S1] I found no program page for the year, and I could not open a printed 2021 festival map that a search summary suggested might list his entries, since the file returns an error. So for 2021 the evidence is photographs and a title.
2024: Venus, and a festival that lists what the archive lacks

Dutch Design Week's program page for Venus names Bart Hess as presenter. It describes a collaboration between Hess and the choreographer and dancer Sedrig Verwoert that explores dance, multimedia and costume design, with costumes treated as an extension of the dancers' bodies. It also describes Woven Bodies, a textile project built around the human skin, using stitching, quilting and embroidery on a large digital print taken from a still of Verwoert's choreography on the intertwining of human bodies. [S6]

Hess's own site gives the credits: concept by Verwoert and Hess, choreography by Verwoert, costume design by Hess and music by Phantom Wizard, with six named dancers. [S10] DDW's own area recap, dated October 25, 2024, calls the NRE site the first hotspot of the Canal area and names the Venus project among its attractions. [S11] The NRE studio's own page lists a DDW 2024 presentation of Bart Hess. [S12] Three sources agree that he presented there that year. None of the 2024 album titles I could list carried his name, and I could not recheck the archive. [S1][S6][S11][S12]
2025 and 2026: the address outlives the exhibit

The same Gashouder 43A has hosted other people's shows. DesignWeb's 2025 guide lists a solo show by the studio ZOWA, Details matter, at Bart Hess | NRE, Gashouder 43A, from October 18 to 26, 2025, 11:00 to 18:00, free. [S28] The NRE studio page lists an Offsite Expo and a Zowa Expo next to the DDW 2024 note for Hess, and it also advertises the space as a rentable photo studio. [S12]

For 2026 the location page gives Gashouder 43A, October 17 to 25, daily 11:00 to 18:00, free entry. The Tuesday row prints the hours backwards as 18:00 to 11:00, which looks like an entry error. [S7] The page lists a single item, Back and forth, and the program page names the presenter as OFFSITE. It is a pop-up café called Café ocho, where the furniture, lamps and vases are made from industrial waste streams, with material credited to Staco, Unilin, Palet, Volta Energy, Brainport Assemblers, Hydro and Befo. It shows a cabinet called Lamella by Nina van Bart and Willem van Doorn and work by Rik van Veen, Structural Aspect, Julius Esser, Rik Frans Jansen and Joris Wintgens, with curtains by Yvonne Mak. [S7][S8]

Nothing on either page says Hess shows work in 2026. DDW lists the address as 5611CR, while the studio's own page gives 5613 CR. [S7][S12] A location name is a label that stays after the show changes, and anyone reading a map the way I do should read the exhibitor line, not the place name.
What the record does not show

Whether Work With Me People ran during Dutch Design Week 2012. The two sources I could open do not say, and the others that might have said so (two design sites that returned HTTP 403 and 503, and a trend service whose text is walled) were not usable, and I stopped asking. [S26][S27]
What the 2017 and 2021 albums show by name. No program page I opened names either body of work. [S1]
Whether the draped bed in the 2016 album is the Royal Latex Bed, and which color the bed was. [S1][S3][S4]
Where his studio stood in each year, and whether Gashouder 43A is the studio he moved into in 2016. [S4][S7]
Whether a 2023 album exists. I did not find one.
Whether Venus was staged elsewhere before the festival, and what Back and forth has to do with Hess beyond sharing his address. [S7][S8]
How Reveries came to be commissioned beyond VPRO's account of the trend report. [S5]
If a location carries a person's name, what would you check before crediting that person with what is inside? [S7]

title: BioArt Laboratories hosts the work, and the record disagrees about where it lived
subtitle: Ten Dutch Design Week shows by one Eindhoven organization, read through its own pages, local reporting, the 2026 listing and five albums in the official photo archive
description: Ten Dutch Design Week shows by BioArt Laboratories, a forest bunker site and a disputed move date, set against five photo albums.

sections.x: The photo archive knows who hosted the show and who took the picture, and it says very little about what stands in the frame or even which building the frame is in. [S1]

I like that gap because it gives a reader something to do. This essay draws on public sources only: BioArt Laboratories' own pages, a residency listing, a university excursion page, Dutch Design Week's program pages, regional reporting, a contractor's project page and the official DDW photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what DDW's location page lists. [S2][S3][S4][S12][S1][S14]
An organization that describes itself as a host

AIR Brabant lists BioArt Laboratories as a residency and gives its self-description: the National Development Institution for the Biological Arts, with programs aimed at practical development and production of work, up to presentation on platforms such as Dutch Design Week. [S4] BioArt's About page calls it a foundation and a gateway where science, nature, technology and creativity meet, and it names the funders that have supported it, among them the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science, the Creative Industries Fund NL, the province of North Brabant and the municipality of Eindhoven. [S2]

The people who show work there change every year. BioArt's page for 2019 describes an annual open call for its Talent Pressure Cooker and a group of makers ranging from product developers to architects. [S10] Its page for the 2020 digital edition says the talents get access to the working environment after submitting a project proposal and receive guidance on turning an idea or prototype into a concept or product. [S11] An organization built like this has a program, and the program has many authors. That matters for a photo archive.

Regional reporting adds a public-policy fact. Brabant Cultureel reported on October 15, 2021 that BioArt Laboratories had been included in the national cultural basic infrastructure that year, on the condition that it could keep developing at its current site. [S9]
A founder with a record before the lab

The founder's own site says Jalila Essaïdi was born in 1980, is best known for the project 2.6g 329m/s, also called Bulletproof Skin, and founded BioArt Laboratories in 2011. [S6] The Bio Art & Design Award says she won a BAD Award in 2010 for that project. [S7] A 2017 excursion page from Burg Giebichenstein University of Art and Design agrees on 2011 and adds that the lab established a physical foothold in Eindhoven in 2012. [S5] AIR Brabant lists the foundation as founded in 2012. [S4] The sources are consistent if 2011 is the founder's start and 2012 the lab's first base, but I have not seen a company-register extract, so I do not state either year as the legal founding date.

Dutch Design Week named her one of its four ambassadors for 2019. In the DDW interview she says she prefers to work with young, not-yet-established talent, and she describes Dutch Design Week as a stage for makers who lack the network or the money to present in prominent places. [S13] That is her account of her own approach, and it fits the shape of the annual open call.
More than an exhibition

The exhibitions are one visible output of a larger operation. BioArt's laboratory page describes a hybrid laboratory that is both a biochemical research station for analysis and cultivation of biomaterials and a traditional atelier for prototyping, and it describes a Materialenbank, a library of bio-based materials that includes slime mold and luminous bacteria. [S25] In a 2017 interview with the materials library MaterialDriven, Essaïdi describes the same Materialenbank, and the interviewer's introduction names the public formats Open Stadslabs and Curiocity Labs. The interviewer's page shows photographs of the lab's Dutch Design Week exhibits for 2015 and 2016. [S26]

That interview also gives the lab's own account of why it sits in Eindhoven: Essaïdi credits the legacy of Philips and the supply of what she calls bright talents. [S26] It is her explanation, and nothing in the other sources tests it. I mention it because the lab's later choice of a Second World War site in a forest is easy to read as symbolism, and no source says that was the intention. [S3][S26]
The site: German Houses in a Strijp forest

The place has a documented history. BioArt's own Village page says the complex is the Duitse Woningen, or German Houses, a bunker complex originally built to house German military officers, five freestanding reinforced buildings disguised as a traditional farmstead in the Heimatstil, on a plot of about 1.5 hectares. [S3] Brabant Cultureel adds that the occupier confiscated the neighboring Constant Rebecque barracks in 1940, that the complex kept a military function until 1996, and that it later served as a center for asylum seekers before it decayed and was looted. [S9] A contractor that worked on the renovation estimate, bureau FRANKEN, gives the figures for five buildings with 3,089 square meters of floor area on 16,255 square meters of land. [S12] That land area is 1.6 hectares, which matches DDW's 2024 page and is slightly more than BioArt's own 1.5. [S3][S12][S15]

BioArt's partner page shows what the renovation has needed: military engineers from the 13th Light Brigade for architectural counsel and landscape work, a firm that traces unexploded ordnance for a risk analysis of the site's history, and companies donating solar equipment, building materials and fire-safety advice. [S16]

Who owns the site is a separate question. Brabant Cultureel says the municipality owned the complex and offered it to BioArt in 2016, and that the municipality later agreed to transfer the land and buildings. [S9] The contractor's page says the purchase was agreed in 2017 and the purchase agreement was signed in 2022, and it also lists the purchase under 2017 in its timeline, so it contradicts itself. [S12] I have not found a municipal document, so I do not give a date for the transfer.
When did the lab move? The sources disagree
The question looks small and has a firm answer. [S3][S8]

BioArt's Dutch Village page says that in 2016 BioArt moved from its 750 square meter lab in Strijp-T to the German Houses. [S3] The English version of the same page contains the same paragraph twice, once with 2016 and once with 2017. [S3] Brabant Cultureel and the contractor both say 2016. [S9][S12]

A contemporary report says otherwise. On June 28, 2017, the IO+ archive wrote that the staff of BioArt Lab would soon be moving into the German Houses, after years of preparing the move from Strijp TQ, where the lab was still located, with an official opening planned for September. [S8] BioArt's own page for Dutch Design Week 2017, titled Lost in Transformation, says that exhibition was the first occasion on which the public got insight into its plans for the new BioArt Village, and its page for 2018 says it had less than a year to refurbish the new location and welcomed the public at the brand new site. [S17][S18]

I settle it this way. The municipality offered the site in 2016, as the regional report says. The move happened in 2017 and 2018, and the first Dutch Design Week show at the Village was in October 2018. The wording "moved in 2016" in BioArt's own pages reads best as the offer date. This matters for the photographs: a 2016 or 2017 album is unlikely to show the Village. [S8][S9][S17][S18]
Year by year, with the claim each source supports

For 2015, BioArt's page says it ran Chilling in a Box at the Veemgebouw, Torenallee 80, between the food market and the Dutch Design Awards, after a half-year collaboration with ten young designers, scientists and local industries. It says the show drew more than 5,000 visitors and that the broadcaster VPRO listed it among ten tips. Those figures are BioArt's own. [S19] The archive has no 2015 album. [S1]

For 2016 the Burg Giebichenstein page names the show The Essence of Things and describes nine projects, among them crystals grown from minerals by Isaac Monte, soap films by Simon Raffy, dissected fish gills by Mandy den Elzen, bone china made without bones by Marloes van Bennekom and Essaïdi's own manure project Mestic. [S5] The page does not say where the show stood. The IO+ report places the lab at Strijp TQ in mid-2017, so the 2016 show was most likely there, but no page I opened states it. [S8] The album of 21 photos by Iris Rijskamp shows a large hall with yellow columns and pink grow lights, which is not the forest. [S1]

For 2017, Lost in Transformation took the theme of metamorphosis, according to BioArt, with a tour through microorganisms and algae. [S17] For 2018, Cybernetic Forest opened at the new Village. [S18] Neither year has an album in the archive. [S1]

For 2019, BioArt's page says it was included in DDW's Bio Design route, with visitors reaching it by hop-on hop-off bus from Strijp-S, that the Symbiocene Forest opened on October 18 with speakers including a European Space Agency MELiSSA scientist and the water board's chief, and that the week included a debate on creative hubs and a storytelling session on water. [S10] The album holds 18 photos by Nick Bookelaar. [S1]

For 2020, the first fully digital edition, the page says eleven artists showed work in a virtual exhibition, and it lists talents from South Africa, the Netherlands, Cyprus, Poland, Russia and Lithuania among them. [S11] For 2021, BioArt's page gives October 16 to 24 and Brabant Cultureel counted work by more than twenty artists and designers, with talents from the Netherlands, the United States, Italy, Turkey, Poland, the Czech Republic and South Africa in its list, and guided tours all week. [S9][S20] For 2022, DDW's program page lists The Symbiocene Forest and says the participating talents' work varies from sculptures and experiments to product design. [S21]

For 2023, BioArt's page says the opening ceremony took place on October 20 with remarks by the North Brabant deputy for energy and culture and an Eindhoven alderman, and that activities ran October 21 to 29. [S22] The archive may or may not hold a 2023 album; the listing I used was incomplete. [S1] For 2024, DDW's page lists The Symbiocene Forest, Coexistence, in a 1.6-hectare forest with hidden bunkers. [S15] BioArt's recap dated October 28, 2024 says more than 53 artists and designers took part, that visitors could enter the first floor of the main exhibition for the first time and that a willow weaving workshop made bracelets. [S23]

For 2026, DDW's location page lists BioArt Laboratories at Oirschotsedijk 14-10 with free access, opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 for all nine days, and a list of exhibition projects that includes a book made from bacteria-derived bioplastic, a clay 3D-printed reef system and a lamp series about time in wood. [S14]
What a reader could test, and what no one has

Two details in the written record could be checked against the albums by someone who has them open. Brabant Cultureel describes a smoking room in the former officers' mess with its original parquet floor and wall paneling. [S9] The 2019 album includes a wood-paneled room with framed botanical prints. [S1] Nothing ties the two together, and the album title does not name a room, so I leave it as a question a visitor to the site could answer.

BioArt's 2024 recap lists a willow weaving workshop in which visitors made bracelets. [S23] Four of the five photographs in the 2024 album show willow being woven. [S1] The workshop and the photographs may be the same event, and the titles give no sign either way.

These two cases show how a single archive can be used in two ways. [S1][S9][S23] A reader who stays inside the album can describe what is visible. A reader who brings a second document can propose a match, and the match is only as strong as the second document's wording.
A theme borrowed from a philosopher

The word Symbiocene runs through every program page from 2019 on. Glenn Albrecht, who wrote the 2019 Ecologist essay I read, uses it for a proposed new era in human-nature relations that he expects to emerge from the Anthropocene. [S24] BioArt's 2019 page states its working principles as full circularity, the elimination of toxic substances, complete and safe biodegradability of materials and organic integration of technology with living systems. [S10] DDW's 2022 page says the lab adopts key principles of the Symbiocene. [S21]

I cannot tell from these pages how much of Albrecht's argument BioArt adopts, because BioArt gives its own principles and does not cite him on the pages I read. I treat the term as borrowed and the list of principles as BioArt's. [S10][S24]
What the titles carry

The archive holds BioArt albums for 2016, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2024, with 21, 18, 25, 54 and 5 photos, a total of 123, and the photographers are named in the titles: Iris Rijskamp, Nick Bookelaar and Cleo Goossens. [S1] A title reads like an inventory number: the organization's name, the photographer and a frame number. The 2022 and 2024 titles add a date and an area code, StrijpTQ and StrijpTR, which are DDW's codes. [S1] DDW's 2026 page places BioArt under Strijp T+R. [S14] No title names a work.

As an anatomist, I am used to specimens that arrive with a tag, and I know how much a tag leaves out. A tag that says who prepared the specimen and when does not say what it is. The photo archive works the same way. It documents the host, the year and the photographer. The identity of the object needs a second document. [S1]

Suppose a reader wants to caption the 2022 photograph of an amber vessel in a lit display case. The scenario is hypothetical. The album title gives the organization and the photographer, and DDW's page gives a show name and a range of media. The maker, the title and the material are still missing, so any caption beyond "from BioArt Laboratories' 2022 album, photographed by Cleo Goossens" would be a guess. [S1][S21]
What the record does not show

I do not know which work any photograph shows. I do not know where the 2016 show stood, though the lab's address in mid-2017 points to Strijp TQ. [S8] I do not know the date the municipality transferred the site, or whether the 2022 purchase agreement the contractor mentions is the signed transfer. [S12]

I could not open the national advice document on which the 2021 inclusion in the basic infrastructure rests, so that fact stands on regional reporting alone. [S9] I do not know whether other albums exist, because the album lists I read were incomplete. [S1]

The 2023 and 2024 numbers of artists come from BioArt's own recaps, and I have no independent count. [S23] Dutch Design Week's 2026 page lists projects, and I do not know how many are by talents of the program and how many are guests. [S14]

Here is a concrete step for a reader: pick one project listed at BioArt Laboratories for 2026, and before reading its description, write the credit line you would need for a photograph of it. Maker, title, year, source. Which of those four could you fill in from the page alone? [S14]

title: The Business Lounge at Dutch Design Week: a room for professionals, a studio behind it and a skate hall around it
subtitle: The official photo archive files two Business Lounge albums, 2024 and 2025. Supplier pages, DDW's ticket page and local sources show who designed the room and what it was for.
description: What DDW's Business Lounge at Area 51 is for, who designed it in 2023 and 2024, and what the photo archive shows for 2024 and 2025.

sections.x: The Business Lounge is the one room at Dutch Design Week built for sitting down, and the photo archive files it under a name that says nothing about who made it. [S11]

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds two albums titled Business Lounge, 4 photographs from 2024 and 73 from 2025, 77 in all. [S11] The written record is thinner than for most places in this series, because the room is a service and not an exhibition, though it is not empty. DDW's ticket page says what the lounge is for, two supplier pages name the studio that designed it in 2023 and 2024, and a few local sources describe the building around it. This essay draws on those public sources only. It reports no visit and no conversation, and it says nothing about the 2026 program beyond what DDW lists. [S1][S2]
What the room is for

DDW's PRO ticket page says the Business Lounge sits at Area 51 on Ketelhuisplein in Strijp-S and that PRO ticket holders can exchange their e-ticket there for a wristband and badge. [S1] The page lists the lounge's facilities as unlimited barista coffee, tea, internet, personal support from DDW staff, and a comfortable place to work and network. [S1] The same ticket includes other things the page lists: access to the Grand Opening, morning sessions in Natlab, a place on a Design Tour, two PRO networking events held in the lounge, an evening called Work in Progress with the Dutch Design Awards, and a bicycle for the nine days. [S1] Tours are reserved in the lounge during the week, and tours that are not full can be joined on the spot. [S1]

So the lounge is a counter and a set of tables with three jobs: pick up credentials, book a tour, and sit down between appointments. That is a hospitality function, which helps explain why the archive photographs show curtains, lamps and chairs more than any single work. [S1][S11]
Which year the ticket page describes

The PRO page carries a header for the October 17 to 25, 2026 edition, but its text describes an earlier one. It says the Grand Opening is on the evening of Friday, October 18, networking events fall on Tuesday, October 22 and Thursday, October 24, and the Design Tours begin on Sunday, October 20 and continue through the week. [S1] Those weekdays fit 2024. October 18 was a Friday in 2024, a Saturday in 2025 and a Sunday in 2026, and DDW's own 2025 press release gives the 2025 edition as October 18 to 26. [S1][S7] The page also gives the last tour, on Friday, the same date it gives for Thursday, which reads like a typo in the source and is not something I can correct. [S1] I therefore use the page for what the lounge offers and treat its dates as 2024's.
Who designed it, in 2023 and 2024
Two supplier pages name the design team. [S3][S4]

For 2023, a case study by the laminate maker Formica says the Business Lounge was designed by the studio Daphna Laurens and Evelien Reich, with the supplier Blok Plaatmateriaal and photography by Ronald Smits. It describes a 12-meter bar in a laminate color called Earthenware that wound through the space and worked as a coffee point, a press and tours desk and a working station for the press. It says the goal was a warm, lively and optimistic room that avoided a black, white or gray palette, and it dates completion to October 2023. [S4]

For 2024, the furniture maker Artifort lists the project as DDW Business Lounge, in Eindhoven, completed October 2024. Its description says soft blues and yellows were balanced with raw metal and glossy earthenware, yellow curtains softened the daylight, and the seating combined customized Orange Slice armchairs with the modular Track sofa. It credits the design to Daphna Laurens in collaboration with Evelien Reich, with photography by Ronald Smits and Daphna Laurens. [S3]

Both pages are the suppliers' accounts of their own products, and neither is a DDW document. They agree with each other on the design team and on the photographer, which is a useful cross-check. [S3][S4]

The studio behind the name is Daphna Laurens, a design duo that, according to a Domus profile of October 31, 2017, opened its firm in Eindhoven in 2008 as Design Academy graduates, joined the Dutch Invertuals collective in 2009, and in 2017 presented four projects at DDW. [S5] A Dutch Design Awards announcement describes Evelien Reich as editor-in-chief of ELLE Decoration in the Netherlands and a member of the awards' main jury, in a version of the page I could not date. [S6] An interview published by Collectible on April 20, 2021 also introduces her as editor-in-chief of ELLE Decoration Netherlands. [S12] The DDW PRO page describes her as the host of the Work in Progress evening and as a former jury chair of the Dutch Design Awards and a former ELLE Decoration NL editor. [S1] I did not find a source that reconciles those two descriptions of her role, so I give each with its source and make no claim about her current position.
What the archive shows

The 2024 album has 4 photographs, all titled October 23, 2024 and credited in the titles to Ronald Smits. [S11] That matches the photographer Artifort names, so the album and the supplier page show the same room in the same week. [S3][S11] The 2025 album has 73 photographs, with titles that name Max Kneefel for 20, Ronald Smits for 21 and a date of October 24 and the name Cleo Goossens for 32 titled DesignTour. The titles do not say that Goossens is the photographer. [S11]

I read the albums at preview size on October 8, 2026 and did not reopen them for this version. In them I saw curtains, round tables, lamps, a checkerboard floor, rows of headsets on a curved table and signs reading TOURS, PRO and PRESS. [S11] Those signs fit the Formica description of a press and tours desk in 2023, which suggests the lounge kept the same functions across years. [S4][S11] They do not show that the 2024 and 2025 rooms were built by the same team. I found no supplier or DDW page that names a designer for 2025, and without one I make no claim.
The DesignTour titles in the 2025 album are a reminder of the PRO ticket's tour booking, but no source links the two, so I leave that as an observation about naming. [S1][S11]
The building around it

Area 51 is better known as a skate hall than a business space. A smow design blog of November 13, 2011 says the venue was established in 2002, covers 3,000 square meters of landscaped wood in an old industrial building on the former Philips estate, and that the blog's writers made a point of visiting it every year during Dutch Design Week. [S8] This is a blog's description, and I have not found an official source for the 2002 date. This is Eindhoven describes Area 51 as the largest indoor skate park in the Benelux, in a building that was a former tool shop and one of the first to be reused after Philips left Strijp-S, an area once closed to everyone but Philips staff. [S9]

The hall changed in the early 2020s. A Brainport Eindhoven article of December 7, 2022 says the skate hall was renovated in 2020 and 2021 with support from the Region Deal Brainport Eindhoven, and quotes a regular skater saying the track is now bigger and that the former separate areas for skaters and for steppers and BMX riders were joined. [S10] So the room hosting the lounge is not the same hall that the 2011 blog described.

DDW's own location page for Area 51 gives the address Ketelhuisplein 18, 5617 AE Eindhoven, daily opening from 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 25, 2026, partial wheelchair access, a wheelchair-friendly toilet, Wi-Fi and dogs allowed. [S2] That page does not mention the Business Lounge, and it offers a "Revisit DDW25" link, so I read it as a standing venue page and not as a 2026 program. Whether the lounge returns in 2026 is not something I can confirm. [S2]
Why a lounge is hard to photograph

The scale of the week explains why the room exists. DDW's 2025 press release expects around 350,000 visitors, more than 2,500 designers, design schools, ministries and brands, and 120 venues. [S7] A professional who has to cover that many venues needs a base, and the PRO page offers the lounge as that base. [S1][S7] A base is hard to picture. A photograph of a lounge shows furniture and light, and the people who matter to the room's purpose are mostly outside the frame. That is a caption problem as much as a photo problem: the room's meaning lives in the PRO page's list, not in the images. [S1][S11]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**Which edition the PRO page describes.** The header says 2026, the text dates fit 2024, and the 2025 edition opened on a Saturday. The weekday arithmetic settles it as 2024's text. [S1][S7]
**Who designed the room.** Formica (2023) and Artifort (2024) name the studio Daphna Laurens with Evelien Reich. For 2025 no source names anyone. [S3][S4]

**Whether the two albums show the same fitted space.** Artifort describes yellow curtains for 2024, while my own preview-size reading of the albums found pale blue and cream curtains in 2024 and violet and blue in 2025. Color at preview size is unreliable, so I do not rest anything on it, and the supplier's description is the stronger source for 2024. [S3][S11]
What the record does not show

I do not know who designed or furnished the 2025 lounge, whether the 2023 lounge was also at Area 51, or how many PRO tickets were sold in any year. I do not know what the other 35 photographs of the 2025 album show, because only 38 of the 73 were viewed in the October 8 reading. [S11] I found no DDW page for the lounge before 2023 and none that says when it began. I have no source for the lounge in 2026. [S2]
If a room exists to let professionals rest between rounds, what would you want its photographs to say about it: the furniture, the people, or the list of what it offered? [S1]
