title: The Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show at Dutch Design Week: five sites, one virtual year and a lease that ends in 2028
subtitle: Ten albums in the official photo archive, the school's own pages for every year from 2012, and what they say about where the show was, how big it was and why one year has no album.
description: Where the Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show stood each Dutch Design Week from 2015 to 2026, why 2020 has no album and what comes after 2028.

sections.x: A graduation show is a school's argument about design, made again each October by a new group of people, and for the Design Academy Eindhoven (DAE) the argument has been made in at least five different places. [S1][S27]

As a medical educator I pay attention to how a school shows what its students can do, because the arrangement of a room teaches as much as the work in it. The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds albums for ten editions of the Graduation Show, 2015 to 2019 and 2021 to 2025, and the school's own website keeps a page for every year from 2012 to 2026. Read side by side, they answer questions the albums cannot: where the show stood each year, how many projects it held, why one year has no album, and where it is going next. This essay uses public sources only. It reports no visit and no interview, and it describes photographs only as far as the archive's titles and my earlier read of the albums allow. [S1][S27]
What the school says the show is

DAE calls its Graduation Show one of the world's most influential exhibitions of work by new designers, staged annually in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week, where bachelor and master students present final projects to thousands of visitors. [S1] That is the organizer's own claim and I report it as one. The same page gives a short history. The show was originally staged in Amsterdam, and in 2001 Li Edelkoort, then creative director of DAE, moved it back to the academy building in Eindhoven when Dutch Design Week launched. DAE partnered with the Dutch Design Foundation, the organization behind the week. [S1] [S1]

The year in that history sits one year away from DDW's own count. In its 2016 press release the Dutch Design Foundation called DDW 2016 the 15th edition, which puts the first edition in 2002. [S26] Both can be true if the show moved in 2001 ahead of the first week, or DAE's year may be a round figure. Neither page says which, so I give both and settle nothing. For scale, the same release counted 430 curated exhibitions and presentations at 100 locations in 2016 and an estimated 295,000 visitors over nine days, so the Graduation Show was one program item among hundreds. [S1][S26] [S1][S26]
The Witte Dame years, and a crowd that outgrew the building

Until 2017 the show was inside the academy's own building. DAE says the 2018 show was the first edition in almost two decades to take place outside the academy's walls. [S8] The building is the Witte Dame, which DAE says was built in 1928 as Philips' first large-scale lighting factory and which the academy shares with a public library and other services, using 10,000 square meters. [S24] The 2013 page shows what that meant in practice: visitors were invited to tour the 4th and 5th floors of the academy and talk to 126 graduate students, and a radio show broadcast sounds from the floors daily. [S3] [S8][S24][S3]

The school's yearly pages give a sense of scale. In 2012 the show was titled Up Close Wide Open, with 137 individual perspectives, curated by Strange Attractors. [S2] In 2014, 155 graduates presented 171 projects. [S4] In 2015, 141 graduates presented 153 projects, dealing with race, dematerialization, tactility and humanizing technology. [S5] In 2016, 171 graduates presented 197 projects under the title In Need Of..., curated by Formafantasma. [S6] In 2017 the overall theme was MINED, which the page ties to the fundamental research in the students' projects; it gives no total. [S7] DAE's own history says the Arena, a live talks platform at the center of the show, began in 2016. [S1] [S2][S4][S5][S6][S7][S1]

IO+ reported on the reason for leaving. Visitor numbers to the show had grown over recent years from 30,000 to 51,000, and the move to the Campina site was meant to give room for that growth. [S9] Creative director Joseph Grima told IO+ that the move would double the available square meters, so that the students' work would be shown better, and that the academy would no longer have to relocate its teaching activities temporarily to make room. [S9] I have the visitor figures from this one report, which is undated in the archive. [S9]
2018 and 2019: a milk factory and eight worlds

DAE's 2018 page describes the move as the first outside the academy in almost two decades, to a venue on the site of the historic Campina milk factory, and says it reflected a major shift in the public's perception of design and the role of DAE. It counted 208 projects by 185 graduates, October 20 to 28, 2018. [S8] IO+ places the site by the Kanaaldijk-Zuid and says DAE had signed an agreement with BPD, the site's owner, for the shows in 2018, 2019 and 2020. BPD had said at the end of 2017 that it wanted to build homes on the site eventually and would make it available for events such as DDW in the meantime. [S9] [S8][S9]

In 2019 the show stayed for a second year at the Campina factory. DDW's own program entry and DAE's page both say so. [S10][S11] The change that year was curatorial. DAE's history says Grima replaced the old system, which arranged work under the title of each bachelor and master program, with projects gathered around themes. [S1] The 2019 page gives the structure: from 120 bachelor projects came eight worlds, named Landscape Amnesia, Unknown Caller, Training Set, Seven Continents, One Ocean, The Scavengers, Hidden Publics, The Guests and Channel Eight, and 61 master projects modeled five characters of designer, Performer, Critical Observer, Material Appropriator, Situated Agent and Empath. [S10] One of the worlds, The Scavengers, matches a banner that shows in a photograph in the 2019 album. [S27] [S10][S11][S1][S27]
2020: the year without a room

The archive has no 2020 album, and the school's own page says why. The 2020 page says that, because of the international nature of the graduates and the scale of the event, it became clear at the eleventh hour that a large-scale exhibition was no longer feasible. It presented the work of 184 graduates in other ways: 3D viewing rooms for each of the eight bachelor and four master departments as part of the virtual edition of Dutch Design Week, a website with a project page for each student, a printed graduation catalog, and the Arena broadcast live from DAE's Instagram twice a day. [S12] [S12]

The 2020 master's projects had a second life. DAE's Moving In Stasis page describes an exhibition of 60 master graduates of 2020 at Het Nieuwe Instituut in Rotterdam, March 8 to April 11, 2021, curated, designed and developed by the graduates themselves, with a mostly digital public because of continued Covid restrictions. [S13] So the show that has no album in the archive does have a record, and part of it ended up in a museum six months later. [S13]
2021 to 2025: a new building almost every year

In 2021 the show ran October 16 to 24 at the Beursgebouw, Lardinoisstraat 10, with 163 projects. [S14] DAE framed it as an index, a navigational tool for the themes, keywords, materials and methodologies of the projects, and added The Stage, a digitally mediated platform alongside the physical exhibition, on which 25 of the 163 graduates presented. [S14] [S14]

In 2022 it ran October 22 to 30 in the Microtuin building, which DAE calls a former telecommunications center in the inner city, taking place there for the first time. The page says the show wound through the building's spaces on a single path and that The Stage grew out of a professorship in transdisciplinary design networks, combining scenography, theater, film and television techniques with extended reality and gaming technologies. [S15] More than 200 projects were shown. [S15] [S15]

In 2023 the show moved to the top floor of the Heuvel shopping center, Heuvel Galerie 133, October 21 to 29. [S16] DAE's opening-day news item counts 220 projects and quotes curators Nadine Botha and Martina Muzi in their opening speech: "Design is not just an object on a pedestal." It describes the choice as setting in-depth projects against the consumer-driven culture of the shopping center, and names three new kinds of space: a bookshop for theses and process books, a workshop area open to the public even without a DDW wristband, and a cinema. [S17] [S16][S17]

In 2024 and 2025 the show was at Microstad, Professor Dr Dorgelolaan 2, October 19 to 27, 2024 and October 18 to 26, 2025, each time with 200 projects. [S18][S20] DDW's program entry for 2024 says that "since the last show in 2022" Microstad has been transformed. [S19] DAE's own December 20, 2024 recap settles what the two names mean: it calls Microstad the former KPN telecoms building on the edge of the city center and puts the video works in the basement garage of the Microtuin, so Microtuin (2022) and Microstad (2024 to 2026) are one complex under two names. [S28][S15][S19] The same recap says that 2024 was the last year in which the show included graduates whose studies had been affected by the pandemic. [S28] The 2025 page names its spaces: an underground Space One for film and sound, a new Garden, Glass Rooms on the ground floor, a Gallery upstairs and a Bookshop. [S20] [S18][S20][S19][S28][S15]
A new organizing idea almost every year

Reading the school's pages in order, the way the projects were grouped changes nearly every year. In 2012 the show had a curator, Strange Attractors, and in 2016 another, Formafantasma. [S2][S6] In 2017 an overall theme, MINED, tied the projects together. [S7] In 2019 the old arrangement by program gave way to eight worlds and five designer characters. [S10] In 2021 it was an index. [S14] In 2022 it was a single path through the building. [S15] In 2023 the concept was proximity, grouping projects so that neighbors complemented each other. [S17] In 2024 a curatorial team led by Martina Muzi, head of the BA studio Technogeographies, organized the projects by typology, which the school's own recap says brought a much-needed clarity to the visitor's experience. [S28] In 2025 the page describes distinct atmospheres, and in 2026 thematic pathways. [S20][S21] I read this as a school treating the layout of the show as part of its teaching, which is my interpretation and not a statement in any source. [S2][S6][S7][S10][S14][S15][S17][S28][S20][S21]

DDW's own magazine described the 2019 show in similar terms. It called the set-up spacious, with projects that could be seen from all sides, a big difference from earlier presentations in the Witte Dame, and named two prize winners: Seok-hyeon Yoon, who won the René Smeets Award for a ceramic project using Korean lacquer, and Irakli Sabekia, who won the Melkweg Award for turning a barbed-wire fence in East Georgia into a radio antenna. [S29] The annual Gijs Bakker, René Smeets and Melkweg Awards are presented at the show; the 2025 page lists a prize of 2,000 euros and a trophy designed by an alumnus. [S20] [S29][S20]
2026, and a correction about where it is

DDW lists the 2026 show as hosted by DAE at Professor Doctor Dorgelolaan 2, October 17 to 25, 2026, with over 200 projects and a DDW ticket required. [S22] This is Eindhoven's September 29, 2026 tip puts it at Microstad, a five-minute walk from the central station. [S23] DAE's page gives the same street address, 200 projects and a theme text about decisions that outlive the rooms they were made in. It says the Arena returns after several years away in an intimate format, and that the awards trophy was designed by DAE alumna Clara Schweers and produced with MAKE Eindhoven. [S21] [S22][S23][S21]

The 2026 show is therefore not at the academy building on Emmasingel 14. [S24][S22] Two dates need care. DAE's 2026 page lists opening times from October 18 to 26, a nine-day sequence that matches its 2025 page, while DDW and DAE's own header give October 17 to 25. [S21][S20][S22] I use DDW's dates, and I cannot tell from the pages whether DAE's opening-times list is a leftover from 2025. [S24][S22][S21][S20]
What comes after the Witte Dame

The school's April 7, 2025 news item says DAE extended its lease at the Witte Dame until 2028, with the city and the landlord, Profinn, arranging a phased handover while the new building is finished. It says the new rental building will stand in the Kanaalzone planning area at Kanaaldijk Zuid 3-5, right next to the former Campina factory site, in a tailor-made building, with 250 student homes in the plan area. [S25] The factory where the show stood in 2018 and 2019 is therefore next door to where the school itself plans to move. [S25][S10] The sources do not say whether the Graduation Show will be held in the new building. [S25][S10]
What the ten albums can and cannot show

The archive holds ten albums with 680 photos in all: 50 in 2015, 69 in 2016, 53 in 2017, 92 in 2018, 50 in 2019, 135 in 2021, 132 in 2022, 35 in 2023, 11 in 2024 and 53 in 2025. [S27] Set against the school's project counts, coverage is uneven. The 2021 album has 135 photos for 163 projects, while the 2024 album has 11 photos for 200 projects, about one picture for every eighteen. [S27][S14][S18] No album can be taken as a record of the show it names. [S27][S14][S18]

Photographer names come from photo titles. Sjoerd Eickmans and Cleo Goossens are credited in 2015, Goossens in 2016, Ruud Balk and Boudewijn Bollmann in 2017, Goossens in 2018 and 2021, Max Kneefel in 2019, Kneefel, Goossens and about.today in 2022, Goossens in 2023, Angelina Nikolayeva and Kneefel in 2024, and Kneefel in 2025. [S27] DAE's own 2019 page captions its photographs with the spelling Sjoerd Eijkmans, where the archive titles say Eickmans. [S1][S27] I could not settle the spelling from the sources I opened, and I would check it with the photographer before a credit is printed. [S27][S1]
Questions the sources settle

Five questions came up. Why there is no 2020 album: the show went virtual, and DAE's page says why. [S12] Where the 2015 to 2017 shows were: inside the academy's building, since DAE says the 2018 move was the first outside its walls in almost two decades. [S8] Where the 2019 show was: at Campina, according to both DAE and DDW. [S10][S11] Whether the 2026 show is at the academy: it is not, since the address is Dorgelolaan 2. [S22][S24] How many projects the 2023 show held: 220 by DAE's opening-day news item, and "more than 200" on its event page. [S16][S17] [S12][S8][S10][S11][S22][S24][S16][S17]
What the record does not show

I do not know why DAE and DDW differ by a year on the start of the partnership. [S1][S26] I do not know how many projects the 2017 show held, because its page gives none. [S7] I do not know which photographs in each album show the Graduation Show hall itself and which show a neighboring DAE exhibition. [S27] I did not find a source for the 2018 attendance after the move, and I did not find the terms of the new building beyond the April 2025 news item. [S25] [S1][S26][S7][S27][S25]
If you look at one of these ten albums, which page would you open to find out where the photograph was taken, the school's, DDW's or neither? [S27][S1][S22]

title: DDW Music, 2015 to 2019: what the press archive counts, what the photo archive holds, and one number that did not hold
subtitle: Dutch Design Week's own pages number four editions of its music program. Read against the photo archive, a venue listing and a 2019 news item, they show where the archive has gaps and where a summary went wrong.
description: DDW Music from 2015 to 2019: editions, venues, lineups, tickets and visitor counts from Dutch Design Week's own pages, checked against the photo archive.

sections.x: Dutch Design Week's own press pages count the music program as a series of editions, and by their count the photo archive skips at least one. [S3][S11]

I read the program that way because the pages are specific, and specific pages can be checked. This essay draws on public sources only: Dutch Design Week's press and news archive for 2015 to 2018, a venue listing, a festival-news item from 2019, a listing site for 2017 and the official photo archive on Flickr as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about a 2026 music program, because I found no page for one. [S1][S11]
The program, edition by edition, by its own count

DDW Music was introduced in 2015. The press page of September 1, 2015 describes daily live performances at various locations in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week, October 17 to 25, free on presentation of a DDW ticket, and calls it a collaboration between Dutch Design Week, the Effenaar and the booking agency Friendly Fire. [S1] The press page of September 14, 2016 calls the next year the second edition. [S3] The wrap-up of November 6, 2017 calls that year the third. [S5] The page of September 4, 2018 calls the 2018 program the fourth edition. [S6] By DDW's own count, then, there were four editions from 2015 to 2018, numbered consecutively, and the numbering is the strongest evidence that 2016 happened. [S1][S3][S5][S6]

The program kept growing in the pages' own terms. The 2016 release says DDW Music drew more than 5,000 visitors in 2015. [S2] The 2017 wrap-up says the third edition had more than 16,000 visitors in total and that three quarters of the performances sold out. [S5] I find those two numbers useful and cannot compare them closely, because neither page says how a visitor was counted. I found no visitor figure for 2016 or 2018 in the pages I opened.

The 2018 page also carries a sentence that is easy to repeat and hard to date: with over 335,000 visitors, it says, the city's population will double for a week. [S6] It is a pre-event description of Dutch Design Week as a whole, and it does not say which year the count belongs to.
One number that did not hold: 2015 had 29 named artists, not 37

My first-pass summary of the 2015 page, which came through a summarizing reader, gave a lineup of 37 artists. The page itself gives a complete line-up of 29 names, which include the two specials announced earlier, Two Gallants at the Effenaar on Thursday, October 22 and Rufus Wainwright at the Muziekgebouw on Sunday, October 25. [S1] The page says twenty new names completed the line-up, and it separately lists two DJs for the Closing Party on Saturday, October 24 at the Effenaar, Kutmah from the United Kingdom and Zes from the Netherlands. [S1] I counted the names myself, and I could find no DDW page that gives 37. The 2016 page, by contrast, speaks of more than 60 artists in 12 locations, and the 2017 page of more than 70 artists. [S3][S4] A fair reading is that the 2015 program was a program of a few dozen named acts that more than doubled within two years. [S1][S3][S4]

I cannot tell from the page whether the 29 names are all of the acts. The page says "to name but a few" about the venues, and it does not use that phrase about the artists, so I give 29 as the number of names the page prints and not as a total. [S1]
Who was booked

The lineups show a program that mixed names a design visitor might know with acts that had only just started. In 2015 the page lists Rufus Wainwright, Ryley Walker, Two Gallants, Charlie Cunningham, K.Flay and Elvis Perkins among its 29. [S1] The first 2016 announcement, on August 3, names Jeremy Loops, Klyne, Benjamin Francis Leftwich and Baauer, and the September 14 page adds Loyle Carner, Palmbomen II, Dillon and Khruangbin. [S2][S3] The 2017 announcement lists Joep Beving, Lefto, Alex Vargas, Lapalux, Phoebe Bridgers, The Weather Station and Vagabon among more than 70. [S4] For 2019 the festival-news item names Altin Gun, Rico & Sticks and Iris Hond as earlier announcements and Blanck Mass and Les Robots among the late additions. [S9] I name these acts only as the pages do, and I did not hear any of them play at the festival.
Where the music went

Each press page lists venues, and the lists show a program that borrowed rooms from the rest of the week. In 2015 the page names the café Altstadt, the Van Abbemuseum, Tuchthuis, Stroomhuis, café Wilhelmina, Arcade, Nul Zes and the Ketelhuisplein, with the specials at the Effenaar and the Muziekgebouw. [S1] In 2016 the list is longer, with twelve locations: the Effenaar, Nul Zes, the Gaslab, FIFTH | NRE, the Van Abbemuseum, Stroomhuis, Altstadt, De Oude Rechtbank, café Wilhelmina, the Muziekgebouw, Calypso and the Ketelhuisplein. [S3] In 2017 it names the Effenaar, TAC, Altstadt, Stroomhuis, café Wilhelmina, The Student Hotel, Piet Hein Eek, FIFTH | NRE, De Oude Rechtbank and de Schuilplaats, and puts experiments on the Ketelhuisplein. [S4] In 2018 the page says three new venues brought the total to eleven locations, "from music halls to bars and ateliers," for over 90 shows, and on October 10, 2018 DDW published an official timetable and a Spotify playlist for the festival. [S6][S7]

Three things follow from reading the lists together. Altstadt, Stroomhuis and café Wilhelmina are on all three of the lists for 2015 to 2017, so a regular could plan a night around them. [S1][S3][S4] Nul Zes is on the 2015 and 2016 lists and not on the 2017 list. [S1][S3][S4] And Piet Hein Eek's complex is new in 2017: the wrap-up calls it a new concert location, with piano shows by Luke Howard and Matteo Myderwyk. [S5] The same complex has its own entry in this series, as a venue with a long guest list. [S5]

A venue listing adds a detail for 2018. The Dynamo venue in Eindhoven lists a DDW Music evening on Saturday, October 27, 2018 with Caro and Sofie Winterson, doors at 19:30, and says it was the first time the festival visited Dynamo's basement. [S8] The same listing describes the festival as having performances by 70 emerging acts over eleven venues, while DDW's own page says over 90 shows in eleven locations. [S8][S6] The two do not conflict if 70 counts acts and 90 counts performances, but neither page says so. The listing also says loose tickets cost 10 euros and were sold only at the door, which is higher than the 5 euros DDW's pages gave for earlier years. [S8][S1][S3][S4] It is a single venue's statement and I do not read it as the festival's price.
The design that stood on the stage

The press pages give the program a design layer that a plain gig listing would not. In 2016 the composer duo Strijbos & van Rijswijk presented a program of interactive installations at the DDW Music Lab on the Ketelhuisplein, open daily from 12:00 to 18:00 and, at weekends, a public workspace for guest musicians and designers, free to enter. [S3] The page asks what it would be like to wander through a composition and what music based on body movement sounds like. [S3] In 2017 the Lab returned, and the wrap-up credits it with interactive installations, lectures and workshops by Jeroen Strijbos, Rob van Rijswijk, the sound designer William Aikman and the producer and vocalist Chagall. [S5] A listing site gives more detail: musical sculptures called Quiver#2 and Quiver#3 by Strijbos & van Rijswijk with Pierluigi Pompeï, Aikman's Self Portrait as a Musical Instrument, a performance by Vito Willems, the Mi.Mu gloves of the electronic performer Chagall, and a sound playground called Sound Scouts. [S10]

Also in 2017, the announcement says five designers made decor and stage design, and the wrap-up says that was a first. [S4][S5] The announcement names four of them, Joost van Bleiswijk, Elvis Wesley, Studio Big Mistake and Tijs Gilde, and the wrap-up names three, Joost van Bleiswijk, Thijs Gilde and Studio Big Mistake, spelling the last name differently. [S4][S5] No page I opened names a fifth designer. A designer of the same name is half of the pair Kiki & Joost, which has its own entry in this series. DDW's pages do not say whether the two are the same person, and TL Magazine's report of October 26, 2017 says the pair had an ongoing project at the Effenaar that week, which fits the music program's main venue without proving the link. [S4][S12]

The same wrap-up reports a dance evening presented with the media partner Dezeen at the Effenaar, by the collective Omnipresent World of Wizkids, with Bart van de Sande, ZES and Polynation. [S5] A listing from October 18, 2017 describes a DDW Music Keynote on Friday, October 27 at the Effenaar from 19:30 to 21:30, with presentations by two women pioneers of electronic music, Sophie Letitre and Chagall, and a demonstration of OWOW instruments. [S10] I could not open the Dezeen page that would date the dance evening, because the site answered my request with an HTTP 403 and I stopped asking. [S5] I therefore do not say the keynote and the dance evening were on the same night, only that both sat at the Effenaar and both involved OWOW.
One artist, three roles

Chagall appears in three places in the 2017 record. The September 2017 announcement lists Chagall among the artists. [S4] The wrap-up names Chagall among the creators of the DDW Music Lab. [S5] The listing places Chagall in the keynote on October 27. [S10] I find that useful for a specific reason. The old dossier for this item recorded two photo titles for the artist, one for the keynote on Friday, October 27 and one for a performance on Wednesday, October 25, and could not say what the second one was. [S11] The line-up supports it: Chagall was booked as an act, so a performance on a weekday evening fits the pattern of the other titles. [S4] I still do not know what the performance was, because no page I opened describes it. [S4][S11]

That one name shows what a program like this was trying to do. A performer who can be an act on Wednesday, a Lab demonstration on a weekend and a keynote speaker on Friday is a performer the program treats as a designer of musical situations, and the three roles are on three different pages. [S4][S5][S10] That is my reading of the pages, and none of them says it.
What the ticket bought

The ticket rule stayed close to the same through the years, and its numbers moved. In 2015 the DDW ticket cost 16 euros online, excluding service costs, and a concert without it cost 5 euros at the door. [S1] In 2016 the ticket was 17.50 euros excluding service costs, with the same 5 euros at the door and individual tickets for specials, with a 5 euro discount for DDW ticket holders. [S3] In 2017 it was 19 euros including service costs, with 5 euros at the door and a free DDW Music Lab even without a ticket. [S4] The three prices look like a rise from 16 to 17.50 to 19, but the first two exclude service costs and the third includes them, so the series is not comparable from the pages alone. [S1][S3][S4] In 2018 the page says a DDW Festival ticket gives access to all DDW locations and to the DDW Music Festival. [S6]

The 2016 page also says the Lab's free admission was made possible by the Effenaar Poplab. [S3] I read the structure as a cross-subsidy between a pop venue and a design festival, and the pages say nothing more about it.
2019 and the end of the old dossier's window

The photo archive window I worked from ends in 2018, and the program did not. A festival-news item of October 3, 2019 says the program of the DDW Music Festival 2019 was complete, lists added acts including Blanck Mass, Kikok, Tim Dawn, Les Robots, Shaemless, Kléo, Meetsysteem and A Million Squeeks Will Do You No Harm, and says the festival is an initiative of the Effenaar and Friendly Fire in collaboration with Dutch Design Week, from October 19 to 27, 2019. [S9] The wording differs from the 2018 page, which says the festival is organized by Dutch Design Week, the Effenaar and Friendly Fire. [S6][S9] It is a different publisher, and I do not know whether the change is a change of roles or only of phrasing. [S6][S9]
I did not find a DDW page for any music program after 2019, and I did not find a DDW Music page for 2026. The sources I opened say nothing about what happened to the name. [S9]
What the photographs add

The old dossier counts three albums in the official archive: 84 photographs for 2015, 63 for 2017 and 112 for 2018, 259 in all, with no 2016 album in the list read on October 8, 2026. [S11] I did not reopen Flickr for this version. The titles carry act, weekday and date, and the 2018 page on DDW's own site adds a credit trail for four 2017 concert photographs: Max Kneefel for Yung Nnelg, Lieke Vermeulen for Alex Vargas, Roos Pierson for Braz and Patrick Spruytenburg for Phoebe Bridgers. [S6] That is a short list of named photographers against a program of 70 artists, and it is a reminder that a credit is a record too. [S6]

Two small mismatches belong here. The dossier lists a title naming Khruangbin among the 2018 photographs, while DDW's September 2016 page lists Khruangbin in the 2016 line-up and the 2018 pages I opened print no line-up. [S11][S3][S6] If that photograph is dated 2018, the band played in both years, and if it is from 2016 it sits in the wrong album. I cannot tell which from the pages. The second mismatch is smaller: a 2017 title reads asiwyfa, and the 2017 announcement lists And So I Watch You From Afar. [S11][S4] The initials fit, and I read the title as that act, but the pages do not confirm it. [S11][S4]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Whether 2016 happened.** The photo archive list has no 2016 album, and DDW's pages of August 3 and September 14, 2016 describe the second edition, which the 2017 wrap-up and the 2018 page then count in their own numbering. The pages settle it: 2016 happened, and the gap is in the archive. [S2][S3][S5][S6]
**How many artists in 2015.** 37 from a summarizing reader, 29 names on the page. The page settles it, and I use 29 as the number of names printed. [S1]
**Seventy or ninety in 2018.** 70 emerging acts on a venue's listing and over 90 shows on DDW's page. I attribute each, and I do not combine them. [S6][S8]
**Who organized 2019.** Organized by three parties in 2018, an initiative of two in collaboration with DDW in 2019. Not settled. [S6][S9]
**Which night the keynote was.** Friday, October 27, 2017 from one listing and the old dossier's photo title. I did not find a second page. [S10][S11]
What the record does not show

I do not know how visitors were counted in any year, and I found no figures for 2016, 2018 or 2019. I do not know what any act played, because titles and lineups name acts and not sets. I do not know who the fifth stage designer of 2017 was, or whether the dance evening and the keynote shared a night. I do not know whether Khruangbin played in 2018 as well as 2016, or what Chagall did on October 25, 2017. I did not open the Effenaar's own pages or Friendly Fire's, so the program's history from the organizers' side is missing here. [S3][S4][S5][S10][S11]

I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts and titles come from the October 8, 2026 reading and need a recheck before posting. [S11] DDW's pages for 2015 to 2018 give the program, and they stop at what was planned and announced, apart from the 2017 wrap-up. Nothing I opened is a review. [S1][S3][S4][S5][S6]
If you had one program page and one photo from the same night, which would you trust for what actually happened? [S5][S11]

title: From Mind the Step to Drivers of Change: how one university exhibition split in two at Dutch Design Week
subtitle: The archive files it from 2015. The organizers' own pages show it began in 2014, split in 2019 and kept showing up in years the archive has no album for.
description: How TU/e, 3TU and 4TU Design United's Mind the Step began in 2014, split in 2019 and kept showing up at Dutch Design Week through 2026.

sections.x: Mind the Step began in 2014, a year before the first album in the official Dutch Design Week photo archive, and by 2019 it had split into two exhibitions that now show up in different places. [S3][S5][S10]

As a content strategist I notice how a name can stay still while the thing it names moves. This essay follows one exhibition lineage through its own pages. It uses public sources only: the 4TU Design United edition pages, TU/e's event and news pages, a TU Delft research record, a University of Twente news item, Dutch Design Week's program pages, press reports and the photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what the organizers' pages list. [S2][S10][S28]
The federation changed its number, and Design United changed its description

In the 2015 brochure, Design United is "the 3TU research institute of the design courses" of Delft, Eindhoven and Twente. [S5] On May 27, 2016 the University of Twente announced that Wageningen University was joining the three technical universities and that the federation would be known as 4TU from then on. [S30] Today Design United describes itself as the 4TU research center for design, "the leading platform for Design Research in the Netherlands," a claim I treat as its own. [S2]

So the same two words describe a three-university institute in one year and a four-university center in another. The edition pages on the 4TU site follow the change quietly: the 2015 brochure speaks of the 3TU institute, and the 2025 and 2026 pages speak of projects from the 4TU and the four Dutch universities of technology. [S5][S27][S34]
2014: an experiment with 68 projects and 25 banners

The 4TU page for 2014 is the earliest edition page on the site. It places Mind the Step at the Klokgebouw from October 18 to 26, 2014 and describes 68 design research projects sorted into six themes: Care, Learn, Live, Make, Move and Sense. [S3] The project leader, Dr. Lucas Asselbergs, writes that the show breaks with the tradition of barely showing the designers and users behind the designs: 25 banners carry their faces and a personal quote on design. He also says the three technical universities' solar-powered racing cars were shown together at Dutch Design Week for the first time. [S3]

The 2015 brochure confirms the order of events. It calls that edition a continuation of what began as an experiment in 2014, a collaboration between several TU/e faculties and Design United. [S5] The photo archive I read holds no album for 2014. [S1] That matters for any caption that says the show started in 2015.
2015 to 2018: Mind the Step in the Klokgebouw

The 2015 edition ran from October 17 to 25 with eight themes: City, Future Mobility, Health, Wearables, Circular Economy, Design Conversations, Home and Material Innovations. [S4] The brochure's welcome is signed by TU/e's vice-president, Jo van Ham, and Design United's science director, Daan van Eijk, and the same two sit on the 2015 steering committee. [S4][S5] Core77's gallery of that week says the design departments of the technical universities in Eindhoven, Delft and Twente teamed up for a group exhibition that took up most of one of the four main exhibition halls at the Klokgebouw. [S31]

The 2016 edition ran from October 22 to 30. Its page quotes the director of Dutch Design Week, Martijn Paulen, calling Mind the Step in just a few years an essential link for the festival, and it lists nine themes, among them Big Data, Design for Debate and Automotive. [S6] The photo archive I read has no album for 2016. [S1]

The 4TU edition list jumps from 2016 to 2018 and has no page for 2017. [S2] A TU Delft research record fills the gap. It calls Mind the Step 2017 the annual exhibition of the 4TU Design United community, shows a project titled Growing Seasons, and gives October 21 to 29, 2017. [S7]

The 2018 page gives October 20 to 28, 2018 and six themes, among them Design for Debate, Health and Wellbeing and The New Mobility. [S8] Innovation Origins visited the hall the day before it opened and reported about 150 students and researchers from Eindhoven, Twente and Delft, with the show open through October 28. It describes a student team's electric car, Vision, meant for the 24 Hours of Le Mans, and conceptual projects such as a Delft machine that matches a family to a migrant, built to start an argument. [S9]
An earlier version of this essay gave the 2018 opening date as October 19. The reporter wrote on the eve of opening and the organizer's page says October 20, so the organizer's date stands. [S8][S9]
2019: one exhibition becomes two, and the dates disagree

TU/e's event page for 2019 says that after five successful years in the Klokgebouw, Mind the Step was merging into two exhibitions, TU/e Drivers of Change and Design United. [S10] Five years fits the counting from 2014 to 2018. [S3][S8][S10] The page places Drivers of Change at Strijp T, building TQ 6, from October 19 to 27, 2019. [S10] A TU/e podcast page describes it as the university's exhibition at Dutch Design Week 2019, with Asselbergs as project leader of both Drivers of Change and Design United. [S11]

The Design United side called its 2019 edition TILT SHIFT, Reframing Futures, with four themes and three named directors. The 4TU page prints October 22 to 30, 2019. [S12] Those dates do not match the festival: BEDA's announcement of September 26, 2019 gives October 19 to 27, 2019, with about 2,600 designers and 120 locations, and TU/e's page agrees. [S10][S13] I treat the 4TU dates as an error on a page that is otherwise reliable. The same page also names a curator and project lead who is not Asselbergs, so the two organizations describe the leadership of the 2019 shows differently. [S11][S12]
2020 and 2021: a talkshow and a campus

In 2020 Design United ran a talkshow format from October 19 to 23 around five themes, among them Hybrids and Crisis. [S14] The edition page for 2021 describes five days at De Effenaar with five themes, from Entangled Ecologies to Evolving Methodologies, and prints the dates as October 18 to 22, 2022. The heading says 2021, and the 2022 edition has different dates and a different venue, so I read the printed year as a slip. [S15][S18]

TU/e, meanwhile, held Drivers of Change on its own campus. Its news item of October 13, 2021 says Dutch Design Week would open officially on the campus that Friday, that the exhibition could be visited from October 15 to 24, and that it presented sixty showcases. [S16] Its calendar entry gives October 16 to 24. [S17] In the same item Asselbergs says that twenty years earlier the university was one of the founding fathers of the festival, then modestly called the Day of Design. [S16] That is TU/e's own account, and I could not confirm it elsewhere. The Design Academy Eindhoven's history says the first Day of Design was organized in 1998 by the Vormgeversoverleg, a designers' collective, that it became a Week of Design in 2002 and took the name Dutch Design Week in 2005. [S32] Neither date matches "twenty years" exactly, and neither source names TU/e among the founders.

The 2021 Flickr album titled TUe, dated October 18, 2021 in its titles, therefore belongs to the campus show. The earlier version of this essay said the 2021 titles named no venue. TU/e's own pages name one. [S1][S16]
2022 to 2024: a square, a lecture hall and a theme

TU/e's own news item for 2022 says Drivers of Change ran from October 22 to 30 at the Ketelhuisplein in Strijp-S, in glass containers, with 23 projects in five themes and a lecture series on campus from October 24 to 28. [S19] The Dutch Design Week archive entry for 2022 names Eindhoven University of Technology as the presenter, and it too says the lectures were on campus. [S20] An earlier note read that presenter line as a location. The exhibition itself stood on the square. [S19][S20]

For 2023 Dutch Design Week's program entry puts Drivers of Change on the Ketelhuisplein, and TU/e's news item gives October 21 to 29 and twenty projects, free to enter. [S21][S22] Design United's 2023 edition ran themes including Politics of Design on Monday, October 23. [S23]

The 2024 record has one more surprise for anyone who works from the photo archive alone, because I found no 2024 album. TU/e's news item says Drivers of Change returned to the Ketelhuisplein from October 19 to 27, 2024, with about fifteen projects linked by the theme Semicon. [S24] The 4TU page says its 2024 expo at the Klokgebouw, with 14 research projects, ran October 19 to 27 and that its dialogues ran October 21 to 25 at the Natlab. [S25]
2025 and 2026: two containers, a joint show and a preview

TU/e's news item of October 13, 2025 describes Future by Design at the Ketelhuisplein, October 18 to 26, 2025: two transparent containers used as mini-labs by the Built Environment and Industrial Design departments. The containers were rented, and the university said it planned its own versions to stand on campus all year and move to Strijp-S for the festival. [S26] The same item says the four universities jointly showed twelve projects at the Klokgebouw under the motto Less Hope, More Action, four of them by TU/e students, and that a festival ticket was needed to enter. [S26][S27]

The photo archive holds four 2025 photos in a Design United album by Boudewijn Bollmann dated October 25, 2025, with banners carrying the same motto. [S1] The containers, the TU/e show of 2025, are not in that album.

For 2026, TU/e's page lists the campus and the Ketelhuisplein, October 17 to 25, 2026. The Ketelhuisplein show is a preview of a larger anniversary exhibition in the Atlas building, where more than 70 projects mark 25 years of Industrial Design in Eindhoven, and the Built Environment department shows three projects on the square. [S28] Dutch Design Week lists TU/e at Ketelhuisplein with free access and daily hours of 11:00 to 18:00. [S33] Design United's 2026 edition is called Design Bridges, runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and its dialogue program begins on Monday, October 19. [S34] Its call for 2026 projects, now closed, asked for work that fits five Dutch Design Week mission days: Living Environment, Thriving Planet, Digital Future, Health and Wellbeing, and Equal Society. [S29]
What was on the floor, as the organizers describe it

The organizers' pages let me list a few exhibits per year, and these are their descriptions, not my findings. In 2014 the exhibition showed an ambulance drone, clothing that holds a music collection and a way to generate wind power around buildings. [S3] In 2015 the City theme included a project called The Twist, and a student project named Trashique presented a museum as a catalog for sustainable reuse. [S4][S5] In 2018 the Innovation Origins reporter found bacteria that produce pigment for coloring textile, a 3D-printed goalkeeper glove and a timber arch held together with about six hundred nuts and bolts, built by a TU/e student who wanted to bend wood without lamination or steaming. [S9]

TU/e's 2019 exhibition featured virtual acoustics, in which visitors hear their own voices in different simulated spaces, a research line on turning plastics into living heart valves, crowd dynamics measured at the train station and a light festival, and photonic chips. [S11] In 2022 the projects included a 3D-printed beetle made of liquid-crystal ink that changes color when it meets moisture, and a spherical test chamber for measuring chip antennas for 6G. The university's Stella Vita solar camper stopped by for the opening. [S19] In 2023 the list included a pavilion built from flax, wood waste and hemp, DNA as a data storage medium, and a hospital robot called CURA. [S22]

In 2024 the headline projects were an EEG-based brain-computer interface, a haptics group and Phoenix, a student-built electric car designed so that up to 75 percent of it can be reused for the next generation, against a closed-loop recycling rate of 21 percent that the page gives for existing cars in Europe. [S24] In 2025 the TU/e containers held a flax-fiber structure tensioned by robotic arms, a study of composting clothing and 3D-printed clay vaults, and the joint Klokgebouw show held a ventilation hose that reacts to touch like a small creature. [S26] In 2026 the university's Built Environment department shows an air-quality project, vibration in timber floors and a nature-inclusive building study at the Ketelhuisplein, and a student team's adaptive building system, MOD[us], is listed at The Body Building in Gashouder 41. [S28]
What the photo archive adds, and what it cannot

The Flickr listing I read holds eight albums and 147 photos for 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2025, with Boudewijn Bollmann credited on most of them. Two albums in 2015 and two in 2019 sit side by side, one for each organization. The album titles name the organization, the year and the photographer, and none names a work. I found no photo-level caption that says which organization a single picture belongs to. [S1]

The written record, taken together, shows the archive missing 2014, 2016, 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2024 under these names, even though the organizers' pages show exhibitions in every one of those years. [S2][S3][S6][S14][S19][S21][S24] The gap reflects what was filed, and I have no source that says why. All Flickr facts in this essay are second-hand from my earlier reading, and I did not reopen the account. [S1]
What the record does not show
Why the archive has no albums for years in which both organizers' pages show exhibitions. [S1][S2]
The founding year of Design United. The pages I opened do not give it, and 2014 is only the start of its collaboration with TU/e at the festival. [S2][S5]
Whether TU/e helped found the Day of Design, as its own account says. [S16][S32]

Which dates are right where the organizers' pages contradict each other: the 4TU pages for 2019 and 2021 carry dates that conflict with other sources, and I settled both from other pages, not from the originals. [S12][S13][S15]
What most of the photographs show. Titles name an organization, a year and a photographer. [S1]
How the 2024 and 2025 TU/e shows appear in the archive. I found no album for either, and I could not reopen the account to look again. [S1][S24][S26]
When you meet a title that names a university or a research center in an archive, which year's organization does it mean, and which page says so? [S2]

title: Designing Society put its own history on a wall, and the record shows how the exhibition was made
subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week exhibitions by the Dutch Design Foundation, read through the organizer's own pages, DDW's archive and the text legible inside the official photographs
description: Two Dutch Design Week editions of Designing Society, a Dutch Design Foundation exhibition, read through DDF pages and photo-archive panels.

sections.x: The clearest sentence about Designing Society in the photo archive is printed on a wall panel, and no photo title says anything like it. [S3]

I like evidence that carries its own label, because a label is the part of an archive I can check. This essay draws on public sources only: Dutch Design Week's press and news archive, pages from the Dutch Design Foundation and its public-sector program PONT, a tourism guide, a 2025 guide on Archipanic and the official photo archive on Flickr, including the text that is legible inside the photographs. It reports no visit and no interview, and for 2026 it repeats only what the organizer's published description says. [S1][S3][S4][S7]
Who makes it: a foundation, not a venue

Designing Society is a Dutch Design Foundation exhibition. The foundation's own pages describe it as a non-profit that runs Dutch Design Week, the Dutch Design Awards and programs that bring designers together with companies, governments and scientists. [S14] The 2024 edition was a consolidation. DDF's program PONT, the Dutch name of which is De Publieke Ontwerppraktijk, described it on September 18, 2024 as an umbrella exhibition of more than 600 square meters with about 40 projects, free to visit at the Ketelhuisplein, and made by four DDF programs: PONT, the World Design Embassies, What if Lab and Maakruimte voor Mooi NL. [S7] DDW's press release of October 29, 2024 says all the World Design Embassies, Labs and PONT joined forces and presented together at Ketelhuisplein in the exhibition Designing Society. [S1] The press release's "Labs" and PONT's "What if Lab" are the same program line in all likelihood, but the two pages do not say so in one sentence, and I treat that as a reading.

The 2024 dates need a note. Dutch Design Week 2024 ran from October 19 to 27, 2024: DDF's calendar entry for the Embassy of Digital Futures at the exhibition gives those dates, and the DDW press release speaks of the 2025 edition running October 18 to 26, 2025. [S6][S1] The 2024 photograph titles carry dates from October 19 to 25, which fits. [S3]
The square it stands on

DDW's own location page calls the Ketelhuisplein one of the festival's largest locations, at approximately 7,000 square meters, an outdoor square on Strijp-S between the Klokgebouw and Microlab Hall, open with free access from 11:00 to 18:00 on each of the nine days in 2026. [S16] A tourism guide published on October 1, 2026 describes the square as a temporary open-air museum for large-scale installations, and lists Designing Society among its recommendations. [S13] The 2026 location page itself lists installations such as Electric Grand, WETHOUSE and the Colonic Cleansing Clinic, and does not list Designing Society by name, so the exhibition's 2026 position on the square is not something I can state. [S16]
The year before: seven Embassies in seven places

The shape of 2024 is clearer against 2023. On October 10, 2023, DDW published a guide to seven themed Embassies of the World Design Embassies program: Circular and Biobased Building, Food, Health, Inclusive Society, Mobility, Safety and Water. Each sat in a different place. The Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building was at Ketelhuisplein, Food in the Evoluon, Health at Foundation We Are, Inclusive Society inside an exhibition at the Van Abbemuseum, Mobility at DONNA, Safety in the Klokgebouw and Water at Stadhuisplein. [S8]

In 2024 those embassies, with the Labs and PONT, came to one square. DDF's calendar entry for the Embassy of Digital Futures says it was part of the exhibition at Ketelhuisplein, and the same entry says the Embassy of Water was part of it too. [S6] I read that as a move from a dispersed program to a single hall, and I mark it as my reading, because no source states the reason. The 2024 PONT page describes the exhibition as built around themes that connect design to the complex challenges of today and tomorrow, and says accessibility features included a physical model at the entrance for visitors with a visual impairment, project signs hung at wheelchair height and free hourly tours. [S7]
The archive: two albums, one photographer

The archive holds one album for each year. The 2024 album has 35 photographs and the 2025 album has 223, 258 in all, and every title I read credits Max Kneefel. [S3] DDF's own pages use the same name in photo credits, including for a 2025 view of the exhibition at the Ketelhuisplein. [S4]

The 2024 photographs show a glass-roofed hall of white rooms, and the text inside them tells me more than the titles do. Flags on the square read Embassy of Safety, De Publieke Ontwerppraktijk and Maakruimte voor Mooi NL. [S3] A wall panel reads Embassy of Inclusive Society and Dutch Design Foundation, with a tall blue school desk behind it holding a clock and a boxing glove. [S3] A plywood board reads, "Good food should be a public service, instead of a commercial product." [S3] Blue signs on the path read Loop nodig risico, Ongemak and Laat je kennen. [S3]

None of that says what each project did or who made it. It says which names stood in one place in October 2024, which fits the description of programs presenting together. [S1][S3][S7] Many 2024 photographs also show visitors, and the carousel leaves those out because they show faces, not projects.

For the Embassy of Inclusive Society, a second document exists. DDF's case page says the embassy was a three-year program from 2023 to 2025 by the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport, the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science and DDF, that The Gym by Gabriel Fontana turned inclusion into something to practice, and that a campaign called Vraagje?! became an interactive installation during DDW24. [S9] That does not identify the blue desk or the boxing glove in the photograph, and I do not say it does.
2025: the same name with a new platform

In March 2025, DDF published a note titled "World Design Embassies and What if Lab continue as Coalitions," dated March 25, 2025. It describes Coalitions as a platform and structural approach for bringing together creative thinkers and doers with science, organizations and governments, built on the earlier programs, with PONT continuing alongside. [S5] The 2025 exhibition therefore ran under a new umbrella.

The 2025 photographs are sharper about projects, because the exhibition printed large panels. One reads Co/Lab: Innovating our defense with society, and a made bed, a helmet and a camouflage backpack stand beside it. [S3] DDF's page for that Co/Lab marks it as completed. It says the Ministry of Defence and DDF selected the design studio Muzus, whose concept Operatie Innovatie invited visitors during Dutch Design Week to contribute ideas to a current challenge of the Ministry. [S10] The page does not mention a bed, helmet or backpack, so the connection between the objects and the page is mine to wonder about and not to state.

Steel letters read The future is fast food above a red menu board headed Geluk, Gemak and Geld, which are Dutch for happiness, ease and money. [S3] A panel reads Sitdown Desk: Pay with time, meet inclusion. [S3] Another is headed Design x Government and carries the PONT name. [S3]

The Archipanic guide of October 19, 2025 quotes DDF's description of Coalitions as a network where designers, governments, experts and challenge holders use the power of design to tackle societal challenges, and gives examples that include design solutions for elderly care professionals and a tattoo shop with an interactive machine. [S2] I read that guide on October 8 and could not reopen it on October 10, because its robots file answered with an access error, so I rely on my earlier reading and treat the quotation as second-hand.
The wall that explains the change

One 2025 panel does something the 2024 material does not. It is titled What history are we making? and the text beside a long timeline of small illustrated ovals describes it as a historical timeline of the former World Design Embassies program, 2017 to 2024, now Coalitions. [S3]

That is the exhibition telling its visitors that the program behind the 2024 flags had changed its name and shape. DDF's March 2025 note says the same thing in prose, so the panel and the foundation agree. [S5] The panel's 2017 start matches the year Baltan Laboratories' annual report gives for the first World Design Event, held October 21 to 29, 2017. [S11] No source I opened says the embassies were created at that event, so I leave the link as a coincidence of dates. The panel is the organizers' account of themselves, and I treat it as their account and not as an independent finding.

One nuance: DDF's case page says the Embassy of Inclusive Society ran through 2025, a year after the panel's end date. [S9] The panel dates the program, and the case page dates one embassy's three-year agreement with two ministries, which is a different unit.
2026: what the organizer says, and what I have not seen

Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I have not seen the exhibition. DDF's news item dated September 29, 2026 describes Designing Society as the foundation bringing designers and researchers together with citizens, public authorities and social organizations on issues that affect everyone, and says visitors may step into an experiment, join a conversation or share a story. It names projects in groups: care for life, with A Healthy Sense of Excitement, The Last Chapter and The First 1000 Days; life in a healthy environment, with Building for Wellbeing, a Building Happiness Score, Declaration of Dependence and Drinkable Nature; and opening up space for change, with a sustainable collective labor agreement experiment, a PONT workshop and the Un/School platform. [S4]

At least one 2026 item, Drinkable Nature, is labeled a Co/Lab, the same word that appears on the 2025 panel. [S4][S10] A tourism guide published on October 1, 2026 describes Designing Society at the Ketelhuisplein as a place to share thoughts on how people want to live, work and care for each other. [S13] A DDF event page lists a Coalition for Safety conference on October 21, 2026 at Microlab, which sits outside the exhibition. [S12] That is all I will say about 2026.
What a title cannot say

A photo title in this archive is a date, a photographer and a camera number. Nothing in it names a project, and I could only match images to projects when a panel or sign in the image did it for me. In anatomy teaching I learned to distrust a specimen without its label, and I read an unlabeled photograph the same way: it shows something real, and I still cannot say whose it is. [S3]
What the record does not show

I viewed 75 of the 223 photographs in the 2025 album, so I cannot describe the other 148. [S3] I found no visitor figure for the exhibition in either year; DDF's Coalitions page cites more than 300,000 visitors for Dutch Design Week as a whole, which is not a count for this exhibition. [S15] I could not reopen the Archipanic guide, so the Coalitions quotation rests on my October 8 reading. [S2]

I do not know how DDF counts the 2024 and 2025 exhibitions together, whether as one series or two, and I do not know why the 2024 exhibition was consolidated. The sources do not say how many of the 2025 projects came from the earlier embassies. [S5][S7]

If I were captioning this archive for a reader, I would write each caption from the panel in the picture, say which year and album it comes from, and leave a project's maker out unless a panel or a program page names one. That makes captions shorter, and a reader can check each one against the photograph in a few seconds. [S3]

If an exhibition prints its own history on a wall, should the archive count that wall as the record, or as one more exhibit? Next time you open a photo set from a show, read the panels in the pictures before you read the captions, and write down which of your sentences each panel supports. [S3]

title: Driving Dutch Design: a business course for young designers, read through five years of photographs
subtitle: The official photo archive files five albums, 2015 to 2019, under a program name. The partners' pages, DDW's archive and the press show when it began, who ran it and what the pictures leave out.
description: Driving Dutch Design, the business course for young designers shown at Dutch Design Week: start year, partners, yearly formats and the 2015 to 2019 albums.

sections.x: The photo archive files five years of Dutch Design Week under the name Driving Dutch Design, and the name sounds like a motor show when it is the title of a business course. [S13]

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds five Driving Dutch Design albums, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019, 89 photographs in all. [S13] The written record is rich enough to say what the program was, when it began, who ran it and how it changed, and it also shows how little of that a stage photograph can carry. This essay draws on public sources only: the program's partners, DDW's own news and magazine archive, a bank's press page, a regional news archive and a design academy's event page. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 edition beyond what DDW lists. [S1][S2]
What the program is

Driving Dutch Design (DDD) is a program for young design studios that want to run a business. ABN AMRO's press page of October 8, 2015 describes it as an initiative of the bank, the Association of Dutch Designers (BNO) and the organizers of Dutch Design Week, in which each designer gets a personal coach and, over ten months, takes part in master classes and co-creation sessions. [S1] DDW's own page for the bank says the program closes at DDW, where participants present designs and business plans to 150 potential customers, and that more than 120 designers had gone through it. [S2] A DDW news item of 2020 lists the content of the monthly master classes: profiling, communication, financing, business operations and presentation. [S6]

The participants are called Drivers. They are not makers in the sense of one studio with one body of work, and that matters for the archive. A DDD album shows a stage, a hall and a crowd, and the studios appear as names on screens. [S13]
When it began

Three start years circulate, and the sources let me resolve them. A DDW page says the bank has supported DDW since 2009 and has been main sponsor since 2011. [S2] That 2011 is the sponsorship, not the program. Innovation Origins, in a five-year look back published on May 24, 2017, says the program was created in 2012, and ABN AMRO's October 2015 page calls that year's group the third since the launch in 2012. [S3][S1] Counting the group of 2015 as the third puts the first class in 2013, and DDW's later edition numbers agree: the class of 2019 is the seventh edition, the class of 2020 the eighth and the class of 2022 the tenth. [S10][S6][S8] The same October 2015 page says alumni of the 2013 and 2014 editions returned to DDW that year. [S1]

So the program was conceived and launched in 2012, and its first class of Drivers was the class of 2013. That reading uses the edition numbers from three different sources and contradicts none of them. [S1][S3][S8]
Why a bank and a trade body

The 2017 look back is the best source on motive, because it quotes the three organizers. Ilona Roolvink of ABN AMRO says entrepreneurship is in the bank's DNA and that young designers make beautiful products but struggle to market them. Martijn Paulen, director of the Dutch Design Foundation, says the three parties saw designers asking for support in professionalizing. Marsha Simon of BNO says the trade body has a large network of designers and of trainers and knowledge partners. [S3] Roolvink also says the ultimate aim is for the program to become unnecessary, because academies would teach enough business. [S3] Those are the organizers' own statements, made on the program's fifth anniversary.

The same piece says the program had 15 to 20 designers a year in an eleven-month workshop track, which differs from the ten months the bank's page uses. [S3][S1] I give each with its source and its date, because the program changed shape from year to year.
2015: a pitch event and a hall in the Klokgebouw

The 2015 album, titled Drivers 2015, has 34 photographs by Jeroen van der Wielen. [S13] The bank's page explains what that year consisted of. Participants showed their results in an exhibition called Momentum, a collaboration of young entrepreneurs, in Hall C of the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, October 17 to 25, 2015, 11:00 to 18:00, and pitched to potential customers at the business event Drivers 2015 on October 20. [S1] It lists fourteen Drivers: Alei Verspoor, Echter Ontwerp, Hats & Tales, Liat Azulay of Nudnik, Mark Vankan of Anidesign, Mianne de Vries, Pim Schachtschabel, Renate Nederpel, Rick Tegelaar, Studio Kars & Boom, Studio TOIMII, Thier&vanDaalen, Thomas Overweg of Glowbots and Tim van de Weerd. [S1] Screens in the album carry the names Glowbots and Studio Mianne de Vries and the words Welcome to the ABN AMRO House. [S13] I cannot tell from the album whether its stage photographs are of the Drivers 2015 pitch or of another session in the same hall.
2016: signs on a dark stage

The 2016 album has 32 photographs, again by Jeroen van der Wielen, of a lit stage whose walls carry phrases such as THE MAKING OF, PERSISTENCE IS FRUITFUL, FOLLOW YOUR GUT and LOVE YOUR EXPERIMENTS. [S13] I found no written source for DDD in 2016: no press page, no participant list, no venue. The 2016 album is therefore all picture and no text, and I leave it at what the signs say.
2017: five years, shown in a loft

In 2017 the album is titled 5 Years Driving Dutch Design, has 4 photographs by Max Kneefel, and its titles name VEEM. [S13] The Royal Academy of Art in The Hague lists, in its page on alumni at DDW 2017 (October 21 to 29), an exhibition called 5 years Driving Dutch Design & Hotspots, curated by Van Eijk & Van der Lubbe, at the Veem building, and lists works by its alumni in the Hotspots retrospective shown there. [S11] The same page lists a second DDD show, Dating Dutch Design, with 21 selected designers, in the Klokgebouw. [S11] The album's titles name VEEM, which fits the Veem exhibition, and nothing in the album points to the Klokgebouw show with the 21 designers. [S11][S13]
Innovation Origins' five-year look back appeared in the same year, on May 24, 2017, five months before the festival. [S3]
2018: a class in the Klokgebouw

The 2018 album has 14 photographs by Jeroen van der Wielen of a dark hall with white cloth walls. A wall text asks What's in it for you? The added value of design, and carries the logos of ABN AMRO, BNO and the Dutch Design Foundation, which is the clearest statement of who ran the program in the archive. [S13] DDW's magazine profile of a Rotterdam trio, the studio Staalslagerij, says they presented with the rest of the DDD class of 2018 in the Klokgebouw during DDW, October 20 to 28, 2018. [S5] The profile adds what the program gave them. A masterclass in storytelling by Paul Hughes taught them to talk about what a project does and not only what it is, and their personal coach pushed them to track which requests turn into paid commissions and why. [S5] That is one studio's account in a partner-run magazine, and it is the kind of outcome the organizers claim.
2019: the Driver, in a circular pavilion

The 2019 album has 5 photographs. Three are credited in their titles to Cleo Goossens and two carry no photographer. [S13] DDW's magazine report on the seventh edition says it was held in Circl-E, the circular pavilion in the Klokgebouw designed by Overtreders W, that twenty designers were supervised over a year by coaches, and that the pitch, moderated by BNO's Marsha Simon, grouped presentations into nine "driving styles" from the Experiencer and the Conscious Driver to the Storyteller and the Futuristic Driver. [S8] It names pitch speakers Onno Adriaanse, Julie Thissen, Mirl van Hoek, Billie van Katwijk, Katinka Versendaal of The Eatelier and Sander Lorier. [S8] A DDW guide of October 21, 2019 lists Driving Dutch Design in Hall 2, Connecting Collaborations, with the Embassy of Health and the Renault concept cars, around ABN AMRO's Circl-E. [S9]

The class of 2019 also published a book, The Driver: Driving Dutch Design, in which the designers introduce themselves, show their studios, and in a chapter called Failing Forward describe their biggest setbacks. DDW reported it in 2020. [S7] A sign in the 2019 album reads THE DRIVER, which is the book's title. [S7][S13]
After the archive stops

The archive has no album after 2019, but the program kept going and DDW's own pages show it. The 2020 class, the eighth, had 26 designers including four duos, took monthly master classes and worked in a Bureau DDD toward an exhibition, a Drivers Pitch Event and a publication. [S6] The 2021 class had 23 designers, started online for the first time, and showed in an exhibition titled I hear what you're seeing, with 17 studios at the Pullman hotel. [S12][S4] In 2022, the tenth anniversary by DDW's count, there was no large joint exhibition: each Driver presented in a way that suited the studio, with DDF support, 21 ABN AMRO coaches, BNO masterclasses and a new alumni club called Club DDD. [S10] In 2024 DDW's program page for Driven by Purpose says 20 studios exhibited together and names BNO, the Dutch Design Foundation and the Stokroos Foundation as the organizers. [S14] That page does not name ABN AMRO. I do not know whether the bank left the program or simply is not named on that page, so I do not claim either.

The change from a joint hall to individual presentations in 2022 and back to a joint exhibition in 2024 is the part the archive misses most. A reader of the 2015 to 2019 albums would conclude the program is a stage in a hall, and the written record says that was one format among several. [S10][S14][S13]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**The start year.** 2011, 2012 and 2013 all circulate. 2011 is the bank's main-sponsor year, 2012 is the launch the organizers give, and 2013 is the first class by the edition numbers. [S2][S3][S1][S10] I use 2012 for launch and 2013 for the first class.

**How many designers and how many months.** Fifteen to twenty and eleven months in 2017, about twenty and ten months in other years, 14 in 2015, 26 in 2020, 23 in 2021. These are consistent across years and I report each with its year. [S3][S2][S1][S6][S12]

**Who ran it.** The 2015 to 2021 pages name ABN AMRO, BNO and the Dutch Design Foundation. The 2024 page names BNO, the foundation and the Stokroos Foundation. Both are true for their year. [S1][S12][S14]
What the record does not show

I do not know what the 2016 sessions consisted of, who the 2016 and 2017 Drivers were, or which album photographs belong to which session within a year. I did not read the program's own website, which answered with an error, and the Dutch Design Daily pages on the 2023 ten-year stage and the 2024 exhibition showed a bot-verification page, so I stopped requests to that site and did not use them. I found no DDW source for 2025. I have no source for the class of 2026. [S13]
If a program says its goal is to become unnecessary, what would you look for in its photographs to tell whether it was getting there? [S3]
