title: Dutch Invertuals at Dutch Design Week: a collective that became a studio, one theme at a time
subtitle: From a Milan group show in 2009 to a listed DDW 2026 location on Fuutlaan. The studio's own pages, a 2018 business plan, trade press and DDW's archive, set against nine years of photo albums.
description: How Dutch Invertuals grew from a 2009 Milan group show into a studio, foundation and academy, and what the DDW photo albums show of its yearly themes.

sections.x: A name that stays the same for sixteen years can hide almost everything that changed behind it, and Dutch Invertuals is a good test of that, because its own pages describe a group show in Milan, a curator's side project, a registered company and a studio, foundation and academy, all under one name. [S1][S2][S4]

As a content strategist I look at how a name is used before I look at what it points to. This essay asks what Dutch Invertuals has been at each Dutch Design Week (DDW) it can be traced to, using the studio's own project pages, a business plan it wrote in 2018, trade press and DDW's program archive, and then asks what the official DDW photo albums can show of that history. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 program beyond what DDW's listing says. [S1][S3][S31]
The start: a hall in Milan, not a design studio

The studio's own history says that in 2009 its founder, Wendy Plomp, was invited to show a group of Dutch designers at the Salone del Mobile in Milan, and that this inaugural exhibition is where the collective began. [S2] The 2018 business plan gives more detail: she was invited to exhibit in the Brera design district, the space was too large for her alone, and she asked other designers to present with her. It names Daphna Laurens, Edhv, Bart Hess, House of Origin, Lotty Lindeman, Pepe Heykoop and Raw Color among the first group. [S3] Plomp told a city-marketing video in 2017 that founding it was almost an accident, that the success in Milan made a second show in Eindhoven during the next DDW obvious, and that from then on she organized and curated two exhibitions a year, one in Milan and one in Eindhoven. [S4] [S2][S3][S4]

The name has an explanation in the plan: Dutch refers to its roots in the Netherlands, and Invertuals is derived from inversion, a process of opposition and reversal, seeing the world upside down from radical new perspectives. [S3] Interior Design gave a similar account in 2018, saying the name derives from inverse. [S6] IO+ wrote in 2016 that Plomp had been the biggest motivation behind the group since the beginning of 2009, that she started as a fellow designer, that she took on a larger role as organizer and curator from 2010, and that it became her full-time job in 2015. [S5] [S3][S6][S5]
Before the photo archive begins

The official DDW albums for the group start in 2015, but the studio's pages list earlier DDW shows. Matter of Time, shown during DDW 2010, used 600-year-old oak wood excavated in 2007 at the Woenselse Poort in Eindhoven as its material. [S24] Conflict was the group's exhibition for DDW 2012. [S25] Cohesion, with 12 designers, was shown in 2014. [S26] Transform, from 2013, carries the location line Milan, so it is a Salone show and not a DDW one. [S27] I found no studio page that names a DDW show for 2011 or 2013. That does not mean there was none, only that I did not find it. [S24][S25][S26][S27]
From collective to company

The business side arrives gradually. IO+ reported in October 2016 that Plomp had made the collective her full-time job the year before, and that the group worked from the edhv design agency on the Fuutlaan, which served as headquarters and as the venue of the annual DDW exhibition. Every two weeks the 13 members of that year's show met there, and for nine days the edhv workspaces were cleared for the exhibition. [S5] In October 2017, Plomp said in the same city video that Dutch Invertuals had been registered as a company with the Chamber of Commerce two years earlier. [S4] I did not look at a register, so the year rests on her statement as the video reports it. [S5][S4]

The March 2018 business plan is the clearest document of what the group thought it was. It counts 18 exhibitions developed so far, with more than 100 new works, mostly made for the Salone and DDW and increasingly moved on to other places such as D'Days in Paris, Kazerne in Eindhoven and the London Design Fair. It counts more than 60 talents scouted and guided. It also says that, although the format was a proven success, the current activities were not yet viable as a business, which is why the plan sets out services under three headings, observe, manifest and create. [S3] Today the About page describes a studio that does spatial and strategic design projects for clients, a foundation that initiates annual research projects, and an academy, an online program for young professionals. [S1] [S3][S1]
2015: No Static, and who made the room

The 2015 DDW exhibition was No Static, curated by Plomp, with exhibition design by Edhv. The studio's page names 11 participants: Aliki van der Kruijs, Alissa + Nienke, Arnout Meijer, Edhv, Jelle Mastenbroek, Jólan van der Wiel, Kirstie van Noort, Martina Lasinger, Noman, Odd Matter and Tijmen Smeulders. [S9] It describes the show as an inquiry into movement, identity and digital life. [S9] TL Magazine reported on it on November 11, 2015 and singled out NOMAN's sliding-door piece Welcome, Arnout Meijer's Feet of Twilight and Martina Lasinger's The Theory of Everything. [S7] [S9][S7]

The DDW album for the year holds 29 photos, 21 of them credited by title to Boudewijn Bollmann and three to Ronald Smits. [S34] The studio's page and TL Magazine both credit Smits for the exhibition photography, and the DDW album title carries the name of the show, which makes this the clearest album in the set. [S9][S7][S34] [S9][S7][S34]
2016: Powerplay on the Fuutlaan

Powerplay, in 2016, looked at a society in which renewable energy has become abundant. The studio's page names thirteen designers and credits exhibition design to Remco van de Craats, Daniel de Bruin, Tijs Gilde and Carlo Lorenzetti, with Plomp as curator. [S10] IO+ reported that the theme was energy overload, that the title was Powerplay and that some of the works would be developed further for Milan, which fits the group's twice-yearly rhythm. [S5] The same report places the DDW exhibition at the edhv headquarters on the Fuutlaan. [S5] [S10][S5]

There are two 2016 albums, both by Nick Bookelaar: Dutch Invertuals with 13 photos and Dutch Invertuals @ Veem with 9. [S34] The first is most likely the Fuutlaan exhibition, because IO+ places it there, though no title says so. The second I cannot explain from 2016 sources. I found none that puts the group at VEEM that year, although DDW's 2019 magazine says that in 2019 the group held the art direction of VEEM, a Strijp-S warehouse used as a parking garage the rest of the year. [S5][S34][S37] [S5][S34][S37]
2017: two shows in one October

In 2017 the group made two exhibitions. Enlighten, made with the window-covering brand Luxaflex, presented six designers experimenting with light and Luxaflex materials. The studio's page names works by Studio Mieke Meijer, by Jetske Visser and Michiel Martens and by Daniel De Bruin, with an exhibition setting by Tijmen Smeulders. [S11] TL Magazine's DDW report, written when the festival was in its 16th edition, picked out Thomas Ballouhey's piece. [S8] That count of editions matches a first edition in 2002. [S8] [S11][S8]

Fundamentals, the second show, was made with the Eindhoven studio Raw Color. The studio's page says 45 Invertuals unearthed more than 800 objects from their studio archives, sorted into nine typologies, from The Workers and The Purists to The Brutalists. Each designer also made a container as a shared archetype. [S12] Plomp told the city video that the participants showed objects normally hidden in their archives, with Raw Color as guest curator. [S4] Interior Design reported that Daphna Laurens designed the exhibition, arranging the objects on a wooden ring 50 feet in diameter, and that Plomp had produced 18 shows in nine years. [S6] Dezeen reported the show on October 27, 2017, a date I carry over from an earlier read because the site now blocks automated requests. [S35] [S12][S4][S6][S35]

The 2017 album holds 19 photos by Boudewijn Bollmann, eight titled enlighten and eleven titled fundamentals, so this is the one year in which the photo titles themselves separate the two shows. [S34] [S34]
2018: Take Away, and a Milan show that shares an album

Take Away asked how design can help to live with less. The studio's page lists ten participants or pairs, describes a circular arrangement with mirrored plinths as part of the exhibition design, and credits photography to Ronald Smits. [S13] Its thanks list names Cultuur Eindhoven, Leeuwerik Plaatmateriaal, Mansveld expotech and Pyrasied. Two image captions on the page read Baars & Bloemhoff and Bone Interieurwerken, and the page does not say what part either company played. [S13] Dezeen reported the show on October 30, 2018, again a date carried over. [S35] [S13][S35]

The 2018 albums hold 12 photos for Take Away by Boudewijn Bollmann, and 8 by Max Kneefel in an album titled Mutant Matter whose photo titles say VEEM. [S34] The studio's page for Mutant Matter, made with the research agency FranklinTill and ten designers, carries the location line Milan. [S14] So the album and the page disagree, or the show traveled; no source says which. A third reading is that the VEEM titles reflect the group's role in organizing that building, as DDW's magazine describes for 2019, and not the show named in the album. [S37] I keep the album and the Milan show apart. [S34][S14][S37]
2019: The Circle, ten years in

The Circle marked ten years. The studio's page says the show was first exhibited in Milan during the Salone del Mobile in 2019 and then in Eindhoven during DDW, that it led to a book and a traveling exhibition series, and that it showed the work of over 40 designers who had played a significant role in the group's beginnings. [S15] The studio's history page recalls it as the celebration of ten years. [S2] Dezeen's report, carried over from the October 7 read, counted more than 20 designers and studios, so the two numbers differ. They may count different editions of the show; no source I opened says. [S35][S15] That same year DDW's magazine says the group's tenth anniversary coincided with its art direction of VEEM, which it transformed into an industrial exhibition space. [S37] [S15][S2][S35][S37]
2020 to 2023: a pause in the gallery, an academy in its place

There is no album for 2020, and the studio's pages name no 2020 exhibition. They do show what it did instead. The Dutch Invertuals Academy was launched in 2020, during the first wave of COVID-19, to keep the group connected to the global design community. [S22] Its first intensive six-week program that year drew 22 designers from around the world. [S23] [S22][S23]

In 2021 the group returned to the gallery with Objects for a New Kind of Society, made with the futures consultancy The Future Laboratory. The studio's page lists eleven participants, Daphna Laurens as exhibition designer, and support from Cultuur Eindhoven, the Dutch Design Foundation and Stichting Stokroo. [S16] AnInteriorMag named it, in its report on DDW 2021, as perhaps the best in show, and said it was developed on the heels of the pandemic-born Academy. [S33] In 2022 came Expedition Æqualis, with The Future Laboratory and Reon Brand of Philips. The page says the show exhibited during DDW 2022 featured eleven designers and used circular pedestals on a sand-covered floor of locally sourced sand, which visitors raked with special tools. [S17] DDW's archive lists an Expedition Æqualis party on October 28 at Fuutlaan 12B. [S29] [S16][S33][S17][S29]

That description lets me connect the 2022 album to the show with more confidence than before. The album's 21 photos, taken October 25, 2022 by Britt Roelse, show raked-sand islands with sculptures, according to the October 7 read. [S34] The studio's description of a sand floor with works on circular pedestals matches that. I count it as a strong match, not a captioned one, since no photo title names the show. [S17][S34] [S17][S34]

In 2023 the group showed Flow with Béla Bezold, Ralf Gloudemans, Teresa Fernández-Pello and Edhv, an installation about a stream of water droplets that the studio says draws visitors away from their daily data flow. [S18] The 2023 album has four photos by Almicheal Fraay of a long line of red and yellow elements on thin metal stands. [S34] I cannot tell from the studio's text whether those four photographs show Flow, so I leave them without a show name. [S18][S34]
2024 and 2025: an anniversary chair and a New York exchange

Specimen, in 2024, marked the 15th anniversary. DDW's listing and the studio's page say 15 designers were each asked to redesign a chair that the studio had made for the 5TRACKS offices, and that the group has worked with over 90 designers. [S28][S19] Daphna Laurens, who took part in the 2009 Milan group, contributed the Di Mama Armchair. [S19][S3] The same year, Circles of Universal Language, commissioned by the municipality of Eindhoven, showed ten designers' proposals for objects in public space at Ketelhuisplein during DDW. The page adds that Queen Máxima visited it. [S20] [S28][S19][S3][S20]

There is no 2024 album titled Dutch Invertuals. The 2024 Fuutlaan album has five photos, and one by Nick Bookelaar, dated October 27, 2024, shows many chairs; its title does not name Specimen. [S34] The chair description fits, and I flag it as an inference. In 2025, DDW lists Objects of Exchange at Dutch Invertuals, Fuutlaan 12B, October 18 to 26, free with a DDW ticket or for 5 euros. [S30] The studio's page describes six designers, three Dutch and three American, each given a pure metal to work with. DDW's listing places the project within Future 400, which it calls a long-term initiative strengthening Dutch-American partnerships. [S21][S36] I found no album for 2025. [S34][S30][S21][S36]
2026: a listed location again

DDW lists the Dutch Invertuals Studio at Fuutlaan 12B, in the Station area, October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00 daily, free with a DDW ticket or for 5 euros. DDW's location page says it is not wheelchair accessible. [S31] A neighboring DDW location, the Design Perron at Fuutlaan 12, lists exhibits from Dutch Invertuals among others. [S32] The sources do not say what the 2026 show is. [S31][S32]
Why the studio's own dates need care

The studio's project pages are the richest list of what it showed, and they carry post dates that cannot all be show dates. The early pages read as contemporary: Matter of Time October 7, 2010, Conflict October 12, 2012, Cohesion October 12, 2014, Powerplay October 28, 2016. [S24][S25][S26][S10] But Enlightened, Fundamentals, Take Away and Mutant Matter all carry October 9, 2023, although the first of them says it was made for DDW 2017, and Circles of Universal Language carries July 25, 2026 for a DDW 2024 show. [S11][S12][S13][S14][S20] My reading is that the later pages were re-published in a site rebuild, and no source says so. I used the pages for what was shown and the press and DDW for when. [S24][S25][S26][S10][S11][S12][S13][S14][S20]
What the record does not show

I do not know why the 2016 VEEM album exists, whether the 2018 Mutant Matter photographs show a DDW presentation, what the 2023 photographs show, or why there is no album for 2020, 2024 or 2025. [S34][S14] I do not know which DDW shows the group made in 2011 and 2013. [S24][S27] I did not see a company register, and I could not reopen the Dezeen reports. [S4][S35] [S34][S14][S24][S27][S4][S35]
When you meet a name that has lasted sixteen years, which line on the page tells you what it was in each of those years: the name, the date or the people credited beside it? [S1][S34]

title: ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week: a program page that names the show, and a Worklife album that no page explains
subtitle: Two editions in the TQ building at Strijp-T. DDW's program archive, a trade-press post and two reports on the building say more than the photo titles do, and still not who made the rooms.
description: ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week 2018 and 2019 in the TQ building at Strijp-T: what DDW's program page, a trade-press post and the photo archive show.

sections.x: Dutch Design Week's recap of October 25, 2019 names ELLE Decoration only as a link, and the page behind the link says more about the exhibition than any caption in the photo archive does. [S1][S2]

That detail matters because this is a thin record, and in a thin record every page counts twice. This essay draws on public sources only: two pages from Dutch Design Week's own site, a trade-press article from November 2018, two reports about the building and the official photo archive on Flickr as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about a 2026 ELLE Decoration show, because I found no page for one. [S1][S2][S3][S10]
The honest length of this essay is short. The sources about ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week run out after a handful of pages, and I have not padded them. [S1][S2][S3]
What the recap says, and what its link says

The recap is a short magazine item of October 25, 2019 in DDW's daily area tour. For Strijp-T and Strijp-R it says that Strijp-T is a popular place among high-tech makers, points visitors to the Innovation Powerhouse, the former Philips power plant, and says the TQ building behind it is also worth a visit, where "you will find the exhibition of ELLE Decoration and the research projects of TUe: Drivers of Change." [S1] The words ELLE Decoration are a link, and the link goes to a page in DDW's program archive titled "ELLE Decoration presents... Fluid Forces." [S1][S2]

That program page is the primary source for the 2019 show. It is marked as part of DDW 2019, presented by ELLE Decoration, in the category exhibitions, and carries the line "Concentrate - Cocreate - Celebrate." [S2] It describes an immersive exhibit "from the world's leading interior magazine in collaboration with Tarkett," and says that, picking up from the previous year's exhibit and building on what was learned since, ELLE Decoration would work from the principle of zoning in the workspace. [S2] The text breaks off mid-word in the archive page, in a sentence about trends, so I do not have the rest of the description. [S2] The image on the page is credited as styling by F. Hofhuis and art direction by D. Westland, with a copyright line for Visual Citizens and Carlfried Verwaayen. [S2] That credit belongs to the promotional image, and the page does not say those people made the exhibit.

An earlier reading of mine, through a summarizing reader, said the recap itself names "ELLE Decoration Presents Fluid Forces." The recap prints only ELLE Decoration, and the title comes from the program page it links to. The difference is small and it changes where the title should be credited. [S1][S2]
What the 2019 page implies about 2018

The program page says the 2019 exhibit picks up from last year's. [S2] That sentence ties the two editions together on DDW's own authority, and it gives the 2018 show a theme. A show that is followed by one about zoning in the workspace was probably also about the workspace, and the 2018 album is titled "ELLE Decoration: Worklife." [S2][S10] I read the two as one thread, and I label that as my inference, because the page does not call the 2018 show Worklife and no page I opened explains the album's title. [S2][S10]

For 2018 itself the written source is thin. Italian Bark, a design blog, wrote on November 13, 2018 that among the exhibits at Strijp-T the author found the setting by Elle Decor NL most interesting, which took the very top of the Strijp-T building and recreated an apartment furnished with design pieces in a white and blue palette. [S3] The same post names a second exhibit nearby, "Body of Work" by OS ∆ OOS, a minimalist setting with a series called Repeated Mirrors made of layers of colored glass. [S3] The blog also writes the exhibitor's name as Elle Decor NL, where DDW writes ELLE Decoration. [S3][S2] I use the album's name, ELLE Decoration, and note that the blog's form is not necessarily a different organization. DDW's 2018 edition ran from October 20 to 28 and the 2019 edition from October 19 to 27. [S8][S9]
The building

The photo titles for both years say TQ, and DDW's 2019 recap places the exhibition in the TQ building. [S10][S1] IO+ wrote in September 2015 that TQ was put up in the 1950s to keep pace with Philips' growth, that companies such as FEI, ASML and the European branch of Fluke trace their origins there, and that it held a Philips nuclear-war bunker from which the company would have been run and rebuilt. [S5] A subsidy consultancy's reference page says TQ has more than 40,000 square meters of floor area, the largest building on Strijp-T, and that it was fully renovated into a shared building for companies with sustainability measures such as insulation and solar panels. [S6] The two pages describe the same place at different moments: the 2015 article says its owner was a bankrupt company and that the bank which financed it had put it up for sale, and the later reference page describes it as renovated. [S5][S6]

That is useful context for the photographs. The 2019 album, by the old dossier's description, shows raw concrete walls, and the 2018 album shows a window over the city. [S10] Neither page tells me which part of TQ the show used, and the Italian Bark post says "the very top" in 2018 only. [S3] I do not claim the 2018 and 2019 sets stood in the same rooms.

The other tenant of the building named in the recap is the Eindhoven University of Technology, whose exhibition Drivers of Change, according to its program page, showed more than 70 exhibits from departments, student teams and start-ups at Strijp-T, from very concrete to fairly speculative. [S4][S1] An interiors magazine and a technical university were in one building in the same week, and DDW's recap puts them in a single sentence. [S1][S4] I find that pairing more interesting than either exhibit's description, though no source says the two were planned together.

IO+ ran a photo gallery on October 23, 2019 whose caption lists Elle, Fontys and the Embassy of Sustainable Design as the Strijp-T, TQ and Innovation Powerhouse exhibitors, and the page has no text beyond the caption. [S7] It confirms the company in one more place and adds no detail about the show. [S7]
What the albums add

The old dossier counts two albums, 9 photographs for 2018 and 14 for 2019, 23 in all, credited in the titles to Britt Roelse (20) and Max Kneefel (3), with the three Kneefel titles beginning 20191025. [S10] I did not reopen Flickr for this version. The 2018 album shows a living room in white and blue with navy poufs, a swirled blue rug with mirrored panels and a gray wall with a yellow hexagon sign that reads qbe next to the ELLE DECORATION logo, and the 2019 album shows concrete walls, curved cream furniture, a gold arch lamp, a dark red room and a mirrored sculpture. [S10] No title names a designer or a piece, and neither DDW page I opened names one. [S10][S2]

The program page names Tarkett as the collaborator on the 2019 exhibit and does not say what Tarkett supplied. [S2] I could not open Tarkett's own site, which refused my first request (robots.txt, HTTP 403), so I say nothing about the company. The yellow qbe sign in a 2018 photograph could belong to a sponsor, but no page I opened says what qbe refers to, and I make no guess. [S2][S10]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**Who named the show.** The old draft credited the recap with the title. The recap links to the program page, and the program page carries the title. The program page settles it. [S1][S2]
**What the exhibitor is called.** Italian Bark says Elle Decor NL, the photo titles and DDW say ELLE Decoration. Nothing I opened separates them, and I use ELLE Decoration. [S3][S2][S10]

**Which building.** Italian Bark calls Strijp-T an area with the former Philips headquarters building. IO+ and the renovation reference describe TQ as a company building from the 1950s with a bunker, and neither calls it a headquarters, so I do not repeat the headquarters label. [S3][S5][S6]
**What Worklife refers to.** Not settled. The 2019 page suggests a workspace thread. The album title is the only source for the word. [S2][S10]
What the record does not show

I do not know who designed or styled either show, which pieces were on display, or what Tarkett supplied. The program page for 2019 breaks off in the middle of its description, so I cannot say what trends it names. I found no DDW program page for the 2018 show and no page from the magazine itself, and I did not find the magazine's own account of either year. [S2][S3] I did not search for earlier or later ELLE Decoration appearances at Dutch Design Week, and my searches turned up none for 2017 or after 2019.

I do not know what the two shows cost to build or how many people saw them. [S1] I did not reopen the photo archive, so the album counts, titles and photographers come from the October 8, 2026 reading. [S10] Nothing here describes an ELLE Decoration show at Dutch Design Week 2026, which runs October 17 to 25, 2026.
If a magazine builds a room for a week and the label by the door gives only the magazine's name, who should the room be credited to? [S2]

title: Envisions at Dutch Design Week: a collective built to show everything but the end product
subtitle: From Products in Process in 2016 to a studio opening in 2026, what the organization says, what the press says and what a photo archive can hold.
description: Envisions at Dutch Design Week, 2016 to 2026: Products in Process, a wood book, a retrospective and a new studio, read against what a photo archive holds.

sections.x: Envisions says it began when its founders left the Milan design fair uninspired by finished products, and the sources show it taking that idea to Dutch Design Week from 2016 on. [S1][S7]

I like a case where the subject's own idea runs against the format that records it. Envisions sets out to show the process and not the product, and a photo archive freezes whatever happens to be on the table the day the photographer comes. This essay uses public sources only: Envisions' own site, design and trade press, a designer's studio page, a university excursion page, Dutch Design Week's own listings and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the published listing says. [S1][S7][S17][S21]
How Envisions tells its own beginning

Envisions' About page says it began in 2016 in Eindhoven, founded by Sanne Schuurman, Simone Post and Iwan Pol, all graduates of Design Academy Eindhoven. After attending Europe's largest design fair in Milan, the page says, they felt uninspired by the focus on finished products and the lack of diversity in design approaches, and the collective grew out of that: a group dedicated to celebrating the design process itself. [S1] The page puts the aim this way: show everything but the final product, by working with designers known for experimental and colorful approaches. [S1]

Its present description is a multidisciplinary design agency that reimagines materials, with three services, Material, Content and Space. [S1][S2] The About page lists five people under Team, with Schuurman as founder and creative director, and a longer list of what it calls envisionaires, which includes Post and Pol. [S1] The headcount has moved with the years and with the definition. It's Nice That pictured eight designers in 2016, the New Material Award described more than 20 designers in 2018, and the site today separates a small team from a wide circle of collaborators. [S1][S7][S11] I read those as three different counts of three different things, not as a contradiction.
That is the organization's account. [S1] A claim that a show is about process rather than product is a statement of intent, and what the archive can add is limited to what was photographed.
2016: Products in Process, in two parts

It's Nice That reported on August 24, 2016 that Envisions, a collective of Design Academy Eindhoven graduates, aimed to "showcase everything but the end product." The show, called Products in Process and also Envisions, had already been shown in New York and Milan and would join Dutch Design Week from October 22 to 30. [S7] Helsinki Design Week, writing in November 2016, calls the Dutch Design Week show Part 2 and says Part 1 was at the Milan design festival in April. [S8]

The magazine names two pieces. Transsaddles by Adrianus Kundert looks at age in design, and Happy Concrete by Iwan Pol asks why the most widely used man-made material so often looks uninspired. [S7] The Dutch Design Week photo archive holds a 2016 album of 23 photographs titled Envisions-DDW16, with the photographer Ronald Smits named in every title. [S21]

Two details about that credit matter. Smits appears on Envisions' own contributor list under photography, and WOTH credits him with the photographs in the 2017 Wood in Process book. [S1][S9] So the archive's 2016 and 2018 albums are credited to a photographer who also works with the subject. I cannot tell from the pages whether he shot those albums for Dutch Design Week or for Envisions, and the answer matters for how the pictures can be reused. [S1][S9][S21]

Where Part 2 stood in 2016 is not in the sources I could open. A page in a collaborator's portfolio and a magazine's venue listing might say, but the first returned a not-found error and the second blocked automated access, so I leave the place open. Envisions' archive also lists an installation called RGB Funfair for the Van Abbemuseum in 2016, with four envisionaires named, but the case page body is placeholder text and I cannot tell whether it belongs to Dutch Design Week. [S3][S5]
2017: a book, a hall and a mistaken launch

WOTH says Envisions launched the book Wood in Process, made with the Spanish wood manufacturer Finsa, during Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, and a photo caption says the book launch was at VDMA during DDW 2017. [S9] The same page says the research collected in the book had been on show at Dutch Design Week 2017, Salone del Mobile 2017, WantedDesign in New York in 2017 and the London Design Fair in 2017. [S9] The photographer is Smits, and the book was designed by Studio Aandacht. [S9]

An earlier version of this essay, and the carousel built from it, said Wood in Process itself launched at VDMA. The page supports less than that: the book launched at VDMA, and the research traveled. [S9] The 2017 album, titled Envisions_VDMA_2017, shows a large hall with many displays, some of which carry other names, so I cannot separate Envisions' objects from the rest by title. [S21] The VDMA was still a Dutch Design Week location four years later: Salone del Mobile.Milano's 2021 report says it was transformed that year into a forest in its courtyard. [S13]

Envisions' home page describes Wood in Process as a laboratory exercise: it set out to find new uses for the full range of Finsa's materials, which it lists as chipboard, medium density fibreboard and high pressure laminates. [S2]
2018: the second chapter, in an ice factory

Studio Simone Post, a founder's own studio, published a post on October 25, 2018 describing Wood in progress as the second chapter of the Finsa collaboration. It says six of the earlier researches were industrially tweaked in Finsa's factories in Spain, shown from October 20 to 28, 2018 at Campinaterrein De IJsfabriek on the Kanaaldijk Zuid, and that the display aimed to shift the viewer's perspective constantly. [S10] The New Material Award, which also listed Wood in Progress for 2018, says six results of the collaboration were developed further in Finsa's factories, and that many of the designs use waste wood that is dyed or pulverized and glued or pressed into new boards. [S11] The studio post adds that Wood in Progress was a nominee for the New Material Award 2018, with the nominees shown at the Veem building. [S10]

Envisions' own press release shows that Eindhoven was the second stop. Wood in progress opened in Milan first, at Officine Savona in Zona Tortona, April 17 to 22, 2018, with a press preview on April 16. [S22] The release names six designers and six works: Aukje Fleur Janssen's Wrapping wood, in which patterned paper is laminated into board under a factory heat press; Elvis Wesley's Undertone, which turns wax finishes on black board into a decorative range of blacks and greys; Strips and stripes by Roos Gomperts and Wesley, which shows the strips that make up veneer; Sanne Schuurman's Open board, a play of repetition and structure that exposes the layers of the board; Simone Post's Wannabe wood, which uses CNC milling to uncover the fiber layers of the material; and Thomas Trum's Fossilised in fibre, dyed fibers pressed into sheets in a pressure press the release calls 500 meters long. [S22] The release also describes the display as a diptych: a conceptual application of handcrafted materials now industrially altered, and a second part about the industrial developments and Finsa's manufacturing process. [S22] These are Envisions' descriptions, and Finsa's own words in the same document say it has more than 12 factories serving 83 countries. [S22]

The 2018 album holds ten photographs titled envisions-wood in progress-ddw18, again with Smits named. [S21] The earlier carousel said the show presented six experimental research projects developed with Finsa. The sources say six of the earlier researches, by six named designers, were reworked in industrial conditions, a narrower statement. [S10][S11][S22]
2021: invitations at the Fuutlaan hall

The 2021 album holds nine photographs by Britt Roelse. One shows a printed curtain that reads envisions invites upcoming talents and says 12 upcoming designers are invited, though folds hide part of the text. [S21] A Berlin art school's excursion plan lists Envisions at Fuutlaan 14i in October 2021, with a meeting with a founder and a participant. [S12]

Salone del Mobile.Milano's report says the Fuutlaan hall that year held Design Perron, Dutch Invertuals and Envisions and calls Envisions Italian, which is an error, since every source I opened places it in Eindhoven. [S1][S13] This shows how a large hall with several groups under one roof gets labeled by whoever writes the caption.
2022: a retrospective and a municipality's cellar

For 2022, Envisions' archive lists More Than This as a self-initiated retrospective exhibition presented at DDW. The case page has placeholder text, so I use only its labels. [S3][S4] Two independent reports describe it. Design Insider Live calls it a 5 year retrospective of the collective's experiments, with work by Post, Schuurman, Studio Truly Truly and Robin Pleun Maas, and says many samples came from challenges by manufacturers such as Finsa and Levi's. [S14] A German design magazine places it in a large tidy warehouse and calls it a five-year retrospective. [S15] The 2022 album has 21 photographs by Roelse, banners that read Because there is more than this, and titles that begin FUUTLAAN_DESIGNPERRON. [S21]

The earlier carousel asked how the Envisions hall related to Design Perron. DDW's own location page for Design Perron gives its home as the Opvallers building at Fuutlaan 12 and lists exhibits from Dutch Invertuals, Envisions and others. [S19] Design Perron's own site calls Opvallers its trusted base. [S20] So Design Perron looks like the umbrella for the hall, and Envisions one of its exhibitors, which would explain the titles. That page describes 2026, though, so I do not know whether its wording about Envisions dates from an earlier year. [S19]

Envisions was also behind a second exhibition that year, which the album does not cover. Its archive lists De Volle Ondergrond, a 2022 exhibition for the municipality of Eindhoven, and Interior Design calls it one of the festival's highlights: organized by the municipality and designed by fffunction studios and Envisions, it examined the jam-packed underground of pipes, sewers, cables and garages. [S3][S6][S16] An archive of albums called Envisions would miss it.
What a retrospective does to an archive

A retrospective gathers earlier work. If More Than This was one, then a 2022 photograph of an object could show something first made years before, and the album year would date the picture, not the object. That is reasoning, and I flag it as such. A caption that says 2022 is true about the photograph and silent about the work. The same logic runs backward: a photograph of a wall of samples dated 2016 does not say which samples were new that year. [S14][S21]

My anatomy training has a parallel. [S14] A dissection is taught layer by layer so that students see how the final structure was reached, and a student who sees only the finished specimen learns the name and misses the order. Envisions' stated idea belongs to that tradition, and a single photograph of a table of samples cannot carry it.
2025: one trace in a craft council's list

For 2025 I found one trace, and it comes from another organization. Crafts Council Nederland's HOW&WOW page for Dutch Design Week 2025 lists 85 makers, and the last entry, [Re]value, spins, weaves and makes felt from local wool and hemp with scalable industrial techniques, with support from Interreg. The entry links to envisions.nl and an Envisions Instagram handle. The page does not say where the exhibit stood. [S23] It is the only evidence in this record that Envisions took part in a Dutch Design Week after 2022, and it describes a material experiment in the way the About page promises. [S1][S23]
2026: a studio opens its door

Dutch Design Week's listing for October 17 to 25, 2026 puts Envisions' new studio at Hallenweg 1E, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 with free access. It says Envisions works there all year on projects from material research and product design to interior design, and that it opens its doors to the public for the first time during the week, in more than 100 square meters. [S17] The program entry, called Treasured, describes a daylit workspace full of treasures, projects, materials and try-outs, finished and in progress. [S18] That is the first Envisions listing in this record that shows the process by its own description, in the place where it happens. The Crafts Council Nederland exhibition WOW NATURE is listed in the same Hallenweg area, at De Fabriek. [S24]
What the record does not show
Where Products in Process Part 2 stood in 2016, and whether RGB Funfair was part of the festival. [S3][S5][S7]
Whether Smits photographed the 2016 and 2018 albums for Dutch Design Week or for Envisions. [S1][S9][S21]

Whether Envisions took part in 2019, 2020, 2023 or 2024. I found no album and no page, and a gap in an archive is not proof of absence. The only trace after 2022 is the 2025 craft-council entry. [S21][S23]
Which objects the 2016, 2017 and 2021 photographs show by name, and who made them. [S21]
How much of More Than This was new in 2022. [S14][S15]
Whether the Design Perron listing describes 2022 or only 2026. [S19]
When you open an album next to a listing, which does the sentence describe: the picture, the object in it or the organization that made it? [S17]

title: GEO-DESIGN left the museum in 2019, and its photographers were never the same people
subtitle: Five Dutch Design Week chapters of a Design Academy Eindhoven series, read against what the school, the festival, a designer and the press wrote about each one
description: Five chapters of the Design Academy Eindhoven and Van Abbemuseum series GEO-DESIGN, set beside organizer pages and six photo albums.

sections.x: GEO-DESIGN left the museum in 2019, and the photo archive recorded that move in the way it sorted its albums. [S8]

I like a series that changes its setting, because the setting is part of what an archive can and cannot prove. This essay draws on public sources only: pages from Design Academy Eindhoven, Dutch Design Week's own magazine articles, an e-flux announcement, the identity designer's project page, a review in Domus and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 festival. [S1][S2][S5][S7][S8]
A school and a museum, with a curator in the middle

Design Academy Eindhoven describes GEO-DESIGN as a platform that explores the social, economic, territorial and geopolitical forces shaping design today. [S1] Its page says the platform transformed the annual exhibition of the Academy's alumni work, produced with the Van Abbemuseum, into an exhibition series. [S1] Dutch Design Week's article on the second chapter calls the series an annual collaboration between the two institutions and says the Academy started it in response to a need for experimentation and support for young designers and researchers. [S2]

The people named around it are few and recur. Martina Muzi curated Sand and Budget Airlines, and DDW says she curated Junk with Joseph Grima, whom it calls director of the Academy. [S2][S3][S6] Domus names the same pair for the first chapter. [S5] Grima is quoted on the Academy's page calling the series emblematic of a shift toward design as systems, strategy and research, and saying it helps the Academy build long-term relationships with alumni. [S1] I read that as a statement of purpose: the series is an alumni program as much as an exhibition.

The page for the platform is dated October 1, 2018 and was later revised, because it also announces the fourth episode, an online exhibition on COVID-19. [S1] That is why the page reads as a running ledger, and it is the main reason I trust the order of the chapters: the Academy numbers the fourth, e-flux numbers the third, and DDW numbers the second. [S1][S2][S3][S4]
One name, two things: an exhibition series and a master's program

The name GEO-DESIGN also belongs to a degree. On November 8, 2019, DesignDigger reported that Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin, who work together as Formafantasma, had been appointed head of a new two-year master's program called Geo Design at the Academy, to be added to the existing master's programs in Social Design, Contextual Design and Information Design. [S9] The report calls the master a logical continuation of the exhibition series and quotes Joseph Grima describing the exhibitions as a breeding ground for ideas and technologies that seep ever further into the Academy's education. [S9] The Academy's own page for the master says it was founded in 2020, calls it the youngest master's program at the Academy and lists Formafantasma as department heads for 2020 to 2023. [S10]

The two share a name and a school, and they are not the same thing: one is a series of shows with the Van Abbemuseum, the other is a course of study. A caption that says "GEO-DESIGN" without saying which one invites a mistake. The Onomatopee publisher's page for the Sand catalog describes the exhibition platform as launched in 2018 by the Academy, which is the clean way to say it. [S11]
2018: Alibaba, in orange

The first outcome was GEO-DESIGN: Alibaba in October 2018, for which the Academy's page says nine graduates were invited to research Alibaba's operational model and its impact on the design field. [S1] Domus, publishing on November 1, 2018, calls the exhibition at the Van Abbemuseum one of the most prominent events of Dutch Design Week 2018 and says it was curated by Muzi and Grima. [S5] The identity designer Irene Stracuzzi gives the dates: October 13 to November 11, 2018 at the Van Abbemuseum, then Salone del Mobile in Milan from April 9 to 14, 2019. [S7] The museum's own page for the show no longer opens, so those dates rest on the designer's page. [S7]

Stracuzzi's page adds a detail that explains what the photographs show. She describes appropriating the orange color recognizable across Alibaba's platforms for the identity, to evoke a new geography of global trade and e-commerce. [S7] The 2018 album holds 17 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge, and they show white rooms, a bed with built-in controls, shoes laid out on a blue mat, screens playing video and a large orange globe printed with trade routes and place names. [S8] The orange is the exhibition's identity, which means orange in a photograph is evidence of the setting and not of any one project. Her page credits Köhlbrugge among several photographers, one of them Peter Cox, whose pictures Domus used. [S5][S7]
2019: Junk moves into the city

Dutch Design Week calls Junk the second chapter and one of the most striking exhibitions of the 2019 edition. [S2] The article says eighteen projects were selected, half shown in the museum and the rest across the center of Eindhoven in places such as De Bijenkorf, Sissyboy and De Witte Dame, and that spreading the show let the makers seek a connection with the city. [S2] It describes two projects in detail: Shahar Livne's study of the plastic life forms of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, which it says visitors explored in videos and recordings, and Noud Sleumer's atlas of the illegal e-waste trade, which it says is built from satellite images. [S2] The article credits its museum photographs to Oscar Vinck and its two city photographs, at De Bijenkorf and at Hutspot, to Köhlbrugge. [S2]

The archive answers that spread with three albums: 20 photographs at the Van Abbemuseum, 7 at Bijenkorf and 6 at Hutspot, 33 in all, every title carrying Köhlbrugge's name and dates between October 19 and 27, 2019. [S8] In the Bijenkorf album a shop window holds a scroll and three green neon waves. In the Hutspot album, rows of pink translucent sheets fill a window, and a banner there carries the word JUNK and the words GEO DESIGN. [S8] DDW's caption names Alissa+Nienke for the Hutspot work. [S2]

That banner is the clearest tie between a photograph and the series in the whole archive, because the picture names itself. Most other photographs depend on the album title and the venue in the file name. [S8]

The sorting is the interesting part. Venue albums exist for Bijenkorf and Hutspot, while Sissyboy and De Witte Dame, named in the article, have no album among those I opened. [S2][S8] A reader who builds a timeline from the albums alone would think two city locations took part, and the article says more did.
2020: Sand, and an exhibition with no room

The 2020 chapter was Sand. An e-flux announcement from the Academy calls it the third chapter, subtitled The Building Block of Modernity, and says it opened on October 17 at the Van Abbemuseum and would stay until November 15, 2020, with nine research-based projects and one long-term research, curated by Muzi. [S4] DDW's article on Sand names several of the projects. Landscope, by Romain Laval and Baiba Soma, looks at sand extraction in Morocco. Nine Dragons, by Bich Tran, concerns river-sand extraction in the Mekong delta. Mica-belt, by Matteo Dal Lago, concerns mineral mining in India. [S3] The article closes with a tribute to Atelier NL's long-running sand research, shown as To See a World in a Grain of Sand, a collection of sand grains sent to the designers from all over the world. [S3]

The archive's album for Sand holds 10 photographs by Max Kneefel, and DDW's article credits its own Sand photographs to Max Kneefel too. [S3][S8] In the album are a cabinet of bottles and a photo wall with a long row of glass vessels. [S8] The article's description of Atelier NL's sample collection makes a match plausible, but nothing ties those photographs to that project, so I do not say they are the same. [S3][S8]

The same announcement presents the fourth chapter, GEO-DESIGN: COVID-19, as an online exhibition that interlinks eight original projects developed by alumni from June to September 2020, curated by Muzi. [S4] It also announces an online archive of all earlier projects. [S4] The Academy's page calls COVID-19 the fourth episode. [S1] The archive has no album for it, which is what you would expect for something made for a screen. I tried to open the archive site, and its security certificate had expired, so I did not use it. [S4]
2021: Budget Airlines

The 2021 edition, GEO-DESIGN: Budget Airlines, We Are All The Jet Set, ran from October 9 to November 14, 2021 at the Van Abbemuseum, according to the Academy. During Dutch Design Week it was open with a DDW ticket only, and afterwards with museum entry. [S6] The Academy's page lists nine research projects, each with its alumni makers, and credits Muzi as curator and Cinzia Bongino with the graphic identity. [S6] One of the nine, For FAQs Sake by The Ironing Board, is described as the exhibition's help center. [S6]

The archive's 2021 album has 8 photographs by Köhlbrugge, among them a lit poster that reads Budget Airlines, an All gates sign, an airplane lavatory and a sculpture with a sign that reads OVERSIZED BAGGAGE DO NOT FEED. [S8] The Academy credits its own photographs to Peter Cox. [S6] A caption that names the project behind the baggage sculpture would claim more than the titles support, because they do not link a photograph to a project. [S6][S8]
The Academy's page does not number this edition. The chapter numbers I can document run from one to four, and 2021 would be the fifth, but no page I opened says so. [S1][S6]
Whose photographs, and who credits them

Four editions yield six albums and 68 photographs. [S8] The archive credits Köhlbrugge for 58 of the 68 and Kneefel for the 10 from 2020. [S8] Meanwhile, the designer of the 2018 identity credits Cox, Marcel de Buck, Köhlbrugge and Nicole Marnati; DDW's Junk article credits Vinck and Köhlbrugge; the Academy's Budget Airlines page credits Cox. [S2][S6][S7] A caption writer has to decide which credit belongs under which picture, and the sources rarely overlap, except where the same photographer appears in both the archive and the organizer's page.
What an album structure can say

The count is a record of what the archive chose to keep and how it sorted it. It does not tell me how many projects each year held, and it cannot show a digital edition. [S8] The Academy's own count of projects is more complete: nine for Alibaba, eighteen for Junk, nine plus one for Sand, eight for COVID-19 and nine for Budget Airlines. [S1][S2][S4][S6] That sums to 54 projects across the five chapters, against 68 photographs in the archive, so the albums cover each chapter thinly.
What the record does not show

I do not know which project any photograph shows, apart from the Hutspot banner. I did not read the museum's own pages for Alibaba and Junk, because they no longer open. [S1][S8] I could not confirm the full list of 2019 city locations. I did not read the project-level archive for any chapter, and I do not know whether the 2021 chapter has a number. [S4]

Nothing I opened says what happened to the exhibition series after 2021, or how the master's program's own graduation work relates to it. [S10] Nothing I opened gives the total number of alumni projects across the chapters. If a series can move into a shop window and then onto a screen, what should its archive record: the objects, the places or the question the series asked?
Next time you read a photo archive, check which of those three it is sorted by, and say so in your caption. [S8]

title: The Grand Opening of Dutch Design Week: a ceremony that changes rooms, read through six photo albums
subtitle: The official photo archive holds opening albums for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2022, 2023 and 2025. DDW's own pages, a ticket page and press fill in the venues, hosts and dates.
description: Where Dutch Design Week opened in 2010, 2022, 2023 and 2025, what the PRO page says about 2024, and what the 2015 to 2025 photo albums leave out.

sections.x: The Grand Opening is the one Dutch Design Week event that is a press moment, a party and a ceremony at once, and the official photo archive files it under three different names across ten years. [S14]

The Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds opening albums for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2022, 2023 and 2025: six editions and 181 photographs. [S14] DDW's own news and press pages describe three of those evenings, a ticket page describes a fourth, and a few outside sources fill in the rest. This essay draws on public sources only. It reports no visit and no conversation, and it says nothing about the 2026 opening, which these sources do not describe. [S3]
An event that moves around

The first thing the record shows is that there is no fixed home. In 2010, when Core77 reported the opening of what it called the 9th edition, the official kick-off took place in the recently renovated Klokgebouw, a former Philips factory building, with guest speakers, premieres of new Dutch design, drinks and live music by a local rock band. [S8] Twelve years later DDW's page puts the opening at MYLC, De Caai, and a year after that at the Area 51 skate park. [S1][S2] In 2025 it was DomusDELA. [S3]

DomusDELA is a rebuilt complex of the Paterskerk, the Augustinianum and the Studentenkapel in Eindhoven, and Omroep Brabant reported in autumn 2020 that its brasserie, hotel and congress center had opened at the end of 2019. [S5] The opening moved from a factory hall to a skate hall to a converted church complex. That is my reading of the sequence of sources, not a statement from any of them. [S1][S2][S5]
The ticket page also describes an opening

DDW's PRO ticket page, whose text describes the 2024 edition, lists access to the Grand Opening as a benefit. It says the Grand Opening takes place on the evening of Friday, October 18, and that after buying the ticket the holder receives an email with an RSVP link, because a place must be reserved in advance for the official part of the event. [S6] October 18 was the day before the first public day, Saturday, October 19, 2024. [S6][S12] I found no DDW news item, press release or album describing that evening, so I know its date and its access rule and not its venue, hosts or program. [S6]
2015 to 2017: parties and halls with no stated venue

The 2015 album is titled WHAT THE IF?! Official #DDW15 Opening Party and holds 20 photographs, eight credited to Nick Bookelaar and twelve to Max Kneefel in the titles, with dates of October 17 and 18, 2015. [S14] ABN AMRO's page of that year gives exhibition dates of October 17 to 25, 2015, which fits a party on the first days of the week. [S15][S14] The album calls it a party, and I have no DDW page that calls it the Grand Opening, so I describe it as the opening party.

The 2016 album is titled Grand Opening DDW and has 16 photographs credited to Jeroen van der Wielen, with no date or venue in the titles. [S14] DDW16 ran October 22 to 30, 2016, and DDW's press page says Queen Máxima visited the festival on Tuesday, October 25, 2016, touring the Klokgebouw and two exhibitions and talking with designers on the Ketelhuisplein. [S7] That was a visit during the week, not the opening, and I do not match it to any album. [S7]

The 2017 album, again titled Grand Opening DDW, has 35 photographs by van der Wielen, and its titles read DDW Opening 2017_10_21. [S14] Innovation Origins' announcement of the theme says the 16th Dutch Design Week took place from Saturday, October 21 to Sunday, October 29, 2017, and the theme was Stretch. [S16] The titles' date is therefore the first day of the week. [S16][S14] Photographs in the album show a screen carrying the word STRETCH, which fits the theme. [S14][S16] I found no source that names the 2017 venue.
2018 to 2021: the years without an album

The archive has no opening album for 2018, 2019, 2020 or 2021, and the written record explains little. For 2019, a DDW welcome item describes nine days, about 2,600 designers and more than 100 locations, and mentions no opening event. [S10] The 2020 edition was a mostly online festival: Core77 reported on October 16, 2020 that it would open the next day, Saturday, October 17, with more than 500 3D viewing rooms, talks and a live studio. [S9] For 2018 and 2021 I found no source about an opening at all. An absent album proves nothing about whether an event took place. [S14]
2022: Get Set, a speech and a farewell

DDW's page titled DDW22 Grand Opening says the opening took place at MYLC, De Caai, hosted by Jess Øberlin of the collective PLASMA and the DDW chairman Jennifer Muntslag. It says the new Creative Head, Miriam van der Lubbe, explained the theme Get Set, and that Gunay Uslu, State Secretary of Education, Culture and Science, spoke about giving space to creativity, designers and makers. [S1] The same page reports that van der Lubbe thanked Martijn Paulen for his dedication to DDW and the design field, that Øberlin talked with the ambassadors Marjan van Aubel and Formafantasma, and that a PLASMA afterparty followed. [S1] Photographs on the page and in the album are credited to about.today. [S1][S14]

The page is dated October 22, 2022 and begins by saying that the opening was "last night." [S1] That puts the opening on the evening of Friday, October 21, 2022, the night before the first public day, and not on October 22 as a quick reading of the date would suggest. I have no second source for the date. [S1]
2023: Picture This in a skate hall

The 2023 page says the Grand Opening was held "in the heart of the skate park at Area 51," hosted by Lynn Zebeda and Cesar Majorana, with a takeover by The New Originals and guests including Phantom Wizard, Fumez, Sokarekta and TNO Sound. [S2] It records that van der Lubbe introduced the theme Picture This, that the year's DDW beacons were Stefan Diez, the founders of Muzus (Sanne and Neele Kistemaker) and Yinka Ilori, and that Cesar Majorana talked with Eindhoven's mayor, Jeroen Dijsselbloem. [S2] Photographs are credited to Lotte Dale. [S2][S14]

This page is dated October 21, 2023, the first public day, and says DDW23 "has officially begun." It does not say which evening the opening was held, so I cannot give the date of the event. [S2] Area 51 is also where DDW's PRO ticket page puts the Business Lounge and the wristband exchange, which I cover in the Business Lounge essay. [S6]

Queen Máxima came to DDW during the 2023 week. HKU reported that she visited its Class of 23 exhibition on Thursday, October 26, 2023. [S11] Omroep Brabant later wrote that 2023 was the last time before 2025 that she had attended. [S4]
2025: a ribbon, a queen and a church-like hall

A DDW press release said Queen Máxima would open the 25th edition on Thursday evening, October 16, 2025. It says she would first visit the exhibition Bridging Minds at the Van Abbemuseum, then join Miriam van der Lubbe in conversation at DomusDELA on the value of Dutch design, and afterward officially open the festival. [S3] DDW25 itself ran October 18 to 26, 2025, so the opening came two days before the public did. [S13]

Omroep Brabant reported that the queen first opened Philips' new headquarters in Amsterdam that Thursday afternoon, then traveled to Eindhoven and appeared on stage in a colorful outfit to open the 25th edition. [S4] The 2025 album has 45 photographs credited in their titles to Bracket Studio, and the ones I viewed show a church-like hall with tall arches and chandeliers lit in blue, teal and magenta. [S14] That fits DomusDELA's rebuilt Paterskerk, but no source says which hall of the complex the photographs show, so I leave it as a fit and not a finding. [S3][S5][S14]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**The date of the 2022 opening.** The page is dated October 22 and says the opening was last night, so the event was on the evening of October 21. The page's own words settled it. [S1]
**The date of the 2023 opening.** The page is dated October 21 and does not name the evening. Unsettled. [S2]

**The edition number.** DDW's press archive calls the 2024 festival its 23rd edition, and its 2025 release calls the next one the 25th. Core77 called 2010 the 9th and Innovation Origins called 2017 the 16th, which fit a first edition in 2002. [S12][S13][S8][S16] The 2025 number, which fits a first edition in 2001, is the odd one out. Both 2024 and 2025 cannot be literally right if every year had one edition, and I could not find a DDW page that explains the count. I use the number each source gives and attribute it.

**Party or ceremony.** The 2015 album calls its event an official opening party, the 2016 and 2017 albums call theirs Grand Opening, and DDW's pages for 2022 to 2025 use "opening" or "Grand Opening." These may be the same kind of event under changing names, and I do not claim they are. [S14][S1][S2][S3]
What the record does not show

I do not know the venue of the 2015, 2016 or 2017 openings, the date of the 2023 opening, or anything about openings in 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2024 beyond the PRO page's date for 2024. I do not know who attended any of them besides those the pages name. I found no source for what MYLC is. I could not read Eindhoven News' reports from 2018 because the site no longer serves them, and I could not read Dezeen's coverage because its server refused access. The album facts are from my reading of the Flickr account on October 7, 2026, which I did not repeat. [S14]
When a festival opens in a different room every year, which would you rather keep: the guest list, the room or the date? [S1]

title: Guest academies at Dutch Design Week: four foreign schools in a former Philips warehouse
subtitle: Nine albums from 2017 to 2019 and what the schools' own pages, DDW's magazine, a student interview and an architect's record say about who showed what in the Veem.
description: Burg Giebichenstein, Central Saint Martins, ECAL and Bauhaus-Universität Weimar at Dutch Design Week, and the Philips warehouse that hosted them.

sections.x: Four foreign design schools turn up in the Dutch Design Week photo archive, and a closer look shows that each left a different kind of paper trail. [S17]

I like a guest because it shows what a host looks like from outside, and a school is a guest that returns with new students every year. This essay asks what the nine guest-academy albums from 2017 to 2019 can be matched to, using the schools' own pages, a DDW magazine article, a student interview, a university excursion program and an architect's record of the building. It reports no visit and no interview, and it names no student. [S17][S5][S11]
The building: a Philips warehouse that was a parking garage

The albums name a place as often as a school: the titles of the Burg and ECAL photos in 2017 and the Burg and Bauhaus photos in 2018 say VEEM. [S17] DDW's own 2019 magazine piece calls VEEM one of the three main locations curated by DDW, with Klokgebouw and Ketelhuisplein, and describes a monumental building that is a parking garage for the rest of the year, entered by a long ramp. [S6] The architects who rebuilt it, Caruso St John, describe the Veemgebouw as a former Philips factory building on Strijp-S, and quote the Architects Journal calling it a listed 1940s warehouse in the former Philips complex. [S14][S15] [S17][S6][S14][S15]

The rebuild, completed in 2022 according to the architects, gave the building workspaces on the upper floors, a car park and a food hall on the ground floor and 38 rooftop homes. [S14] So the four schools showed in a building that was in its last years in the form DDW's magazine describes. The 2019 article adds that the Dutch Invertuals collective, which was celebrating its tenth anniversary, held the art direction for VEEM that year and turned it into an industrial exhibition space. [S6] [S14][S6]

The guests were not alone in the building. A university excursion program for October 2017 lists, besides Weimar and Halle, Crafts Council Nederland, Plaatsmaken & Grind the Gap and the Dutch Design Awards at the Veem. [S12] In 2018 the KABK alumni guide places Crafts Council Nederland's HOW&WOW studio there, with participants symbolically moving their workshops into the building. [S16] In 2019 DDW's article names representatives of Dutch schools such as Creative Craftsman and KABK, and students from the Royal College of Art, Burg Giebichenstein, Aalto University and Central Saint Martins. [S6] The Veem is still a DDW location in 2026: DDW lists VEEM floor 8, home of Manifestations, at Torenallee 100, October 17 to 25, fully wheelchair accessible. [S18] [S12][S16][S6][S18]

DDW also tells readers that the week grows more international every year, with more foreign academies taking part. [S5] That sentence is the organizer's claim about the whole festival, and the Veem is where it can be checked at the level of single schools. [S5]
Burg Giebichenstein: a diary of seven years

The school in Halle, Germany, has the longest written record. It announced that its students would make their premiere at DDW 2014 with Materials and Making at the Burg, ten selected projects at the Klokgebouw, October 18 to 26, 2014. [S1] In 2016 almost 20 of its students took part through the Burg Roadshow in the 9 Days of Making exhibition, and a page about the trip carries a photo captioned Veemgebouw. [S2] In 2017 nine projects were shown in a curated exhibition called Mastering the Material, from October 21 to 29, and the school describes DDW as one of the yearly stops of the Roadshow program. [S3] [S1][S2][S3]

The 2018 page says the school was at DDW for the fifth year in a row, which agrees with a first appearance in 2014. It names ten students and alumni at two locations, the theme Immaterial - Ultramaterial at the stand on the second floor of the Veem and the Rotor 3D light installation in the Area 51 basement, and lists the disciplines: industrial design, fashion design, textile design and interior architecture, plus ceramics and jewelry. It describes DDW 2018 as the largest design festival in northern Europe, with more than 2,600 designers and 335,000 visitors, under the title If not us, then who?, and says the festival has existed since 2002. [S4] [S4][S1][S2][S3]

DDW's 2019 article describes the school's last archived show. Eight practical experiments explored how human civilization should reposition itself on the planet, through dialogues with animals, speculative scenarios, unstable matter and artworks looking for an identity, and a robot called Fiffy helped visitors take the first steps toward alternative solutions. [S5] The 2019 album holds 17 photos, and a sign in one reads Meet the future ...and Fiffy the robot. [S17] [S5][S17]
Central Saint Martins: a collective that returns every year

DDW's 2019 article says that in the VEEM, Central Saint Martins presented United Matters, a one-time collective named for the master's graduates of Material Futures who work at the edge of craft, science and technology. [S5] The program entry says United Matters is a London-based collective of Central Saint Martins graduates from MA Material Futures. [S7] A 2020 entry describes a collective of graduates from MA Material Futures 2020, and a 2021 entry says that for the fifth year United Matters would be part of DDW with the 2021 graduates. [S8][S9] Next Nature Network repeated that fifth year in a row. [S10] [S5][S7][S8][S9][S10]

Five years counted back from 2021 puts the first appearance in 2017, if every year counts, and 2020 was a virtual festival. That would make the archive's 2017 album titled Central Saint Martins and its 2018 album titled MA Material Futures the first two United Matters shows, although neither album names the collective. [S9][S17] I give that as an inference from the count, not as a caption. In the 2018 album a panel is headed Wine Matters, which no page I opened explains. [S17] [S9][S17]
Bauhaus-Universität Weimar: a student show, found by a magazine

For the Weimar university I had only an album title and a sign until a German design site published an interview with the student group in 2017. Six students from a project called Design a sustainable value chain, supervised by a visiting researcher, Tjeerd Veenhoven, and a bachelor graduate, showed experimental material studies. They said the idea came at the end of the previous semester, that the exhibition was realized through student initiative, and that they were on floor 3 of the Veemgebouw. [S11] A university excursion program for October 21 to 24, 2017 independently lists Bauhaus Uni Weimar and Burg Giebichenstein Uni Halle among the visits at the Veem. [S12] [S11][S12]

The project names in that interview line up with what the 2017 album shows, which the October 8 read describes as fiber and sheet material samples, a helmet and jackets on stands. [S17] The interview mentions a raincoat made from biodegradable paper, a fireproof jacket and gloves from basalt fiber, grown textiles made into two jackets and a dress, and a chitosan study. [S11] I read the match as likely and not certain, since no photo title names a project. The 2018 album of 13 photos, titled with VEEM, has a sign for the Bachelor of Arts graduates of 2018 in Product Design and Visual Communication, and I found no page about that show. [S17] [S17][S11]
ECAL: one page, one aisle

ECAL in Lausanne says that from October 21 to 29, 2017 it presented ECAL Graphic Design, an exhibition of projects by students of its Bachelor Graphic Design and its Master Art Direction. [S13] The archive's ECAL album has five photos, dated October 24, 2017 in the titles and titled VEEM, showing printed posters on perforated panels along an aisle. [S17] That is a page, a date and a place that agree, and nothing more than that. [S13][S17]
What the nine albums can prove

The archive holds nine albums and 90 photos, all credited to Max Kneefel: four albums in 2017 with 7, 7, 9 and 5 photos, three in 2018 with 13, 7 and 13, and two in 2019 with 17 and 12. [S17] The 2017 photo titles carry the date October 24, 2017, which settles two albums whose ids looked misfiled. [S17] Set against the written record, the picture is uneven. Burg Giebichenstein has a page and an album for 2017, 2018 and 2019, and pages for 2014 and 2016 besides. [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5] Central Saint Martins has an entry for 2019, a count that points back to 2017 and albums for 2017 and 2018. [S7][S9][S17] Weimar has a magazine interview for 2017 and a sign for 2018. [S11][S17] ECAL has a page for 2017. [S13] [S17][S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S7][S9][S11][S13]

A title can prove a date and a place. It cannot show the course, the brief or the people, and a school's page rarely lines up with a Flickr title. When I caption a photograph from a visiting school, I want the school's name, the year and the exhibit each to have its own source, and I want to say so when one is empty. [S17]
Questions the sources settle

Three earlier doubts have answers. Whether the Bauhaus albums belong to Weimar: the 2017 interview and the excursion program both name Weimar. [S11][S12] When Burg Giebichenstein started: its own 2014 page says 2014, which fits the fifth year in 2018. [S1][S4] Whether the archive's Central Saint Martins albums for 2017 and 2018 are the same collective as in 2019: a fifth-year count says they probably are. [S9] [S11][S12][S1][S4][S9]
What the record does not show

I do not know what Bauhaus-Universität Weimar showed in 2018, what the Wine Matters panel belonged to, or whether any of these schools came back after 2019 under the same banner, apart from United Matters, which DDW lists in 2020 and 2021. [S17][S8][S9] I did not find a record of why these four are the only guest schools with albums, since DDW's 2019 article lists others, including the Royal College of Art and Aalto University, that have none in this set. [S6] I also do not know how the DDW art direction of VEEM, credited to Dutch Invertuals in 2019, worked in 2017 and 2018. [S6] [S17][S8][S9][S6]
If you open one of these albums, which of the three lines, school, year or exhibit, would your own captions fail on first? [S17]
