title: HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 at Dutch Design Week: a bamboo square, a bar with a new host each night, and a coin track in a studio
subtitle: From a bamboo maze on the Ketelhuisplein in 2016 to a coin track at the studio in 2019, the pages give three kinds of place and the photo archive gives four albums of very different size.
description: HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 at Dutch Design Week 2016 to 2019: the bamboo installation, the Inwisselbar, a museum commission and a coin track, read against the photo archive.

sections.x: HeyHeydeHaas filled a square with bamboo in 2016, ran a bar in the middle of it for two Dutch Design Weeks, and by 2019 had moved its Dutch Design Week project into its own studio, and the photo archive records each of those years at a different size. [S2][S7]

I like a project that changes scale from year to year, because it shows what an archive keeps and what it drops. This essay draws on public sources only: the agency's own pages, a profile from 2016, regional and local news, a bamboo studio, a heater maker, an Italian design magazine, DDW's own magazine pages and the official photo archive on Flickr as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about 2026 beyond what a tourism page lists for the square. [S2][S7][S14]
Who the two names are

HeyHeydeHaas calls itself a Dutch creative agency based in Eindhoven and operating worldwide, working on design, brand and identity development in both physical and digital work, and describes its approach as research-, insight- and instinct-driven. [S2] In November 2016 a regional business site ran a profile in its Share the Vibe series under the line "three people, one agency," naming Erik Sjouerman, Elske van der Putten and Eric de Haas. [S8] In the profile de Haas says Eindhoven leaves much room for randomness and that designers coming up from below had lifted the city in recent years. [S8] That is his opinion, given to a journalist, and the same page is the only source I opened that gives the agency's size.

Biki90 is harder to place. A project page by the designer Guy Verbeek, one of its members, says Biki90 is an Eindhoven-based collective that "started off in 192005" as friends kicking local parties, that more people joined and the parties grew, and that the yellow illuminated letters that lit its venues were damaged, which led him to start a "partymachine project." [S4] The page credits Labolleur for materials and frame-building, Maikel Engels for organizing and transport, De Vinyl Snijderij for last-minute milling, and Max Kneefel for the photography. [S4] I cannot read "192005" as a date, and I do not guess one. I could not find a Biki90 page of its own, because its former website now shows something else.

The regional broadcaster Omroep Brabant joins the two names. Its tips for the 2016 festival, published on October 21, 2016, describe the Inwisselbar as a large bamboo promenade with a cafe at its glowing center and a different host every day, and call it a collaboration between the Eindhoven concept developers of HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90. [S1] It is one outside source, and I would keep the wording as a report and not as a fact the two groups have confirmed.

The agency's home page lists other projects that show the range around the three at Dutch Design Week: a publication for MozFest called How to MozFest, an installation for the STRP festival 2019 made with Desirée Hammen and Pol Tijssen as part of the festival's identity, brand identity and research-based web archives for a pair of long-term partners, a script and copy project made with an animator, and entries labeled St. Joost School of Art & Design, AtelierNL, Het Zuidelijk Toneel, MU and Stedelijk Museum, which carry no description in the text I read. [S2] I list them to show that a bar, a bamboo maze and a coin track are a small part of a long list, and that the page gives no dates for most of the others. [S2]
2016: a bamboo maze on the festival's central square

DDW's own magazine calls the Ketelhuisplein the beating heart of the festival, one of three main locations curated by DDW, with Klokgebouw and VEEM. [S11] That text was written for the 2019 edition. In 2016 the square's curated theme was sustainability: Omroep Brabant wrote on October 28, 2016 that the Ketelhuisplein had been turned into a large exhibition on that theme, with the main installation Agri meets Design bringing farmers and designers together in four installations, among them one about the egg economy called The EGGCHANCE. [S10] The bamboo and the bar sat in the same square, and the broadcaster's text does not mention them. [S10]

The agency's site says its Bamboolala was an open-air installation within the art direction of the Ketelhuisplein during Dutch Design Week 2016, commissioned by the Dutch Design Foundation, and that the bamboo scaffolding connected the participants on the square and turned the open space into a maze of bamboo and design. [S2] Neon Moire's festival guide of October 13, 2016 lists it as Bambooh Lala, October 22 to 30, 11:00 to 22:00, a "never finished" bamboo construction that would connect everything and everyone on the square, with the Inwisselbar at its center hosting a different party each night between 5 and 8 in the evening. [S5]

The bamboo was built by a partner. Studio Jeroen Wand writes that for the agency's Bamboohlala it filled the Ketelhuisplein with bamboo structures for a festival vibe, thanks its team of Daan Hesseling, Wouter Corvers, Ellis Holman and Roy de Regt, and opens with the words "Again we did an amazing project with HeyHeydeHaas," so the two had worked together before 2016. [S3] The studio's page credits Sam Walravens for the photographs. [S3] Jeroen Wand has his own entry in this series.

The installation has three spellings in three sources: Bamboolala on the agency's site, Bambooh Lala in the festival guide and Bamboohlala on the bamboo studio's page. [S2][S3][S5] I use the agency's spelling because it is the maker's own, and I tell a reader about the others so they can search for them.

The archive has two albums for 2016. The old dossier counts 26 photographs in the one titled for the Inwisselbar and 9 in one titled Biki90: The making of a hangover, whose full title adds Official opening party, and says the 9 photographs show a silent disco in a decorated hall with colored headphones, DJs and a crowd, with no photographer named. [S7] I found no page that describes that party, and DDW's pages I opened say nothing about it. [S7] The Inwisselbar album shows bamboo scaffolding under a tent roof, signs reading Bambooh La La and DDW Music Lab, and a bar banner that reads "Iedere dag een andere party," every day another party, with a host listed for each day. [S7] The music lab sign has an explanation in DDW's own words: its press page of September 14, 2016 says a special stage would be built on the Ketelhuisplein for the DDW Music Lab. [S15]
2017: the bar without the bamboo

A heater maker's news item, published on October 23, 2017, says the company warmed the Ketelhuisplein during Dutch Design Week from October 21 to 29 in collaboration with the Inwisselbar, with wood stoves creating a cozy place and a lit fire. [S6] It adds that at the end of each day the Inwisselbar would open the evening with music, a drink and a special guest, as the perfect lead-in to the DDW Music performances. [S6] The page names neither the agency nor Biki90, and it does not mention bamboo. [S6]

The archive's 2017 album carries both names in its title and holds 34 photographs, the largest of the four. [S7] The title is how I link the 2017 bar to the two groups, and I would say so in a caption. The photographs are dated October 23 and 27, 2017 and show a yellow umbrella tent with string lights, wood stoves, a food truck and a clock whose dial spells Inwisselbar, so the bar is confirmed for that year. Titles dated October 23 name OWOW x Hutspot, one of the nightly hosts. [S7] OWOW, the Omnipresent World of Wizkids, is also named in DDW's 2017 wrap-up as the collective behind a dance evening at the Effenaar, which is the same week and the same collective name, though no page I opened ties the bar's night to that event. [S16][S7]
2018: a museum, a website and no album

The archive has no album for 2018, and the record is not empty for that year. The Italian magazine Domus reported on October 12, 2018 on A Balancing Act, a group exhibition at Kunsthal KAdE in Amersfoort that ran from September 15, 2018 to January 6, 2019, and its image captions list HeyHeydeHaas, 50/50, 2018 among the installations. [S9] The agency's site says the 50/50 coin track was commissioned by Kunsthal KAdE in 2018. [S2] Two sources, then, agree on a museum commission in 2018, and the museum show sits outside Dutch Design Week.

The agency also left a mark on another lab in this series. Baltan Laboratories' post of December 22, 2017 says its new website was developed by the team of Heyheydehaas, and the page for Baltan's Frankenstein Symposium on October 22, 2018 credits its header image to HeyHeydeHaas. [S12][S13] A design agency can be present at Dutch Design Week through other people's pages, and the archive's album titles will not show it.
2019: a coin track in a studio

The agency's site describes 50/50 as an enormous coin track: 80 meters of custom-made, clear, recycled acrylic track whose only purpose is to carry 50 cent coins from one point to another. It says the piece was on display during Dutch Design Week 2019 at the HeyHeydeHaas studio, with free entrance and 50 cents as the price of taking part. [S2] The studio's address on the same site is Gashouder 30 in Eindhoven. [S2]

The 2019 album titled HeyHeydeHaas holds only 6 photographs by Iris Rijskamp, and the old dossier says they show a track of clear acrylic tubes in a studio and a small sign reading 50 eurocent only, which matches the agency's description of the coin track, with visitors including children on a scaffold. [S7][S2] DDW's 2019 magazine page about the Ketelhuisplein does not mention the agency, and the 2019 square was devoted to sustainable architecture and society. [S11] In 2019 the agency's Dutch Design Week project was not on the square at all.
What a small archive can carry

Four albums, 75 photographs and three kinds of place: a public square, the same square a year later and a private studio. [S7] The sizes run from 6 photographs to 34, and the largest album belongs to the bar. [S7] That fits a festival archive that follows crowds, but it also means the quietest project here, the coin track, has the fewest pictures.

A timeline built from the albums alone would say the work peaked in 2017. The text sources say something else. In 2016 the festival organizer commissioned the installation, in 2018 a museum commissioned a piece that never appeared at the festival, and in 2019 the same piece was shown at the agency's own studio. [S2][S9] The albums record a camera's attention and not the size of a commission.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Who made the 2016 bar.** Omroep Brabant says HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 together. The agency's own page claims the bamboo installation and does not mention the bar or Biki90. The albums' titles carry both names. I attribute the bar to the pair as a report and the bamboo to the agency. [S1][S2][S7]

**Whether the 2017 bar was the same project.** The heater maker's page names only the Inwisselbar. The album title names both groups. I treat the link as the archive's, and I do not claim the 2017 bar was a new commission. [S6][S7]

**Where 50/50 was seen.** The agency's site says Kunsthal KAdE commissioned it in 2018, and Domus lists it in the 2018 show there. The agency says it stood at its studio in 2019. These are two showings of one piece, and they do not conflict. [S2][S9]
**What Biki90 says about itself.** Nothing first-party was found. The collective's start date is written as 192005 on one member's page, and I leave it unread. [S4]
What the record does not show

I do not know what the 2016 Official DDW opening party was beyond its album title and photographs, who the hosts of each night's Inwisselbar were in 2016 or 2017, or whether Biki90 describes itself as a partner in the bamboo. I do not know whether the 2017 bar was a HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 commission, because the one page about it names neither. I did not find a DDW program page for the bamboo, the bar or the opening party. The agency's own pages do not mention the bar at all. [S2][S7]

I did not reopen the photo archive, so the album counts, dates, titles and what the photographs show come from the dossier's October 8, 2026 reading and should be checked again before posting. [S7] I do not know why there is no 2018 album, and nothing I opened says what the agency will show in 2026. A tourism page of October 1, 2026 mentions a pop-up spot called The Bar on the Ketelhuisplein for this year's week, and no source ties it to the Inwisselbar. [S14]
When a project has two names on it, which source would you ask first about who made what, and which one would you trust last? [S1]

title: HOW&WOW at Dutch Design Week: a craft council, a Philips warehouse and a plinth label
subtitle: Crafts Council Nederland's own record from masterclasses in 2014 to WOW NATURE in 2026, read against what the Dutch Design Week photo archive holds.
description: Crafts Council Nederland at Dutch Design Week, 2014 to 2026: masterclasses, three HOW&WOW editions at VEEM, flax, baskets and WOW NATURE.

sections.x: Crafts Council Nederland was at Dutch Design Week years before it had a show called HOW&WOW, and by its own list the show with that name began in 2017. [S2][S6]

I like evidence that is small and checkable, because it shows how far a caption can honestly go, and the most useful evidence in the HOW&WOW photo archive is a white label on a teal plinth. This essay draws on public sources only: the pages Crafts Council Nederland keeps for each of its presentations, Dutch Design Week's own 2026 listing, a building page from Strijp-S, the national monument register and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the listings say. [S2][S17][S19][S20]
A council for craft, founded in 2012

Crafts Council Nederland, which I will call CCNL, says on its About page that it was founded in 2012 and is the platform for creative craftsmanship. Its stated mission is to connect makers to socially urgent themes, and it lists five goals, from supporting makers to mapping and passing on craft knowledge, enabling research, offering a stage and encouraging crafts in other sectors. [S1] The page adds that it follows the Cultural Governance, Diversity and Inclusion and Fair Practice codes. [S1]

Its presentation index says it presents excellent makers every year at Dutch Design Week, and lists items from 2014 to 2025, with WOW NATURE for 2026. [S2] That index changes the starting point of this story.
Before HOW&WOW: masterclasses, a map and indigo

CCNL's 2014 page says masterclasses had already run during Dutch Design Week 2013 and that in 2014 (October 18 to 26) Etsy, CCNL and the Fonds voor Cultuurparticipatie, with the Center for Folklore and Intangible Heritage, offered nine daily masterclasses called Meet the Master. The masters taught laminating wood, painting Delftware, Staphorst dot painting, papermaking, gold embroidery, stained glass design, hat-making, weaving and felting. [S3] The same page describes Dutch Darlings, a competition for contemporary souvenirs based on traditional Dutch techniques. [S3]

In 2015 the page says the online Craftsmap, a search engine for makers, was presented to the public for the first time at the festival, with an offline version on the theme of glass. [S4] In 2016, CCNL sent four maker-designers to Kyushu, Japan, to study indigo dyeing with Japanese masters in September, and presented the results at Kazerne in Eindhoven from October 22 to 30, 2016. [S5] One of the four, Adrianus Kundert, returns later in this story. [S5][S10]
So CCNL's HOW&WOW had three earlier formats at the festival: a teaching program, a map and an exchange. None of them is in the photo archive under CCNL's name as far as I read it. [S20]
The building: a warehouse with a national monument number

CCNL's pages place HOW&WOW in 2017, 2018 and 2019 at Veem, or VEEM, on Strijp-S. [S6][S7][S8] Strijp-S says the Veemgebouw was built during World War II as a Philips warehouse, that the developer Trudo acquired it in 2009, that several floors host pop-up exhibitions during Dutch Design Week, and that three layers with 39 homes were added in 2021. [S18]

The national monument register is more exact. It dates the Veemgebouw to 1942, to a design by the Philips engineering bureau with expressionist elements, and lists it as part of the Philips complex on Strijp-S. [S19] A craft show about hands and materials therefore stood in a concrete industrial warehouse, and neither source comments on the contrast. I note it and leave it there.
2017 to 2019: three editions at VEEM

The 2017 page says CCNL curated the show and that it presented exceptional making processes and current developments in creative craft. It lists no makers and credits photography to Theodoor Adriaans. [S6] The 2018 page is titled HOW&WOW, Studio at VEEM. It names 25 makers and groups, among them Agustina Bottoni, Boris de Beijer, Sara Ricciardi and the weaving company De Ploeg, and credits photography to Adriaans and Max Kneefel. [S7]

The 2019 page gives the dates, October 19 to 27, 2019, and describes HOW&WOW as an initiative of CCNL in collaboration with Dutch Design Foundation, made possible in part by the Fonds voor Cultuurparticipatie and Forbo. It names 38 participants, including a museum, a flooring company that is also a funder and the exhibition design studio, Studio ZwartFrame, with graphic design by Daniël Maarleveld. [S8] Its one-sentence description of the show runs from wood carving to polyurethane casting, from emerging makers to seasoned artisans. [S8]

The photo archive holds one album per edition, with 14, 25 and 25 photographs, 64 in all, and the photographer Kneefel named in every title. The 2017 titles start with 20171022 and the page for the first photograph gives October 22, 2017. I read the albums in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand. [S20] CCNL credits Adriaans for 2017 and Adriaans with Kneefel for 2018, while the archive credits Kneefel for every photograph. Both can be true, since the organizer and the festival could each have had a photographer, and no page explains the difference. [S6][S7][S20]
Where a label closes the gap

In 2018 the plinths carry names. One photograph shows a teal plinth with a large raffia piece, a purple woven vase, a dark chair frame and two small hanging baskets, and white letters on the plinth read Agustina Bottoni and Sara Ricciardi. Both are on CCNL's 2018 list. [S7][S20] Another shows two round plinths, one green with colored glass bowls and one purple, each carrying the name Boris de Beijer, who is also on the list. [S7][S20]

Anatomy teaching left me with one habit: read the label before you trust the specimen. Here the habit pays off and also sets a limit. A label sits beside several objects, and the photograph does not show which object belongs to which name. For the Bottoni and Ricciardi plinth I cannot say whether the raffia belongs to one name and the baskets to the other. For the de Beijer plinths I can say the name is there and that one plinth holds glass bowls. That is a smaller claim than a caption usually makes, and it is the one the photograph supports. [S7][S20]
2020 and 2021: flax, then baskets

For 2020, CCNL describes HOW&WOW Linen as a group exhibition about flax and linen. A video series called HOW follows the crop from blue flowers in the polder to processing, and in WOW a group of makers interprets what they learned. It names 15 participants, funders including the Bankgiro Loterij Fonds and the Province of Gelderland, and credits an exhibition designer, a text writer and film maker. [S9] The festival was largely online that year, and CCNL's page calls its presentation a special online edition. [S2][S9]

The flax work did not stop. The Linen Project, which CCNL says it started with the ArtEZ master's program Practice Held in Common and which is based in Arnhem, had thirty stewards growing and processing flax from 2020, and CCNL presented stewards' work at Dutch Design Week 2021 and again in a 2024 show titled The Linen Economy. [S2][S11] A Linen Project show ran at Museum Arnhem from May 22 to June 16, 2024, as part of State of Fashion. [S2]

HOW&WOW BASK IT! followed in 2021, an initiative of CCNL with Adrianus Kundert, designer and co-founder of Basketclub. CCNL describes Basketclub as an Instagram community that Kundert and Jamie Wolfond founded during the pandemic, with a monthly emoji challenge. The page lists more than 40 participants, among them Hella Jongerius, Bertjan Pot, Sebastian Herkner and Simone Post, and it includes loans from the national basketry museum in Noordwolde. [S10] One exhibit is a funeral basket of willow, another a rattle woven from seven willow twigs holding seven stones, and another a machine meant to weave three-dimensional volumes. [S10] The page does not name the venue.
Kundert is a thread across these pages. He is one of the four makers CCNL sent to Japan in 2016, and he led the 2021 basketry edition with CCNL. [S5][S10]
2022 to 2024: from a map of makers to a school

In 2022 CCNL presented iAtelier, NEW CRAFTS, which it describes as bringing artisans and digital makers together for knowledge exchange, with 18 makers named and funding from the Creative Industries Fund NL and the Creative Europe program. [S12] In 2023 the Crafts Academy exhibition ran from October 21 to 29 at Sectie C, Daalakkersweg 16, for 36 young makers who had learned calligraphy and decorative painting, embroidery, basket weaving and kite making in three Wereldmuseum locations. [S13] In 2024 the exhibition (w)aardewerk gathered twelve contributors around sustainable futures for ceramics, curated by three CCNL staff, with exhibition design by Elvis Wesley. [S14] These pages do not name the HOW&WOW title, and they show CCNL moving from showing makers to teaching them.
2025 and 2026: 85 makers, then 40 and a landscape

In 2025 CCNL used the HOW&WOW name again for a catalog of 85 numbered makers, from bronze casting to glassblowing, with Forbo, Artek and Iittala as partners. [S15] The last entry, [Re]value, spins, weaves and felts local wool and hemp and is linked to the Eindhoven design agency Envisions. [S15] The page does not name the venue.

For 2026 the listing is WOW NATURE: 40 craft experts, October 17 to 25, free, 11:00 to 18:00, at De Fabriek, Baarsstraat 38, in the Hallenweg area. [S16][S17] The exhibition design is by Scheltens & Abbenes, whose composed still lifes the page cites, and it describes an artificial landscape assembled from craft objects made from natural materials. [S17] The page asks what can still be considered natural, given how much of the Dutch environment is managed by people. [S17]
Who comes back

CCNL's pages let me count recurring names. By my count of the printed lists, 20 names appear in more than one edition among 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025. Babs van den Thillart, Saar Scheerlings and Rik van Veen each appear in three, and Esmé Hofman in 2019, 2021 and 2022. [S7][S8][S9][S10][S12][S14][S15] A show that returns the same weavers, ceramic artists and basket makers across eight years gives a photograph archive a practical problem, because a photograph of a woven object in 2025 may show a method first seen in 2018, and the caption year says only when the picture was taken.
What the record does not show
Who made what in the 2017 photographs: CCNL lists no makers for that year. [S6]
Which object a plinth label refers to when it stands beside several. [S20]
Where the 2021 and 2025 HOW&WOW shows stood. CCNL's pages do not say. [S10][S15]
Why the archive credits Kneefel for every HOW&WOW photograph while CCNL credits other photographers for some years. [S6][S7][S20]
Whether DDW's archive holds photographs of HOW&WOW or WOW NATURE after 2019. I did not find them and could not reopen the account. [S20]

If you caption a craft photograph from this archive, three lines can carry the claim: the label in the picture, the title in the archive and the organizer's list. Which will you let carry the sentence, and what will you leave out when none can? [S7]

title: In No Particular Order left a factory for a white museum room, and the fund that made it kept its own count
subtitle: Four editions of a talent exhibition by the Creative Industries Fund NL at Dutch Design Week, read through the fund's own pages, the press and three albums
description: Four editions of the Creative Industries Fund NL talent show In No Particular Order, 2014 to 2017, set beside three photo albums.

sections.x: The Dutch Design Week photo archive shows In No Particular Order moving from a raw industrial hall to a white museum room, and the way the pictures look changes with the room. [S6]

I like to start from what the pictures can show before I trust any caption. This essay draws on public sources only: the Creative Industries Fund NL's own announcements and talent platform, a Dutch industry news site that republished the fund's text, a Core77 report, a 2017 preview and the official photo archive on Flickr, including text visible inside the photographs. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 festival. [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6]
Who made it, and how many editions there were

The organizer is stated plainly in the fund's own pages. The Creative Industries Fund NL, known in Dutch as the Stimuleringsfonds Creatieve Industrie, is named as the initiator of the exhibition on its 2015 and 2016 announcements, and its talent platform lists four editions of In No Particular Order. [S2][S3][S4]

The platform says the first edition took place in the Schellens Factory during Dutch Design Week 2014, built on the questions of what makes someone a talent and how talent is shaped, with curator Agata Jaworska. [S4] The fund's own page for it says the show presented recent work by 21 young creatives in architecture, design and e-culture who had received a year of support in 2013/2014, with an exhibition and a publication, and quotes Jaworska, an alumna of Design Academy Eindhoven, saying that there is no uncontroversial standard for what counts as a talent. [S8] The second edition, in 2015, was staged in the Veem Building. [S4][S1] Core77 calls the 2015 show the second edition of a showcase of promising young Dutch designers, curated by Jaworska, which agrees. [S1] The fund's announcement of October 2016 calls that year's show the third edition, and the platform describes the fourth edition at the Van Abbemuseum in 2017. [S3][S4]

So the photo archive's three albums cover editions two to four. The first edition, in 2014, has no album with this name in the archive that I know of, and I did not search for 2014 photographs elsewhere. [S6]
What the fund pays for

The exhibition is a showcase for a grant. The fund says talent development is one of its five objectives, that about 30 highly promising designers and makers are selected each year for a stipend, and that the program includes coaching toward entrepreneurship and professionalism. [S3] The talent platform adds that grants run for twelve months and that participants must have graduated within the last four years. [S4] The grants cover new work such as research, materials, equipment and projects at home or abroad. [S3]

That matters for reading the photographs, because the exhibition does not show a curator's choice of the best young designers. It shows the results of one cohort's grant year, selected by an independent committee, and the fund says so in 2016. [S3]
2015: thirty-six designers and a wall of image archives

The fund's announcement, republished by CLICKNL on September 18, 2015, says the exhibition showed the newest work and ways of working of 36 promising designers, makers and architects, opening on Saturday, October 17 at 1:00 p.m. in the Veemgebouw. [S2] It says Jaworska asked each designer to assemble a collection of images and photographs that reveal their artistic vision and the development of their practice, and that a media wall showed their personal image archives. [S2] The credits list the fund as initiator, Jaworska as curator, Rana Ghavami as editor, Studio Remco van Bladel and Andrea Spikker for graphic design, three interaction designers and Bendewerk for production. [S2]

Core77's November 16, 2015 gallery names five works from the show, which the archive's titles never do: Ricky van Broekhoven's Solid Vibration, Marjan van Aubel's Current Window, Mark Sturkenboom's Ark (Volume 2): Paradigm Shift, Bora Hong's Cosmetic Surgery Kingdom and Maurizio Montalti's The Growing Lab, Mycelia. [S1] Core77 also places the exhibition in the Veemgebouw with the Dutch Design Awards exhibition and Transnatural. [S1]

The 2015 album holds 10 photographs by Nick Bookelaar, each titled Veemgebouw_expositie. [S6] They show small screens on poles across a bare hall, nine round lenses with images of sea and sky, a lamp before a round white projection and a rainbow-colored projection on a wall. [S6] The fund's description of a media wall of image archives fits the screens, but no page ties the screens in the photographs to that wall, and I do not say they are the same. The lamp is a candidate for the Sturkenboom lighting object that Core77 describes, and again nothing connects them. [S1][S2][S6]
Two of the 2015 photographs show faces on screens, and the carousel leaves them out, because a face on a screen is still a person's face and no title says whose it is. [S6]
2016: thirty-two designers on the eighth floor

The fund's announcement of October 12, 2016 gives more detail than any other source. It says the fund presents the work of 32 young designers in In No Particular Order, the third edition of the annual talent showcase, curated by Jaworska, on the eighth floor of the Veemgebouw from October 22 to 30, 2016. [S3] The designers came from all disciplines of the creative industries and were selected by an independent committee, and each received a year-long grant. [S3]

The announcement names all 32. Among them are the architecture studio KNOL, Elejan van der Velde, the digital-culture makers Karel van Laere and Polina Medvedeva, the textile designer Marjanne van Helvert, the product designers Olivier van Herpt and Sabine Marcelis, the biodesigner Teresa van Dongen and the food designer Chloé Rutzerveld. [S3] It describes three of their works: van Helvert launched a publication at a symposium, KNOL made a mirror piece about what it calls modern loneliness, and van Dongen showed a light installation powered by living micro-organisms. [S3]

Jaworska's question that year, in her words as the announcement quotes them, was how emerging designers organize their practice and what it means to have one. [S3] The announcement links that question to the Dutch Design Week theme The Making Of. [S3] The fund's platform says the designers answered with audio recordings and sketches. [S4] A program of artist talks, tours, performances and workshops ran on a stage nearby, and the fund also presented two other exhibitions, Intensive Care and Making School, on the same floor. [S3]

That last fact is a caution for the albums. The 2016 album holds 12 photographs by Bookelaar, and the fund's own announcement says the floor held three exhibitions. [S3][S6] A bench-filled hall or a large printed face in the album could belong to any of them, and the titles do not say. [S6]

In one 2016 photograph a translucent screen hangs in the hall with white text that reads het stimuleringsfonds creatieve industrie is, and the same words appear reflected backward on the floor. [S6] The announcement confirms the fund's role in plain words, which makes the screen's unfinished sentence part of the exhibition's own branding. [S3]

Other 2016 photographs show a cube lined in blue-green plaster with one visitor facing a small screen, a visitor pressing both hands against a white frame in a black wall and a blue torpedo-shaped craft with a round fan at its tip. [S6] The announcement's list of works does not tell me which, if any, of these is by a named designer. [S3]
2017: a curator who was also a participant, and a show in a basement

The fund's retrospective, dated October 30, 2017, calls the 2017 show the fourth exhibition on talent development, held in the Studio of the Van Abbemuseum during Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29, 2017. [S7] It says the fund received about 5,000 design professionals and led 230 students on tours. [S7] The fund's platform describes it as a collective statement on the plurality of contemporary design practice, with nine installations on the themes of Position, Inspiration, Working Environment, Representation, Money, Happiness, Language, Discourse and Market. [S4]

The curator was Jules van den Langenberg, who was himself a participant in the talent program in 2017. [S4][S7] In 2014 to 2016 the curator was Jaworska; in 2017 the curator came from the cohort. [S4] The retrospective quotes him saying that, instead of showing individual projects or end products, the exhibition showed the back side of design practice in the basement of the museum. [S7] I do not know whether the change of curator was a deliberate shift and no source says.

The retrospective describes how the nine installations were made. Each of the 32 participants contributed to each theme through characteristic objects and fragments, from their own clothes and chairs to prototypes and books that inspired them, and Van den Langenberg then invited nine thinkers and makers to build an installation from those collections. [S7] For Position, each participant packed a suitcase of things they would take to found a new society, and Jurgen Bey opened several suitcases each day to build a visual dictionary. [S7] For Representation, each participant gave a garment to the fashion designer Duran Lantink, who made three composite portraits, and a performance artist wore one of the outfits during the week. [S7] For Working Environment, participants described and drew their ideal workspace, and the architect Anne Dessing, herself an alumna of the program, presented an analysis on a curtain whose folds link the sketches. [S7] For Discourse, daily talks were held on chairs the participants had brought, placed on a floor by the artist Simon Becks. [S7]

Set that beside the 2017 album, and the fit is striking. The album's eight photographs, credited to Tommy Köhlbrugge, show a white room with suitcases and chairs on a floor, coats and a red cap on a wall, a tall curtain printed with small drawings, shelves of small photographs and rolls of colored tape on a white table. [S6] Suitcases, garments, chairs and a drawn curtain are the kinds of objects the fund's text assigns to the Position, Representation, Discourse and Working Environment installations. [S7] That is a fit between a description and a picture, and not a documented match: no title names an installation, and the fund's text does not describe a red cap or rolls of tape. [S6][S7] I use the fit to say what kind of objects the room held and not to caption any frame as a particular installation.

The fund also credits its own retrospective photographs to Lonneke van der Palen and Hanneke Wetzer, not to Köhlbrugge, so the archive's pictures are a second set. [S7] A preview of August 23, 2017 puts the show at the Van Abbemuseum with nine installations by talent stipend recipients, and it mentions that the festival that year included the new World Design Event. [S5] The word to notice is "preview": it says the recipients will exhibit, and it is not a report on what happened. [S5]
The room in the 2017 pictures is white and bright, which is the opposite of the Veemgebouw. [S6]
After 2017: the name stops, the show continues under others

The platform shows what followed. In 2018 the fund presented 24 minute-long film portraits of the 2017/2018 grant recipients in an installation in the Veem Building, in 2019 portraits shown with performances at MU, in 2020 a program called Talent Tours and in 2021 and 2022 portrait installations at the Klokgebouw and MU. [S4] None of those pages uses the name In No Particular Order. [S4]

I read that as the series ending in 2017 under that name, while the fund's yearly presence at Dutch Design Week continued in a different form. That is my reading of a list of titles, and no page says the name was retired. [S4]
What the change of room does to the evidence

The darker Veemgebouw photographs let a reader see the work as light, screens and shapes. The 2017 photographs show it as objects against white walls. A reader comparing the albums is comparing two photographers and two rooms as well as three exhibitions, and I do not think the archive lets me separate them. [S6] In my own field I learned that a specimen photographed on a dark cloth and the same specimen on a white tray look like different specimens, and I treat these albums the same way.

The titles stay steady in one respect: each names a place. The Veemgebouw appears in 2015 and 2016 and the Van Abbemuseum in 2017, which agrees with the fund's pages. [S3][S4][S6] If I had to caption these albums for a reader, I would write the year, the place from the title and the credit, and describe what is visible and nothing about who made it, unless a named page or a legible label does the matching.
What the record does not show

I do not know which designer any photograph shows. Core77 names five 2015 works and the fund names 32 designers for 2016, but neither connects a work to a frame in the archive. [S1][S3][S6] I did not read the fund's talent pages for individual designers. I could not open Metropolis M's review, because the site answered with an access error (403), and I did not retry.

I do not know which installation any 2017 photograph shows. [S6][S7] I do not know whether the 2014 edition left photographs in the archive. The fund's retrospective lists 32 participants for 2017, and I have not matched any of them to a photograph. [S7]

When a show changes rooms from one year to the next, should its archive stay faithful to the room or to the work? Next time you open a multi-year album, look at the first and last photograph of each year, and write down what changed in the setting before you decide what changed in the exhibition. [S6]

title: Jelle Mastenbroek asked for your data twice: a card swipe in a living room and an ID chip in a forest
subtitle: The official photo archive holds two albums, 2017 and 2019, with no work named. His own site, DDW's interview, museum and press pages fill in 2015 to 2022.
description: Jelle Mastenbroek's Data Orchestra and The Robin Who Wondered If He Was a Nightingale, and what the DDW photo albums for 2017 and 2019 leave out.

sections.x: Jelle Mastenbroek built a piece that plays music from your bank card and, three years later, one that makes mechanical birds sing from the chip in your ID, and the photo archive holds two small albums that show neither process. [S18]

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds two albums under his name: 2017, titled Jelle Mastenbroek/MIR, with 6 photographs credited to Ronald Smits, and 2019, with 16 photographs credited to Max Kneefel. [S18] That is 22 photographs, and none of the titles names a work. The written record is much fuller, and it also shows he was at DDW in 2015 and 2016, years the archive does not cover. This essay draws on public sources only: his own site, DDW's interview series, museum and press pages, and a broadcaster's festival guide. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about 2026. [S1][S7]
In anatomy teaching, consent is the first document on file, so I notice how little a card swipe records of it. That is a perspective, not a claim about his work. [S7]
Who he is, from the record

Jelle Mastenbroek is an artist and designer who works from Eindhoven. A 2015 profile on the Creative Industries Fund NL's talent site says he graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2012, is a member of the studio collective Collaboration O, takes a humorous and playful approach and uses storytelling to reflect on society, often through interactive installations made with musicians, composers and programmers. [S11] VPRO's festival guide in 2019 places the Collaboration O studio at Sectie-C, the former factory site on Daalakkersweg that opens its studios during DDW. [S16] His own site lists dozens of works, grouped by theme, with money, porcelain and sound recurring. [S1]
2015: a cuckoo clock named Frank

In 2015 the Creative Industries Fund NL presented 36 emerging designers under the title In No Particular Order. [S11] Mastenbroek's entry was Frank, a cuckoo clock with an animated character who is, according to Mastenbroek, an expert on time and being punctual, made in collaboration with the artist Niels Hoebers. The profile says it offers a playful view of the nine-to-five routine. [S11] The page I read does not give the exhibition's venue, so I cannot say where in Eindhoven it stood. There is no album for 2015 in the archive under his name. [S11][S18]
2016: the card, the living room and an award

Data Orchestra is the work that made his name. VPRO Medialab describes it as an installation in which visitors swipe a credit card, or another card with data, through a reader and receive a composition played on everyday objects such as cutlery, plates, pens and glasses, so that personal data are exchanged for a piece of music. [S8] Designboom, in a May 5, 2016 post that its editors say came from reader submissions, adds that the work was made with the agency OWOW and sets itself against how influential companies collect data and trade it. [S12]

In April 2016 the installation was shown in Milan. The Dutch technology site Bright reported it as part of a group of Dutch designers presenting in the Lambrate district, with Data Orchestra at Via Massimiano 23 from April 11 to 17, and quoted Mastenbroek saying personal data is a new kind of currency. [S10] His site and VPRO Medialab both say the jury of the Milano Design Award rewarded it with the prize for Best Technology among 1,600 exhibitors. [S4][S8] The award is the organizer's claim on the artist's site and the broadcaster's page, and I did not find the award organizer's own page. [S4][S8]

The first Dutch showing came on Saturday, May 14, 2016, at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, in a free evening called Klokgebouw viert de toekomst, connected to the 125th anniversary of Philips, according to VPRO Medialab. IO+ reported the same evening. [S8][S9] That event was not part of DDW. [S8][S9]

At DDW 2016, theme The Making Of, DDW published an interview with him. He said Data Orchestra began as a design for a music festival, that the sound side came from OWOW's software and electronics and the acoustics from him, and that the Creative Industries Fund helped him present it in Milan. [S7] He said the scanner can read bank and credit cards and also the chips of driving licenses and passports, that he does not store the data though in principle it could be stored, and that people react very differently: some swipe at once, some realize afterward what they handed over, and some refuse for privacy reasons, which he reads as a sign of awareness. [S7] He also said that he was showing work at Ketelhuisplein and in his studio at Sectie-C, where mirrors hang. [S7] The page is dated November 3, 2016, but its text says DDW would be over next week, so the interview was written during the festival and the date on the page is probably a later republication. [S7]
There is no DDW album for him in 2016. The DDW interview and the Sectie-C studio are the evidence that he took part. [S7][S18]
2017: a museum show, a competition and a second DDW

Between March 24 and October 9, 2017, his site says, Music Box No.1 and Data Orchestra were on show in New Icons: Rietveld Now at Kazerne in Eindhoven. [S3] IO+ describes the side room at Kazerne where Data Orchestra could be activated with any chip card, and lists Mastenbroek and OWOW among the New Icons participants, with Atelier NL, Maarten Baas, Studio Drift and others. [S14]

On May 16, 2017, IO+ reported that he had won the What if Lab: Marathon Eindhoven, an initiative of Marathon Eindhoven and the Dutch Design Foundation in which five studios pitched ideas for the finish of the 34th Eindhoven Marathon. His idea put runners' own motivations on banners and on boards along the route, with boards at the toughest points that recognize a runner by a chip and show a personal message. Jury member Arne Hendriks said the jury was moved by experiencing the marathon as a collective. [S15] I found no source that says the design was built as pitched. [S15]

His site lists Dutch Design Week 2017 as October 21 to 29. [S2] Interior Design's roundup of November 2, 2017 described Sectie C as four former factory buildings turned into studios and wrote that he showed musical crockery vending cabinets, Data Orchestra and new pieces, including a lightbox with a twirling dancer, all coin-operated. It credits its photograph of the vending cabinets to Ronald Smits, the same photographer the 2017 album's titles name. [S13][S18] The archive's 2017 photographs show a wall panel headed Data Orchestra, wooden cabinets, lit frames and a model, with no people. [S18] The album title ends in MIR, which no page I opened explains.
2019: a forest that sings from your ID

The 2019 album shows a yard with young trees and ferns on wood chips, small domes on poles and visitors reading stands. [S18] VPRO's DDW tips of 2019 identify the work behind that setting as The Robin Who Wondered If He Was A Nightingale: a miniature forest with mechanical birds that sing according to the data on your ID card, passport or OV-chip, at Sectie-C, Daalakkersweg 16. [S16] His own page describes improvisations by an orchestra based on your identity and the natural environment, with woodpeckers delivering percussive rhythms and the forest's acoustics playing a large role. It lists the musicians, from nightingale and cuckoo to four species of woodpecker, and says the work was commissioned by Oerol and curated by Marin de Boer and Atelier NL. [S5]

Atelier NL is the Eindhoven studio of Nadine Sterk and Lonny van Ryswyck, and the credit shows how small the circle is: a festival commission curated by a studio that had been a DDW ambassador. [S5][S14] I could not find which Oerol edition the piece first appeared in, so I do not date the commission. [S5]
The piece traveled. His site says it was on show from June 20 to August 20, 2022 at the Crossrail Place Roof Garden in Canary Wharf, London. [S6]
What came after the archive

Much of what is known about his later work is on his own site and in museum news. On January 14, 2026, Museum Speelklok announced it had bought his Porcelain Piano, a piece that combines a china cabinet and a piano and whose 48 porcelain plates each have their own tone. The museum said it was the first work by a contemporary artist to enter its permanent collection. [S17] His site also lists Shell Symphony for Oerol 2024. [S1] I found no DDW album or program page for him after 2019.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**When the DDW interview was published.** The page carries November 3, 2016, and its text says DDW would be over next week. The text settled it: it was written during the festival. [S7]

**Whether the 2017 pieces were at Kazerne or Sectie C.** Both. His site lists Data Orchestra at Kazerne from March 24 to October 9, 2017, and Interior Design places Data Orchestra at Sectie C during DDW, October 21 to 29. A work can be shown in two places in one year, though I cannot say if there were two copies. [S3][S13][S2]
**Whether the 2019 yard is Sectie-C.** VPRO places The Robin at Sectie-C. The album does not name a place. I read the match from the trees and domes only. [S16][S18]
What the record does not show

I do not know what MIR means, which photographs in the 2017 album belong to which work, where the 2015 exhibition stood, or which Oerol edition commissioned The Robin. I could not read the Vimeo page for The Robin because the site showed a bot-verification page, and I could not read the Canary Wharf press release because its robots file excludes my request. I did not find the Milano Design Award organizer's own page. [S5][S18]
The works ask for your data in exchange for pleasure. When you swipe a card for a song, what do you think you are giving, and what do you think you are getting? [S7]

title: Jeroen Wand at Dutch Design Week: a Hallenweg workshop, five objects in a museum and albums that never name a work
subtitle: A studio that opened its doors on the Hallenweg in 2015, the Boijmans records and presentation that followed, a move in 2019, DDW pages from 2023 to 2026 and what the three archive albums can and cannot show.
description: Designer Jeroen Wand's Hallenweg studio at DDW, the five objects Boijmans holds, the DDW pages through 2026 and what the official photo albums can show.

sections.x: In 2015 a designer on the Hallenweg in Eindhoven described his workspace as a small free state, and by 2018 the Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive had three albums for it, none of which names a single work. [S1][S2]

I like a studio that opens its doors, because a visit leaves a record that finished objects cannot. This essay asks what the sources say about Studio Jeroen Wand at DDW, from a 2015 article, a 2017 trade-magazine profile and the museum's own records to the studio's news and DDW's program pages for 2023 to 2026, and then asks how far the three archive albums can be tied to that story. It reports no visit and no interview, and it names no one who appears in a photograph. [S1][S3][S4][S2]
The place: a post-war industrial street

This is Eindhoven writes that the Hallenweg came into being after the Second World War as an economic recovery project, that metal and welding companies were its first tenants, that the buildings follow the Delft School style and are hidden behind the Hoogstraat, and that the street now holds studios and ateliers including Vij5, HeyHeydeHaas and the church of Atelier NL. [S5] Eindhovens Dagblad, via De Erfgoedstem, reported on January 9, 2016 that the business halls at Hallenweg 1 to 7c were among seven postwar buildings newly designated as municipal monuments. [S6] That is the setting for the 2015 to 2018 albums, a protected row of working halls and not a gallery district. [S5][S6]

A June 28, 2017 profile in the trade magazine ArchitectuurNL gives a picture of the workshop itself without naming the street: a large workshop on a site full of creative activity, chickens outside, a trainee cutting veneer inside, racks of sorted wood and veneer, and a wall of small labeled bins of screws and bolts with the word GAMMA, in the writer's phrase a wink, over the hardware cabinet. Upstairs is what Wand calls his memory, a cabinet arranged like a candy shop and filled with material tests, from plaster and glass to porcelain and PVC pipe. [S3] The chickens match the 2015 description of the Hallenweg workspace, so I read the two as the same place, though the 2017 article does not say so. [S3][S1]
The designer and the studio

The studio's own page says it was founded by Jeroen Wand in 2007, that it specializes in interior design, furniture and products, and that it alters traditional combinations of materials and techniques, for example with paper laminating and plaster rotation molding. It gives his birth year as 1985, a product design education at the academy in Maastricht and a master's degree at the Sandberg Institute in Amsterdam in 2008. [S7] The Boijmans record gives Heerlen as his birthplace. [S8] ArchitectuurNL adds that he graduated in Maastricht in 2006, finished at Sandberg in 2008 and also holds a welding diploma, and that he applied to the academy at 16, a year early, with a portfolio of clothing, jewelry, lamps and furniture. [S3]

The graduation piece was the Paper Chair. The museum's text says Wand made it in 2006 as his graduation project from many layers of 160 gram paper, strong enough to sit on, and that the museum bought it in 2008. [S9] A Vij5 interview from 2023 says he ended up in Eindhoven by chance: a friend found a studio too big for one person, and Wand was working in Geldrop at the time. [S10] He describes the studio as three pillars, free work made in-house, commissions, and executive work for other designers, says the workshop runs on solar power and that the veneer used for its products is a residual stream, and says the 's-Chair that Vij5 sells has been tested to NEN-EN 16139, level 2. [S10] Those are his statements as an interviewer for his publisher recorded them. [S10]

One number does not line up. The studio says it was founded in 2007. [S7] DDW's program text for 2023 says the studio had existed for 15 years, which counted back from 2023 gives 2008. [S11] A studio can be counted from the year it was registered or the year it began to show work, and neither page explains its count, so I do not choose between them. [S7][S11]
2015: Same place, New stuff

The e52 program and Dutch Design Daily chose Wand as one of nine hidden gems of DDW 2015, in an article that the IO+ archive carries. The article, by Renske Mehra, calls his workspace on the Hallenweg a small free state, with a large outdoor area, a few chickens, a radio playing and a lot of hard work going on. His newest work would be exhibited in his own studio under the title Same place, New stuff. [S1]

The show was to include new Phases vases, which he had shown at the Milan design fair that year. According to the article, each vase's basic shape comes from one mold; after the first version hardens it is immersed in liquid plaster, giving an irregular, uncontrolled outer layer, and the process is repeated several times, so that the inside stays sleek while the outside gets rougher. A second new piece was a laminated table, made in part during a stay with an Italian furniture maker in South Tyrol as an artist in residence. Other designers, among them Jo Sijen and Wouter Corvers, were invited to show experiments in ceramics and construction, and Wand would explain the exhibition himself at a meet and greet on Wednesday, October 21, 2015, at 16:00. [S1]

ArchitectuurNL tells the residency story differently. It places the artist residency in what it calls Swiss Bolzano (translated from the Dutch), says he learned there something with paper that he then translated to veneer, using the discarded offcuts of a nearby factory, and says he presented the first products of this collection at the Milan design fair in 2015. It adds that he built his own vacuum bag to press the layers together. [S3] The two accounts differ on the country, and I use IO+'s version, which was written during the 2015 festival and names a region. The Milan 2015 date agrees in both. [S1][S3]

The official archive's 2015 Hallenweg album, with 18 photos credited by title to Ralph Roelse, shows a courtyard with signs for Studio Jeroen Wand, according to my October 8 read. [S2] So the 2015 show is in the archive, filed under the area and not under his name. [S2]
Five objects in one museum

Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen holds five Wand objects, not two. The artist page in its online collection lists a Paper Chair, a Paper stool, two vases titled Phases and a Laminated Table. [S8] The records give the detail:

The Paper Chair (V 2506, made 2006, laminated and pressed paper, 75.5 centimeters high) and the Paper stool (V 2507, made 2006, 40.5 centimeters high) were both bought in 2008 with the support of the Mondriaan Fund. [S12][S13] The first Phases vase (V 3106, made 2013, plaster with a polyurethane coating, 44.5 centimeters high) was purchased in 2016. [S14] The second (V 3107, made 2015, plaster and polyurethane coating, 45 centimeters high) came to the museum as a gift from Jeroen Wand in 2016. [S15] The Laminated Table (V 3193, made 2015, veneer and glue, 50 centimeters high, 121 wide and 70 deep) was bought in 2017 with the support of the Mondriaan Fund. [S16] The Montreal Museum of Fine Arts holds a further vase, from the series Phases IV, dated 2015, bought as the Suzanne Caouette Bequest purchase and inventoried 2016.2. [S17] One of the two Boijmans vases is therefore a gift from the maker and not a purchase, and the museum's purchases are the chair and stool (2008), one vase (2016) and the table (2017). [S8][S15]

All five Boijmans records list the same exhibition, Studio Jeroen Wand. Een gelaagde collectie (2017), which can be read as A layered collection. [S12][S13][S14][S15][S16] The records label it an internal exhibition and do not say where it was held. The museum's own exhibition page, which I read through an Internet Archive capture of July 16, 2019 because the live address now redirects, answers that: the presentation was shown in the Paviljoen, and the page says the plaster vases in it were built layer by layer, two of them acquired in 2016, and that the Laminated Table and the Sarentino Chair from 2016 are the result of his latest experiment with laminating wood and integrating the legs into the gluing. [S9] ArchitectuurNL, in its issue 03/2017, says the exhibition could be seen until and including August 27, 2017. [S3]

A second source disagrees about the year. The Meer arts calendar, in an entry dated August 23, 2018, gives the dates of the presentation as August 1, 2018 to January 13, 2019 and repeats the museum's text word for word. [S18] The records and the trade magazine say 2017, and Meer says 2018 to 2019. The museum's page, as captured in 2019, carries no dates, so it settles the place but not the year. [S9][S18] I take 2017 as the documented date, because two sources and the museum's own records agree on it, and I list the 2018 to 2019 entry as unexplained: it may be a second showing, an extension or an error in the calendar. [S12][S3][S18]

The table has a date problem of its own. Boijmans dates it to 2015, and IO+ called a laminated table new in October 2015. [S16][S1] The museum's exhibition text dates the Laminated Table and the Sarentino Chair to 2016. [S9] Kazerne, the Eindhoven exhibition house, writes in 2020 that a table in its show is a reinterpretation of Wand's first Laminated Table, presented in 2012. [S19] I cannot tell from these pages which iteration the museum owns, and I cannot connect the Sarentino Chair to a place or a source beyond the museum's text. [S9][S19]
2016 to 2018: three albums and one dated recap

The archive's Wand albums are Hallenweg: Jeroen Wand for 2016 with 7 photos and for 2017 with 9, and Jeroen Wand for 2018 with 12, 28 in all, every title crediting Iris Rijskamp. [S2] The photos show a cluttered workshop with glaze jars, a moped and a hand press and a workbench covered in rows of small vases in 2016, pendant lamps, a white cabinet with bottles and white vases beside black candlesticks in 2017, and a bright hall with a long table of vases, wooden chairs and screens in 2018. [S2]

A Berlin art university's program for its DDW trip of October 21 to 24, 2017 lists a visit to the Hallenweg for Vij5 and friends and Jeroen Wand, which puts the studio on a visitor's route in the year of the 2017 album, though a program is a plan and not a report. [S20] Only 2018 has a DDW page that names him. DDW's recap of Day 3, October 23, 2018, says that during the week the designers of the Hallenweg welcome visitors into their studios and that Jeroen Wand and Maarten Baptist were also exhibiting, one of eight design areas of the festival. [S21] Wallpaper*'s 2018 guide places Wand's veneer, PVC, porcelain and paper creations in The Young Collectors II, a three-story 1960s house of the studio Thier&vanDaalen on Populierenweg, not on the Hallenweg. [S22] So in 2018 his work was in at least two places, and the album does not say which one it shows. [S21][S22][S2]

The same year he showed abroad. A July 3, 2018 note from the London agency Zetteler lists Eindhoven's Studio Jeroen Wand, which it describes as known for raw and unpolished pieces that challenge conventions of beauty, among the highlights of that year's Dutch Stuff selection at London Design Fair, held at the Old Truman Brewery. [S23] Kazerne's designer page lists him in its exhibitions Open World (2014 to 2015), with a vase of PVC pipe, two small pieces of round timber and a hand-molded reservoir, and Fundamentals (2018 to 2019). [S24]
After 2018: a move, a prize and a different address

The studio's news says it moved to a new address, Bayeuxlaan 7, on March 14, 2019, which ends the Hallenweg workshop of the album years. [S25] On June 26, 2019 it posted that COS was showing its work in the retailer's Coal Drops Yard store in London. [S26] That September it took part in Dutch Design in NYC, shown from September 12 to December 20, 2019 by Ventura Projects with the designers' co-op Colony in SoHo. [S27] Design Milk lists it as one of seven designers in a show curated by Jean Lin of Colony and Margriet Vollenberg of Ventura Projects, at 324 Canal Street, and Interior Design adds that the project was supported by Dutch Culture USA, a program of the Dutch consulate general in New York. [S28][S29] The studio's Laminated Coffee Table won the ARC19 Award for best piece of furniture on a post dated November 14, 2019. [S30] The collection page confirms the prize and describes the table as part of the Re-veneer collection, in which leftover veneer is pressed together. [S31] MaterialDistrict, which published an entry for Re-veneer on May 26, 2021, says the pieces are industry leftovers pressed with a vacuum technique that needs no complicated molds. [S32]

The 2020s pages show a studio that works in several directions. Kazerne showed a Wand Laminated Table in its exhibition The Circle in 2020 and lists him in New Melancholy for 2020 to 2021. [S19][S24] A post from November 2020 describes a vase experiment a day during the first lockdown, a post of April 2021 announces the Design Open route in Eindhoven from June 13 to 17, a post of April 16, 2021 shows a custom interior for Design Museum Helmond made with HeyHeydeHaas, and a post of November 1, 2021 reports a new shop interior for the Haags Historisch Museum. [S33][S34][S35][S36] In 2023 Vij5 described the 's-Chair and 's-Table, designed for the education space of the Stedelijk Museum 's-Hertogenbosch, now the Design Museum Den Bosch, as part of its collection. [S10][S31]
What DDW's own pages list from 2023 to 2026
DDW's program has pages that bear on the studio in 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, though only the 2024 recap and the 2026 location page state their edition. [S11][S37][S38][S4]

The 2023 entry is Making, 15 years. It says the studio exists 15 years and shows its way of making in a retrospective of works with new interpretations added, that the outcome of 15 years includes a paper chair and glazed constructions, that visitors can browse a sample sale, and that the studio and workspace, in an old garage building hidden behind a gas station, are open to look into the workshop. It credits a plate made in collaboration with Cor Unum. [S11] The page prints no year. The image files attached to it carry upload dates of August 29, 2023, which is why I place it in DDW 2023. [S11]

The 2024 entry is Stacking. Multiple shapes are immersed in liquid plaster that unites them almost like a weld; the position of the shapes must be decided instantly while the plaster sets, and the page calls Stackings a continuation of the Phases project. [S37] The year again comes from the page's image upload date, September 27, 2024, and from DDW's own DDW24 area recap, which tells visitors in the Hallenweg area not to miss Studio Jeroen Wand for unconventional designs such as Stacking and EXO. [S37][S38] I found no program page for EXO.

For 2025 the program names Wand among the Dutch designers invited to make coat racks for To Come and to Go at Design Daily's gallery at Gestelsestraat 234, October 18 to 26, 2025. DDW lists that project under the Hallenweg area, but the address is not the studio's. [S39] DDW lists Studio Jeroen Wand for 2026 in the Hallenweg area, D8, at Bayeuxlaan 7, October 17 to 25, free to enter, 11:00 to 18:00 daily and fully wheelchair accessible. [S4] The Hallenweg is therefore an area label and not a street address for his studio today. [S4][S25]
What the albums can and cannot prove

A title in these albums can prove a year, a photographer and a place. It cannot show a work. The 2016 vase with a layered band tempts a caption, since the Boijmans records describe plaster vases with a coating, but no photo title names Phases, so I do not join them. [S2][S14] The 2017 album coincides in year with the museum presentation, and nothing connects the two. [S2][S9]

There is also a data question. Flickr album ids rise with creation time, and the series plan's list of 493 albums shows that the ids of the 2017 album (72157662464553208) and the 2018 album (72157675404555828) sit among ids of albums created in late 2015 and autumn 2016. [S40] That pattern appears in dozens of albums, including guest-academy albums whose photo titles carry the 2017 date, so it may reflect how DDW created and filled albums and not a wrong year. [S40] I cannot check the photographs' taken dates without contacting Flickr, so I treat it as a flag for checking and not as a finding. [S40][S2]
What the record does not show

I do not know which work any photograph in the three Wand albums shows, what the 2016 and 2017 shows were called, or whether the studio exhibited at DDW 2019 to 2022 under its own name; I found no program page for those years that I could open. [S2][S11] A search summary pointed to a studio post about a 2022 show, but it sits on a professional-network site that I did not open, so I use nothing from it. [S11] I did not open the studio's downloadable CV, a Word file, because it was a file download, and the About page's list of exhibitions appears to live there. [S7]

I do not know which Boijmans year is right for the presentation in the Paviljoen, 2017 or 2018 to 2019, or which version of the Laminated Table the museum holds. [S9][S18][S19] I do not know how the studio counts its 15 years. [S7][S11] Dezeen and Archello, which carry coverage of the 2019 New York show and a studio profile, refused automated requests, and I stopped there.
When you meet a studio through an archive of its open days, which would you rather have next to the picture, the year or the name of the piece? [S2]
