title: Manifestations at Dutch Design Week: eleven editions that count themselves, and five that the photo archive keeps
subtitle: A media art festival publishes a site for every year and numbers its own editions. Read against its funder, an academy and the official albums, the sites settle some questions and open others.
description: Manifestations, the media art festival at Dutch Design Week: eleven editions by its own count, edition sites, themes, venues and what the photo archive holds.

sections.x: Manifestations counts its own editions, and the count settles a question its edition sites leave open: Dutch Design Week's 2025 listing calls that year the tenth in a row and the 2026 listing the eleventh, which puts the first edition in 2016. [S17][S18]

That kind of self-counting is why this festival is easy to read and hard to check. The organizers publish a website for every edition, with themes, dates, floors, artist lists and sometimes visitor numbers, and the official photo archive holds albums for only five of the years. This essay reads the two against each other. It draws on public sources only: the festival's edition sites, its organizer's own site, a curator statement, a 2017 news item, two Royal Academy of Art pages, DDW's program listings, the funder's 2026 announcement and the photo archive as I recorded it on October 7 and 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 show beyond what those pages state. [S1][S9][S12][S20]
What the festival says it is

Manifestations calls itself a media art festival with an expo during Dutch Design Week, under the tagline Art, Tech & Fun. [S6][S7] Its 2026 about page says it is an initiative of Stichting Art & Technology and its creative director and curator, Viola van Alphen, and that it is free for everyone. [S10] The organizer's own site gives the foundation's name as ViolaVirus, Stichting Art & Technology, in Nijmegen, and says ViolaVirus is a split from PLANETART that arose in 2008 and is known for the projects GOGBOT, the Twente Biennale and TEC ART. [S12] Every edition site from 2018 to 2024 closes with the line "a production of ViolaVirus." [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6][S7]

The festival describes its method on the 2026 page: each year the curators go through the graduation shows of Dutch art and design academies looking for promising talent, which, the page says, makes the festival a springboard for beginning makers who are then noticed by scouts from festivals and museums. [S10] The same page lists a 2026 team of staff, floor managers, volunteers and guest curators and scouts, among them former exhibitors, and credits exhibition design to St Lucas College. [S10] That is the organizer's account of itself, and it fits what the edition sites show: lists of mostly young makers, with a Young Talent Award each year. [S1][S5][S10]

Curator statements are the other place to hear the festival's voice. In a statement for the ISEA2020 symposium, van Alphen writes that during Dutch Design Week, which she puts at 350,000 visitors, the festival presents 50 to 100 artists, that it works with a pool of more than 5,000 international artists, and that its focus is art with a human dimension, "always critical, playful, recognizable and awe-inspiring." [S13] In the same statement she lists four artists with the year each work was shown: Tim Dekkers' The Parasitic Humanity in 2018, Maartje Dijkstra's four works in 2019, Jip van Leeuwenstein's A Diverse Monoculture in 2017 and Daniëlle Ooms' Apple-based Material in 2019. [S13] Those are the only dated work titles in the sources that tie to a year outside the edition sites themselves.
The editions, one table
Year · Dates · Place · Theme or frame the site gives
2016 · October 22 to 30 [S21] · not stated in the page I read [S21] · the first edition by the 2026 count; "Best of DDW" winner per the 2018 site [S18][S1]
2017 · October 21 to 29, the dates of DDW 2017 [S22] · floors 8 and 9 of the Veemgebouw, plus a satellite show in the Eindhoven library [S14] · Will the Future Design Us? [S14]
2018 · October 20 to 28, 11:00 to 18:00 [S1] · floors 8 and 9, Veemgebouw [S1] · Will The Future Design Us? [S1]
2019 · October 19 to 27 [S2] · floor 9, Veemgebouw [S2][S16] · Superpowers (KABK's page title) [S16]
2020 · October 17 to 25 [S3] · virtual, in Second Life, Sansar and Mozilla Hubs [S3] · Monsters [S3][S2]
2021 · October 16 to 24, 11:00 to 18:30 [S4] · De Caai, the former Campina Melkfabriek, plus virtual worlds [S4] · not stated in the page text [S4]
2022 · October 22 to 30 [S5] · floor 8, Veemgebouw, plus virtual worlds [S5] · Bubbles [S5]
2023 · October 21 to 29 [S6] · floor 8, Veemgebouw [S6] · Vision, Think Bigger, Make Smarter Choices [S6]
2024 · October 19 to 27 [S7] · floor 8, Veemgebouw [S7] · Invisible Enemies [S7]
2025 · October 18 to 26 [S8] · VEEM, Strijp-S [S17] · Happy End? [S7]
2026 · October 17 to 25 [S9] · VEEM floor 8 [S18] · MUTE [S9][S18]

Three cells need a note. The 2016 place is not in the page text I could read, because the 2016 site refused my request twice with an HTTP 403 on its robots.txt, the second time after a 10-minute wait, and I made no further request to that host. [S21] The 2017 dates are those of Dutch Design Week 2017 in DDW's own music announcement, because the 2017 site itself is a blog without a date range in the text I read. [S22][S11][S14] And the 2019 theme name rests on the Royal Academy's listing, not on the festival's own 2019 page. [S16][S2]

The 2018 page also carries a number that does not hold still. It prints 4,500 square meters in one block and 6,000 in two other blocks, with the same wording around them. [S1] I report both and do not choose. Other sources give other sizes: the organizer's site describes the 2017 festival as three locations, 5,000 square meters and 50,000 visitors, and DDW's 2025 listing says Manifestations is 3,000 square meters. [S12][S17] None of the sources says how floor area was measured, and the numbers are a reminder that the festival's size varied with the floors it used. [S1][S12][S17]
What the early years looked like

The first public account of 2017 I found is a news item of September 27, 2017. It says the exhibition in the Veemgebouw shows the work of more than a hundred designers, fills the eighth and ninth floors with cyberpunk, brain-controlled robots, virtual reality, fashion-tech and a Museum of the Future, and includes smart nails, fantasy organs, an electronic house doctor, a robot that eats oak processionary caterpillars and interactive stick-on tattoos. [S14] It also reports a satellite exhibition in the Eindhoven library, The Internet of Women Things, where technology with a feminine edge is the subject, and quotes van Alphen saying that internet and technology are too often made by men for men. [S14] The festival's 2017 site is a blog of about 95 program posts with categories such as Young Talent (35 posts), High Tech Presentations (30) and Internet of Women Things (30), and a December 15, 2017 post says pictures and videos were online and that the site would not be updated to 2018 yet, to prevent copycats. [S11]

For 2016 the organizer's own site says the exhibition Manifestations: Will the Future Design Us? won the title Best of Dutch Design Week 2016 and lists press mentions it attributes to RTL-Z, de Volkskrant, De Telegraaf, Dezeen's best tips, a High Tech Campus tip and E52 as the most critical event of the week. [S12] The 2018 edition site repeats that the 2016 edition won Best of DDW, and the 2019 to 2024 sites close with "Manifestations was Winner Best of DDW." [S1][S2][S7] The 2026 about page gives the award without a year, and the 2016 date comes from the 2018 and organizer pages. [S10][S1][S12] I could not open any of the press items themselves, so these are the organizer's list.

The question Will the Future Design Us? was the title in 2016 and 2017 and again the 2018 site's frame. [S12][S14][S1] An essay that treats it as the 2018 theme alone would be wrong, and a caption should say the question was a standing heading across three editions. [S1][S12][S14]
2018 and 2019: works with names

The 2018 page lists works with their makers, among them Tim Dekkers' The Parasitic Humanity, Annemiek Höcker's The Search for Submission, Pelle Schilling's Incandescence, Esmee Kiewiet's OBJECTS, Pia Walter's AWE, Caio Vita's Imprecisely Human, Freerk Wieringa's Exoskeleton, Alexandra Ehrlich Speiser's USELESS WEAPONS, Jeanine Verloop's Reawaken, Dan Chen's End of Life Care Machine and Nicole Spit's NeoBio, and it names the 2018 Young Talent Award winners: Diego Grandry, Marie Cantenys and Sissel Tolaas from the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague took the award given with the sponsors GBO and Sioux, and Alexander van Bakel of the Rietveld Academy came second. [S1] The page's header text has been updated to advertise 2019, so the works list may mix years; Dekkers' 2018 date is confirmed by the curator statement. [S1][S13]

The Royal Academy's own page for Dutch Design Week 2018 says curator Viola van Alphen selected works showing the interaction between man and technology from different perspectives, lists alumni and students on floor 9 of the Veem, and names among them works such as Peer to Peer, Home in a Bag, Airphone, Responsive Tactility: 4D Printed Skins, George.io and The Undesirables. [S15] For 2019 the same academy lists the show as Manifestations - Superpowers on the ninth floor, with work by young talents and recent graduates, calls out the newest fashion and wearables, "botox," human mutations and post-apocalyptic design, and says two of its alumni were nominated for the Young Talent Award. [S16] The 2019 site gives the Young Talent Award winners as Pia-Marie Stute and Katja Trinkwalder for Accessories for the Paranoid, from the Köln International School of Design. [S2]

This is the best match between the festival's text and the photo archive. The old dossier read the 2018 and 2019 albums as 19 and 21 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge showing glass sculptures, mannequins in garments, a robotic arm and a person in a headset. [S20] The titles name none of the works, so I do not pair a photograph with a name from the lists above, and a caption should not either. [S20][S1]
2020 to 2022: virtual worlds and a cap on visitors

The 2020 site says the edition would take place virtually on manifestations.nl, on ddw.nl and in several virtual worlds, naming Second Life, Sansar and Mozilla Hubs, and that the festival hoped to be physical again at a later time at Sectie-C. [S3] That sentence resolves the puzzle in the old notes, which read the page as both virtual and located at Sectie-C. The address was a hoped-for later location. The page also gives the theme as Monsters on the 2019 page's header and asks visitors whether they might be the monster themselves. [S2][S3] The 2020 page is no longer a 2020 page: its text says the exhibition runs October 16 to 24 and that the 2021 site was coming. [S3]

For 2021 the site says the edition would take place in the Melkhal De Caai, the former Campina Melkfabriek, and online in the same virtual worlds, with entry free from 11:00 to 18:30. [S4] It sets a limit of 250 visitors inside at once, in a space the page says was calculated for many more, with constant ventilation and a tip to come between 11 and 13 hours. [S4] On masks the page says visitors could choose, and it names the World Health Organization and the German national institute's guidance instead of the Dutch national institute's. [S4] I report that as the organizers' statement and take no position on it.

In 2022 the festival returned to the Veem, on floor 8, with the same 250 cap and the theme Bubbles. [S5] The 2022 page sorts roughly 35 projects into four sections: Known Circles or Different Worlds?, Masks & Uniform, Conflict & Confidence, and Soap Bubble & Transience, and tags 21 projects as nominated for the Young Talent Award by named academies. [S5] It names the French collective RYBN's The Great Offshore, a research project on offshore finance co-produced with several French and European institutions, as one work, and notes that a design and art shop was being set up next door with Emmaus Eindhoven where artists could sell without charge. [S5] A visitor looking at the 2022 album would meet a staged bedroom with a retro computer, according to the old dossier, and the page does not say which project that was. [S5][S20]
2023 and 2024: the same floor, different questions

The 2023 page gives the theme as Vision, Think Bigger, Make Smarter Choices and groups its works under headings including Mens? and Duurzaam. [S6] The 2024 page gives Invisible Enemies, with headings on the human as creator and destroyer, social injustice and victim blaming, and technological influences and alternative realities. [S7] Both pages list between 30 and 40 projects with short texts, and both say the festival was on floor 8 and in virtual worlds, with entry free. [S6][S7]

Names recur across the three years from 2022 to 2024. Viola Renate appears in 2022 and again in 2023, Nonna Hoogland and Agnes van Dijk appear in 2023 and 2024, and the Emmaus Eindhoven design shop is on both the 2023 and 2024 pages. [S5][S6][S7] The 2026 team page lists Agnes van Dijk as supervision and a guide, and names Abel Kamps, Tom Haakman and Aïsha Dingemans among guest curators and scouts, so exhibitors turn into curators. [S10] I draw one conclusion from this: the festival keeps its own alumni near it. I do not know how many of the roughly 35 projects a year are new, because the pages do not say. [S5][S6][S7][S10]
2025 and 2026: counted by DDW

DDW's own program listings are the plainest source for the last two years. The 2025 listing says Manifestations is 3,000 square meters, with 50 artists of the future, robots, e-fashion and kids, at VEEM on Strijp-S, with free entrance. [S17] The 2026 listing says it is hosted by Manifestations, Art & Technology, on floor 8 of the VEEM building, with free access, open daily from 11:00 to 18:30, and describes more than 50 works by mostly young, recently graduated artists, tours that open three days earlier for tours and press, and wheelchair access at the back. [S18] The 2026 listing also says it is the largest art and tech event during Dutch Design Week, and I treat that as the organizer's claim. [S18]

The funder describes the 2026 festival too. The Creative Industries Fund NL's announcement of January 14, 2026 says the fund considered 31 proposals in a festival grant scheme, selected 21, and lists Manifestations 2026 among them as a 10-day free festival with some 50 works whose theme MUTE touches on silence, censorship and self-censorship. [S19] That description says ten days where the festival's own dates give nine, October 17 to 25, and the difference may count an earlier opening for tours. [S19][S9][S18] The 2026 edition is covered by its own piece in this series, and this essay stops there.
What the albums keep

The old dossier counts five albums for 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2024, with 19, 21, 83, 100 and 8 photographs, 231 in all, credited in the titles to Tommy Köhlbrugge, about.today and Cleo Goossens. [S20] I did not reopen Flickr for this version. What the albums show is mostly mood: lit glass, mannequins, a staged bedroom, visitors reading paper scrolls. [S20] The festival's own sites hold what the albums lack, which is the names of works, makers and themes. [S1][S5][S20]

The albums miss 2016, 2017, 2020, 2023 and 2025 by the dossier's reading. [S20] Between them, the festival's sites show that Manifestations took place in each of those years, so a timeline built from the archive alone would skip five of the eleven editions. [S11][S3][S6][S8][S20]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**When it began.** The edition archive on the sites runs back to 2016, and the DDW listings count the 2025 edition as the tenth and the 2026 edition as the eleventh. The count settles 2016, including the virtual 2020 edition. [S17][S18]
**What "Best of DDW" refers to.** The 2026 page gives it without a year. The 2018 site and the organizer's site say the 2016 edition won it. [S10][S1][S12]
**Where the 2020 edition was.** Online, in virtual worlds, with a physical edition at Sectie-C only hoped for later. [S3]
**How big 2018 was.** The 2018 page prints both 4,500 and 6,000 square meters. Not settled. [S1]
**Whether the question was a 2018 theme.** It was the title in 2016 and 2017 as well. [S1][S12][S14]
**How long the 2026 festival runs.** Nine days by its own dates, ten by the funder's summary. Not settled. [S9][S18][S19]
What the record does not show

I do not know where the 2016 edition stood, what it showed or how many visited, because the 2016 site was not open to me. I do not know how many visitors any edition drew apart from the organizer's own 50,000 for 2017, which sits on its site without a method. [S12][S21] I do not know which works the photographs in the albums show, or whether the albums include works from the lists above. I did not find independent reviews of any edition, and the press items the organizer lists were not opened. [S12]
The photo archive counts and titles come from the October 7 and 8 readings, not from this pass. [S20]

If a festival numbers its own editions, keeps a website for each and then moves on to the next year's site, which of those pages would you trust to tell you what happened in a year you did not attend? [S17][S18]

title: Modebelofte, then New Order of Fashion: a graduate platform that kept changing its organizer, its name and its building
subtitle: What the curators' pages, the trade press and Dutch Design Week's listings say about one fashion platform, 2014 to 2026, and what the photo archive can hold.
description: One fashion platform at Dutch Design Week, 2014 to 2026: two names, changing organizers and buildings, and what a photo archive can hold.

sections.x: Modebelofte's own curators credit one organizer for its first three Dutch Design Weeks and another for the next three, and a photo archive that files every year under one name cannot show either change. [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5]

As a content strategist I read a rename as a content problem: the thing keeps moving and the label has to keep up. This essay follows one fashion platform through its own curators' pages, trade and design press, Dutch Design Week's listings and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the published listings say. [S1][S12][S17][S20]
Two names, and a start date that depends on who is counting

Modebelofte is Dutch for fashion promise. Studio Harm Rensink, the studio that designed and curated it, calls it an international platform for fashion talents that presents graduates of international bachelor and master courses. [S2] FashionUnited reported on October 26, 2018 that Modebelofte would continue after that edition as New Order of Fashion, and a year later said 2019 was the first edition under the new name, chosen to make the international character of the platform clear. [S12][S13]

The curator's own page for 2018 is already titled New Order of Fashion, while FashionUnited and the photo archive call the 2018 edition Modebelofte, so the name changed inside a window and not on a single day. [S5][S12][S20]

Start dates disagree in a useful way. Studio Harm Rensink says it has worked on the creative direction and exhibition design since 2014. [S5] FashionUnited wrote in 2017 that the platform was founded five years earlier as part of Dutch Design Week, and in 2018 that it had been part of the festival for six years. [S11][S12] Both counts point to 2012. Dezeen's 2025 report, which I read in an earlier pass and could not reopen, also gives 2012 as the year Ellen Albers started it. [S22] I read these as one story told by different people: the platform began around 2012, and this studio has shaped it since 2014. The trade counts are loose, so I say around 2012 and not 2012.
2014 to 2016: the retailer years

For the first three editions in the studio's records, the credit lines name a local retailer. The pages for 2014, 2015 and 2016 say the show was initiated and organized by You Are Here, with the exhibition design by Studio Harm Rensink and HeyNiek. [S1][S2][S3] The 2017 and 2018 pages instead say initiated by Ellen Albers. [S4][S5] No page I opened explains the handover, and FashionUnited calls Albers the initiator of Modebelofte in 2017. [S11] That leaves the earlier years of her role open.

The 2014 edition was called Seductive Precursors and filled an abandoned, slightly notorious disco club with floating mannequins, black walls, directional light and white dust on a granulated floor. The studio describes the mood as Tim Burton's Corpse Bride going clubbing. [S1] The 2015 edition, Performing Advancers, took its sports theme to the home of PSV, the Philips football stadium. [S2] Dezeen counted 42 designers from 15 courses and gave the dates as October 14 to 25, 2015. [S21] The photo archive holds 42 photographs for 2015 too, and I treat the match as coincidence, since a count of photographs is a count of what was posted. [S20]

In 2016, under the theme Adaptive Travelers, the platform took over de Bijenkorf, one minute from Eindhoven Central Station, using the shop windows, part of the first and third floors and the roof for about 30 graduates. [S3] Neon Moire's guide to the fifteenth Dutch Design Week listed it at the Bijenkorf roof, October 22 to 30, 2016, 10:00 to 18:00, entrance 2 euros, with a talk show at the Van Abbemuseum on October 23. [S9] Visi, reporting from the festival, wrote that fashion students showed how clothes might become resources for shelter, safety and energy in an apocalyptic world. [S10]
2017: a department store with the lights half off

Digital Realists in 2017 showed 18 international designers in what the studio calls an abandoned V&D warehouse and FashionUnited calls the former V&D store on the Vrijstraat. [S4][S11] FashionUnited gives the size as 2,500 square meters, made available by the owner of the building to Albers, and says the ground floor also held a small coffee shop, a design hair salon and a robot space, and that Vlisco showed creations on the floor where clothing collections used to hang. [S11] The curators were Rensink and Lisanne Fransen, and the reporter noticed that they left out mannequin silhouettes, so gender did not show, and let masks, headwear and shoes carry the human presence. [S11]

The studio's credits show how many hands a platform like this has. Production was by Fabian Briels, artwork and animation by Leeza Pritychenko and music by a Gothenburg electronic duo, with photography by Barbara Medo. [S4]
2018 and 2019: the rename year, then the new name

The 2018 edition, Shape Shifters, ran to October 28 with a 2 euro ticket. FashionUnited names 21 participants, one of them a studio, among them Sinéad O'Dwyer, Kota Okuda, Pierre-Louis Auvray, Emma Wessel and Paolo Carzana, and two collaborations with New Order of Fellowships, a concept it says was introduced in 2017: Ecco Leather and Kobe with Kira Goodney, and with the duo AnoukxVera. [S12] The studio's text asks what fashion does with our shape and with our concept of self. [S5] An earlier version of this essay said FashionUnited counted twenty individual designers. The page lists 21 names and states no count. [S12]

In 2019 the exhibition moved to a vacant former V&D store at Rechtestraat 8, open through October 27, under the theme The End is Near, Time for New Beginnings. [S6][S13] The studio describes a tilted world where walls were about to collapse, airbrushed artwork provided by the graduates, and a Talks program at the center of the exhibition. [S6] FashionUnited quotes Rensink saying the dark entrance hall signals a world at a tipping point. [S13] The report lists a coat made of used tea bags by Benedetta Marcucci, a dress of old plastic car parts strung on metal chains by Valentine Tinchant, and a graduation project by Laura Frandsen that was a cart of discarded clothes instead of a collection. [S13]

FashionUnited notes the earlier venues, the old V&D building several times, the Bijenkorf roof and the Philips stadium, and that earlier partnerships included Ecco and Vlisco. In 2019 the partners were instead textile-innovation parties: Unseam, which makes seamless fabric from digital 3D shapes and researches a leather alternative from jellyfish, and Sunbrella with the designer Wendy Andreu. [S13] The studio's 2019 page thanks Albers, Emma Wessel, Frank Verkade, Grietje Schepers and Jelle Smidt as the team that supports the exhibitions through the year, and credits the photography to Ronald Smits. [S6]
2020 to 2023: a lab, a school and a theme

I found no written source for 2020, when the festival was largely online. The archive's 2020 album has nine photographs of a New Order Fashion Store, as I read it earlier, and nothing in the pages I opened describes that show. [S20]

For 2021, FashionUnited reported the show, Do It, A joint Catalyst for Change, at Strijp S from October 16 to 24, with 16 entries in its list of graduates (Jessica Guzman appears twice, so the list holds 15 names). The graduates were mentored by Rensink as creative head, Pauline van Dongen as artistic research mentor, Matthew Needham and Stina Randestad, and their work would stay in the platform's circular lab and fashion atelier. [S14] The report names the supporters as Cultuur Eindhoven, Het Nieuwe Instituut, the Prins Bernhard Cultuurfonds, Regiodeal Brainport Eindhoven and the Stimulation Fund Creative Industries, and lists partners that include Aalto University, Fashion for Good, Kniterate and The Student Hotel. [S14]

By 2022 the FashionUnited route for fashion fans placed a New Order of Fashion Lab on the Torenallee, with recent graduates' work and material and artistic research by the makers around the lab, and an embroidery atelier at The Student Hotel near the station with workshops by Martine van 't Hul and Woo Jin Joo. [S15] Design Milk's report on the 2023 exhibition, Regeneration: Fashion From The Ground Up, says it explored regeneration through three lenses, Earth Care, People Care and Fair Share, and describes projects such as a needle-lace dress of lavender seeds grown over two summers and a garment woven as a whole. [S16] The photo archive I read has no 2023 album. [S20]
2024 to 2026: the lab with a wool theme

For 2024 the only source I have is the archive's five-photograph album titled with the lab, as I read it earlier, and nothing describes the show. [S20] For 2025, Dezeen reported a wool exhibition, Wool (Re)discovered, in the platform's makerspace at Strijp-S, noting that 1.5 million kilograms of wool are discarded each year in the Netherlands, and named Haiko Huvenaars as director. I read that article in the earlier pass and could not reopen it. [S22]

For 2026, Dutch Design Week lists the New Order of Fashion LAB at Torenallee 22-06, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, October 17 to 25, with the exhibition Regeneration: Fashion from the Source. [S17] The program entry Flock, Folk, Field is a wool exhibition in three parts, Flock, Folk and Field, that follows wool from animals and landscapes to the people who shape it. The entry describes the organization as a talent development and knowledge platform with three pillars, Explore, Educate and Activate. [S18] A second item at the same address, With Reflection, shows ten textile veils by the Brussels designer Antoine Guitou. [S19]
The curator's other work

The same studio that curates the platform designed the Bart Hess retrospective Future Bodies at the Stedelijk Museum in 's-Hertogenbosch in 2017, transforming 500 square meters of exhibition space, and shared the exhibition design credit with Hess for BodyDrift in 2020. [S7][S8] That is the kind of fact an archive of fashion albums cannot hold.
What an archive can and cannot do for a platform like this

The photo archive holds ten albums, with 42, 23, 18, 17, 19, 9, 23, 51, 5 and 21 photographs, 228 in all. I read them in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so the Flickr facts are second-hand. [S20] The photographer credits in the archive titles differ from the credits on the curator's pages. The studio credits Barbara Medo for 2014, 2015, 2017 and 2018, Gert Jan van Rooij for 2016 and Ronald Smits for 2019, while the archive's titles name other photographers. Festival and studio photographers can differ, and the pages do not say. [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6][S20]
What the record does not show
What the 2020 and 2024 shows were. [S20]
Whether Albers was part of the organization in 2014 to 2016, when the credit line names You Are Here. [S1][S2][S3][S4]
Details of the 2025 show beyond one article I could not reopen. [S22]
Why the archive has no 2023 album although a 2023 show is documented. [S16][S20]
Where the 2018 and 2022 shows stood; no page I opened names the 2018 venue. [S12]
When you read a timeline of a moving platform, which line tells you who was organizing it in a given year, and which only tells you where? [S5]

title: MVRDV built a hotel in 2017 and a walk-through in 2018, and the city kept the argument
subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week editions of an architecture office whose founder was also the city's supervisor, read through MVRDV's pages, the press, the municipality and the official photo archive
description: MVRDV at Dutch Design Week 2017 and 2018: a nine-room folly, a city-center pavilion and the supervisor role behind them.

sections.x: In 2017 MVRDV put a nine-meter hotel on a town square, and in 2018 it asked visitors to walk through a city center that did not exist yet. [S1][S3]

I like an architecture office that shows its argument at full size, because the photographs then have something to prove. This essay draws on public sources only: MVRDV's own news posts and project pages, a VPRO interview, two Dutch architecture-news reports, the municipality of Eindhoven's own policy page and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what MVRDV shows at the 2026 festival. [S1][S3][S7][S8][S10][S13]
An office, a festival role and a city job

MVRDV says it was founded in 1993 by Winy Maas, Jacob van Rijs and Nathalie de Vries, works from Rotterdam, Shanghai, Paris, Berlin and New York, and has a team of over 300. [S11] The Dutch Design Week archive holds four MVRDV albums, two for 2017 and two for 2018, 53 photographs in all, 43 for 2017 and 10 for 2018. [S13]

The photographs show the work of an office, and the sources show that Maas wore two other hats in these years. MVRDV's post of October 18, 2017 begins with his role as ambassador of Dutch Design Week 2017, in which he, The Why Factory, the municipality of Eindhoven, the Eindhoven University of Technology and the festival curated four interventions on what he called future city products. [S1] In the VPRO's interview of the same day he says he first came to the festival four years earlier and has not missed an edition since, and the interviewer notes that the municipality had recently named him supervisor of the city center. [S7]

Architectenweb later put the start of that supervisor job in 2017, and MVRDV's own announcement of February 25, 2022 describes almost five years in the role. [S8][S6] The exhibitions of 2017 and 2018 therefore sit at the start of a municipal appointment. I could not open the municipality's own announcement of it, because the city's website refused the request, so the appointment date rests on the two news items. [S6][S8]
2017: four interventions, not two

MVRDV's project page for the same week lists a slightly longer partner line than the post does: MVRDV, The Why Factory, the municipality, the Eindhoven University of Technology, IIT Chicago and Dutch Design Week. [S4] MVRDV's post names four interventions, and the shorthand of a hotel and a masterclass leaves two out. [S1] The Future City is Wide was a film at the entrance of the Klokgebouw exhibition center, sorted by agenda point, showing hundreds of ideas from students of The Why Factory. [S1] The Future City has Memories was a presentation and book launch of the Why Factory's Copy Paste: A Badass Copy Guide at the Klokgebouw, which the post says treats works of architecture as if they were science, so that a famous bridge could become a hospital. [S1] The VPRO adds a datingbank for designers and plants in the Veemgebouw, a board with a thousand packets of seed, as a prelude to the Floriade 2022 in Almere, which it says MVRDV would design. [S7] The two interventions the archive photographed are the other two: (W)ego and ICI Eindhoven. [S1][S13]
(W)ego: a hotel of nine wishes

The post calls (W)ego The Future City is Flexible, an installation on the Markt square with nine rooms made from an idealistic but egoistic perspective, including a panorama room, a stair room and a sky room. [S1] A second post dated October 20, 2017 gives the opening dates, October 21 to 29, 2017, and quotes Maas on the hypothesis that the maximum density could equal the maximum of desires. [S2] It adds that the installation represents a frozen moment of a living, flexible vision from The Why Factory, in which future dwellings adapt in real time to their users, and that a film in one of the rooms details that vision. [S2] The first post describes it as a walkable folly nine meters high with nine hotel rooms. [S1]

The idea is a negotiation. Users share a limited space and must deal with the dream rooms of others, so that ego becomes wego. [S1][S2] The VPRO quotes Maas describing a labyrinth of small rooms, some vertical and some horizontal, a puzzle in which you feel close to the neighbor and still have privacy, and it says the intention was that the public could really sleep a night there. [S7] MVRDV's own posts do not mention overnight stays, so I cannot say whether anyone slept in it. [S1][S2][S7]

The archive's (W)ego album holds 21 photographs, 16 credited in the titles to Ossip van Duivenbode and 5 to Ruud Balk. [S13] In one view, rooms in green, orange, pink and blue glow on a black platform at dusk, with café umbrellas and old buildings behind. In another, a single red room has slatted shutters, a round basin and a toilet. [S13] Titles name no rooms. That is the problem with photographing a building made of wishes: the whole facade can stand for the project, while what each room was for goes unrecorded. I can say the archive shows the rooms, and I cannot say which wish belongs to which. [S1][S13]

The idea did not end with the week. The Why Factory's own news page lists a Wego exhibition at the TU Delft on October 7, 2021, as part of the Together! exposition, describing the research as a desire-based design process that brings residents' wishes into the construction and adaptation of housing, with a book in its Future Cities series planned with NAi010 Publishers. [S14] The same page announces a launch of the Why Factory's book (w)Ego, with a lecture by Maas, dated May 18, 2022. [S14] The folly on the Markt was, on that evidence, one stage of a research project that ran at least four and a half years. [S2][S14]
ICI Eindhoven: the kick-off

The fourth intervention, The Future City is Eindhoven, was the presentation on Stadhuisplein of a masterclass on the intensification of uses in the city center, in which students from several universities showed a wide variety of towers that could one day be built there. [S1] MVRDV's post says the event was the kick-off for Maas's supervisory role for Eindhoven's inner city and that he began by asking citizens and discussing the future of their city. [S1]

The archive's album for it holds 22 photographs, all credited to Ruud Balk. [S13] A gray pavilion carries cut-out letters that spell COME beneath the words Future Downtown Eindhoven, and inside, a round table is covered with an aerial photograph and a white block model of the city center. [S13] At night a panel on the pavilion reads WE ARE HERE BECAUSE OF and lists logos, among them Eindhoven, Dutch Design Week Eindhoven, TU/e, MVRDV, TU Delft and De Meeuw. [S13] The post names several of the same partners among the sponsors: De Meeuw, Dutch Design Week, the municipality, Van Beek Art Supplies, TU Delft, TU Eindhoven and Keeper Development. [S1]

Here the photographs do more than the titles. Lettering and a partner panel are text a reader can check, and they tie the pictures to the project in the project's own words. A city-scale argument needs more than one author, and the sponsor list says so in plain terms. [S1][S13]
2018: Future Downtown, with the job already running

MVRDV's post of October 19, 2018 dates the week October 20 to 28 and lists three things. A talk by Winy Maas was set for Wednesday, October 24 at 14:00 at the VDMA complex, supported by Architectuur Centrum Eindhoven and the municipality. An exhibition ran there all week, and Virtual Future Downtown, an augmented reality walk, stood in a large glass greenhouse on Stadhuisplein, made with the municipality and Dutch Rose Media as Future040. [S3] The post says that in his role as supervisor of the city center Maas was asked to guide the vision and planning of the inner city, and that the exhibition's pavilion shows the work on upgrading the center, on radical greenification and on intensifying urban life, with an invitation to add more and talk about your Future Downtown Eindhoven. [S3] An MVRDV event page gives the talk's address as 31T Vestdijk and says tickets sold out and the lecture was live-streamed. [S5]

The archive answers with two albums, 6 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge and 4 by Ruud Balk. [S13] A window sign reads Future Downtown Eindhoven and the words intense, accessible, green, for everybody and wonderful. A white block model carries small green trees. A greenhouse of glass pavilions carries the words Virtual Downtown Eindhoven on its panes. [S13] It is tempting to put the greenhouse and the walk in the foreground, but the post puts the exhibition and the talk at the VDMA first, and the six-photograph album most likely belongs there, given its title. [S3][S13]

One caution on names: the album is titled Virtual Future Downtown, while its four photo titles read Near Future Downtown. [S13] MVRDV's own post uses Virtual Future Downtown, so I use that name and note the difference. [S3] The augmented reality walk itself cannot appear in a photograph of a greenhouse, so the archive shows the container and not the experience.
What came of it

The exhibitions were not self-contained. MVRDV's announcement of Maas stepping down describes the Inner City Densification Vision, adopted by the city council at the end of 2020, as an important achievement of the supervision, with two layers, an Eindhoven layer capped at 17 meters at ground level and a Brainport layer on top that reaches 45, 75, 105 or even 160 meters for individual buildings. [S6] The municipality's own page for the vision confirms that the council adopted it on December 15, 2020, unchanged, and that the council embraced two motions, to keep the green wedges free of housing and to evaluate every large building project completed in the center. [S10] Architectenweb reported that 39 of the 45 council members voted for it. [S9]

The numbers differ. MVRDV writes that the vision shows tens of thousands of additional homes can be created through densification alone. [S6] Architectenweb wrote that up to 10,000 new homes could be realized. [S9] The municipality's page says a tactical study found room for at most 21,000 homes within the ring road, provided that conditions on mobility, green space and water are met, against a regional agreement to build 35,000 to 40,000 homes in Eindhoven by 2040. [S10] I take the municipality's 21,000 as the best-sourced ceiling and note that neither "tens of thousands" nor 10,000 matches it exactly.

The ending was contested. Architectenweb reported that the contract with Maas as supervisor was not extended and ended on December 31, 2021, that the municipality said the decision was taken in good consultation, and that local politicians had criticized a double role as supervisor and architect, after which a new supervisor would not be allowed to combine the two. [S8] MVRDV said the new conditions made a proper fulfillment of the role impossible, and Maas said he wanted to do things himself and would focus on projects such as De Heuvel and the city office. [S6][S8] The municipality said the area visions had been adopted and the phase had moved from plan to development. [S8]

I mention this because the 2017 and 2018 photographs can look like architecture alone. They are also a record of a public role being introduced to the public at a festival, and the role's later dispute is part of what those exhibitions were for. The sources say that Maas's DDW work was framed as the start of the supervisory role. They do not say whether the dispute affected how the festival later treated MVRDV. [S1][S3][S8]
What an archive count cannot tell us

I would not read 43 photographs against 10 as a measure of how big each year was. An archive count records what was photographed and kept. MVRDV's posts give no visitor counts for its own projects, and the 2018 post's total refers to the whole of Dutch Design Week, with a figure of more than 335,000 visitors that matches the number Baltan Laboratories gives for the 2017 edition, so I do not use it for 2018. [S3][S12] Credits show the same partial record: three photographers cover the four albums, and no title names a designer at MVRDV. [S13] Two editions are enough to compare and not enough to call a trend. The archive may also hold more MVRDV photographs under other album titles, and I did not search for them.
What the record does not show

I do not know whether anyone slept in (W)ego. I could not open the municipality's announcement of the supervisor appointment, or the festival's own programme pages for the 2018 events, which no longer open at the old addresses. I do not know which of the 2018 photographs were taken at the VDMA and which on Stadhuisplein. [S3][S13]
If a project asks you to imagine a city, is the model the exhibit or the evidence? Next time you photograph a model, photograph its label too. [S13]

title: Next Nature went from a job agency for robots to a museum in a landed spacecraft
subtitle: Four Dutch Design Week editions of Next Nature, 2017 to 2025, read from Next Nature's own pages, DDW's program archive and the photo archive.
description: Next Nature's HUBOT job agency in 2017, RetroFuture in the Evoluon in 2022, and the 2024 and 2025 museum shows, against the DDW photo albums.

sections.x: Next Nature began its Dutch Design Week story in this archive as a job agency for people and robots in an electronics store, and it appears in the later albums as the museum inside a building that looks like a landed spacecraft. [S1][S3]

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds four Next Nature albums, 2017, 2022, 2024 and 2025, 62 photographs in all. [S12] Next Nature's own pages are unusually detailed about what it was doing in each of those years, and DDW's program pages let me test them. This essay draws on public sources only. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what the museum will show in the 2026 edition beyond what its pages list. [S7][S9]
I like a maker whose projects grow in size while the question stays the same, because it lets me test whether an archive can follow. [S10]
An organization that describes itself as a radar

Next Nature's about page calls it a non-profit of creatives, thinkers, educators and supporters, with members in 44 countries and a museum in the Netherlands, and says it explores how technology becomes so omnipresent, complex, intimate and autonomous that it becomes a nature of its own. [S10] Its colophon lists Koert van Mensvoort as founder and CEO, a core team based in Eindhoven, and a set of named ambassadors that includes the astronaut André Kuipers, the philosopher Jos de Mul and the biotechnologist Mark Post. [S11] I found no founding year on those pages, so I give none.

Next Nature's project pages describe earlier work in the same register. One is the NANO Supermarket, a mobile exhibition disguised as a shop that presents 50 speculative nanotech products, which its page says had received more than 75,000 visitors in cities including Eindhoven, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Pamplona, Milan and Stavanger. [S13] That page gives no dates and does not mention DDW, so I treat it as background and not as a DDW presentation. [S13]
2017: HUBOT, in a store window

In a story dated October 4, 2017, Next Nature introduced HUBOT as the job agency for people and robots. It said the virtual office would open on October 12, and that HUBOT could be found at the MediaMarkt in Eindhoven from October 21, during Dutch Design Week 2017, and would travel the world afterward. It named three partners: Next Nature Network, Start Foundation and Gemeente Eindhoven. [S1]

The story describes 16 professions, "jobs from the future," in which technology lets people do work they could not otherwise do, and offers examples such as a mover in a robotic suit, a gaming farm manager and a six-armed masseur. [S1] The project page adds an air traffic security worker who flies an eagle drone to keep birds away from planes, and a home healthcare professional whose cleaning drone leaves time to talk with patients. [S2] It also says the exhibition could be hired for events, with two self-driving robots, a career test and four trained agency workers. [S2]

The 2017 album is titled HUBOT | Next Nature Network and holds 19 photographs by Ralph Roelse. Its photo titles name MediaMarkt and the dates October 21 to 29, 2017, which matches the story. [S12][S1] The photographs show a store with displays set among the shelves: a clear robot torso with white tube arms beside a screen reading Uitzendbureau voor mens en robot, a robotic suit on a plinth, and a wooden sign headed HUBOT - The job agency for people and robots. [S12] The suit and the torso fit the jobs the pages list, but no sign I could read names the six-armed masseur, so I do not say that is what the torso is. [S1][S12]
The building Next Nature took on

Next Nature's New Evoluon page says the Evoluon was built in 1966 as a technology and science museum on behalf of Frits Philips, to celebrate the 75th anniversary of Philips; that it drew over 500,000 visitors by 1970 with interactive exhibits; and that it was withdrawn from operation in 1989 despite many protests. [S3] The page says the building's design reminds one of a spacecraft that landed in Eindhoven, announces a collaboration between Next Nature and the Evoluon Foundation, and proposes a plan in four rings: geosphere, biosphere, technosphere and mindsphere. [S3] It says that in the fall of 2021 the building became a VR Time Machine, and that the first major exhibition, RetroFuture, would debut on September 24, 2022. [S3] These are Next Nature's own statements, and they carry its enthusiasm. I did not find an independent source for the visitor count or the closure date.
2022: RetroFuture

DDW's program lists RetroFuture as a DDW 2022 project presented by Next Nature, in the Evoluon, with ten tunnels across 3,000 square meters and work by Studio Drift, Maison de Faux with Esmay Wagemans, Driessens & Verstappen, Audrey Large, Tabita Rezaire, Michael Mandiberg and Studio Smack. [S5] It describes a fairground area with ten ideas on contemporary topics, among them the Microbial Vending Machine by Emma van der Leest, a converted snack machine with products made from algae and enzymes in place of croquettes, a VR Time Machine, a haunted house and a slot machine about the future of money. [S5] Next Nature's own project page gives a figure of over 50,000 tickets sold and says visitors could create a deepfake of themselves in the funfair. [S4] The ticket figure is Next Nature's claim, and the page gives no date for the count. [S4]

The 2022 album is titled Evoluon and holds 22 photographs: 16 by Tommy Köhlbrugge titled RetroFuture and dated October 22 and 23, 2022, and six by about.today titled with the spelling VRPO. [S12] They show a glass tunnel of robots, a wall of historic photographs, an atrium with a spiral stair, banners reading Inclusion in many languages and a DeLorean with an Evoluon plate. [S12] The spelling VRPO is probably a typo for VPRO, but no page I opened says so. [S12]
2024: a recap with names and no dates

The DDW24 area recap, dated October 24, 2024, says the West area is home to the Evoluon, which it calls the Next Nature Museum, and names projects such as Microbial Oasis, A House of Salt and Meet Meat: Rourou's Adventure, and a Breathing Session with Geoffrey Lillemon. [S6] It prints no dates for them. [S6] The 2024 album is the smallest in the set, with 7 photographs dated October 19, 20 and 23 that show a yellow dome with hand-drawn walls, a dome of seed images and visitors lying on mats in a dark dome. [S12] No title names a work. [S12]
2025: fifty talents under one dome

Next Nature's page for Digital Futures says the museum presented it in collaboration with DDW, with the works of 50 pioneering talents and makers in the Dome from October 18 to 26, 2025, free to visit as part of the DDW program, while a museum ticket was needed for RetroFuture and the Digital Wellness Center. [S8] It describes Econario by Woven Studio as a 5-meter-high robotic plant driven by predictions from the Natural History Museum's Biodiversity Intactness Index, and Apathos by Studio Falkland as a human-sized phone from the front and a server from the back that shows how scrolling and liking lead to recommendations. [S8] It describes Bloomlight S by Justus Bruns as a lamp whose stem bends toward someone who approaches, an example of slow tech. [S8] Those are the museum's descriptions of works. The 2025 album holds 14 photographs, several with visitors in headsets gesturing in the air, and no title names a work, so I cannot match a photograph to any project above. [S12]
The plan that changed

In 2022 the New Evoluon page said the aim was a fully reopened Evoluon from 2025. [S3] The museum's current "on show" page says something different: it lists Once Upon a Time… the Earth as the first chapter of Enter Spaceship Earth, the permanent exhibition being developed at the Evoluon, alongside a Quantum Escape Room, a Facebook Museum, the Digital Wellness Center and RetroFuture. [S9] So by October 2026 the permanent exhibition is under development and has not fully opened, and the 2025 date in the old plan has passed. [S3][S9] I do not know why the schedule moved, and no source I opened says. DDW's location page lists the Next Nature Museum at Noord Brabantlaan 1A with opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 daily during October 17 to 25, 2026. [S7]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**Where HUBOT stood.** An earlier timeline could not place the album at the Evoluon. Next Nature's story and the photo titles agree on the MediaMarkt, which settles it. [S1][S12]
**The Evoluon's reopening.** The 2022 page promises a full reopening from 2025, and the current page describes a permanent exhibition in development. The current page is the later statement. [S3][S9]
**Visitor numbers.** Over 500,000 by 1970 (the Evoluon) and over 50,000 tickets (RetroFuture) are Next Nature's figures, undated and with no outside source. [S3][S4]
What the record does not show

I do not know the founding year of Next Nature, the dates of the 2024 projects, what any 2024 or 2025 photograph shows beyond its description, or what the Evoluon's 2023 album adds, since it belongs to the Evoluon venue timeline. I did not find a DDW program page for HUBOT. Next Nature's press page lists a media kit titled Eindhoven viert 60 jaar Evoluon, and I did not find its text. [S14] The album facts are from my reading of the Flickr account on October 8, 2026, which I did not repeat. [S12]
If an organization's address changes from a store to a spaceship, what would you ask a photograph to prove before you let it tell you the story? [S12]

title: NUL ZES at Dutch Design Week: a gasworks site, a collective of studios and the makers the archive files under three names
subtitle: The NRE terrein, the studios of Lotte de Raadt, Kirstie van Noort and Alissa+Nienke, and what five albums from 2018 to 2025 can and cannot show of them.
description: The NRE terrein, the NUL ZES collective since 2013, the studios of Lotte de Raadt, Kirstie van Noort and Alissa+Nienke, and what the DDW albums show.

sections.x: One corner of Eindhoven, a former gasworks, appears in the Dutch Design Week photo archive under a collective's name, under the names of two sets of makers, and under a show title that a 2018 review ties to a third maker. [S1][S2][S3]

I like an archive that makes me sort names before I write a caption. This essay uses the places' own pages, a city guide, a municipal planning document, DDW interviews and program pages, the founders' and makers' own accounts, regional and trade press from 2017 to 2023, and the DDW photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it does not call the makers young, because no source I opened does. [S4][S5][S6][S1]
The place: a gasworks that became a utility, then a neighborhood

This is Eindhoven says the NRE-terrein has been a gasworks site since 1899, owes its name to the Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven (the utilities of the Eindhoven region) that were there from 1989 to 2010, and was then bought by the municipality and turned into a creative neighborhood where working, living and culture come together. [S4] A concept appendix of justifications for the municipality's plan, dated September 10, 2015, shows the idea in its working form. It identifies the site as a possible breeding ground (broedplaats) for the creative industry, plans up to 10,000 square meters of housing and up to 11,500 square meters for offices, businesses and community uses, and lists a 1,000 square meter event location called FIFTH among the leisure uses, adding that the current users together occupy 1,700 square meters. [S5]

The 2019 IO+ article describes the change from the inside: new residents such as the jazz club Fifth and the cycling cafe Cyklist, apartments rising on the site, and a group of people over 50 who converted monumental building number 2 into housing. [S7] Omroep Brabant, writing in late 2021 when the NRE-terrein was a finalist for the Brabantse Stijlprijs, adds that one of the first initiative groups saw the empty utility buildings as a place for a housing group for people over 55, that eleven former factory buildings now hold residents of all ages, designers and craftspeople among them, and that the municipality helped the initiators develop their plans themselves without a developer in between. [S8] Both are local accounts, and both fit the city guide's picture of empty utility buildings turned into a mixed neighborhood of housing and creative use. [S4][S7][S8]
NUL ZES in its own words, and in others'

DDW's location page for 2026 says NUL ZES is the home of more than 18 creatives, from designers to architects and form researchers to illustrators, in two redeveloped buildings on the industrial NRE terrain, at Gasfabriek 3A. It is open October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 20:00, and the page says it is not wheelchair accessible. [S3] This is Eindhoven describes a multidisciplinary collective of individual companies whose motto is that their work is their mission. [S9]

The collective's start has a date in its founder's own words. In an IO+ hidden-gem profile published on October 14, 2017, Renee Scheepers, a designer who graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven and the founder of NUL ZES, says she started it after graduating because she had wanted a place of her own in Eindhoven for a long time, with different people under one roof, and that "in 2013, we started on the NRE-area." She says empty sites in a city are often filled temporarily with creatives, who are then pushed out for bigger companies, and that when the land on the NRE terrain went up for sale the group decided it wanted to be that established order itself and planned to buy its own space with an investor. [S10] That is the founder's account, published four years after the start. The profile settles a question the earlier version of this essay left open, the year the collective began: 2013, according to the person who started it. [S10]

The next account comes from the people who rented there. In a DDW interview with Alissa+Nienke, NUL ZES arose out of necessity: after their studies at Design Academy Eindhoven they wanted an affordable workspace with shared facilities, knowledge and networks, wrote a ten-year proposal to the municipality as a group and found someone willing to invest. [S6] The 2019 article counts seventeen members at that point and describes separate workspaces, brainstorming places and their own ceramics, wood and metal workshop, where the first layout of one large open space had stopped working as the group grew. [S7] An undated VPRO Dorst page about Dutch Design Week, which gives the festival dates as October 19 to 27, describes ten people who turned an old building on the NRE terrain into a workshop and hangout, from studio to stage and bar to office, and it counts the group as ten. [S11] The counts differ because the accounts date from different years, and none of them gives a registered founding date for the collective. [S10][S7][S11]

An official visit puts a date on the standing of the place. On February 16, 2023 Queen Máxima made a working visit to designers in Eindhoven, and the Dutch Design Foundation, reporting it on February 17, 2023, says she went first to NUL ZES, which it describes as a designer collective and creative laboratory for designers, architects and researchers, where she met its founder Renee Scheepers and designers Alissa van Asseldonk and Nienke Bongers of Alissa+Nienke, and talked about their preparation for Milan Design Week 2023. [S12] A royal-house social media post, as quoted by a fan blog, says the same. [S13]
Lotte de Raadt and Kirstie van Noort: iron sludge as pigment

The two ceramic designers have separate studios and share a ceramics workshop in the collective. [S14] Lotte de Raadt told Vij5 that she applied to the Design Academy at sixteen, started her studio straight after her studies, graduated on tap water with three drinking-water carafes inspired by the three kinds of Dutch water source, and turned to ceramics in an anti-squatting studio, where she found she loved it. The Water Research Knowledge Center KWR then asked her for a commission, and she remade her carafe in terracotta, which cools water by evaporation. [S15] Kirstie van Noort's own page says she graduated from the Design Academy's department Man and Well-Being in 2011, has run her own studio in Eindhoven since 2012, received the Material Award in 2012 for design research in Cornwall and did a two-month residency on porcelain in Arita, Japan, in 2014. [S16]

The OER project, whose name is the Dutch word for iron sludge, has been in development since 2016, according to Vij5, which says KWR asked them to find uses for the residual stream of tap-water production that would otherwise go back into the sewer. [S14] Van Noort's own page describes the sludge as a residual waste product from water production, deep red, usable as a source of ceramic pigment, and says the work produced a pink-to-red coloring on ceramics and a line of wall tiles. [S17]

The tiles are the long project. DDW's program page for Van slib naar tegel, From sludge to tile, says Inbo designed a new circular groundwater production plant for Brabant Water in Eindhoven, that more than a thousand liters of iron sludge would be processed into 10,000 tiles for one wall, that the design refers to the reflecting character of water, and that Koninklijk Tichelaar was producing the tiles with the plant's realization planned for 2023. It invites visitors to the designers' studio at Nul Zes to see the first results. [S18] The page prints no year. A MaterialDistrict entry dated February 21, 2023 repeats the same sentences, with the plant still described as planned for 2023, and I found no source that says whether the wall was installed. [S18][S19]

The tableware is the other branch. Vij5 describes porcelain mixed with iron sludge, drawn from the buffer pond of the water production company, dried, ground and sifted into a rust-colored powder, poured into plaster molds, glazed on the inside and fired at 1250 degrees Celsius, so that the pigment turns beige with dark brown specks, and says it has been in its collection since 2023. [S14] Vij5's interview adds how the link to the shop came about: Lotte de Raadt says she met Vij5's founders through her colleagues Alissa and Nienke, and that her products have been in the Vij5 collection since 2017. [S15]

The DDW record for them is older than the 2018 album. Van Noort's own exhibition list says OER was shown at DDW 2017 in the Crafts Council exhibition HOW&WOW, and that she took part in the Dutch Invertuals shows No Static in 2015 and Fundamentals in 2017. [S16] A 2018 review says the duo presented OER at NRE as ceramics decorated with oxidized iron, spelling her first name Kristie, as the archive's 2018 and 2021 album titles do. [S2][S1] I use the spelling on her own site. [S16]
Alissa+Nienke: A+N Studio, from porcelain to woven walls

A+N Studio's own page says it is a material research and design studio founded in 2014 by Alissa van Asseldonk and Nienke Bongers, who met at Design Academy Eindhoven, with its studio at Gasfabriek 3A on the NRE terrein, and it names Dior, Fendi and the Municipality of Eindhoven among the organizations it has worked for. [S20] In a January 3, 2018 interview Alissa van Asseldonk says they met at the academy during internships, started with a "material get-together" that became their porcelain line Pigments & Porcelain, and later widened the studio to manipulating flat materials so that they pop up, move or elevate. [S21] Vij5 sells Pigments & Porcelain as cups made of colored porcelain in limited series. [S22] The DDW program listing for 2026 describes A+N Studio as founded by the same two people, so the album titles Alissa_Nienke and the 2026 listing refer to one studio. [S20][S23][S1]

The October 9, 2019 article describes what they brought to DDW that year. They had spent months exploring 3D weaving with EE Exclusive, a family business in Heeze that makes jacquard fabrics, supported by the Creative Industries Fund NL, and had run at least 300 tests for woven textiles that can serve as wall coverings, room dividers or acoustic coverings. The Fringes & Floats textile collection was shown in a smaller building behind their studio, and The Sun Show, a materials vision on awnings, in the studio itself. The article also mentions paneled drapes they developed for the office of the Minister of Education, Culture and Science. [S7] DDW's own program page for Fringes & Floats, credited to Alissa+Nienke x EE Exclusives, describes it as a total overview of the research, from samples to large surface applications. [S24]

The DDW interview adds their view of the festival: they say they take part because the studio is in Eindhoven, because guests and business relations from abroad come, and because DDW allows more research-oriented presentations than the sales-oriented one they had at the Salone del Mobile in 2018. [S6] For 2026 DDW lists Weave / Weld, in which A+N and EE Exclusives test what happens when woven recycled PET is welded instead of sewn. It says the exhibition ranges from tiny weld points to large-scale structures and a process wall of sketches, tests and samples, and that it is not wheelchair accessible. [S23][S3]
The third name in 2018: Crush on Nature

The 2018 album carries a title the earlier sources did not explain, CrushOnNature. The Italian blogger whose 2018 round-up places Lotte de Raadt and Kristie van Noort at NRE also writes that, always at NRE, Fabrique Céramique showed in an exhibit together with Liesbeth Bulk, who with Crush on Nature makes objects from glass and synthetic resin, and mentions the ceramics of Hester de Wolff. [S2] That is one blog, and the album title is the only other place the name appears, so I read it as a lead and not a record. [S2][S1] It does show that the NRE terrain in 2018 held more makers than the three names in the album, and that the album's single CrushOnNature photograph probably belongs to a fourth presentation. [S2][S1]
Five albums, four years

The archive holds five albums for these names: 2018 with 13 photos, titled for Lotte and Kristie, Alissa+Nienke and NulZes; 2019 with 12, for Alissa+Nienke; 2021 with 12 for Lotte & Kristie and 9 for Alissa & Nienke; and 2025 with 68 for NUL ZES, 114 photos in all. [S1] Nick Bookelaar is credited by title for 2018 to 2021, and the 2025 titles name no photographer. [S1]

The 2018 album mixes presentations: of its 13 photos, 5 are titled Alissa_Nienke, 4 Lotte_Kristie, 3 NulZes and 1 CrushOnNature. [S1] The review and Van Noort's list explain the Lotte and Kristie part, because OER was shown at NRE that year, and the review explains the CrushOnNature photo. [S2][S16] For 2019 the article names two shows, and the 12 photos name neither. [S7][S1] For 2021 the albums show pink and orange tiles and discs, and freestanding panel walls in blue, pink and gray. The DDW program page for From sludge to tile is the closest match for the first album, since the tiles are pink to red, but the page prints no year and the album titles name no work, so I treat the match as a lead. [S18][S1]

The 2025 album's titles name Friend & Friends of Friends, Rematerialised and Oori Apparel by Cleo Goossens, with the date October 19, 2025. None names the four makers. [S1] DDW's 2026 location page lists four exhibitions at NUL ZES: Touch On Connection by Plura Studio, Workroom in progress by Tessa van der Wey and Oori Apparel, Atlas by Cleo Goossens and Oori Apparel, and Weave / Weld by A+N Studio. [S3] So the collective is a venue for several makers' shows, not a single exhibitor. [S3][S1]
Questions the sources settle

Does the A+N name in the 2026 listing mean the Alissa+Nienke of the albums? Yes: A+N Studio's page and the DDW listing give the same founders, and the studio's 2019 DDW interview names the same pair. [S20][S23][S6] Did Lotte and Kirstie show only at NRE? No: Van Noort's list puts OER at DDW 2017 in HOW&WOW as well. [S16] Is the OER project old or new? It has been in development since 2016, and its tiles were planned for a plant due in 2023. [S14][S18] When did NUL ZES start? In 2013 on the NRE-area, per its founder. [S10]
What the record does not show

I do not know what the 2021 photographs show by name, whether any 2025 photograph shows work by these makers, who took the 2025 photographs, or when each maker joined the collective. [S1] I could not open the municipal EU ROCK document on the NRE site, because its host's robots.txt returned 403, and Eindhoven's monument register PDF for the gasworks answered with a rejection page, so the site's dates after 1899 rest on the city guide, the planning appendix and the press. [S4][S5] The collective's own website redirected to an empty page, so I have no statement from NUL ZES about itself beyond DDW's page and its founder's interview. [S3][S10] I do not know whether the Brabant Water wall was installed, how the collective financed its own building, or whether it bought it. [S18][S10]
When you sort an album's titles into collective, studio and show, which of the three has a source in front of you, and which is a guess? [S1]
