title: VPRO at Dutch Design Week, from a lab turned exhibition to a kick-off in an auditorium
subtitle: Seven albums of talk shows and talks from 2015 to 2022, read against VPRO's own pages for 2015 to 2025 and the official photo archive.
description: What VPRO's own pages say it did at Dutch Design Week each year, from the 2015 Medialab exhibition to the 2025 kick-off, and what its talk albums show.

sections.x: VPRO has been a media partner of Dutch Design Week for years, and its own pages show the same broadcaster changing what it did there, from a lab turned into an exhibition, to talk shows, to talks made with the festival, to a kick-off event in an auditorium. [S2][S3][S6][S9]

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds seven albums with VPRO's name or its talk formats: two for 2015, and one each for 2016, 2017 and 2022, and two for 2020, 115 photographs in all. [S11] VPRO is unusual among the subjects of this series because it writes down what it plans, which gives me something to set beside the photographs. This essay draws on public sources only: VPRO's own pages, two outside listings and the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 festival beyond what VPRO lists. [S1][S8]
I like a media partner for that reason: a plan on paper is something a photograph can confirm or contradict. [S2]
Who VPRO is, in its own words

VPRO describes itself as an independent media organization that traces its public broadcast heritage back to 1926, working on television, radio, a weekly magazine, websites, apps and live events, and as a media pioneer that has won Emmy Awards and Prix Europa among other prizes. [S1] That is its own description, and I use it only to say who the partner is. The festival-specific pages call it a media partner of Dutch Design Week and say it pays attention to the festival with tips, broadcasts and interviews. [S6][S8]
2015: a lab turned inside out

VPRO's page of October 6, 2015 lists what it planned. It promised daily video portraits of nominees for the Dutch Design Awards from October 10, a Tegenlicht broadcast titled Gimme Shelter on Sunday, October 18 at 21:05 on NPO2 about new ideas for the growing flow of refugees, and a Tegenlicht meet-up on Thursday, October 22 at 19:00 in the Designhuis in Eindhoven. [S2] It said VPRO Medialab and VPRO Dorst would turn the lab into an exhibition and living studio, De omroep van de toekomst, misschien, made over the previous months with St. Joost and the Design Academy, open October 17 to 25 from 13:00 to 17:00 at NatLab. [S2] It also listed the VPRO Peepshow, a virtual reality experience from the Medialab, on Ketelhuisplein from October 17 to 25, and sessions recorded by the music program 3voor12 with artists playing at DDW Music, among them Rufus Wainwright, to be heard on 3FM from October 19 to 22. [S2]

The same page ties the documentary channel NPO Doc's NatureTech series to the festival's talk show, which it calls the Future Now talk show, theme Forward to Nature. It says the show would be live on NPO Doc on Thursday, October 22 at 20:30, with Koert van Mensvoort as the main guest and Pieter van der Wielen as presenter. [S2] The archive calls the same series Now Future Talkshow, and a screen in the 2015 album reads Now Future Talkshow #3, what if our notion of nature changed?, and Thu 22 Oct 2015, beside the logos of VPRO and DDW. [S11] The date on the screen matches the date on VPRO's page, which settles that the two names are one series and that the album is of that evening's stage. [S2][S11] Next Nature's colophon lists Koert van Mensvoort as its founder and CEO. [S12]
2016: the fourth talk show

A trade site's copy of the 2016 program puts the Now Future Talkshow on Thursday, October 27 at 19:30 in the Klokgebouw and calls it the fourth edition, organized by DDW with VPRO, with Pieter van der Wielen talking to Bas van Abel, Luna Maurer and Robert Suarez about the research and processes behind their designs. [S3] The count agrees with the 2015 screen, which said #3. [S3][S11] The same page lists a VPRO Tegenlicht broadcast on Sunday, October 23 about Bas van Abel's Fairphone, a meet-up on October 26 at Pakhuis de Zwijger in Amsterdam, a daily design program, Dagelijkse dosis design, hosted by Elfie Tromp on NPO Cultura from October 24 to 28 at 20:30, and a HoloLens mixed-reality experience from VPRO Medialab from October 22 to 30 in the VDMA building. [S3] The HoloLens piece lets visitors live two hundred years of Maarten Baas's Tree Trunk Chair, a chair that grows inside a young tree and can be harvested in 2216, according to the page. [S3]

The archive holds 29 photographs under Now Future Talkshow for 2016, showing a stage branded The Making Of, with a screen reading Persistence is fruitful, and the audience from behind. [S11] The trade site's own date field reads 1999, which is wrong, and I trust its text only because the dates and ambassadors it names fit the 2016 festival. [S3]
2017: a debate about devices

A culture site's tip list of October 18, 2017 describes We Know How You Feel Tonight, an English-language debate evening organized by VPRO Medialab on Wednesday, October 25 from 19:00 to 21:30, about devices and the data they collect about us and our emotions, with executives of large organizations and writers from Stichting Gr1p, entrance five euros. [S4] The same page says VPRO pays plenty of attention to DDW on television in the program De toekomstbouwers and on radio in Nooit Meer Slapen. [S4] The archive has an album titled VPRO Medialab with 9 photographs whose own description names Dutch Design Week 2017. [S11] The photographs show an installation in a dark room with visitors lying on mats inside cones of colored light, and the file titles name Design Perron. [S11] No page I opened links the album to the debate evening, so I do not, and I cannot name the work. [S4][S11]
2019 and beyond: where the archive is silent

The albums this timeline uses stop after 2022, with none for 2018, 2019, 2021 or 2023 to 2025, but VPRO's pages are not silent. Its ten tips for 2019 list The Robin Who Wondered If He Was A Nightingale at Sectie-C and say the television program De toekomstbouwers, VPRO's program about DDW, would be recorded that year at Sectie-C in the studio of Collaboration O, with viewers invited to attend on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday. [S5] For 2022, VPRO's ten tips begin with Manifestations on the eighth floor of the Veem building and mention works such as Love Letter Generator and gURL. [S7] VPRO's DDW hub lists ten-tip articles for 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, and a Tegenlicht project in 2024 in which Medialab built an intervention to bring physical and online audiences together around an episode about new building materials. [S8]

In 2025 VPRO organized its own kick-off program on Sunday, October 19, from 10:15 to 13:00 in the Natlab auditorium, with four speakers: Pauline van Dongen on the Umbra Pavilion on Ketelhuisplein, Daan Sonnemans of Kantamanto Social Club, Eleni Soerjo of Philips on 100 years of Philips design, and Tom van Veen of Accenture on AI in the physical world. It was introduced by Miriam van der Lubbe, the Creative Head of DDW, and Tom Klaassen of VPRO, and the ticket price included a DDW ticket at 25 euros. [S9] Its ten tips for 2025 include Designing Democracy at the Foundation We Are, Ambient Care by Plectrum at Matchbox on Strijp-S, and the Zandkorrelverspreider on Nieuwe Emmasingel. [S10] The kick-off and the tips are VPRO's announcements, and I describe them as such.
2020: three talks made with the festival

In 2020 VPRO says DDW and VPRO made three talks in which ambassadors, makers and designers explore the future. [S6] The first, according to VPRO's teaser for it, has Chris Kijne in conversation with the DDW20 ambassador Lidewij Edelkoort and Lucas de Man, founder of Biobased Creations. The third, published on October 21, 2020, has Pieter van der Wielen with the ambassador Sabine Marcelis and the urban planner Winy Maas about the green future of the city, new ways for designers to exhibit digitally and why architects and filmmakers are alike. [S6] VPRO's talk pages credit their photographs to about.today and Oscar Vinck. [S6] The archive holds 10 and 12 photographs for the first and the third talk, showing the same studio set in a large hall, with a sign reading vpro ambassadeurs talks DDW, two or three people at a long table and camera crews at the sides. [S11]

A talk is the hardest kind of event for a caption to improve on, because the words matter and the picture shows a room. The pages above give the topics the speakers were meant to cover and not what was said, so any sentence about the content of a talk would need a recording I have not opened. [S6]
2022: a program with no page

The archive album for 2022 is titled VPRO - De wereld van Dutch Design and holds 12 photographs of a television set with a round table, guests, a presenter standing, a seated audience and a screen reading wereld van dutch design. [S11] No page I opened describes that program, so I give it no date. VPRO's ten tips, published on October 22, 2022, are a different thing: they point viewers to works around the city. [S7]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Future Now or Now Future.** VPRO's 2015 page writes Future Now talk show, while the 2016 program copy and the album screen write Now Future Talkshow. The screen's date and VPRO's date for the live broadcast match, which settles that they are one series. [S2][S11]
**The date of the 2016 page.** The trade site says 1999 and describes the festival starting on October 22, which fits 2016. [S3]
**Whether the 2017 album belongs to the debate evening.** Unsettled: nothing links them. [S4][S11]
What the record does not show

I do not know what was said in any of the talks, what the 2022 television program was about, or who made the installation in the 2017 album. I did not find VPRO pages for 2018, 2021 or 2023 beyond the ten-tip articles listed on its hub. The album facts come from my reading of the Flickr account on October 8, 2026, which I did not repeat. [S11]
A talk leaves a speaker list, a date and a few rooms. If you caption a talk photograph, which of those three can you actually source? [S11]

title: World Design Embassies at Dutch Design Week: eight Octobers of themed embassies, 24 albums and a program that closed in 2025
subtitle: From the first World Design Event in 2017 to eight embassies in 2024: who ran each one, where it stood, what the Dutch Design Foundation says about its end, and what the photo archive can and cannot show.
description: The Dutch Design Foundation's World Design Embassies, 2017 to 2024: curators, venues, the 2025 close and Coalitions, and what the DDW photo albums show.

sections.x: A program that calls its exhibitions embassies has to explain what they represent, and the Dutch Design Foundation's World Design Embassies did it by naming a social question for each one and handing it to a curator. [S1][S2]

This essay follows the program through the Dutch Design Week (DDW) pages that describe it, the Dutch Design Foundation's own pages for each embassy, the partners' pages, press from 2017 to 2024 and the 24 embassy albums in the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview. I read the embassies the way I would read a medical case series: each one is a case of a design question meeting a venue, and the useful comparison is across years. [S1][S3][S4]
What the program was

A DDW page about Dutch Design Foundation (DDF) says the foundation organizes DDW and the Dutch Design Awards and, throughout the year, manages programs under the flag of Design Works, among them World Design Embassies, What if Lab and Driving Dutch Design. [S1] Design Works is described as the part of DDF that builds business relationships between designers and companies, organizations and governments. [S1] A Dutch article for DDW 2022 says DDF started the program five years earlier, to explore how design helps with the social questions of the time, and that eight themed embassies would show the society of the future with designers and partners. [S2]

The program began as something else. On March 27, 2017, IO+ reported on the opening of DDF's year, at which the foundation announced a new festival, the World Design Event, that would run every four years alongside DDW, with eight embassies for the future as creative breeding grounds for food, care and climate, and a People's Pavilion by the design studio Overtreders W with the firm SLA. [S5] The four-year rhythm did not last. The embassies came back every October, and in 2024 DDW's page described World Design Embassies as a year-round program that culminates during DDW, with eight embassies. [S6] Pakhuis de Zwijger, the Amsterdam debate house, filed twenty talks under a World Design Embassies series between October 15, 2020 and March 31, 2022, and describes the program in the same year-round terms. [S7]

DDF's own pages count the years differently from the festival. The pages for the Embassies of Health, Water and Safety, written after the program ended, begin with the same sentence, that over the past seven years DDF brought designers, governments, businesses and knowledge institutions together through the program. [S3][S8][S9] The Embassy of Health page lists its creative leads from 2018, which gives seven editions from 2018 to 2024, while the Safety page counts six years and the Inclusive Society page four. [S3][S9][S10] The festival's own count runs from the first World Design Event in 2017 to 2024, eight Octobers. [S11][S6] I use both and say which I mean.
2017: the first World Design Event

IO+ announced that the Innovation Powerhouse in Eindhoven would open to the public for the first time as the Embassy of Health, next to the new studio of the design agency VanBerlo, with the exhibition Chronic Health: Designing a Healthy Future. It named projects such as Outrospectre by Frank Kolkman, the LifeSaver CPR guidance concept by VanBerlo, the High Risk Pregnancy Toolkit by Philips and the DIY Toolkit for Dementia by Waag Society, and said Waag Society curated the exhibition. [S11] Waag adds that the embassy was formed with VanBerlo, Philips, U CREATE and the Máxima Medical Center, that Sabine Wildevuur of its Creative Care Lab was one of the curators, and that the exhibition was open daily from 11:00 to 18:00, October 21 to 29. [S12]

The Embassy of Food stood on Ketelhuisplein. DDF's retrospective, published on September 10, 2020, says visitors saw The Future of Food, Looking Back to Now in a big greenhouse, curated by the eating designer Marije Vogelzang, with a daily dinner by the food designer Chloé Rutzerveld, a conference on food waste and the first Future Food Design Awards. It says the exhibition drew about 26,000 people and about 800 took part in the program, and that the embassy was organized by the province of Noord-Brabant with ZLTO, DDF and the Ministry of Economic Affairs. [S13] Those are the organizer's figures, written three years afterward. [S13]

The Robot Love Embassy was a different kind of embassy. Its own page says the Niet Normaal Foundation presented it, from October 21 to 29, 2017, in the former V&D department store in the center of Eindhoven, with the Technological Universities of Delft and Eindhoven and the University of Twente, where robots learned from their interactions with humans, and it reports 63,000 visitors, which is the organizer's figure. [S14] A 2018 press release from the same foundation repeats the number as 63,000 visits counted in nine days. [S15] The page lists a 2018 edition at the Campina milk factory on Kanaaldijk-Zuid, September 15 to December 2, 2018. [S14]

The 2017 albums are Embassy of Food (17 photos), Embassy of Health (13), Embassy of Intimacy (7) and Embassy of Robot Love (10). [S4] The Health album shows a DNA donation contract table, a case of medical equipment, a pregnancy simulator and visitors at a VR station, which fits the healthcare themes in the press descriptions, though no title names a project. [S4][S11] The Intimacy album's titles name Ketelhuisplein and the MU, not an intimacy exhibit, so I cannot say what it shows, and I found no page I could open that describes the Embassy of Intimacy. [S4]
2018: six embassies, two albums

DDW's 2018 dossier page lists six embassy pages: Water, Mobility, Urban Transformation, Health, Circularity and Food. [S16] The Embassy of Health returned to the Innovation Powerhouse, now described as on the Strijp-T terrain, with the exhibition Chronic Health: If not us then who?, echoing the 2018 festival title, and with the same six partners: Waag, VanBerlo, Philips, the Máxima Medical Center, DDF and U CREATE. Its curator was Sabine Wildevuur of Waag, and its examples included an artificial womb, a bicycle for elderly and insecure cyclists and a game helping teenage girls cope with the loss of a father or brother. [S17]

The other pages give each embassy a place and a person. The Embassy of Food, curated again by Marije Vogelzang, was a smaller Micro Embassy on microbes and food, in her words. [S18] The Embassy of Water stood in AtelierNL's church on Bergmannstraat, with Anouk van der Poll, owner of vanderPolloffice, as curator and two themes, Water-Sensitive Urban Design and Nature-Based Solutions. [S19] DDF's retrospective, published on July 25, 2019, adds that the embassy was initiated by her as a platform for water-related design and credits its photographs to Iris Rijskamp. [S20] The Embassy of Mobility stood in the former V&D building, with the consultant Nienke Dijkstra in charge of the program and the urban developer Harm Rensink designing the exhibition and a test circuit for electric vehicles. [S21] The Embassy of Urban Transformation was a collaboration between the Rotterdam design agency A/BZ and The Student Hotel, using Eindhoven's District E as a playground for experiments. [S22] The Embassy of Circularity, curated by Marieke Rietbergen of Design Innovation Group, asked how to produce 2020 entirely circular apartment buildings by 2020 with partners that included ABN AMRO, DEMEEUW, CIRCO, New Horizon and the Urban Mining Collective. [S23]

The archive has two 2018 albums, Embassy of Health with 21 photos by Ruud Balk and Embassy of Water with 15 photos whose titles read AtelierNL, by Iris Rijskamp. [S4] The Water album's title now has an explanation, since AtelierNL's church is where DDW's own page puts the embassy. [S4][S19] The other four 2018 embassies have no album. [S16][S4]
2019: six embassies and a change of structure

On October 17, 2019, IO+ listed six embassies for DDW, October 19 to 27: Safety and Circular & Biobased Building on Ketelhuisplein, Sustainable Design across Strijp-S and Strijp-T, Health in the Klokgebouw, Mobility behind Radio Royaal and Water at the Campina terrain. [S24] The roster had changed from 2018: Safety, Sustainable Design and Circular & Biobased Building appear for the first time on the list, Circularity, Food and Urban Transformation do not, and Water moved from the church to Campina. [S16][S24]

The Embassy of Sustainable Design was curated by Leonne Cuppen of Yksi Connect with VanBerlo, as part of DDW's theme If not now, then when, and was spread over Strijp-S and Strijp-T, the Innovation Powerhouse, Gloeilampenplantsoen and Yksi Expo. Yksi Connect names partners from IKEA Netherlands and NS to TU Delft, Design Academy Eindhoven and FrieslandCampina. [S25] DDF's Embassy of Health page names Jetske van Oosten as creative lead from 2019 to 2022 and describes the 2019 exhibition Chronic Health: It's Only Human?. [S3] The 2019 archive has albums for Embassy of Mobility (11 photos) and Embassy of Sustainable Design (7), both credited to Britt Roelse. [S4]
2020: a virtual house and a talk series

DDW 2020 was virtual. On October 18, 2020, DDW TV posted a video in which Lucas De Man walks viewers through The Exploded View, a detached house rebuilt with circular methods and biobased materials. [S26] DDF's Health page calls the 2020 edition Chronic Health: Happily Ever After?, held in a digital setting. [S3] The year-round side shows in the Pakhuis de Zwijger series, whose livecast talks that autumn took one embassy a week: Rethinking Plastic on November 5, then Circular & Biobased Building, Water, Health, Mobility, Food and Safety, the last on December 17, 2020. [S7] The 2020 albums are Circular & Biobased Building with 26 photos and Rethinking Plastic with 11. [S4]
2021: no album and a new embassy

There is no embassy album for 2021, yet the program was there. The DDW article for 2022 says the Circular & Biobased Building embassy built a circular and biobased house at DDW the year before, and calls the 2022 Inclusive Society embassy the second edition. [S2] DDF's own page for the Embassy of Inclusive Society says it was in its inaugural year at DDW 2021, asking how designers can contribute to a society in which everyone feels seen and represented, and names Jorn Konijn as creative lead for 2021 and Shay Raviv for 2022 to 2024. [S10] Its photograph credits for the Embassies of Health, Water and Safety also list DDW21 images. [S3][S8][S9] The Pakhuis de Zwijger series ran six talks in 2021, on circular thinking, a healthy environment, food and water systems, a safe and inclusive society, living with water, and mobility with livability first. [S7]
2022: the largest year in the archive

The DDW article for 2022 shows how the roster worked. Food, with food designer Chloé Rutzerveld as curator, built three scenarios for the supermarket of 2050 in the Klokgebouw. Water, with Anouk van der Poll, argued for regenerative housing at the Designhuis Eindhoven. Urban Mobility, with Rob Adams, worked on liveable streets in the Klokgebouw. Safety, with Tabo Goudswaard, took the theme In makers we trust. Inclusive Society, with Shay Raviv, was in its second edition at the Van Abbemuseum. Health, with curator Marleen van Bergeijk, was in its sixth year in a row, in the Klokgebouw. [S2]

Two more embassies in that article mark the end of a thread. Rethinking Plastic, with Leonne Cuppen as curator, was in what the article calls its very last year, at Yksi Expo, and Circular & Biobased Building, curated by Lucas De Man and Pascal Leboucq, was building a modular exhibition on Strijp-S inspired by the circular and biobased house it had built the year before. [S2] DDW's program page adds that Rethinking Plastic ran changing exhibitions, lectures and workshops through the year, with students from several design schools in a Rethinking Plastic Academy. [S27] Yksi Connect lists a Rethinking Plastic exhibition at Yksi Expo from September 2, 2022 as the start of a two-year program, and a traveling version in Bucharest in June 2021. [S25] The two statements about 2022 differ, since one calls it the last year and the other the start of a two-year program, and I do not resolve them. [S2][S25]

The 2022 archive is the largest: eight albums for the embassies (Inclusive Society 43 photos, Urban Mobility 14, Health 17, Rethinking Plastic 48, Circular & Biobased Building 32, Safety 11, Food 40) plus a 63-photo conference album titled Ch.. Ch.. Changes. [S4] The Water embassy, which the article places at the Designhuis, has no 2022 album, although DDF's Water page lists a DDW22 conference photograph. [S2][S4][S8]
2023: seven embassies

For 2023, DDW lists seven embassies, each with a creative lead and venue. Circular & Biobased Building, led by De Man and Leboucq, stood on Ketelhuisplein. Food, led by Barbara Vos, was in the Evoluon, showing a farm of the future. Health, led by Marleen van Bergeijk, explored health as currency at Foundation We Are. Inclusive Society, led by Shay Raviv, built a spatial gym for training an inclusivity muscle at the Van Abbemuseum. Mobility, led by Joost van der Made, ran a living lab across the city with a permanent exhibition at DONNA. Safety, led by Goudswaard, had the theme Making (amends) in the Klokgebouw. Water, led by Van der Poll, built a pavilion at Stadhuisplein. [S28] DDF's later page names the gym's designer, Gabriel Fontana, and a companion installation that visualized guidelines for inclusive and accessible presentations. [S10] The 2023 archive has six albums, 116 photos in all, and none for Food. [S28][S4]
2024 and the end

DDW's program page for 2024 lists eight participating embassies, Circular & Biobased Building, Digital Futures, Food, Health, Inclusive Society, Mobility, Safety and Water, as part of the exhibition Designing Society, for October 19 to 27, 2024. [S6] Digital Futures is the one name that does not appear in earlier years. [S6][S28] DDF's account of the Inclusive Society embassy says that in 2024 it took part in Designing Society and focused on turning isolated inclusive initiatives into sustained practice. [S10] My reading of the archive stops at 2023, and I did not check Flickr for 2024 embassy albums. [S4]

The end is on record. On March 25, 2025, DDF announced that World Design Embassies and What if Lab would continue as Coalitions, a platform and structural approach that builds on both programs, with the first products called Co/Labs, collaboration trajectories in which design teams work with organizations that own a societal challenge. [S29] DDF's pages for the individual embassies, written afterward, say it plainly: since 2025, the World Design Embassies program has come to a close, and DDF is building on its legacy with Coalitions. [S10][S3] DDF's current About page describes a foundation that builds coalitions with partners from business, policy and science and does not list World Design Embassies. [S30] An earlier version of this essay said no page announced the end. DDF's own pages do, and they use the word close. [S10][S29]

Brainport Eindhoven's article of October 11, 2024 gives the funder's view. It says that with funding from the Regio Deal Brainport Eindhoven, DDF set up programs that link designers to government and industry, that DDF's Head of Design Works, Marianne Aarnoudse, is responsible for programs such as the What if Lab and the World Design Embassies, and that in the embassies DDF acts as director, bringing the relevant parties together with designers. It also quotes the DDF leadership saying that they might make themselves redundant in the coming years, if the design world penetrates traditional markets. [S31]
Who led each embassy

DDF's embassy pages carry the creative leads by year, which makes them the best single record of who stood behind each name. Health: Sabine Wildevuur (2018), Jetske van Oosten (2019 to 2022) and Marleen van Bergeijk (2022 to 2024), with the partners Alles is Gezondheid, AMS-IX, Health Holland, Philips, the Máxima Medical Center, Waag, the province of Noord-Brabant and the Creative Industries Fund NL among others. [S3] Water: Anouk van der Poll, with Brabant Water, the City of Eindhoven, the province of Noord-Brabant and the water board De Dommel. [S8] Safety: Tabo Goudswaard, with the Ministry of Justice and Security, the police, the Public Prosecution Service and the Probation Service. [S9] Inclusive Society: Jorn Konijn (2021) and Shay Raviv (2022 to 2024), with ActiZ, two ministries, the Van Abbemuseum, the Vriendenloterij and the VSB Fonds. [S10] A reader of the albums sees the name of an embassy. The leads and partners explain why the same name looks different from year to year. [S3][S10]
What the archive can and cannot show

The embassy albums hold 522 photos: 47 in 2017, 36 in 2018, 18 in 2019, 37 in 2020, 268 in 2022 and 116 in 2023. [S4] There is no album for 2021, although the 2022 article says the Circular & Biobased Building embassy built a house at DDW the year before, DDF says Inclusive Society began that year, and Yksi's pages place a traveling Rethinking Plastic show in Bucharest in June 2021. [S2][S10][S25][S4] The same name appears in many years, Health in 2017, 2018, 2022 and 2023, Mobility in 2019, 2022 and 2023, Circular & Biobased Building in 2020, 2022 and 2023, and the curator, the venue and the question change under it. [S4][S2][S28] A caption that says only Embassy of Health tells you the program and not the year, the room or the people. [S4][S3]

One credit needed checking. The archive's 2017 Robot Love album credits Iris Rijskamp by title, while the Robot Love page credits a photo of the Pepper robot to Iris Rijswijk of Dutch Design Week. [S4][S14] DDF's own Water retrospective spells the photographer Iris Rijskamp, as the archive does, so I read the Robot Love page's spelling as a misspelling, though a printed credit should still be checked with DDW. [S20][S14]
What the record does not show

I do not know what the Embassy of Intimacy showed in 2017, what the 2019 Sustainable Design and Mobility albums show beyond their titles, what the Digital Futures embassy showed in 2024, or how many visitors each embassy had apart from the two organizer figures for Food and Robot Love. [S4][S6][S13][S14] I could not read DDF's public annual reports for 2021 to 2024, which are the likely place for program-level numbers, because the files returned errors at the addresses a search listed and an archive copy came back empty. I did not find the date the program was first called World Design Embassies instead of World Design Event, although the 2017 announcement already names the embassies. [S5] Dezeen's guide to the 2017 embassies is on a host that refused my automated request, so I used nothing from it.
When one name is reused for eight Octobers, which part of the caption would you check first: the curator, the venue or the question? [S4][S2]

title: Yksi at Dutch Design Week: one name, four organizations, and an exhibition space that changed hands in 2023
subtitle: The curator's own pages, two press releases and DDW's listings give themes, dates and credits for the years the photo archive labels only Yksi.
description: Yksi Expo on Strijp-S, 2011 to 2022: Dutch Design Week exhibitions, Rethinking Plastic, the 2023 handover to Foundation We Are, and what the photo archive holds.

sections.x: Yksi's own record of its Dutch Design Week years is a list of curated exhibitions, and each of them has a named theme, a date and a photographer credit, which the photo archive's titles mostly do not. [S5][S13]

I like that gap, because it shows what each kind of record is good for. This essay draws on public sources only: the pages of Yksi Expo's curator, two press releases, an exhibition announcement, a lecture listing, Dutch Design Week's program pages, a building page from Strijp-S and the official photo archive as I recorded it on October 7, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it describes the 2026 week only through what a DDW location page lists. [S2][S3][S5][S12][S13]
One name, four organizations

The Yksi home page links three parts, called ontwerp, expo and connect, and in the version I could read on October 9 it carried nothing else. [S1] The pages behind the names describe different organizations. Yksi Ontwerp says it has been active in the design world since 1991 and calls itself an initiator of Dutch Design Week, with a team of an interior designer, an industrial designer and a founder, working on interiors and products, among them a design label called JAPTH. [S4] Yksi Expo was a foundation with a gallery. Its December 2022 press release says Yksi began in 1991 as a design studio with a foundation and gallery next to it, to give Dutch design and above all young designers a platform, that after some years in the Designhuis near the city hall the foundation settled on Strijp-S in 2011, and that the foundation was later separated from the studio by mutual agreement. [S2] Yksi Connect is the company that Leonne Cuppen founded, in her words more than seven years ago, to connect designers with the field. [S6]

A fourth organization enters at the end of the story. Foundation We Are, founded in 2018, took over the space in 2023, as the release explains below. [S2] I keep the four apart because the archive's albums say only Yksi.
The building, and what the dates do not say

Yksi Expo's address is Torenallee 22-04 on Strijp-S, and its 2021 press release describes the space as the ground floor of the Apparatenfabriek. [S3] Strijp-S's building page says that in 1928 three large buildings known as the Hoge Rug rose at great speed, among them the Apparatenfabriek, formerly known as building SK, which was built as the first radio equipment factory, where the first Philips radios were produced and, after the war, television sets. [S11] The same page says the housing corporation Trudo transformed the building in 2013 into a business center with more than 100 workspaces. [S11]

Those dates sit side by side awkwardly. Yksi's release says it settled on Strijp-S in 2011, and the building page dates the conversion to 2013, so Yksi may have been in the building before the conversion. [S2][S11] Neither page says so, and I do not know which part of the building Yksi used before 2013. The curator's page puts the size of the space at 600 square meters. [S5]
What the curator's page says about each year

The best written account of Yksi Expo's Dutch Design Week years comes from Leonne Cuppen's curation page, which lists her exhibitions with dates, themes and photographers. [S5] I report what it says as her own account.

The 2017 edition is documented by an exhibition announcement posted on an architects' site under the name Yksi Ontwerp: for the 16th Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29, 2017, Yksi Expo at Torenallee 22-04 presented twenty-five projects, presentations and products, with attention to material experiments and design for the circular economy. [S8] It names Material Sense Lab's Bio-Boost, with a living fungus as natural black paint, paper pulp as a base for building elements and tiles and a festival token made of bioplastic, fish skins from NYVIDD, Daria Biryukova's research on reusing waste for glazes with Van Gansewinkel, the label Pour by Julie van der Boorn and the launch of the brand Zooi, which makes lifestyle articles from residual material. [S8] It also lists craft furniture by students of the Koning Willem I College, the results of the Masters of Materials design competition organized by Baars & Bloemhoff, and an exhibition called Austrian Design Compositions as a contrast to Dutch design. [S8]

In 2018 the curator's page gives Yksi Expo's Dutch Design Week program as October 20 to 28, about twenty designers and companies, on sustainability, circular design and social design, tied to that year's festival motto, which she renders as "If not us, then who." [S5] The same page lists two exhibitions before the festival, Like Leather, from July 4 to September 29, and Paper Generations, which she curated as a tribute to her father, and a larger show called Clean Revolution: Dutch Design for a Better World, which she lists for the Global Climate Summit in San Francisco on September 12 and 13, for Dutch Design Week October 20 to 28 in the Veemgebouw, and for Yksi Expo. [S5] An Innovation Origins listing of the lectures on Monday, October 22, 2018, lists two lectures at "Yksi, Torenallee 22-04," at 14:00 and 16:00, both titled KVGO and Print Pakt. [S9] The page is Innovation Origins' list, not DDW's own schedule. [S9]

For 2019 the page gives Yksi Expo's program as October 19 to 27, about sustainability and circular design, with several thematic exhibitions and some twenty presentations by designers, small and medium businesses and schools, and says Yksi Expo formed part of the Embassy of Sustainable Design, which Cuppen curated with the design agency VanBerlo. [S5] It lists Beyond Coffee at Yksi Expo from July 19 to November 3, 2019, and a long partner list for the Embassy that includes IKEA Netherlands, Renewi, NS, FrieslandCampina and several universities. [S5] The Embassy was a program of the World Design Event during Dutch Design Week 2019, under the theme If not now, then when. [S5]
2021 and 2022: plastic

For 2021 the press release of September 13, 2021 describes Yksi Expo's Dutch Design Week, October 16 to 24, as entirely about plastic. [S3] It describes a 50 square meter studio space furnished with products of recycled plastic, bioplastic or sustainable alternatives, a complete house of plastic called the Rethinking Plastic House, built with companies and institutes of the Brightlands Chemelot Campus, a Rethinking Plastic Academy for projects by students and young designers, a small recycling workshop from the foundation Sparkling Plastic, the platform Solaris with products made of ocean plastic from Thailand, and the winners of the No Waste Challenge and the Green Product Award. [S3] It says the program had run for more than a year and that it formed the Embassy of Rethinking Plastic, part of the World Design Embassies of the Dutch Design Foundation. [S3] The curator's page adds TNO's Torwash, a technology that dissolves bioplastic so it can be reused, and three designers' results shown at Yksi Expo during the festival. [S5]

Dutch Design Week's own program archive lists Rethinking Plastic as part of DDW 2022, presented by Yksi Expo, with a main exhibition photographed by Jeroen van der Wielen, and mentions Wint designLab and a project from the Vilnius Academy of Art. [S10] The archive has no Yksi album for 2022. [S13]

One date does not line up. The curator's page dates the exhibition Rethinking Plastic at Yksi Expo from September 2 to December 31, 2022 and calls it the start of a two-year program, while the September 2021 press release says the program had already run for more than a year. [S5][S3] The most consistent reading is that the page's 2022 is a slip for an earlier year, but I cannot settle it from the pages, and the press release is the dated document. [S3][S5]
The handover in 2023

Yksi Expo's press release of December 10, 2022 says Cuppen stops with the foundation on January 1, 2023, after more than 31 years, and hands on the baton to the younger generation. [S2] It says that a plan for members of the Yksi Expo Young Talent team to continue the work could not be realized, and that the new tenant of the Torenallee space is the foundation We Are, founded in 2018 to bring the creative sector and experts in societal transitions together, which began on Sectie C and then sat on the former Campina site. [S2] DDW's 2026 location page lists Foundation We Are at Torenallee 22-04, calls it a design collective that began eight years ago with eight designers and is now a young cultural organization, and lists an exhibition there for the 2026 week. [S12] The foundation has separate albums in the archive and belongs in a different timeline. [S13]

Cuppen's own pages say she continues with Yksi Connect, and that more recently she has been curator of the materials fair MaterialDistrict and a guild master of a maker place called Nieuw Zwanenburg, which she describes as a place in the making. [S7] I describe those as her pages' account and do not add to them.
The claim about Dutch Design Week itself

Two Yksi pages say Yksi was among the initiators of Dutch Design Week, and Cuppen says in her own words that she was one of the initiators of the Dutch Design Week and the Designhuis in Eindhoven. [S4][S6] That is a self-description. I found no DDW page that confirms it, so I report it only as a claim made by Yksi and leave it out of any statement about the festival's history. [S4][S6]
What the albums keep

The old dossier counts six Yksi albums, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021, with 11, 16, 20, 14, 17 and 6 photographs, 84 in all. [S13] The photographers named in the titles are Patrick Meis for 10 of the 11 in 2015, Iris Rijskamp for 2016 to 2019 and Max Kneefel for 2021, while the curator's page credits Jeroen van der Wielen for exhibitions of 2018 and later and Oscar Vinck for the 2019 Embassy. [S13][S5] The dossier describes banners in the 2018 album that read Online Department Store of the Future and name Indigo People and Planq, and a 2019 panel on green coffee beans that fits the Beyond Coffee show. [S13] I could not tie those to the written sources beyond that one match. [S13][S5] The old dossier also records that Dezeen's 2016 festival guide listed Yksi among venues with international exhibitions, a fact I did not reopen because Dezeen refused my request. [S13]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**What the 2018 lecture list is.** The old draft called it DDW's schedule. The page is Innovation Origins' list. [S9]
**When Yksi arrived on Strijp-S.** 2011 per Yksi, and the building's conversion is dated 2013 by Strijp-S. Not settled. [S2][S11]
**When Rethinking Plastic started.** The September 2021 release says more than a year before; the curator's page says September 2022. The dated release is the stronger source. [S3][S5]
**Whether Yksi initiated Dutch Design Week.** Two Yksi pages say so; no DDW page does. Not settled. [S4][S6]
**Who the Torenallee space belongs to.** Yksi Expo until January 1, 2023, then Foundation We Are. The press release settles it. [S2][S12]
What the record does not show

I do not know what most of the archive photographs show, because titles after 2015 do not name works, and I do not know why 2020 and 2022 have no album. I do not know what Yksi Expo showed in 2015 and 2016 beyond the album titles and a trade listing, or which part of the Apparatenfabriek it used before 2013. I did not open Yksi Expo's own website. [S13][S5]

I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts, titles and descriptions come from the dossier's October 7, 2026 reading. [S13] Nothing here describes Foundation We Are's 2026 program beyond DDW's listing. [S12]

If a single address held a curator's exhibition space for thirty-one years and then a younger collective's, which name would you put on a caption for a photo from a given year, and which document would you show to prove it? [S2][S12]

title: Area51 and Area West sound like one place, and the sources say they are two
subtitle: A skatepark in a former Philips hall on Strijp-S and a Dutch Design Week area south of it, followed through planning and press records, the organizers' own pages and the official photo archive
description: A Strijp-S skatepark and a DDW area south of it: what planning, press and program records say about each, from 2006 to DDW 2026.

sections.x: Area51 and Area West sound like one place in Eindhoven, and every source I opened treats them as two. [S1][S23]

In anatomy I learned to check whether two names point at one structure before I assume they do, because a shared name is where wrong assumptions start. This essay uses public sources only: a tourist board, a district site, contractor and developer pages, trade and local press, Dutch Design Week's own pages and its photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what is on show during DDW 2026 beyond what the published listings say. [S1][S32]
Area51 is a hall on Strijp-S with a skatepark at its center

Area51 is an indoor skatepark at Ketelhuisplein 18 on Strijp-S. [S3][S4] The tourist board calls it "the largest indoor skate park in the Benelux," and I treat that as the venue's and the tourist board's own claim, since no source I opened ranks it against other parks. [S1][S2] The venue's site describes a street section with ledges and rails, a park section with a six-meter vertical wall, a small bowl, a foam pit, a café overlooking the course, an event space and a basement venue. [S4] The tourist board adds four dance studios and the Academy 51 lessons. [S2]

So the building holds more than skating, and that matters for the archive question later. A label that names a skatepark gets attached to dance, design fairs and a conference lounge, and the label keeps working because the address does. [S2][S5]
The hall is a Philips building, and it has a code: SEU

The district site for Strijp-S calls the building SEU and says it is split in two. Area51 occupies one part and several other parties use the other, among them 040 BMX Park. The same page describes SEU as a former Philips machine factory, tall enough inside for BMX riding. [S8] The tourist board's A to Z gives a different description: the building was a former tool shop and was among the first on the site to be repurposed after Philips left. [S1] A machine factory and a tool shop can be the same place described two ways, and I do not claim to settle it. Neither page gives a construction year or says which Philips unit worked there. I found no heritage record for the building. A 2015 report quotes Trudo's director calling it architecturally unremarkable but charming, which is an opinion and not a register entry. [S10]

The same 2015 report places the hall between the residential building Anton and the Klokgebouw. [S10] Strijp-S as a whole gives the frame. The district's history page says VolkerWessels and the municipality of Eindhoven bought the fenced Philips site in 2002 and leased it back to Philips, who stayed as the main user for several years. It says the fence was moved back gradually as Philips parts relocated, so that the first buildings became available for new use, and it ties Dutch Design Week choosing Strijp-S as its new home to the same period without giving a year. [S9] The tourist board repeats the local nickname for the closed site, the forbidden city. [S1]
Skating here since 2006, and an older story about Meerhoven

Three sources date the use of the hall as a skatepark to 2006. A roofing contractor's project page says the hall has been in use since the fall of 2006. [S7] A news item from the district site, dated January 16, 2023, says Area51 has been at Ketelhuisplein since 2006. [S6] A skate magazine's park review of September 2014 says the same, and it adds an older story: the park opened in 2000 in an old aircraft hangar in Meerhoven, which is where the name Area51 comes from. [S11]

Another source disagrees on the founding. A design furniture retailer's blog, writing in November 2011 after a visit during Dutch Design Week, says Area 51 was established in 2002, in an old industrial building on the former Philips estate. [S12] The 2002 and 2000 dates cannot both be right for the first park, and only the magazine mentions Meerhoven. I settle one thing and leave one open. The move to Strijp-S in 2006 has three sources that do not obviously copy each other, a contractor, a district site and a skate magazine. The year the first park opened, and where, has one source for 2000 and one for 2002, and I treat both as second-hand.

The blog gives a useful picture of the hall in 2011 all the same. It says the writers make time at every Dutch Design Week to leave the design fair and visit the skatepark, describes about 3,000 square meters of landscaped wood, and says Area 51 shows that city planning needs space for teenagers too. [S12] That makes the hall a stop for design visitors years before the photo archive in this series begins. It is a blog's account, and it does not say anything was exhibited there.
The hall nearly went, and then homes were built over it

In 2015 the hall's future was open. Innovation Origins reported on October 10, 2015 that the urban plan for the site called for the old factory hall, between Anton and the Klokgebouw, to make way for housing. It says the hall was supposed to be gone already, to give way to a residential tower with a technology and media museum called Volt at its base, and that one of the museum's initiators, the Hilversum museum Beeld en Geluid, withdrew at the end of 2013, which put the tower and the demolition on hold. [S10]

Jack Hock, the Trudo director responsible for developing Strijp-S, then proposed keeping the hall and building homes across it: three levels of apartments on a structure that would span the skatepark and the BMX hall like a bridge. The report quotes him saying the site had lost too much to demolition already, and it quotes the Area51 manager as pleased and cautious, since the municipality and VolkerWessels would decide. [S10]

That plan became Haasje Over. Trudo's page says the Amsterdam architect VMX designed it, with a tower of 19 floors, about 70 meters high, and a bridge building of two residential layers across the existing skatehal, with homes of social rent. [S13] The builder Stam + De Koning describes the bridge as an air bridge of about 50 homes, six meters high, running over the skatehal, and speaks of the building in the past tense, as finished. [S14] The consultancy Tielemans's project page describes two bridges of 50 meters each, built as trusses and carrying dwellings above the existing hall, and a footbridge from Haasje Over to the roof of Anton on the tenth floor. [S15] Trudo's page expected the first homes to be delivered in January and February 2021. [S13]

The sources differ on the tower's lofts: Trudo's pre-completion page counts 136, the builder's page counts 134. [S13][S14] Neither figure matters to Area51, so I name both and leave it. What the sources do not say is how building above the hall changed daily life inside it. The district's history page only says the hall is no longer to be demolished and is fitted into the new plans. [S9]
Two parks became one in a rebuild around 2020 and 2021

The next change came from the inside. On November 9, 2018 Innovation Origins reported that an upgrade of Area 51 was among the first ten projects to receive money from the Regio Deal Brainport Eindhoven, a program in which the national government would invest 130 million euros and the region 240 million over four years in the area's business climate. [S16] A quote in the report says the upgrade would create a location with wide pull in the region and abroad, where both recreational and top athletes could train. The amount awarded to Area51 is not in the text I read, and I leave it out. [S16]

A Brainport Eindhoven profile of a regular tells the rest in a teenager's words. It says renovation work ran in 2020 and 2021, that the venue used to have one area for skaters and another for scooter riders and BMX riders, and that the course is now much bigger. It reports that people now come by train from other cities, and that more visitors come from abroad. [S17] The profile is undated in the text I read, and it is a feature written to show what the program paid for.

The venue's own pages describe the result today. The course is given as 3,000 square meters, with the street section's 750 square meters serving as an event floor, a cellar of 355 square meters with its own entrance on Ketelhuisplein, a café with room for 350 people and a multi-purpose room of 190 square meters. [S5] The tourist board's location page says 2,800 square meters. [S2] I use "about 3,000 square meters" for the course because the venue's page gives that figure, and I name the venue as the source.
Before the archive: a blog visit in 2011 and the opening night of 2023

Dutch Design Week came into the hall twice in ways the photo archive does not show. The first is the 2011 visit above. The second is the Grand Opening of DDW23. A DDW news item dated October 21, 2023 says the week began with a Grand Opening in the heart of the skatepark at Area 51, hosted by Lynn Zebeda and Cesar Majorana, with a takeover by The New Originals and guests named as Phantom Wizard, Fumez, Sokarekta and TNO Sound. It says the creative head of DDW opened with the theme Picture This. [S18]

Area51's own event-location page lists the opening of Dutch Design Week among the non-urban-sports events it has hosted, next to Club Vrijdag and the Storioni Festival. [S5] The two pages agree. The news item's date is the date of the page, and it does not say which evening the opening was. I did not find the evening elsewhere. [S18]

In the archive albums I read on October 7, 2026, the 2023 Area51 album holds five photos, all of an artists' collaboration. It has no photo of the opening night. [S39] A single exhibition stands for the venue in 2023, and the biggest night of the week there is not in the album. I did not check every album in the account, so I limit the point to the albums I read.
2023: a drawing machine and four hands

The 2023 album's photos are titled Antigoon 2023, and they credit Almicheal Fraay. [S39] A listing in DDW's own program explains the project. The listing says that before and during DDW 2023 Antigoon and the graphic design duo Thomas & Jurgen would make new work, to see what happens when a human and machine collaboration meets a human and human one, and that the results would be presented at Area 51. [S19] It describes Antigoon as building machines that combine a program's binary logic with intentional anomalies from the human programmer, and Thomas & Jurgen as working with self-made tools to move ink or paint across glass, perspex or brick. [S19] St. Joost School of Art & Design separately lists its tutor's display as Antigoon X Thomas & Jurgen at Area 51. [S20]

All three artists are part of UC MASTERS, which the listing says gives talented artists a grant and guidance. It is a project by EMOVES, supported by Cultuur Eindhoven, the province of North Brabant and the national education and culture ministry. [S19] The tourist board says Area51, the youth center Dynamo and The Ruggeds form EMOVES together, which places the venue inside the organization behind the program, as I read it. [S1][S19]

The photos show a bright white-brick hall with tall windows, a flat-bed drawing machine on a black table, a person drawing on a window, framed prints on the floor and a black display wall. [S39] The listing's description fits what the photos show. I cannot say which machine in a photo belongs to Antigoon, and I describe the objects by how they look.
2024: a design fair takes the building, and the archive tags another place

In 2024 Isola Design, a design platform that also stages a Milan showcase, took over Area51. Its press text, as Archisearch reported it on October 22, 2024, says this was its sixth consecutive participation in Dutch Design Week, which ran from October 19 to 27, 2024, with more than 100 exhibitors in four exhibitions that would share the building with the skaters' regular activities. [S21] DDW's program listing says the same four exhibitions were inspired by the theme This Future is Currently Unavailable. [S22]

The sources place the exhibitions floor by floor. Disclosure took the basement, with more than 40 independent designers and studios. Forms Unfolding and Routes to Roots took the ground floor, where the second was a traveling show made with a cultural center in Saudi Arabia and seen earlier in Saudi Arabia and in Milan. The Floor is Yours took the first floor, in a dance studio. The café on the first floor served as the meeting and talk area. [S21][S22]

The sources disagree on one number. Archisearch gives the basement space as 350 square meters and DDW's listing as 300. [S21][S22] The venue's own page gives the cellar as 355. [S5] I take "about 350" because two of the three agree and the venue's measurement sits beside it, and I name that as a reading, since I found no measurement.

The photo archive has no Area51 album for 2024. It has two albums tagged AreaWest in their photo titles, Fashion Tech Farm with 11 photos and Next Nature Museum at the Evoluon with seven, both by Tommy Köhlbrugge. [S39] A reader scanning the archive for Area51 in 2024 would find nothing and might conclude the venue was unused. The press says it was full.
Area West is a label on DDW's own map

DDW's own pages explain the second name. The 2024 area recap says the West area lies just south of Strijp-S and is home to the Evoluon, which it calls the Next Nature Museum. [S23] The 2026 locations list gives West as a filter of its own, next to Canal, Center, Hallenweg, Sectie-C, Station, Strijp-S and Strijp T+R. [S24] The Fashion Tech Farm's 2026 listing gives its address as Zeelsterstraat 80 in the West area. [S25] DDW's page for Area 51 lists the area as Strijp-S. [S32]

So the archive labels follow DDW's labels, and the confusion belongs to a reader. The tag AreaWest in a 2024 photo title is accurate for the farm and the Evoluon. The label "Area51" in 2023 and 2025 is accurate for the skatepark. I found no source that ties the two names together. In the record they share a sound and nothing else. [S23][S24][S32]
2025: four exhibitions, one album of 73 photos and a lounge

DDW's program pages for 2025 place four projects at Area 51. Next, Now, Then by the German Design Council presents German graduation projects. Hochschule Trier's news item says it showed 25 projects from October 18 to 26, 2025, curated by the studio Raw Colour. [S26][S27] Red Box, a program on design that strengthens the position of women, names Stoov as its main sponsor and lists 15 participants, with talks and workshops at several locations in the city. [S28] Seeds of Hope shows the work of 15 Fontys graduates in Trend Research and Concept Creation in Lifestyle, five new exhibitors every three days. [S29] Shaping the future of care, from the elder-care organization Anna Ouderenzorg and a dementia and technology center at the university in Eindhoven, listed a workshop at Area51 on Monday, October 20 from 10:00 to 12:00. [S30]

The archive holds two Area51 albums for the year. The first is nine photos of the German show by Max Kneefel. The second is a Business Lounge album with 73 photos by Kneefel and Cleo Goossens in the 24 titles I read. [S39] The other three exhibitions have no Area51 album in the list I read. The year's archive coverage of the venue is one exhibition and one lounge.

The lounge now has an answer, with a limit. DDW's 2026 frequently asked questions say the Design Tours start at the DDW Business Lounge in Area51 on Ketelhuisplein. [S31] One of the 2025 lounge photos carries a Design Tour title dated October 24, 2025, which fits. [S39] I read this as the lounge being a base for tours in both years, and the 2025 half is my inference from one photo title. The sponsors on the lounge sign are visible in the photographs, and I did not find a page saying who they were.

The four 2025 program pages I opened name other organizers, and I found no page placing Isola Design at Area51 in 2025. That does not prove it was absent, and the question stays open. [S26][S28][S29][S30]
The archive leans on one year

The Area51 albums hold 87 photos and the two AreaWest albums 18, which makes 105. The 2025 albums hold 82 of them, 78 percent, and the Business Lounge album alone holds 73. The 2024 albums hold 18 and 2023 holds five. [S39] Anyone counting photos per year would conclude 2025 mattered most. The counts show what was photographed and uploaded, and I would not read more into them than that.
2026: four items on DDW's list

DDW's 2026 page for the location lists nine days of opening hours, October 17 to 25, from 11:00 to 18:00, and free access. [S32] It lists four items. Fontys for Society, run all week, is a Fontys exhibition in five zones named Think, Create, Tech, Apply and Reflect, according to a FRITS news item that also says visitors need no DDW ticket. [S33][S34] SpaceTeen, also all week, is a research and design project in which young people work with designers and scientists on alternatives to social media, from a University of Amsterdam research group, a design studio, a digital design agency and a social design agency. [S35] Philips Design. Soul & Science runs across the Philips Museum, Area51 and the streets, and its description puts the part at Area51 under the heading care felt. The credits on the listing include a board member of Area51 as an exhibition host. [S36]

The fourth is Open Socials Social Club on Friday, October 23, by Waag Futurelab, a party that marks the soft launch of an open social media platform and puts on stage artists the listing says Meta had banned. [S37] A party in a skatepark belongs to a hall with a basement venue and an event floor. [S5][S37]

The venue's own Dutch Design Week page needs a careful reading. When I opened it on October 9, 2026, it still said that Dutch Design Week 2025 was getting closer, and the home page teasers for the festival carried placeholder text. [S38][S4] I read both as leftover text, and I rely on DDW's listing for 2026.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**When skating began on Strijp-S.** 2006, from three sources. A 2011 blog says Area 51 was established in 2002 and a 2014 magazine says the park opened in 2000 in Meerhoven. I use 2006 for Strijp-S and leave the first park's year open. [S6][S7][S11][S12]
**What the hall was.** A machine factory in one source and a tool shop in another. Not settled, and the phrase "former tool shop" is the tourist board's. [S1][S8]
**How big it is.** 2,800 square meters on the tourist board's page, 3,000 on the venue's. I use the venue's figure for the course and name it. [S2][S5]
**The basement exhibition.** 300, 350 and 355 square meters. I use about 350 and name the venue's cellar figure. [S5][S21][S22]
**Haasje Over's lofts.** 136 on Trudo's page, 134 on the builder's. [S13][S14]
**One place or two.** DDW's own labels settle it. Area51 is in the Strijp-S area, and West is a separate area south of Strijp-S. [S23][S24][S32]
What the record does not show
I do not know the year the SEU hall was built, which Philips unit used it, or whether it is a registered monument. I found no heritage record for it. [S8][S9]

I do not know when the first Area51 opened, or whether it began in Meerhoven in 2000 or elsewhere in 2002. [S11][S12] I do not know what building Haasje Over above the hall changed for the skatepark's daily use. [S9][S15]
I do not know the amount the Regio Deal gave Area51, and I could not open the news item that reportedly states it. [S16] I do not know the date of the Brainport profile. [S17]

I do not know which evening the DDW23 opening took place, or whether other albums in the archive hold photos of it. [S18][S39] I do not know why the archive has no Area51 album for 2024, whether Isola Design returned in 2025, or who the sponsors on the lounge sign were. [S21][S31][S39] I read only 24 of the Business Lounge album's 73 titles, and I did not reopen the photo archive for this version. [S39]

If you look up a venue in an archive, try three questions. Is the label a building or an area? Does the album title match the place in the photo? And does the archive skip a year the venue was in use? Area51 gives a clear answer to the last one, because 2024 is missing from its albums and full in the press. [S21][S39]

title: Design Perron sounds like a station platform, and its address is a building on Fuutlaan
subtitle: A former freight-forwarding building a five-minute walk from Eindhoven's central station, the venue's own history, and nine editions in the official photo archive
description: Design Perron in Eindhoven from 2013 to a final edition at Fuutlaan 12 in 2026: the building, the DDW record and what the sources leave open.

sections.x: The name Design Perron points to a railway platform, and the sources I opened point to a building on Fuutlaan that was once used to move freight. [S1][S21][S22]

DDW's 2026 page for the location says Design Perron is held in the building of Opvallers at Fuutlaan 12 and calls it a five-minute walk from the central station. It lists opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 24, 2026 and 11:00 to 17:00 on October 25, with free access. [S1] Design Perron's own 2026 notice adds something the older records could not: the area is being redeveloped, the building's tenant has to move, and this will be the last edition at Fuutlaan 12. [S10] This essay uses public sources only: Design Perron's pages, DDW's program pages and archive, a regional archive record, a property listing, press from 2013 and 2014 and the municipality's project page. It reports no visit and no interview.
The name points to the station, and DDW files the place under "Station"

Perron is the Dutch word for a station platform. Design Perron's English page uses the line "a track full of design stories," and its 2026 notice calls the building a station of ideas, materials, encounters and new designs for nine days. [S4][S10] The national monuments register lists Eindhoven's station, built in 1956 to a design by K. van der Gaast and registered on March 29, 2010, and its protected parts include the platforms, perrons in Dutch. [S26]

DDW adds to the confusion without meaning to. Its 2026 locations list sorts places by area, and Design Perron sits in the area called Station. [S1][S2] DDW's 2024 recap of the Station area walks through projects around the station building. [S17] Earlier years used other words. A DDW magazine recap of 2018 called the area from the station to the NRE site Central, and the 2019 area text said the central station marks the heart of a new design area and sent visitors to Design Perron alongside the railroad track. [S15][S16]

As an anatomist I learned that a structure's name and its location are two separate facts, and that a good atlas gives both. A venue name needs the same treatment. Read the name for what it suggests and the address for where the place is. [S1][S3]
The building: freight shed, theater premises, office

Fuutlaan 12 has a longer record than the festival. The regional historical center for Eindhoven holds a photograph titled Fuutlaan 12, forwarding company Van Gend & Loos, 1973. [S21] A commercial property listing for one unit, Fuutlaan 12 E1, says the complex lies directly against the railway beside the central station, was formerly used by Van Gend & Loos to move goods from trucks to rail wagons, and dates from 1956 according to the national address register. [S22] The same listing names Opvallers among the creative businesses around it. [S22]

A fire brigade report on a fire of October 8, 1955 describes a 150-meter freight shed of the railways, with the Van Gend & Loos loading station, burning in the direction of the station building, and it says the new shed would be in use within months. [S23] The report does not give a street, so I cannot tie the fire to Fuutlaan 12. The dates are consistent with a replacement shed in 1956, and I leave it at that.

Design Perron's own history adds the next layer. Its team page says the building Opvallers showed founder Meike van Schijndel in 2013 was the old premises of the theater company Het Zuidelijk Toneel. [S3] A Utrecht news site, writing on December 11, 2013 about that October, says she showed the Delta vase in the old Zuidelijk Toneel building. [S20] That is independent support from 2013 for the building's earlier use, though it is one line in a profile and I have found no record of the theater company's years there. Opvallers describes itself on its own site as a company that runs face-to-face campaigns and events, with nearly 25 years of work and a team of 350. [S24]
2013: twelve exhibitions, a vase and a boulevard

Design Perron says it was founded in 2013. Van Schijndel was looking for a location for an exhibition during Dutch Design Week to honor the relaunch of the Delta vase of 1981, designed by her father, the architect Mart van Schijndel, who lived from 1943 to 1999. After a long search she met Martin Damen of Opvallers on Fuutlaan, and the first year brought twelve exhibitions in and around the building, according to Design Perron. [S3] The Utrecht news item confirms the vase, the 1981 date and the Eindhoven showing in October 2013, and adds that the glass vase is assembled from three plates bonded with silicone rather than blown. [S20]

Press at the time counted differently. Core77's highlights from October 31, 2013 describe three long warehouses next to the central station that were partly emptied to make room for Design Perron, a set of ten exhibits, and a separate exhibit by the collective Dutch Invertuals. [S18] Twelve and ten are not the same count, and neither source says how it counted. I take both as honest and different.

Design Perron's own page says the first year was held in and around the Opvallers building. Core77 places Design Perron in warehouses next to the station. Together they make it very likely that the 2013 warehouses and the Opvallers building are one site, and I say "very likely" because no single page states it in both vocabularies. [S3][S18]

The 2014 edition was the second. A shop's news item gives the dates as October 18 to 26, 2014 at Fuutlaan 12 to 14, calls Design Perron a boulevard of bold design talent, and says about ten exhibitions stood outside in containers, with Dutch Invertuals and JSPR as resident exhibitors and a drinks evening on Wednesday, October 22. [S19] In 2016 Design Perron's own page says it was taking place for the fourth time at Fuutlaan 12 to 14, with new halls, a lecture room of about 238 square meters, a pop-up shop and a Design Meets Brands program planned with Opvallers. It also says a group called Working Friends would occupy the back of the building that fall and that the café would again serve coffee, tea and organic rolls. [S7]
Foundation, team and the scale it claims

The team page says Van Schijndel started Design Perron in 2013 as an ad hoc DDW location. An interior designer joined in 2014 and an architect in 2015, which made the first real team, and since June 2016 it has been a foundation. [S3] Both of those early team members have since left, and Chris Ruhe took on a larger role from 2025. [S3] The page says the event now has more than 50 exhibitors and over 16,000 visitors a year. Those are the organizer's own figures, and I found no independent count. [S3]

For 2025, the info page gives Fuutlaan 12, 12A and 12E, with the designer market in 12 and 12A, a light lab at 12A and the graduates at 12E, October 18 to 26, 2025, open only during DDW, and free. It puts the walk at about five minutes from the central station, past the Effenaar. [S4] A DDW notice dated September 30, 2025 about new exhibition clusters called HUBS names a Young Graduates HUB at Fuutlaan 12. [S14]
Who shows there: schools, collectives and brands

The exhibitor mix has stayed close to what the 2013 format promised. The 2014 notice lists Dutch Invertuals and JSPR as residents and names Cor Unum Ceramics, a second-year Design Academy Eindhoven master's group, a Utrecht platform for beginning talent and a Rotterdam group of creatives among many others. [S19] Design Perron's 2016 page says a hall fitted out by Sint Lucas the year before could be rented for lectures and events. [S7] In 2023 seven design graduates of the Berlin University of the Arts showed under the title U don't Know at Fuutlaan 12, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 with free admission during DDW23, October 21 to 29, 2023, according to the university's own page. [S28]

The former-exhibitors page is a long run of image galleries by year, and the labels on its images name schools such as ArtEZ, Artemis Academy, Cibap, HKU, the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and the Willem de Kooning Academy, next to studios, ceramicists and brands. [S9] I read those as labels set by Design Perron, and I did not count exhibitors. The 2026 mix repeats the pattern: a Swedish textile school, a brand and designer pairing, a designer market and a disability arts organization. [S1][S12][S13]
What the archive and the venue's own site show for each year

The official DDW Flickr archive holds albums named Design Perron for nine editions: 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2025, with 157 photos in total. [S27] The photographers are credited in the titles. In 2015 the 15 photos credit Cleo Goossens and Boudewijn Bollmann and name Hamerhaai and Studio Ineke van der Werff, and one shows a sign reading opvallers. The venue's own pictures page for 2015 carries labels such as Cor Unum, Ineke van der Werff, Ultra Studio, MVOS and Hamerhaai, which match some of the photo titles. [S29] The 2016 album has 26 photos by Tommy Köhlbrugge. The 2017 album has 11 by Bollmann, including a painted sign reading "Een spoor vol design," Dutch for a track full of design. [S27]

Britt Roelse shot the eight photos of 2018, Nick Bookelaar the eight of 2019, whose titles name the designer Marlou Beentjes, and Roelse again the 24 of 2021 and 22 of 2022, both titled FUUTLAAN_DESIGNPERRON. Almicheal Fraay shot the 19 of 2023, and Goossens the 24 of 2025, all titled DesignPerron_Station_DDW25. [S27] The DDW 2018 magazine says the venue again offered a stage to many designers. [S15] In 2023 DDW listed a drinks evening for ten years of Design Perron from 17:00 to 20:00 at Fuutlaan 12. [S11]

The 2025 file titles have a likely explanation. Station is DDW's area label for the venue, and the titles begin DesignPerron_Station. [S1][S27] The titles do not say why the photographers chose the word, so that reading is mine.
Two missing years that were not missing

The archive has no album named Design Perron for 2020 or 2024, and I first read that as a gap in the event. The venue's own site says otherwise. Its info page for 2020 sets out the pandemic rules: every DDW location needed a DDW ticket that year, checked at the door, and Design Perron could only be entered with one. [S8] Its former-exhibitors page carries a gallery for every year from 2013 to 2025, 2020 and 2024 included. [S9] So the event ran in 2020 by its own page, and the 2024 gallery label points the same way. The archive does not file photographs of those years under its name.

For 2024 the archive has two small albums with related titles, Fuutlaan with five photos and Centraal Station Eindhoven with two, neither named Design Perron. A 2023 album titled Fuutlaan 12C holds 14 photos by Fraay, and a 2025 album titled Centraal Station Eindhoven holds 27 by Max Kneefel. The archive does not link any of these to Design Perron. [S27] An album named for the station tells you where a photographer stood and not which venue the pictures show.
2026: the last edition at Fuutlaan 12

DDW's page for 2026 lists 11 entries at the location, among them the Swedish School of Textiles show EXIT26, a furniture and textile exhibition, a workshop that appears twice, a mahjong project, a shelving system and a vase exhibition by Special Arts in which creators with disabilities answer the question what a vase is. [S1][S13] Brands & Designers pairs brands and designers and was originally developed for a three-day festival in Amsterdam. It was designed by Van Schijndel, and four of its original eight houses are shown here. [S12]

Design Perron's drinks notice invites visitors on Monday, October 19 from 17:00 to 20:00 to celebrate 13 years and 13 editions on Fuutlaan 12 and thanks Damen and the Opvallers team for their hospitality. [S10] By the site's own year galleries, 2013 to 2025 is 13 editions, which would make 2026 the fourteenth. Either "13 editions" counts through 2025 or it counts elapsed years, and the page does not say which. [S9][S10]

The two sources also disagree on where the graduates will be. Design Perron's 2026 home page places a Young Graduates Hub with 30 graduates at Kennedyplein 300, a second location. [S5][S6] DDW's 2026 locations list shows Design Perron at Fuutlaan 12 and I found no Kennedyplein 300 entry on it, and DDW's own notice names the Young Graduates HUB at Fuutlaan 12, though that notice dates from September 30, 2025. [S2][S14] I do not know which is current. DDW's 2026 page for the venue also says other exhibits there come from Dutch Invertuals, Envisions, Spoor K, JSPR and others. [S1]
The area is being redeveloped

Design Perron says the area is being redeveloped and Opvallers has to move. [S10] The municipality's project page for the Nieuwe Fuutlaan says the city council adopted a Fuutlaan area framework in 2024, that the first step is a new road between Stationsweg and the Insulindelaan ring, and that the city, NS and ProRail carry it out. It gives a schedule: research in 2026, a design phase and permit procedure in 2027, and execution from 2028 to 2030. [S25] The page does not name Opvallers, the building or Design Perron, so the link between the two statements is Design Perron's own. I did not find a document naming the building.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**Platform or building.** DDW's address and the property record settle it. The venue is a building on Fuutlaan, and the station appears as a walking reference. [S1][S22]
**Twelve exhibitions or ten.** Design Perron's own count for 2013 is twelve, Core77's is ten. Not settled. [S3][S18]
**Whether 2020 and 2024 happened.** They did, by the venue's own pages. The archive lacks albums under the name. [S8][S9][S27]
**Where the graduates will be in 2026.** Fuutlaan 12 on DDW's list, Kennedyplein 300 on Design Perron's page. Not settled. [S2][S5][S14]
**Thirteen editions.** Counted from the galleries, 13 ends in 2025. Not settled. [S9][S10]
What the record does not show

I do not know who owned the Fuutlaan 12 complex over the years, or whether the Opvallers building is the replacement shed that the 1955 report anticipates. I did not find a heritage record, and that report does not give an address. [S21][S22][S23]

I do not know how long Het Zuidelijk Toneel used the building, or in what way. The company is named in Design Perron's account and in one news profile, and I found no record from the theater side. [S3][S20]

I do not know why the archive files no photographs under Design Perron for 2020 and 2024, whether the 2024 Fuutlaan photographs show the venue, or who the exhibitors are in photographs whose titles carry no name. I read the album pages on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen the archive for this version, so counts and credits come from that reading. [S27]
I do not know where the venue will go after 2026, or whether the Young Graduates Hub is at Fuutlaan 12 or Kennedyplein 300. [S5][S10][S14]

If you plan to visit during DDW 2026, check the address on DDW's location page before you set out. When you open a venue's photo archive, which would you trust first: the name, the file title, or the address on this year's listing? [S1][S27]
