title: A building made to show the future has to keep updating it
subtitle: The Evoluon in Eindhoven, from Philips's 1961 decision to its 2018 sale and the Next Nature Museum, read through the records and four Dutch Design Week archive years
description: The Evoluon from the 1961 Philips decision to the Next Nature Museum and four DDW photo albums, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: A museum built to show the future has to keep revising the future it shows, and the Evoluon in Eindhoven was designed on that principle in 1961. [S1]

The Philips Museum's own account says the exhibition inside the Evoluon was meant to look ahead, to avoid being a showroom for Philips products, and to avoid lingering in the past. [S1] That plan makes the later history easier to read. The Evoluon closed as a museum in 1989, spent years as a congress center, was sold by Philips for a new use and reopened in 2022 as the Next Nature Museum. [S2][S3][S4] This essay follows the building through public records: Philips's museum, heritage and planning news, trade and regional press, Next Nature's own pages and annual report, and the official Dutch Design Week program and photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview.

In medical education I have seen what happens to a teaching collection that never updates, because it ends up teaching a past generation's anatomy. A science museum has the same problem on a larger scale, and the Evoluon is a good place to watch it. [S1]
Planned in 1961, opened on September 24, 1966

The Philips Museum records that on January 2, 1961 the board agreed to a proposal by Frits Philips: instead of taking part in world exhibitions, Philips would build a house for a museum and an ever-renewing exhibition of its products. The board's reasons included a spectacular marker for the company's 75th anniversary and a place to receive the many visitors who could not be taken through the factories. After the Brussels world exhibition of 1958, where Philips made a good impression with its own pavilion, the board had decided against joining further fairs. [S1]

Philips had shown products in Eindhoven before. The museum lists a prewar history museum in the company school, destroyed in a bombing raid on December 6, 1942, a Demonstration Laboratory of 1951, which is today's Philips Museum, and a product studio of 1948. [S1] The museum also names a possible inspiration, the Dome of Discovery at the Festival of Britain in 1951, for which Kalff gave lighting advice, and it notes that he also advised on the lighting of the festival's pleasure gardens in Battersea Park, designed by James Gardner, who later shaped the Evoluon exhibition. [S1]

Louis Kalff, who the museum says headed Philips Design from 1925 to 1960, made the first sketches. According to Frits Philips's autobiography as the museum quotes it, the building that looked like a spaceship was drawn over lunch on the back of a menu. [S1] A heritage site tells the story differently: a dinner at which Kalff drew three designs, one of them the flying saucer, and it adds that this is tradition. [S5] Omroep Brabant has a lunch with a menu. [S2] I take the menu as the story's fixed point and leave the meal open. The museum cites the founder's autobiography for its version, the heritage site and Omroep Brabant call theirs tradition, and none gives a date.

Kalff worked with the young architect Leo de Bever, who lived from 1930 to 2015. [S6] Brabants Erfgoed calls Kalff an already retired artistic adviser to the Philips board. [S6] The Philips Museum gives a different picture, since it lists him as head of Philips Design until 1960 and still active in the project. [S1] The two descriptions are compatible, because a man can leave a post and stay an adviser.

The name came from the exhibition expert Jacques Kleiboer, the museum says, who meant it as an essentially optimistic concept. The physicist Jan F. Schouten supplied the philosophy: a show of the relationship between people and technology, dynamic and looking ahead, not a catalog of products. The museum adds that 120 company specialists worked in 18 groups, and that the English exhibition designer James Gardner was brought in. [S1] The building went up between 1962 and 1966, according to the heritage news site De Erfgoedstem. [S7] Prince Bernhard and Frits Philips opened it on September 24, 1966. [S4]
What the saucer is made of

The numbers are consistent across sources, and I give them here once. The dish has a diameter of 77 meters and the building is almost 32 meters high. It rests on twelve V-shaped column pairs, which Omroep Brabant counts as 24 columns. [S2] The Dutch architecture database describes two shells on twelve 8-meter V-shaped columns around a glass entrance hall, 48 windows in the rim of the upper shell, an 8-meter plexiglass skylight, a shell built from 822 hexagonal concrete elements of 1,200 kilograms each, ring-shaped steel cables with a combined length of 169 kilometers, and a total weight of 15,000 tons. It gives 6,000 square meters of exhibition space reached by a hydraulic lift with a glass shaft, and a 60-meter concrete mast beside the building. [S8] A 2026 profile in a regional magazine repeats these figures and adds that the pond in the park has the same 77-meter diameter as the dish. [S9]

Some of the park was never built as drawn. The artists Constant, Volten, Haber and Clough designed the park, and Philips rejected their design. [S8] The architecture database says so, and the 2026 profile agrees. [S9]
Half a million visitors a year

The numbers on visitors come as three different kinds of figure. The Philips Museum says the millionth visitor arrived on November 21, 1968. [S1] Omroep Brabant gives 527,000 visitors in the peak year 1970 and an average of 475,000 a year until 1980. [S2] Brabants Erfgoed says about ten million visitors had been counted when the Evoluon closed to the public in 1989. [S6] Next Nature's own page says "over 500,000 visitors by 1970," which could be read as a cumulative figure, and Omroep Brabant's yearly figure shows it was one year's count. [S10][S2] Taken together the figures fit: a million by late 1968, a peak year near 527,000 and a lifetime total near ten million.

Visitors turned knobs and ran experiments, which the Philips Museum says was new to the Netherlands and was imitated by later science centers such as NEMO in Amsterdam. [S1] A 2026 profile by a former student worker adds details such as a counter of four red tubes in the hall that tracked the number of people inside, and a fire-code cap of 2,000 visitors at once. [S9] That is one person's memory in a magazine, and I treat it as color and not as a measurement.
Closed in 1989, and what came after

Sources give different reasons for the closure. The Philips Museum says it was no longer justifiable for Philips to carry the high operating costs. [S1] Omroep Brabant says the museum became too expensive. [S2] Next Nature's page says declining visitor numbers and changing views on science communication. [S11] Those readings are compatible, since a costly museum with falling attendance is hard to defend. They share one claim, which is that the company stopped.

After 1989 the building became a closed reception center for Philips and later a congress center, according to Omroep Brabant. [S2] The architecture database says congress use dates from 1994 and that new buildings were added on the 5.8-hectare site. [S8] A magazine profile says an auditorium was built next to the building. [S9] The year the congress function began is not settled in the sources I could open, and English-language references give other years. In January 1994 the city's executive board designated the building a municipal monument, as NOS recalled in 2018. [S12]

The record shows temporary life in the building as well. A regional magazine says the first temporary exhibition, about the human brain, was organized in 2012, and the German band Kraftwerk played there in 2013. [S13] The tourist board counts four concerts. [S14]

The heritage status rose in 2018. NOS reported on February 20, 2018 that the municipality had announced the Evoluon was designated a national monument, and that the city's earlier municipal status would be withdrawn. [S12] The trade site Architectenweb adds that the decision was the minister's, Ingrid van Engelshoven's, and De Erfgoedstem, a day later, calls the building an icon of the postwar rebuilding period. [S15][S7] NOS also reported one idea floated that year, to place a national design museum in the building. [S12]
Sold by Philips, effective January 1, 2019

The building was not the city's property in the way the word gift suggests. The tourist board writes that Philips gifted the Evoluon to the city for the company's 75th anniversary, and Omroep Brabant calls it a present from Philips to the city. [S14][S2] But on December 20, 2018 Innovation Origins reported that the combination Hurks, Foolen & Reijs would become the new owner on January 1, 2019, "the current owner" being Philips. [S3] I read the gift as a gift in spirit to the citizens, with ownership staying with Philips for 52 years.

The report describes a process Philips started in the fall of 2017. Fifteen parties applied, seven presented plans in the summer, and a committee led by the president of Philips Nederland chose the Eindhoven partnership of Foolen & Reijs Vastgoed and Hurks vastgoedontwikkeling. A new Evoluon Foundation was to program the building, with Philips as a member. Philips and the buyers agreed a clause against speculation, a chain clause against splitting up the site, and an intention to make the Evoluon available free for at least half the time for technology, design, education and culture. Renovation and the new program were to start in the summer of 2021, and the tenant Regus stayed until then. [S3] The buyers' own vision text says the icon would reopen to the public in 2021 with a park around it. [S16]

The price is less well documented. A heritage trade site, writing in January 2021, says the building was sold in 2018 for 4.2 million euros, a relatively modest sum, on condition it become accessible again. [S17] I found no second source for the figure.
Next Nature moves in

In September 2020 the TU/e campus paper reported that the national government would release 2 million euros over four years for a futurelab for design and technology, led by Koert van Mensvoort of Next Nature, with the Evoluon as its planned home. It quotes him planning a first project in 2021 and a complete futurelab by 2025, and it names Jan Mengelers, president of the Evoluon Foundation, as the contact. [S18] The paper notes that the plan had first lost out to Waag in the Council for Culture's advice and was rescued by a motion in the House. [S18]

On June 30, 2021 Next Nature announced that its plans had received 7.6 million euros from the Region Deal Brainport Eindhoven. From January 1, 2022 it would be the new crew of the monument, and it named Lichtstad Erfgoed as the owner it works with. [S19] The announcement does not say how Lichtstad Erfgoed relates to the buyers named in 2018, and I did not find a register entry that links the names. In the fall of 2021 Next Nature turned the building into a virtual reality time machine, and it planned a full reopening from 2025. [S10]

The public reopening came in stages, and on September 24, 2022, fifty-six years to the day after the opening, the building reopened with RetroFuture, which KIVI says used 3,000 square meters on four rings. [S4] Next Nature describes ten tunnels of fiction and facts, with works by Studio Drift, Driessens & Verstappen and others, and funding from several cultural funds and public bodies. [S20] The interior studio M+R says its brief was to restore the monument's clarity with limited means. It cut visual clutter, painted existing furnishings in one blue and filled the public rooms with chairs by designers from Eindhoven and Brabant such as Maarten Baas and Piet Hein Eek, each item labeled for auction after use. [S21]

The plan Next Nature published for the full building divides the story into four rings: the origin of the universe and Earth, the origin of life, technology as a force on the planet, and the visitor's own role as crew of what it calls spaceship Earth. [S10] The original exhibition space is described elsewhere as three rings, so the fourth ring may be Next Nature's own count. [S9]
By summer 2024, a regional magazine says, only the building was called Evoluon and the museum was the Next Nature Museum. [S13]
Dutch Design Week, from 2022

The archive question has a clear answer from Dutch public broadcaster VPRO's tips for DDW 2022, which says the Evoluon is a DDW location for the first time that year. [S22] That explains why the photo archive has no earlier Evoluon album, and I found no evidence that DDW used the building before. The 2017 album titled HUBOT, which I could not place before, belongs elsewhere: Next Nature's own page says HUBOT was at the MediaMarkt in Eindhoven during DDW 2017. [S23]

The 2022 album holds 22 photos. Six are credited to about.today and show a person in a virtual reality headset, and 16 are credited to Tommy Köhlbrugge and titled West_Evoluon_RetroFuture, dated October 22 and 23, 2022. [S24] The 2023 album holds 13 photos by about.today dated October 20, 2023, showing geodesic domes. [S24] The domes belong to Spacefarming: the future of food, which Next Nature says ran from September 2023 until July 2025, with a list of 28 names that includes SPACE10, Solar Foods, Wageningen University & Research and the European Space Agency. [S25] A design press story from 2023 describes domes housing lab-grown meat substitutes and an insect-powered cookbook. [S26]

The 2024 album holds seven photos by Köhlbrugge, dated October 19 to 23. [S24] DDW's recap of the West area names Microbial Oasis, A House of Salt, Meet Meat: Rourou's Adventure and a Breathing Session with Geoffrey Lillemon, and the album shows a breathing session on the floor. [S27] Spacefarming was still on view, which is consistent with the algae dome in the album. [S25][S24]

The 2025 album holds 14 photos by Almicheal Fraay, and it includes a blue reception desk that fits M+R's blue scheme. [S24][S21] DDW listed a Digital & AI hub called Digital Futures with 31 presentations at the Next Nature Museum, whose entrance DDW lists as partially paid. [S28] Next Nature's annual report adds the Next Nature Conference 2025 on bio design and a Design Debate on Saturday, October 25 in the Philips Hall, led by Tracy Metz and Wouter van Noort. [S29]

For 2026, DDW's page for the Next Nature Museum lists nine opening days from October 17 to 25, with 11:00 to 18:00 shown for October 17, partly paid entry, and four items. Quantum Safari Game is an exhibition of six interactive quantum installations by Next Nature and QDNL, open all week. [S30][S31] A symposium on the creative economy with Peter Wennink among the speakers is listed for Monday, October 19. [S32] The National Design Debate 2026, titled Shaping Europe, takes place in the Philips Hall on Friday, October 23, and Waag announced a three-year partnership with the museum to hold it. [S33][S34] A conference called PROMPT, on AI as an artistic material, is listed as well. [S35]
A new future on view almost every year

The program titles show what the building keeps updating. In 2022 the future on view was the past's version of it, in RetroFuture. From 2023 to 2025 it was food, in Spacefarming. At DDW 2025 it was digital life and AI, and in 2026 DDW lists quantum physics and a debate on European design. [S4][S25][S28][S31][S33] That is a reading of titles and not of the exhibitions themselves, which I did not see. It does match the principle in the Philips Museum's account: a show about technology that does not stand still. [S1]

The cost of that principle appears in the annual report for 2025. Paying visitors rose from 54,837 in 2023 to 62,651 in 2024 and 76,636 in 2025, and the museum aims for 150,000 visitors a year by 2030. The report also records a loss of 168,514.50 euros in 2025, the first red figures in the organization's history, multi-year commitments of more than a million euros a year from the state, province and municipality for 2025 to 2028, building costs of about the same size, and a park development that was taking longer than hoped. [S29] On the park, the landscape studio LOLA says the city commissioned a framework for a 15-hectare park, and that the council approved plans that include two new buildings with affordable housing. [S36]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Who owned it.** The gift framing says the city, and the sales report names Philips as the owner until January 1, 2019. The sales report is the later and more specific document, and I use it. [S14][S3]
**The columns.** Twelve V-shaped columns in one source and 24 columns in another. They describe the same structure, twelve V-shaped pairs. [S8][S2]
**Where Kalff drew it.** Lunch, dinner, menu card. Not settled, and the versions differ. [S1][S5][S2]

**Three rings or four.** The original exhibition space is described as three rings, and both KIVI and Next Nature's plan speak of four. I cannot tell whether the fourth is the top ring or a count Next Nature made for itself. [S9][S4][S10]
**The 1970 count.** Next Nature's page reads as a total and Omroep Brabant's as one year. Omroep Brabant's yearly figure fits the other totals. [S10][S2]
**Whether DDW used the building before 2022.** VPRO's statement and the absence of earlier albums agree. [S22][S24]
**The 2017 HUBOT album.** Next Nature places it at a store, not at the Evoluon. [S23]
What the record does not show
I do not know when the congress function began, whether in 1989 or 1994 or in between, and I found no Philips document that says. [S8][S2]
I do not know how Lichtstad Erfgoed relates to Hurks, Foolen & Reijs, or the price of the 2018 sale, which rests on one trade report. [S19][S17]
I do not know why Kalff's sketch story varies, or which meal it was. [S1][S5]

I cannot say what the visitors to the 2022 to 2025 DDW exhibitions saw beyond what the program texts and album titles say, and I read the Flickr albums on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them for this version. [S24]

If you visit during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at what the building asks you to imagine and when that vision was first proposed. Which of today's futures on show do you expect a visitor to find quaint in thirty years, and which do you expect to hold up? [S30]

title: Hallenweg is a street of workshops, and the archive follows its tenants
subtitle: A post-war row of business halls in Eindhoven, the design area that took its name, and seven editions of the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: Hallenweg in Eindhoven from post-war halls to a Dutch Design Week area that now reaches beyond the street, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: Hallenweg is a street of post-war business halls, and by 2026 the Dutch Design Week area that carries its name reaches well beyond the street. [S1]

That sentence is easy to miss if you read the archive the way the archive is filed. The photo albums say Hallenweg, Vij5, Jeroen Wand or Atelier NL, and a reader could take all four for neighbors on one street. [S2] The sources I opened say something more careful: the street is one place, the DDW area is another, and the tenants who made the area known have moved around inside it and out of it. This essay uses public sources only: the tourist board, a heritage news item, DDW's area recaps, location pages and program items, the studios' own pages and the DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. [S3][S4]
A post-war scheme for small industry

The tourist board's roundup of Eindhoven's design areas says Hallenweg came into being after the Second World War as an economic recovery project. It says the first tenants were mostly metal and welding firms, that the buildings were constructed in the style of the Delft School, and that they are hidden behind the Hoogstraat. [S3] That is the whole published description I could open. It gives no architect and no date.

The city's own history page sets the scene. The war left Eindhoven damaged, with the Philips factories bombed and the Demer shopping street destroyed in the bombing of December 6, 1942, and afterward the city rebuilt quickly and became the fastest-growing city in the Netherlands, with a housing shortage, a ring road and new districts in Woensel and Gestel. [S5] A scheme of halls for small industry fits that period, though the city's page does not mention Hallenweg.

DDW's 2026 pages repeat the story with one more detail. The Hal2 location page says Hallenweg was originally built as part of the city's post-war reconstruction in 1951, and the Muziek&Ko page, for Hallenweg 7, says it was built after the war as an economic recovery project in the Delft School style and keeps its industrial character. [S6][S7] The 1951 date is DDW's own, and I could not check it against the city's monument file.

A heritage news item of January 9, 2016 adds the status of the halls. Eindhoven had designated seven new buildings from the reconstruction period as municipal monuments, out of 24 that the city's executive board had proposed in 2014, and the item lists the business halls at Hallenweg 1 to 7c among them. The other 17 were to be decided in March or April. [S4]

The same list of seven includes the power station at Strijp-T on Beukenlaan. [S4] That may be why the two places get linked, because they appear together in a single municipal decision. The tourist board still lists Strijp-T and Hallenweg as separate entries, and I found no source that places Hallenweg inside the Strijp-T area. [S3][S4]

I could not read the city's own monument file. The city's monument dossier host answered with a rejection page when I asked for it, and I did not try again, so the register's architect and construction year stay out of this essay. [S4]
Metal shops first, then studios

The street's present life shows up in tenants' own words. The interior design-and-build company Hal2 says it started twenty years ago at Hallenweg 2, the second hall, and has now grown into a renovated Hallenweg 3. The page is undated, and I read "twenty years" as relative to its writing. [S8] In October 2015 Innovation Origins described the workspace of the designer Jeroen Wand on Hallenweg, with a large outdoor area, chickens outside and a radio inside. It said his newest work would be shown in the studio during DDW 2015, alongside guests including Jo Sijen and Wouter Corvers, and listed his Phases vases among the pieces. [S9]

Vij5 describes itself as a publisher of design products, and its own site gives a studio, workshop and showroom address in Den Bosch. [S10] DDW's program for 2021 says Vij5 was celebrating its fifteenth birthday, and the DDW 2026 listing for its anniversary show is titled "20 jaar Vij5," which puts the label's start around 2006. [S11][S12] A designer interview on Vij5's site says Wand settled in Eindhoven when a friend found a studio too big for one person, and that his studio now has several employees. [S13]
DDW's own pages, year by year

DDW's recap of 2018, which says the festival has eight design areas, tells visitors that the designers of the Hallenweg welcome them in their studios. It names Vij5 with a project called Kies Kleur, in which the public chooses a color, and it lists Jeroen Wand and Maarten Baptist as exhibitors. Atelier NL appears with the sentence that the church of Atelier NL is just a stone's throw away, and the recap adds that Atelier NL was the previous year's ambassador of Dutch Design Week. [S14] The recap says "a stone's throw away," which places the church near the street and not on it.

In 2019, now counting nine areas, DDW's recap sends visitors to Vij5, which showed the origins of its collection, to Atelier NL's church for an indoor forest, and to a ceramics presentation called Arita. It also names Studio van der Zandt and an enormous coin track called 50/50 by the agency HeyHeyDeHaas. [S15] A design site's 2019 report places the area in the south-west of the festival map and describes it as private studios opened to the public, with projects on interaction, sustainability and ceramic craft combined with technology. [S16] In 2021 the area preview, back at eight areas with Hallenweg marked G on the map, lists Vij5's anniversary candles, Atelier NL's natural-materials exhibitions including a flax project and a water school, and two shows at De Fabriek. [S11]

The 2024 recap says the hidden gems of Dutch Design Week are in the Hallenweg area, and it names De Fabriek with Polluted Plants to Pottery and (w)aardewerk, Studio Jeroen Wand with Stacking and EXO, and Atelier NL's Meanderende Maas and a dinner called Smaak van de Bodem in the Atelier NL church. [S17] Vij5 says in a blog post that its 2024 exhibition, Introducing Tomorrow, could be found in its workshop on Hallenweg, with six new and four renewed designs. [S18] I found area recaps titled for 2021 and 2022 as videos with no text I could read, and none for 2023 or 2025.
What seven editions of photographs show
The official archive holds Hallenweg-related albums for seven editions: 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2024. Together they hold 11 albums and 143 photos. [S2]

The 2015 album has 18 photos by Ralph Roelse with number titles, showing a courtyard with Studio Jeroen Wand signs, a shipping container and workshop rooms with ceramics and pendant lamps. In 2016 the archive splits the street into two albums: 7 photos of Wand's workshop by Iris Rijskamp and 39 of Vij5 whose titles read "image by Vij5," meaning the label supplied them. In 2017 and 2018 each studio again has an album, and Rijskamp took all of them. The 2019 album of Vij5 has 5 photos and the 2020 album has 30, credited in the titles I read to Max Kneefel. The 2024 album has 5 photos by Anwyn Howarth and is titled Atelier NL (Hallenweg), showing a mound of earth among tables of ceramics. [S2]

The archive follows the tenants. The street name appears in album titles in 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2024, and after 2017 the albums are named for the studio. I cannot say from the titles that the 2019 and 2020 Vij5 albums were photographed on the street. [S2]
The label travels

DDW's 2026 location pages show how far the area label has stretched. The Dutch locations page lists, under the Hallenweg area, Atelier Fig. at Hallenweg 11, Atelier NL at Bergmannstraat 76, De Fabriek at Baarsstraat 38, Design Daily's at Gestelsestraat 234, Hal2 at Hallenweg 3, Muziek & Ko at Hallenweg 7, Studio Jeroen Wand at Bayeuxlaan 7 and Studio Tast at Gestelsestraat 238. [S1] DDW's 2026 pages give a flavor of the area's tenants. Muziek&Ko at Hallenweg 7 shows Design by Resonance, instruments shaped by sound, with workshops and live music. [S7] Atelier Fig shows its Fringe technique in an industrial warehouse that the page says was made available by a natural stone specialist. [S19] De Fabriek lists a group exhibition of master projects from two LUCA schools in Belgium among its items, and Studio Tast invites visitors to test neuro-inclusive solutions for education and work. [S20][S21] Teun Zwets is on Hallenweg itself: the DDW page says his studio found a new home in early 2026, with workshop, showroom, office and canteen under one roof, and a show of 50 chairs. [S22] Wand's page gives Bayeuxlaan 7, in the Hallenweg area and not on the street, where in 2015 his workspace was on Hallenweg. [S23][S9]

Atelier NL's own site gives Bergmannstraat 76 as its address, and DDW's 2026 page says it is situated in the former Bergmann Church on Bergmannstraat. [S24][S25] So the church counts as part of the Hallenweg area on DDW's map and as a neighbor of the street in the 2018 recap, and it is not on Hallenweg. The 2024 album title "Atelier NL (Hallenweg)" reads as the area label. [S1][S14][S2]

Vij5 is the other change. Its 2026 anniversary show is listed under the Canal area at APTUM, in the NRE site, at Gashouder 13, not in the Hallenweg area. [S12] That does not mean Vij5 has left the street for good, and I found no 2026 source that says where its workshop is.
For October 17 to 25, 2026, DDW lists the Teun Zwets and Wand shows as free and open from 11:00 to 18:00 on the first day. [S22][S23]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Strijp-T or not.** The tourist board lists Hallenweg and Strijp-T as separate areas. The municipal monument decision of January 2016 lists both, which is likely why they get linked. I use the tourist board's listing for the areas. [S3][S4]

**Where Atelier NL is.** The 2018 recap says near the street, Atelier NL's own site says Bergmannstraat 76, and DDW's 2026 list says the same address under the Hallenweg area. These agree once the area is separated from the street. [S14][S24][S1]

**Where Vij5 is based.** Vij5 describes a studio, workshop and showroom in Den Bosch, while its 2024 blog places an exhibition in a workshop on Hallenweg. Both can be true if the festival showroom and the base are different places, and that is my reading. [S10][S18]
**Eight areas or nine.** DDW said eight in 2018, nine in 2019 and eight in 2021. The recaps do not say what changed. [S14][S15][S11]
What the record does not show

I do not know who designed the halls at Hallenweg 1 to 7c or when they were built. The tourist board names a style and the heritage news item gives a status, and neither gives an architect or a year. [S3][S4]
I do not know when DDW first used the street, why 2021 to 2023 and 2025 have no album, or whether the 2019 and 2020 Vij5 albums show Hallenweg. [S11][S2]
I do not know where Vij5's workshop stands in 2026, and I did not find an exhibitor list for the area in 2025. [S12]

If you walk the area during DDW 2026, you could try the archive's test on a studio door. Does the sign name the street, the studio, or only the work, and which of those would still tell a reader where they were ten years from now? [S1]

title: A power plant for Philips factories, now a stage for design questions about AI
subtitle: The Innovation Powerhouse in Eindhoven, from a Philips energy plant of the 1950s to a design and technology building, followed through planning, press and Dutch Design Week records
description: The Innovation Powerhouse in Eindhoven from Philips energy plant TR to a Dutch Design Week venue, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: The Innovation Powerhouse was built to make power for Philips factories, and Dutch Design Week now lists it as a place where design asks questions about AI. [S1][S2]

I like a building whose first job is on the record, because it gives me something firm to hold while the exhibitions change. This essay draws on public sources only: an architecture and planning record, the city's image bank, trade press, the building's developers and architects, Dutch Design Week's pages and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. [S3][S1][S2]
A power plant that grew in stages

The Eindhoven architecture center's walking guide, published in January 2021, says the energy plant TR was born at the start of the 1950s on the drawing boards of Philips's own Architects and Engineers Bureau. It was delivered with a single chimney, and the second chimney, like the first 76 meters high, dates from 1953. The plant was extended in 1956 and 1960, and the turbine hall was extended in 1970. Over those years it burned coal, then oil and finally natural gas. [S3]

Other sources compress the same history into four stages. The firm that supplied the windows for the conversion and the Dutch architecture site Architectuur.nl both say the plant was built in four phases between 1953 and 1972 and supplied the Philips factories on Strijp R, S and T. Architectuur.nl places the turbines and generators in the low volume, the coal transport and storage in the narrow high-rise, and the steam boilers in a third volume to the north, while Reynaers puts the steam boilers in the high volume. [S4][S1] Both name the architect of the 1953 design as C. Last. [S1][S4] The architecture site urbanNext gives the same 1953 to 1972 span. [S5]

One source gives an earlier year. A story on the city's image bank says that in 1951 Philips built its own coal-fired power station on the Zwaanstraat to meet growing demand, that the coal came by a rail line crossing the Beukenlaan, and that a viaduct was built so traffic and freight trains could pass. It adds that in the 1960s, when the Netherlands moved to natural gas, the plant was converted to gas and the coal line lost its function. [S6] The 1951 date and the 1953 design date are not the same milestone, and I cannot tell from the pages which is the earlier stage of one project. I use "the early 1950s" and name the sources.

Philips called it building TR. [S1][S4] The wider site had its own history. The same walking guide says Philips owned the Strijp-T land before the war but developed it only after it, with a carton factory and a paper factory as the first large buildings, designed by Philips's bureau. [S3]
The spine that was never finished

The plant's silhouette was meant to be symmetrical. The coal chutes in the narrow central high-rise were built in the third phase, and in 1972 the owners decided to build only the lower volume that was needed, so the 1953 design stayed unfinished. [S1] The reason, the sources agree, was the change of fuel: coal chutes were no longer needed. [S5][S1]

The 2018 conversion completed the silhouette with a steel frame that holds terraces, a glass elevator, emergency stairs and a vertical garden, and a glass extension on the other side. [S5][S1] The five-meter-wide middle section still has concrete coal chutes hanging at a height of 28 meters. [S5][S1] The conversion was nominated for the Dirk Roosenburg prize in 2019, and since 2020 the chimneys have carried a light artwork, according to the architecture center. [S3]
A municipal building, then a private conversion

Ownership changed in the middle of the story. Reynaers, whose aluminum profiles were used in the conversion, says the building belonged to the municipality from 2011, and after an asbestos remediation by the municipality, a remediation company and the developer Geva Vastgoed, the municipality sold it to Geva for redevelopment. [S1] Ad van Berlo, founder of the design agency VanBerlo, told the Eindhoven IO+ archive in July 2015 that he looked up the first photograph he took of the plant, dated March 9, 2011, that the building was full of asbestos and unfit to work in, and that he expected it to host his agency and about ten other innovative companies in two years. [S7] The same architecture sources say he asked the architect Margriet Eugelink in 2011 to study how such a program could fit, and that in 2015 Geva commissioned three architects, Janne van Berlo of Atelier Van Berlo, Eugelink and Stefan de Bever, to design the transformation. [S1][S4]

Two openings appear in the record. IO+ wrote in May 2019 that Van Berlo could finally celebrate the official opening of the building in September 2017. [S8] A Strijp-T news item written at the move-in says that VanBerlo had moved into the former plant, that public visitors had to wait, and that the official opening of the Innovation Powerhouse would take place during Dutch Design Week, with a first exhibition on the ground floor between the concrete pillars titled Chronic Health: Designing a Healthy Future. [S9] The first looks like the opening of VanBerlo's own offices and the second like the opening to the public. That is my reading and neither source says it.

The architecture site says the VanBerlo office covers 2,300 square meters around a two-story atrium, and that the atrium's wooden stairs served as a tribune at presentations and for television recordings of De Toekomstbouwers during DDW 2018. [S4] An organizer's page says the 2018 exhibition belonged to an Embassy of Health, organized by Waag, VanBerlo, Philips, Maxima Medical Center and U Create, and called Chronic Health: If not then Who?, an open lab for care applications. [S10]

A municipal listing has protected the plant since 2016. A heritage news item of January 9, 2016 names the energy plant Strijp-TR on Beukenlaan among seven new municipal monuments from the reconstruction period, in the same decision that listed the Hallenweg halls. [S11] The plant is a typical example of reconstruction-period factory architecture, according to the architecture site. [S4]
Tenants, and a district around it

IO+ reported in February 2018 that the owner of Strijp-T, the real estate company Geva, was recruiting companies, and that earlier users of the site such as Smurfit Kappa and Draka had moved in after Philips gradually left. It said a new phase had started with the arrival of VanBerlo the year before. [S12] In May 2019 IO+ said the power plant, now called Innovation Powerhouse, was fully rented, with the buildings behind it also let. It named VanBerlo, Additive Industries, CTOUCH, Amber and Thermo Fisher Scientific among the companies on the site, and Ad van Berlo as chair of the first board of a new foundation to connect them. [S8]

The site around the plant describes itself in strong terms. IO+ in February 2018 called Strijp-T the terrain Philips developed right after Strijp-S, said spin-offs such as NXP and ASML emerged there, and called it the birthplace of the Brainport region, and its 2019 report adds that the cd and the dvd were invented there. [S12][S8] Those are promotional claims in trade press and I have not checked them against a Philips source. The same 2018 report says the fence around the 27-hectare site, a standard feature in Philips times, was slowly disappearing. [S12]

VanBerlo is now part of Accenture. Accenture's press release of February 19, 2020 says it had acquired the Eindhoven-based agency, which then had more than 90 professionals in Eindhoven and The Hague and joined Accenture's Industry X.0 practice. [S13] That helps explain why Accenture's design teams are the repeat host in DDW's pages for this building. DDW names Accenture Industry X | Industrial Design in 2023, Accenture Industrial Design in 2025 and Accenture in 2026. [S14][S2][S15] No page I opened lists the building's other current tenants.
Dutch Design Week, year by year

The earliest DDW-related record I found for this place is 2018, with the Chronic Health exhibition and the official opening described above. [S9] In 2019, in a piece on its nine design areas dated October 25, 2019, DDW sent visitors to the Innovation Powerhouse "formerly the Philips power plant" to see the Embassy of Sustainable Design and noted the TQ building behind it. [S16] I found no DDW page for the building in 2020, 2021, 2022 or 2024.

In 2023 DDW lists The Language of Sustainability, presented by Accenture Industry X | Industrial Design. Its text says storytelling and visual thinking help designers see how ecology, sociopolitical systems and products connect, and it names TU Delft with a project on composite material waste and two Accenture projects, Wings for Aid and Designing Sustainable North Stars. [S14] The page prints no location. So I cannot say from it that the exhibition stood in this building, and I do not caption a 2023 photograph with its title unless a sign does. [S14]

The archive of the DDW Flickr account holds an album titled Innovation Powerhouse for 2023 with 13 photos, all by Tommy Köhlbrugge, with titles dated October 21, 24 and 26, 2023. I see a hall of raw concrete with a large folded cardboard drone under a sign that reads Wings For Aid, a white model plane hanging from wires, glass domes with small objects and a courtyard with colored chairs in front of container huts. [S17] Wings for Aid is one of the Accenture projects DDW lists for the exhibition. [S14]

For 2025 DDW names the building. Accenture Industrial Design hosted an exhibition called Designing Interaction with Physical AI at Strijp T+R, Innovation Powerhouse, free of charge, from October 18 to 26, 2025, 11:00 to 18:00. [S2] The text asks what changes when everyday products begin to perceive, learn and respond, and it picks the kitchen as the place to test that, a room it calls one of the most human spaces of all. [S2] Those are the host's questions, and the page gives no result. The 2025 album has 7 photos by Almicheal Fraay of a kitchen island with a hob, visitors around it and a black panel with the exhibition title. [S17][S2]

For 2026, DDW's location page lists Zwaanstraat 31a, open 11:00 to 18:00 on October 17 and daily to October 25, and links an Accenture item called The Hornet Trap: Designing for Living Systems. [S18][S15] Its text describes a smart trap meant to target the invasive yellow-legged hornet while limiting harm to native insects, developed with the Arvespa Foundation and informed by beekeepers, with a prototype as the starting point. [S15] I have not seen this exhibit and nobody should read this essay as a review of it.
What a thin record can still teach

Across the years the host's questions change. In 2018 the question was health care and open design, in 2019 sustainability, in 2023 storytelling for sustainability, in 2025 physical AI in the kitchen and in 2026 technology that protects biodiversity. [S10][S16][S14][S2][S15] That pattern comes from the program texts, and it is a pattern of titles. The photographs fit it only loosely.

The building history and the program pages come from different kinds of source, and each answers a different question. A power plant that supplied Philips factories tells me what the walls were made for. A program page tells me what a host wanted visitors to think. The archive photographs show what a camera saw on certain days. A caption that mixes the three without saying so will claim more than any one of them can support. [S1][S2][S17]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**1951 or 1953.** The city image bank says a coal power station was built in 1951, while the architecture sources date the design and the second chimney to 1953 and the plant's four phases to 1953 to 1972. Not settled. [S6][S3][S1]
**When it opened.** IO+ gives September 2017 for the official opening, and the Strijp-T item places the official opening in DDW 2018. These can be two events. [S8][S9]

**Whether the 2023 show was here.** The program page prints no address and the photo album carries the building's name. The album settles where the photographs were taken and not the exhibition's title. [S14][S17]
What the record does not show

I do not know the exact date the plant stopped operating, and I did not find a document that says so. The building sources describe it as no longer used for power, and a plant to its west is described as still operating. [S4]
I do not know who owns the building today or who all its tenants are. [S8]
I do not know why the archive has albums only for 2023 and 2025, whether DDW 2024 had a program in the building, or what the 2026 exhibit looks like inside. [S17][S15]

If you open one of its albums, write down the year, then look for any sign, label or title that names an exhibit before you decide what you are looking at. Which of the two lists would you trust more in a caption: the one from the wall, or the one from the program? [S2]

title: Before it was De Caai: a dairy, two graduation shows and a Canal area
subtitle: What council papers, trade press, the organizers' own pages and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive say about the former Campina dairy site in Eindhoven, from construction in 1957 to the furniture show of 2025
description: The former Campina dairy in Eindhoven, from its 1957 to 1961 construction to the 2018 graduation show and the 2025 furniture show.

sections.x: Dutch Design Week had already used the former Campina dairy site in 2018 and 2019, seven years before the 2025 show that its photo archive files under De Caai. [S11][S12][S6]

That matters because the archive makes De Caai look like a newcomer. The albums that carry the area's label, Canal, cover 2023, 2024 and 2025, and the former dairy appears in only one of them. [S34] The paper trail is older and longer than that: a cooperative built the dairy, a company announced its closure in 2013, a council wrote a zoning plan around its buildings, a design school borrowed the factory for two graduation shows, and a designer duo opened a workshop at its edge. This essay follows those records. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what is on show in the area during DDW 2026 beyond what the published listings say.

I read buildings the way I was trained to read a specimen: ask what the structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For a dairy, the first answer is easy to find, and the later answers are scattered across council papers, trade press and festival pages. [S17][S22]
A cooperative built the dairy between 1957 and 1961

The first record is a heritage dataset for the factory at Dirk Boutslaan 2, credited to G. Korenberg and F. Haans and archived with the DANS data station for archaeology. It says the cooperative dairy association De Kempen commissioned a milk and ice cream factory, that the plans produced the name Campina (a Latin name for the Kempen region), that the name was also given to the new factory, and that construction ran from 1957 to 1961. [S17] I read only the catalog record, not the full report that sits behind it, so everything below that depends on the report's contents stays out.

The city's later papers agree on the end of that range. A news item written when the site was being sold says the Campina complex on Dirk Boutslaan was put into use in 1961. [S18][S19] One more start date, 1960, reached me only through a search summary of a building-renovation trade page that answered my request with an access refusal, so I did not open it and do not use it. I use 1961, because it comes from pages I read and sits at the end of the heritage record's 1957 to 1961 construction period. [S17][S18]

One more claim about the factory's rank comes only from a developer's side. Mei architects and planners, who designed one of the new towers, describe what was once the most modern milk factory in the Netherlands. [S24] That is a promotional sentence from a firm that works for the developer, and I found no independent ranking behind it.
The closure was announced on October 31, 2013, and production ended in September 2015

FrieslandCampina told employees and unions on Thursday, October 31, 2013, that it would restructure Dutch fresh dairy and close the Eindhoven production site and a distribution center in Woerden. Fresh dairy production from Eindhoven, where 142 people worked, would move to Rotterdam and Maasdam in mid-2015. [S29][S28] Trade press counted 246 jobs cut, offset by 72 new jobs at a distribution center in Maasdam. [S28]

The date needs care, because an English-language news item about it is dated November 5, 2013. [S30] The Dutch trade site Melkvee published the announcement on October 31, 2013, and FoodNavigator's report of November 4, 2013 says employees were informed "last Thursday," which is the same day. [S29][S28] The November 5 item is a later rewrite of the same news, not the announcement.

The plan said mid-2015. A development article in the IO+ archive, which I could not date from its text, says FrieslandCampina ended production on Dirk Boutslaan in September 2015, after which the factory was dismantled. [S18] The same fact appears in a second IO+ item on the sale. [S19] A water assessment filed with the zoning plan, written for the engineering firm BRO and dated December 7, 2020, also calls the factory vacant since 2015. [S35]

What the site looked like in between is on record in an IO+ report written after the departure and before the rest of the site emptied. It describes machines and loose equipment still inside, a cold store, main building, canteen and production center that had lost their function, five anti-squat students living in part of the complex, and two break-ins for copper. [S20] The council group D66, the report says, put questions to the city about what the owner and the city wanted to do with the grounds. [S20]
The city, the owner and the buyer set the terms between 2015 and 2021

The council's own papers give the sequence. In late 2015 the city's executive decided that the canal zone could change character, and on July 5, 2016 it adopted a starting memo for the southern canal zone. [S22] The council adopted a development framework for the Campina site on March 21, 2017. [S22] Before that vote, according to IO+, the council had taken a preparatory decision to protect the valuable buildings, FrieslandCampina had said in a letter that nothing would be demolished during the sale, and the city planned to designate some buildings as municipal monuments after the sale. [S21]

FrieslandCampina offered the site for sale in March 2017, and the developer BPD bought it. [S18][S19] An IO+ interview quotes the then alderman for finance and spatial planning, Wilbert Seuren, saying that the city would keep five industrial monuments. [S19] The same item quotes the architect Arie van der Neut of Studioninedots describing a car-free area of shared spaces in which factory halls get new uses. [S18]

Then the zoning plan. A council proposal for the "Campinaterrein" plan, with an executive date of July 13, 2021, says the plan allows up to 700 dwellings and up to 21,500 square meters of floor area for other functions. It says about 20,000 square meters of existing, partly cultural, property would be transformed. [S22] An agreement with BPD dated July 3, 2020 required at least 25 percent of the new homes to be cheap to mid-priced, and the program in the proposal goes further: 555 of 694 homes, or 80 percent, in the social to mid-price range. [S22] Objections were open from March 18 to April 28, 2021. The proposal's decision line names the council meeting of September 22, 2021; I did not open the adopted plan itself. [S22] It also states that the chimney is a municipal monument and is kept. [S22]

The site is larger than a single building. The same paper puts it at just over three hectares, about a third of the whole canal zone. [S22] That is why the city treated it, in its own words, as the starting point for a later redevelopment of the entire zone. [S22]
Graduates took over the milk factory in 2018 and 2019

This is the part the Canal albums do not show. Design Academy Eindhoven's own page for the 2018 Graduation Show says it was the first edition in almost two decades to take place outside the academy's walls, in a venue on the site of the historic Campina Milk Factory. The show ran from October 20 to 28, 2018, during Dutch Design Week, and presented 208 projects by 185 graduates. [S11] Wallpaper called the venue a much larger location than the school's own building and named it the former Campina milk factory. [S15]

The 2019 show, October 19 to 27, 2019, continued for a second year at the factory, according to both the academy and DDW's own program listing. [S12][S14] The 2020 show was not held as a large exhibition: the academy says it had become clear at the eleventh hour that a large-scale exhibition was no longer feasible, and the graduates' work went into a virtual edition of DDW. [S13]

So the statement that De Caai appears only in 2025 needs a precise reading. The archive's Canal albums show it once. The site had hosted a much larger DDW presence in 2018 and 2019, under the name of the milk factory. [S11][S12] Whether those halls are the hall called De Caai in 2025 I cannot say. No source I opened ties a 2018 or 2019 room to a 2025 room.
Kiki and Joost opened a workshop at the edge of the site in 2019

A DDW magazine item from the 2019 festival reports that the design duo Kiki&Joost founded a new studio "at the edge of the former Campina site," under the name Future Workspace, and opened it on the first Saturday of DDW 2019. [S16] That Saturday was October 19, 2019. The item describes a renovated, somewhat dilapidated building with a timber-framed central hall for exhibitions, an office and showroom upstairs, and space for machines and steel on the ground floor. The alderman for mobility, culture and design, Monique List-de Roos, opened it by welding two pieces of steel together, because Joost believed that cutting a ribbon symbolized separation. [S16]

The item also records the alderman saying that the pair had worked from several places, including squatted and anti-squat buildings, and that the city now wanted designers to have a permanent place. [S16] That is a municipal statement made at an opening, and I treat it as the city's stated aim, not as an outcome.

I cannot say that this Future Workspace is the same address as the studio DDW describes in 2023 and 2024. DDW's 2026 listing says the 190 square meter exhibition space, built from Douglas wood, is the latest addition to the adjacent studio and workshop at Gabriël Metsulaan 1, with the entrance on Kanaaldijk Zuid, joined by a new garden of nearly 300 square meters. [S2] The two descriptions are consistent with one site. No page I opened says so.
In 2023 and 2024 the Canal area was a studio

DDW's own area recap for 2023 calls the NRE grounds the first hotspot in the Canal area, five minutes by bike from the station. It adds that, following the canal, visitors come to Kiki and Joost's studio and its exhibition Perpetuum Mobile, and then to the Koelhuis. [S3] The photo archive's 2023 album, with 20 photos credited in the titles to Nick Bookelaar and dated October 22, 2023, shows a timber-framed hall with a pink-lit wooden sculpture, wall pieces of black cord, ceramic vases and glaze swatches. [S34] No source says which of those objects was Perpetuum Mobile, so the description stops at what the pictures show.

The 2024 recap points to "the newly built exhibition space of Kiki and Joost." [S4] DDW's program page says DDW would host the international debut of the new exhibition space with a show titled Carte Blanche, in which Kiki van Eijk unveiled Sprout, Joost unveiled Intentional Coincidence, and both showed collaborations with WEEEF. [S5] The page also says the building doubles as a storage facility with public access to a curated collection, and hosts workshops, lectures and community events. [S5] The 2024 album holds five photos credited in the titles to Anwyn Howarth, dated October 23, 2024. The album title carries the spelling Kanal, which DDW does not use anywhere else I looked. [S34]
In 2025 there were three different hosts on the canal

In 2025 the area's best-documented hall was De Caai. DDW's program page for Forward Furniture gives the location as Canal, De Caai, De Kade, Kanaaldijk-Zuid 1 D, the dates as October 18 to 26, 2025, and the entry rule as a DDW ticket. [S6] It describes a 2,000 square meter raw industrial hall in the historic Campina former dairy factory and says the show would bring together 60 to 100 international participants. [S6] The page was written before the event. A DDW update dated October 7, 2025 says over 100 designer studios presented work, and that Liv Vaisberg conceived and curated the show. [S7] Both numbers are DDW's, and I did not count participants myself.

A gallery that represents three Lithuanian designers confirms the dates and place in a news item dated November 14, 2025. [S32] An announcement from the Karlsruhe University of Arts and Design, dated October 18, 2025, repeats the size and adds that the building was being presented for the last time before its demolition. [S31] That last claim is secondhand. DDW's own program page, which I read in full, does not say it, and I found no demolition permit or council paper that names this hall. It stays an unverified claim in this essay.

The same street address carried a second DDW listing the same year. The HUB Bouw aan Morgen, an exhibition on sustainable construction hosted by Biobased Creations with BPD and Rabobank, is listed at "de Melkfabriek," De Kade, Kanaaldijk-Zuid 1 D, October 18 to 26, 2025, with a DDW ticket required. [S8] DDW gives the two listings different postal codes, 5613 LH for Forward Furniture and 5613 LE for the HUB. [S6][S8] So the festival's own data use two names, De Caai and Melkfabriek, for what its address field gives as one street number, and the codes disagree. I cannot tell from DDW's pages whether these are two halls, one hall, or one entry with a typing error.

The third host is Onomatopee. DDW's page for its project says "How to enter from the exit" is a curatorial experiment reimagining cultural institutions through collaboration, installations and shared living, shown at Onomatopee Project Space, Lucas Gasselstraat 2a, in the Canal area, from October 18 to 26, 2025. [S9][S10] The archive's album simply named Canal holds ten photos, and each title names the Onomatopee project. [S34] An album named for the area therefore shows a different host from the album named for De Caai. Of the 49 photos in the Canal - De Caai album, I read only the first 24 titles on October 7, 2026, and those name no photographer. [S34]
What De Caai means now

De Caai is the name of the redevelopment. DELVA Landscape Architecture says that it and Studioninedots, commissioned by BPD, are redeveloping the Campina site into De Caai, and writes of "the redevelopment of the dairy called 'De Caai'." [S27] Mei used the name in a June 24, 2021 item about a tower sketch, and the official it quotes, Yasin Torunoglu, whom Mei's English text calls a councilor, said the plan sets the tone for the rest of the canal zone redevelopment. [S23] The IO+ items about the sale, which refer to the March 2017 offer, call the district "De Zuivelfabriek," the dairy, so the current name came later. [S18][S19] I could not date those items from their text, and I found no page that explains where "Caai" comes from.

Construction of the first two towers, Flow and Fresh, was officially started on Wednesday, July 6, 2022, when alderman Mieke Verhees drove the first pile, according to Mei. The same item gives the whole plan as about 700 homes and 18,000 square meters of other facilities. [S24] KAAN Architecten, which designed Fresh, gives the project as about 700 homes in three lower blocks and five towers plus 20,000 square meters of commercial space inside the factory buildings, and places Fresh between the Milk Factory and the Ice Factory. [S25] The numbers differ across the council proposal (21,500 square meters), Mei (18,000) and KAAN (20,000). They measure different things at different dates, and the council's figure is the only one that carries legal weight, so I use it for the zoning limit. [S22][S24][S25]

The architects LEVS, who designed two residential blocks, say in a news item that the development is in its final phase, that the factory buildings are the architectural starting point for all new construction, and that completion by the contractor is expected in autumn 2026. [S26] That is a statement from a firm involved in the project, and I treat the date as an expectation.

One practical consequence follows for DDW 2026. This is Eindhoven's area tip dated October 1, 2026 describes the canal zone as home to the former Campina site and the NRE grounds and points visitors to Onomatopee and the Melkfabriek. [S33] It also recommends the HUB Bouw aan Morgen, which DDW's own archive files under 2025, so parts of the tip may be carried over from last year. [S33][S8] I could not tell from that page, or from the DDW pages I read, whether a hall at this address is a 2026 location, so I make no claim about it.
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it
Four conflicts came up. Three are settled below on the evidence, and the fourth is reported as open. [S6][S8][S29]

The start of production. One unopened page is reported as giving 1960; the news items and the heritage record's construction range support 1961 as the year the complex went into use. [S17][S18] I use 1961.

The announcement date. November 5, 2013 is the date of an English-language news item; October 31, 2013 is the date of the Dutch trade-press report and matches FoodNavigator's "last Thursday." [S29][S28][S30] I use October 31, 2013.

The name. DDW writes Canal for the area, Melkfabriek and De Caai for halls at the same street number, and Kanaalzone appears in the city's tourism text. [S1][S6][S8][S33] The word Kanal appears in the 2024 album title only. [S34] I use Canal for the festival area and Kanaalzone for the district.

The size. DDW's 2,000 square meters for the Forward Furniture hall is a pre-event description, repeated by the Karlsruhe announcement and not measured by anyone I read. [S6][S31] I report it as DDW's figure and leave it unresolved.
What the record does not show

Which building the 2025 Forward Furniture hall was, and whether it is the same space the academy used in 2018 and 2019, is open. Whether that hall was demolished or is due to be, beyond one university announcement's phrase, is open. [S31] Why the 2024 album title says Kanal is unknown. Whether the Future Workspace opened in 2019 sits at the same address as the studio of 2023 and 2024 is not stated by any page I opened. [S16][S2] Who took the 2025 De Caai photos is not named in the titles or on the photo pages I read on October 7, 2026, and I could not reopen Flickr in this pass. [S34] The IO+ items I used are undated in their text, so the order of the sale, the handover to BPD and the name change from De Zuivelfabriek to De Caai is only partly known. [S18][S19]

I could not open the monument records, the heritage vision that the council paper says is attached to the plan, the Eindhoven city archive, or the design academy's own news item about the move, which timed out. [S22] The Dezeen preview of the 2025 show answered with an access refusal, and I stopped there.

Next time you open a festival archive, try three checks. Is the label the organizer's, or a photo tag? Does an album named for the area show the place you expect, or only the host that filed under it? And is the place new, or has the festival used the same ground under another name? [S11][S34]
