title: Kazerne: a barracks bought in 1824, a fire station, a warehouse and a design hall
subtitle: A former military police barracks and a former municipal warehouse in Eindhoven, followed through heritage records, the organizers' own pages and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: Kazerne in Eindhoven, from a barracks bought in 1824 to a Dutch Design Week venue, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: Kazerne sits in a former military police barracks with a former municipal warehouse beside it, and no source I opened connects it to Philips. [S1][S2]

In Eindhoven an industrial brick hall invites the guess that it belonged to Philips, so the point is worth making early. Kazerne's heritage page and the national heritage day entry describe a barracks and a warehouse, and neither mentions Philips. [S1][S2] One of the exhibitions the place has hosted did include light work made for Philips, which shows how easily the two names travel together, but that is a commission and not a landlord. [S12] This essay uses public sources only: Kazerne's pages, a heritage encyclopedia, news reports, DDW's pages, one design magazine and the DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview.

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A building that has been a barracks, a fire station, a garage, a theater rehearsal room and a hotel invites that question, and it turns out the record answers more of it than the place's own marketing does. [S2][S3]
The land was bought in December 1824

The most detailed account of the early years comes from the Eindhoven encyclopedia, a digital reference that says it is still being compiled and that lists as its sources a building-history and cultural-history study of the site from January 2014 by J.A. van der Hoeve and J&B Hüsken and a 2006 book on Eindhoven's hidden past. [S3] Kazerne's heritage page says a constructive and cultural-historical study was carried out in 2014 and is available on request. [S1] The dates match, and I take it to be the same study, though neither page says so. I have not seen the study itself.

According to the encyclopedia, the municipality bought a plot of land on the Grote Berg in December 1824 to build a barracks. To reach the stables it needed a right of way along the Paradijslaan, which belonged to a linen manufacturer named Smits, owner of the area called Het Paradijs. The barracks followed in 1825, designed by the master builder Peter van Driel and built by Arnoldus Ader, a mason from Tilburg. The encyclopedia gives the building cost as 5,825 guilders, financed by a loan of 6,400 guilders from Smits. [S3] The national heritage day entry lists Peter van Driel in its architect field, with a building period of 1824 to 1900. [S2] Two sources agree on the name, and the second is not independent of the first in any way I can check. A field covering 1824 to 1900 cannot describe one hand, so I attribute only the 1825 barracks to him.

The encyclopedia describes a block-shaped, two-story building with a hipped roof, a central corridor and three rooms on each side on both floors, plus an L-shaped addition against the back wall that held stables and a holding room for prisoners. The facades were plain brick. [S3] The heritage day entry says the complex began as quarters for the Royal Marechaussee, with horse stables and outbuildings around a courtyard. [S2] The encyclopedia supports the word: it records that a lieutenant colonel of the Royal Marechaussee applied in 1895 for a permit to rebuild the horse stables. [S3] Both pages support the word.

Kazerne calls the barracks one of the first military police barracks of the Netherlands, dated 1825. [S1] The heritage day entry says one of the oldest. [S2] No page I opened ranks the barracks against others, so I use "one of the oldest" and attribute "first" to the owner.

Later changes are documented in the encyclopedia: a new roof in 1864, a partial demolition of the stables recorded in 1886, a renovation in 1888, and in the mid-1890s the rebuilding of the stables into an extension of the main building and three outbuildings around a courtyard, with drawings dated 1898. [S3] Kazerne dates its coach house to 1898, which agrees with those drawings. [S1][S3]
A fire station and a cleaning service shared the site

In 1905, the encyclopedia says, the complex was split. The part behind the Grote Berg stayed a barracks, and the buildings on the Paradijslaan, two storerooms, became a fire pump house with a stable. A permit of 1909 led to a rebuilt brick front on the Paradijslaan in an eclectic style, seven bays wide, decorated with concrete diamond heads, and the encyclopedia says firefighters worked from it during the first half of the twentieth century. It adds a detail I like: the entrance of the later theater, built as a link between two wings of the stables in 1909, was originally a large manure pit. [S3]

By 1934, according to the encyclopedia's reading of the city address book, the address Paradijslaan 2c belonged to the fire brigade, to the local air-protection service and to the municipal cleaning service. [S3] The heritage day entry says the site later gained a garage for the cleaning service and that the service left in 1977. [S2] Kazerne dates the adjoining warehouse to 1925 and the heritage day entry to 1924 to 1925. [S1][S2] The encyclopedia says that in 1955 the municipality, as owner, was assessed for property tax for the first time, which it reads as the end of the building's public function. [S3]

Annemoon Geurts, one of the founders, remembered the large building in a 2015 interview as a garage for the city's garbage trucks that had been boarded up and derelict for many years. [S6] That agrees with the heritage day entry's garage for the cleaning service, and with a 2017 news report that part of the complex had been a warehouse for the municipal cleaning service. [S2][S8]
Temporary users, and a decaying hall

After the cleaning service left in 1977 the complex had various temporary users. The heritage day entry names Theater Het Klein, the Wereldwinkel and the foundation Eindhoven in Beeld. [S2] The encyclopedia dates the conversion of a garage into a rehearsal room for Theater Het Klein to 1981, places the Wereldwinkel shop on the Grote Berg from 1998, and lists several other tenants in 1990, among them a poetry-poster foundation, a journalists' collective and a mosque. It says Eindhoven in Beeld moved out in 2015. [S3]

Kazerne's heritage page describes the whole as standing more or less empty and in decay for decades. [S1] The encyclopedia's tenant list does not read that way. The two can be reconciled if the large warehouse sat unused while the smaller buildings were let, and Geurts's recollection of a boarded-up garage fits that reading. [S3][S6] That is my inference, and the sources do not state it.
Pop-up dinners in 2006, a request to the city in 2007, a hall in 2014

Kazerne's heritage page says its two founders, Geurts and Koen Rijnbeek, ran several successful pop-up pilots during Dutch Design Week before they saw the potential of the site. It does not say where or when. [S1] Two other sources do. In the 2015 interview, published on May 18, 2015, Geurts says that around Dutch Design Week 2006 she and Rijnbeek organized their first Eat Drink Design event, a pop-up restaurant where guests dined among and on design works, repeated it in 2007 by pairing Eindhoven designers with local restaurants in seven projects, and then decided to create a permanent platform. She says they asked the city for a venue on December 7, 2007 and that Kazerne opened in October 2014. [S6] A design magazine's 2024 interview with Geurts also traces the venture to a do-it-yourself exhibition during Dutch Design Week in 2006. [S7]

The two accounts differ on one point. The magazine says that after nearly five years of exhibitions and events, the city proposed the use of Kazerne in 2012. [S7] Geurts's 2015 account has the request in 2007 and the opening in 2014 and does not mention a 2012 proposal. [S6] They fit together as a sequence, request in 2007, offer of this site in 2012, opening in 2014, but neither source says the 2012 offer answered the 2007 request.

Geurts says in the 2015 interview that she and her husband lived close by and had not known the building was there. [S6] By her account the first goal was to get the large hall operating and earning, and a second phase with more function rooms, two restaurants and seven apartments was hoped to be finished by the end of 2016. [S6] The hotel opened in 2019, as I describe below. [S20]

Public money entered the story later. On September 28, 2017 Omroep Brabant reported that the province of North Brabant wanted to lend 750,000 euros to the foundation Stichting ter behoud van Klein Paradijs, for plans to show Design Academy graduation work permanently alongside a restaurant, a hotel and meeting rooms. It said the cabinet had announced 9.5 million euros for the Eindhoven region in 2016, to be matched by the province, and that the buildings, long owned by the municipality, were now in private hands. [S8] Kazerne's heritage page calls the site "Klein Paradijs," the same name the news report gives the foundation. [S1][S8]
What Kazerne put on, year by year

Kazerne's own pages preserve the early exhibitions, which the photo archive does not cover. The opening exhibition, Open Mind, ran from winter 2014 to summer 2015, curated by Geurts with exhibition design by Moon/en/co, which the 2019 opening announcement describes as Geurts and Rijnbeek's design studio. [S20] Its featured list is long and includes Maarten Baas, Studio Drift, Kiki van Eijk and Joost van Bleiswijk, and a group called ICE that includes Jeanine Eek Keijzer and Piet Hein Eek. [S9] During Dutch Design Week 2014, October 18 to 26, Open Mind was supplemented with work by Bokja, Klaas Kuiken, and Van Eijk and Van Bleiswijk, among others. [S10]

The 2015 page settles a question the photo archive left open. A wall in a 2015 photograph reads "Open Ended - Lidewij Edelkoort," and I could only say that a photograph showed it. Kazerne's page for Dutch Design Week 2015, October 17 to 25, says the running exhibition was OPEN ENDED, Lidewij Edelkoort, supplemented with work by David Derksen, Christien Meindertsma, Dirk van der Kooij, Lucas & Lucas, Kazerne Lab and others. [S11] Edelkoort's name therefore appears in the organizer's own program in the first year the archive covers.

Escape, which Kazerne's page dates from fall 2016 to spring 2017, featured Studio Drift's kinetic installation In 20 steps, which the page says was made for the Venice Biennale in 2015, and a light and sound installation by Paul Thursfield and Simon Rycroft made for Philips. [S12] That is the Philips connection I mentioned at the start: a commission shown in the hall, with no bearing on who owned it. In 2017, a news item on a design prize says the first design prize of the Culture fund of North Brabant was awarded to Piet Hein Eek at "Design Center Kazerne Eindhoven" on October 28 during Dutch Design Week, with a jury chairman's quote and a prize of 10,000 euros. [S13] The page carries a July 3, 2017 date but describes the ceremony in the past tense, so I treat the ceremony date as reported and not independently confirmed.

The Dutch Design Week archive on Flickr holds Kazerne albums for nine editions, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024 and 2025, with 240 photos in all, and none for 2021 or 2022. I read them on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen the Flickr account for this version, so the counts and captions here are from that reading. [S14] The photographer named in titles through 2019 is Ralph Roelse, and the credits widen after that. [S14] Titles in the 2017 album mention a plinth marked Maarten Baas x Cor Unum and in 2019 an exhibition called Circular Materialists. [S14]

The 2018 album titles read Eat Drink Design Softwear For Google. [S14] Eat Drink Design is the name Geurts gives to the founders' own format from 2006, so the title suggests that format returned in 2018. [S6][S14] No source I opened describes the 2018 program, so that is an inference from a name, and I describe nothing about what the show contained.

In 2020 the program was a double exhibition with the Van Abbemuseum. Kazerne's event page dates New Melancholy, Van Abbemuseum x Lidewij Edelkoort x Kazerne, from October 17, 2020 to June 30, 2021, and quotes Edelkoort describing melancholy carried by humor and distance, shown in both places. [S15] An Interior Design roundup of Dutch Design Week 2020 called it a double exhibition between Kazerne and the museum. [S16] The two 2020 albums name both venues and do not say which room is which, so I make no claim from the photographs about where any object stood. [S14]

In 2022 the Edelkoort collection show, called The collection is... De Edelkoort collectie, ran at the Van Abbemuseum from October 8 to November 6, 2022, and the DDW listing says a second showing was held at Kazerne until spring 2023. It names Piet Hein Eek among the prominent pieces and credits Geurts as initiator and founder of Kazerne. [S17] The archive has no album for 2021 or 2022. [S14]

Kazerne's page for Dutch Design Week 2023 fills in an album the titles alone could not explain. It describes 2,000 square meters of recent work and two exhibitions: Evolving Harmony, a group show curated by Geurts, and Everyday Paradise, Outsider Arts & Crafts, co-curated by Lilli Tedde and Edelkoort. It lists projects including Blossoming Food Chains by Biotope Brainport, a challenge to feed 10,000 people in one day with regional ingredients, House of Dreams by ConverseLab and Futon Factory, on how artificial intelligence may change sleep, and a tribute to the designer Thomas Eyck, who lived from 1964 to 2023. [S18] The 2023 album titles name Everyday Paradise and House of Dreams. [S14] Those titles name two of the exhibition's main strands.

For 2024 and 2025 the record is thinner. The design magazine interview from December 18, 2024 says the Kazerne Foundation would run two rotating exhibitions a year, a weekly innovation café, and a program focused on nature-inclusive design for which it had funding for four years, with the results of a development table of ten people to be presented at Dutch Design Week 2025. [S7] Kazerne's news page lists a Kazerne Design Award 2025 won by Antonia Vincenza Schreiber for a project called Local Shit, dated May 14, 2025, and a May 22, 2024 item on Back to the Flax. [S19] The archive holds a five-photo album for 2024 and a 23-photo album for 2025. [S14] I could not open a Kazerne page describing either year's exhibition.
The hotel, the club and the 2024 split

On May 7, 2019 a trade site republished an opening announcement for Kazerne, describing a hotel of eight lofts and suites, a private members club, and six brick structures, the oldest from 1825, restored by Moon/en/co together with Van Helmond Architecten. It says the Hay Loft sits in the former stable attic and the Corner Duplex in the former barracks, built around a converted historic prison cell, and that the members club occupies the first floor of the coach house. [S20] It is a promotional text, and I use it for the description of the buildings and not for any claim about quality. Kazerne's own mission page says the hotel and members club opened at the beginning of 2019. [S4] The announcement is dated May 7, 2019, so the exact opening date cannot be settled from these two. I say "in 2019."

The heritage day entry says the redevelopment from 2014 to 2019 came in two phases, first the warehouse as restaurant and exhibition hall, then the barracks house, coach house, cells and stables, with the exterior brought back as close as possible to its historic look and new volumes, staircases and an elevator added, and the wooden roof structures left visible. It credits the design to Harrie van Helmond in close collaboration with Geurts and Rijnbeek. [S2]

Ownership and operation then changed. Kazerne's organization page says the Kazerne Foundation, a public-benefit non-profit, was the sole shareholder of Kazerne BV until the end of 2024, that the BV has been independent since autumn 2024, and that the Foundation now focuses on design programming as a guest in the building, ten years after Kazerne officially opened. [S5] The heritage day entry says the hospitality operations were transferred in 2024 to Bram Bijnen and Dick Spierenburg, while Geurts and Rijnbeek remain responsible for the design program. [S2] The magazine interview gives the reasoning in Geurts's words: she says the decision to let someone else take over the restaurant and hotel was made in 2023, after ten years, and the magazine adds that she wanted to spend more time on curating and less on staff and hotel concerns. [S7] The decision was taken in 2023 and took effect in autumn 2024, and the sources agree on that sequence.
What DDW lists for 2026

The Dutch Design Week location page for 2026 is titled "Kazerne - Design Lab," gives the address Paradijslaan 8, and lists opening hours of 11:00 to 23:30 from October 17 to 24 and 11:30 to 22:00 on October 25. [S21] Kazerne's own agenda lists an exhibition called "Dutch Design Week 2026 @ Kazerne," October 17 to 25, and a book launch with a talk and signing by Li Edelkoort and Philip Fimmano on October 18. [S22]

The DDW page needs a careful reading. Its description still says visitors can see recent work by "over 40 leading designers" and uses the phrase "Also this DDW'25." That is last year's text, and I read it as carried over. The page's own list for 2026 shows 19 program items, among them an iF Design network event on October 20 and several exhibitions by studios such as Studio Noff, HAK Studio and Back to the Flax. [S21] The page does not support "over 40" as a 2026 fact. The DDW page also says admission is free with a DDW ticket or entrance fee, while Kazerne's home page says entrance is free and open to all. [S21][S22] Both can be true for different parts of a visit, and I cannot tell which applies to which.

Before Dutch Design Week, the heritage day entry for September 12 and 13, 2026 described a show in the former warehouse of the nominated projects for the Kazerne Design Award 2026, by ten recent Design Academy graduates, under the national theme of resilient heritage. [S2]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Size.** Kazerne's heritage page and the heritage day entry give 2,500 square meters for the complex. Kazerne's mission page and the 2024 magazine interview give 2,600. [S1][S2][S4][S7][S20] The 2023 program page speaks of 2,000 square meters of work, which describes exhibition space. [S18] I found no measurement. I use "about 2,500 square meters" for the complex because Kazerne's heritage page and the heritage day entry agree on it, and I name them as the source. The 2019 announcement applies the same number to exhibition space, which I treat as a loose use.
**The warehouse date.** 1925 on Kazerne's page, 1924 to 1925 on the heritage day entry. [S1][S2] Both agree on 1925 as the year it was finished, so I use 1925 and name the owner.
**"First" and "oldest."** Settled above by attributing "first" to the owner. [S1][S2]

**The architect.** Peter van Driel, named by the encyclopedia and by the heritage day entry, for the 1825 barracks only. The heritage day site's second entry for the same address lists "various architects" instead. [S2][S3][S23]
**"Royal."** Supported by the heritage day entry and by the encyclopedia's 1895 permit. [S2][S3]
**The 2019 opening.** Beginning of 2019 against a May 7, 2019 announcement. Not settled. [S4][S20]
**Fire station move.** The encyclopedia gives one street for a new fire station in the 1950s and another elsewhere in the same entry. I left it out. [S3]
What the record does not show

I have not seen the 2014 building-history study that the encyclopedia cites, and I cannot say whether it names the architect or fixes the warehouse date. [S1][S3] I have not found the municipal monument designation itself, only Kazerne's statement and the heritage day entry's listing that the barracks, stables and coach house are a municipal monument. [S1][S2]

I cannot say what the 2018 exhibition contained, why the archive has no album for 2021 or 2022, or what Kazerne showed in 2024 and 2025 beyond what titles and news items suggest. [S14][S19] I do not know which photographs in the 2020 albums show which building. [S14]

I do not know what Kazerne is planning for the main exhibition of Dutch Design Week 2026 beyond its agenda line. [S22] The sources also leave open why Kazerne counts 2,500 square meters in one place and 2,600 in another, and whether the 2012 offer from the city answered the 2007 request. [S4][S6][S7]

If you go to Kazerne during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at the signage and ask which building you are standing in and who wrote the text on the wall. When two pages give 1925 and 1924 to 1925 for the same warehouse, which date would you print? [S1][S2]
Sources

title: Ketelhuisplein: a fenced factory yard, a boiler house and a square that is rebuilt every October
subtitle: One outdoor square on Strijp-S, followed through the Philips years, the 2002 sale, ten editions of the official Dutch Design Week photo archive and the building next to it that is under construction now
description: Ketelhuisplein on Strijp-S, from the fenced Philips works and the 2002 sale to ten editions of Dutch Design Week and a new building beside it.

sections.x: The ground that Dutch Design Week now calls Ketelhuisplein lay inside the fenced Philips works at Strijp-S, and the fence began to come down only after the site was sold in 2002. [S1][S2]

That is about all the public record says about the ground before the festival, and the gap is the reason I wanted to write this. [S1][S2] A square is the hardest kind of venue to date, because the ground stays and everything on it leaves. This essay reports no visit and no interview. It uses the Strijp-S site's own history page, the national monument register, a heritage story, a 2018 heritage calendar, architects' and artists' project pages, local news, Dutch Design Week's own pages and the festival's photo archive on Flickr, and it says nothing about what is on the square during DDW 2026 beyond what published listings say.

I was trained to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. A square built for nothing in particular is an odd specimen, so I followed the buildings around it, and then the things that have been put on it. [S1][S3]
The site was a closed Philips works until 2002

The Strijp-S site's history page says Philips had its first factory at Strijp-S built in 1916, a glass factory for lamp bulbs, followed by a cardboard factory, a gas factory and the physics laboratory known as the NatLab, and that the company became self-sufficient there, from raw material to finished product and transport. [S1] A heritage story from Erfgoed Brabant, adapted from a 2014 book by Jan van Oudheusden and published online on November 15, 2017, calls the works of roughly thirty hectares an Eindhoven version of the Forbidden City, open only to Philips staff. [S2] The Strijp-S history page gives the same nickname and says some 10,000 people worked there every day in the 1970s, behind fences and barriers, with entry by pass. [S1]

The turn is dated. In 2002 VolkerWessels and the municipality of Eindhoven bought Strijp-S from Philips, the company leased parts back, and the buyers set up a public-private company, Park Strijp Beheer. [S1] Some summaries give 2004, and the site's own history page says 2002, which I use. [S1] The page says the urban plan by West 8's Adriaan Geuze was developed between 2002 and 2005, and that an important part of the old factories was designated as municipal or national monuments, with the NatLab municipal and the Hoge Rug and Klokgebouw national. [S1]
The name comes from a boiler house, and the register does not list it

The square carries the name of the Ketelhuis, the boiler house. The Strijp-S building page says the building used to heat the entire old Philips industrial area and has held catering, studios and exhibition space since 2011. [S3] Erfgoed Brabant says the Ketelhuis and the Machinekamer, the machine room, date from 1929 and supplied the whole complex with compressed air and electricity. [S2] A heritage calendar published in 2018 under the theme of power stations gives 1929 for the machine room as well, saying it supplied Strijp-S with electricity, steam and compressed air and now houses a restaurant. [S4] So 1929 for the Machinekamer has two sources, and 1929 for the Ketelhuis itself has one, which is the Erfgoed Brabant story. [S2][S4]

No page says the square was named for the building. The link is likely, because the square lies beside it, and I treat it as likely and not established. [S3][S5] A caution about names: the national monument register has a Ketelhuis at Dr Poletlaan 45, dated about 1918, and that is a different building. [S6]

The register entry for the Philipscomplex Strijp S, complex number 518768, protects three parts: the buildings SA, SDM, SBP/SAN/SK and SF. [S7] The register gives the main object's address as Klokgebouw 300, calls SDM the Veem building and SF a pump building, and the Strijp-S history page places the Hoge Rug factories among the national monuments. [S7][S1] The Ketelhuis is not among them. The register says the terrain's layout was developed by A.I.J. de Broekert, who worked for Philips, and describes a six-story factory building with a water tower, designed by A. de Broekert of the Philips engineering office, that came about in two phases in 1928 and 1929. [S7] Whether the Ketelhuis has municipal monument status I could not find. The Strijp-S history page names the NatLab as municipal and the Hoge Rug and Klokgebouw as national monuments, and does not mention the Ketelhuis. [S1]
What the ground has been given since the fence came down
Three things have been built or placed at the square's edge, and each can be dated. [S8][S9][S10]

The Leidingstraat, the elevated pipe street beside the square, was turned into a raised garden in 2014 by the landscape architect Piet Oudolf and the lighting designers Har Hollands, according to the architects MVRDV. [S8] The Strijp-S history page says the Philips-era pipe system was kept. [S1]

A mosaic by Gé Verhulst, signed and dated 1963, was moved to the facade of the Ketelhuis after the Van der Putt Lyceum, a building that began as a retail trade school designed by the architects Geenen-Oskam, was demolished. [S9] The art register's record gives the text as 2021 and its "year of placement" field as 2020, so the year of the move is not settled. [S9] The register's address field for the work reads Ketelhuisplein 1. [S9]

The third is a pair of floor paintings. In April 2024 the artist Cox Janssens painted a work of about 35 by 35 meters, more than 1,200 square meters, on the square as part of the art festival The Art Department, which the foundation Playgrounds ran at the Klokgebouw. [S10] The Omroep Brabant report, published on April 13, 2024, says a year earlier the artist Toscana Banana had made a huge floor painting on the same square. [S10] That is all I found about the 2023 work.
From 2015 on, the square is assembled each October

I do not know when Dutch Design Week first used the square. The photo archive's Ketelhuisplein albums start at 2015, and a 2014 note from the university TU/e is about a move into the Klokgebouw, not the square. [S11][S12] The photo archive holds a Ketelhuisplein album for ten editions between 2015 and 2025, with no album for 2020, the digital edition. [S11] The counts are 33 photos in 2015, 67 in 2016, 38 in 2017, 20 in 2018, 28 in 2019, 38 in 2021, 190 in 2022, 58 in 2023, 30 in 2024 and 76 in 2025, for 578 in all. I read those counts on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen Flickr in this pass. [S11]

Two outside records help date the early years. A local news report from the 2016 edition says the square had been turned into a large exhibition about sustainability, Agri meets Design, with four installations, including The EGGCHANCE, on the economy around eggs. [S13] DDW's own 2019 magazine says the three main locations curated by DDW that year were the Klokgebouw, the Veem and Ketelhuisplein, calls the square the beating heart of the festival, and names the pavilions Biobasecamp, built on pillars of tree trunks from trees felled along the A2, the Growing Pavilion, made of mycelium, an ABN AMRO pavilion and the Embassy of Safety. [S14] It also says permanent residents named YKSI and Broeinest open their doors during DDW, and that a bench made of tree trunks from Atelier NL's Stormhout project stands on the square. [S14]

The album titles fit those records. In 2015 the titles name a series called Overzicht, which is Dutch for overview, along with VPRO, a greenhouse and ABN AMRO. In 2017 they show ABN AMRO, a DDW Music stage and flags that spell the square's name. In 2018 they name an NS train-carriage pavilion, Renault and Brabant Living Lab. In 2019 they name BioBaseCamp, the Growing Pavilion, an ABN AMRO hotspot, Floriade and an Embassy of Safety. [S11] The later albums add De Stoelendans, VPRO, The Bar and aerial frames credited to about.today in 2022, nine or more projects in 2023, Brabant Ontmoet and Fix Your Phone in 2024, and a glasshouse called Boeren Poorten in 2025. [S11] The albums show only the first two dozen photos through the tool I used, so they may hold more.
The two neighbors that DDW's listing names

DDW's location page places the square between the Klokgebouw and Microlab Hall, and the building histories show how different those two are. [S5] The Klokgebouw is the Philite factory, building SA, completed in 1928 and 1929, where a bakelite-type plastic was made for radio housings, according to a building-history survey that the site owner commissioned in 2022. [S15] The Microlab hall is in building SFH, the former TV factory, built in 1977 and 1978 on the footprint of an older building that was not rebuilt after the bombing of December 6, 1942. [S15] The same survey says the site was almost fully built up shortly before the Second World War. [S15] So the square lies between a 1920s radio-era factory and a 1970s television factory, and the Ketelhuis beside it sits in the older layer.
A building is being built to watch the square

The newest change is not on the square. MVRDV's Strijp-S Tribune, a building of 56 apartments, 44 of them social rent and 12 mid-market rental, over a two-story commercial base, steps down to two stories beside the Ketelhuisplein so that residents can watch events on the plaza from terraces. [S8] MVRDV says the stepped shape mediates between the open square, the high-rise Haasje Over, the factory building Anton and the Area 51 building, and adds a public lookout over the Leidingstraat at the corner of the square. [S8][S16] The architects also say the timber facade refers to wood pavilions shown at DDW, with Biobasecamp of 2019 as the example. [S8]

MVRDV's news item says the housing association Trudo celebrated the start of construction on Tuesday, November 11, with the contractor Stam + De Koning Bouw and alderman Stijn Steenbakkers. [S16] The item prints no year. November 11 fell on a Tuesday in 2025, and the project page lists the status as on site, so I read the date as November 11, 2025. [S16][S8] That is my inference, and MVRDV or Trudo can confirm it.

The Strijp-S history page describes the same turn in a general way: from about 2016, it says, new buildings adapt to the monuments, and Haasje Over was built over the old Area51 hall instead of replacing it, with a new wave of about 2,000 homes planned. [S1] A square used for a festival has a neighbor that is being built.
What the square is in the 2026 listings

DDW's location page lists Ketelhuisplein as an outdoor Strijp-S location with free access, postal code 5617 AE and hours of 11:00 to 18:00 on each day from October 17 to 25, 2026. It describes it as one of DDW's largest locations, with approximately 7,000 square meters, between the much-visited Klokgebouw, Microlab Hall and other DDW locations. [S5] The tourism site This is Eindhoven, in a tip dated October 1, 2026, calls it a festival ground in itself and a temporary open-air museum, says it lies practically next to Strijp-S station and names four installations: Blind Spots, Designing Society, Wuerstelhocker and If Soil Could Speak, plus a pop-up spot called The Bar. [S17] I treat those as published descriptions, not as a report of what stands there.
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it
The sale year. Some summaries give 2004. The Strijp-S site's own history page gives 2002 for the purchase by VolkerWessels and the municipality. [S1] I use 2002.

The Klokgebouw's year. Erfgoed Brabant gives 1928 for the Klokgebouw; a register entry in the same complex describes a factory building with a water tower built in two phases in 1928 and 1929. [S2][S7] The register is the primary record, so where an entry gives two phases, both years are right for that building. The Ketelhuis's 1929 stays a single-source date. [S2][S7]
The year of the mosaic's move. The record text says 2021 and the same record's field says 2020. [S9] I leave it open.
What the record does not show

I do not know when Dutch Design Week first used the square, why 2020 has no album beyond the festival having gone digital that year, or what stood on the ground before the Philips buildings around it. I do not know whether the Ketelhuis has municipal monument status, who designed it, or whether the square is named for it. I could not find a building-history report for the Ketelhuis, although the site owner commissioned such reports for other Strijp-S buildings. [S15] The Tribune's construction year is my inference from a weekday. The photo counts and credits are from my October 7 reading of Flickr. [S11]

If you look at one of these album photos, try a plain test. What is the ground telling you, and what is only the structure on it? And which of the buildings at the edge of the frame will still be standing in the same shape in the next album? [S11][S8]

title: The Klokgebouw was built in two phases, so its two dates were never in conflict
subtitle: A former Philips factory on Strijp-S, followed through the national monument register, a 2022 building-history survey, the Strijp-S redevelopment and nine editions of the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: The Klokgebouw on Strijp-S dated 1928 and 1929, resolved with the national register and a 2022 survey, plus nine editions of Dutch Design Week photos.

sections.x: The Klokgebouw's two dates, 1928 and 1929, come from a single fact that the national register states in one sentence: the building came about in two construction phases, in 1928 and in 1929. [S1]

Ask three public sources when the Klokgebouw was built and you can get two years. The Strijp-S site says it was originally built in 1929 for Philips' synthetic material Philite. [S2] A heritage story from Erfgoed Brabant says it dates from 1928, and a hostel inside the building says it was completed in 1928. [S3][S4] A walking-tour guide says 1929. [S5] Two construction phases would let every one of those sources be right, and two separate records, the register and a 2022 building-history survey, say exactly that. I set out both below. This essay reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what is on show in the building during DDW 2026 beyond what published listings say.
The register gives two phases, and the address list ties it to the venue

The monument is number 518769 in the national register, registered on February 16, 2004, and part of complex 518768, the Philipscomplex Strijp S. [S1][S6] The entry describes a multi-story factory building with a factory water tower, designed by A. de Broekert of the Philips engineering office, which came about in two construction phases in 1928 and 1929 in a functionalist style. [S1] It describes a six-story building under a flat roof, made of two square masses, with a tower-like mass of eight levels on the north side that holds a water reservoir, built entirely in concrete with wide windows in metal frames. [S1] The value statement calls it a building of general importance, a rare example of a built-in water tower, and part of a coherent industrial landscape that is becoming rare. [S1]

A reader might doubt that the register entry is the venue, because the entry's main address is Klokgebouw 300 and the venue's own site gives Klokgebouw 50. The register's address list for the monument settles that: it includes Klokgebouw 50, 5617 AB, among more than a hundred Klokgebouw addresses. [S1][S7] The entry for the complex adds that the layout of the whole terrain was developed by A.I.J. de Broekert, who worked for Philips, and that the protected buildings are SA, SDM (the Veem building), SBP, SAN and SK, and SF (a pump building). [S6]
A second record agrees

In 2022 the site owner, Park Strijp Beheer, commissioned a building-history survey of several buildings on the south-east side of the terrain, carried out by the office of J.A. van der Hoeve. Its survey of building SFH, the former TV factory that houses Microlab, gives a short history of the whole terrain. [S8] It names the Philite or Klokgebouw as building SA, dated 1928 and 1929, and says a plastic was made there that served among other things as housing for radios, a variant of bakelite. [S8] The survey is by a building historian who is not the register's author, it draws on earlier literature and the municipal building files, and it matches the register.

So the one-year sources each name one of two real years. Strijp-S and the walking-tour guide give the year of completion, 1929, and Erfgoed Brabant and the hostel give the year the work began or the first part was finished, 1928. That reading is still mine, because none of those pages says it, but the register and the survey now make it the simplest explanation. [S1][S8][S2][S3][S4][S5]
What was made there, and how the building was used

Philite was a Philips plastic. The 2022 survey calls it a variant of bakelite used among other things for radio housings. [S8] The walking-tour guide calls it a hard plastic and says the building was originally the center of Philite production. [S5] Erfgoed Brabant says bakelite for radios was made at the Klokgebouw. [S3] The Museum of Design in Plastics at Arts University Bournemouth says Philips first began production of Philite in 1923 and describes 1930s plaques made of Philite as compression-moulded urea formaldehyde, a different resin from phenol formaldehyde bakelite. [S9] Those two descriptions do not match, and a heritage booklet explains why they may both be right: it lists twelve types of Philite by 1938, including a standard grade, a tropical grade, a transparent grade and sheet materials impregnated with resin. [S10] The booklet is by an amateur heritage publisher and says it draws on Philips' staff magazine of January 1930, which I did not open, so I use it for color and not for any date I rely on. That a family of materials carried one name is my reading of the booklet, and it fits both descriptions.

The booklet gives a fuller picture of the building's first use. It says the Philite factory, coded SA, was the last building delivered on the terrain in 1929, that it came into use in 1930 with about 750 employees, that its central hall held 600-ton presses for complete radio cabinets and more than a hundred smaller presses, and that the pressing powder was prepared next door in building SAC. [S10] It says the factory worked in three shifts with a night crew of twenty-five, and that when radio sales fell in the 1930s it made ashtrays, tobacco jars, tableware and inkstands to keep staff. [S10] It credits the design to the company architect J.R. Bouten working under A.I.J. de Broekert, head of Philips' technical department, with the concrete structure drawn and calculated by staff of the Hollandsche Beton Maatschappij. [S10] The walking-tour guide gives the same two names. [S5] The register names only De Broekert. [S1]

The booklet adds a detail that touches the clock. It says the north-west end was raised into a tower of sixty meters with three clocks only at the end of the 1930s, that the building got its nickname from it, and that the reinforced concrete of that raising was replaced by glass blocks in a restoration in 1996. [S10] None of the other sources I read dates the tower or the clock, so this stays a single-source statement. The register describes a tower-like mass of eight levels that holds a water reservoir and does not mention clocks. [S1] DDW's listing says the building is recognizable by the blue Philips clock. [S11]

The survey places the building within a larger works. Philips' first building on the terrain was a glass factory, dated 1915 in the survey and 1916 on the Strijp-S history page, and the radio factory that grew from the mid-1920s included the concrete production buildings SK, SAN and SBP, dated 1927, 1929 and 1930, in a group called the Hoge Rug. [S8][S12] The survey calls the radio factory one of the largest in the world and says the terrain was almost completely built up shortly before the Second World War. [S8] The December 6, 1942 bombing hit the Philips complex heavily, according to the survey. [S8]
The fence came down in stages

Philips sold the roughly 27-hectare terrain in 2002 to Park Strijp Beheer, a partnership of the municipality of Eindhoven and VolkerWessels, according to the Architectuurcentrum Eindhoven's walking-tour guide. [S5] The Strijp-S history page agrees on the year, and says the plan by West 8 followed between 2002 and 2005. [S12] The guide says serious redevelopment began in 2006. [S5]

A sale date of 2004 turns up in some web summaries. I use 2002, because the site owner's own history and the architecture center's guide agree on it. [S12][S5] The register entry for the Klokgebouw is dated February 16, 2004, which may be where a 2004 slip comes from; I cannot show that. [S1]

The Klokgebouw was among the first buildings to be reused. The Strijp-S history page says the Klokgebouw, under the leadership of Trudo, and the Glasgebouw led the way after the fencing began to come down. [S12] The Strijp-S building page says Trudo has owned it since 2007 and calls it the cultural heart of Strijp-S, with a hotel, a music café and many studios. [S2] The building's own site says the skaters of Area51 and the climbers of Monk were the first pioneers, that it now holds more than 100 workspaces on 30,000 square meters, and that its culture halls take events from 100 up to 10,000 visitors. [S13]

The renovation was by Van Helmond | Zuidam architecten, now FAAM architects and Van Helmond Architecten, and included a new main entrance, according to the walking-tour guide. [S5] The hostel says the Blue Collar Hotel opened in the building in 2014 and was taken over by Stayokay after ten years, and that the building was nominated for the Brabant Cultural Prize in 2010. [S4] The hostel's page is a marketing text and carries no date, so I treat those two dates as the hostel's own account.
Dutch Design Week and the building

I could not find when Dutch Design Week first used the Klokgebouw. A 2014 note from the university TU/e says the Klokgebouw was a new location for the university's DDW presence, which had earlier been in the Hoofdgebouw hall and on the second floor of Vertigo, and that the university expected a bigger audience there. [S14] That dates the university's move, not the festival's first use. The festival's photo archive has Klokgebouw albums from 2015 on. [S15]

By 2019 DDW curated the Klokgebouw as one of its three main locations, with the Veem and Ketelhuisplein, with a focus on technology and innovation and an art director, Bas van Tol of Studio Muller van Tol. [S16] The same page describes the layout as Hall 1, the DDW Lounge, Hall 2, Connecting Collaborations, Hall 3 on technology, design and research, and Hall 4, Urban Habitat, while its own text speaks of three halls. [S16] DDW's 2026 location page says four halls, 7,500 square meters of exhibition space, block B4, and gives opening days of October 17 to 25, 2026. [S11]

The photo archive holds Klokgebouw albums for nine editions: 2015 with 50 photos, 2016 with 48, 2017 with 26, 2018 with 29, 2019 with 61, 2021 with 278, 2022 with 134, 2024 with 41 and 2025 with 112. [S15] Three more 2021 albums are listed, a 2025 Class of 25 album of 56 photos and an Industrial Design HUB album of 38. [S15] I found no album for 2020, the digital edition, or for 2023. I read those counts on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen Flickr in this pass. [S15]

The titles show a building that changes its show each year. The 2015 album is a numbered series of hall views, display cases and an orange robot arm credited to Sjoerd Eickmans. In 2016 the titles name Mind the Step, a frame shop, Volvo and Fontys. In 2019 they name Driving Dutch Design and the Embassy of Health. In 2021 they name Cabinet of Collaborations and Class of 21 banners. In 2022 Hall 1 carries banners reading Get set for global wellbeing. The 2024 titles are only dates and frame numbers. [S15]
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

The construction year. 1928 versus 1929: settled by the register's two phases and the 2022 survey. [S1][S8] The booklet adds that the factory was delivered in 1929 and came into use in 1930, which is consistent with a building begun in 1928. [S10]
The resin. The survey says a bakelite variant and the plastics museum describes a urea formaldehyde Philite; I read Philite as a family name, which is my inference. [S8][S9][S10]
The sale year. 2002 versus 2004: settled by the Strijp-S history page and the architecture center's guide, which agree on 2002 and name the buyer. [S12][S5]
The register address. Klokgebouw 300 versus 50: settled by the register's address list, which holds both. [S1]

The number of halls. Three in one sentence of the 2019 magazine, four in the same page's list and in the 2026 listing. [S16][S11] I use four, because the list names four halls, and note that the text has three.
What the record does not show

I do not know when Dutch Design Week first used the building, why 2020 and 2023 have no album in the archive pages I read, or who took the photos whose titles carry no name. I could not open any Philips Company Archives page on the Philite process, so what Philite was rests on the survey, the guide and Erfgoed Brabant. The hostel's dates for the hotel and the 2010 nomination are single-source. The register does not mention the clock, and the clock's date rests on one booklet. [S1][S10]

If you stand in front of the Klokgebouw during DDW 2026, you could try a question the register answered for me. When two accurate dates seem to clash, are you looking at one building or two phases of one? And which date would you print on the wall? [S1][S10]

title: Microlab was a TV assembly plant first, and its building history is no longer a gap
subtitle: A hall in the former Philips SFH building on Strijp-S, followed through a 2022 building-history survey, the founders' own account, the Dutch Design Awards exhibitions and four editions of the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: Microlab on Strijp-S sits in a Philips building designed in 1977 for TV assembly and testing. Its history, the Dutch Design Awards and four editions of photos.

sections.x: The building that houses Microlab was designed in 1977 by Philips' own architects and engineers as a TV assembly, testing and development plant, and a 2022 building-history survey says it served that purpose only briefly. [S1]

The survey answers a question that the public pages leave open: what the building was for. Microlab is a name with two lives, a workspace building on Strijp-S and a hall that Dutch Design Week has used, and public pages join the two only in places. The Strijp-S site calls the building the former Philips SFH building, the survey describes it in detail, and Microlab's own history page names it as a former TV factory. [S2][S1][S3] This essay uses those records, the festival's own pages and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what is on show at Microlab during DDW 2026 beyond what the published listing says.
I was trained to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. SFH is an easy case once the survey is on the table, because the plan of the floors shows the function. [S1]
The survey dates the building to 1977 and 1978

Park Strijp Beheer, the owner of the terrain, commissioned a cultural-history survey of four buildings on the south-east side of Strijp-S, carried out by the office of J.A. van der Hoeve with R. Stenvert, with fieldwork on May 5, 2022 and a report dated June 2 and August 11, 2022. [S1] Its chapter on SFH, the TV factory that houses Microlab, tells the following story.

In the early 1970s Philips drew up a reorganization plan for the south-east of the terrain for its new audio and video industry groups. It started with a new head office, building SFF, built from 1972 to 1975. Then the old glass factory and neighbors made room for the TV assembly plant, SFH, dated 1977, and the video lab, SFJ, dated 1979. [S1] The survey says SFH was designed in 1977 by Philips' own architects and engineers' office, and that, unlike SFF and SFJ, it was not given to the architects Bakker en Bakker, probably because it had a less prominent position and purpose. [S1]

The paper trail is specific. The design of May 25, 1977 went to the municipal aesthetics committee on June 23, 1977 and received a negative opinion because it was too symmetrical, which led to the tall block being pushed into the low base and projected forward to mark the entrance. [S1] The city executive granted the building permit on November 2, 1977. [S1] The contractor was Boele & Van Eesteren of The Hague, the prefabricated concrete facade panels came from Basto Beton of Oudenbosch and were approved in November 1978, the steel trusses of the first floor came from Hollandia, and the light roof panels from Durox. [S1] Four older buildings had to be demolished for the site: SGG (1924), SEE (1925), SVV (1920 and 1924) and SWW (1916). [S1]
What it was for, and how briefly

The survey is explicit that the building was not meant for producing TVs in the sense of manufacturing the parts, but for assembly, testing and development. [S1] The ground floor held goods receiving, warehouses and packing; the mezzanine and first floor held assembly rooms; the second floor a canteen with offices; the third floor a laboratory and workshop; the fourth design space and a laboratory; the fifth measuring rooms; and the sixth floor was entirely offices. [S1] The big low base carried the logistics and the assembly, and the laboratories and offices were concentrated in the tall block. [S1]

It did not last. The survey says TV production and assembly moved elsewhere around 2000, leaving a test and research laboratory, and that the building functioned only briefly for its original purpose. [S1] Philips sold the terrain in 2002 to Park Strijp Beheer, a public-private partnership of the municipality of Eindhoven and VolkerWessels, and left in stages; SFH stayed in use by Philips for a long time, and one floor was still used by a Philips department when the survey was written. [S1] The survey names the last Philips presence at Strijp-S as Philips MMD Micro Devices on the first floor of the west wing. [S1]

Some uses between Philips and Microlab are on record. In 2014 the first floor of the east wing was refitted for Amazon-Liquavista to a design by OIII Architects of Amsterdam. [S1] Part of the ground floor of the east wing stood empty and was used for a time to shelter war refugees from Ukraine. [S1] I could not date that sheltering from the survey, which was written in 2022.
How Microlab came to the building

Microlab's own history page tells it as a story about two brothers. Luuk Visser made furniture on his balcony and then in his living room, found no public wood and metal workshop in Eindhoven, and in January 2014 phoned his brother Rik; in May 2014 they had a plan for a place called Atelier Eindhoven, a first crowdfunding campaign raised enough to equip a workshop of 650 square meters on Strijp-T, which volunteers built in six weeks. [S3] It opened in October 2014, just before Dutch Design Week, with five members, and the page says the young business also hosted that year's Dutch Design Awards expo, with almost 20,000 visitors in its first two weeks. [S3]

A local news guide published on October 18, 2014 agrees on the place: it says the Dutch Design Awards exhibition was on Strijp-T and showed all the entries that qualified. [S4] So the Awards and the brothers' workshop meet in 2014, two years before the SFH building.

The move to SFH follows in the same account. After a search the brothers found a former TV factory, known as the SFH building on Strijp S, signed contracts in December 2015, moved at the end of January 2016, and reopened in June 2016 as Microlab with twenty studios and eight offices. [S3] The page says that over the next two years the team of sixteen converted the Philips offices into a co-working space, and that by April 2018 it housed more than 120 companies and 500 people. [S3] The survey says Microlab was set up gradually from 2015, which fits the December 2015 contracts. [S1][S3]

An article in the IO+ archive published on December 10, 2019 counted 230 companies and 800 members on 10,000 square meters over six floors, and reported that Microlab's owners would also run the top four floors of the old V&D department store in the city center, with more than 400 flexible workplaces, after two years of works. [S5] I found nothing on how that project ended, and the current Microlab site lists a location in Rotterdam and the one on Strijp-S, not a V&D building. [S6] The Strijp-S building page, which is undated, describes 150 offices, 60 workstations and 80 studios, status "existing" with redevelopment in phase 4. [S2] Microlab's events page now speaks of more than 250 companies and 1,500 members, six floors, a skybar and a playground. [S7]
How the Dutch Design Awards came to the hall

The Awards show moved around. In 2014 it was on Strijp-T. [S4] In 2019, the Awards' own report says, the work of all winners and nominees could be seen in a nine-day exhibition on the third floor of the Veem building. [S8] Microlab's own history page gives the same 2014 account from the other side. [S3][S4]

For 2021, two photographs of signs in the archive read "Things that Matter @ Microlab Hall" and list Dutch Design Awards among the participants; they are pictures of signs, and they do not say where in the hall the Awards were shown. [S9] For 2022 DDW wrote that all projects of the nominees and winners could be visited in the nine-day overview exhibition of DDA22 at Microlab Hall, with 24 nominees, and says the winners were announced at the Award Night on October 27. [S10] For 2023 DDW's news item placed the Awards exhibition in Microlab during DDW, October 21 to 29, with QR codes for a public vote that closed on Thursday, October 26, at 12:00. [S11] The 4TU Design United show of 2023 also gave Microlab, Kastanjelaan 400, as the address for its dialogues. [S12]

After that the trail changes. DDW's 2024 program page says the Dutch Design Awards chose a year of reflection and connection, working with ten former winners or nominees in the Young Designers category, each introducing one new young designer. [S13] A partner foundation's page confirms the ten-plus-ten format and says the work was shown in the annual Awards exhibition during DDW 2024. [S14] Neither page names the venue, so the 2024 exhibition cannot be tied to Microlab from these sources. [S13][S14]

In May 2025 the Awards announced a new direction centered on emerging talent, with communication moving to the Dutch Design Foundation and the Awards website becoming an archive. [S15] The renewed Awards named fifteen nominees for an Emerging Talent Award in October 2025 and three winners, who received their awards on the evening of Saturday, October 18, 2025, with 10,000 euros each. [S16][S17] For 2026 fifteen finalists are named and the awards ceremony is set for Saturday, October 17, 2026, by invitation, during DDW. [S18] None of those pages gives a venue. [S15][S16][S17][S18]
What four editions of photographs show

The archive holds Microlab albums for four editions, 2021 to 2024, in five albums and 344 photos. [S9] I read the album pages on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen Flickr in this pass. The 2021 album is titled Things that matter - Microlab and has 116 photos by Boudewijn Bollmann, with signs reading Things that Matter @ Microlab Hall, large black inflatable tubes, glass panels carrying text and long tables under a pale sheet. [S9] In 2022 there are two albums: Dutch Design Awards, 79 photos by Nick Bookelaar dated October 22 and 26, 2022, with black display frames in a blue-lit hall and a sign reading Stem hier, Vote here; and Things that Matter, 88 photos credited to about.today and Nick Bookelaar, with ceramic tiles and a panel reading 450 years Koninklijke Tichelaar. [S9]

The 2023 album has 44 photos by Nick Bookelaar, dated October 21, 2023. The 2024 album, titled only Microlab, has 17 photos by Max Kneefel, dated October 19 to 23, 2024, with a Microlab Hall banner at the entrance, a workshop table under a Crafted Connections sign and a rusted metal and glass structure. [S9] I found no Microlab album for 2015 to 2020 or for 2025. [S9]
DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and its listing names the venue Microlab - Playground, at Kastanjelaan 400, with a single opening slot on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, from 09:00 to 12:30. [S19]
Where the sources disagreed, and what settled it

What the building was. A search snippet had once suggested a TV factory with no page behind it. The survey and Microlab's history page now both say so, with the qualification that it was an assembly, test and development plant. [S1][S3]

When Microlab came to SFH. The survey says gradually from 2015; Microlab's history gives signed contracts in December 2015, a move at the end of January 2016 and a reopening as Microlab in June 2016. [S1][S3] The company's own dates are more specific and consistent with the survey, so I use them.
Size. Microlab's page now speaks of 250 companies and 1,500 members, and its earlier descriptions gave other numbers, 230 and 800 in 2019. [S7][S5] These are different dates and not a conflict.
What the record does not show

The record does not say which part of the building DDW calls Microlab Hall, or whether the hall is the whole base, one wing or a floor. It does not name the 2024 and later Awards venues. I could not date the use of the east-wing ground floor for refugees. I did not open the municipal building files that the survey used, and the survey notes that the files have gaps. [S1] The year-by-year photo counts and credits are from my October 7 reading of Flickr. [S9]

If you look through the 2021 to 2024 albums yourself, which caption would you want first: the year, the photographer, or the name of the show? And when a hall has been a TV plant, a workshop and an exhibition stage, which of those would you put on the wall? [S1][S9]

title: MU Hybrid Art House: a radio factory, a Japanese character and twelve Octobers of Dutch Design Week
subtitle: An Eindhoven art house followed through the national monument register, its own exhibition archive and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: MU Hybrid Art House on Strijp-S, from a Philips radio factory to Dutch Design Week shows, with what its own archive and the register do and do not say.

sections.x: MU Hybrid Art House has occupied the ground floor of a former Philips radio factory on Strijp-S since 2013, and its exhibition archive shows what it put in that building each autumn since. [S1][S2][S3]

This essay uses public sources only: MU's own pages and exhibition archive, the national monument register, Dutch government and housing-corporation pages, press coverage and the official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. MU's current website loads its text with scripts and is hard to read, but its older website still holds the full exhibition archive, and that archive settles several questions that look open elsewhere. I say below which source settled each one. [S3]

I also have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A building that made radios and now makes arguments about artificial intelligence is a fair test of that habit. [S4]
MU began in 1998 and carries a Zen word

MU describes its own history in a short text on its website. It says MU began in 1998 in De Witte Dame, a former Philips factory in the center of Eindhoven, as a merger of several small initiatives in visual art, architecture, pop culture and design. [S1] It has belonged to the national cultural infrastructure since 2005, as a small presentation institution until 2012 and as a large one since. [S1]

A 2023 interview in Brabant Cultureel adds the people. It says the director and artistic leader, Angelique Spaninks, took over in 2005 from Ton van Gool, who started MU in 1998 as a place where, at the initiative of the municipality of Eindhoven, several small initiatives in visual art, design, architecture and pop culture were to come together. Spaninks says in that interview that she built on his lines and added bio art and design, engaged art, digital media and performance. The same article says she came to MU from the regional newspaper Eindhovens Dagblad. [S5]

The name is explained on MU's About page. It comes from a Japanese character that stands for synergy, and in Zen the term goes beyond either-or thinking and leaves room to postpone judgment. [S1] The Brabant Cultureel article renders the same character as nothing or emptiness and adds the sentence that anything can arise from nothing. [S5] I note both readings because the character is used differently in different places, and MU's own text chooses synergy.

MU has three stated pillars: public presentations, talent development and education. [S1] Its 2017 to 2020 activity plan, which the Cultuur Eindhoven foundation publishes, adds numbers. It says MU's projects drew about 40,000 to 90,000 physical visitors a year, with Dutch Design Week and Glow Next named as the peaks. It reports 105,098 digital sessions by 78,207 unique visitors on MU's websites in 2015, against 70,807 sessions by 53,603 unique visitors in 2013. [S6] Those are the organization's own figures and I have found no later ones.
The building: a radio factory on the Hoge Rug

Which building is MU in? The answer is on MU's old news page. It announced that MU was turning 15 and opening a second space on Strijp-S: one thousand square meters on the ground floor of the building called Gerard, at Torenallee 40-06, with an opening party on Saturday, May 18. [S2] The page carries no year. MU was founded in 1998, so its 15th birthday is in 2013, and May 18, 2013 was a Saturday. That date arithmetic is mine, and it matches the year MU gives for its move in every other text. [S1][S2][S6]

One source disagrees. The housing corporation Trudo, which redeveloped the building, says on its project page that the art space MU was established there in 2014. [S7] MU's own archive explains how both can be right. It lists five shows in a series called MUtate from February to June 2014, and a Studio LONK project page describes MU's last five months in De Witte Dame as a monthly relay of artists before the move to Strijp-S, without a year. [S3][S8] I read that as the Strijp-S space opening in May 2013 and the old home closing in mid-2014. I have not seen a source that says so in one sentence, and a 2014 local news item about the farewell exhibition turned up in a search but could not be opened, so that part is second-hand.

Gerard and its neighbor Anton are two of the Philips radio-factory buildings on the Hoge Rug, a row of concrete production buildings at Strijp-S. A building survey for the municipality, written by a firm of building historians, says a new radio factory took over most of the site from the mid-1920s and that the concrete production buildings SK (1927), SAN (1929) and SBP (1930) still stand. [S9] The national register lists these three as one rijksmonument, number 518771, registered on February 16, 2004, with a design credited to the Philips engineer A. de Broekert, and the address list for that monument includes Torenallee 40-06 itself. The register adds that the interiors have changed greatly through changed use. [S10] So MU's building is a national monument, which matters because the Dutch government's transformation database says the monument status restricted the conversion and that uncertainty about the restrictions raised its cost. [S4]

That database, from the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), also records what the work was. The former radio factories SAN (Anton) and SBP (Gerard) became 276 lofts plus commercial space, finished in 2013, with an address range of Torenallee 30 to 60 and an original construction year of 1927 for the project. [S4] Trudo says all 276 lofts were let and that it placed the art space on the ground floor because public functions belong there. [S7]

Here the sources split, and I cannot settle it. RVO says Gerard is the former SBP. A French database of architecture says Gerard is the former SAN and dates it to 1929. [S4][S11] The register entry does not label the three buildings by name. [S10] If RVO is right, MU's building went up in 1930, and if the French database is right, in 1929. I lean to RVO because it is a government record, but a government page can carry the same error as a database, and I did not find the primary drawing or permit that would settle it.
Strijp-S: a fenced city that opened in the 2000s

The site's own owners tell a short history. Strijp-S's website says Philips had its first factory built there in 1916, a glass factory making bulbs for lamps, and that the company became self-sufficient on the site, from raw material to finished product. It says the area was called the Forbidden City because it was fenced and you needed a pass, and that about 10,000 people worked there in the 1970s. [S12] The national register gives the same starting point from the heritage side: a need for its own glass factory during the First World War started the new complex. [S10]

The sale date needs care because sources differ. Strijp-S's history page says 2002, when VolkerWessels and the municipality of Eindhoven bought the site from Philips and leased it back for a time. [S12] A German architecture trade site says production stopped and the site was sold in 2004. [S13] I trust the site owner's own history over a trade summary, and I did not find a deed. The Strijp-S page also says Dutch Design Week chose the area as its new home after the first buildings opened up, and that the Klokgebouw and the Glasgebouw led the redevelopment. [S12]
What the archive shows, year by year

The official DDW photo archive on Flickr holds MU albums for 2015 to 2022, 2024 and 2025, ten editions and 658 photos by my October 6 count. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so every count and photographer credit below comes from that earlier reading and stays second-hand. [S14] What changed is that MU's own exhibition archive now lets me say what was on show in each of those Octobers.

**2015.** The album is titled Collective [Ir]Rationality. MU's page says it ran from October 5 to 25, 2015, and was a spatial installation by Studio KNOL on the herd behavior of festival crowds. It says that MU had been visited by more than 36,000 people in nine days during the previous year's DDW. [S15] That is the only DDW-week visitor count for MU that I found.

**2016.** For Play, Shaping Sexuality ran from October 7 to November 13, 2016, curated by Sanne Muiser and Tom Loois, with more than 30 invited artists and designers. [S16] The same page lists the other things MU did in DDW week: a daily design talk show called Create Out Loud, an art-book pop-up shop and The Parliament of Things, which it places at the MU container at Plug-In-City. [S16] That settles where the Parliament of Things stood: at a container, and not in the building. The archive's 24 photographs under that title therefore show the container. MU's activity plan says it had managed two containers at Plug In City since 2015 as an outside presentation and development space. [S6] I leave the content of For Play at its title, because the show deals with adult themes and nothing in this essay depends on it.

**2017.** Materialising the Internet ran from October 6 to November 12, 2017, curated by Nadine Roestenburg and Spaninks, with more than 20 international artists and designers. [S17] The artists listed include Joey Holder, who appears again in 2025 as the maker of Ambiogenesis. [S17][S18]

**2018.** The New Newsroom, subtitled Reporting Redesigned, ran from October 12 to November 11, 2018, under the same two curators, with a newsroom set up inside the exhibition. [S19] Domus, the Italian design magazine, called it the most interesting show of that DDW and confirms the closing date. [S20]

**2019.** The Object Is Absent ran from October 19 to 27, 2019, an exhibition that, by its own description, replaced objects with designers acting, singing and dancing. Four people are named for concept, curating and realization: Alexandre Humbert, Tom Loois, Lucas Maassen and Spaninks. [S21] It was later a nominee in the product category of the Dutch Design Awards, whose page quotes the jury calling the absence of objects perhaps necessary to generate new ways of designing. [S22]

**2020.** The Self Design Academy ran from September 18 to November 22, 2020, as a joint initiative of MU and the Image Society, curated by Mieke Gerritzen and Spaninks, with 18 artists and designers, shown both at MU and online. [S23] In December MU opened Evolutionaries for the tenth anniversary of the Bio Art & Design Award. [S3][S24]

**2021.** This year needs care. The album is titled Bio.Stories, but MU's archive has no exhibition by that name. MU's show that October was LAWKI-Alive, by the collective ARK, from October 14 to November 28, 2021, curated by Spaninks and Paulien Dresscher. [S25] Bio.Stories was a separate event hosted in MU: a forum series curated by the design consultancy Faber Futures with the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Synthetic Biology, which a participant announced for MU at Torenallee 40-06 on October 19, 2021. [S26] So the 141 photographs titled Bio.Stories document a forum held in MU's hall, and the album title is accurate about what it shows.

**2022.** The album has 245 photographs, the largest, and titles that name no show. MU's archive supplies one. Reproduction Otherwise, on view from October 7 to November 27, 2022, looked at designers' and artists' scenarios for human reproduction through seven makers. [S27] The Creative Industries Fund NL was also in MU that week, with a video installation of one-minute portraits of 51 talents and a live program, and its own report credits photographs of it to Max Kneefel, the photographer named across the MU album. [S28] I connect the album to Reproduction Otherwise by date, since it was the MU exhibition on show on October 22, 2022, and not by any title. As an anatomist, I know reproduction as a chapter of structure and function. MU's exhibition text treats it as a set of social, religious, medical and economic systems, which is a different way into the same subject, and I take no position on its argument here.

**2023.** I found no 2023 album, and I cannot say whether one exists. What I can say is that MU was open with a show during DDW 2023: TIMELESSTIME by MAISON the FAUX, an installation with scheduled performances, running from September 15 to November 26, 2023, with its DDW-week performances on October 21, 22 and 25 to 29, from 2 to 5 p.m. [S29] The BAD Award exhibition followed on December 15, 2023. [S30]

**2024.** Poetics of Prompting, a collaboration between The Hmm and MU, ran from October 4 to November 24, 2024. MU's page describes it as exploring new languages between AI and human creativity. [S31] DDW's press page, read on October 6, names it as MU's show for that DDW. [S32] The album has eight photographs.

**2025.** Other Intelligences ran from October 10 to November 23, 2025, curated by Sabine Himmelsbach, Marlene Wenger and Spaninks. MU's page says twelve artists took part but prints thirteen names, and I cannot tell which count is right. [S18] The album's titles name works including Plant Machete by David Bowen and PL_AI by Špela Petrič. [S14] MU's 2017 to 2020 plan had already listed Petrič among the artists MU was in conversation with. [S6]
Beyond the main show, and who pays

The archive also lists smaller DDW-week items that the photo albums fold into one title. A daily design talk show called Create Out Loud appears in the archive on October 18, 2015, October 21, 2016, October 22, 2017 and October 21, 2018. [S3] MU's activity plan says MU set it up with the Design Academy Eindhoven, the Creative Industries Fund NL and Dutch Design Week, and that it wanted a daily moment of reflection on design that the festival lacked. [S6] Other DDW-week entries include Dries Verhoeven's Guilty Landscapes IV in 2016, Embassy of Intimacy in 2017 and The Scene Is Here in 2019, each listed with a start date and nothing more in the list view. [S3] The albums cannot tell a reader which of these a photograph belongs to.

MU's money is public and mixed. Its organization page says it is structurally supported by the Ministry of OCW, the province of North Brabant and the Cultuur Eindhoven foundation with the municipality, and that it receives project support from funds including Fonds21, Kunstloc Brabant, the Creative Industries Fund NL, the VSB Fonds and the Cultural Participation Fund. [S33] The 2017 to 2020 plan describes a three-part model of income from its own activities, sponsors and media, and outside funds, with public subsidy named as the most important source. It also says the staff then consisted of eight listed roles, with the director's time partly lent to the STRP biennial. [S6] The Brabant Cultureel article adds that the national subsidy has to be requested again every four years. [S5] I mention this because a venue that depends on fixed funding periods tends to plan in blocks, and MU's calendar reads that way.
Threads that run through the years
Three patterns show up only when the exhibition archive is read next to the photo archive. [S3]

First, the calendar. In most years MU opens its autumn show in the first half of October and keeps it up for weeks after the festival ends: October 5 to 25 in 2015, October 7 to November 13 in 2016, October 6 to November 12 in 2017, October 12 to November 11 in 2018, October 7 to November 27 in 2022, October 4 to November 24 in 2024 and October 10 to November 23 in 2025. 2019 is the exception, with The Object Is Absent running only from October 19 to 27. For 2026, MU's press page gives the opening as October 9 and the exhibition page as October 10. [S15][S16][S17][S18][S19][S21][S27][S31][S34][S35] The activity plan explains one reason for the long runs. It says each changeover closes the space to the public for at least two weeks and that MU therefore planned no more than six presentations a year in its own space. [S6]

Second, the director's hand. Spaninks is named as curator or co-curator of the DDW-season show in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2025 and 2026. [S17][S18][S19][S21][S23][S25][S35] In 2016 the co-curators were Muiser and Loois. [S16] Loois returns in 2019. [S21] That is a pattern of a standing house curator working with a changing guest, and I take it from the credits and not from any statement by MU.

Third, return visits. Joey Holder is in the 2017 and 2025 exhibitions. [S17][S18] MAISON the FAUX made TIMELESSTIME in 2023 and returns in 2026 with Everything Moist Seems Alive. [S29][S35] The bio artist behind this year's Bar Mycelium, Dasha Tsapenko, was one of the three winners of the 2020 Bio Art & Design Award. [S24][S36] MU says on its About page that the award is on hold for now while it looks for partners and funds. [S1]
What MU lists for DDW 2026

DDW 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and MU's own page for it lists six items. [S37] The main one is Everything Moist Seems Alive by MAISON the FAUX, which MU's page calls an installation and string of live performances that drips, flows, splashes, seeps, leaks and sweats. It is a co-production of the foundation This is not an Office, MU and Studio Boekman, and it runs to January 3, 2027, with live performances daily in DDW week except October 19 and 20. [S35][S37] Bar Mycelium is in the MU container at Plug-In City, a bar grown from mycelium with a mycologist and a biotechnologist, with free admission to the bar and booked slots for cocktail sessions. [S36] The page also lists Small & Slow AI by the Visual Methodologies Collective, an AI workshop program from The Hmm for ages 8 and up, a presentation by the Creative Industries Fund NL and a pop-up bookshop by Motta Art Books. [S37] I describe these only as MU lists them.

One more item concerns the organization more than the program. A report on the local news site eindhoven.nieuws.nl says the art and technology festival STRP will stop at the end of 2026, and that its digital archive and website will go to MU. [S38]
What the record does not show

I cannot say whether Gerard is the former SAN, built in 1929, or the former SBP, built in 1930. RVO and a French database disagree, and the register entry does not label the buildings. I also cannot say what Philips made on MU's particular floor, beyond the site being a radio-factory complex. [S4][S10][S11]
I do not have a source that explains Trudo's 2014. I have reasoned that the Strijp-S space opened in 2013 and the old home closed in 2014, but I have not seen it written in one place. [S2][S3][S7]
Every Flickr count and photographer credit rests on my October 6 reading, which I could not repeat. I do not know whether a 2023 album exists, or why the 2024 album has only eight photographs. [S14]

I have visitor figures only for DDW 2014 and for the 2017 to 2020 plan's general range, nothing for later years. The 2025 to 2028 multi-year plan that MU links from its site was not retrievable. [S6][S15][S39]

Two sites that carry coverage of these shows, Dezeen and Faber Futures, refused my requests with an access-denied answer, so I stopped asking and did not open them. Where this essay needs facts from them, it takes them from MU's own archive or from a participant's announcement. [S21][S26]

If you want to test this record yourself, take the year you remember best, find its dates in MU's exhibition archive, and ask what that show, which usually ran for weeks, left out of the one festival week the photographs cover. [S3]
