title: Natlab: a physics laboratory from 1923, a cinema since 2013, and a design week that keeps asking it about research
subtitle: A former Philips research building on Strijp-S, followed through heritage writing, the organizers' own archives and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: Natlab on Strijp-S: a Philips laboratory founded in 1914, in its own building from 1923, a cinema since 2013, and a Dutch Design Week venue.

sections.x: Natlab is older than its building: the Philips physics laboratory began in 1914 inside a lamp factory and moved into the Kastanjelaan building in 1923. [S1][S2]

Two founding dates are in circulation for the NatLab, and they describe different things; the sources below explain how. I use public sources only: heritage writing from the Eindhoven architecture center, a 2002 book review in a Dutch academic magazine, the municipality's and the architects' own descriptions of the conversion, the archives of the lab Baltan, which works inside the building, the Dutch Design Week (DDW) program listings and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. This essay reports no visit and no interview. [S1][S2]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A research building that now holds a cinema, a school, a lab for artists and a professionals' conference is a fair test of that habit. [S1]
The laboratory began in a lamp factory in 1914

The historian Klaas van Berkel, reviewing a dissertation on the lab in 2002, says the NatLab officially begins in 1914, when Gilles Holst came to Eindhoven as its first director, and calls that a fairly arbitrary starting date. [S2] Gerard Philips was already doing chemical experiments in the factory in the 1890s. In 1908 he hired a chemical engineer, J.C. Lokker, who got a small laboratory on the fifth floor that the staff called the little pharmacy. In 1913 a second engineer, L. Hamburger, arrived and became the first Philips researcher to do fundamental scientific work. Van Berkel adds that Dutch patent law, in force since 1912, gave companies a reason to do their own research. [S2] Holst's group got space on the fourth floor, and staff called the chemists' lab Lab V and the physicists' lab Lab IV. [S2]

A TU/e page agrees on the date and the motive. It says the NatLab was founded in 1914 after a direct decision by Gerard and Anton Philips, who wanted in-house research to support product development, a patent portfolio and less reliance on other firms' patents. [S3]

The separate building came later. Van Berkel says the lab outgrew the factory floors and was housed in its own laboratory in Strijp, then at the edge of Eindhoven, so that in 1923, almost ten years after Holst arrived, "the actual NatLab" was born. [S2] The Eindhoven architecture center, Architectuurcentrum Eindhoven, gives the same year and adds the details. The lab had been housed in the Philips complex on the Emmasingel. In 1923 it got its own building on Strijp-S, designed by the architect Dirk Roosenburg, with the Philips building code SMM. [S1] The same article says there were 15 researchers and 20 assistants in 1923 and 106 researchers and 360 assistants by 1939. [S1]

So the two dates are both right. 1914 is the laboratory, and 1923 is this building. A plaque with the words Natuurkundig Laboratorium 1923 is among the details the architecture center lists in the building. [S1] It would therefore be wrong to say that Philips opened the laboratory here in 1923. Philips moved an existing laboratory into this building in 1923.
What happened inside it

The architecture center's article says Albert Einstein visited in 1923 and caused a stir in Eindhoven. It says short-wave radio broadcasts to the Dutch East Indies started from the NatLab, and that in 1927 Queen Wilhelmina and Princess Juliana addressed the colony from the building, which is why one room is still called the Queen's Room. [S1] The Strijp-S site's own history page confirms the Queen's radio address from the laboratory. [S4]

Television came next. The article says an annex of the NatLab served as a television studio from 1946, and that between 1948 and 1951 Philips made 264 experimental broadcasts with transmitters on the top floor of the Veemgebouw, another Strijp-S building, topped by a wooden mast. [S1] The article calls them experimental broadcasts, and I do not claim more than that. [S1]

Then there is sound. A 2010 text from the VPRO radio archive by the journalist Marten Minkema, now hosted on a site about the lab's history, says the composers Tom Dissevelt and Dick Raaijmakers were given modern equipment in an acoustics department between 1956 and 1960 to experiment with electronic sound, which produced the piece Song of the Second Moon and puzzlement elsewhere in Philips. [S5] Strijp-S's history page says Philips saw nothing in the project and put no more energy into it. [S4] The architecture center explains where the name Baltan comes from. Raaijmakers recorded as Kid Baltan, which is Natlab and Dik read backwards. [S1]

The lab was also a social place. A mural by the artist Albert Troost, in the auditorium, was presented on December 21, 1957 by the 1,300 staff then working at the NatLab, at the opening of a new wing and the 40th anniversary of Philips Research. [S1] The mural's own contents, as the architecture center quotes the local newspaper's 1957 description, show an inventor handing a crystal on until humanity benefits, and a falling figure surrounded by fire for the misuse of inventions. [S1]

After the war, Minkema writes, the lab grew under its director Hendrik Casimir and gained a function above the company's, with more room for basic research that had nothing to do with shavers or irons. In the mid-1970s it cost 250 million guilders a year and employed 2,000 people, and a 1990 cost-cutting operation ended its special position inside the group. [S5] The architecture center says the NatLab moved to Waalre in 1963 and that the campus, opened to other companies in 2003, is now the High Tech Campus. [S1] The TU/e page says the move happened in the early 1960s, which matches. [S3]
How a research building became a cinema

The building is a municipal monument. Strijp-S's history page says so, and so does the architecture firm that converted it. [S4][S6] N Architecten of Maastricht, working for the municipality of Eindhoven, gives 2011 to 2014 as the design and realization period for what it calls Natlab 2.0, a re-use as a cultural center. It says the hardest task was placing a 200-seat hall in the existing building, which the firm solved with a visibly different element in weathering steel that rises above the roof line and is visible through the old windows. The café-restaurant went into the former boiler house. [S6] The architecture center adds that the floors of the halls, the window frames and Troost's mural were kept. [S1]

The film theater Natlab opened officially on October 11, 2013, with five screens, a multipurpose stage hall, two exhibition spaces and a café-restaurant. [S1] The tenants named in the article include the film theater Plaza Futura, the film platform Broet, Baltan, Architectuurcentrum Eindhoven and the school SintLucas. [S1] Another part of the old complex became a SintLucas building in 2016, designed by Cepezed and Arup with Laride, and was nominated in 2017 for the municipal architecture prize named after Roosenburg. [S1]

In October 2017 the European Physical Society gave the building its Historical Site distinction. The EPS list includes The Philips NatLab, Eindhoven (2017). [S7] The architecture center says the plaque hangs at the entrance and calls it Historical Site number 36. A TU/e page says the distinction came on October 5, 2017 and was the second given to an industrial research lab. [S1][S3] The plaque is therefore at the entrance of the building that is now the film theater. [S1]
A lab inside the lab

Baltan Laboratories is the organization most tied to the archive years below. Its About page says it was founded as a two-year pilot to explore what the media lab of the future could look like, and ties its identity to the NatLab and to Strijp-S, which it calls the former forbidden city. It says the renovated Natlab building opened officially with Baltan as a key inhabitant, with openings celebrated by projects inspired by Raaijmakers. [S8] The Mediamatic listing for a 2009 session of a monthly series called BALTAN goes NATLAB puts Baltan's presentations in the auditorium of the former Philips NatLab already in May 2009. [S9] Baltan's 2015 annual report says its offices and lab spaces in the building, which looked generous when it moved in during 2013, had become too small at full occupancy by the end of 2015. [S10] The 2016 report says it then took office space elsewhere on Strijp-S, at the Apparatenfabriek owned by Trudo, though the lab's events kept using the Natlab address. [S11][S12]
What the archive shows, year by year

The official DDW photo archive holds Natlab albums for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2025. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so every album count and photographer credit below stays second-hand from my October 6 reading. What I could do is find, for each year, the organizer's own account of what was on. [S13]

**2014 (no album).** Baltan and the aid organization Hivos began Age of Wonderland that year. Baltan's page for an Open Social Innovation Lab on October 2 to 4, 2014 says it was a chance to work with the six international artists of the Age of Wonderland program. [S14] The archive's tag for Natlab contains eight photographs from that year, outside the range of the albums. [S13]

**2015.** The second Age of Wonderland took the theme Balancing Green and Fair Food. The Creative Industries Fund NL, which granted 40,000 euros, describes a platform and incubator program with the curator Arne Hendriks, six designers from Kyrgyzstan, Indonesia, Tanzania and Bolivia, and a six-week residency, with results shown at DDW 2015. [S15] Baltan's annual report mentions a well-attended Future Food Seminar in Natlab and a fellow from Bishkek who researched the traditional feast Toi, which often has more than 800 guests. [S10] The album has 23 photographs. [S13]

**2016.** The third edition was Big Data. Big DADA? Hivos says six creatives from Africa, Asia and Latin America would research big and open data and show their work at DDW, October 22 to 30, in an exhibition and workshops, with Natlab as their temporary studio from September 26 and a seminar called The Big Data/Dada Dialogues. [S16] Baltan's report adds a pop-up radio station in Natlab during DDW and a traffic-counting system that collected real-time data on visitors to the building, a first step in a Tanzanian fellow's work to map his home city. [S11] The two sources disagree on the fellows' home countries. Hivos names fellows from Guatemala, Indonesia and Tanzania, and the Baltan report names Indonesia, Chile, Tanzania and Iran. [S11][S16] The album has 62 photographs, of which I could reach 24. [S13]

**2017.** The final edition was 100 Days of Learning. Baltan's year-end note says teachers from all over the world answered the question of what we need to learn to make the world better, in workshops and an exhibition, and that the exhibition would travel to another show in January. [S17] The album has six photographs. [S13]

**2018.** Baltan's Frankenstein Exhibition, titled It's Alive, ran from October 20 to 28, 2018, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, on whether AI and robotics will decide for us, with us or against us. Its works include a mirror room by We Are Data, a robotic lifeform called Cluster by Quintus Glerum, a digital persona by Arthur Elsenaar and an AI training center by Bureau Moeilijke Dingen. [S12] A Frankenstein Symposium on October 22 ran from 11:00 to 20:30 at Natlab, organized by Baltan and Robot Love, with a regular ticket price of 50 euros. [S18] The album has 12 photographs. [S13]

**2019.** The program was Homo Sensorium, October 19 to 27, 2019. Baltan's page lists experiments, workshops, talks, dinners, tours, films and a Brainwave Wedding Lab, in which EEG sensors measure the brain activity of couples during a kiss. [S19] I cannot say which activity the album's clear dome belongs to, and the page does not mention a dome. [S13][S19] That uncertainty from my earlier reading stays. The page does settle the name of the 2019 program.
**2020.** No Natlab album exists in the archive for 2020, and I did not find a Baltan program for that year. [S13]

**2021.** Mediamatic of Amsterdam and Baltan hosted Inhuman Carnaval at Natlab from October 17 to 22, 2021, with an open costume lab, exhibitions, workshops and talks on species from earthworms to fungi. Nearly 70 names and organizations are listed for it. [S20] The album has nine photographs dated October 21. [S13]

**2022 to 2024.** No Natlab album exists for these years. The sources show where Baltan went. In 2023 it and Onomatopee presented the DDW Gym at Sectie-C, and a selection of the project moved to Baltan's exhibition space in Natlab from November 8, 2023 to January 7, 2024. [S21] In 2024 its Decentralized Futures exhibition on blockchain and digital art was hosted at Koelhuis District Eindhoven. [S22] Natlab itself was still in use for DDW in 2024. A CLICKNL notice says the public design program PONT held three sessions at Natlab, part of the DDW Mission Days. [S23] I found no 2022 program.

**2025.** Mission Days is a DDW program of curated sessions for professionals around the festival's five guiding missions. [S24] TU Delft's page for DDW 2025 lists Design United Dialogue sessions at Natlab from 9:30 to 12:30 on October 20, for Living Environment, and October 21, for Thriving Planet, and says sessions continued through October 24 with registration. [S25] The album has 112 photographs of what its titles call Mission Days, with a stage and round tables in the first ones I viewed. [S13] That is a conference, and it is a different use of the building from any earlier year.
Who paid for the research on view

Baltan's own reports show how thin the funding behind these shows could be. The 2015 report says a small team of three permanent staff, plus freelancers, interns and volunteers, produced that year's work, and that Baltan worked structurally with the Holst Centre, an open innovation technology center. [S10] The 2016 report is blunter. It says an application to the Creative Industries Fund NL for basic infrastructure was rejected, that Age of Wonderland had to pull out all stops after refusals from the fund and from Brabant C, and that Baltan responded by creating a partner program, MEET : IMPACT, whose first partner event took place in October during DDW and Age of Wonderland. [S11] The December 2017 note says the Creative Industries Fund NL granted Baltan's program for the following year, with continued partnership with the Holst Centre and Sensiks. [S17] Research on public view in this building was, in other words, financed project by project.
A reading of the sequence

Read in order, the years describe a building that first showed research to the public and later hosted professionals who talk about it. [S22][S25][S26] From 2014 to 2021 the organizer's own accounts describe residencies, exhibitions, a radio station, a symposium and a costume lab, all of them open to visitors. From 2024 on, the sources describe sessions for professionals, some of them with registration. The 2026 listing fits that pattern.

The DDW 2026 location page gives Natlab weekday hours of 9:30 to 13:30 from October 19 to 23 and shows the building closed on October 17, 18, 24 and 25. [S26] The four items it shows at the time of reading are a regional care seminar by the Catharina Hospital on October 22, the Design United Dialogues from October 19 to 23, a workshop called Repositioning Circularity on October 20 and a Netherlands China Design Symposium on October 19. [S26] The page may list more, because it offers a link to all program items.

That is my reading, and the evidence for it is uneven. Baltan's DDW shows were held elsewhere in 2023 and 2024, which fits the pattern, and a single Mission Days album does not prove a trend. The Baltan expo space in Natlab was still showing projects in November 2023. [S21]
What the record does not show

The building history here rests on the architecture center's article, a book review and a radio feature, which cite an unpublished 2008 building-history report by Suzanne Fischer and a book on the lab that I did not read. I did not find an open primary document for the Einstein visit or the 1927 radio address. The Strijp-S history page confirms the radio address only. [S1][S2][S4]

Two places that would help did not answer: the cinema's own site returned a server error to my robots.txt request, and an Italian web magazine that covered Baltan returned an access-denied answer, so I stopped asking and used neither. [S1]

I do not know why there is no album for 2020 or 2022, what happened at Natlab in DDW 2022, which activity the 2019 dome belonged to, or how many people visited in any year. Baltan's reports give some counts for its own events, and none for DDW weeks. The Flickr counts and credits come from my October 6 reading. [S10][S11][S13]

One more thing remains unclear. Baltan's About page dates the official opening of the renovated building to its 2014 to 2015 period, while the architecture center says October 11, 2013, and the architects give 2011 to 2014 for design and realization. I take the architecture center's date for the film theater's opening, and the other dates may describe other parts of the work. [S1][S6][S8]

If you go during DDW 2026, check the hours first. Then look for the plaque by the entrance, and ask which of the two stories on the 1957 mural still describes this building: the crystal passed from hand to hand until humanity benefits, or the figure falling through fire. [S1][S26]

title: The NRE terrein: a gasworks from 1899, a bombed gas holder and a neighborhood built by the people who use it
subtitle: A former municipal energy site in Eindhoven, followed through heritage writing, the planners' and architects' own accounts and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: The NRE terrein in Eindhoven, from an 1899 gasworks to a creative neighborhood and Dutch Design Week venue, with what the sources do and do not show.

sections.x: The NRE terrein in Eindhoven began as a gasworks in 1899 and was rebuilt in the 2010s by its future users, without a project developer. [S1][S2]

The dates for this site conflict across the sources, so I say below which source supports which year. This essay uses public sources only: the provincial heritage body Erfgoed Brabant, the architects and planners who worked on the site, the collective NUL ZES, the city's tourism pages, Dutch Design Week (DDW) location pages and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. A few pages I wanted refused automated requests, and I name them at the end. [S3]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was for before I ask what it is now. A gasworks, a power station and a set of workshops for the city's utilities are a good place to practice it, because each of them kept the city's lights and stoves running and none was built to be looked at. [S1]
A gasworks moved to the canal in 1899

Erfgoed Brabant Verhalen, the heritage body's story site, dates the start of the site to 1899, when Eindhoven's first gasworks was moved out of the inner city to a spot on the Eindhovens Kanaal. The canal meant the city's residents would suffer less from the plant, and coal could be unloaded straight from the water. The building was designed by Louis Kooken, the city architect, and some years later large gas holders were added to store gas. [S1]

In 1909 the company Maatschappij de Peelcentrale began building an electricity plant on the site, finished in 1912, and in 1924 the site gained the Zuiverhuis, a purification house where gas was cleaned with water. [S1] The gasworks itself fell out of use as early as 1930, because technical progress allowed gas to travel farther, and the city took cheaper mine gas from the state mines. A receiving station for mine gas came instead. The water-gas plant stayed in use, the article says, because Philips still needed it. [S1]

That last sentence matters for a series about Eindhoven's technology history. Philips appears here as a customer of the water-gas plant, not as the owner, and the site remained a municipal utility site. [S1]

The firm Diederendirrix gives the setting. The Eindhovens Kanaal was dug in 1846 and made it cheap to move coal, wood and heavy machines, so factories collected at its end near the city. The wood company N.V. Picus began around 1883 and went bankrupt in 1993. Hub van Doorne started the workshop that became the truck maker DAF behind a brewery on the same stretch in 1928, and the linked buildings on the Tongelresestraat that remain now hold the DAF Museum. [S4] The whole former industrial estate covered 6.5 hectares, held buildings from 1899 to 1992, and was kept alive by re-use and temporary use until a selection of buildings designated as monuments remained. [S4]
The gas holder called Goliath

In 1941 one of the gas holders, the 84-meter Goliath, was hit in a British bombing raid and burned out. In 1944, during the liberation, other holders were damaged. In 1953 a new office building by the Eindhoven architect Cees Geenen was added. [S1] A local photo-history site gives more detail from the same event: it says the holder, built in 1930, was a landmark for pilots at 84 meters and burned out in the night of March 3 to 4, 1941, and that its flame lit up the whole city. [S5] That site is a collection of photographs and reader comments, so I treat its details as local memory and not as a record. It also says the holder was demolished in 1970, after a fire during demolition work on September 29 of that year. [S5] The heritage article says the holders were removed in the 1960s. [S1] I could not reconcile those two, and the site's own stories do not need the answer.

In the 1960s, the heritage article continues, storage and distribution left the complex, the holders were demolished and the offices and workshops stayed. In 1989 the municipal utilities for gas, water and electricity were merged into the company NV Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, NRE, which gives the terrain its name. [S1] The utility later moved to another location. [S1]
The dates line up once the sources are read together

Several sources give different-looking accounts of the end of the utility years, and most of the difference disappears when the urban designers' history is added. Diederendirrix, the architecture and urban design firm that wrote the first vision for the area, says the gasworks premises became part of Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, that NRE became part of the grid operator Enexis and that it left the premises in 2010. After that, it says, a number of municipal services moved into the existing office building and workplaces. [S4] The city tourism page agrees that the utilities were on the site from 1989 to 2010 and that the municipality bought the site afterwards. [S3] A heritage re-use site says that NRE became Endinet in 2007, that it was already clear Endinet would leave, and that the municipality bought the complex in 2010. A second page by the same site repeats the 2010 purchase. [S6][S7]

Two dates in the record then look out of place. A 2019 municipal report written for an EU project, which I read on October 7 and could not open again because its host now refuses my requests, says the municipality acquired the site in 2004 and that Endinet left in 2012. [S8] The 2004 has a likely source. Diederendirrix says it started in 2004 with an urban development vision for the area, so I read the 2004 in that report as the vision and not the purchase, though no page says so. [S4] The 2012 is a single second-hand statement against several pages for 2010, and I leave it aside. [S3][S4][S8]

One more date needs care. Most sources date the gasworks to 1899. Diederendirrix says the coal gas factory opened in 1900 at the Havenhoofd, the head of the canal. [S4] A start of building in 1899 and an opening in 1900 would fit both, but that reconciliation is mine.
Ten years of building it from the inside

The planners' and architects' accounts agree on an unusual method. The urban design firm Van Tuijn Stedenbouw says the terrain was long a blank spot on the map, closed to most people, and that during the planning years it was opened to temporary activities and became a creative hotspot. Its description of the process says there was no fixed master plan, that only end users and stakeholders took part, and that the area was shaped cooperatively with the new residents and businesses. [S9] The architects Houben / Van Mierlo describe the same arc: after a period of temporary use the municipality issued buildings and building plots to private initiators, whose first generation drew up, with their advisers, the municipality and the TU/e's Bauhütte, a framework plan called Nieuwe Energie, new energy. [S10]

The planning economists Metafoor, who worked for the municipality, give dates: the development process started in 2013 with small private parties and end users, with no housing corporations or project developers; the site covers 2.1 hectares; a provincial subsidy helped pay for cleaning up the ground and replacing the sewer; and the last phase of public space was due to be delivered in 2022. [S11] Houben / Van Mierlo add that the plan Made by NRE was selected by the municipality in early 2018 to redevelop the last four plots. It is a collective of residents, entrepreneurs, designers and makers, and it produced four buildings called Ambachtsdorp, Park NRE, Werkgebouw and Body Building. The firm says that with Made by NRE the transformation of the terrain is complete. [S10]

The monument status is disputed. The re-use site lists the former gasworks building as a municipal monument, with Louis Kooken as the original architect and De Bever architecten for the transformation. [S6] Diederendirrix says a selection of buildings designated as monuments remained. [S4] Van Tuijn says the existing buildings have no monumental status but do have cultural-historical value. [S9] Two of the three say there are designated buildings, and I cannot tell from these pages which buildings or what level of designation, so the municipal monument list is the place to check. The re-use site also gives two transformation years for the same building, 2013 on one page and 2019 on the page about the jazz club that occupies it. [S6][S7]

An undated guide from the Eindhoven-Now site lists eleven remarkable factory buildings on the terrain and, from the temporary period, the Atelierdorp with 24 studios, a bakery, a coffee bar and an exhibition space, and the events venue FIFTH|NRE waiting for its planned conversion to a jazz club. [S12]
NUL ZES, the collective that says it grew up here

NUL ZES is a collective of creative professionals at Gasfabriek 3A. Its own site says it grew up at NRE, that the old industrial buildings and all the new plots were developed by their end users with no project developer, and that NUL ZES took part as first-time placemakers, helped found the neighborhood association and developed the identity of NRE, including a logo. It offers private studios for a limited number of members, shared wood, metal and ceramics workshops, and event spaces. [S2] For DDW 2026 its page on the festival site lists it as a free location open from 11:00 to 20:00 each day, with items that include Touch On Connection by Plura Studio and a presentation by NUL ZES members. [S13]
What the DDW archive shows

The DDW photo archive on Flickr holds albums titled NRE for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2024 and 2025, six albums and 77 photos by my October 7 count. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so all counts, credits and picture descriptions in this section are second-hand. [S14]

The 2016 album has 13 photos by Iris Rijskamp, showing a long table of photographs in a dark hall, a yard with a yellow van and brick sheds, and weathered halls with plinths. The 2017 album has 10 photos by Nick Bookelaar, including a white wall of small framed works, a brick workshop with ceramics and the front of the NulZes building with bicycles. The 2018 album has 13 photos by the same photographer, and its title names three sets of makers: Lotte de Raadt with Kirstie van Noort, Alissa and Nienke, and NulZes. The 2024 album has 11 photos by Anwyn Howarth, with a rooftop garden pavilion called Cooling Down the City and exhibition rooms called Lighting for Wellbeing. The two 2025 albums, Finished Forms with 26 photos and Zowa with four, are by Cleo Goossens. [S14] There is no album titled NRE for 2015 or 2019 to 2023, though albums under maker or event names exist for several of those years. [S14]

For the festival's own account I used its 2026 location pages. Make Eindhoven, at Gasfabriek 12, offers workshops for graphic techniques, glass, metal and CAD/CAM and sits in what the page calls the former workshop of the energy companies on the NRE site. It is free and open from 11:00 to 18:00. [S15] Fifth, at Gasfabriek 5, describes itself as set in the industrial and cultural NRE site. [S16] Bart Hess I NRE is at Gashouder 43A, and its page calls the terrain a small-scale but lively creative area on the edge of the center with several design studios and creative agencies. [S17] The city's Kanaalzone tip of October 1, 2026 says there are fifteen DDW projects at the NRE site. [S18]

The first year the site was used for DDW remains unknown. The 2019 municipal report says it hosted DDW and GLOW years before the buildings were sold, and names no year. [S8] GLOW's own page for the work Waterfalls of Light says the light festival covered the facade of the three-story NRE office building at the head of the canal, built in 1992, with 40,000 small lights; the text I read gives no year. [S19]
A reading of the site

Read together, these sources describe a place whose use changed in stages that were each decided by its users: the utility that left, a period of temporary tenants who made it a hotspot, and then a set of buildings issued piece by piece to the people who had been using them. [S2][S9][S10] A nine-day festival fits that pattern of temporary use, and the archive's gaps in 2019 to 2023 may say more about how the albums were titled than about what happened on site. That second point is a guess, and I cannot confirm it. [S14]
What the record does not show

I take 2010 for both the departure of the utility and the municipal purchase, on the strength of four pages, but I did not find a deed or a council decision, and the one document that says 2004 and 2012 could not be re-opened. [S3][S4][S6][S8]

I do not know when DDW first used the site, or what the 2016 album shows beyond its photographs, because I could not reopen Flickr. I do not know which buildings are designated monuments. I do not know when the large gas holder was demolished. The heritage article says the 1960s and a photo-history site says 1970. [S1][S5][S14]

The most detailed document I could not read is a zoning-plan explanation for the area, hosted on a viewer site that refused my request, and a European heritage hub that also refused. I stopped asking both and did not look for copies elsewhere. [S8]

If a gasworks can become a festival venue, a neighborhood and a set of private workshops within a decade, which of its records would you ask the city to keep: the plans, the temporary tenants' agreements, or the photographs? [S9]

title: The Ontdekfabriek: a radio-equipment factory, a children's workshop and a move planned for the end of 2026
subtitle: A hands-on making space in a former Philips building on Strijp-S, followed through the building's register entries, the foundation's own reports and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: The Ontdekfabriek on Strijp-S: a Philips radio-equipment factory, a children's workshop since about 2010, and a move planned for the end of 2026.

sections.x: The Ontdekfabriek has spent about sixteen years as a children's workshop on the ground floor of a former Philips radio-equipment factory on Strijp-S, and a May 2026 report says it has to leave that building at the end of this year. [S1][S2]

That makes this a good moment to read its record. This essay uses public sources only: the foundation's own website and annual reports, the national monument register, the Strijp-S developers' pages, trade-press reports on the move and the official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. I describe the venue's audience only as the venue describes it, and I mention no participant in any photograph. [S3]

As a medical educator, I care about how people learn by handling things, so the venue's own account of its method is the part I read most closely. I read it as a description of a teaching sequence and I take no position on how well it works. [S2]
The building was a radio-equipment factory

Strijp-S's page for the Apparatenfabriek, which means appliance factory, says it was formerly better known as building SK and was built as the first radio equipment factory. It says the first Philips radios were produced there and that after the Second World War it made television sets. Housing corporation Trudo turned it into a business center in 2013, with a national monument status noted on the page. [S4] The same page says three buildings rose in 1928 on the Hoge Rug: Anton, Gerard and the Apparatenfabriek. [S4]

That year does not match the building historians. A survey written for the municipality of Eindhoven by the building-history firm of J.A. van der Hoeve gives SK as 1927, SAN as 1929 and SBP as 1930, and says the buildings belong to a radio factory that took over most of the site from the mid-1920s. [S5] The national monument register lists the three buildings as one monument, number 518771, and says they were built in 1930, 1929 and 1927 to a design by the Philips engineer A. de Broekert. Its address list for the monument includes Torenallee 22, the Ontdekfabriek's address. [S6] Philips's own media library says the company introduced its first radio in 1927, built entirely from Philips components. [S7] I take 1927 for SK, because two documents that rest on the buildings themselves agree, and treat Strijp-S's 1928 as a round year for the row.

The developers describe what came after. Driehoek Strijp-S says the Apparatenfabriek was still in Philips use until shortly before its transformation, that the ground floor and first floor were rebuilt for public functions, and that the ground floor housed the Ontdekfabriek, Capital D, Yksi, the 5Minuten Museum and Caffee Allee. [S8]
Founded in 2009, open from about 2010

Three sources give three founding years, and they turn out to be counting different things. The foundation's own ANBI page, the Dutch tax status for charities, says Stichting De Ontdekfabriek was established on May 18, 2009. [S9] A 2020 article on the Driehoek Strijp-S site, published on February 11 to mark ten years of the venue, says it started in the building that now holds the Urban Shopper, with very few facilities, and was open only on Sundays at first, under Anne Veenstra, who had run Plan-2 in the Klokgebouw. [S2] A 2017 article by E52 in the IO+ archive quotes the co-founder Chris Voets saying he started the venue with Hugo Vrijdag seven years earlier, which points to 2010. [S10]

So the foundation dates from 2009 and the public venue from about 2010. The first reading is a legal date and the second is an opening date, and I say that on my own reasoning. The foundation's 2024 report is consistent with 2009, since it carries a caption about celebrating its 15th anniversary. [S11]

The 2020 article adds three facts. At the ten-year party Trudo handed over the brand name De Ontdekfabriek, which it had owned. The venue had already expanded to Breda under the name De Uitvindfabriek. And the location in the Apparatenfabriek was uncertain from the start, because the building was at one point to be demolished, until a decision that it would stay for at least five more years. [S2] A national monument and a demolition plan sit oddly together, and I cannot explain it from these pages. [S2][S4]
How the venue describes its own method

Chris Voets, quoted in the 2020 article, says three quarters of the visitors are parents with children who come to play without a reservation, and that the venue is fun from about age five or six. He describes a sequence: first a film room for inspiration, then a workshop to make something, then a presentation of the result with tools that include a film studio. He says the basic concept is ten years old, that the venue is hands-on and uses few digital tools, and that it aims to teach the creative step that comes before programming. [S2] The E52 article records the same idea in his words: a child should get a first spark, and the point is doing and making, not education as such. [S10]

The foundation's statutes, as its site quotes them, set the mission as stimulating a positive attitude toward innovation, technology, science and creativity in children, with a sustainable society as a source of inspiration, by running a play-workshop and hands-on museum and offering cultural education programs. [S3] The site describes a storytelling approach in which children and young people are inspired to investigate, design, build and present in their own way. [S3]

On ages, the venue's own pages disagree with each other. Its profile page says 4 to 18. Its practical-information page gives an indication of 4 to 12 for a family adventure. Its 2025 to 2028 policy plan says 7 to 15. [S3][S12][S13] Voets's remark about age five or six is a fourth figure. I print no single range.
What the reports count

The policy plan for 2025 to 2028 says the foundation, established in 2009, reaches 30,000 children and young people a year, half through school and half in their free time with parents, and that it is a regional institution that works with Brainport, the culture-education center CultuurStation, the Dutch Design Foundation, the light festival GLOW and its sister institutions in Breda and Utrecht. [S13]

The 2025 report gives a table. It counts 231 public openings with a reach of 21,322, against a planned 165 with 21,875, and 249 school-bound activities with a reach of 13,734. Together with company events, the venue's physical reach was 21,957 in 250 offerings. The report says the foundation was open nine more days than the year before, that school visits from the city of Eindhoven rose from 37 to 50 percent of primary-school visits, that it organized 33 events, and that a children's light project for GLOW reached an estimated 15,000 children, a number kept out of the venue's visitor figures. It also reports a record turnover of just over 1.2 million euros and a surplus of 22,000 euros, which it put into a reserve in anticipation of extra work and relocation and housing costs in 2026 and after. [S14]

The report for 2024 calls that a record year for the number of activities, and says competition from a free ASML program for primary schools lowered school visits from that sector. [S11] The numbers are the foundation's own and have not been audited by me.
Work outside the building

The 2025 report shows how much of the work already happens elsewhere. The foundation says educational activities increasingly take place at school locations, reached by an electric bus, an electric cargo bike and bicycles with trailers, and that the number of pupils it served externally, in primary and secondary schools, rose by 82.5 percent. It gives a reason that bears on the building: visits from secondary and vocational schools to Torenallee 22 fell by 64 percent, and the report says these schools often want to serve very large groups at once, which touches the limits of what the foundation can offer well given its space, machines and materials. [S14] Among the 33 events it ran, the report names projector building at the Philips Stadion for a school challenge, car building at a discovery festival, and the final of a project called Jouw Eindhoven van de Toekomst in the Eindhoven city hall. [S14] It also reports that a program for young people aged 14 to 18 stalled in 2025 and that it applied with the Association of Science Centers for funding from ASML to restart work with that age group in 2026. [S14] That fits the plan's emphasis on a renovated space with a place for young people in their free time. [S13]
What the DDW archive shows

The DDW photo archive on Flickr holds Ontdekfabriek albums for 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2018, four albums with 56 photos in all by my October 7 count, and none after 2018. I could not reopen Flickr for this pass, so every count, credit and description in this section is second-hand. [S15] The 2015 album has 20 photos by Boudewijn Bollmann, the 2016 album 13 by Nick Bookelaar, and the 2017 and 2018 albums 11 and 12 by Max Kneefel. The pictures I viewed then show workbenches with drill presses, pendant lamps, a green-screen room, a container workshop at the entrance, a gear wall and soldering and laser-cutting benches. They show the equipment and the rooms and I say nothing about the visitors. [S15]

I found no organizer's account of what the venue did for DDW in those four years, and the foundation's reports for 2024 and 2025 do not mention DDW by name. The 2025 to 2028 plan names the Dutch Design Foundation, which organizes DDW, among its cultural partners. [S11][S13][S14] On the festival's 2026 location list, which I read on October 9, the Ontdekfabriek does not appear. Other organizations are listed at the same building: Community Square and Foundation We Are at Torenallee 22-04 and New Order of Fashion LAB at Torenallee 22-06. [S16] The list may not be complete, and I cannot say why the archive stops after 2018.
The move

The policy plan describes an Ontdekfabriek 2.0: a trilogy of new adventures, a renovated space, a creative breeding ground for young people and a rehousing that is necessary because the building the foundation occupies is to be renovated, planned with the owner Trudo and the area developer Park Strijp Beheer. [S13] The 2025 report says a permit has been applied for to build the 2.0 location in the Evoluonpark, on the Toekomst Campus, that there are agreements for an option to buy this circular building, that the province of North Brabant intends to lend part of the purchase price, and that the foundation is looking for more funding, including from the municipality. [S14]

Architecture trade press says what the building is. The Natural Pavilion, a nearly fully bio-based and demountable pavilion designed by DP6 for the Dutch government at the Floriade Expo 2022 in Almere, is to be moved to the park behind the Evoluon, on the spot where the Smartest Home of the Netherlands once stood, as the new home of the Ontdekfabriek. Because of a renovation the foundation must leave its current location in the Apparatenfabriek at the end of the year, and the ambition is to bring the building into use at the end of 2026. [S1][S17] Het Houtblad, a timber trade magazine, gives the same ambition and adds that the son of the Evoluon's architect Leo de Bever is advising on its position in the park. [S17]

So the 2026 edition of Dutch Design Week may be the last one that falls while the foundation is still at Torenallee 22. That is my inference from the move dates in the reports, and I have no source that says the foundation will or will not take part this year. [S1][S14]
What the record does not show

I do not know what the Ontdekfabriek did at DDW in 2015 to 2018, why the archive stops after 2018, or whether it takes part in 2026. I do not know when the move will actually happen, because the end of 2026 is an ambition stated in trade-press reports and I found no later confirmation. [S1][S17]

I do not know which age range to print, because the foundation itself gives three. I cannot explain why a national monument was once expected to be demolished. And I could not reopen Flickr, so the albums remain a second-hand record. [S2][S3][S12][S13][S15]

If you pass Torenallee 22 in DDW week, ask what a radio-equipment factory, a children's workshop and a pavilion rebuilt for its third life have in common, and which of the three you would keep a record of. [S1][S4]

title: Sectie-C: a switchboard factory, a creative district, and a city purchase in progress
subtitle: A former factory complex in Eindhoven's Tongelre district, followed through municipal documents, the owners' pages, local press and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: Sectie-C in Eindhoven, from a Philips-built complex and a Nolte and Stork factory to a Dutch Design Week venue and a planned city purchase.

sections.x: By the accounts I could find, parts of Sectie-C were built for Philips, the complex became an electrical factory in 1970, it stood empty after 2007, designers moved in from 2010, and in March 2026 the city of Eindhoven decided in principle to buy it. [S1][S2][S8][S11][S12]

It is easy to file Sectie-C with the Philips sites of Eindhoven, and just as easy to file it with the Stork factories of Hengelo. The record supports a little of each label and all of neither, so this essay follows the place through the documents that name it. I use public sources only: the city's area framework, the developer's pages, the tenants' own site, local and trade press, a design magazine and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. This essay reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe what the published pages say about it without claiming to have seen any of it. [S2][S7][S17]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. A hall that made switchboards and traffic signs, then held a swimming pool in a shipping container, is a good test of that habit. [S13]
The name is a land-registry term, and the neighbor is a landmark

A local history column in Groot Eindhoven says Sectie-C is a cadastral name for the terrain, meaning it comes from the land registry rather than from a company or a designer. [S8] The site lies in Tongelre, on the east side of the city. The city's area framework, adopted in November 2024, describes it as bounded by the Eindhoven to Venlo railway line, the TenneT high-voltage station, Urkhovenseweg and Daalakkersweg, next to the green of the Zeggen, about ten minutes by bike from the center. [S1][S2]

Next door is 't Karregat, which matters more to the story than a neighbor usually does. The framework says the neighborhood center was completed in 1973, designed by Frank van Klingeren (1919 to 1999), and originally put two primary schools, a library, a neighborhood center, a supermarket and a café under one roof. It sits in Herzenbroeken, a district built between 1968 and 1973 as a deliberate experiment in letting residents shape their surroundings. The city gives 't Karregat cultural-historical status and treats Sectie-C as a possible second heart for Tongelre. [S2] The tenants have taken up the connection themselves. Sectie-C's own pages list an outdoor film screening about 't Karregat on October 11, 2024, and an evening on December 9, 2024 on Van Klingeren's ideas and what Sectie-C might learn from them. [S7]

The sources do not agree on how big the place is, and the disagreement runs inside the city's own documents. NICE Developers calls it a former factory site of 6 hectares. The Open Eindhoven page puts the plan area at almost 8 hectares, and a trade-press report in March 2026 repeats "almost 8." The area framework itself says the total area is 11.3 hectares. [S1][S2][S3][S12] No source says what each figure includes, and I have not seen the boundary map that would show it, so I give none as the size of the place.

The address varies too. Dutch Design Week gives Daalakkersweg 2-14, This is Eindhoven's area tip gives 2-16, and the developer's plan site gives Daalakkersweg 2. [S4][S16][S17] A March 2026 trade report repeats 2-14. [S11] I use "Daalakkersweg" and no number.
Built for Philips, taken over by Nolte in 1970

The oldest layer of the story comes from one source. A local history column published in Groot Eindhoven on October 5, 2024 says parts of the complex were built for the Installatie en Service Bureau of Philips. It says that in 1970 the firm Nolte Elektrotechnische en Mechanische Industrie, until then at Tongelresestraat 209, took the complex over, settled there and expanded it, making switchboards, lampposts and traffic signs. [S8] The city's own framework points the same way without using the word Philips for the site itself: it asks for landmarks that keep alive the memory of Stork Nolte and the related industry around Philips. [S2] No other source I opened mentions the Philips service bureau, so I treat that part as one local historian's account that I could not confirm.

Dating the buildings is harder than naming the owner. Open Eindhoven says the buildings were put up in the 1970s and 1980s. An undated student presentation hosted on a Dutch teaching platform says the buildings date from around 1970. [S1][S18] Those two statements fit a complex that grew in stages after Nolte arrived, which is also what the local column says Nolte did. They do not fit buildings that all predate 1970, and none of these sources dates an individual hall.
Stork, a spelling problem and a closing in 2007

The step from Nolte to Stork has a contemporary record. On June 14, 1989 the Reformatorisch Dagblad reported that Nolte Groep BV of Eindhoven would almost certainly be taken over by Verenigde Machinefabrieken Stork NV. The report gives Nolte a turnover of about 225 million guilders and about 1,900 employees, says the talks had been going for about five weeks, and quotes a board member saying it would still take a few months. Nolte was to operate inside Stork as a separate group in industrial services. [S9] The report is about the company and says nothing about the Daalakkersweg site.

After that the chain is thinner. The Groot Eindhoven column says Nolte became Stork-Nolte and was then taken over by Strukton, and that production at the site stopped in 2007. [S8] A trade-press report in February 2025 says Stork Nolte, "later VDL," made switchboards, lampposts and traffic signs there until 2007. [S10] These two accounts name different later owners. I opened VDL's group history page and found no mention of Stork or Nolte, so it settles nothing. [S20] Both agree on 2007, and the city's framework independently dates the closing of the Stork Nolte factory to 2007. [S1][S2]

Even the company's full name wobbles. NICE Developers writes Stork-Nolte Elektrotechnische en Mechanische Industrie, and the city's framework writes "Elektronische" in the same place. [S2][S3] The 1989 report calls Nolte an electrotechnical company and says its electrotechnical and electronic activities would fit Stork's, so both words have a footing. [S9] I use "electrotechnical," following the developer and the newspaper, and I cannot say which form the company registered.
Empty after 2007, occupied from 2010

The city's framework gives the shortest account of what came next: from 2010 new entrepreneurs settled on the old industrial site, and a handful of young artists and designers took over the property that had been left behind, drawn by how much could be made of the empty spaces. The framework says the name of the place became Sectie-C. [S2] The tenants' own site agrees on 2010 as the start of the development into a creative ecosystem. [S7] The Groot Eindhoven column says a designers' collective saw the possibilities in 2010. [S8]

The most vivid account is an interview on the developer's news site with Niels Hoebers, a stop-motion animator and artist whose studio has been at Sectie-C for 16 years. He says his group had been in a hall on Heezerweg, had to leave, and saw possibilities in what he calls the forgotten area, the former Stork Nolte location. He describes it as a playground for adults and says the group began as a collective, Collaboration O. [S5] That is one tenant's recollection in an interview published by the developer, so I treat it as testimony and not as a settled history. It fits the 2015 description from Core77, which called Collaboration O a shared studio space housing over a dozen young designers. [S14]
Design Week: 2011 or 2012?

This is Eindhoven says Sectie-C's Dutch Design Week role started in 2011 as an accidental counterpart of the Design Week at Strijp-S, and that it has grown to more than 25,000 visitors each year. [S15] The Groot Eindhoven column says the tenants together became a main location in 2011 and had about 25,000 visitors "then." [S8]

A contemporary report complicates the date. On October 26, 2012 the Dutch technology site Bright called Sectie C "the new location" and the biggest surprise of that year's Design Week, where even the taxi driver had to search. The reporter places it well east of the center and describes a large gate with yellow letters, a jumble of buildings and design studios, a five-meter lamp, a swimming pool in a container and a hot tub over an open fire. Sectie C is described as a breeding ground of about 80 small businesses, with the studios of Floris Wubben and Nacho Carbonell, an exhibition by the Royal College of Art from London, free design rides from the city, and opening only after 4 p.m. so that the studios could work first. [S13]

Two readings fit both sources. Sectie-C could have had a small first presence in 2011 that the 2012 reporter did not know about, or the 2011 date may be a looser reconstruction made later. I found no 2011 program, so I cannot choose. The official photo archive does not help, because its Sectie-C albums begin in 2015. [S19]
What the archive and the tenants' pages show, year by year

The Dutch Design Week Flickr account holds Sectie-C albums for eight editions between 2015 and 2024, nine albums with 402 photos in all. I read those album pages for the earlier version of this research on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass, so the photo counts and photographer names below carry that date. [S19] Where I can, I set them beside what Sectie-C and the press said the same year.

**2015.** The album has 49 photos, with fifteen titled 91_OXI. The photographers named in titles are Iris Rijskamp, Tommy Köhlbrugge and Boudewijn Bollmann. [S19] Core77's report of November 16, 2015 most likely explains the title: "OXI" was a group exhibition at Club-C, curated by Justine Kontou, with designers whose studios were nearby. The photo captions name Nacho Carbonell, Tessa Koot, Victor Sonna, Sabine Marcelis with Brit van Nerven, and Sander Wassink with Luuk van den Broek. Core77 also shows Studio Plott, Fleur Hulleman's "Soft Ceramics" in a small group show called "Behind the Screens," and a group exhibition called "Change of State." [S14]

**2016 and 2017.** The 2016 album is the largest, with 112 photos, 19 of them titled 94_SECTIEC and some dated October 26, 2016. The 2017 album has 47, with titles dated October 25, 2017. The photographers named are Rijskamp and Köhlbrugge for 2016, and Max Kneefel and Köhlbrugge for 2017. [S19] The tenants' own site hosts a press set labeled DDW 2017. [S7]
**2018.** The album has 31 photos, all credited in their titles to Max Kneefel and dated October 20, 23 and 28, 2018. [S19]

**2019.** The album has 25 photos. Sectie-C's own page lists 18 items for October 19 to 27, 2019, including an exhibition on the Swiss watch brand Enicar, a project by Florian de Visser called Tourist-Site-Seeing with a Hidden Gem Shop, Wikkelhouse, and a rug collection by Studio Daniel Costa. [S7][S19]

**2020.** The archive's album is titled Oost-C, not Sectie-C, and holds 10 photos by Kneefel. [S19] The tenants' site resolves the name. For October 17 to 25, 2020 it lists "Living Space," where, in its words, Oost-C presents itself in the large hall of Carte Blanche on Sectie-C. Studio Speciaal, described as the only design studio within Oost-C, curated it, with work by Gijs van Bon, Tijs Rooijakkers and Frits Achten, and the arrangement of objects changed through the week. The page also lists "Papercut," shown in a virtual exhibition space, from October 17 to December 31, 2020. [S7] So Oost-C is a name used on the site for a group exhibiting inside Sectie-C. I could not check whether the 10 archive photos show this exhibition.

**2021.** There are two albums, VANTOT with 35 photos and a general one with 13. [S19] The tenants' page for "Press Play: Dutch Design Week" gives October 16 to 24, 2021, with opening hours of 11:00 to 20:00 until October 23 and 11:00 to 18:00 on October 24. It describes Sectie-C as studios of more than 100 designers, artists and photographers and as a main location with more than 25,000 visitors a year. [S7]

**2022 and 2023.** The 2022 album has 86 photos credited to about.today and Max Kneefel, with CollaborationO-titled photos that carry the names Fleur Hulleman and Willem van Hooff. [S19] The titles do not say whether those two names are makers or photographers. Two other pages lean toward makers. Core77 showed a ceramics work by Fleur Hulleman at Sectie C in 2015, and Sectie-C's page lists Willem van Hooff as an exhibitor, with Olga Flor, in The Pool from May 6 to 24, 2022. [S7][S14] That is a lean and not a proof, because the titles themselves do not say. I found no 2023 album in the archive, although the album list I could see in the earlier pass was incomplete, and Sectie-C's list of past events has no entry dated 2023 and none for Design Week 2022. [S7][S19]

**2024.** The archive's album has only 4 photos, by Almicheal Fraay. [S19] Sectie-C's page has a heading for Design Week 2024, October 19 to 27, titled "The Last Edition: MAYBE," with no description in the text I read. [S7] A December 2024 exhibition called Undercurrents, hosted at Sectie-C, calls the site artist spaces that will soon undergo residential development. [S7]

**2025.** The archive listing as I read it on October 7, 2026 has no Sectie-C album. [S19] The tenants' own list for October 18 to 25, 2025 has 31 items, including a run of shows in Punt-C, several Open O studio presentations, a collaboration with 1m2 Collective, the Kunstacademie Maastricht and Rietveld alumni. [S7] That is the clearest warning in the record. The week with the most detailed tenant listing is the week the official photo archive does not cover, so the archive shows what a photographer was sent to shoot and not how busy the site was.

**2026.** Dutch Design Week lists Sectie-C open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 25, 2026. [S17] The tenants' page lists 31 items for the week. They include "A Home of Many Addresses," in which current and former residents share fifteen years of stories around the mailbox, an audio tour of listening points scanned by QR code, a project called Flavors of Sectie-C that archives the terrain's sensory memory, and a second "Radicale Wegbereiders" program with a local activity center. For neighbors, two guided tours are listed on October 17 and October 24, at 11:00 in Dutch and 15:00 in English, and a Design Week ticket is required. [S7][S16]
Between the Design Weeks

The tenants do not wait for October. Their list shows a "Design Open" in December 2020 that joined more than ten Eindhoven designers and locations, including Piet Hein Eek, Kazerne, Kiki&Joost, Sectie-C and NRE, after the fairs they would normally show at fell away. [S7] Later editions are listed for June 2021, December 2021, April 2022 and November 2024. The first Atelier-Sale was held on July 19, 2020 and drew on tenants who the page says number more than 250 on the former Stork-Nolte terrain. [S7]

The place also keeps small institutions of its own. The Pool is described on the site as the cultural clubhouse of Sectie-C. Anker Studio, a rehearsal and recording space, held the fourth edition of its Ankerfest on August 23, 2025. [S7] In an interview on the developer's news site, the three founders of Anker Studio say about 150 musicians rehearse there each week, which is their figure and not an audited count. [S6] "The Window" is a two-month artist residency on the theme of ownership. In 2025 it hosted a residency that ended with the launch of a prototype called Sectie-C Contacts on July 18, 2025, then another that ran from August 17 to October 12. [S7]

The organization behind this is two bodies. Vereniging Sectie-C represents tenants and subtenants toward the landlord, the foundation and the municipality. Stichting Sectie-C says its goal is to grow, refine and secure the creative ecosystem over the long term, and it publishes annual reports for 2023 to 2025, which I did not open. [S7]
1,300 homes, a 19,500 square meter promise and a purchase in principle

The ownership story is the part of the record that moved most recently, and the old version of the question, who owns Sectie-C, now has an answer with a caveat. The city's framework says that since 2019 Focus on Impact has been mostly the owner, and that it owns about 90 percent of the area. It also says the municipality owns no land there beyond the public space around the plan area, so its role is facilitating. [S2] Open Eindhoven names the owner and developer as TBFOS, short for Ten Brinke en Focus on Sectie-C. [S1] NICE Developers says Focus acquired the complex in 2019 to safeguard its value as a breeding ground. [S3]

The planning timeline starts with the city adopting the area framework in November 2024. On February 24, 2025, Focus on Impact and Ten Brinke announced the redevelopment, with at least 1,300 homes and 30,000 square meters of business space. [S1][S10] A sketch design was presented to neighbors and stakeholders in April 2025, and a preliminary design was presented at two participation meetings on October 27 and November 12, 2025. [S1] The municipality's framework sets a floor of 19,500 square meters of creative workspace. The developer's plan site repeats about 19,500 square meters of creative breeding ground, next to about 5,800 square meters of facilities, 426 student units and about 72 percent affordable housing. [S2][S4]

The city's own page gives different figures from the developer's. It says 1,400 new homes, 85 percent affordable. The developer says 1,300 homes, about 72 percent affordable. The framework's own range is 1,100 to 1,400 homes. [S1][S2][S4] I cannot tell whether these are different versions of the plan or different definitions of affordable, and I report both.

The step with the most consequence came in March 2026. A trade report of March 12, 2026 says the college of mayor and aldermen took a decision in principle to buy Sectie-C from TBFOS and to keep renting out the space, at an average rent of 85 euros per square meter of gross floor area, excluding VAT, at 2025 prices. Two other scenarios were dropped, one in which TBFOS stays owner and rents for up to 15 years and one in which the foundation becomes owner. The report gives a 50-year operating period, a first-year shortfall of about 500,000 euros and a positive result of about 600,000 euros at the end. [S11] A second report the next day says the foundation would become main tenant and handle subletting and management, that the proposal answers a council motion of October 1, 2024 on securing creative workspace, and that 250,000 euros is set aside for the next steps. It also records that tenants are cautiously positive, worried about crowding, and unsure whether all kinds of makers can be housed, and that tenants had asked for tall spaces for mezzanines which make buildings more expensive. [S12] Earlier, in October 2024, the tenants' association and the foundation's members had said 19,500 square meters was too little and that at least 25,000 would be needed. [S8]

This was a decision in principle. I found no source showing that the purchase has been completed, and the developer's plan page, read on October 10, 2026, presents the project as a Ten Brinke and Focus on Impact development without mentioning a municipal purchase. [S4]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Philips or Stork.** The label depends on which decade you ask about. One local historian says parts were built for Philips, the 1989 newspaper shows Stork buying Nolte, and the city says the site's industry was Stork Nolte and related industry around Philips. I give each its own era and rest the Philips claim on a single source. [S2][S8][S9]
**Who ran the factory at the end.** Strukton (Groot Eindhoven) against VDL (PropertyNL). Not settled, and the 2007 closing date is the only point on which they agree. [S8][S10]
**How big it is.** 6 hectares (NICE Developers), almost 8 (Open Eindhoven, repeated by Stadszaken) and 11.3 (the area framework). I could not reconcile them and use none. [S1][S2][S3][S12]

**How many people work there.** Sectie-C's site says more than 250 businesses and uses "more than 100" for designers, artists and photographers in its Design Week pitch. The city's framework says about 280 tenants. This is Eindhoven's main page says over 250 artists, designers, musicians, writers and artisans and its area tip says more than 100 creatives. A 2012 report counted about 80 small businesses. [S1][S2][S7][S13][S15][S16] Because the city's number is from a planning document about tenants and the "more than 100" comes from promotional text about Design Week, I use about 280 for tenants and 100 only as the tenants' own Design Week claim.
**The 2020 album.** Settled enough to use: the tenants' site places Oost-C inside Sectie-C in 2020. [S7]

**The start year.** The city and the tenants agree on 2010 for the new users. 2011 for Design Week is attributed to This is Eindhoven and a local column, but a 2012 report calls Sectie C new. Not settled. [S7][S8][S13][S15]

**Visitors.** The 25,000 figure appears on This is Eindhoven and on the tenants' 2021 page, so it is the tenants' own claim, repeated by the city's tourism site. [S7][S15] An undated student presentation gives about 350,000 visitors a year, which no other source supports. I did not use it. [S18]
What the record does not show

I have not found a building-by-building history. Nothing I opened dates the Philips service bureau structures, says which halls Nolte added, or says how many square meters were built when. The council's March 2026 letter is known to me only through two trade-press reports, and the council information site timed out when I tried to open a related letter, so I did not read any council document directly. A cooperation agreement between the municipality, the developer and Sectie-C is mentioned by one of those reports and I have not seen it. [S11][S12]

I cannot say who operated the factory at the end, or whether Stork-Nolte was one business or several by 2007. I have no source for what happened to the Nolte brand name after the 1989 deal. I did not open the foundation's annual reports, and I did not re-read the Flickr albums, so every photo count and name in the year-by-year section carries its October 7 date. [S7][S19]

I do not know why the archive has no album for 2023 or 2025, what the 10 photos of 2020 show, or whether 'Sectie C' as a land-registry term can be traced to a registry entry. I have not seen the registry itself. [S8]

If you go to Sectie-C during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at what the signs and the guided tours say about the buildings, and ask what each one is built on. When a place has had a Philips-built service complex, an electrical factory, an artists' district and a prospective city landlord, which of its names would you put on the wall? [S2][S7][S8]
