title: Stadhuisplein: a city hall that took thirty years to finish, a courthouse turned design house, and a square Design Week keeps borrowing
subtitle: What municipal brochures, local press, council papers and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive show about Eindhoven's city hall, the former courthouse beside it, and the square between them
description: Eindhoven city hall, the former courthouse and Stadhuisplein, from a 1938 competition to Dutch Design Week 2026, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: Eindhoven's city hall was the subject of a design competition in 1938, was opened by Queen Juliana on September 18, 1969, and the square in front of it was already a Dutch Design Week venue by 2009. [S1][S2][S11]

The official Dutch Design Week photo archive holds albums for this place in 2015, 2016 and 2025, and it is tempting to take those three years as the shape of the record. The wider sources say otherwise. The square carried a Brainport Greenhouse for the Dutch Design Awards in 2009, the building next to the city hall was a design house for years, and in 2026 the same building is a Design Week location again. [S6][S7][S11][S12] This essay follows the three places, the city hall, the former courthouse and the square, through the architecture center's heritage writing, council papers, local press and Dutch Design Week's own pages. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe what its pages list without claiming to have seen any of it. [S8]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it is used for now. Here the building at Stadhuisplein 3 has been a court, a design house and a remembrance center within about sixty years, which makes it a good place to practice. [S3][S4]
Three places that share one name

Stadhuisplein is the square, and the city hall stands on it. A municipal notice from January 2026 places the residents' service desk, the Inwonersplein, in the city hall at Stadhuisplein 1. [S5] The former district courthouse sits at Stadhuisplein 3, diagonally behind the city hall beside the Dommel river, and has been called the Designhuis since 2007 and Het Hornemann Huis in recent years. [S3][S4] Dutch Design Week lists that building as "Het Hornemann Huis (voormalig Designhuis)." [S6] I keep the three names apart because the archive, the programs and the history all do.
The city hall took more than thirty years

The architecture center's Open Monumentendag brochure of 2020, written by René Erven and Peter Thoben, gives the fullest account I found. Eindhoven merged with its neighbors on January 1, 1920, and the council decided on December 28, 1928 to build a new city hall on a vacant field called the Studentenwei between the Wal and the Stratumseind. From 1929 the city's government used a large villa in Stratum as a temporary seat. [S1]

A public competition followed in 1938. Out of 110 entries four were picked, and a jury report dated May 11, 1939 favored the proposal of the Leiden architect J.A. (Jan) van der Laan, mainly for how it fitted the city. On April 16, 1940 the council approved his worked-out design, which carried the name Broleto. The war stopped the work. [S1][S2] After the war a part of the plan was built first as an emergency secretariat building. The first pile went in on August 2, 1949, the first stone was laid on October 18, 1950, and the mayor opened the building on January 19, 1952. It is a three-story brick building in a traditional style, and it now serves as a court building. [S1]

The main building changed a great deal in the meantime. Van der Laan finished a revised design in 1956, then told the council in 1957 that the 1939 concept might no longer be wise, and in 1958 presented a far more modern sketch with a ten-story office tower and a square-shaped ceremonial block around a central hall. The first pile of that building went in on November 4, 1965. [S1][S2] Van der Laan died in 1966, and the building was finished by his colleagues Kirch, Hermans and Van der Eerden, with the Eindhoven architect Hans Thomassen as project staff member. [S1] Queen Juliana opened it on September 18, 1969, during the commemoration of 25 years since the city's liberation, and the mayor who received her had refused to approve the building plans in 1956 as minister of construction. [S1][S2] The next day, September 19, 1969, the Van Abbemuseum opened an exhibition with the model of the Cityplan by Van den Broek and Bakema, which the architecture center reads as a companion statement of the same modern course. [S2]

Four artists made the monumental works inside and on the building: Ad Dekkers (the wall relief in the council chamber), Peter Struycken (the tile relief near the lifts), André Volten (a hanging sculpture of 1,500 square meters of moving steel plates in the citizens' hall) and Arthur Spronken (the bronze figure on the facade). The carillon of 45 bells was first played at the opening. [S1][S2] The building was renovated in 2001 by architecten|en|en with buro Staal Christensen, whose main change was a glass roof, and again by the !MPULS alliance, delivered at the start of 2020, with a green entrance under the tower and the residents' desk moved back from the Stadskantoor on the Wal. The brochure says 95 percent of the materials released in the rebuild were reused. [S1][S2]
The square: a field, a grid and a stage

The ground has its own history. The brochure says the Studentenwei lay where the city moat branched off the Dommel, near the Stratum watermill that had been in use since the fourteenth century. In 1812 a textile manufacturer bought the mill and built two factory buildings called Den Bouw, and the brochure says the first industrial steam engine in the Netherlands went into use there in 1820. The factory burned in 1896 and its ruins were cleared in 1928. [S1] I treat the steam engine as the brochure's claim and did not check it elsewhere.

The square in front of the finished secretariat building was left as lawn for years. The Liberation Monument, designed by the sculptor Paul Gregoire with a stone surround by Van der Laan, was unveiled on September 18, 1954 and later moved about 50 meters to its present corner. The brochure dates the move to 1965 and the architecture center's own walking route dates it to 1969. [S1][S2] The present square was delivered in 1997. It measures about 50 by 50 meters and is divided in squares of about 10 meters, a grid that echoes the 1952 layout of concrete tiles, and five specially designed lamp posts stand for the five districts added to the city since the 1920 merger. [S1][S2] Light and art were the design principles, light because of Eindhoven's reputation as a city of lighting innovation, and art through a route called De Rode Loper, which the Van Abbemuseum started by inviting the American artists Lawrence Weiner and Matt Mullican to propose ideas. [S2]

One object on the square is easy to miss. Gerrit Rietveld designed a bus shelter that doubled as an advertising column for the city in 1962. Only one was built, around 1965 on the Hendrik Staetslaan, and it was moved to its current place in the 1990s (the brochure says 1990). [S1][S2]
The courthouse that became the Designhuis

The building at Stadhuisplein 3 was designed as a district court by Johannes (Jo) Kruger for the national government's buildings agency, with design work in 1958 and 1959. It was finished in 1964, cost about two million guilders, a quarter of which went into the interior, and stood empty for months because the Danish furniture had been ordered too late. It was officially opened on May 21, 1965. [S3][S4] Inside, a large atrium carried a brick mosaic of 140 square meters by Theo van Amstel showing the biblical negotiation over the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah, which the Eindhovens Dagblad of the time called a symbol of modern case law. Judges and detainees shared one route through the building, while visitors, witnesses and counsel came through the central hall. [S3]

The court was abolished with the district courts in 2002, and in 2007 the building opened as the Designhuis after a conversion by the architect Peer van Ling. The mosaic disappeared behind a white wall. [S1][S3] The brochure names Lidewij Edelkoort, then head of the Design Academy Eindhoven, as the driving force. [S1] The house was a Design Week venue from the start of its life. In October 2009 Bright reported that it showed "Talent 2009," Edelkoort's selection of 175 objects and installations by 2009 graduates of thirty European institutions, open until November 30, 2009. The same article reports that the municipality, the only grant-giver, had announced the house's closing in July and then let it organize two final exhibitions, and that the staff contracts would not be renewed after two years under Edelkoort. [S11]

The money story is in council papers. A party's published questions of February 1, 2013 and the college's answers say the municipality signed a five-year lease with Stichting Designhuis in 2007, that the co-financing from others fell short so the municipality became the only financier, and that from 2010 the municipality covered the building costs while others funded the content. A Vitra exhibition called "Hidden Heroes" was bought in for October 2010 to May 2011, and from summer 2011 the design institute Premsela funded exhibitions while Capital D, which the questioners describe as the organizer of Dutch Design Week, directed the volunteers. [S12] The questioner's figures, including a rent debt of 210,000 euros, come from a political party and I cannot confirm them. The college's answer says only that the remaining debt was booked as a doubtful receivable. [S12]

After the design years the house held the local broadcaster Studio 040 and the Stichting Cultuur Eindhoven, per the 2020 brochure. [S1] The Hornemann Huis, a remembrance center that tells the story of two Jewish brothers from Eindhoven murdered by the Nazis, moved in recently, according to the architecture center. Its article announces Open Monumentendag openings on Saturday, September 14 and Sunday, September 15, a weekend pairing that fits 2024, though the page text gives no year. [S3] The Open Monumentendag entry for 2026 calls the building a municipal monument and lists it open on September 12 and 13, 2026. [S4]
What Design Week has done here, as far as the record shows

The earliest record I found is from 2009, when Bright lists the winning work of the Dutch Design Awards at the "Brainport Greenhouse" on Stadhuisplein, open 11:00 to 22:00 and until 20:00 on Sunday, October 25. [S11] In 2013 a blog recap describes a display of XL posters with self-portraits made by parents and their children on the square. [S13]

For 2015 the evidence is the photo archive. The Stadhuis album has 14 photos and the Stadhuisplein album 16, and the photo pages credit Sjoerd Eickmans. I read those album pages on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass. Inside the city hall they show wall posters of faces with captions, a table of small objects and a wooden clock. On the square they show a large steel wheel of colored balls, glass pavilions, a shipping container shop signed Kunstblok, a sign reading Treasure Light and a poster reading Design for Kids. Many show children, so I describe objects only. [S19] I found no program text for these items, and no source says the glass pavilions were the Awards greenhouse of earlier years. [S19]

The 2016 record is fuller. IO+ reported on October 24, 2016 that the municipality's design show was in the city hall during Design Week, that Mieke Fiers of the social design office Tante Netty designed it, and that it played on the verb "Eindhoof." The show covered five themes, including the NRE terrain and a game for newcomers, and let visitors weigh in on a redesign of the Vestdijk. [S15] The photos show stacked wooden walls with panels titled Fun op straat and Slim licht and a window reading Eindhoof je mee? [S19] Outside, VPRO's tips of October 23, 2016 put the Solar Cabin by Bram Zondag and Arjan de Nooijer on the square, one of six winners of a competition called A Home Away From Home from the asylum seeker reception agency COA and the Rijksbouwmeester, Floris Alkemade. [S14]

For 2025 DDW's program page for touching cellulose_SENSE OF CRAFTING gives City Hall Square as the location and October 18 to 26, 2025 as the dates, free of charge, with students from TU Delft and TH Köln and visitors building a wooden EduCrafting Pavilion, with two daily introduction sessions. The archive album has 21 photos credited to Cleo Goossens in the titles. [S9][S19]

For 2026 the picture is double. Dutch Design Week lists Het Hornemann Huis, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 and free, with "Objects on Trial," a group exhibition by Bureau.parso and Meeseek in the former courthouse. The program text says the show uses the building's rooms of judgment, observation and waiting as a curatorial frame, with an Examination Room of samples and prototypes. [S6][S7] The program text does not mention the museum, and I draw no connection. On the square, DDW lists FIELD by Isabel + Helen, a wind-powered interactive installation of turbines on wheels, among eight large-scale installations that are free to visit. [S8] The locations list also names a Raadzaal, the council chamber, at Stadhuisplein 1 and a "City Hall Square" entry. [S20]

The organizer describes why the square gets this use. Its 2025 call for Grand Projects names Stadhuisplein, Markt and Ketelhuisplein as high-visibility locations and calls them key squares that attract tens of thousands of visitors. [S10] That is the organizer's description and I read it as one.
A square about to change

The city council adopted a master plan for the public space on September 30, 2025, which the project page says will turn the stony surroundings into a green, lively place over about ten years. The plan builds on a vision by Bygg Architecture & Design from November 2023 and aims to lead a branch of the Dommel across the square as a "Binnendommel" and to link green roofs of the surrounding buildings by four gates and bridges into a public lookout called the Belvedère. It prefers an underground link between garages that would remove the garage entrance, so cars no longer cross the square. Large events such as carnival, King's Day and a PSV championship celebration stay possible, with first estimates of 20 percent fewer visitors for King's Day and 25 percent fewer for the celebration. [S16] Omroep Brabant put the last celebration at 19,000 supporters and the new capacity at about 15,000. [S17] On August 25, 2026 it became known that the permit for Citywall, three mixed buildings on the north side with 330 homes, had been granted. [S18]

The idea of the square as an event stage is older than the plan. At a meeting of the architecture center on October 1, 2019, the city's supervising architect Winy Maas called the future square the "new dance floor" of Eindhoven. [S1][S2] The 2025 and 2026 Design Week programs fit that stage, but no source says they were chosen with it in mind.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

**Who designed the city hall.** Short accounts say "Jan van der Laan." The architecture center's brochure and walking route give the fuller account: his Leiden office designed it, he died in 1966, and colleagues finished it. I describe it as designed by his office and completed by his successors. [S1][S2]
**When the Liberation Monument moved.** 1965 (brochure) against 1969 (walking route). Not settled. [S1][S2]

**When the courthouse became a municipal monument.** The architecture center's walking route of 2020 says it became one "this spring." The municipal gazette of January 28, 2026 says the college decided in 2015 to designate Stadhuisplein 3, that the decisions were sent to interested parties but by mistake not published for third parties, and that publication in 2026 repairs this. [S2][S5] The gazette is the primary text and I follow it for the 2015 decision. I cannot say whether the 2020 date refers to a second step. [S2][S5]

**Spelling and dates of the artists.** The architect of the courthouse is Kruger in the brochure and Krüger in the walking route, and the mosaic's artist Theo van Amstel is given as 1927 to 2010 in one and 1927 to 2004 in the other. I use Kruger and give no death year. [S1][S2]

**Whether the archive's years are the venue's years.** The archive holds albums for 2015, 2016 and 2025, and the sources above show Design Week on the square in 2009, 2013 and 2026 and in the Designhuis in 2009. The archive is therefore a sample of what photographers shot, and not a record of use. [S11][S13][S19]
What the record does not show

I did not find a program for the 2015 items, a building-by-building account of the square before 1952, or a source for the Awards greenhouse in any year other than 2009. I did not find DDW programs at the city hall or on the square for 2010 to 2012, 2014 and 2017 to 2023, and the archive's single 2024 photo with Stadhuisplein in its title is not enough to say what it showed. [S19]

I cannot say how often Design Week used the Designhuis after 2011, which hand the city hall's show took in other years, or whether the 2015 glass pavilions were a greenhouse. I have not seen the council's own master plan, because the municipal website answered one request with an access refusal and I stopped using that host. I know it only through a project page of the Open Eindhoven site and the press. [S16][S17]

If you stand on the square during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at the three buildings that face each other and ask which of them was built for the function it has now. When a courthouse becomes a design house, a design house becomes a remembrance center, and the remembrance center hosts an exhibition about judging objects, which of those uses would you say the building was made for? [S4][S6][S7]

title: Strijp-S: a Philips company district, a Forbidden City, and a design week that filled it
subtitle: The former Philips factory district in Eindhoven, followed through the national monument register, planning research, the owners' history and ten editions of official Dutch Design Week photo albums
description: Strijp-S in Eindhoven, from a 1916 Philips glass factory and the Forbidden City to Dutch Design Week, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: Philips began building on Strijp-S in 1916, decided in 1999 to leave it, sold it in a deal that two sources date to 2002 and two others date to 2004, and by 2007 Dutch Design Week was already using its Klokgebouw. [S1][S3][S6][S7][S10]

The common shorthand for Strijp-S is "the old Philips site that became a design district," and each half of that sentence hides a lot of paperwork. The site was a planned industrial landscape with a designer, a grid and a building code. It was closed by fences for decades. It was sold in stages, redeveloped in a partnership that nearly collapsed, and opened to the public in part through temporary uses before the permanent ones arrived. This essay follows that sequence through public sources: the national monument register, an urban-development research essay, the owners' history page, heritage and trade writing, contemporary press and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list. [S12]
I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For Strijp-S the register answers that question with unusual precision. [S2]
A planned industrial landscape, south of the railway

The Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed describes the "Philipscomplex Strijp S" as a rectangular site south of the railway line. It says the need for a glass factory of Philips's own during the First World War was the first push toward a new complex, laid out next to the existing Philips buildings at Emmasingel and Philipsdorp. The layout was developed by A.I.J. de Broekert, who worked for Philips, and applied a high degree of rationality. From the 1920s the site was filled systematically with industrial buildings. [S2]

The register's description of the protected buildings is blunt about method. They are mostly three-aisle, multi-story factory buildings with a wide central street, built with a reinforced concrete skeleton, identical steel profiles from Krupp, pumice-concrete roof cassettes and long horizontal bands of daylight, a type developed by Philips. The register values the complex as an example of the industry's social and economic development, as a record of how large-scale industrial high-rise developed, and as a rare coherent industrial landscape. [S2] That is the national government's reading, and it explains why the planners later treated the buildings as the backbone of the district.

The register also settles some dates that other sources blur. The Klokgebouw was built in two phases, in 1928 and 1929, to a design by de Broekert of the Philips engineering bureau, and includes a factory water tower. [S3] The Veemgebouw was built in 1942 by the same engineering bureau and has expressionist elements. [S16] Three multi-story factory buildings on the Leidingstraat, the "industrial boulevard" later called the Hoge Rug, date from 1930, 1929 and 1927, also to designs by de Broekert. [S17] The Strijp-S owners' page says the Klokgebouw dates from 1929, a heritage article by Jan van Oudheusden gives 1928, and the architecture center's walking route says the Veemgebouw was finished in 1943. [S1][S5][S8] I follow the register for all three.
What the owners say about the first decades

Strijp-S's own history page gives a plain timeline. Gerard Philips began making light bulbs in a small factory on the Emmasingel in 1891. Philips had its first Strijp-S factory built in 1916, a glass factory making glass balloons for lamps, so it would not depend on suppliers, followed by a cardboard factory, a gas factory and the Physics Laboratory, the NatLab. From 1928 the pace increased: the Klokgebouw, a factory for Philite, the Philips name for bakelite, then the appliance factories of the Hoge Rug, an engine room, a boiler house and the Veemgebouw. The page says Philips became completely self-sufficient on the site, "from raw material to finished product." [S1]

The NatLab date varies by source. The architecture center says the physicist Gilles Holst was appointed head of the laboratory in 1914 and that the research department moved into its own building in 1923, designed by Dirk Roosenburg. [S4] Van Oudheusden dates the laboratory building to 1922. [S8] I use 1923 and name the architecture center. The laboratory had a long reach. Strijp-S's history page says Queen Wilhelmina addressed the Dutch East Indies by wireless radio from the lab, that Einstein visited, and that the researcher Dick Raaijmakers took the first steps toward synthesizers there and made electronic music with them, a project it says Philips did not pursue. [S1] The European Physical Society lists "The Philips NatLab, Eindhoven (2017)" among its Historic Sites. [S21]

The site was large, and the sources do not agree on how large. Strijp-S and the architecture center say 27 hectares, the Inventing Europe essay by Hans Schippers says 25 and Van Oudheusden says "about thirty." [S1][S4][S8][S9] I give 27 hectares and attribute it.

The district was also a target. On Sunday, December 6, 1942, the Royal Air Force bombed the Philips factories on the Emmasingel and on Strijp-S in the raid known as the Sinterklaas bombing, code name Operation Oyster. The national committee for commemoration says the raid was flown by 94 aircraft, that sixteen did not return, and that the monument unveiled on December 6, 2011 remembers about 150 civilian victims, since many bombs hit shops, homes and churches. [S22] A local history site puts the civilian toll at about 138 dead and 161 injured, says 14 aircraft were lost, and says production was running again after about half a year. [S23] The two accounts differ on the numbers and I give both. The raid shows that the factories were a wartime asset of the occupied city as well as a company campus.

In the 1970s, the owners' page says, some 10,000 people worked on the site every day, and Eindhoven nicknamed it the Forbidden City because fences and barriers surrounded it and you only got in with a pass. [S1] Schippers adds that Philips, with its own schools, sports clubs and cultural institutions, was often called a state within the city. [S9] Van Oudheusden repeats a story that the Torenallee boulevard was laid out as a sightline so that Frits Philips could see the Philips light tower from his house. He writes that it "appears" to be so, and I treat it as a legend. [S8]
Leaving, selling and the argument about 2002 and 2004

The departure was gradual. The architecture center places the turning point in the late 1980s, when Philips ran into economic trouble, and says that under Jan Timmer from 1990 the "Operation Centurion" reorganization closed factories and sold business units, and even the head office moved to Amsterdam. [S4] A research essay by Simon van Zoest of the TU Delft program on urban transformation says Philips decided in 1999 to move its activities and that VolkerWessels won the tender for the area together with a pension fund investor. After the crisis that followed 2001 the investor withdrew, the whole transformation was in doubt, the municipality joined because it feared decay, and a public-private partnership of the municipality and VolkerWessels was born. [S6] The renovation-oriented site Herbestemming adds that Philips organized a tender in 2001 and that the best plan came from VolkerWessels. [S5]

On the sale, each source is right about a different step. Strijp-S's history page says that in 2002 VolkerWessels and the municipality bought Strijp-S from Philips, that the fenced area was transferred and leased back to Philips, and that the partners set up Park Strijp Beheer. [S1] The architecture center also gives 2002 and says the site of about 27 hectares was sold to the municipality and VolkerWessels partnership that year. [S4] The Driehoek Strijp-S site says Philips sold the site to Park Strijp Beheer in 2004. [S7] Herbestemming puts it in sequence: letter of intent in 2001, master plan in 2002, and in 2004 Park Strijp Beheer takes over the land from Philips, renting back the buildings Philips still used. [S5] I read 2002 as the purchase agreement and 2004 as the transfer of the land. That reading comes from reconciling those sources and not from a deed, so I use "2002" only with the word "agreement" and say that the handover is dated 2004 elsewhere.
The plan, the partnership and the crisis

Strijp-S's history page says the plan was developed from 2002 to 2005 under Park Strijp Beheer, with the landscape architect Adriaan Geuze of West 8 drawing the urban plan and acting as supervisor. It says the zoning plan followed in 2005 and 2006, and that part of the old factories were designated as a municipal monument (the NatLab) and national monuments (the Hoge Rug and Klokgebouw). [S1][S3] Herbestemming dates the approved zoning plan to 2008 and a program for art and culture on Strijp-S to 2007. [S5]

The Van Zoest essay describes how the plan changed. It began as a fairly blueprint-driven plan with a lot of demolition and new building. While the first buildings were being demolished, friction grew inside the partnership, which led to a new governance structure with a "Board of Inspiration" of VolkerWessels, the municipality, the housing corporations and the supervisor Geuze. The 2008 credit crisis then forced changes, including a parking concept and more heritage preservation, and a large skate hall that was meant to be temporary became permanent. [S6] Strijp-S's own page agrees on the outcome: in 2012 and 2013 the demolition of many Philips factories was postponed and later canceled, and development in four phases moved from the edge toward the center. [S1] Van Zoest's account says the area now holds about 500 new residents and 700 companies, a figure from 2019. [S6]

The housing corporations carried much of the early reuse. The architecture center says the housing corporation Trudo developed the buildings around the Driehoek, including the Klokgebouw, and that old factory buildings became open studios, music stages, restaurants, schools and small shops, with some housing. Herbestemming says Woonbedrijf built the first new homes, with construction starting in 2010 and the first residents arriving at the end of 2012. [S4][S5] Herbestemming says the city bought the Klokgebouw in 2006 and that its transformation to studios, a music venue and event halls was delivered in 2010. [S5] The Strijp-S history page says that, in the latest phase, new buildings adapt to monuments: Trudo's Haasje Over project is built over the former Area51 hall, and the partners plan 2,000 more homes and 25,000 square meters for creative businesses. [S1]
When Design Week arrived

The owners' history page says the 2005 and 2006 consortium investment "resulted in Dutch Design Week choosing Strijp-S as its new home." [S1] I found independent evidence from 2007. A car magazine's news item of October 15, 2007 says the Citroën C-Buggy would be shown for the first time in the Netherlands at the Design On Wheels show in the Klokgebouw Strijp-S during Design Week from October 20 to 28. [S10] In 2009 Bright lists a Design On Wheels stand in the Klokgebouw, a student show on Strijp-S and its own stand in hall 4 of the Klokgebouw. [S11] By 2012 Bright reported that the biggest concentration of young talent had moved out of the Klokgebouw to a video lab elsewhere on Strijp-S. [S13] I did not find a source for the first year. The history page's "2005 and 2006" is the owners' account, and 2007 is the earliest date I can support from outside.
What the photo archive shows, year by year
The albums below are the ones read for the earlier Strijp-S research on October 6, 2026, and I did not reopen them in this pass. They show the district as a sequence of squares, not factories. [S14]

**2015 to 2019.** Ketelhuisplein has albums for 2015 (33 photos), 2016 (67), 2017 (38), 2018 (20) and 2019 (28). Titles name Cleo Goossens, Tommy Köhlbrugge, Almicheal Fraay, Dick Rennings, Ruud Balk, Max Kneefel and Oscar Vinck. The pictures show the square from above, banners, stages, a green ABN AMRO box, a train-carriage pavilion and, in 2019, a raised wooden pavilion and a BioBaseCamp. [S14]

**2021 to 2025.** The 2021 album (38 photos, October 16 and 17, 2021) shows timber houses, and 2023 (58) shows market tents and greenhouses. In 2022 the album is for Trudotorenplein (43 photos), beside residential towers. In 2024 the subject is Microlab Hall (17 photos), and for 2025 the album is an introduction with 6 photos of orange and purple pavilions. No album in this set covers 2020. [S14] The Strijp-S building pages describe the Trudo Tower as a 70-meter tower by Stefano Boeri Architetti with 125 social housing lofts, a new building with no Philips function, and Microlab as flexible workspace in the former Philips SFH building. [S18][S19]

DDW's own 2026 location list groups about forty entries under Strijp-S, among them Area 51, Bakkie 040, a Community Square, Plug in City, the Ketelhuisplein Greenhouse, the Klokgebouw, Matchbox, MU Hybrid Art House, Natlab, a passage at the Trudo tower, Radio Royaal, SintLucas, Skybar Microlab and VEEM floor 8. [S12] The count and the names are DDW's grouping and not a statement about ownership or history.
The doubts about the success story

The success story has a counter-voice, thin but present. In March 2026 Stadszaken reported a Sectie-C tenant who hoped that site would not go the way of Strijp-S, where "ruimte voor creativiteit onder druk" is said by those involved to have come under pressure. That is a second-hand characterization inside an article about another place, and I did not find a study or a named case that supports it. [S15] The Van Zoest essay calls the transformation widely seen as successful and notes that it won a national renovation prize and a developers' award. [S6] The question of who the district's cheap space serves today is not one the sources I opened answer.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**The sale.** 2002 (owners, architecture center), 2004 (Driehoek, Herbestemming for the land transfer). Reconciled as agreement and handover, but not settled by a primary document. [S1][S4][S5][S7]

**Building dates.** Settled by the national register: Klokgebouw 1928 and 1929 in two phases, Veemgebouw 1942, Hoge Rug 1927, 1929 and 1930. The architecture center's separate dating of the Hoge Rug buildings (the SK building to 1928, SBP to 1930, SAN to 1929) differs for one of them, so I give the register's set only. [S3][S4]

**The first light bulbs.** Herbestemming and Strijp-S's own Glasgebouw page say the very first light bulbs were made in the Glasgebouw; Strijp-S's history page puts the first bulbs in the Emmasingel factory in 1891, before any Strijp-S building. I follow the history page and leave the Glasgebouw claim out. [S1][S5][S20]
**Size.** 25 hectares (Schippers), 27 (owners, architecture center), about 30 (Van Oudheusden). Not settled. [S1][S4][S8][S9]
**The NatLab building.** 1922 (Van Oudheusden) against 1923 (architecture center). Not settled. [S4][S8]

**Whose account it is.** Much of the district's history comes from the owners' own page and a housing-corporation partner's site. Where I could, I set them beside the register and the research essay. [S1][S2][S6][S7]
What the record does not show

I have not read the sale or transfer deeds, the 2001 tender documents or the master plan itself, and I have not seen the council's papers. The council information site was not reachable in this pass. I cannot say what Design Week used on Strijp-S before 2007, why the photo selection has no 2020 album, or what the 2025 introduction album's street is called. I did not reopen the Flickr albums, so counts and credits carry their October 6 date. [S14]

I do not know how many creative tenants have left or stayed since the first temporary uses, and I could not verify the claim about creative space under pressure. I also have no source for the 1916 factory's later fate or for which buildings were demolished in the first phase beyond the general statements above. [S1][S6]

If you walk Strijp-S during Dutch Design Week 2026, find a building on the register and read its plate against the dates in this essay. When a district's year of sale depends on whether you mean the agreement or the handover, which date would you put on the wall? [S2][S5]

title: TAC: a Philips office from 1930, a temporary art centre from 2004, and a building it now says it owns
subtitle: A former Philips office building near the stadium in Eindhoven, followed through the venue's own timeline, a building-history researcher, trade and local press, and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: The Temporary Art Centre building in Eindhoven, from a Philips office of about 1930 to a Dutch Design Week venue, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: The building that houses the Temporary Art Centre in Eindhoven was built for Philips around 1930, held a school, sales offices, a wartime head office, a staff shop and a museum depot, and in 2025 reopened in part after a renovation that tore down another part of it. [S1][S2][S4]

The Temporary Art Centre publishes a long timeline on its own site, and most of the building's history rests on it. I looked for other sources and found a building-history researcher, a demolition contractor and TAC's own pages on its renovation, which let me check parts of the timeline. The result is a better-supported building history and a less certain account of the organization. This essay follows both. I use public sources only: TAC's pages, the researcher's note, trade pages on the renovation, a design magazine's 2012 report, This is Eindhoven, the Dutch Design Week pages and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list. [S7]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For this building the list of earlier uses is long, which is the point of the exercise. [S1][S3]
An office building for a lamp company

TAC's timeline begins in 1927, when Philips submitted a planning application for an office building. It lists the years 1930 to 1992 as "Philips," a Philips ULO school and training center for office staff in 1933 and 1934, and the Dutch Sales Department from 1930 to 1964. [S1] A building-history researcher, Gerrit Korenberg, gives the independent anchor. His project note says the office building was built in 1930 for the N.V. Philips Gloeilampenfabriek. [S3] A 1927 application and a building in use by 1930 fit together, and two sources agree on 1930. I treat 1930 as the year the building came into use and 1927 as the year the plan was filed. The researcher's note gives no exact day and no architect.

The timeline continues with the war. It lists the German authorities occupying the building from 1940 to 1945. It says Frits Philips established his office there from 1942, and that the building served as a temporary Philips head office from 1943 to 1964. [S1] Korenberg's note explains why: when the Philips head office was hit in a bombing in 1942, the directors were housed in this building, which got a new main entrance and upgraded offices. [S3] The bombing was most likely the RAF raid of December 6, 1942 on the Philips factories on the Emmasingel and Strijp-S, though the researcher's note does not name the date. [S3][S5][S6] The two sources differ on the years. The timeline says the temporary head office ran from 1943, and the researcher says the directors moved after the 1942 bombing. I give both.

The temporary arrangement ended with a new building. The architecture center says the Philips Nederland office building VB on the Boschdijk was opened on December 29, 1964, after four years of construction, and gathered about 1,300 employees who had worked at five locations in Eindhoven. [S8] The TAC timeline ends the Dutch Sales Department and the temporary head office in 1964. [S1] I read those as the same event seen from two ends, which is my inference and not a statement in either source.
Offices, a canteen, a staff shop and a gap

After 1964 the timeline lists a housing and land company and a Philips canteen until 1988, then social services, a personnel department, a housing office, a tax advisory office, sports and recreation services from 1965 onward, and from 1978 a support fund, a travel agency, a reproduction department and the works council's office. It gives the staff shop 1972 to 1992. [S1] Korenberg also mentions the staff shop from about 1972. [S3] The demolition contractor's page, describing the renovation, calls the part being demolished the place "where the Philips staff shop was once housed." [S9]

One entry matters for the building's present shape: in 1985 a large section along the Gagelstraat was demolished. [S1] The building TAC took over in 2004 was therefore already smaller than the one Philips built, and the renovation of the 2020s removed another part. The timeline says the building became vacant in 1992. [S1]
The Van Abbemuseum years, and a date that disagrees

From 1995 to 2003 the timeline says the Van Abbemuseum used the building as a depot and as its temporary location during the rebuilding of its own premises. [S1] Korenberg writes that the museum was temporarily housed there from 1995 to 2002 and that TAC has been there since 2002. [S3] The energy company Ennatuurlijk, in an August 2025 news item about reconnecting the building to its heat network, also says it has been a cultural breeding ground since 2002, and describes the building as originally built as a Philips office in the 1930s. [S17] The museum's own page on its director Jan Debbaut says the museum moved to a temporary location in 1995, without naming the building, and stayed until 2002, which matches the researcher's dates. [S20] The disagreement is a year on the museum's departure and two years on TAC's arrival, since TAC's own timeline says it became a foundation, an organization and a physical space in 2004. [S1] TAC's text on the Petri complex adds that its original plans for TAC Living date from 2003, "a year before we moved into the TAC building." [S1] I follow TAC for its own move, 2004, and report 2002 as the date two outside sources use. The outside sources may be counting from the first use of part of the building, but none says so.
How an art centre began in a pub

TAC's own words are that it "was born at a pub bar in 1999," as a concept scribbled on a beer coaster. [S1] In 2004 it became a foundation, an organization and a physical space, a base for emerging artists, designers, musicians, theater makers and architects who move on as they grow, which the timeline gives as the reason for the word temporary. [S1] This is Eindhoven repeats that explanation: at TAC they do not say contemporary but temporary, because that is how the Temporary Art Centre began. [S10]

The early years produced a magazine. TAC's about page says that after just over a year it published VAN TAC, in several editions between 2004 and 2008. [S2] The timeline records a street festival, Via Ventosa, launched in 2005, and the hope in that year, with the municipality, the Ventoseflat association and the housing corporation Woonbedrijf, to redevelop the neighboring Ventoseflat. It says the plans for what it called the Petri complex, a breeding ground for art with living space, were put on hold in 2006 and that new plans were revived in 2017. [S1]
Design Week at TAC

I found one independent early record of TAC at Design Week. In October 2012 Bright wrote that TAC, "next to the Philips Stadium," always produces surprises, in a roundup of that year's venues. [S11] TAC's home page lists Dutch Design Week 2026, October 17 to 25, among its events. [S4]

The Flickr archive begins in 2015. I read its album pages for the earlier version of this research on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass, so the counts and names below carry that date. Six editions have TAC albums, seven albums and 145 photos in all. [S12] The 2015 albums hold 9 photos by Cleo Goossens, six of them titled Overzicht, and 17 photos by Nick Bookelaar of a Late Night Bingo Show. The 2016 album has 16 photos with number titles, 2017 has 12 with titles naming Sint Joost and WDKA, and 2018 is the largest with 56, of which the earlier pass could read 24: lamps, mineral samples and a staged bedroom. The 2019 album has 13, nine of them titled WATTBA, with a banner reading What a Time to Be Alive. The 2020 album has 22 photos by Max Kneefel of installed rooms with almost no visitors. [S12] The 2020 week ran online as well as offline, with visits by appointment, according to CLICKNL, which may explain the empty rooms. [S13]
The move out and the rebuild

TAC's timeline says that in 2021, with the renovation about to begin, TAC moved with most of its members to a former school building at Kronehoefstraat 30A and another group moved to Sectie-C. [S1] A TAC page on its future describes public events at three other locations during the renovation, including exhibitions at the old address, programs at United Cowboys on Kleine Berg and a stage at the High Tech Campus. [S14]

The plans and the money changed along the way. The same page says the building was originally going to be demolished entirely, that TAC found a partner in Focus Real Estate and that the decision was to preserve it in part. It names the architecture firm KCAP and Atelier Boetzkes in the preliminary design, with 80 studios for 200 artists and 230 new homes, and says the iconic entrance will be kept. It expected the move back in early 2024 and the housing a year later. [S14] The contractor who carried out the demolition says a residential tower of about 249 apartments for Woonbedrijf is being realized by Huybregts-Relou, that a part of the historic building will be demolished entirely and that the other part is kept as a cultural center. [S9] The 230 and 249 figures differ and I give both with their sources. A Brainport Eindhoven page on the national Regio Deal lists TAC Vastgoed B.V. as the beneficiary of a project running from October 1, 2019 to December 31, 2025, with a national contribution of 3,100,000 euros, regional co-financing of at least 7,571,429 euros and a total of 10,671,429 euros, with Focus Real Estate and the municipality as partners. It describes the plan as keeping about 4,800 square meters of studios, makerspaces, exhibition space and hospitality in place and as giving TAC a self-standing, independent form, "TAC 2.0." [S18] An architecture firm's page on the same project says TAC had the old Philips building on loan from the municipality, that the original plans for the area had no place for it, and that an agreement with the municipality now keeps TAC on the site in exchange for creating affordable housing. [S19] Ennatuurlijk says the renovation started in 2024 and was carried out by TAC Vastgoed B.V., and expected activities in the building again at the end of 2025. [S17]

TAC's timeline says the first phase was completed in 2025, with the exhibition spaces, the Ballroom and the Vault, ready for their first exhibitions. [S1] TAC's home page says that on November 5 (the year is not shown) it became official that the building belongs to TAC, and invites visitors to the first two exhibition spaces. [S4] An Open Eindhoven news item of December 2, 2025, read for the earlier research and not reopened because that host later answered with an access refusal, reports the opening of the renewed TAC with about 80 studios in 4,800 square meters and TAC Living with 249 apartments. [S15]
What the Design Week listing says for 2026

DDW lists TAC for October 17 to 25, 2026, with opening hours from 11:00 until 21:00 or 23:00 on most days and until 20:00 on the last Sunday. The text says TAC offers promising makers the chance to develop and present their work, with more than 100 young designers, artists and musicians in 60 studios. [S16] The location page shows the address Vonderweg 1, while TAC's own home page gives Ventoselaan 1 for its office and studios and its exhibitions. [S4][S16] TAC's future page uses Vonderweg 1 for exhibitions during the renovation, so both addresses are TAC's own. [S14] The studio count is also TAC's own on both sides: 60 on the Design Week page and 80 on TAC's about page. [S2][S16] I use neither.
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**When the building came into use.** The 1927 filing and the 1930 use fit together, and the researcher's 1930 settles it as far as one independent note can. [S1][S3]
**When the Philips directors arrived.** After the 1942 bombing (researcher) or from 1943 (TAC's timeline). Not settled. [S1][S3]
**When TAC moved in.** 2004 (TAC) or 2002 (researcher and the energy company). I follow TAC and flag the rest. [S1][S3][S17]
**The museum's years.** 1995 to 2003 (TAC) against 1995 to 2002 (researcher). Not settled. [S1][S3]
**Studios and homes.** 60 or 80 studios, 230 or 249 homes. Different dates and different documents, not settled. [S2][S9][S14][S16]
**Address.** Vonderweg 1 and Ventoselaan 1 are both used by TAC. [S4][S14][S16]
What the record does not show

I have not seen the building's heritage assessment, a drawing or an architect's name for the 1930 office, or a record of its monument status. I did not look for archive or heritage records beyond those named above. I cannot say what TAC showed at Design Week before 2015 beyond the 2012 mention, why the photo archive has no TAC album after 2020, or what the 32 unseen photos of the 2018 album show. I also have no source for the exact date and terms on which TAC acquired the building. [S4][S12]

If you walk past the building during Dutch Design Week 2026, look for the entrance that survived the demolition and ask what the rest of the facade once belonged to. When a building has been a school, a head office, a staff shop and a museum depot before it became an art centre called temporary, which of those names would you leave on it? [S1][S14]

title: The Van Abbemuseum: a cigar maker's gift to the city, ninety years of directors, and a Design Week partner since at least 2009
subtitle: A museum from 1936 in Eindhoven, followed through its own history pages, the national monument register, the Design Week program archive and seven editions of official photo albums
description: The Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, from a cigar maker's 1936 gift to a Dutch Design Week venue, with its directors, building and what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: The Van Abbemuseum opened on April 18, 1936 in a building paid for by a cigar manufacturer, and by 2009 it was one of the places a Dutch Design Week pass opened. [S2][S12]

The usual way to read a museum in a design-week archive is as a list of exhibition titles, and that is how the photo albums present it. The museum's own history gives the titles a context. Six directors, a rebuilt building and a long relationship with the Design Academy Eindhoven sit behind them. This essay uses public sources only: the museum's own pages, the national monument register, the architecture center's heritage writing, Design Week's program archive, design and trade press, and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list. [S23]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. This building was built to hold paintings, was later joined to a tower for a growing collection, and in 2026 is described by its director as a sundial. [S3][S22]
A gift from a cigar manufacturer

The museum is named after H.J. van Abbe, whom it describes as the cigar manufacturer who financed the building and set aside a sum for purchases and running costs in the first years. [S2] The national monument register adds that he gave the museum to the city of Eindhoven together with paintings and a sum of money for buying art. [S1] The register dates the building to 1936 and names A.J. Kropholler (1882 to 1973) as the architect. It describes a square plan of 40 by 40 meters, dark red brick, copper roofs, a clock tower over the front, and two rearing horses by the sculptor John Raedecker beside the steps. [S1] The architecture center's walking route says the building went up in the years 1933 to 1935 and opened in 1936, and gives Kropholler's birth year as 1881. [S11] I follow the register for 1882 and note the difference.

The museum says it officially opened on April 18, 1936 with the exhibition Hedendaagsche Nederlandse Kunst, Contemporary Dutch Art. At the opening the first director, Dr. W.J.A. Visser, hoped the museum would become "part of the living community." The name was a problem from the start: the inscription "Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum" was put on a memorial stone by mistake just before the opening, and because the public already used that name, the council changed it officially on April 10. [S2]
Directors and what they bought

The museum's own pages sketch the directors in some detail, and the sketches explain why its exhibitions look the way they do. Edy de Wilde, who took over in July 1946 at the age of 26, laid the foundation of the modern collection, dismissed the roughly 70 prewar paintings as incomplete, and in 1952 bought Chagall's Hommage à Apollinaire as the start of a core collection. Picasso's Femme en vert, bought for 114,000 guilders, caused public commotion. [S5] Jean Leering, director from April 1964, was a structural engineer interested in architecture, urban planning and design. His program mixed New York artists with historical retrospectives of El Lissitzky, Moholy-Nagy, Van Doesburg and Tatlin. In 1968 he bought 86 works by Lissitzky, which the museum says made its holdings the largest outside Russia. [S6] That ranking is the museum's claim and I did not check it elsewhere.

Rudi Fuchs, director from February 1975, argued for the autonomy of art and turned the program toward German, Austrian and Italian artists. [S7] Jan Debbaut took over in January 1988. In 1990 the architect Abel Cahen was given the assignment to draw up a rough plan for a new building. In 1995, in anticipation, the museum moved to a temporary location under the slogan Van AbbeMUSEUM entr'acte, where it stayed until 2002. [S8] Charles Esche led the museum from August 2004 to 2024, and Defne Ayas took over in September 2025, ahead of the museum's 90th birthday in spring 2026. [S9][S10]

One exhibition connects the museum to the city around it. On September 19, 1969, the day after Queen Juliana opened the new city hall, the museum opened an exhibition with the model of the Cityplan by the Rotterdam firm Van den Broek and Bakema, which the architecture center reads as a companion statement to the new city hall's modern course. [S11]
An old building and a new tower

The register describes the museum as a monument, and a 2003 rebuild joined it to something very different. The museum's architecture page says the listed old building by Kropholler was renovated and integrated in 2003 into Abel Cahen's design for a new building. The new part has a 27-meter tower with inward-sloping walls, a facade of gray slate from Lapland, interiors by Maarten van Severen and a front garden by Piet Oudolf. The landscape architects H+N+S widened the Dommel into an "inner lake," and John Körmeling's footbridge, a small pink house with lighted words on its roof, followed in 2006. [S3] The two buildings carry different addresses: the register lists the old building at Bilderdijklaan 10, and the museum and Dutch Design Week give Stratumsedijk 2. [S1][S2][S23] The first is the monument's registered address and the second is the museum's address today.
Design Week at the museum, year by year

The earliest record I found is from 2009. Bright's guide to that year's Design Week says a pass of 22 euros gave access to the Design Academy, the Dutch Design Awards greenhouse, TU/e, the Van Abbemuseum, the Klokgebouw and the Designhuis. [S12] In 2012 Bright reported that the DOEN materials prize had landed, less accessibly than usual, in the Van Abbemuseum. [S13] The Flickr archive, which begins in 2015, holds albums for seven editions, 193 photos in all. I read those album pages for the earlier research on October 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass. [S25]

**2017.** Beyond Generations, October 7 to November 5, was a group exhibition of work by designers of different generations who studied at the Design Academy Eindhoven, which was founded in 1947 and was approaching its 75th anniversary. The curator was Annemartine van Kesteren of the Boijmans Van Beuningen museum. The museum's record says the show used eight frames of thinking, each marked by a dialog between two iconic products set beside a work from the museum's collection. The opening on October 7 was addressed by Esche and by a member of the academy's executive board. [S14] The album has 26 photos by Tommy Köhlbrugge. [S25]

**2018.** The Design Academy's page says its GEO-DESIGN platform, produced with the Van Abbemuseum, began in October 2018 with GEO-DESIGN: Alibaba, for which nine graduates researched Alibaba's operating model and its effect on design. [S15] The album has 17 photos titled GEO-DESIGN. [S25]

**2019.** GEO-DESIGN: Junk, which DDW's program archive calls a city-wide exhibition produced in collaboration with the museum, showed 18 projects by academy alumni. [S16] The album has 20 photos with dates of October 19, 23 and 27. [S25]

**2020.** Interior Design listed New Melancholy by Lidewij Edelkoort as a double exhibition between Kazerne and the Van Abbemuseum, showing pensive work from the collections of Edelkoort and the museum. [S17] The two albums hold 43 photos and name both venues, so I cannot say which room is which. [S25]

**2022.** The museum's DDW program item "De collectie is... De Edelkoort collectie" ran from October 8 to November 6, 2022 in ten rooms of the old building. It put design objects from Edelkoort's private collection beside contemporary art from the museum, with pieces by Maarten Baas, Jurgen Bey, Nacho Carbonell, Piet Hein Eek, Hella Jongerius and Studio Job, and a second showing at Kazerne until spring 2023. [S18] The album has 35 photos. [S25]

**2024.** museum.nl lists the museum's Design Week program from October 19 to 27, 2024: the exhibition Soils, complemented by work from Design Academy students, Jeroen Erosie's living mural Alternative Entrance and four stations by the collective De Onkruidenier about how design shapes a food such as the tomato. [S19] The album has seven photos by Boudewijn Bollmann. [S25]

**2025.** The archive's one museum album is titled for a visit by Queen Máxima and holds 45 photos by Max Kneefel with file names dated October 16, 2025. [S25] DDW's press release says that evening she opened the 25th Dutch Design Week, and that before the opening she visited the exhibition Bridging Minds, 100x design for change at the museum. Dutch Design Week co-founder Miriam van der Lubbe curated it, with about 100 designers and artists including Formafantasma and Klarenbeek and Dros. [S20][S21]

**2026.** DDW lists the museum open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 on October 17 to 25, with a DDW ticket required, and a program item called Museum as Sundial. The text says Ayas conceived it as an exercise in reorientation, that the building, designed ninety years ago in relation to the sun, becomes a sundial with the central gallery as a point of orientation, and that it brings together contemporary art, design, archaeology and play, with participants including Kiki & Joost, Gala Porras-Kim, Paul Panhuysen and John Körmeling. [S22][S23] The claim about the 1936 design is the museum's own, and I could not check it against the register, which says nothing about the sun.
What the pattern shows

Across those years the Design Academy appears in the program of 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2024, and Edelkoort in 2020 and 2022. [S14][S15][S16][S17][S18][S19] The architecture center's brochure also names Edelkoort as the driving force behind the Designhuis in 2007, and her collection show at the museum had a second showing at Kazerne, so the museum's Design Week program is partly the same small circle seen from different buildings. [S18][S28] That is a pattern in the program, and the albums only record it. A separate venue with a similar name belongs to a different story: DDW lists the van Abbehuis, at Bilderdijklaan 19, as the former villa of the van Abbe family and an experimental project space for some 200 artists in recent years. The page does not mention the museum. [S24] The archive holds a 2023 album titled Albert van Abbehuis with 9 photos and a 2025 album titled Van Abbe Huis with 8, and I count neither among the museum's. [S25]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**Kropholler's birth year.** 1882 in the register, 1881 in the architecture center's route. I follow the register. [S1][S11]
**The address.** Bilderdijklaan 10 (register, the historic building) against Stratumsedijk 2 (the museum and DDW, the present entrance). Both are right for different things. [S1][S2][S23]

**The temporary location.** The museum says it moved to a temporary location in 1995 and stayed until 2002, without naming the building. The Temporary Art Centre's timeline says the museum used its building from 1995 to 2003, and a building-history note on that building says 1995 to 2002. The museum's own dates agree with the note. [S8][S26][S27]
**Whether the museum is a Philips site.** No source I opened links it to Philips. The founder was a cigar manufacturer. [S2]

**Self-descriptions.** The museum's own pages say "one of the first public museums for contemporary art to be established in Europe," while the Design Week 2026 location text says "one of the leading museums." These are the museum's words in different places, and I attribute them rather than rank them. [S4][S23]
What the record does not show

I did not find the museum's own press releases for 2018, 2019 or 2025, because its press pages answered not found, so exact dates for those shows and the dates of Bridging Minds rest on Design Week's pages. I cannot say why the archive has no museum album for 2021 or 2023, which galleries held the 2020 show, or whether the van Abbehuis has any tie to the museum. I did not reopen the Flickr albums, so counts and credits carry their October 7 date. [S25]

If you visit during Dutch Design Week 2026, check which title DDW's listing gives for the museum before you go. When a program calls a 1936 brick building a sundial, which of its own earlier uses would you ask it to show you first? [S22]

title: The Veemgebouw: a Philips warehouse with a television mast, a food hall and car park, and a festival home since 2019
subtitle: The Philips warehouse on Strijp-S followed through the national monument register, an architecture journal, the owners' pages, the organizers' own sites and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive
description: The Veemgebouw on Strijp-S, from a 1942 Philips warehouse and television mast to a food hall, car park, housing and Dutch Design Week home, with what the records do and do not show.

sections.x: The Veemgebouw in Eindhoven was built in the early 1940s as a Philips warehouse, carried an experimental television antenna in the late 1940s, and has been converted into a food hall, a car park, housing and the home of a media-art festival that has used it in most Design Weeks since 2019. [S1][S2][S9][S11][S15]

A building's history gets tidier every time someone retells it, and the Veemgebouw is a good place to watch that happen. The Dutch Design Week photo albums call it VEEM, the monument register calls it the "veemgebouw," and the architects who rebuilt it call it Veemgebouw. This essay follows it through those documents and through the organizers' own sites for the exhibitions inside it. I use public sources only. It reports no visit and no interview. Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I describe only what its pages list. [S14]

I have a habit from anatomy, which is to ask what a structure was built to do before asking what it does now. For a warehouse the answer is simple, which makes the later answers easier to compare. [S1]
Built as the end of the line

The national monument register describes the Veemgebouw as built in 1942 to a design of the Philips engineering bureau, with expressionist elements, on the west edge of the Philips site along the Beukenlaan, in line with a series of concrete warehouses. It is one of the buildings of the register's Philips complex on Strijp-S. [S1][S3] Caruso St John, the architects who later rebuilt it, say the building was constructed in 1943 and is the most prominent of the large industrial buildings at the heart of the site. [S2] The architecture center's walking route says it was finished during the war, in 1943. [S4] Strijp-S's history page describes it as a new building of the war years with typical rounded corners, meant for storing parts and products. [S8] I credit 1942 to the register and note that the other two sources say 1943, which may mean completion and not the start.

The Architects' Journal, in a building study of October 24, 2022, explains what the building was for. The line of factory blocks on Strijp-S followed Philips's motto "from sand to customer," raw materials entering at one end and finished goods leaving at the other, and the Veem, short for Veemgebouw, was the end of the line, where finished products were stored before distribution. It stood next to the ring road and a railhead. On its tenth floor sat offices, marked by an illuminated mast and resembling a ship's bridge, where executives worked beside a showroom, which in the journal's words gave the building a representative role. [S5] The structure is a grid of thick concrete columns with splayed tops at six-meter centers, ceilings only 2.8 meters high and floors over 35 meters deep. [S5] The monument register describes the building as of general interest as part of the coherent Philips industrial landscape. [S1]
The mast and the first Dutch television

The story that a first Dutch television broadcast came from the Veem's roof is too big. The supported version is smaller and still good. Omroep Brabant reported in 2021 that Philips sent experimental programs, called Philips Experimentele Televisie, three evenings a week from 1948 to 1951, 264 test broadcasts in all, with an antenna on the roof of the Veemgebouw that reached forty kilometers. People who had received a set from Philips, often higher Philips staff, and radio dealers with a set in the window could watch. The presenter was often a Philips secretary, and the first live football match on television, PSV against EVV, was shown in 1950. [S6] The same article says the first national broadcast, on October 2, 1951, came from a studio in Bussum rented by Philips, which was more central and nearer to Hilversum. [S6] The Canon van Nederland confirms the date and that Philips began making programs itself in 1948, reachable only near Eindhoven. [S7] The architecture center adds that a wooden mast stood on the roof for years and was used for the experimental television broadcasts of the late 1940s. [S4]
Philips leaves, Trudo arrives

The Architects' Journal says Philips closed manufacturing on the site in 1996 and that the site was sold in 2002 to Park Strijp Beheer, the partnership of the city and VolkerWessels. [S5] Strijp-S's own page for the building says the housing corporation Trudo acquired the Veem in 2009 and decided to redevelop it, and that because the building has low floor heights and small windows it is less suitable for housing, so Trudo chose a mixed use. [S9] The journal gives a different order: it says Trudo decided in 2007 to hold an ideas competition for the building, which Caruso St John won. [S5] The architects' own page agrees with 2007 and dates the project 2007 to 2022, with the competition's first prize. [S2] I cannot say how an ideas competition came in 2007 for a building the owners' page says Trudo bought in 2009. The owners' page may be dating a formal purchase, and Trudo's own statement in the journal says it has owned the building for a long time. [S5]

The design idea was to leave the deep warehouse as it was and add three floors of housing on top. The journal says the housing design dates to 2011 and was redesigned as penthouse apartments that year, after which the project was put on ice for several years; the retrofit of the main building went ahead in 2015 and work on the housing began in 2019. [S5] Trudo's project leader says the ground-floor market hall was realized in 2015 and that an opportunity for the housing arose in 2020 when the facades were being maintained. [S5] Strijp-S's page says Trudo had the three layers built in 2021, and Trudo's page says it realized the 39 homes in 2021 and 2022, replacing 11,500 window panes in the facade work and holding the building since 2009. [S9][S23] The completion year the journal gives is 2022. [S5]

What the building holds now is well documented. The Strijp-S page lists a supermarket, a restaurant, specialty shops and a brewery on the ground floor, then a parking garage, a VR experience center and several floors used for pop-up exhibitions during Dutch Design Week. [S9] The architects describe a food market hall across the whole width of the deep ground floor, nine middle floors holding parking for six hundred cars for residents of the whole site, and offices and about forty apartments around a landscaped courtyard on top. [S2] The journal explains the car park: Dutch law then required 1.2 parking spaces per new home, and reusing the storage floors for car storage needed minimal conversion. It reports a gross floor area of 30,000 square meters and a construction cost of 55 million euros. [S5] The count of homes varies. Strijp-S and Trudo's own page say 39 homes, made of 19 studios, 19 maisonettes and one house, the architects say forty apartments, and Trudo's project leader in the journal says 38 studios and maisonettes. [S2][S5][S9][S23]

The Dutch renovation platform NRP's page for the building carries a jury report that praises the care of the renovation and the idea of turning a warehouse into a car park, and says parking was expanded from three floors to five, with the remaining floors left to temporary tenants. [S24] The architects' news page lists a RIBA International Award and the gold prize of the Erich Mendelsohn Award for brick architecture, in the housing and residential category. [S2] I did not find the years on that page.
Earlier Design Weeks, and the festival that moved in

Core77's report on Dutch Design Week 2015, dated November 16, 2015, places the Dutch Design Awards exhibition, the show "In No Particular Order" and "Transnatural" in the Veemgebouw, and shows a view of the rest of Strijp-S from an eighth-floor corner window of the "storage building." [S22] So the building was a Design Week venue by 2015 at least, a year before the archive's first VEEM album.

The most important fact for Design Week after that is a festival. Manifestations, a media-art, technology and fashion festival, says on its own sites that it has held its exhibition at the Veem during Dutch Design Week in several years. Its 2019 edition lists October 19 to 27, 2019, free admission, daily 11:00 to 18:00, at the Veemgebouw. [S10] Its 2020 site says the 2020 edition was virtual, on its own site, on ddw.nl and in virtual worlds, and hoped to be physical again later at Sectie-C. [S11] Its 2021 site says the 2021 edition would take place in the Melkhal at De Caai, the former Campina site, and online. [S12] From 2022 the sites name the Veem: October 22 to 30, 2022, October 21 to 29, 2023, October 19 to 27, 2024 and October 18 to 26, 2025, each announced as running at the Veem "and longer." [S13] For 2026 the festival's site announces October 17 to 25, 2026 at the Veem, and Dutch Design Week's own location page lists "VEEM floor 8 - home of Manifestations," free of charge, at Torenallee 100, open from 11:00 to 18:30 most days, with more than 50 participants, a food court and a brewery downstairs. [S13][S14][S15] The 2026 theme on the festival's site is MUTE, about censorship and taboo. [S13]

Crafts Council Nederland has also shown at the Veem. Its pages record the exhibition HOW&WOW at the Veem during Dutch Design Week 2017, a studio version, HOW&WOW Studio, at the Veem in 2018, and a group exhibition from October 19 to 27, 2019 at the Veem. [S16][S17][S18]
What the photo archive shows, edition by edition

The official archive holds albums naming VEEM for six editions between 2016 and 2024, 265 photos in all. I read those album pages for the earlier research on October 6 and 7, 2026 and did not reopen them in this pass, so the counts and credits below carry those dates. [S19]

The 2016 album is titled Dutch Invertuals @ Veem, with 9 photos by Nick Bookelaar. This is the one row I now doubt. Domus gave the address of the Dutch Invertuals show "Power Play" at Design Week 2016 as Fuutlaan 12b, and the Neon Moiré guide gave NS Loods / studio Edhv, October 22 to 30, 2016. [S20][S21] I found no source that puts that show at the Veem, and I cannot reopen the album to compare its photos. It is possible that the album title is loose or that the collective showed something in the Veem that I could not find. [S19][S20][S21]

The 2017 album is the largest, with 113 photos by Max Kneefel, and its titles name guest academies including Bauhaus Universität, Burg Giebichenstein, Central Saint Martins and ECAL. Outside sources confirm the Veem for HOW&WOW that year, but I found none for the academies. [S16][S19] The 2018 album, titled Bauhaus Universität, has 13 photos by Kneefel, and each photo title names VEEM. HOW&WOW Studio was at the Veem that year. [S17][S19] The 2019 album has 22 photos, matching the Manifestations and HOW&WOW dates. [S10][S18][S19] The 2022 album, VEEM - Manifestations, has 100 photos credited to about.today and Tommy Köhlbrugge. [S13][S19] The 2024 album has eight photos by Cleo Goossens, four titled with Veem and four with only Strijp-S. [S19]

The archive has no VEEM album for 2020, 2021, 2023 or 2025. The festival's own sites explain 2020 and 2021, since the exhibition was online in 2020 and at De Caai in 2021. For 2023 and 2025 they place Manifestations at the Veem, so those gaps look like gaps in the archive's list and not absences from the building, which fits the earlier note that the list I could read was incomplete. [S11][S12][S13][S19]
Where the sources disagree, and what settled it
**The build year.** The register says 1942; the architects and the architecture center say 1943. I use 1942 and name the register. [S1][S2][S4]
**When Trudo came in.** 2007 (competition) against 2009 (acquisition, per Strijp-S, Trudo and the renovation platform NRP). Not settled. [S2][S5][S9][S23][S24]
**The number of homes.** 38, 39 or 40, from four descriptions of the same project; 39 has the most support. [S2][S5][S9][S23]
**The 2016 album.** Its title says Veem and two outside sources place that show elsewhere. Not settled. [S19][S20][S21]

**The first television broadcast.** Settled by the Canon and Omroep Brabant: Eindhoven sent experimental programs from 1948 to 1951, and the national start on October 2, 1951 came from Bussum. [S6][S7]
What the record does not show

I have not seen the original construction drawings that the architects used, so I cannot describe the building's first layout beyond what the register and the journal say. I cannot say whether the guest academies of 2017 exhibited in it, or what the 2024 photos titled only Strijp-S show. I did not reopen the Flickr albums. [S19]

If you ride the lift to floor 8 during Dutch Design Week 2026, look at the columns and ask what they were built to carry. When a warehouse for finished goods becomes a food hall, a car park, a set of homes and a festival floor, which of those jobs would you say it was designed for? [S5][S15]
